<margin>St. Jerome's <term>Prologue</term><note>A formal introduction written by the 4th-century scholar Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin.</note> to the Pentateuch</margin>

I have received the longed-for letters of my friend Desiderius <note>original: "Desiderii mei"</note>, who, by a certain omen of the future, shares a name with Daniel <note>The name Daniel can be interpreted as "God is my Judge," while Desiderius means "Longed-for."</note>, entreating that I should translate the volumes of the <term>Pentateuch</term><note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> from the Hebrew language into the Latin tongue. This is certainly a dangerous work, exposed to the barking of detractors, who claim that I am attempting to subvert the Hebrew language and the new translation... <note>Jerome is defending himself against critics who preferred the older Greek translation, the Septuagint. The OCR here is heavily abbreviated and contains several errors in the original Latin transcription.</note> ...they think they see light in others while I am in darkness... how can I criticize the work of another? ...lest I seem to be waking the dead... those who know how to slander and ignore... the truth of the matter remains... as it is found written in the Hebrew books. First is the book of Moses, second is the Law... third in Zechariah, fourth in Proverbs, fifth in Isaiah... all these testimonies... <note>Jerome argues that to understand the Bible's origins, one must return to the Hebrew source material rather than relying solely on later Greek translations.</note>

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK
## OF GENESIS WHICH
## IS CALLED <note>original: "BRESIT"</note> BERESHIT
## THESE ARE THE FIVE BOOKS
## OF MOSES, AMONG THE
## HEBREWS CALLED
## THE <note>original: "THORA"</note> TORAH, BUT AMONG US
## THE PENTATEUCH.

<note>Inscription at bottom right:</note>
Abbot Dionysius <unclear/> 1340—1366 <note>Likely the name and dates of the high-ranking monk who commissioned or owned this manuscript.</note>

<summary>This page serves as the instructional and formal opening to a medieval Bible, providing the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin alphabets as scholarly tools followed by St. Jerome's defense of his Latin translation from the original Hebrew. It establishes the book's academic and religious authority before the text of Genesis begins.</summary>

### [Column 1]

<unclear>And God blessed Noah and his sons, saying: "Increase and multiply, and fill</unclear> the earth. And let the fear and dread of you be upon all the animals of the earth, and upon all the birds of the air, and with everything that moves upon the earth; all the fish of the sea are delivered into your hands.

Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; even as the green herbs have I delivered all things to you. Except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood <note>original: "carnem cum sanguine." This refers to the dietary laws later expanded in the Torah.</note>. For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast, and from the hand of man; from the hand of a man and his brother will I require the soul of man. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed; for man was made in the image of God. You, however, increase and multiply, and go forth upon the earth, and fill it."

This also God said to Noah, and to his sons with him: "Behold, I will establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you, and with every living soul that is with you, as well among the birds as the cattle and all the beasts of the earth that have come out of the ark, and all the wild animals of the earth. I will establish my covenant with you, and never again shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of a flood, nor shall there henceforth be a flood to waste the earth." And God said: "This is the sign of the covenant which I give between me and you, and every living soul that is with you, for everlasting generations. I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. And when I cover the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant with you, and with every living soul that gives life to flesh; and the waters of a flood shall no more be for the destruction of all flesh. And the bow shall be in the clouds, and I shall see it, and I will remember the everlasting covenant which was made between God and every living soul of all flesh that is upon the earth." And God said to Noah: "This shall be the sign of the covenant which I have established between me and all flesh upon the earth."

**A**<note>The scribe uses 'A' instead of 'E' for the acrostic.</note>rant <note>original: "Erant," meaning "They were."</note> therefore the sons of Noah who came out of the ark: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Moreover, Ham himself is the father of Canaan. These three are the sons of Noah, and from these was the whole race of men spread over the entire earth.

**R**<note>The scribe uses 'R' instead of 'C' for the acrostic.</note>epit <note>original: "Coepit," meaning "He began."</note> then Noah, a man of agriculture, to till the earth, and he planted a vineyard. And drinking the wine, he became drunk, and was naked in his tent. Which when Ham, the father of Canaan, had seen—namely, that his father’s private parts were naked—he told his two brothers outside. But Shem and Japheth put a cloak upon their shoulders, and walking backward, they covered the private parts of their father. And their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s nakedness. And Noah, waking from the wine, when he learned what his younger son had done to him, said: "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers." And he said: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." And Noah lived after the flood three hundred and fifty years. And all his days were fulfilled as nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.

**I**<note>The scribe uses 'I' instead of 'H' for the acrostic.</note>ee <note>original: "Hae," meaning "These."</note> these are the generations of the sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. Moreover, the sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. And the sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. By these were the islands of the Gentiles divided in their regions, each according to his tongue and their families in their nations. And the sons of Ham: Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan. And the sons of Cush: Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Moreover, Cush begot Nimrod; he began to be a mighty one on the earth. And he was a robust hunter before the Lord. Because of this, the proverb went out: "Like Nimrod, the robust hunter before the Lord." And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar. From that land went out Asshur, and built Nineveh, and the streets of the city, and Calah. Resen also between Nineveh and Calah: this is a great city. Mizraim, however, begot Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim.

**B**<note>The scribe uses 'B' instead of 'C' for the acrostic.</note>hanaan <note>original: "Chanaan."</note> moreover begot Sidon, his firstborn, Heth, and the Jebusite, and the Amorite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Arkite, the Sinite, and the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite. And after these the peoples of the Canaanites were spread abroad. And the borders of Canaan were for those coming from Sidon as far as Gerar toward Gaza, until you enter Sodom and Gomorrah, and Admah and Zeboiim, even to Lasha. These are the sons of Ham in their kindreds and tongues and generations and lands and their nations.

**H**<note>The scribe uses 'H' instead of 'E' for the acrostic.</note>e <note>original: "Et," meaning "And."</note> to Shem also were born children, the father of all the sons of Eber, and the elder brother of Japheth. The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash. Moreover, Arphaxad begot Shelah, from whom was born Eber.

### [Column 2]

<unclear>begot Eber.</unclear> And to Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg <note>meaning "Division."</note>, because in his days the earth was divided; and his brother's name was Joktan. Which Joktan begot Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, Jerah, and Hadoram, and Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, and Abimael, Sheba, and Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan. And their dwelling was from Mesha as one goes toward Sephar, a mountain in the east.

**O**<note>The scribe uses 'O' instead of 'H' for the acrostic.</note>i <note>original: "Hi," meaning "These."</note> These are the sons of Shem according to their kindreds and tongues and regions in their nations. These are the families of Noah according to their peoples and nations. By these were the nations divided on the earth after the flood.

**H**<note>The scribe uses 'H' instead of 'E' for the acrostic.</note>rat <note>original: "Erat," meaning "It was."</note> and the earth was of one tongue and of the same speech. And when they were wandering from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and dwelt in it. And each said to his neighbor: "Come, let us make bricks, and bake them with fire." and they had bricks for stone, and bitumen for mortar. And they said: "Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower, the top of which may reach to heaven; and let us make our name famous before we are divided into all lands." But the Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building, and he said: "Behold, the people is one, and they all have one tongue; and they have begun to do this, nor will they desist from their thoughts until they accomplish it in deed. Come, therefore, let us descend and there confound their tongue, so that no one may hear the voice of his neighbor." And thus the Lord divided them from that place into all lands, and they ceased to build the city. And therefore its name was called **Babel** <note>related to the Hebrew word 'balal,' meaning to confuse.</note>, because there the tongue of the whole earth was confounded; and from there the Lord dispersed them over the face of all regions.

**A**<note>The scribe uses 'A' instead of 'H' for the acrostic.</note>ee <note>original: "Hae," meaning "These."</note> these are the generations of Shem. Shem was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the flood. And Shem lived after he begot Arphaxad five hundred years, and begot sons and daughters. Moreover, Arphaxad lived thirty-five years, and begot Shelah. And Arphaxad lived after he begot Shelah four hundred and three years, and begot sons and daughters. Shelah also lived thirty years, and begot Eber. And Shelah lived after he begot Eber four hundred and three years, and begot sons and daughters. And Eber lived thirty-four years, and begot Peleg. And Eber lived after he begot Peleg four hundred and thirty years, and begot sons and daughters. Peleg also lived thirty years, and begot Reu. And Peleg lived after he begot Reu two hundred and nine years, and begot sons and daughters. Reu lived thirty-two years, and begot Serug. And Reu lived after he begot Serug two hundred and seven years, and begot sons and daughters. And Serug lived thirty years, and begot Nahor. And Serug lived after he begot Nahor two hundred years, and begot sons and daughters.

**H**<note>The scribe uses 'H' instead of 'V' for the acrostic.</note>ixit <note>original: "Vixit," meaning "He lived."</note> Nahor also lived twenty-nine years, and begot Terah. And Nahor lived after he begot Terah one hundred and nineteen years, and begot sons and daughters. And Terah lived seventy years, and begot **Abram**, and Nahor, and Haran. These however are the generations of Terah. Terah begot Abram, and Nahor, and Haran. Moreover, Haran begot Lot. And Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans. And Abram and Nahor took wives; the name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. But Sarai was sterile, nor did she have children. Therefore Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans, that they might go into the land of Canaan. And they came as far as Haran, and dwelt there. And the days of Terah became two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.

**D**ixit <note>Matches 'D' for the acrostic.</note> And the Lord said to Abram: "Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from the house of your father, and come into the land which I shall show you. And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you; and in you shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed." Abram therefore went out as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran. And he took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all the substance which they possessed, and the souls they had acquired in Haran; and they went out to go into the land of Canaan. And when they had come into it, Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem, even to the illustrious valley...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Patriarchs from the Book of Genesis. Having previously followed the lineage of Noah and the call of Abram, the text now details Abram's journey into Egypt, his separation from his nephew Lot, the rescue of Lot from the warring kings, and the establishment of the covenant—including the change of his name to Abraham and the promise of a son, Isaac.</meta>

# The Acts of the Patriarch Abraham

The Canaanite was then in the land <note>original: "Chanaaneum autem erat in terra." This indicates that the land promised to Abram was already inhabited.</note>. And the Lord appeared to Abram and said: "To your offspring I will give this land." And he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him. And moving from there to the mountain that was toward the east of Bethel, he pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. He also built there an altar to the Lord and invoked His name. And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south. Now there came a famine in the land, and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was very severe in the land.

And when he was near to entering Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: "I know that you are a beautiful woman, and that when the Egyptians see you, they will say: 'She is his wife,' and they will kill me, but they will keep you alive. Say, I beseech you, that you are my sister, so that it may be well with me because of you, and that my soul may live for your sake." Therefore, when Abram had entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful. And the princes told Pharaoh, and praised her before him, and the woman was taken into the house of Pharaoh. Moreover, they treated Abram well for her sake; and he had sheep and oxen, and asses, and menservants and maidservants, and camels. But the Lord struck Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife. And Pharaoh called Abram and said to him: "What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? For what reason did you say she was your sister, so that I might take her to me for a wife? Now, therefore, here is your wife; take her and go." And Pharaoh gave orders to his men concerning Abram, and they sent him away, with his wife and all that he had.

<margin>Chapter 13</margin>
And Abram went up out of Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, toward the south. Now he was very rich in the possession of gold and silver. And he returned by the way that he had come, from the south to Bethel, even to the place where he had previously fixed his tent, between Bethel and Ai, in the place of the altar which he had made before; and there he invoked the name of the Lord. But Lot also, who was with Abram, had flocks of sheep, and herds, and tents. Nor was the land able to hold them, so that they might dwell together; for their substance was great, and they could not dwell together. Wherefore there arose a strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s cattle and the herdsmen of Lot’s cattle.

At 그 that time the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelt in that land. Abram, therefore, said to Lot: "Let there be no quarrel, I beseech you, between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers. Behold, the whole land is before you; depart from me, I pray you. If you go to the left hand, I will take the right; if you choose the right hand, I will go to the left." Lot, therefore, lifting up his eyes, saw all the region around the Jordan, which was watered throughout, before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the paradise of the Lord <note>original: "parady(us) dñi," referring to the Garden of Eden.</note>, and like Egypt as one comes to Zoar. And Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan, and he departed toward the east; and they were separated one from the other. Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, and Lot stayed in the towns that were around the Jordan, and dwelt in Sodom. Now the men of Sodom were very wicked, and sinners before the Lord beyond measure. And the Lord said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him: "Lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you now are, to the north and to the south, to the east and to the west. All the land which you see, I will give to you, and to your seed forever. And I will make your seed as the dust of the earth; if any man can number the dust, your seed also shall be numbered. Arise and walk through the land in its length and in its breadth, for I will give it to you."

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>
Now four kings waged war against five. It came to pass in that time that Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Pontus, and Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites, and Tidal king of nations, entered into war against Bera king of Sodom, and against Birsha king of Gomorrah, and against Shinab king of Admah, and against Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and against the king of Bela, which is Zoar. All these gathered together in the woodland valley, which is now the Salt Sea <note>original: "mare salis."</note>. For they had served Chedorlaomer twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they revolted from him. Therefore, in the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who were with him, and they struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, and the Zuzim with them, and the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in the mountains of Seir, even to the plains of Paran, which is in the wilderness. And they returned and came to the fountain of Mishpat, which is Kadesh, and they struck all the region of the Amalekites and the Amorites, who dwelt in Hazezon-tamar. And the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and also the king of Bela, which is Zoar; and they drew up their battle array against them in the woodland valley; that is, against Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites, and Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Pontus: four kings against five. Now the woodland valley had many pits of bitumen <note>term: "bituminis" — a naturally occurring asphalt or tar often found in the Dead Sea region.</note>. So the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah turned their backs and fell there; and those who remained fled to the mountain. And they took all the substance of Sodom and Gomorrah, and their food, and went their way. They also took Lot, the son of Abram’s brother, who dwelt in Sodom.

But Abram, hearing that his brother Lot was taken captive, numbered of his servants born in his house three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them even to Dan. And dividing his company, he rushed upon them in the night, and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is to the left of Damascus. And he brought back all the substance, and Lot his brother with his substance, the women also and the people. And the king of Sodom went out to meet him, after he returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, in the valley of Shaveh, which is the King’s Valley. But Melchizedek, the king of Salem <note>note: Salem is traditionally identified with Jerusalem.</note>, bringing forth bread and wine—for he was the priest of the most high God—blessed him and said: "Blessed be Abram by the high God, who created heaven and earth. And blessed be the high God, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands." And he gave him tithes of all. And the king of Sodom said to Abram: "Give me the persons, and the rest take for yourself." But he answered him: "I lift up my hand to the Lord God the most high, the possessor of heaven and earth, that from the very thread of the web to the shoe-latchet, I will not take of any things that are yours, lest you should say: 'I have enriched Abram.' Excepting those things which the young men have eaten, and the shares of the men who came with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre; these shall take their shares."

<margin>Chapter 15</margin>
The vision of the Lord came to Abram by a vision, saying: "Fear not, Abram, I am your protector, and your reward is exceedingly great." And Abram said: "Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go childless, and the son of the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus." And Abram added: "To me you have given no seed, and behold, my servant born in my house shall be my heir." And immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying: "This man shall not be your heir, but he who shall come out of your own body, him shall you have for your heir." And He brought him forth abroad, and said to him: "Look up to heaven, and number the stars, if you can." And He said to him: "So shall your seed be." Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice. And He said to him: "I am the Lord who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land, and that you might possess it." But he said: "Lord God, whereby may I know that I shall possess it?" And the Lord answered and said: "Take me a cow of three years old, and a she-goat of three years old, and a ram of three years, a turtle-dove also, and a pigeon." And he, taking all these, divided them in the middle, and laid both parts opposite each other; but the birds he did not divide. And the fowls came down upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.

And when the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark horror invaded him. And it was said to him: "Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, and they shall bring them under bondage, and shall afflict them for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation which they shall serve, and after this they shall come out with great substance. As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age. But in the fourth generation they shall return here: for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete, even to the present time." Therefore, when the sun had set, there arose a dark mist, and there appeared a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire passing between those divisions. On that day God made a covenant with Abram, saying: "To your seed will I give this land, from the river of Egypt even to the great river Euphrates: the Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites, and the Hittites, and the Perizzites, the Rephaim also, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites."

<margin>Chapter 16</margin>
Now Sarai, the wife of Abram, had brought forth no children. But having an Egyptian handmaid named Hagar, she said to her husband: "Behold, the Lord has shut me up, that I should not bear; go in unto my handmaid, if perhaps I may at least have children by her." And when he agreed to her request, she took Hagar the Egyptian, her handmaid, ten years after Abram had begun to dwell in the land of Canaan, and gave her to her husband as a wife. And he went in unto her. But she, seeing that she had conceived, despised her mistress. And Sarai said to Abram: "You do me wrong. I gave my handmaid into your bosom, and she, seeing that she has conceived, has me in contempt. The Lord judge between me and you." Abram answered her: "Behold, your handmaid is in your hand; use her as you please." And when Sarai afflicted her, she fled away. And an angel of the Lord found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, which is in the way to Shur in the desert, and he said to her: "Hagar, handmaid of Sarai, whence come you? And whither go you?" She answered: "I flee from the face of Sarai, my mistress." And the angel of the Lord said to her: "Return to your mistress, and humble yourself under her hand." And again he said: "Multiplying, I will multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered for multitude." And further: "Behold," he said, "you have conceived, and you shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael <note>term: Ishmael — meaning "God hears."</note>, because the Lord has heard your affliction. He shall be a wild man: his hand shall be against all men, and all men's hands against him; and he shall pitch his tents over against all his brethren."

<margin>Chapter 17</margin>
And when he was ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said to him: "I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be perfect. And I will make my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly." Abram fell flat on his face. And God said to him: "It is I, and my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of many nations. Neither shall your name be called any more Abram, but you shall be called **Abraham**, because I have made you a father of many nations. And I will make you increase exceedingly, and I will make you into nations; and kings shall come out of you. And I will establish my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you in their generations, by a perpetual covenant: that I may be your God, and the God of your seed after you. And I will give to you, and to your seed, the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, for a perpetual possession, and I will be their God." Again God said to Abraham: "And you, therefore, shall keep my covenant, and your seed after you in their generations. This is the covenant which you shall observe between me and you, and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised. And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be for a sign of the covenant between me and you. An infant of eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every male-child in your generations. He that is born in the house, as well as the bought servant, shall be circumcised, and whoever is not of your stock; and my covenant shall be in your flesh for a perpetual covenant. The male, whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised, that soul shall be destroyed out of his people: because he has broken my covenant." God said also to Abraham: "Sarai your wife you shall not call Sarai, but **Sarah**. And I will bless her, and of her I will give you a son, whom I will bless, and he shall become nations, and kings of people shall spring from him." Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, saying in his heart: "Shall a son, think you, be born to him that is a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bring forth?" And he said to God: "O that Ishmael might live before you." And God said to Abraham: "Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name **Isaac**, and I will establish my covenant with him for a perpetual covenant, and with his seed after him. As for Ishmael also, I have heard you. Behold, I will bless him, and increase him, and multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve chiefs, and I will make him a great nation. But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time in the next year." And when He had left off speaking with him, God went up from Abraham. Abraham then took Ishmael his son, and all that were born in his house, and all whom he had bought: every male among the men of his house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskin immediately on that very day, as God had commanded him. Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin. And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old at the time of his circumcision. On the same day was Abraham circumcised, and Ishmael his son. And all the men of his house, as well they that were born in the house as the bought servants and strangers, were circumcised together. <margin>x1</margin>

<margin>Chapter 18</margin>
And the Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre as he was sitting at the door of his tent, in the very heat of the day. And when he had lifted up his eyes, there appeared to him three men standing near him. And as soon as he saw them, he ran to meet them from the door of his tent, and bowed down to the ground. And he said: "Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, pass not by your servant. But I will fetch a little water, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. And I will set a morsel of bread, and strengthen your heart, afterwards you shall pass on; for therefore are you come aside to your servant." And they said: "Do as you have spoken." Abraham made haste into the tent to Sarah, and said to her: "Make haste, temper together three measures of flour, and make cakes baked upon the hearth." And he himself ran to the herd, and took from there a calf, very good and tender, and gave it to a boy, who made haste and boiled it. He took also butter and milk, and the calf which he had boiled, and set before them; but he himself stood by them under the tree.

<margin>Chapter 17 [18]
1</margin>
And he was in the tent. And they lived <note>The text here follows the visit of the three angels to Abraham at Mamre</note>. "I will surely return to you at this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." Having heard this, Sarah laughed behind the door of the tent. Now they were both old and advanced in years, and the manner of women had ceased for Sarah. She laughed secretly, saying: "After I have grown old and my lord is an old man, shall I have pleasure?" And the Lord said to Abraham: "Why did Sarah laugh, saying, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, who am an old woman?' Is anything difficult for God? According to the agreement, I will return to you at this same time next year, and you shall have a son." Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was terrified. But the Lord said: "No, but you did laugh."

**T**he men set out from there and directed their eyes toward Sodom. Abraham walked with them, seeing them on their way. And the Lord said: "Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do, since he is to become a great and very robust nation, and in him all the nations of the earth are to be blessed? For I know that he will command his children and his house after him to keep the way of the Lord, and to do judgment and justice, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham everything he spoke to him." And the Lord said: "The outcry of the Sodomites and those of Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin is exceedingly heavy. I will go down and see whether they have fully completed the work according to the cry that has come to me, or if it is not so, that I may know." And they turned from there and went toward Sodom. But Abraham still stood before the Lord, and approaching, he said: "Will you indeed destroy the righteous with the wicked? If there are fifty righteous men in the city, will they perish together? And will you not spare that place for the sake of the fifty righteous, if they are in it? Far be it from you to do this thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous become like the wicked; this is not your way, you who judge all the earth; you will by no means do such a judgment." And the Lord said to him: "If I find in Sodom fifty righteous in the middle of the city, I will forgive the whole place for their sake." Abraham answered and said: "Since I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord, though I am but dust and ashes. What if there are five fewer than fifty? Will you destroy the whole city for the sake of forty-five?" And He said: "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there." And he spoke to Him again: "If forty are found, what will you do?" He said: "I will not strike it for the sake of forty." He said: "I beseech you, let the Lord not be angry if I speak. What if thirty are found there?" He answered: "I will not do it if I find thirty there." Since he had once begun, he said: "I will speak to my Lord. What if twenty are found there?" He said: "I will not kill them for the sake of the twenty." He said: "I beseech you, let the Lord not be angry if I speak yet once more. What if ten are found there?" He said: "I will not destroy it for the sake of the ten." The Lord departed after He ceased speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.

<margin>Chapter 18 [19]
2</margin>
**A**nd two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gates of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them, and bowed prostrate to the ground and said: "I beseech you, lords, turn aside into the house of your servant and stay there. Wash your feet, and in the morning you shall go on your way." They said: "Not at all, but we will stay in the square." He compelled them greatly so that they turned aside to him; and when they entered his house, he prepared a feast, baked <term>unleavened bread (azymos)</term>, and they ate.

**B**efore they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house, from the young to the old, all the people together. And they called Lot and said to him: "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out here so that we may know them." Lot went out to them, closing the door behind his back, and said: "I beseech you, my brothers, do not do this evil. I have two daughters who have not yet known men; I will bring them out to you, and you may use them as it pleases you, provided you do nothing evil to these men, because they have entered under the shadow of my roof." But they said: "Stand back!" and again, "You entered," they said, "as a stranger; are you now to act as a judge? We will afflict you yourself more than these." And they used extreme force against Lot. They were already near to breaking down the doors, when behold, the men reached out their hands and pulled Lot in to them, and closed the door. And those who were outside they struck with blindness, from the smallest to the greatest, so that they could not find the door. And they said to Lot: "Do you have anyone of your own here? A son-in-law, or sons, or daughters? Lead everyone who is in the city out of this way, because we are destroying this place, because the outcry of them has grown great before the Lord, who sent us to destroy them." So Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, and said: "Arise and get out of this place, for the Lord will destroy this city." And he seemed to them as if he were joking.

**A**nd when it was morning, the angels urged him, saying: "Arise and take your wife and the two daughters you have, lest you also perish in the wickedness of the city." As he lingered, they took his hand, and the hand of his wife, and of his two daughters, because the Lord spared him. And they led him out and placed him outside the city; and there they spoke to him, saying: "Save your life. Do not look back, nor stay in any of the surrounding region, but save yourself in the mountain, lest you also be snatched away." And Lot said to them: "I pray you, my lord, because your servant has found grace before you, and you have magnified your mercy which you have shown me, that you might save my life; I cannot be saved in the mountain, lest perhaps evil overtake me and I die. This city is nearby, to which I can flee—it is small—and I shall be saved in it. Is it not a modest place, and my soul shall live?" And He said to him: "Behold, even in this I have heard your prayers, that I will not subvert the city of which you have spoken. Hurry and be saved there, because I cannot do anything until you enter it." Therefore the name of that city was called <note>original: "Segor" — known as Zoar in most English translations</note> Segor. The sun had risen over the earth, and Lot entered Segor. Therefore the Lord rained sulfur and fire from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and He overthrew these cities and the whole surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and all the green things of the earth. And his wife, looking back behind her, was turned into a statue of salt. But Abraham, rising in the morning where he had stood before with the Lord, looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole region; he saw embers ascending from the earth like the smoke of a furnace. For when the Lord overthrew the cities of that region, He remembered Abraham and delivered Lot from the destruction of the cities in which he had lived. And Lot went up from Segor and stayed in the mountain, and his two daughters with him. For he had been afraid to stay in Segor, and he stayed in a cave, he and his two daughters with him. And the elder said to the younger: "Our father is old, and no man remains on the earth who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole world. Come, let us make him drunk with wine and sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they gave their father wine to drink that night, and the elder entered and slept with her father. But he did not perceive when the daughter lay down, nor when she rose. On the next day, the elder said to the younger: "Behold, I slept yesterday with my—

---

—father; let us give him wine to drink this night also, and you go in and sleep with him, so that we may save offspring from our father." And that night they gave the father wine, and the younger daughter entered and slept with her father. Thus the two daughters of Lot conceived by their father. And the elder bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this present day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ammon, that is, the son of my people; he is the father of the Ammonites until today.

3</margin>
**A**braham set out from there into the southern land and lived between Kadesh and Shur, and he sojourned in Gerar. And he said of Sarah his wife: "She is my sister." Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent and took her. But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: "Behold, you shall die because of the woman you have taken, for she has a husband." Now Abimelech had not touched her, and he said: "Lord, will you kill an ignorant and just nation? Did he not say to me, 'She is my sister,' and she herself said, 'He is my brother'? In the simplicity of my heart and the purity of my hands I have done this." And God said to him: "I also know that you did this with a simple heart, and therefore I kept you from sinning against me, and I did not allow you to touch her. Now therefore, restore the wife to her husband, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you will not restore her, know that you shall die the death, you and all that are yours." And immediately rising in the night, Abimelech called all his servants and spoke all these words in their ears, and all the men were greatly afraid. Abimelech also called Abraham and said to him: "What have you done to us? How have we sinned against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin? You have done to us things that you ought not to have done." And again: "What did you see, that you dared to do this?" Abraham answered: "I thought to myself, saying: Perhaps the fear of God is not in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife. Furthermore, she truly is my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother, and I took her as a wife. After God led me out from my father’s house, I said to her: 'You shall do me this mercy in every place to which we come: say that I am your brother.'" Therefore Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and servants and handmaids, and gave them to Abraham, and restored to him Sarah his wife, and said: "The land is before you; live wherever it pleases you." To Sarah he said: "Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother; this shall be to you a covering of the eyes before all who are with you, and wherever you go; and remember that you were caught." When Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech and his wife and his handmaids, and they bore children. For the Lord had closed every womb of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.

**A**nd the Lord visited Sarah as He had promised, and fulfilled what He had spoken. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time God had predicted to her. And Abraham called the name of his son, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac. And he circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had commanded him, when he was a hundred years old. Indeed, at this time Isaac had been born to him. And Sarah said: "God has made laughter for me, and whoever hears of it will laugh with me." And again she said: "Who that hears it would believe Abraham, that Sarah should suckle a son whom she bore to him now that he is old?" So the child grew and was weaned; and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning. And when Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with Isaac, she said to Abraham: "Cast out this handmaid and her son; for the son of a handmaid shall not be an heir with my son Isaac." This matter distressed Abraham bitterly on account of his son. To whom God said: "Let it not seem harsh to you concerning the boy and your handmaid. In all things that Sarah has said to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac shall your offspring be named. But I will also make the son of the handmaid into a great nation, because he is your offspring."

**S**o Abraham rose early in the morning, and taking bread and a skin of water, he placed it on her shoulder and handed over the boy, and sent her away. When she had departed, she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. And when the water in the skin was consumed, she cast the boy under one of the trees that were there. And she went away and sat opposite him, as far off as a bow can shoot; for she said: "I will not see the boy dying." And as she sat opposite, she lifted up her voice and wept. And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of the Lord called Hagar from heaven, saying: "What are you doing, Hagar? Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy from the place where he is. Arise, lift up the boy and hold his hand, for I will make him into a great nation." And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went and filled the skin and gave the boy a drink, and He was with him. He grew and lived in the wilderness, and he became a young archer. He lived in the desert of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

**A**t the same time, Abimelech and Phicol, the prince of his army, said to Abraham: "God is with you in all that you do. So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and both of them struck a covenant. And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart. But he said: "You shall receive seven ewe lambs from my hand, that they may be a testimony to me that I dug this well." Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because both of them swore there, and they entered into a covenant for the well of the living one. Then Abimelech and Phicol, the prince of his militia, arose and returned to the land of the Palestinians. But Abraham planted a grove in Beersheba and called there upon the name of the eternal Lord, and he was a dweller in the land of the Philistines for many days.

**B**ehold, the angel of the Lord called to Abraham from heaven a second time, saying: "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not spared your son, I will bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand which is on the seashore. **A**braham then lived in Beersheba. After these things were done, it was reported to Abraham that Milcah had also borne sons to his brother Nahor: Uz the firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of the Syrians, and Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel, from whom Rebekah was born. <margin>Gen. 23</margin>
**T**he years of Sarah were one hundred and twenty-seven, and she died in the city of Arba, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn and weep for her. And when he had risen from the duty of the funeral, he spoke to the sons of Heth <note>The Hittites</note>, saying: "I am a stranger and a pilgrim among you. Give me the right of a burial place with you, so that I may bury my dead." The sons of Heth responded: "Hear us, lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in our choice tombs; no one can prevent you from burying your dead in his own monument." Abraham rose and bowed to the people of the land, namely the sons of Heth, and said to them: "If it pleases your souls that I should bury my dead, hear me and intercede for me with Ephron the son of Zohar, that he may give me the double cave <note>Original: "speluncam duplicem," referring to Machpelah</note> which he has at the end of his field. For a fair price let him hand it over to me in your presence as a possession for a burial place."
Now Ephron lived in the midst of the sons of Heth. And Ephron responded to Abraham in the hearing of all who entered the gate of that city, saying: "Not so, my lord, but rather listen to what I say. I give the field to you, and the cave that is in it, in the presence of the sons of my people. Bury your dead." Abraham bowed before the people of the land and spoke to Ephron while the people stood around: "I pray that you hear me. I will give money for the field; accept it, and so I will bury my dead in it." Ephron responded: "My lord, hear me. The land you ask for is worth four hundred shekels <note>A "shekel" was a unit of weight for silver used as currency</note> of silver; that is the price between me and you. But what is that? Bury your dead." When Abraham heard this, he weighed out the money that Ephron had asked for in the hearing of the sons of Heth: four hundred shekels of silver of the common public currency. And the field that was once Ephron's, in which was the double cave facing Mamre—both the field itself and the cave, and all the trees in its circuit throughout its entire border—was confirmed as Abraham's possession in the sight of the sons of Heth and all who entered the gate of that city. And so Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the double cave of the field which faced Mamre; this is in the land of Canaan. And the field and the cavern that was in it were confirmed to Abraham as a possession for a monument by the sons of Heth.
<margin>Gen. 24</margin>
**A**braham was now an old man of many days, and the Lord had blessed him in all things. And he said to the senior servant of his house, who was in charge of all that he had: "Put your hand under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I live, but that you will set out for my own land and kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac from there." The servant responded: "If the woman is unwilling to come with me to this land, must I lead your son back to the place from which you departed?" Abraham said: "Beware that you never lead my son back there. The Lord God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore, saying: 'To your seed I will give this land'—He will send His angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman is unwilling to follow you, you shall not be bound by the oath. Only take care not to lead my son back there." So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his lord and swore to him concerning this matter. Then he took ten camels from his lord’s herd and departed, carrying all his lord's goods with him; he set out and went into Mesopotamia of Syria, to the city of Nahor.
And when he had made the camels lie down outside the town near a well of water in the evening, at the time when women were accustomed to come out to draw water, he said: "O Lord, God of my lord Abraham, meet me today, I beseech you, and show mercy to my lord Abraham. Behold, I stand near the spring of water, and the daughters of the inhabitants of this city will come out to draw water.
**A**nd the young woman to whom I shall say, 'Tip your pitcher that I may drink,' and who shall respond, 'Drink, and I will also give drink to your camels'—she is the one you have prepared for your servant Isaac; by this I shall understand that you have shown mercy to my lord."
He had not yet finished these words within himself when behold, Rebekah came out, the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, having a pitcher on her shoulder; a young woman of very beautiful countenance, and a virgin unknown to man. She had gone down to the spring and filled her pitcher and was returning. The servant ran to meet her and said: "Give me a little water to sip from your pitcher." She responded: "Drink, my lord." And she quickly lowered the pitcher onto her arm and gave him a drink. And when he had drunk, she added: "I will also draw water for your camels until they have all drunk." And pouring out the pitcher into the troughs, she ran back to the well to draw water, and having drawn it, she gave it to all the camels. But he contemplated her in silence, wanting to know whether the Lord had made his journey successful or not. After the camels had drunk, the man brought out golden earrings weighing two shekels and two bracelets worth ten gold pieces, and said: "Whose daughter are you? Tell me. Is there a place in your father’s house to stay?" She responded: "I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor." And she added, saying: "There is plenty of straw and hay with us, and a spacious place to stay." The man bowed himself and adored the Lord, saying: "Blessed be the Lord God of my lord Abraham, who has not taken away His mercy and truth from my lord, and has led me by the right path into the house of my lord's brother."
The girl ran and reported in her mother’s house everything she had heard. Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, who hurriedly went out to the man at the spring. When he had seen the earrings and the bracelets on his sister’s hands, and had heard all the words she recounted, the man spoke. He came to the man who stood by the camels near the spring of water and said to him: "Enter, blessed of the Lord. Why do you stand outside? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels." And he led him into the lodging and unharnessed the camels; he gave them straw and hay, and water to wash the feet of the camels and of the men who came

with him. And bread was set before them. But he said: "I will not eat until I have spoken my message." Laban responded: "Speak." And he said:
"I am the servant of Abraham. And the Lord has blessed Abraham greatly, and he has been magnified; He has given him sheep and oxen, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and donkeys. While I was turning these things over silently within myself, Rebekah appeared, coming with a pitcher which she carried on her shoulder; she descended to the spring and drew water. And I said to her: 'Give me a little to drink.' She quickly lowered the pitcher from her shoulder and said to me: 'Both you drink, and I will provide a drink for your camels.' **L**aban and Bethuel responded: "The word has come from the Lord; we cannot speak anything else against His pleasure. At that time, Isaac was walking along the way that leads to the well named "Of the Living and Seeing One" <note>Beer-lahai-roi</note>. For he lived in the southern land. **A**braham then took another wife named Keturah, who bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan begot Sheba and Dedan. Isaac therefore went to Abimelech, the king of the Philistines, in Gerar.

The Lord appeared to him and said: "Do not go down into Egypt, but rest in the land which I shall tell you. Live there as a stranger, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and your offspring I will give all these regions, fulfilling the oath which I swore to your father Abraham. I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give to your descendants all these regions; and in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my precepts and my commands, and observed my ceremonies and laws." So Isaac remained in Gerar. When he was questioned by the men of that place about his wife, he responded: "She is my sister." For he had been afraid to confess that she was joined to him in marriage, fearing they might perhaps kill him because of her beauty. When many days had passed and he continued to stay there, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looking through a window, saw him playing <note>The Latin *iocantē* suggests affectionate or intimate behavior, revealing they were more than siblings.</note> with his wife Rebekah. Calling for him, he said: "It is clear that she is your wife. Why did you lie, saying she was your sister?" He responded: "I feared lest I might die because of her." And Abimelech said: "Why have you done this to us? Someone from the people could have slept with your wife, and you would have brought a great sin upon us." And he commanded all the people, saying: "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall die the death." Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold harvest in that same year. The Lord blessed him, and the man became wealthy, and he went on progressing and growing until he became exceedingly great. He also possessed sheep and herds and a very large household. Because of this, the Philistines envied him and blocked up all the wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug at that time, filling them with earth. It reached the point that Abimelech himself said to Isaac: "Depart from us, because you have become much more powerful than we are." And departing from there, he came to the torrent of Gerar to live in the valley. He dug other wells again, which the servants of his father Abraham had made and which the Philistines had blocked after his death; and he called them by the same names by which his father had called them before. They also dug in the torrent and found living water <note>original: "aquā viuam"; this refers to fresh, flowing spring water as opposed to stagnant cistern water.</note>. But even there, a dispute arose from the shepherds of Gerar against the shepherds of Isaac, saying: "The water is ours." For this reason, he called the name of the well "Strife" <note>original: "esec"</note> because of the false claim that had occurred. They dug another, and for that one too they contended; he called its name "Enmity" <note>original: "inimicitias", referring to the Hebrew Sitnah</note>. Moving from there, they showed a well for which they did not contend; therefore he called its name "Room" <note>original: "latitudo", referring to the Hebrew Rehoboth</note> saying: "Now the Lord has given us room and made us grow upon the earth."

From there he went up to Beersheba, where the Lord appeared to him on that very night, saying: "I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not fear, for I am with you; I will bless you and multiply your offspring for the sake of my servant Abraham." Therefore he built an altar there and invoked the name of the Lord. He pitched his tent and commanded his servants to dig a well. When Abimelech, and his friend Ahuzzath, and Phicol the commander of the soldiers had come to that place from Gerar, they spoke to him of peace. He brought them into his lodging and made a feast for them. After eating and drinking, they rose in the morning and swore an oath to one another, and they departed from him in peace. On that same day, Isaac's servants came and reported to him about the well they had dug, saying: "We have found water." Wherefore he called it "Abundance," and the name of the city was set as Beersheba <note>original: "bērsabee"; meaning "Well of the Oath" or "Well of the Seven"</note> even unto the present day.

Truly, Esau, at forty years old, took as wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon from the same place. Both of these offended the souls of Isaac and Rebekah. Isaac had grown old and his eyes had become dim. He called Esau, his elder son, and said to him: "My son?" He replied: "What is it, my lord?" Isaac had finished his speech, and just as Jacob had gone outside, Esau came and brought the cooked meat from his hunting to his father, saying: "Rise, my father, and eat of your hunting, so that your soul may bless me."

To which Isaac said: "Who then are you?" He responded: "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau." Hearing his father's words, Esau roared with a great and violent cry, and being dismayed, he said: "Bless me also, my father." He said: "Your brother came deceitfully and received your blessing." But he added: "He is rightly called by the name Jacob <note>The name Jacob is associated with 'heel-grasper' or 'supplanter'.</note>, for he has supplanted me now a second time. ### The Rivalry of the Sisters
<image-desc>Large ornamental red initial C</image-desc>Seeing that she was unfruitful, Rachel envied her sister and said to her husband: "Give me children, otherwise I shall die." Jacob, angry with her, replied: "Am I in the place of God, who has deprived you of the fruit of your womb?" But she said: "I have my handmaid Bilhah; go in to her, so that she may give birth upon my knees, and I may have children through her." So she gave him Bilhah in marriage. When she was joined to the man, she conceived and bore a son. Rachel said: "The Lord has judged me and heard my voice, giving me a son." And for that reason, she called his name **Dan**. And again Bilhah, conceiving, bore another. Regarding him, Rachel said: "God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed." And she called him **Naphtali**. Leah, sensing that she had ceased bearing, gave Zilpah her handmaid to her husband. After conceiving, she brought forth a son. "Happily!" she said. And for that reason, she called his name **Gad**. Zilpah also bore another. And Leah said: "This is for my happiness; for indeed, women shall call me blessed." Therefore, she called him **Asher**. 

Now Reuben, going out into the field at the time of the wheat harvest, found mandrakes <note>Mandrakes were anciently believed to aid in fertility and conception.</note> which he brought to his mother Leah. Rachel said: "Give me a portion of your son's mandrakes." She replied: "Does it seem a small thing to you that you have taken my husband from me, unless you also take my son’s mandrakes?" Rachel said: "Let him sleep with you tonight, then, in exchange for your son's mandrakes." And when Jacob returned from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said: "You shall come in to me, because I have hired you for a price with my son's mandrakes." He slept with her that night, and God heard her prayers; she conceived and bore a fifth son and said: "God has given me my reward, because I gave my handmaid to my husband." And she called his name **Issachar**. Again Leah conceived and bore a sixth son and said: "God has endowed me with a good dowry; even this time my husband will be with me, because I have borne him six sons." And for that reason, she called his name **Zebulun**. After this, she bore a daughter named **Dinah**.

### Jacob’s Prosperity and the Peeled Rods
<image-desc>Large ornamental red initial R</image-desc>The Lord also remembered Rachel and heard her, and opened her womb. She conceived and bore a son, saying: "God has taken away my reproach." And she called his name **Joseph**, saying: "May the Lord add to me another son." 

Now when Joseph was born, Jacob said to his father-in-law: "Dismiss me so that I may return home to my own country. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, so that I may depart. For you know the service with which I have served you." Laban said: "Let me find grace in your sight; I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you. Appoint the wages that I should give you." But he replied: "You know how I have served you, and how much your possession has been in my hands. You had very little before I came, and now you have become wealthy; the Lord has blessed you at my coming. It is just, therefore, that I should also provide for my own house at some point." 

Laban said: "What do you want me to give you?" But he said: "I want nothing; but if you will do what I ask, I will again feed and keep your flocks. I will go through all your flocks and separate all the speckled and spotted sheep; and whatever is dark and spotted and varied, both among the sheep and among the goats, shall be my wages. And tomorrow my justice shall answer for me, when the time of the agreement comes before you; and anything that is not varied and spotted and dark, both among the sheep and the goats, shall prove me a thief." 

Laban said: "I am pleased with what you ask." And on 그날 that day, he separated the goats and the young sheep, and the rams that were varied and spotted; but the entire flock of a single color—that is, the white and the black ones—he delivered into the hands of his sons. And he put a distance of a three days' journey between himself and his son-in-law, who was feeding the rest of his flocks. 

Jacob then took green rods of poplar and almond and plane trees, and partially peeled them. When the bark was stripped away, whiteness appeared in the parts that had been bared, while the parts that were intact remained green; and in this way, a variegated color was produced. He placed them in the troughs where the water was poured out, so that when the flocks came to drink, they would have the rods before their eyes and would conceive while looking at them. And it happened that in the heat of mating, the sheep looked at the rods and brought forth young that were spotted and varied and sprinkled with different colors. And Jacob did this likewise, placing the rods before the eyes of the rams. Some were white and some were black, which belonged to Laban, but the rest Jacob separated. Whenever the sheep were first coming into season, Jacob would place the rods in the troughs before the eyes of the rams and sheep so they would conceive while contemplating them. But when it was the later mating and conception, he did not place them. Thus, those that were late-born became Laban's, and those of the first season became Jacob's. And the man was enriched beyond measure; he had many flocks, male and female servants, camels, and donkeys.

### The Flight from Laban
After he heard the words of Laban’s sons saying, "Jacob has taken everything that was our father's and has become very wealthy from his resources," and he noticed from Laban’s face that he was not toward him as he was yesterday and the day before—especially when the Lord said to him, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you"—he sent and called Rachel and Leah into the field where he was feeding the flocks and said: "I see your father’s face, that it is not toward me as it was yesterday and the day before; but the God of my father has been with me. And you yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength. But your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times; and yet God did not allow him to harm me. Whenever he said, 'The speckled shall be your wages,' all the sheep bore speckled offspring; but if he said, 'The white shall be taken as your wages,' all the flocks bore white. Thus God has taken your father's substance and given it to me. For after the time for conception arrived, I lifted my eyes and saw in a dream the males leaping upon the females, variegated and spotted and of diverse colors. And the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob.' And I responded, 'I am here.' He said, 'Lift your eyes and see the males ascending upon the females, varied, sprinkled, and spotted. For I have seen everything Laban has done to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and made a vow to me. Now arise and depart from this way and return to the land of your birth.'" 

Rachel and Leah responded: "Do we have anything left in the resources and inheritance of our father’s house? Has he not treated us like strangers and sold us and consumed our price? But God has taken from our father and added to us. Now therefore, do everything that God has commanded you." 

So Jacob arose and, having placed his children and his wives upon camels, he departed. He took all his substance and flocks and whatever he had acquired in Mesopotamia, proceeding to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.

### The Pursuit and the Stolen Idols
<image-desc>Large ornamental red initial E</image-desc>At the time when Laban had gone to shear his sheep, Rachel stole her father’s idols <note>Original: *ydola*. These were household gods or 'teraphim' that represented family inheritance and legal status.</note>. Jacob did not want to confess to his father-in-law that he was fleeing. And when he had gone, both himself and all that belonged to him, and having crossed the river, he headed toward Mount Gilead. It was told to Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled. Taking his brothers with him, he pursued him for seven days and caught him on Mount Gilead. And he saw the Lord in a dream saying to him: "Take care that you do not speak anything harshly against Jacob." 

Now Jacob had already pitched his tent on the mountain, and Laban settled with his brothers on Mount Gilead. Laban said to him: "Why have you acted in this way, to lead away my daughters in secret like captives of the sword? Why did you want to flee without my knowledge, and did not tell me, so that I might follow you with joy and songs and timbrels and harps? You did not even permit me to kiss my sons and daughters. You have acted foolishly. And now indeed my hand has the power to return evil to you; but the God of your father said to me yesterday: 'Beware that you do not speak anything too harsh against Jacob.' And even if you desired to go to your people and longed for your father’s house, why did you steal my gods?" 

Jacob responded: "I say to you that I departed in secret because I feared you might violently take away your daughters. As for your charge of theft, with whomever you find your gods, let him be put to death before our brothers. Search whatever you find with me and take it." In saying this, he did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols. 

Laban therefore entered the tents of Jacob and Leah and of both the handmaids, and found nothing. When he entered Rachel’s tent, she quickly hid the idols under the camel's straw and sat upon them. And though he searched the whole tent and found nothing, she said: "Let my lord not be indignant that I cannot rise before you, for the custom of women <note>A euphemism for menstruation.</note> has now happened to me." Thus the diligence of the searcher was eluded.

### The Covenant at Galaad
<image-desc>Large ornamental red initial R</image-desc>Jacob, being provoked, said: "What is my fault and what is my sin, that you have so burned after me and searched all my furniture? What have you found from all the substance of your house? Set it here before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between me and you. Behold, I have been with you for twenty years. Your sheep and goats were not sterile; I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I show you what was caught by a beast; I made good every loss. Whatever was lost by theft you demanded from me. Day and night I was parched by heat and frozen by frost, and sleep fled from my eyes. Thus for twenty years in your house I served you: fourteen for your daughters and six for your flocks. You also changed my wages ten times. Unless the God of my father Abraham and the fear of Isaac had been with me, perhaps you would have sent me away empty-handed now. God has looked upon my affliction and the labor of my hands, and he rebuked you yesterday." 

Jacob <note>This likely refers to Laban's response, though the OCR continues with Jacob's name.</note> replied to him: "The daughters are mine and the sons are yours, and the flocks and all that you see are mine. What can I do to my children and grandchildren? Come therefore and let us enter into a covenant, so that it may be a testimony between me and you." 

Thereupon, Jacob took a stone and set it up as a monument, and said to his brothers: "Bring stones." They gathered them and made a heap, and they ate upon it. Laban called it "The Heap of Witness," and Jacob called it the "Galeed" <note>Original: *garitum testimoniū*. In the Bible, Laban uses the Aramaic *Jegar-sahadutha* and Jacob uses the Hebrew *Galeed*.</note>, each according to the property of his own language. Laban said: "This heap shall be a witness between me and you today." And therefore its name was called **Gilead** and **Mizpah** <note>Original: *roeb testirul[us]*. Likely referring to Mizpah (Watchtower).</note>, for he said: "May the Lord watch between us when we have departed from one another. If you afflict my daughters, and if you bring in other wives over them, no one is witness to our speech except God, who is present and watches." 

And he said again to Jacob: "Behold this heap and the stone which I have set up between me and you shall be a witness: this heap, I say, and the stone as a monument. If I pass over it toward you, or if you pass over it thinking evil against me, may the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their fathers, judge between us." Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac. Having sacrificed victims on the mountain, he called his brothers to eat bread. When they had eaten, they stayed there. But Laban, rising in the night, kissed his sons and daughters and blessed them, and returned to his own place.

### The Meeting with Esau
Jacob also went on the journey he had begun, and the angels of God met him. When he saw them, he said: "These are the camps of God." And he called the name of that place **Mahanaim**, that is, "The Camps." He also sent messengers before him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, in the region of Edom. And he commanded them, saying: "Thus shall you speak to my lord Esau: 'Thus says your servant Jacob: I have lived as a stranger with Laban and have been there until the present day. I have oxen and donkeys, and sheep, and male and female servants. And I now send a delegation to my lord, that I may find grace in your sight.'" 

The messengers returned to Jacob, saying: "We came to your brother Esau, and behold, he is hurrying to meet you with four hundred men." Jacob was greatly terrified and distressed. He divided the people who were with him, as well as the flocks, oxen, and camels, into two companies, saying: "If Esau comes to one company and strikes it, the other company which remains will be saved." 

And Jacob said: "O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, Lord who said to me, 'Return to the land of your birth and I will do good to you,' I am less than all the mercies and the truth which you have fulfilled for your servant. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies. Rescue me from the hand of my brother Esau, because I fear him greatly; lest perhaps coming he should strike the mother with the children. You spoke that you would do well for me, and that my offspring would be spread out like the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered because of its multitude." 

And when he had slept there that night, he separated from those things he had as gifts for his brother Esau: two hundred female goats, twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes, twenty rams, thirty milch camels with their colts, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty she-asses and ten of their colts. And he sent these by the hands of his servants, each flock separately. He said to his servants: "Go before me, and let there be a space between flock and flock." And he commanded the first one, saying: "If you meet my brother Esau and he asks you, 'Whose are you?' or 'Where are you going?' or 'Whose are these things you are following?' you shall answer him: 'Your servant Jacob's. He has sent gifts to my lord Esau, and he himself comes after us.'" Similarly, he commanded the second and third, and all who followed the flocks, saying: "Speak these words to Esau when you find him..."

He said: "Your servant Jacob comes behind us." For he said: "I will appease him with the gifts that go before me, and afterward I will see him; perhaps he will be gracious to me." Jacob, lifting his eyes, saw Esau coming with four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah and Rachel and the two handmaids. He himself, going before them, bowed down to the ground seven times until he approached his brother. Be favorable to me and receive the blessing I have brought you, which God, who grants all things, has bestowed upon me." Only after his brother insisted did he accept it, saying: "Let us walk together, and I will be the companion of your journey." Jacob answered: "My lord knows that I have tender children, and sheep and nursing cattle with me; if I make the flocks labor too much in walking, they will all die in one day. Let my lord go on before his servant, and I will follow slowly in his footsteps, as I see my little ones are able, until I come to my lord in Seir." Esau replied: "I pray you, let some of the people who are with me remain as companions for your way." He said: "It is not necessary. I need only this one thing: to find grace in the sight of my lord." So Esau returned that day by the way he had come to Seir, and Jacob came to **Succoth** <note>Meaning "Booths" or "Tabernacles."</note>. He then passed over to Salem, a city of the Shechemites in the land of Canaan, after returning from Mesopotamia of Syria, and lived near the town. He bought the part of the field where they had pitched their tents from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs. Having erected an altar there, he called upon the most mighty God of Israel.

<margin>Genesis 34</margin>
Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that land, saw her, he fell in love with her. He seized her and slept with her, violating the virgin by force. But his soul was knit to her, and he comforted her with soft words. He said to his father Hamor: "Take this girl for me as a wife." When Jacob heard this, his sons being away occupied with the livestock, he remained silent until they returned. Hamor, the father of Shechem, went out to speak to Jacob. Behold, the sons came in from the field, and hearing what had happened, they were very angry because Shechem had done a foul thing in Israel, and by violating Jacob's daughter, had committed an illicit act. Hamor spoke to them: "The soul of my son Shechem clings to your daughter. Give her to him as a wife, and let us join in marriages with one another. Give your daughters to us and take our daughters, and live with us. The land is in your power; cultivate it, trade in it, and possess it." Shechem also said to her father and brothers: "Let me find grace before you, and whatever you establish, I will give. Increase the dowry and the requested gifts, and I will gladly give what you ask; only give me this girl as a wife." The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father deceitfully, being enraged by the defilement of their sister. "We cannot do what you ask, nor give our sister to an uncircumcised man, which is unlawful and wicked among us. But in this we can be allied: if you will be like us, and every male among you is circumcised. Then we will give and receive our daughters mutually, and we will live with you and be one people. If you will not be circumcised, we will take our daughter and depart." Their offer pleased Hamor and his son Shechem. The young man did not delay in fulfilling what was asked, for he loved the girl greatly, and he was the most noble in all his father's house. Entering the gate of the city, they spoke to the people: "These men are peaceful and want to live with us. Let them trade in the land and cultivate it; it is spacious and wide and needs tillers. We shall take their daughters as wives and give ours to them. There is only one thing that delays such a great good: we must circumcise our males according to the rite of their nation. If we do, their substance, their cattle, and everything they possess will be ours. Let us only agree to this, and by living together, we shall become one people." All agreed with Hamor and Shechem. Every male was circumcised. On the third day, when the pain of the wounds is most severe, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took their swords and entered the city boldly. They killed all the males, including Hamor and Shechem, and took their sister Dinah from Shechem's house. After they left, the other sons of Jacob fell upon the slain and plundered the city in revenge for the violation. They took their sheep, herds, donkeys, and wasted everything in the houses and fields; they led away the little ones and the wives as captives. Jacob said boldly to Simeon and Levi: "You have troubled me and made me hateful to the strangers and the wild inhabitants of this land. We are few; if they gather together, they will strike me, and I and my house will be destroyed." They answered: "Should they have used our sister like a harlot?"

Meanwhile, the Lord spoke to Jacob: "Arise and go up to Bethel and live there. Make an altar to God, who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau." Jacob, having called together all his household, said: "Cast away the foreign gods that are in your midst, be cleansed, and change your garments. Jacob came to Luz (which is in the land of Canaan, known as **Bethel** <note>Meaning "House of God."</note>), he and all the people with him. Jacob erected a stone monument in the place where God had spoken to him, pouring out drink offerings and oil upon it. He called the name of that place Bethel.
