Judah said to his brothers: "What does it profit us if we kill our brother and hide his blood? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites so that our hands are not defiled, for he is our brother and our flesh." The brothers agreed to his words. And as the Midianite merchants passed by, they pulled him out of the cistern and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They led him into Egypt. When Reuben returned to the cistern and did not find the boy, he tore his garments and went to his brothers, saying: "The boy is not there, and I, where shall I go?" They took his coat and dipped it in the blood of a goat they had killed, sending men to carry it to their father and say: "We found this; see whether it is your son's coat or not." When the father recognized it, he said: "It is my son's coat; a wild beast has eaten him, a beast has devoured Joseph." Tearing his clothes, he put on sackcloth, mourning his son for a long time. Though all his children gathered to ease their father's pain, he would not receive consolation, saying: "I will go down to my son in the grave <note>original: 'infernum'—referring to the place of the dead</note> mourning." While he continued in his weeping, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

**A**t that time, Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a certain Adullamite named Hirah. He saw there the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua, and taking her as his wife, he went in to her. She conceived and bore a son, and called his name Er. Again she conceived and bore a son whom she called Onan. She bore a third, whom she called Shelah; after his birth, she ceased to bear children. Judah took a wife for his firstborn Er, named Tamar. But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and was slain by Him. Judah then said to Onan his son: "Go in to your brother’s wife and marry her, so that you may raise up offspring for your brother." Knowing that the children would not be his own, whenever he went in to his brother's wife, he spilled his seed on the ground so that no children would be born in his brother's name. Therefore the Lord struck him down because he did a detestable thing. Wherefore Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law: "Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up." For he feared that he too might die like his brothers. She went away and lived in her father’s house. After many days had passed, Shua's daughter, the wife of Judah, died. After his mourning, Judah received consolation and went up to Timnah to his sheep-shearers, himself and Hirah the Adullamite, his companion. It was told to Tamar that her father-in-law was going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. She laid aside her widow’s garments, took a veil, and changing her attire, sat at the crossroads on the way to Timnah; for she saw that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife. When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face so she would not be recognized. Going to her, he said: "Let me come in to you." For he did not know she was his daughter-in-law. She answered: "What will you give me to sleep with me?" He said: "I will send you a young goat from the flocks." She replied: "I will agree, if you give me a pledge until you send what you promise." Judah said: "What do you want given to you for a pledge?" She answered: "Your ring, your bracelet, and the staff you hold in your hand." By that one union she conceived, and rising, she went away. After she had put off the attire she had taken, she put on her widow’s garments. Judah sent the goat by his shepherd, the Adullamite, to receive the pledge he had given the woman, but he did not find her. He asked the men of that place: "Where is the woman who sat at the crossroads?" They answered: "There was never a prostitute in this place." He returned to Judah and said: "I did not find her, and the men of that place said no prostitute ever sat there." Judah said: "Let her keep the things; surely she cannot accuse me of a lie. I sent the goat I promised, and you did not find her."

**A**nd behold, after three months, it was told to Judah: "Tamar your daughter-in-law has played the harlot, and her womb seems to swell." He said: "Bring her out to be burned." As she was being led to her punishment, she sent to her father-in-law, saying: "By the man to whom these belong, I have conceived. Look at whose ring, bracelet, and staff these are." Recognizing the gifts, he said: "Tamar is more just than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah." Yet he did not know her again. When the time of birth was at hand, twins appeared in her womb. At the moment of delivery, one put out a hand, on which the midwife tied a scarlet thread, saying: "This one shall come out first." But as he drew back his hand, the other came out, and the woman said: "Why has the wall been breached for you?" For this reason his name was called Perez <note>meaning 'breach'</note>. Afterward his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and he called him Zerah. Meanwhile, Joseph was led into Egypt, and Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh and captain of the army, an Egyptian man, bought him for a price from the hands of the Ishmaelites who had brought him there. The Lord was with him, and he was successful in all things, living in the house of his master. The master saw that the Lord was with him and that all he did was guided by His hand. Joseph found favor in his master's sight and served him. Being placed in charge, he governed the house entrusted to him and all that was there. The Lord blessed the house of the Egyptian 

because of Joseph, and multiplied everything both in the house and in the fields. The master knew nothing of his own affairs except for the bread he ate. Now Joseph was beautiful of face and handsome in appearance. After many days, his mistress cast her eyes upon him and said: "Sleep with me." But he, by no means consenting to the deed, said to her: "Behold, my master has entrusted everything to me and does not even know what he has in his house. There is nothing that is not in my hand, nor has he withheld anything from me except you, who are his wife. How then can I do this evil and sin against my master?" Though she spoke such words to him every day, the woman was a burden to the young man, and he refused the adultery. It happened one day that Joseph entered the house to do some work without witnesses. She, catching him by his cloak, said: "Sleep with me." Leaving his cloak in her hand, he fled and went outside. When the woman saw the garment in her hands and that she was rejected, she called the men of her house and said to them: "See, he has brought in a Hebrew man to insult us. He came in to me to lie with me, and when I cried out and he heard my voice, he left the cloak I was holding and fled outside." To prove her story, she kept the cloak until her husband <note>original: 'mercurio'—likely a scribal error for 'marito' (husband)</note> returned home, and said: "The Hebrew servant you brought came in to me to mock me. When he heard me cry out, he left his cloak and fled outside." Hearing this, the master, being too ready to believe the words of his wife, was very angry. He delivered Joseph into the prison where the king's prisoners were kept, and he was shut in there. But the Lord was with Joseph and showed him mercy, giving him favor in the sight of the chief of the prison. He put all the prisoners held in custody into Joseph's hand, and whatever was done was under him. The keeper did not check anything, trusting him with all.

**A**fter these things, it happened that two officials sinned: the cupbearer of the king <margin>Go.</margin> of Egypt and the baker of his lord. Therefore Pharaoh was angry with them—for one was chief of the cupbearers and the other chief of the bakers—and he sent them into the military prison where Joseph was bound. The keeper of the prison entrusted them to Joseph, who served them. Some time passed while they were held in custody, and both saw a dream in one night, each with its own interpretation. When Joseph went in to them in the morning, he saw they were sad. He asked them: "Why is your face sadder today than usual?" They answered: "We have seen a dream, and there is no one to interpret it for us." Joseph said to them: "Does not interpretation belong to God? Tell me what you saw." The chief cupbearer told his dream first: "I saw before me a vine on which were three branches, which grew little by little into buds, and after the flowers, the grapes ripened. Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I took the grapes and pressed them into the cup I held, and I gave the cup to Pharaoh." Joseph responded: "This is the interpretation of the dream. The three branches are yet three days, after which Pharaoh will remember your service and restore you to your former rank. You shall give him the cup according to your office, as you were formerly accustomed to do. Only remember me when it is well with you, and show me mercy by suggesting to Pharaoh that he bring me out of this prison, for I was stolen away from the land of the Hebrews, and here I am innocent, though cast into this pit." The master baker, seeing that he had wisely solved the dream, said: "I also saw a dream, that I had three baskets of meal upon my head. And in the one basket that was highest, I carried all manner of baked meats, and the birds ate them." Joseph answered: "This is the interpretation: the three baskets are yet three days, after which Pharaoh will take off your head and hang you on a cross, and the birds shall tear your flesh." Then on the third day, it was Pharaoh's birthday, and making a great feast for his servants, he remembered among the banquet the chief cupbearer and the prince of bakers. He restored one to his place to offer the king his cup; the other he hanged on a gallows, as Pharaoh's truth was conjectured. And yet, when prosperity followed for the chief cupbearer, he forgot his interpreter.

**A**fter two years, Pharaoh saw a dream. He thought he stood by a river, from which came up seven beautiful and very fat cows, and they fed in marshy places. Seven others also emerged from the river, foul and wasted with thinness, and they fed on the very bank of the river in green places. They devoured those whose appearance and body was wonderful. Pharaoh, terrified, woke up and then fell asleep again. He saw another dream: seven ears of grain grew on one stalk, full and beautiful. Seven other ears, thin and blasted by the wind, sprang up and devoured all the beauty of the former. Pharaoh woke after his rest, and in the morning, overcome with fear, he sent for all the diviners and wise men of Egypt. Having summoned them, he told the dream, but there was no one who could interpret it. Then at last, the chief cupbearer remembered and said: "I confess my sin. The king was angry with his servants and ordered me and the chief baker to be thrust into the prison of the captain of the guard, where in one night we both saw a dream foretelling the future. There was a Hebrew youth there, a servant of the same captain, to whom we told our dreams and heard what later proved to happen. I was restored to my office, and the other was hanged on a cross." Immediately, by the king’s command, Joseph was brought out of prison; they shaved him, changed his clothes, and presented him. The king said to him: "I have seen dreams, and there is no one who can explain what I saw. I have heard that you are most wise in interpreting." Joseph answered: "Without me, God shall give a prosperous answer to Pharaoh." Pharaoh then told what he had seen: "I thought I stood on the bank of the river, and seven cows came up from the stream, very beautiful and fat-fleshed, which fed in the marshy pastures. And behold, following these, seven other cows came out, so thin that I never saw such in the land of Egypt; they devoured and consumed the first, but it made no difference; they remained just as thin and foul. Waking again, I saw a dream: seven ears grew on one stalk, full and most beautiful. Seven others, struck by the wind, arose and devoured the beauty of the first. I told the diviners, but no one can explain it." Joseph answered: "The king's dream is one: what God is about to do, He has shown to Pharaoh. The seven beautiful cows and the seven full ears are seven years of plenty; they comprise the same dream. The seven thin and meager cows that came up after them, and the seven thin ears struck by the burning wind, are seven years of coming famine. Seven years of great plenty shall come to the land of Egypt, which seven years of scarcity shall follow, so that all the former abundance shall be forgotten. Famine shall consume all the land. As for the dream being seen twice, it is a sign of certainty, for the word of God is fixed and shall be fulfilled quickly."

# Now, therefore, a man of exceptional wisdom and a marvel of modesty and royal efficiency:
one who proved by his constancy that he was a persuader of regions; whom luxury did not inflate, nor the foulness of arms terrify; who, having joined the assembly of all virtues, does not shrink back. He brought together all the high officials of the impious Pharaoh; he served in the city; and with equal care, he took charge of the famine that was pressing upon them, so that the empire would not be consumed. This counsel pleased Pharaoh and all his ministers, and he spoke to them: -> "Can we find such a man, who is full of the spirit of God?" <- And he said to Joseph: "Because God has shown you all that you have spoken, could any man be found wiser than you? You shall be over my house, and the people shall be obedient to the command of your mouth; only in the throne of the kingdom will I precede you." And Pharaoh said again to Joseph: "Behold, I have appointed you over the entire land of Egypt." And when he had drawn the ring from his hand, he clothed him in garments; and with a robe of fine linen <note>original: *stola byssina*</note>, he placed a gold chain around his neck. He made him ascend upon his second chariot, with a herald crying out that everyone should bow their knee before him. Thus he was set over the entire land of Egypt. The king also said to Joseph: "I am Pharaoh; without your command, no one shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt." And he changed his name, and called him in the Egyptian tongue "Savior of the World" <note>original: *salvatorem mundi*, a Latin translation of the Egyptian name Zaphenath-Paneah</note>. And he gave him as a wife Aseneth, the daughter of Potipherah, the priest of Heliopolis. So Joseph went out into all the land of Egypt; he was thirty years old when he stood in the sight of Pharaoh, and he traveled through all the regions of Egypt. And the fertility of the seven years came, and the crops were reduced into bundles and gathered into the storehouses of Egypt. Every abundance of grain was stored in the individual cities. Furthermore, there was such a multitude of wheat, like the sands of the sea, that it was equaled; and the quantity exceeded measurement. But before the famine came, younger sons <note>The text likely means "sons before the famine," referring to Manasseh and Ephraim</note> were born to him, whom Aseneth, daughter of Potipherah the priest of Heliopolis, bore to him. And he called the name of the firstborn Manasseh <note>from a Hebrew root meaning "to forget"</note>, saying: "God has made me forget all my labors and my father's house." And the name of the second he called Ephraim <note>from a Hebrew root meaning "to be fruitful"</note>, saying: "God has made me grow in the land of my poverty."

If something should happen to him <note>referring to Benjamin</note> on the journey, you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave. When he <note>Judah</note> comes to your servant, our father, and the boy is missing—since his life depends on the boy’s life—seeing that he is not with us, he will die; and your servants will bring down his gray hairs with grief to the grave. I, your servant, personally took responsibility for him and promised my father, saying: "If I do not bring him back to you, I shall be guilty of a sin for all time." Therefore, I, your servant, will remain in the service of my lord in place of the boy, and let the boy go up with his brothers. For I cannot return to my father while the boy is absent, lest I witness the calamity that is bound to overwhelm my father. Joseph could no longer restrain himself before the many standing by; therefore, he commanded that everyone go outside, so that no stranger would be present at their mutual recognition. He raised his voice with weeping, which was heard by the Egyptians and all the house of Pharaoh, and he said to his brothers: I am Joseph. Is my father still alive? His brothers could not answer him, being terrified by a great fear. To whom he spoke gently: "Come near to me," he said. And when they had come close, he said: I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Do not be afraid, nor let it seem a hard thing to you that you sold me into these regions; for God sent me before you into Egypt for your safety. For it is now two years since the famine began in the land, and five years still remain, in which there can be neither plowing nor harvesting. God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved on the earth and have food to live on. It was not by your counsel but by the will of God that I was sent here; He has made me like a father to Pharaoh, and lord of his entire house, and a prince in all the land of Egypt. Hurry and go up to my father, and say to him: "Your son Joseph sends this message: God has made me lord of all Egypt; come down to me and dwell in the land of Goshen. You shall be near me—you, your children, your grandchildren, your sheep, your herds, and all that you possess. There I will feed you, for there are still five years of famine remaining, lest you and your house and all you possess should perish." Behold, your eyes and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see that it is my own mouth speaking to you. Report to my father all my glory and everything you have seen in Egypt. Hurry and bring him to me. And when he had fallen upon the neck of his brother Benjamin, he wept; and Benjamin likewise wept upon his neck. He kissed all his brothers and wept over each one. After this, they dared to speak to him. The news was heard and spread by common talk in the king's court: "Joseph's brothers have come." And Pharaoh rejoiced with all his household. He told Joseph to command his brothers, saying: "Load your beasts and go into the land of Canaan; take your father and your kindred from there and come to me, and I will give you all the good things of Egypt, that you may eat the marrow of the earth <note>original: *medullam terrae*, meaning the best or most fertile parts of the land</note>." He also commanded them to take wagons from the land of Egypt for the transport of their little ones and wives, and said: "Take your father and hurry as fast as you can. Do not worry about your household goods, for all the riches of Egypt shall be yours." And the sons of Israel did as they had been commanded. Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharaoh's command and food for the journey. He ordered two robes to be brought out for each man; but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver along with five of the best robes. He sent the same amount of money and clothing to his father, adding ten male donkeys to carry all the riches of Egypt, and as many female donkeys carrying wheat and bread for the journey. So he sent his brothers away, and as they were departing, he said to them: "Do not be angry on the way." Going up out of Egypt, they came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. They told him, saying: "Joseph is alive, and he rules over all the land of Egypt." Hearing this, Jacob felt as if he were waking from a heavy sleep; yet he did not believe them. They, on the other hand, related the whole sequence of events. When he saw the wagons and everything Joseph had sent, his spirit revived, and he said: "It is enough for me if my son is still alive; I will go and see him before I die."

<margin>Gen. 46</margin>
### Israel set out with everything he had and came to the Well of the Oath <note>original: *puteum iuramenti*, referring to Beersheba</note>. He offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac, and he heard God calling to him in a vision at night, saying: "Jacob, Jacob." He replied: "Here I am." God said to him: "I am the most mighty God of your father; do not fear. Go down into Egypt, because I will make you a great nation there. I will go down there with you, and I will bring you back again when you return. Joseph shall also place his hand over your eyes <note>A gesture performed at the moment of death</note>." Jacob rose from the Well of the Oath, and his sons carried him with their children and wives in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry the old man. Taking all they had possessed in the land of Canaan, they came into Egypt with all their offspring: his sons, grandsons, daughters, and all his progeny together.

<margin>Gen. 46</margin>
### These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with their children. The firstborn was Reuben. His sons: Enoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. However, Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were born: Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Iob, and Shimron. The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. These were the sons of Leah whom she bore in Mesopotamia of Syria, along with her daughter Dinah. All the souls of her sons and daughters were thirty-three. The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishuah, Isui, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel. These were the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah. She bore these to Jacob: sixteen souls. The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin. To Joseph were born in the land of Egypt Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Aseneth, daughter of Potipherah the priest of Heliopolis, bore to him. The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. These were the sons of Rachel born to Jacob; all souls, fourteen. The son of Dan: Hushim. The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. These were the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel; she bore these to Jacob; all souls, seven. All the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob, who were his direct descendants—excluding the wives of his sons—were sixty-six. The sons of Joseph born to him in Egypt were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy.

### He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to announce his arrival, and so that Joseph might meet him in Goshen. When he arrived there, Joseph yoked his chariot and went up to meet his father in that same place. Seeing him, he fell upon his neck and wept as they embraced. The father said to Joseph: "Now I can die happy, because I have seen your face and I leave you still alive." Joseph spoke to his brothers and to all his father's house: "I will go up and announce this to Pharaoh, saying: 'My brothers and my father's house, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. They are men who are shepherds of sheep,

<column-break/>

and they have their flocks and herds with them for their livelihood, and they have brought everything they could own.' When he calls you and asks: 'What is your occupation?' you shall answer: 'Your servants have been shepherds from our youth until the present day, both we and our fathers.' Do this so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, because the Egyptians detest all shepherds of sheep." So Joseph entered and reported to Pharaoh, saying: "My father and brothers, their sheep and herds, and everything they possess have come from the land of Canaan, and behold, they are staying in the land of Goshen." He also presented five of the last <note>meaning the youngest or most humble</note> of his brothers before the king. Pharaoh asked them: "What is your occupation?" They answered: "Your servants are shepherds of sheep, both we and our fathers. We have come to stay as travelers on our way, because there is no grass for the flocks of your servants; for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. We ask that you order your servants to stay in the land of Goshen." Pharaoh said to Joseph: "Your father and your brothers have come to you. The land of Egypt is before you; settle them in the best place, and give them the land of Goshen. If you know of any industrious men among them, appoint them as masters over my own livestock."

<margin>Gen. 47</margin>
### After this, Joseph brought his father to the king and stood him before him. Jacob blessed him, and when asked by the king: "How many are the days of the years of your life?" he answered: "The days of my pilgrimage are one hundred and thirty years; they have been few and difficult, and have not reached the days of my fathers during their own pilgrimages." Having blessed the king, he went out. Joseph gave his father and brothers a possession in Egypt, in the best part of the land, in Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. He provided for them and his father's entire household, giving food to each person. For there was famine in the whole world, and it oppressed the land of Egypt, especially Egypt and Canaan. From these, Joseph gathered all the money in exchange for the sale of grain and brought it into the king's treasury. When the buyers ran out of money, all Egypt came to Joseph saying: "Give us bread. Why should we die while you look on? Our money is gone." He replied: "Bring your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for them if you have no money." When they brought them, he gave them food in exchange for horses, sheep, cattle, and donkeys; he sustained them that year in exchange for their livestock. They came in the second year and said to him: "We will not hide from our lord that since our money is gone, our livestock are also gone; it is not hidden from you that we have nothing left except our bodies and our fields. Why should we die before your eyes? Both we and our land shall be yours. Buy us into the king’s service and provide seed, so that the land does not become a wilderness because the farmers have perished."

### And so Joseph claimed all the land of Egypt as the king's possession, as each man sold his land due to the hunger. He subjected it and all its people to Pharaoh, from the farthest borders of Egypt to its extreme limits, except for the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king. They were provided with fixed rations from the public storehouses, and therefore they were not forced to sell their possessions. Joseph then said to the people: "Behold, you see that Pharaoh now possesses both you and your land. Take seed and sow the fields so that you may have crops. You shall give a fifth part to the king; the remaining four parts you shall take for yourselves for sowing and for food for your families and children." They answered: "Our salvation is in your hand; let our lord only look upon us with favor, and we will gladly serve the king." From that time until the present day, in all the land of Egypt, a fifth part is paid to the kings, and it became like a law—except for the priestly land, which was free from this condition.

<margin>Exo. 1</margin>
### Israel lived in the land of Egypt, that is, in the land of Goshen, and possessed it; he grew and multiplied greatly. He lived there for seventeen years, and the total days of his life were one hundred and forty-seven years. When he saw the day of his death approaching, he called his son Joseph and said to him: "If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand under my thigh, and show me mercy and truth: do not bury me in Egypt. But I shall sleep with my fathers; you must carry me out of this land and bury me in the tomb of my ancestors." Joseph replied: "I will do what you have commanded." And he said: "Swear to me then." As he swore, Israel worshipped God, turning toward the head of his bed.

### After these things were done, it was reported to Joseph that his father was sick. Taking his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, he went to him. It was said to the old man: "Behold, your son Joseph is coming to you." Strengthening himself, he sat up in bed, and when Joseph entered, he said: "The Almighty appeared to me in Luz <note>Bethel</note>, which is in the land of Canaan; He blessed me and said: 'I will increase and multiply you, and I will make you into a multitude of peoples. I will give this land to you and your offspring after you as an everlasting possession.' Therefore, your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came here shall be mine. Ephraim and Manasseh shall be counted as mine just like Reuben and Simeon. But any others you father after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the names of their brothers in their inheritance. For when I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel died in the land of Canaan during the journey. It was springtime, and as I was entering Ephrath, I buried her near the road to Ephrath, which is also called Bethlehem." Seeing Joseph's sons, he said to him: "Who are these?" He replied: "They are my sons, whom God gave me in this place." Joseph brought them near and said: "Bless them for me." For Israel’s eyes had grown dim from great old age and he could not see clearly. When they were brought to him, he kissed them and embraced them tightly. "Suddenly deprived of the sight of you," he said, "God has now shown me even your offspring." When Joseph had taken them from his father’s lap, he bowed low to the ground and placed Ephraim at his right hand (which was Israel’s left) and Manasseh at his left (which was his father's right); he brought them both to him. But Israel, stretching out his right hand, placed it upon the head of Ephraim, the younger brother, and his left hand upon the head of Manasseh, who was the firstborn, switching his hands. He blessed Joseph’s son and said: "May the God in whose sight my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me from my youth until this present day, the Angel who rescued me from all evils, bless these boys; and may my name be invoked upon them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth." Joseph, seeing that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, took it poorly; he tried to lift his father’s right hand from Ephraim’s head to move it to Manasseh’s. He said to his father: "It should not be so, father, for this one is the firstborn. Place your hand upon his head." But he refused and said: "I know, my son, I know. This one too shall become a people and shall be multiplied, but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall grow into nations." He blessed them at that time, saying: "In you shall Israel be blessed, and it shall be said: 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh. And he said to his son Joseph: "Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. I give to you one portion more than your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow." Then Jacob called his sons and said to them: "Gather together, so that I may tell you what will happen to you in the days to come. Gather together..."

Listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father. Reuben, my firstborn, my strength and the beginning of my sorrow; first in gifts, greatest in power. You are poured out like water—may you not grow—because you climbed into your father’s bed and defiled his couch. Simeon and Levi, brothers, vessels of warring iniquity. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my glory not be in their assembly, for in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they broke down a wall. Cursed be their fury because it is stubborn, and their indignation because it is harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies; your father’s sons shall adore you. Judah is a lion’s cub; to the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you crouched like a lion, and like a lioness; who shall rouse him? The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent <note>This refers to the "Shiloh" prophecy, often interpreted in a Messianic sense</note>, and he shall be the expectation of the nations. Tying his young donkey to the vineyard, and his she-ass, O my son, to the vine. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk. Zebulun shall dwell on the seashore, and in the station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon. Issachar is a strong donkey dwelling within the borders; he saw that rest was good and the land was excellent, and he bowed his shoulder to carry, and became a servant to tribute. Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe of Israel. Let Dan be a snake in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward. I will wait for your salvation, Lord. Gad, girded for battle, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded from behind. Asher’s bread shall be fat, and he shall provide delicacies for kings. Naphtali is a deer let loose, giving words of beauty. Joseph is a growing son, a growing son and beautiful to behold; his sons ran upon the wall, but they exasperated him and quarreled, and those with arrows envied him. His bow sat in strength, and the bands of his arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the powerful one of Jacob; from there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel. The God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you with the blessings of heaven above, with the blessings of the deep that lies below, with the blessings of the breasts and the womb. The blessings of your father are strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the eternal hills should come; let them be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the one set apart <note>original: "nazarei"</note> among his brothers. Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil. All these are the twelve tribes of Israel; and this is what their father spoke to them, and he blessed each one with their own blessings. And he commanded them, saying: "I am being gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the double cave <note>This is the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron</note> which is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a possession for a burial place. There they buried him and Sarah his wife; there Isaac was buried with Rebekah his spouse; there Leah lies buried." And when he had finished the commands by which he instructed his sons, he drew his feet onto the bed and died; and he was gathered to his people. Seeing this, Joseph fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him. And he commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father with spices. While they were fulfilling the orders, forty days passed; for this was the custom for embalmed bodies. And Egypt wept for him seventy days. When the time of mourning was finished, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh: "If I have found favor in your sight, speak in the ears of Pharaoh because my father made me swear, saying: 'Behold, I am dying; in my tomb which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, you shall bury me.' I will go up therefore to bury my father and return." And Pharaoh said to him: "Go up and bury your father as you were made to swear." When he went up, all the elders of Pharaoh’s house went with him, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, the house of Joseph with his brothers, except for the little ones and the flocks and herds which they had left in the land of Goshen. He also had in his company chariots and horsemen, and it became a great multitude. And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is situated across the Jordan, where they celebrated the funeral rites with a great and vehement mourning for seven days. When the inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw this, they said: "This is a great mourning for the Egyptians." And for that reason, they called the name of that place "The Mourning of Egypt." Therefore, the sons of Jacob did as he had commanded them, and carrying him into the land of Canaan, they buried him in the double cave, which Abraham had bought with the field for a burial possession from Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre. And Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all his company after his father was buried. When he was dead, his brothers, fearing and speaking among themselves lest he should remember the injury he suffered and return to us all the evil we did, sent word to him: "Your father commanded us before he died that we should say these words to you from him: 'I pray that you forget the crime of your brothers, and the sin and malice they practiced against you.' We also pray that you forgive all the injury of the servants of the God of your father." Hearing this, Joseph wept. And his brothers came to him, and prostrating themselves on the ground, they said: "We are your servants." To whom he replied: "Do not fear. Can we resist the will of God? You thought evil against me, and God turned it into good so that he might exalt me as you see at present, and save many people. Do not fear; I will feed you and your little ones." And he comforted them and spoke kindly and gently. And he lived in Egypt with all his father’s house. And he lived one hundred and ten years, and he saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation; the sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were also born on Joseph’s knees. To whom he spoke thus: "After my death, God will visit you, and will make you go up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." And when he had made them swear, saying: "God will visit you; carry my bones with you from this place," he died, having completed one hundred and ten years of his life; and being embalmed with spices, he was laid in a coffin in Egypt. THE END OF GENESIS.

When they were summoned to him, the king said: "What is this that you have chosen to do, that you would save the boys?" They replied: "The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation. Go and gather the elders of Israel, and you shall say to them: 'The Lord God of your fathers has appeared to me, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, saying: Visiting, I have visited you: and I have seen all that has happened to you in Egypt. And I said that I would lead you out of the affliction of Egypt into the land of the Canaanite, and the Hittite, and the Amorite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite, to a land flowing with milk and honey.' And they shall hear your voice.

And you and the elders of Israel shall enter to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: 'The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us. We will go a three days' journey into the wilderness, to sacrifice to the Lord our God.' But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, except by a mighty hand. For I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders which I shall do in the midst of them. After these things he will let you go. And I will give grace to this people before the Egyptians, so that when you depart, you shall not go empty. But every woman shall ask of her neighbor and of her hostess for vessels of silver and gold, and clothing; and you shall put them upon your sons and your daughters, and you shall spoil Egypt." Moses answered and said: "They will not believe me, nor hear my voice. But they will say: 'The Lord has not appeared to you.'" Therefore He said to him: "What is that which you hold in your hand?" He answered: "A staff." The Lord said: "Cast it on the ground." He cast it, and it was turned into a serpent, so that Moses fled from it. And the Lord said: "Stretch out your hand and take it by the tail." He stretched it out and held it, and it was turned into a staff. "That they may believe," He said, "that the Lord God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you." And the Lord said again: "Put your hand into your bosom." And when he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out leprous, like snow. "Draw back your hand," He said, "into your bosom." He drew it back, and brought it out again, and it was like his other flesh. "If they will not believe you," He said, "nor hear the voice of the first sign, they will believe the word of the following sign. But if they will not believe even these two signs, nor hear your voice, take water of the river and pour it upon the dry land: and whatever you draw from the river shall be turned into blood." Moses said: "I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday or the day before; and since you have spoken to your servant, I have a more impeded and slower tongue." <margin>Who made the mouth of man?</margin> The Lord said to him: "Who made the mouth of man? Or who fabricated the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I? Go therefore, and I will be in your mouth: and I will teach you what you shall speak." But he said: "I beseech you, Lord, send whom you are going to send." And the Lord, being angry at Moses, said:

<margin>Aaron the brother</margin> "Is not Aaron your brother the Levite? I know that he is eloquent. Behold, he himself comes out to meet you, and seeing you, he will be glad in his heart. Speak to him, and put my words in his mouth: and I will be in your mouth and in his mouth, and I will show you what you ought to do. He shall speak for you to the people, and shall be your mouth; but you shall be to him in those things that pertain to God. Take also this staff in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs."

<margin>Moses departed</margin> And the Lord said to Moses in Midian: "Go and return to Egypt, for all those are dead who sought your life." Moses therefore took his wife and his sons, and set them upon a donkey, and returned to Egypt, carrying the staff of God in his hand. The Lord said to him: "When you have returned to Egypt, see that you perform all the wonders which I have put in your hand before Pharaoh. I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go. And you shall say to him: 'Thus <margin>Behold, I will kill</margin> says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Let my son go, that he may serve me; and you would not let him go. Behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'" And when he was on his journey in an inn, the Lord met him and sought to kill him. Immediately, Zipporah took a very sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son, and touched his feet, and said: "A spouse of blood you are to me." <note>This "spouse of blood" incident is an ancient and mysterious passage; it appears Zipporah's action saves Moses from divine wrath.</note> And He let him go after she had said "a spouse of blood" because of the circumcision. Now the Lord said to Aaron: "Go to meet Moses in the desert." And he went to meet him at the mountain of God, and kissed him. And Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord by which He had sent him, and the signs He had commanded. And they went together and gathered all the elders of the children of Israel. And Aaron spoke all the words which the Lord had said to Moses: and he performed the signs before the people, and the people believed. And they heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel and that He had looked upon their affliction: and they bowed down and adored. After these things, Moses and Aaron entered and said to Pharaoh: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the desert." But he answered: "Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." But they said: "The God of the Hebrews has called us, that we may go a three days' journey into the wilderness, to sacrifice to the Lord our God, lest perhaps pestilence or the sword happen to us." The king of Egypt said to them: "Why, Moses and Aaron, do you distract the people from their works? Go to your burdens." Pharaoh also said: "The people of the land are many. You see that the crowd has increased; how much more if you give them rest from their works?" Therefore he commanded on that day the overseers of the works and the taskmasters of the people, saying: "You shall no longer give

<column-break/>

straw [to make bricks]; they must remain as they were before, and you shall not diminish anything from the measure of bricks which they previously gave: for they are idle, and therefore they cry out, saying: 'Let us go and sacrifice to our God.' Let them be overwhelmed with works, and let them fulfill them, so that they do not yield to lying words." The overseers of the works and the taskmasters therefore went out and spoke to the people: "Thus says Pharaoh: I do not give you straw; <margin>Go yourselves</margin> go yourselves and collect it wherever you can find it; yet nothing shall be diminished of your work." And the people were dispersed through all the land of Egypt to collect straw. And the taskmasters urged them, saying: "Complete your work daily, as you were accustomed to do before when straw was given to you." And those who were over the people of Israel were beaten by Pharaoh’s taskmasters, saying: "Why have you not fulfilled the measure of bricks, as yesterday?" And the leaders of the children of Israel came and cried out to Pharaoh, saying: "Why do you act thus against your servants? Straw is not given to us, and yet bricks are demanded of us. But we your servants are beaten with lashes, and your people are unjustly accused." He said: "You are idle and lazy, and therefore you say: 'Let us go and sacrifice to our God.' Go therefore and work: straw shall not be given to you, and you shall return the usual number of bricks." And the leaders of the children of Israel saw themselves in a bad state, because it was said: "Nothing shall be diminished of the bricks for each day." And they met Moses and Aaron, who stood opposite them as they came out from Pharaoh, and they said to them: "May the Lord see and judge, for you have made our odor to stink before Pharaoh and his servants, and you have provided him a sword to kill us." And Moses returned to the Lord and said: "Lord, why have you afflicted this people? Why did you send me? For since the time that I entered to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has afflicted this people, and you have not delivered them."

Then the Lord said to Moses: "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh: for by a mighty hand he shall let them go, and with a strong hand he shall cast them out of his land." And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: <margin>Then the Lord</margin> "I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty: and my name ADONAI <note>original: "Adonay." A Hebrew name for God, substituted here for the Tetragrammaton.</note> I did not make known to them. And I established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their pilgrimage, in which they were strangers. I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel, with which the Egyptians have oppressed them: and I have remembered my covenant. Therefore say to the children of Israel: I am the Lord who will lead you out from the workhouse of the Egyptians, and will deliver you from servitude, and will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments. <margin>The Lord who</margin> And I will take you to myself for a people, and I will be your God: and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who led you out from the workhouse of the Egyptians, and led you into the land over which I lifted up my hand, to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: and I will give it to you to possess. I am the Lord." Moses therefore told all these things to the children of Israel. <margin>This is Aaron</margin>

Because the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt.
The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "I am the Lord. Speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, all that I speak to you." And Moses said before the Lord: "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips; how will Pharaoh hear me?" <margin>Because he spoke</margin>

And the Lord said to Moses: "Behold, I have appointed you as the god of Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak to him all that I command you, and he shall speak to Pharaoh, so that he may let the children of Israel go out of his land. But I will harden his heart, and I will multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt. And he will not hear you; and I will lay my hand upon Egypt, and lead out my army, my people the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt by very great judgments. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, who stretched out my hand over Egypt, and led the children of Israel out from the midst of them." Moses and Aaron did just as the Lord had commanded; so they did. Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh. <margin>Behold, I appointed</margin> And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: "Take your staff and cast it before Pharaoh, and it shall be turned into a serpent." So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and did as the Lord had commanded. Aaron took the staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it was turned into a serpent. But Pharaoh called the wise men and the sorcerers: and they also, by Egyptian incantations and certain secrets, did in like manner. And they each cast down their staffs, which were turned into dragons. But Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs. And Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not hear them, just as the Lord had commanded. Then the Lord said to Moses: "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he will not let the people go. Go to him in the morning; behold, he will go out to the waters; and you shall stand to meet him upon the bank of the river: and the staff which was turned into a dragon, you shall take in your hand. And you shall say to him: 'The Lord God of the Hebrews has sent me to you, saying: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the desert. And until now you would not hear.' Thus therefore says the Lord: 'In this you shall know that I am the Lord. Behold, I will strike the water of the river with the staff that is in my hand, and it shall be turned into blood. And the fish that are in the river shall die, and the waters shall rot, and the Egyptians shall be afflicted drinking the water of the river.'" And the Lord said to Moses: "Say to Aaron: 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, and over their rivers, and over the streams and marshes, and all the pools of water, that they may be turned into blood: and let there be blood in all the land of Egypt, as well in vessels of wood as of stone.'" And Moses and Aaron did so, as the Lord had commanded. And lifting up the staff, he struck the water of the river before Pharaoh and his servants: and it was turned into blood.

<summary>This page covers the pivotal calling of Moses at the burning bush, the revelation of the Divine Name, and the initial confrontation with Pharaoh which results in increased hardship for the Israelites. It concludes with the first of the ten plagues, where the Nile is turned into blood, and includes a genealogy of the tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the account of the Israelites' exodus from Egypt. The previous page ended with God calling Moses from the burning bush to lead the people out of bondage; this page recounts their journey through the wilderness, the miracle of the manna, the battle with Amalek, and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai.</meta>

<margin>Exodus</margin> **T**hey came into Elim where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters. Setting out from Elim, the whole multitude of the children of Israel came into the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt. And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. They said to them: "Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over the meat-pots and ate bread to our fill. Why have you led us out into the desert, to kill this whole multitude with hunger?"

<margin>Moses & Aaron</margin> **T**he Lord said to Moses: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you. Let the people go out and gather what is sufficient for each day, so that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. But on the sixth day, let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather each day." And Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel: "In the evening, you shall know that the Lord has led you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see His glory. For He has heard your murmuring against the Lord. But what are we, that you mutter against us?" And Moses said: "The Lord will give you meat to eat in the evening, and bread to your fill in the morning, because He has heard your murmurings with which you have murmured against Him. For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord." Then Moses said to Aaron: "Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: Approach before the Lord, for He has heard your outcry." And while Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "I have heard the murmuring of the children of Israel. Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God." And so it happened in the evening that quails came up and covered the camp. In the morning, a dew lay all around the camp. And when it had covered the surface of the earth, there appeared in the wilderness something small and as if pounded by a pestle, like hoarfrost upon the earth. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another: **M**anhu? <note>original: "Manhu?"</note> which means, "What is this?" For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them: "This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat. This is the word which the Lord has commanded: Let everyone gather as much as is sufficient to eat, a gomer <term>gomer: an ancient Hebrew unit of dry measure, roughly equivalent to 2 liters</term> for every head, according to the number of your souls that dwell in the tabernacle, so shall you take it." And the children of Israel did so, and they gathered, some more, some less. And they measured it by the measure of a gomer; he who gathered more did not have extra, nor did he who prepared less find less, but each gathered according to what they were able to eat. Moses said to them: "Let no one leave any of it until morning." They did not listen to him, but some of them left it until morning, and it began to swarm with worms and it rotted. And Moses was angry with them. They gathered it every morning, as much as was sufficient for food; and when the sun grew hot, it melted. But on the sixth day they gathered double the food, that is, two gomers for every person. And all the leaders of the multitude came and told Moses. He said to them: "This is what the Lord has spoken: Tomorrow is the rest of the Sabbath, sanctified to the Lord. Whatever you wish to cook, cook it; and whatever is left over, lay aside until morning." And they did as Moses had commanded, and it did not rot, nor was any worm found in it. Moses said: "Eat it today, because it is the Sabbath of the Lord; it will not be found today in the field. Gather it for six days; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord, therefore it shall not be found."

<margin>Rephidim</margin> **T**he whole congregation of the children of Israel, having set out from the desert of Sin by their stages, according to the word of the Lord, camped in Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. Quarreling against Moses, they said: "Give us water that we may drink." Moses responded: "Why do you quarrel against me? Why do you test the Lord?" So the people thirsted there for lack of water, and murmured against Moses, saying: "Why did you make us leave Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?" Moses cried out to the Lord, saying: "What shall I do with this people? A little more and they will stone me." And the Lord said to Moses: "Go before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel; and take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there upon the rock of Horeb; you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, so that the people may drink." Moses did so before the elders of Israel. And he called the name of that place "Temptation" <note>original: "temptatio," referring to Massah</note> because of the quarrel of the children of Israel, and because they tested the Lord, saying: "Is the Lord among us or not?" <margin>Amalek</margin> Then Amalek came and fought against Israel in Rephidim. Moses said <margin>Joshua</margin> to Joshua: "Choose men, and go out and fight against Amalek; tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill, having the rod of God in my hand." Joshua did as Moses had spoken, and he fought against Amalek. But Moses, Aaron, and Hur ascended to the top of the hill. And when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel prevailed; but if he lowered them a little, Amalek overcame. But Moses' hands became heavy. Therefore, taking a stone, they put it under him, and he sat upon it. Aaron and Hur sustained his hands on both sides. And it came to pass that his hands did not grow weary until the setting of the sun, and Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword. **M**oses prayed to the Lord, and wrote it for a memorial in a book, and delivered it to the ears of Joshua: "For I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." And Moses built an altar and called its name "The Lord is my exaltation" <note>original: "Dominus exaltatio mea," translating the Hebrew Yahweh-Nissi</note>, saying: "Because the hand of the Lord alone and the war of the Lord will be against Amalek from generation to generation."

<margin>Midian</margin> **A**nd when Jethro, the priest of Midian, the kinsman <note>original: "cognatus," meaning kinsman or specifically father-in-law</note> of Moses, heard all that God had done for Moses and for Israel His people, because the Lord had led Israel out of Egypt, he took Zipporah, the wife of Moses whom he had sent back, and her two sons—one of whom was named Gershom, for his father said, "I have been a stranger in a foreign land," and the other Eliezer, "for the God of my father is my helper and has delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh." And Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the desert where he was camped near the mountain of God. And he sent word to Moses, saying: "I, your kinsman Jethro, am coming to you, and your wife and your two sons with her." Moses went out to meet his kinsman, and bowed down and kissed him; and they greeted each other with words of peace. When he had entered the tabernacle, Moses told his kinsman all that the Lord had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel's sake, and all the labor

<column-break/>

which had befallen them on the journey, and how the Lord had delivered them. Jethro rejoiced over all the good things that the Lord had done for Israel, because He had delivered them from the hand of the Egyptians. And he said: "Blessed be the Lord who has delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh, who has rescued His people from the hand of Egypt. Now I know that the Lord is great above all gods, because they acted proudly against them." Then Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, offered burnt offerings and sacrifices to God; and Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with him before God.

**O**n the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, who stood by Moses from morning until evening. When his kinsman saw this—namely, all that he did for the people—he said: "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people wait from morning until evening?" Moses answered him: "The people come to me seeking the judgment of God. And when any dispute happens to them, they come to me so that I may judge between them and show them the precepts of God and His laws." But he said: "The thing you are doing is not good. You are consuming yourself with foolish labor, both you and this people who are with you; the business is beyond your strength; you cannot sustain it alone. But hear my words and advice, and the Lord will be with you. Be a representative for the people in those things that pertain to God, so that you may report what is said to Him. Show the people the ceremonies and the ritual of worship, and the way in which they ought to walk, and the work they must do. Moreover, provide from all the people powerful men who fear the Lord, in whom there is truth and who hate avarice; and appoint from them captains of thousands, and captains of hundreds, and captains of fifties, and captains of tens, who shall judge the people at all times. Whatever is a major matter, let them report to you, but let them judge only the minor matters. It will be lighter for you, the burden being divided among others. If you do this, you will fulfill the command of God and be able to endure His precepts, and all this people shall return to their places in peace." Having heard this, Moses did all that he had suggested; and having chosen strenuous men from all Israel, he appointed them as leaders of the people: captains of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, who judged the people at all times. Whatever was grave they reported to him, judging only the easier things. And he dismissed his kinsman, who returned to his own land.

<margin>.xxx.</margin> **I**n the third month of Israel's departure from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. For having set out from Rephidim and arriving at the desert of Sinai, they camped there; and there Israel pitched their tents opposite the mountain. But Moses ascended to God. And the Lord called him from the mountain and said: "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and announce to the children of Israel: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, how I carried you on eagles' wings and took you to myself. If, therefore, you will hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my own possession among all peoples. For all the earth is mine. And you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. These are the words you shall speak to the children of Israel." Moses came and, having called together the elders, he set before them all the words which the Lord had commanded. And all the people responded with one voice: "All that the Lord has spoken, we will do." When Moses had reported the words of the people to the Lord, the Lord said to him: "Behold, I will now come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you, and may believe you forever." Moses then reported the words of the people to the Lord. And He said to him: "Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their clothes and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend before all the people upon Mount Sinai. You shall set boundaries for the people all around, and say to them: Take care that you do not ascend the mountain, nor touch its edges. Everyone who touches the mountain shall die the death. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be overwhelmed with stones or pierced with arrows; whether it be beast or man, he shall not live. When the trumpet begins to sound, then let them ascend the mountain." Moses descended from the mountain to the people and sanctified them. And when they had washed their clothes, he said to them: "Be ready for the third day; do not approach your wives."

**A**nd now the third day had come, and the morning had grown bright; and behold, thunders began to be heard and lightnings to flash, and a very thick cloud to cover the mountain, and the blare of the trumpet sounded very loudly. The people who were in the camp feared. And when Moses had led them out from the place of the camp to meet God, they stood at the foot of the mountain. All of Mount Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire; and the smoke ascended from it as if from a furnace, and the whole mountain was terrible. And the sound of the trumpet grew louder little by little and was drawn out longer. Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him. The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, on the very top of the mountain, and called Moses to its summit. When he had ascended, He said to him: "Go down and charge the people, lest they wish to pass the boundaries to see the Lord, and a great multitude of them perish. Let the priests also, who approach the Lord, be sanctified, lest He strike them." Moses said to the Lord: "The common people will not be able to ascend Mount Sinai. For you have testified and commanded, saying: Set boundaries around the mountain and sanctify it." The Lord said to him: **G**o, descend; and you shall ascend, and Aaron with you. But let not the priests and the people pass the boundaries nor ascend to the Lord, lest He perhaps kill them. So Moses descended to the people and told them everything.

<margin>9.</margin> **T**he Lord spoke all these words: **I** am the Lord your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall not have foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image nor any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth below, or that is in the waters under the earth; you shall not adore them nor worship them. I am the Lord your God, mighty and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. For the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes the name of the Lord his God for a useless thing. Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do all your works. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it: you, and your son, and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, your beast of burden, and the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea, and all things that are in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it. Honor your father and your mother, so that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God will give you. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not commit theft. You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor's house, nor shall you desire his wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is his. **A**ll the people saw the voices <note>original: "voces," here meaning the thunder</note> and the lamps <note>original: "lampades," here meaning the flashes of lightning</note> and the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain; and being terrified and struck with fear, they stood far off, saying to Moses: "Speak you to us, and we will hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die." And Moses said to the people: "Do not fear; for God came to test you, so that His terror might be in you and you would not sin." And the people stood far off. But Moses approached the darkness in which God was.

**F**urthermore, the Lord said to Moses: "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves. You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall offer upon it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen, in every place where the memory of my name shall be. I will come to you and bless you. But if you make a stone altar for me, you shall not build it of hewn stones; for if...
