<meta>This page continues from the narrative of the Israelites' journey through the wilderness. Having arrived at Mount Sinai, the text transitions from the story of their travels to the specific judicial and moral laws delivered by God to Moses, followed by the ratification of the covenant and instructions for building the Tabernacle.</meta>

<margin>Chapter 40</margin>
**T**hese are the judgments which you shall set before them. If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve for six years; in the seventh year, he shall go out free for nothing. With whatever garment he entered, with such he shall depart. If he has a wife, his wife shall go out with him. But if his master gave him a wife and she bore him sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, but he himself shall go out with his own clothing. But if the servant should say, "I love my master and my wife and children; I will not go out free," his master shall bring him to the gods <note>In this context, "gods" refers to the judges or magistrates acting with divine authority.</note> and he shall be brought to the door and the doorposts; he shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be his servant forever. If anyone sells his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as female slaves are accustomed to do. If she displeases the eyes of her master to whom she was delivered, he shall let her go. He shall not have the power to sell her to a foreign people if he has rejected her. But if he betroths her to his son, he shall deal with her according to the custom of daughters. If he takes another wife for him, he shall provide for the girl's marriage, clothing, and shall not deny the price of her modesty <note>Original: "pretium pudicitie," referring to her conjugal rights.</note>. If he does not do these three things, she shall go out free without money. He who strikes a man intending to kill him, let him die the death. But he who did not lie in wait, but God delivered him into his hand, I will appoint for you a place to which he ought to flee. If anyone kills his neighbor by design and by treachery, you shall pluck him from my altar so that he may die. He who strikes his father and mother, let him die the death. He who curses his father or mother, let him die the death. If men quarrel and one strikes another with a stone or a fist and he does not die but lies in his bed, if he rises and walks outside upon his staff, the one who struck him shall be innocent, provided that he restores his lost work and his expenses for doctors. He who strikes his servant or maid with a rod and they die in his hands, he shall be guilty of a crime. But if the person survives for one or two days, he shall not be subject to punishment, because they are his money. If men quarrel and someone strikes a pregnant woman and she miscarries, but she herself lives, he shall be subject to a fine as much as the woman's husband demands and the judges determine. But if death follows her, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise. If anyone strikes the eye of his servant or maid and makes them one-eyed, he shall let them go free for the eye he plucked out. If he also knocks out a tooth of his servant or maid, he shall likewise let them go free. If an ox strikes a man or woman with its horn and they die, it shall be overwhelmed with stones and its flesh shall not be eaten, and the owner of the ox shall be innocent. But if the ox was a gorer from yesterday and the day before, and they warned its owner, and he did not shut it up, and it kills a man or woman, the ox shall be overwhelmed with stones and they shall kill its owner. But if a price is imposed on him, he shall give for his life whatever is demanded. If it strikes a son or daughter with its horn, he shall be subject to a similar sentence. If it strikes a servant or maid, he shall give thirty shekels of silver to the master, and the ox shall be overwhelmed with stones. If anyone opens a cistern and digs it and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall restore the price of the beasts, but that which is dead shall be his. If one man's ox wounds another's ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price, and they shall divide the carcass of the dead one between them in proportion. But if he knew that the ox was a gorer from yesterday and the day before and its owner did not guard it, he shall restore ox for ox and shall receive the whole carcass. If anyone steals an ox or a sheep and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep. If a thief is found breaking into a house or digging under it and is killed by a wound, the striker shall not be guilty of blood. But if he does this after the sun has risen, he has committed homicide and he himself shall die. If he does not have what he may restore for the theft, he himself shall be sold. If that which was stolen is found alive with him, whether ox, donkey, or sheep, he shall restore double. If anyone damages a field or vineyard and lets his beast loose to graze on another's property, he shall restore the best of whatever he has in his own field or vineyard according to the estimation of the damage. If fire spreads and catches thorns and heaps of grain are consumed, or standing crops in the fields, he who kindled the fire shall restore the damage. If anyone entrusts money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping and they are stolen from the one who received them, if the thief is found, he shall restore double. If the thief is hidden, the master of the house shall be brought to the gods and shall swear that he did not extend his hand toward his neighbor’s property to commit fraud, whether in ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, or whatever can cause loss. The cause of both shall come before the gods, and if they judge him guilty, he shall restore double to his neighbor. If anyone entrusts to his neighbor an ox, donkey, sheep, or any beast for safekeeping and it dies, or is weakened, or captured by enemies, and no one saw it, an oath shall be between them that he did not extend his hand toward his neighbor’s property; the owner shall accept the oath, and the other shall not be compelled to restore it. But if it was taken by theft, he shall restore the damage to the owner. If it was eaten by a beast, let him bring that which was killed to him, and he shall not restore it. If anyone asks for a loan from his neighbor and it is weakened or dies while the owner is not present, he shall be compelled to restore it. But if the owner was present, he shall not restore it, especially if it had come hired for the price of its work. If a man seduces a virgin not yet betrothed and sleeps with her, he shall endow her and have her as his wife. If the father of the virgin is unwilling to give her, he shall restore money according to the measure of the dowry which virgins are accustomed to receive. You shall not permit sorcerers <note>Original: "maleficos," often translated as witches or practitioners of harmful magic.</note> to live. He who copulates with a beast, let him die the death. He who sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone. You shall not sadden a stranger nor afflict him, for you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt. You shall not harm the widow and the orphan. If you hurt them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry, and my fury will be kindled, and I will strike you with the sword, and your wives shall be widows and your children orphans. If you give a loan of money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not urge them like an extortioner, nor shall you oppress them with usury. If you take a garment from your neighbor as a pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun sets. For that is the only thing by which he is covered, the clothing of his flesh, nor does he have anything else in which to sleep. If he cries out to me, I will hear him, because I am merciful. You shall not disparage the gods <note>Meaning the judges or rulers.</note>, nor shall you curse the prince of your people. You shall not delay to offer your tithes and your firstfruits. You shall give the firstborn of your sons to me. You shall do similarly with your oxen and sheep. For seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day, you shall return it to me. You shall be holy men to me. You shall not eat meat that has been pre-tasted by beasts, but throw it to the dogs. You shall not accept a false report, nor join your hand to speak false testimony for the wicked. You shall not follow the crowd in doing evil, nor shall you agree with the sentence of the majority in judgment so as to deviate from the truth. You shall not even pity a poor man in a legal matter <note>This instructs the judge to be impartial, not favoring the poor out of misplaced pity.</note>. If you happen upon your enemy’s ox or wandering donkey, lead it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him. You shall not turn aside in the judgment of the poor; you shall flee from a lie. You shall not kill the innocent and the just, because I turn away from the wicked; nor shall you accept gifts which blind even the wise and subvert the words of the just. You shall not be troublesome to a pilgrim. For you know the souls of strangers, because you yourselves were pilgrims in the land of Egypt. For six years you shall sow your land and gather its fruits, but in the

<column-break/>

seventh year you shall let it be and make it rest, so that the poor of your people may eat, and whatever is left over, the beasts of the field may eat. So you shall do in your vineyard and in your olive grove. For six days you shall work; on the seventh day you shall cease, so that your ox and donkey may rest, and the son of your maidservant and the stranger may be refreshed. Keep all the things I have said to you. You shall not swear by the name of foreign gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth. Three times each year you shall celebrate festivals. You shall keep the feast of unleavened bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new things, when you went out from Egypt. You shall not appear in my sight empty-handed. And the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits of your work, whatever you have sown in the field; also the feast at the end of the year, when you have gathered all your crops from the field. Three times a year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God. You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim upon leaven, nor shall the fat of my feast remain until morning. You shall bring the firstfruits of the crops of your land into the house of the Lord your God, nor shall you boil a kid in its mother’s milk.

**T**he Lord had also said to Moses: "Come up to the Lord, you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel, and you shall adore from afar. Moses alone shall come up to the Lord, and they shall not approach, nor shall the people come up with him." Moses therefore came and set forth to the people all the words of the Lord and the judgments. And all the people answered with one voice: "All the words of the Lord which He has spoken, we will do." Moses then wrote down all the speeches of the Lord, and rising early, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. And he sent young men from the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of bulls to the Lord. And so Moses took half the blood and put it in bowls, and the remaining part he poured upon the altar. And taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people. They said: "All things that the Lord has spoken, we will do, and we will be obedient." He indeed took the blood and sprinkled it on the people and said: "This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words." And Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up. And they saw the God of Israel. Under His feet was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear. Nor did He lay His hand upon those of the sons of Israel who had withdrawn far off. And they saw God, and they ate and drank.

**A**nd the Lord said to Moses: "Come up to me on the mountain and be there; and I will give you stone tablets and the law and the commandments which I have written, so that you may teach them." Moses arose, and Joshua his minister, and going up into the mountain of God, he said to the elders: "Wait here until we return to you. You have Aaron and Hur with you; if any question arises, you shall refer it to them." And when Moses had gone up, a cloud covered the mountain, and the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it with a cloud for six days. On the seventh day, He called him from the midst of the darkness. Furthermore, the appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the peak of the mountain in the sight of the children of Israel. And Moses, entering into the midst of the cloud, went up onto the mountain; and he was there for forty days and forty nights.

**T**he Lord also spoke to Moses, saying: "Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take firstfruits for me. From every man who offers willingly, you shall receive them. These are the things you ought to receive: gold, silver, and bronze; blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet; fine linen, goats' hair, and rams' skins dyed red, and violet-colored skins <note>Original: "pelles ianthinas," likely referring to skins of sea cows or fine leathers dyed violet.</note>, and acacia wood <note>Original: "ligna setthim."</note>; oil for preparing lights, spices for ointment, and sweet-smelling incense; onyx stones and gems for adorning the ephod and the breastplate. And they shall make a sanctuary for me, and I will dwell in the midst of them. According to the whole likeness of the tabernacle which I will show you, and of all the vessels for its worship, so you shall make it. Construct an Ark of acacia wood, the length of which shall have two and a half cubits, the breadth a cubit and a half, and the height likewise a cubit and a half. And you shall overlay it with the purest gold inside and out, and you shall make a golden crown around it. Also four golden rings, which you shall place at the four corners of the Ark: two rings on one side and two on the other. You shall also make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, and you shall lead them through the rings which are on the sides of the Ark, so that it may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings, nor shall they ever be drawn out of them. And you shall put into the Ark the testimony which I will give you. You shall also make a mercy seat <note>Original: "propitiatorium," the lid of the Ark where atonement was made.</note> of the purest gold; its length shall hold two and a half cubits, and its breadth a cubit and a half. You shall also make two golden cherubim, hammered out, on both sides of the oracle. Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other. Let them cover both sides of the mercy seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle, and they shall look at each other with their faces toward the mercy seat with which the Ark is to be covered, in which you shall put the testimony that I will give you. From there I will command you, and I will speak to you from above the mercy seat and from the middle of the two cherubim who shall be over the Ark of the testimony, all the things which I will command through you to the children of Israel. You shall also make a table of acacia wood, having two cubits in length, a cubit in width and a half, and a cubit and a half in height. And you shall overlay it with the purest gold, and make a golden lip around it, and for the lip itself a carved crown four fingers high, and over that another golden crown. You shall also prepare four golden rings and put them in the four corners of the same table at each foot. The rings shall be above the crown, so that poles may be put through them and the table can be carried. You shall make the poles themselves of acacia wood and surround them with gold for carrying the table. You shall also prepare dishes, bowls, censers, and cups in which the drink offerings are to be offered, of the purest gold. And you shall place the bread of the presence <note>Original: "panes propositionis," literally "bread of the setting forth."</note> upon the table in my sight always.

<margin>the tabernacle</margin>
**H**e also made the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twisted linen, and of violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet. They were woven with embroidered work and great variety. Each curtain had a length of twenty-eight cubits and a width of four cubits. All the curtains were of one measure. And he joined five curtains to one another, and the other five he coupled together in the same way. He also made violet loops on the edge of the first curtain on its side, and similarly on the edge of the second curtain, so that the loops might meet each other and be coupled together. He also made fifty gold clasps which would catch the loops of the curtains, so that it might become one tabernacle.

<margin>Curtains</margin>
**H**e also made eleven coverings <note>Original: "saga," referring to tent cloths made of hair.</note> of goats' hair to cover the roof of the tabernacle. One covering had a length of thirty cubits and a width of four cubits. All the coverings were of one measure. He joined five of them by themselves and the other six by themselves. And he made fifty loops on the edge of one covering and fifty on the edge of the other, so they might be joined together. And he made fifty bronze buckles with which the roof might be knit together, so that it would become one tabernacle. He also made a cover for the tabernacle of ram skins dyed red, and another covering above that of violet-colored skins <note>Original: "ianthinus," likely referring to the skins of the dugong or "tahash" mentioned in Hebrew, often translated as badger or violet skins.</note>.

<margin>boards</margin>
**H**e also made the boards for the tabernacle of standing acacia wood <note>Original: "lignis sethim," referring to the durable wood of the Shittah tree.</note>. The length of each was ten cubits and the width was one and a half cubits. There were two tenons in each board so that one might be joined to the other. Thus he did for all the boards of the tabernacle. Twenty of these were for the southern side, with forty silver bases. Two bases were placed under one board on both sides of the corners where the joints of the sides end at the corners. For the second side of the tabernacle, which faces the north, he made twenty boards with forty silver bases: two bases for each board. For the western side, he made six boards, and two other boards for the corners of the tabernacle at the back, which were joined from bottom to top and held in a single binding. Thus he did on both sides in the corners. So there were eight boards in total, and they had sixteen silver bases, specifically two bases under each board.

<margin>bars</margin>
**H**e also made bars of acacia wood: five to hold together the boards of one side of the tabernacle, and five others for the boards of the other side. Besides these, he made five other bars for the western side of the tabernacle toward the sea. He made the middle bar to pass through the boards from one end to the other. He overlaid the boards themselves with gold, and made their rings of gold through which the bars could be passed. These bars he also covered with gold plates.

<margin>veil</margin>
**H**e also made a veil of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen, varied and distinguished with embroidered work. And he made four columns of acacia wood, which he overlaid with gold along with their tops, casting silver bases for them.

<margin>screen</margin>
**H**e also made a screen for the entrance of the tabernacle of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen, with embroidered work. And he made five columns with their capitals, which he covered with gold, and he cast bronze bases for them.

<margin>the ark</margin>
**H**e also made the ark of acacia wood, having two and a half cubits in length, and one and a half cubits in width; the height was also one and a half cubits. And he clothed it with the purest gold inside and out. He made a golden crown for it all around. And he cast four gold rings for the four corners of the ark: two on one side and two on the other. He also made poles of acacia wood which he clothed with gold. And he put them into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry it.

<margin>the mercy seat</margin>
**H**e also made the mercy seat <note>Original: "propitiatorium," also called the "oracle." This was the gold lid of the Ark.</note> of the purest gold. It was two and a half cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. He also made two cherubim of hammered gold, which he placed on both sides of the mercy seat. One cherub was on the top of one side, and the other cherub on the top of the other side. They extended their wings and overshadowed the mercy seat, looking toward each other and toward the seat.

<margin>the table</margin>
**H**e also made the table of acacia wood, two cubits in length and one cubit in width, which had a height of one and a half cubits. He surrounded it with the purest gold and made a golden lip around it. For the lip itself, he made a carved crown four fingers high, and above that another golden crown. He cast four gold rings, which he placed at the four corners of the table at each foot against the crown. He put poles into them so the table could be carried. These poles he also made of acacia wood and surrounded them with gold. And he made the vessels for the various uses of the table: dishes, bowls, cups, and censers of the purest gold in which the drink offerings are to be offered.

<margin>the lampstand</margin>
**H**e also made the lampstand of hammered pure gold. From its shaft proceeded branches, cups, spheres, and lilies. Six on each side: three branches from one part and three from the other. There were three cups in the shape of almonds on each branch, along with spheres and lilies. And on the lampstand itself were four cups in the shape of almonds, with spheres and lilies for each. There were spheres under every two branches in three places, which together make six branches proceeding from one shaft. He also made seven lamps with their snuffers and the vessels where the snuffs are extinguished, all of the purest gold.

<margin>altar of incense</margin>
**H**e also made the altar of incense of acacia wood, being one cubit square and two cubits high. From its corners proceeded horns. He clothed it with the purest gold, along with its grating, walls, and horns. He made a golden crown for it all around, and two gold rings under the crown on each side, so that poles could be put into them and the altar could be carried. He made the poles of acacia wood and covered them with gold plates. He also composed the oil for the anointing of sanctification and the incense of the purest spices, the work of a perfumer.

<margin>altar of burnt offering</margin>
**H**e also made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood: five cubits square and three cubits in height. Its horns proceeded from the corners, and he covered it with bronze plates. He made various bronze vessels for its use: pots, tongs, flesh-hooks, hooks, and fire pans. He made its grating like a net of bronze, and under it, in the middle of the altar, a hearth. He cast four rings at the ends of the grating to receive the poles for carrying. These poles he also made of acacia wood and covered them with bronze plates. He put them into the rings that protruded from the sides of the altar. The altar itself was not solid, but hollow, made of boards and empty inside.

<margin>basin</margin>
**H**e also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle.

<margin>the court</margin>
**H**e also made the court: on its southern side were curtains of fine twisted linen, a hundred cubits long. There were twenty bronze columns with their bases. The capitals of the columns and all the carvings were of silver. Likewise on the northern side, the curtains, columns, bases, and capitals were of the same measure, craftsmanship, and metal. On the western side, there were curtains of fifty cubits. There were ten columns with their bronze bases. And the capitals of the columns and all the carving were silver. Furthermore, in the east, he prepared curtains of fifty cubits. On one side there were fifteen cubits of curtains and three columns with their bases. And on the other part—because between the two he made the entrance to the tabernacle—there were likewise curtains of fifteen cubits, three columns, and as many bases. All the curtains of the court were woven of fine twisted linen. The bases of the columns were bronze. Their capitals and all their carving were silver. But he also overlaid the columns of the court with gold. The screen at the entrance of the court he wove with embroidered work of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen. It was twenty cubits in length, but the height was five cubits, according to the measure that all the curtains of the court had. The columns at the entrance were four with bronze bases, and their capitals and carvings were silver. He also made the pegs of the tabernacle and the court all around of bronze.

In the first row was a sardius stone, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper. In the third, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. **T**his is the measurement of the tabernacle of the testimony, which was numbered according to the precept of Moses for the ceremonies of the Levites by the hand of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. Which Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, had completed, as the Lord commanded through Moses. Joined with him was his companion Ooliab <note>Commonly known as Aholiab.</note>, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, who was himself a distinguished craftsman in wood, a weaver, and an embroiderer in violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. All the gold that was spent in the work of the sanctuary, and which was offered in gifts, was twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels <note>Original: "siclorum."</note>, according to the measure of the sanctuary. The silver, however, from the numbered multitude of the people, was collected in a hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels, according to the measure of the sanctuary. A beka for each head, that is, half a shekel, according to the measure of the sanctuary. For all those who were numbered from twenty years and upward, from six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men of arms. There were besides a hundred talents of silver, from which the bases of the sanctuary and the entrance where the veil hangs were cast. A hundred bases were made from a hundred talents, calculating one talent for each base. From the one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels, he made the capitals of the columns and overlaid them with gold. Of bronze, seventy-two talents and four thousand shekels were offered. From these were fashioned the bases at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony, and the bronze altar with its grating, and all the vessels that belong to its use. And the bases of the court, both all around and at its entrance, and the pegs of the tabernacle and the court round about.

<margin>exod. 39</margin>
**O**f violet and purple, scarlet and fine linen, they made the garments in which Aaron was to be clothed when he ministered in the holy places, as the Lord had commanded Moses. Therefore, he made the ephod of gold, violet, and purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, with embroidered work. He hammered the gold into thin plates and cut them into threads so they could be twisted with the weaving of the previous colors. And he made two edges on each side of the tops, so they might be joined into one. The belt was also of the same colors, as the Lord had commanded. He also bound and enclosed two onyx stones in gold, engraved with the skill of a jeweler with the names of the sons of Israel. And he placed them on the sides of the ephod as a memorial for the sons of Israel, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

**A**fter these things, he presented the work of the breastplate <note>Original: "rationalis."</note> of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, with embroidered work. It was four-square, double, of the measure of a span. And he placed four rows of stones in it. In the first row was a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper. In the third, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. In the fourth, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl. They were enclosed and surrounded with gold in their rows. And these twelve stones were engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, each by its own name. Moses caused these to be made just as the Lord had commanded.

He also placed the golden altar under the roof of the testimony against the veil, and burned upon it the incense of spices, as the Lord had commanded Moses. He also set up the court around the tabernacle and the altar, drawing the screen at its entrance. After all things were perfected, the cloud covered the tabernacle of the testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it. Nor could Moses enter the tent of the covenant, for the cloud covered all things, and the majesty of the Lord shone brightly, because the cloud had covered everything. Whenever the cloud left the tabernacle, the children of Israel set out by their troops. If it hung above, they remained in the same place. For the cloud of the Lord rested over the tabernacle by day, and fire by night, in the sight of all the people of Israel through all their dwellings.

<meta>This page continues the divine instructions for the Tabernacle from Exodus 29, transitioning from the consecration of priests to the daily offerings, the construction of the incense altar, the census tax, the holy anointing oil, the appointment of master craftsmen, and finally the episode of the Golden Calf and Moses’ subsequent intercession for the people.</meta>

**The one who offers** shall do so according to God’s decree, wherever he visits the tabernacle. Furthermore, they shall weave the curtains and cook the meat in a holy place, because it is the "Holy of Holies" for the sons <note>referring to the priests, the sons of Aaron</note>. Whoever has sworn in the ministry of the Tabernacle of Witness shall also eat the bread; let the sacrifice not be pleasing to them otherwise. After they have offered the gift, if any of the meat remains from the ministry of the Holy of Holies, they shall burn it in a holy fire; they shall not burn its remains in the morning. Indeed, every day you shall perform the judgments which are commanded to you upon the altar and in just proportion: the Lord says: He will consecrate their hands. And you shall offer a calf for sin each day for atonement. **How** you shall cleanse the altar when you have sacrificed the victim of expiation: and you shall anoint it for sanctification. For seven days you shall atone for the altar and sanctify it; and it shall be holy. Anyone who touches it shall be sanctified.

**This** is what you shall do on the altar: two lambs of one year old every single day continually; one lamb in the morning and the other in the evening. A tenth part of fine flour mixed with beaten oil which has the measure of a fourth part of a <term>hin</term> <note>Original: "hiĩ." A hin was an ancient Hebrew liquid measure, roughly 4 to 6 liters.</note>, and wine for a libation of the same measure for the first lamb. The other lamb you shall offer in the evening according to the rite of the morning offering: and according to those things we have said, for a sweet odor in sacrifice to the Lord, a perpetual offering throughout your generations, at the door of the Tabernacle of Witness before the Lord, where I will appoint and speak to you. And there I will command the children of Israel, and the altar shall be sanctified in my glory. **I will sanctify** also the Tabernacle of Witness with the altar: and Aaron with his sons, so that they may perform my priestly function. And I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel: and I will be their Lord God: and they shall know that I am the Lord their God, who led them out of the land of Egypt so that I might remain among them: I am the Lord their God.

**You shall make** also an altar for the burning of incense out of <term>acacia wood</term> <note>Original: "lignis sethim." Shittim or acacia wood was prized for its durability in the desert.</note>: having one cubit in length and another in width—that is, a square—and two cubits in height: horns shall proceed from it. And you shall overlay it with the purest gold: both its grate and its walls round about, and its horns. And you shall make for it a small golden crown round about, and two golden rings under the crown on each side, so that the poles may be put into them, that the altar may be carried by them: which poles you shall make of acacia and overlay them with gold. And you shall place the altar against the veil that hangs before the Ark of the Witness before the propitiatory <note>The "mercy seat" or lid of the Ark.</note> which is the sanctuary: where I will speak to you. There Aaron shall burn incense of sweet fragrance. In the morning, when he dresses the lamps, he shall burn it. And when he sets them out in the evening, he shall burn a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout your generations. You shall not offer upon it incense of any other composition, nor offering and victim, nor shall you pour libations. And Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year with the blood that was offered for sin: and they shall make atonement upon it throughout your generations. It shall be the Holy of Holies to the Lord.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: When you take the census of the sum of the children of Israel, according to their number, each shall give a price for their souls to the Lord: and there shall be no plague among them when they are enrolled. **This** every one who passes into the census shall give: half a <term>shekel</term> <note>Original: "sicluĩ." The shekel was the standard weight for currency.</note> according to the measure of the temple. A shekel is twenty <term>obols</term> <note>Original: "obolos." Also known as gerahs; the smallest unit of Hebrew weight.</note>: the half part of a shekel shall be offered to the Lord. **He who is** in the count, from twenty years and above, shall give the price. The rich man shall not add to the half shekel, and the poor man shall diminish nothing. And you shall give the money which is collected from the children of Israel for the uses of the propitiatory of the Tabernacle of Witness, that it may be a monument of them before the Lord, and he may be merciful to their souls.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: You shall also make a bronze basin with its base for washing. You shall place it between the Tabernacle of Witness and the altar: and having put water in it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet when they are about to enter the Tabernacle of Witness, and when they approach the altar to offer incense to the Lord, lest perhaps they die. It shall be a perpetual law for him and his seed throughout their successions.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: Take for yourself spices: of the first and chosen myrrh five hundred shekels, and of cinnamon half as much, that is two hundred and fifty shekels; of calamus similarly two hundred and fifty; of cassia five hundred shekels, in the weight of the sanctuary; and of oil from olives the measure of a hin. And you shall make the holy oil of anointing, an ointment composed by the work of a perfumer. And you shall anoint with it the Tabernacle of Witness, and the Ark of the Testament, and the table with its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altars of incense and of holocaust <note>The altar of burnt offerings.</note>, and all the furniture that pertains to their worship. And you shall sanctify all things, and they shall be the Holy of Holies. **Whoever** touches them shall be sanctified. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons and sanctify them so that they may perform the priesthood for me. You shall say to the children of Israel: **This** oil of anointing shall be holy to me throughout your generations. The flesh of man shall not be anointed with it; and according to its composition, you shall not make any other, because it is sanctified and shall be holy to you. Whatever man shall compose such a thing and give of it to a stranger, he shall be exterminated from his people.

**The Lord** said to Moses: Take for yourself spices: <term>stacte</term> <note>A fragrant gum resin.</note> and <term>onycha</term> <note>The operculum of certain mollusks, used as incense.</note>, <term>galbanum</term> <note>A bitter, aromatic gum resin.</note> of good odor, and the clearest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. And you shall make incense of a composition like that of a perfumer, mixed with diligence and pure, and most worthy of sanctification. And when you have ground it into a very fine powder, you shall place it before the Witness in the Tabernacle of the Testament, in which place I will appear to you. The incense shall be the Holy of Holies to you. **Such** a composition you shall not make for your own use, because it is holy to the Lord. Whoever makes the like to enjoy its odor shall perish from his people.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah: and I have filled him with the spirit of God, and with wisdom and intelligence and knowledge in every work, to devise whatever can be made of gold and silver and bronze, marble and gems and variety of woods. And I have given him as his companion Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan: and in the heart of every learned man I have placed wisdom, that they may make all things that I have commanded you: the Tabernacle of the Covenant and the Ark of the Witness, and the propitiatory which is upon it, and all the vessels of the tabernacle, the table and its vessels, the purest lampstand with its vessels, and the altars of incense and of holocaust and all their vessels, the basin with its base, the holy garments for the ministry of Aaron the priest and his sons, that they may perform their office in holy things; the oil of anointing and the incense of spices in the sanctuary. They shall do all things that I have commanded you.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: See that you keep my Sabbath, because it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you. **Keep** my Sabbath, for it is holy to you. **He who** pollutes it shall die the death. **He who** does work on it, his soul shall perish from the midst of his people. Six days you shall do work; on the seventh day is the Sabbath, a holy rest to the Lord. **Everyone** who does work on the holy day shall die. **Let** the children of Israel keep the Sabbath and celebrate it throughout their generations. **It is** a perpetual covenant between me and the children of Israel and a perpetual sign. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he ceased from work. And the Lord, having finished these words on Mount Sinai, gave to Moses two stone tablets written by the finger of God. **However**, the people seeing that Moses made a delay in descending from the mountain, gathered against Aaron and said: **Rise up**, make for us gods who may go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who led us out of the land of Egypt, we know not what has happened to him. **And** Aaron said to them: **Take** the golden earrings from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me. **The people** did as was commanded, bringing...

**When** he had received them, he formed them with a founder’s work and made from them a molten calf. **And** they said: **These** are your gods, O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt. **When** Aaron had seen this, he built an altar before it, and with the voice of a herald he cried out, saying: **Tomorrow** is the solemnity of the Lord. **And** rising in the morning, they offered holocausts and peace victims: and the people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses: **Go**, descend; for your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt, have sinned. **They have** quickly turned aside from the way which you showed them; they have made for themselves a molten calf and have adored it, and sacrificing victims to it, they said: **These** are your gods, O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt. **And** again the Lord said to Moses: **I see** that this people is stiff-necked. Let me be, that my fury may be kindled against them, and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation. **But** Moses prayed to the Lord his God, saying: **Why**, O Lord, is your fury kindled against your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt with great strength and a robust hand? **Lest** perhaps the Egyptians say, "He craftily led them out that he might kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth." **Let** your anger cease and be appeased over the wickedness of your people. **Remember** Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, saying: **I will multiply** your seed like the stars of heaven: and all this land of which I have spoken I will give to your seed, and you shall possess it forever. **And** the Lord was appeased from doing the evil which he had spoken against his people.

**Moses turned** from the mountain, carrying the two tablets of the witness in his hand, holy on both sides and made by the work of God. **The writing** also was of God, engraved on the tablets. **But** Joshua, hearing the sound of the people shouting, said to Moses: **The howling** of battle is heard in the camp. **He** replied: **It is not** the cry of those encouraging to battle, nor the voice of those compelling to flight, but the voice of singers I hear. **And** when he approached the camp, he saw the calf and the dances. **And being** very angry, he threw the tablets from his hand and broke them at the foot of the mountain. **And** snatching the calf which they had made, he burnt it and ground it into powder, which he scattered into water: and he gave it to the children of Israel to drink. **And** he said to Aaron: **What** did this people do to you, that you should bring upon them a very great sin? **To which** he replied: **Let not** my Lord be indignant. **For** you know this people, that they are prone to evil. **They said** to me: **Make** for us gods who may go before us; for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we know not what has happened to him. **To whom** I said: **Whoever** of you has gold, [bring it]. **They took** and gave it to me: and I threw it into the fire, and this calf came out. **Moses** seeing therefore that the people were naked—for Aaron had stripped them because of the ignominy of their filth, and had set them naked among their enemies—stood in the gate of the camp and said: **If anyone** is for the Lord, let him join me. **And** all the sons of Levi were gathered to him. **To whom** he said: **Thus** says the Lord God of Israel: **Let** every man put his sword upon his thigh. **Go** and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let every man kill his brother and friend and neighbor. **The sons** of Levi did according to the word of Moses, and there fell on that day about twenty-three thousand men. **And** Moses said: **You have consecrated** your hands today to the Lord, every man in his son and in his brother, that a blessing may be given to you.

**It happened** on the next day, Moses spoke to the people: **You have sinned** a very great sin. **I will ascend** to the Lord, if by any means I might entreat him for your sin. **And** Moses returned to the Lord and said: **I beseech** you, this people has sinned a very great sin, and they have made for themselves golden gods; either forgive them this trespass, or if you do not, delete me from your book which you have written. **To whom** the Lord replied: **He who** has sinned against me, him will I delete from my book. **But you**, go and lead this people where I have spoken to you. **My angel** shall go before you. **But I**, in the day of vengeance, will visit also this sin of theirs. **The Lord** struck the people for the sin of the calf which Aaron made.

**The Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: **Go**, ascend from this place, you and your people whom you led out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: **To your seed** I will give it. And I will send before you an **Angel** as your guide, that I may cast out the Canaanite, and the Amorite, and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite: and that you may enter into a land flowing with milk and honey. **For** I will not ascend with you, because the people are stiff-necked, lest perhaps I destroy you on the way. **The people**, hearing this very bad word, mourned, and no one put on his ornaments according to custom.

**The Lord said**: **My face** shall go before you, and I will give you rest. **And** Moses said: **If you yourself** do not go before, do not lead us out of this place. **For in what** can it be known that I and your people have found grace in your sight, unless you walk with us, and we be glorified above all the peoples who dwell upon the earth? **The Lord** said to Moses: **This word** also that you have spoken I will do. **For** you have found grace before me, and I have known you by name. **He** said: **Show** me your glory. **He replied**: **I will show** all good to you, and I will call in the name of the Lord before you: and I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be merciful to whom it shall please me. **And again** he said: **You cannot** see my face. **For** man shall not see me and live. **And again**: **Behold**, he says, there is a place by me; you shall stand upon a rock. <meta>This page continues the narrative of the construction of the Tabernacle. Following the divine instructions given to Moses on Mount Sinai in the previous chapters, the text now transitions to the practical execution of the work. It details the call for materials, the overwhelming generosity of the Israelites, and the appointment of the master craftsmen Bezalel and Oholiab to oversee the creation of the sacred vessels and the structure itself.</meta>

<margin>Exod. 35.</margin>
And Moses spoke to the whole assembly of the sons of Israel, saying: This is the word which the Lord has commanded, saying: Set aside from among yourselves first-fruits for the Lord. Let every person of a willing and prompt mind offer them to the Lord: gold, and silver, and bronze; blue, and purple, and double-dyed scarlet, and fine linen; goat hair and ram skins dyed red, and violet-colored skins; **shittim wood** <note>Original: "lignis sethim." This is acacia wood, known for its durability.</note>; and oil for preparing the lamps, and for the creation of the ointment and the sweetest incense; onyx stones and gems for the decoration of the ephod and the breastplate. Whoever among you is wise, let him come and do what the Lord has commanded: namely, the tabernacle and its roof, the covering, the rings, and the boards with their bars, the pegs and the bases; the ark and the poles, the mercy seat, and the veil which is hung before it; the table with its poles and vessels, and the bread of presence; the lampstand to support the lights, its vessels and lamps, and the oil for the nourishment of the fires; the altar of incense and its poles, and the anointing oil and the incense made of spices; the hanging for the door of the tabernacle; the altar of burnt offering and its bronze grating with its poles and all its vessels; the basin and its base; the curtains of the court with their columns and bases; the hanging at the doors of the vestibule; the pegs of the tabernacle and of the court with their cords; the vestments used in the ministry of the sanctuary; the garments of Aaron the high priest and of his sons, so that they may perform the office of the priesthood for me.

<margin>v. 20.</margin>
And when the whole multitude of the sons of Israel had gone out from the presence of Moses, they offered with a most prompt and devoted mind first-fruits to the Lord to do the work of the tabernacle of testimony. Whatever was necessary for the worship and for the sacred vestments, they provided. Men and women alike gave bracelets and earrings, rings and armlets. If anyone had blue and purple, double-dyed scarlet, fine linen, and ram skins dyed red, and violet skins, silver and bronze and metals, they offered them to the Lord; and shittim wood for various uses. Moreover, the skilled women gave the things they had spun: they contributed blue, and purple, and vermilion, and fine linen, and goat hair, all of their own accord. The princes offered onyx stones and gems for the ephod and the breastplate; also spices and oil for preparing the lamps, and for making the ointment, and for composing the incense of sweetest odor. All the men and women with a devoted mind offered gifts, so that the works might be made which the Lord had commanded by the hand of Moses. All the sons of Israel dedicated voluntary offerings to the Lord.

<margin>v. 30.</margin>
And Moses said to the sons of Israel: Behold, the Lord has called by name **Bezalel** <note>Original: "beseleel."</note>, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And he has filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom and intelligence and knowledge in every kind of learning, to devise and to perform work in gold and silver and bronze, and in the carving of stones and in carpentry; whatever can be skillfully invented, He has put into his heart.

<margin>v. 34.</margin>
**Oholiab** <note>Original: "Ooliab."</note> also, the son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan. He has instructed both of them in wisdom, so that they may do the work of the silversmith, the polisher, and the embroiderer in blue and purple and double-dyed vermilion and fine linen, and that they may weave all things and find out new designs.

<margin>c. 36.</margin>
Therefore, Bezalel and Oholiab and every wise man to whom the Lord gave wisdom and understanding in these matters, did the work; so that they might know how to work skillfully the things that are necessary for the uses of the sanctuary, and those things which the Lord had commanded. And when Moses had called them and every learned man to whom God had given wisdom and understanding, and who had offered themselves of their own accord to do the work, he delivered to them all the gifts of the sons of Israel. While they were busy with the work, the people brought votive offerings every day in the morning. Whereupon the craftsmen were compelled to come and say to Moses: The people offer more than is necessary.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 6.</margin>
Moses therefore commanded that it be announced by the voice of a herald: Let neither man nor woman offer anything more for the work of the sanctuary. And so they ceased from offering gifts, because the things offered were sufficient and more than enough.

<margin>v. 8.</margin>
And all those who were wise of heart to complete the work of the tabernacle made ten curtains of fine twisted linen, and blue, and purple, and double-dyed scarlet, with varied work of stripes and the art of the embroiderer. One curtain had in length twenty-eight **cubits** <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>, and in width four. There was one measure for all the curtains. And he joined five curtains to one another, and the other five he coupled together. He also made loops of blue on the edge of one curtain on both sides, and similarly on the edge of the other curtain, so that the loops might meet one another and be joined together. Wherefore he also cast fifty gold circles which might catch the loops of the curtains, and the tabernacle might become one. He also made eleven curtains of goat hair to cover the roof of the tabernacle. One curtain had thirty cubits in length and four cubits in width. All the curtains were of one measure. Five of these he joined by themselves, and the other six by themselves. He made fifty loops on the edge of one curtain, and fifty on the edge of the other curtain, so that they might be joined to one another; and fifty bronze buckles with which the roof might be fastened, so that one covering might be made of all the curtains. He also made a covering for the tabernacle of ram skins dyed red, and another covering above that of violet-colored skins.

<margin>v. 20.</margin>
He also made the boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood, standing upright. The length of one board was ten cubits, and the width was one and a half cubits. There were two tenons <note>Original: "mastra."</note> in each board, so that one might be joined to the other. Thus he did for all the boards of the tabernacle. Twenty of these were on the southern side toward the south, with forty silver bases. Two bases were placed under one board on each side of the corners, where the notch of the sides ends in the corner. Also on the side of the tabernacle that looks toward the north, he made twenty boards with forty silver bases, two bases for each board. But toward the west, that is, toward that part of the tabernacle which looks toward the sea, he made six boards, and two others at each corner of the tabernacle behind, which were joined from the bottom even to the top, and were held together in one joint. Thus he did on both sides at the corners, so that there were eight boards in all, and they had sixteen silver bases, namely, two bases under each board. He also made bars of shittim wood: five to hold together the boards of one side of the tabernacle, and five others to fit the boards of the other side; and besides these, five other bars at the western side of the tabernacle toward the sea, which he also covered with gold; and he gilded the boards themselves, and cast gold rings for them through which the bars might be inserted, and these too he covered with gold plates.

<margin>v. 35.</margin>
He also made a veil of blue, and purple, and double-dyed vermilion, and fine twisted linen, varied and distinguished with embroidery work; and four columns of shittim wood, which he gilded along with their capitals, casting silver bases for them. He also made a hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle of blue, purple, double-dyed vermilion, and fine twisted linen, with needlework; and five columns with their capitals, which he covered with gold, and he cast their bases in bronze.

<margin>c. 37. v. 1.</margin>
And Bezalel made the **Ark** of shittim wood, having two and a half cubits in length, and a cubit and a half in width; the height was also one cubit and a half. And he covered it with the purest gold inside and out. And he made a gold crown for it round about, casting four gold rings for its four corners: two rings on one side, and two on the other. He also made poles of shittim wood, which he covered with gold, and which he put into the rings that were on the sides of the ark to carry it.

<margin>v. 6.</margin>
He also made the **Mercy Seat**—that is, the oracle—of the purest gold: two cubits and a half in length, and a cubit and a half in width. Also two **cherubim** of hammered gold, which he placed on both sides of the mercy seat: one cherub on the top here, and another cherub on the top there, so that they were on both sides of the mercy seat. The cherubim were spreading their wings and covering the mercy seat, looking toward one another and toward it.

<margin>v. 10.</margin>
He also made the table two cubits in length and one cubit in width, which was a cubit and a half in height. And he gilded it with the purest gold. And he made a gold lip for it round about, and for the lip itself a gold crown of four fingers' breadth; and over the same crown another small gold rim. He also cast four gold rings, which he placed at the four corners at each foot of the table near the crown. And he put the poles into them, so that the table could be carried. And he made the vessels for the various ministries of the table: the bowls, the cups, and the censers of pure gold, in which the libations are to be offered.

<margin>v. 17.</margin>
He also made the **lampstand** of hammered work from the purest gold, from the shaft of which proceeded branches, cups, bowls, and lilies. There were six branches on its sides: three branches on one side, and three on the other. There were three cups in the shape of a nut on each branch, with bowls and lilies; and three cups like a nut on another branch, with bowls and lilies together. The work of the six branches proceeding from the stem of the lampstand was equal. On the stem itself were four cups in the shape of a nut, and bowls for each, and lilies. And there were bowls under two branches in three places, making six branches in all proceeding from one shaft. And the bowls and branches were of one piece, all of hammered work from the purest gold.

<margin>v. 23.</margin>
He also made seven lamps with their snuffers, and the vessels where the snuffed wicks might be extinguished, of the purest gold. He spent a talent of gold on the lampstand with all its vessels.

<margin>v. 25.</margin>
He also made the **altar of incense** of shittim wood, being one cubit square and two in height, from the corners of which proceeded horns. And he covered it with the purest gold, with its grating and walls and horns; and he made a gold crown for it round about, and two gold rings under the crown on each side, so that the poles might be put into them and the altar could be carried. But the poles themselves he made of shittim wood and covered with gold plates.

<margin>v. 29.</margin>
He also composed the oil for the anointing of sanctification, and the incense of the purest spices, by the work of a perfumer.

<margin>c. 38.</margin>
He also made the **altar of burnt offering** <note>Original: "altare holocausti."</note> of shittim wood, five cubits square and three in height; its horns proceeded from the corners, and he covered it with bronze plates. And for its use he prepared from bronze all the vessels: pots, tongs, flesh-hooks, hooks, and fire pans. And he made its grating in the manner of a net of bronze; and under it, in the middle of the altar, a hearth. He cast four rings at the four corners of the net to receive the poles for carrying; these poles he also made of shittim wood and covered with bronze plates. And he put them into the rings that stood out from the sides of the altar. The altar itself was not solid but hollow, made of boards and empty within.

<margin>v. 8.</margin>
He also made the bronze **basin** <note>Original: "labrum eneum." A large basin for ritual washing.</note> with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle.

<margin>v. 9.</margin>
And he made the court: on the southern side of which were hangings of fine twisted linen, a hundred cubits long. There were twenty columns with their bronze bases; the capitals of the columns and the entire carving of the work were of silver.

<margin>v. 11.</margin>
Similarly, on the northern side, the hangings extended a hundred cubits.

...of the columns, that is, the measurements which were worked and measured in height. In the court, on the side which looks toward the west: there were hangings of ten cubits. <note>Original: "uelarū .x. cubitorū." A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches.</note> Fifty [cubits] for the sons of [Israel] and the silver caps of the columns were cast. Furthermore, toward the east: fifty cubits in a space of one hundred: where seven columns with two bases were on one side. and on the other part: seven on each side made the curve. which were eleven equal sections: they were tents. the caps of these and the bases were of bronze. All the hangings were woven of twisted fine linen. The bases of the columns were of bronze, but their caps with their engravings were of silver. but they also clothed the columns themselves with silver. and he made the hanging for the entrance of the court with embroidery of purple, scarlet, and twisted fine linen, which had a length of twenty cubits. The height was also five cubits, according to the measure which all the hangings of the court had. The columns of the entrance were four with their bases: with their bronze caps and silver engravings. He also made the pegs of the tabernacle and of the court all around of bronze.

These are the instruments of the tabernacle of testimony which were numbered according to the command of Moses in the ceremonies of the Levites by the hand of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. Which **Bezalel** <note>Original: "beselhel." The chief artisan of the Tabernacle.</note>, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, had completed as the Lord commanded through Moses: joined by his companion **Oholiab** <note>Original: "ooliab."</note>, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, who was himself an outstanding worker in wood: and a weaver of many colors and an embroiderer in hyacinth <note>Original: "iacinto." Often translated as blue or violet.</note>, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. All the gold that was spent in the work of the sanctuary: and what was offered in gifts: was twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels, according to the measure of the sanctuary. It was offered by those who passed to be numbered from twenty years and above, from six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty armed men. There were, moreover, a hundred talents of silver, from which the bases of the sanctuary and the entrance where the veil hangs were cast. A hundred bases were made from a hundred talents: one talent being calculated for each base. Moreover, with one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five [shekels], he made the caps of the columns, which he also clothed with silver. Of the bronze offered, there were seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels, from which the bases for the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony were cast, and the bronze altar with its grating, and all the vessels which belong to its use, and the bases of the court, both around and at the entrance of the sanctuary, and the pegs of the tabernacle and the court all around. Moreover, the vestments were made of scarlet and purple and fine linen, which they wore when they ministered in the holy places, just as the Lord commanded Moses.

He also made the **ephod** <note>Original: "superhumerale." A garment worn over the shoulders by the High Priest.</note> of gold, hyacinth, and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen with multi-colored work. And so he made thin plates of gold and cut them into threads so they could be twisted with the weaving of the previous colors. [The ephod] was joined at both sides of the top, and a belt of the same colors, as the Lord commanded Moses. They also prepared two onyx stones, bound and enclosed in gold and carved with the art of a jeweler with the names of the sons of Israel; as the Lord commanded Moses. He also made the **breastplate** <note>Original: "rationale."</note> with multi-colored work according to the work of the ephod, of gold, hyacinth, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen; it was square and double, a span in length and width. And he placed in it four rows of gems. In the first row were a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second: a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper. In the third: a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. In the fourth: a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl; surrounded and enclosed in gold in their rows. And the stones themselves were carved with the twelve names of the twelve tribes of Israel, each with the name of one. They made on the breastplate chains linked to one another of purest gold, and two hooks and as many gold rings. Furthermore, they placed rings on both sides of the breastplate, from which two gold chains would hang, which they fastened to the hooks that stood out from the corners of the ephod. These met both in front and in back, so that the ephod and breastplate were fastened together, bound by the belt and the rings which the breastplate and ephod held, so they would move together, as the Lord commanded Moses.

And he made the robe of the ephod entirely of hyacinth, and an opening in the upper part to hold it, with a border around the edge, and at the feet were pomegranates of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and twisted fine linen, and bells of purest gold, which they placed between the pomegranates at the bottom part of the robe all around: a gold bell and a pomegranate, so that they sounded as he went in and out when he performed his ministry; as the Lord commanded Moses. They also made the linen tunics of woven work for Aaron and his sons, and miters with their small horns of fine linen, and linen breeches of fine linen, and a girdle of twisted fine linen, hyacinth, purple, and scarlet, distinguished with the art of embroidery; as the Lord commanded Moses. They also made the plate of sacred veneration of purest gold and wrote on it, in the measure of a shekel: **HOLY TO THE LORD** <note>Original: "sc̄m d̄no."</note>. And they bound it to the miter with a hyacinth ribbon; as the Lord commanded Moses. All the work of the tabernacle and the roof of the testimony was finished. And the sons of Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses. And they offered the tabernacle and the roof and all the furniture: rings, boards, bars, columns, and bases; the covering of ram skins dyed red, and another covering of hyacinth skins; the veil, the ark, the poles, the mercy seat, the table with its vessels and the bread of presence; the lampstand, the lamps, and their utensils with the oil; the gold altar and the ointment, and the incense made of spices, and the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle; the bronze altar, the grating, the poles, and all its vessels; the basin with its base, the hangings of the court, and the columns with their bases; the hanging at the entrance of the court, its cords, and pegs. Nothing of the vessels was missing which were commanded to be made for the service of the tabernacle and for the tent of the covenant. Moreover, the vessels which the priests use in the sanctuary, namely Aaron and his sons, the sons of Israel offered, just as the Lord commanded Moses. And after Moses saw all things completed, he blessed them.

But the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: On the first day of the first month you shall erect the tabernacle of testimony. And you shall place the ark in it, and hang the veil before it. And having brought in the table, you shall place upon it the things that are commanded by rite. The lampstand shall stand with its lamps; and the gold altar on which incense is burned before the ark of testimony. You shall place the hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle, and before it the altar of burnt offering. The basin between the altar and the tabernacle which you shall fill with water. And you shall surround the court with hangings, and its entrance. And taking the oil of unction, you shall anoint the tabernacle with its vessels so they may be sanctified. The altar of burnt offering and all its vessels. The basin with its base; you shall consecrate all things with the anointing oil, so that they may be the Holy of Holies. And you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the doors of the tabernacle of testimony, and having washed them with water, you shall clothe them in sacred vestments, so that they may minister to me, and their anointing shall be for a perpetual priesthood for all time. And Moses did all things that the Lord commanded. Therefore, in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was set up: and Moses erected it and placed the boards and bases and bars, and set up the columns. And he spread the roof over the tabernacle, placing the covering over it, just as the Lord had commanded. He also placed the testimony in the ark, with the poles placed underneath, and the mercy seat above. And when he had brought the ark into the tabernacle, he hung the veil before it to fulfill the Lord’s command. He also placed the table in the tabernacle of testimony on the north side outside the veil, with the bread of presence arranged before it, as the Lord commanded Moses. He placed

<column-break/>

the lampstand in the tabernacle of testimony opposite the table on the south side: the lamps being placed in order according to the command of the Lord. He also placed the gold altar under the roof of the testimony before the veil, and burned spice incense upon it, as the Lord had commanded. He also placed the hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle, and the altar of burnt offering in the vestibule of the testimony, offering upon it the burnt offering and sacrifices as the Lord had commanded. He also set the basin between the tabernacle of testimony and the altar, filling it with water. And Moses and Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet in it when they entered the court of the covenant and approached the altar, as the Lord had commanded. He also erected the court around the tabernacle and the altar, with the hanging drawn at its entrance. After all things were finished, a cloud covered the tabernacle of testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it. Nor could Moses enter the tent of the covenant while the cloud covered all things and the majesty of the Lord was flashing, because the cloud had covered everything. Whenever the cloud left the tabernacle, the sons of Israel set out by their companies; if it hung above, they remained in the same place. For the cloud remained over the tabernacle by day, and fire by night, in the sight of the people of Israel through all their dwellings. **END OF EXODUS.**

the Lord from the tabernacle of testimony, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: A man among you who offers a sacrifice to the Lord of animals: that is, of cattle and of sheep, offering victims. If his offering be a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer an unblemished male at the door of the tabernacle of testimony to appease the Lord toward him. He shall also place his hand upon the head of the victim, and it shall be acceptable and profitable for his expiation. And he shall immolate the calf before the Lord, and the sons of Aaron the priests shall offer its blood, pouring it around the altar which is before the door of the tabernacle. And having pulled off the skin of the victim, they shall cut the limbs into pieces, and they shall put fire on the altar, having arranged a pile of wood. And the members that are cut up they shall arrange above: namely the head and all things that adhere to the liver. The intestines and feet being washed with water, the priest shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet odor to the Lord. But if the offering is from the flocks: from the sheep or from the goats, a burnt offering, they shall offer an unblemished one without spot. And they shall immolate it at the side of the altar which looks toward the north before the Lord. The sons of Aaron shall pour its blood upon the altar all around. And they shall divide the members and all that adhere to the liver, and they shall place them upon the wood, under which the fire is to be put. But the intestines and feet they shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all the offered things upon the altar as a burnt offering and a most sweet odor to the Lord. But if the offering to the Lord be a burnt offering of birds: of turtledoves or young pigeons, the priest shall offer it at the altar, and having twisted back the head and broken the wound, he shall make the blood run down upon the edge of the altar. The crop and the feathers he shall cast before the altar toward the east side in the place where the ashes are usually poured out. And he shall break its wings, but shall not cut them, nor violate them with iron. And he shall burn it upon the altar, wood having been placed under it. It is a burnt offering and an offering of most sweet odor to the Lord.

When a soul offers an offering of sacrifice to the Lord, his offering shall be of fine flour. and he shall pour oil upon it and place frankincense: and it shall be brought to the sons of Aaron the priests, one of whom shall take a handful of the flour and oil and all the frankincense, and he shall place it as a memorial upon the altar as a most sweet odor to the Lord. But what remains of the sacrifice shall be for Aaron and his sons, the Holy of Holies, from the offerings to the Lord. If your offering be from a frying pan of fine flour mixed with oil and without leaven, it shall be divided into small pieces, and you shall pour oil upon it. But if the sacrifice be from a gridiron, likewise fine flour shall be mixed with oil: which the one offering it to the Lord shall deliver into the hands of the priest. Who, when he has come to the altar, shall take a memorial from the sacrifice and burn it upon the altar as a most sweet odor to the Lord.
