And again Gaal said: "Behold, a people is descending from the center <note>original: "umbilico"; literally 'navel' or center-point</note> of the land, <margin>A</margin> and one company is coming by the way that looks toward the oak." Zebul said to him: "Where is your mouth now, with which you were speaking? 'Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?' Is this not the people you despised? Go out and fight against him."

So Gaal went out, preceding the people of the Shechemites, and fought against Abimelech, who pursued him as he fled and forced him into the city; and many on his side fell, even to the gate of the city. And Abimelech stayed in Arumah. But Zebul expelled Gaal and his companions from the city, nor did he allow them to remain in it. On the following day, the people went out into the field. When this was reported to Abimelech, he took his army and divided it into three companies, laying ambushes in the fields. And seeing that the people were coming out of the city, he rose and rushed upon them with his company, attacking and besieging the gate of the city; while the other two companies followed the adversaries through the field. Furthermore, Abimelech attacked the city all that day. He took it, having killed its inhabitants, and the city itself was destroyed, so that he scattered salt over it.

When those who lived in the tower of the Shechemites heard this, they entered the temple of their god Berith, where they had struck a covenant with him, and from which the place had taken its name, which was very strongly fortified. Abimelech also, hearing that the men of the tower of Shechem were gathered together, ascended Mount Zalmon with all his people; and taking an axe, he cut a branch from a tree, and carrying it on his shoulder, he said to his companions: "What you see me doing, do quickly." Therefore, vying with one another, cutting branches from the trees, they followed the leader. Surrounding the stronghold, they set it on fire. And so it happened that by smoke and fire a thousand people were killed, men and women alike, inhabitants of the citadel of Shechem.

But Abimelech, proceeding from there, came to the town of Thebez, which he surrounded and besieged and captured. There was, however, a high tower in the middle of the city, to which the men and women had fled, along with all the princes of the city; and with the entrance most firmly closed, they stood upon the roof of the tower in the defense works. Abimelech, coming near the tower, fought bravely; and approaching the door, he endeavored to set fire under it. And behold, a certain woman, throwing a fragment of a millstone from above, struck the head of Abimelech and broke his skull. He quickly called his armor-bearer and said to him: "Draw your sword and strike me, lest it be said: 'I was killed by a woman.'" He, performing the orders, killed him. When he was dead, all the men of Israel who were with him returned to their homes. And God repaid the evil that Abimelech had done against his father, killing his seventy brothers. To the Shechemites also, what they had worked was repaid; <margin>P</margin> and the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal came upon them.

After Abimelech, there arose as leader in Israel Tola, the son of Puah, the uncle of Abimelech, a man of Issachar who lived in Shamir in the mountains of Ephraim; and he judged Israel for twenty-three years. And he died and was buried in Shamir. He was succeeded by Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years, having thirty sons sitting upon thirty donkey colts, and who were princes of cities, which he called by his name Havoth-Jair, that is, the villages of Jair, even to the present day in the land of Gilead. And Jair died and was buried in a place called Kamon.

But the children of Israel joined new sins to their old ones, doing evil in the sight of the Lord, and worshiping the idols of the Baals and Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria and Sidon, and Moab, and the children of Ammon, and the Philistines. And they forsook the Lord and did not worship Him. Being angry against them, He delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and the children of Ammon. They were afflicted and vehemently oppressed for eighteen years—all who lived across the Jordan in the land of the Amorite which is in Gilead; except for one man, across the Jordan they devastated Judah and Benjamin and Ephraim. And Israel was afflicted excessively; and they cried to the Lord and said: "We have <margin>Q</margin> sinned against you, because we have forsaken the Lord our God and have served the Baals." To whom the Lord spoke: "Did not the Egyptians and the Amorites, and the children of Ammon and the Philistines and the Sidonians and Amalek and Canaan oppress you, and you cried to me, and I rescued you from their hand? And yet you have forsaken me and have worshiped foreign gods; therefore I will not add to deliver you further. Go and call upon the gods you have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of distress." They...

Fleeing and avoiding them, he lived in the land of Tob. Men who were poor and living as outlaws gathered to him, following him as their leader.

He also made a vow to the Lord, saying: "If you deliver the sons of Ammon into my hand, whoever is the first to come out of the doors of my house and meets me when I return in peace from the sons of Ammon, him I will offer as a burnt offering to the Lord." And Jephthah crossed over to the sons of Ammon to fight against them, whom the Lord delivered into his hand. And he struck them from Aroer until one comes to Minnith...

<margin>31</margin>
When Jephthah came to his home in Mizpah, his only daughter met him with timbrels and dances. For he had no other children. Upon seeing her, he tore his clothes and said: "Alas for me, my daughter, you have deceived me, and you yourself are deceived. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do otherwise." She responded to him: "My father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord, do whatever you have promised, since vengeance and victory over your enemies have been granted to you." And she said to her father: "Grant me only this which I pray: Let me go for two months so that I may wander the mountains and bewail my virginity <note>In this context, she mourns that she will die without children, which was considered a great tragedy in ancient Israel</note> with my companions." He responded: "Go." And he sent her away for two months. When she had gone with her friends and companions, she wept for her virginity on the mountains. After the two months were finished, she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed; and she had never known a man. From then on, a custom grew in Israel, and the practice has been kept, that after a year’s cycle the daughters of Israel gather together to bewail the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days.

<margin>34</margin>
Behold, however, a rebellion arose in Ephraim. For crossing over toward the north, they said to Jephthah: "Why, when going to fight against the sons of Ammon, did you not want to call us to go with you? Therefore we will burn down your house." To whom he responded: "There was a fierce dispute between me and the sons of Ammon; I called you so that you might provide me help, and you did not want to do it. Seeing this, I took my life in my hands <note>original: "uictoriā meā: posui i manu meā"; literally "I placed my victory in my hand," an idiom for risking one's life</note>, and I crossed over to the sons of Ammon, whom the Lord delivered. Therefore he called to himself all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim because the Gileadites had occupied the fords of the Jordan through which Ephraim had to return. ...they would test him. "Say **Shibboleth**" <note>original: "Orca sebolis"; "Shibboleth" means an ear of corn</note>. When he responded "**Sibboleth**" <note>original: "ceboleh"</note>, as they were not able to express the same letter with the same sound, they would immediately seize him and slit his throat at the very crossing of the Jordan. And forty-two thousand from Ephraim fell at that time. Jephthah the Gileadite judged Israel for six years; and he died and was buried in his city, Gilead. After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel, who had thirty sons and as many daughters, whom he sent abroad and gave to husbands; and he took wives for his sons of the same number, bringing them into his house. He judged Israel for seven years, and died and was buried in Bethlehem. Elon the Zebulunite succeeded him; he died and was buried in Zebulun. After him, the judge of Israel was Abdon the son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, who had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode upon donkey colts, and he judged Israel for eight years; he died and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, on the mountain of Amalek. And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord, who delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.

### OF SAMSON:
### AND THE BIRTH OF THE MAN.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial E with red and blue flourishes and penwork scrolling.</image-desc>

There was a certain man of Zorah and of the stock of Dan, named Manoah, having a sterile wife. To her an angel of the Lord appeared and said to her: "You are sterile and without children, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Beware, therefore, that you do not drink wine or strong drink <term>siceram: an alcoholic beverage made from grain or fruit other than grapes</term>, and do not eat anything unclean, because you shall conceive and bear a son, whose head a razor shall not touch. For he shall be a **Nazirite** <term>Nazareus: a person consecrated to God by a special vow, involving refraining from alcohol and cutting hair</term> of the Lord from his infancy and from his mother’s womb, and he himself shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines." When she had come to her husband and said to him: "A man of God came to me having an angelic countenance, exceedingly terrible. When I asked him who he was and by what name he was called, he would not tell me, but responded this: 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. Beware that you do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean. For the boy shall be a Nazirite from his infancy and from his mother’s womb until the day of his death.'" Therefore Manoah prayed to the Lord and said: "I beseech you, Lord, that the man whom you sent may come again and teach us what we ought to do concerning the boy who is to be born."

<image-desc>Large decorative initial C in red with internal floral patterns.</image-desc>

And when he had been born, they called his name Samson. And the boy grew, and the Lord blessed him. And the Spirit of the Lord began to be with him in the camp of Dan, in the land of Zorah and Eshtaol.

Samson therefore went down into Timnah, and seeing there a woman from the daughters of the Philistines, he went up and told his father and mother, saying: "I saw a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines, whom I ask that you take as a wife for me." To whom his father and mother said: "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your brothers, or in all my people, that you wish to take one from the Philistines who are uncircumcised?" And Samson said to his father: "Take this one for me, because she has pleased my eyes." Now his parents did not know that the matter was being done by the Lord, and that he sought an occasion against the Philistines. For at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel. Samson therefore went down with his father and mother to Timnah. And when they had come to the vineyards of the town, a young lion appeared, raging and roaring, and met him. Then the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, and he tore the lion into pieces as if he were tearing a young goat, having nothing at all in his hand; and he did not want to tell this to his father and mother. And he went down and spoke to the woman who had pleased his eyes.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial E in red with elaborate interior penwork.</image-desc>

And after some days, returning to take her, he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the mouth of the lion and a honeycomb. When he had taken it in his hands, he ate it on the way; and coming to his father and mother, he gave them a portion, and they also ate; yet he did not want to tell them that he had taken the honey from the body of the lion. And so the father went down to the woman and made a feast for his son Samson. For so young men were accustomed to do. Now when the local inhabitants saw him, they gave him thirty companions to be with him. To whom Samson spoke: "I propose a riddle to you; if you solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and as many tunics. But if you cannot solve it, you shall give me thirty linen garments and the same number of tunics." They responded to him: "Propose the riddle so that we may hear it." And he said: "Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness." Nor could they solve the proposition for three days. And when the seventh day was present, they said to Samson's wife: "Coax your husband and persuade him to show you what the riddle means. If you will not do this, we will burn you and your father's house. Did you call us to the wedding for this reason, to strip us bare?" And she poured out tears...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Book of Judges, specifically the life of Samson (Judges 14–16) and the migration of the tribe of Dan along with the story of Micah’s idols (Judges 17–18). It follows the previous page's account of Jephthah.</meta>

Samson was hiding and they sought him, saying: "Because you have been appointed to serve the common people, you have chosen to expose the children of those who fear them." But he replied: "I would not even tell my father and mother; how would I be able to tell you?" As was expected by all, she wept before him, and finally on the seventh day, because she was persistent, he explained it to her. She immediately told her fellow citizens. And they said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down: "What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?" He said to them: "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle." <note>This "heifer" is a metaphor for Samson's wife, whom the Philistines used to get the answer to his riddle.</note>

Therefore, being angry, the spirit of the Lord came upon Samson and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men there; he gave their clothes, which he had stripped from them, to those who had solved the riddle. And being exceedingly angry, he went up to his father's house. But his wife took as a husband one of his friends and wedding companions. After some time, when the days of the wheat harvest were near, Samson came wanting to visit his wife, and he brought her a young goat from the flock. And when he wanted to enter her chamber in the usual way, her father prevented him, saying: "I thought you hated her, and therefore I gave her to your friend. But she has a sister who is younger and more beautiful than she; let her be your wife instead." Samson replied: "From this day I shall be blameless against the Philistines, for I will do you harm." And he went and caught three hundred foxes and tied their tails together and fastened torches in the middle. He set these on fire and let them run about here and there. They immediately went into the grain fields of the Philistines. When these were set on fire, both the grain already gathered and that still standing in the stalk were consumed by the fire, so that the flame even consumed the vineyards and olive groves. And the Philistines said: "Who did this thing?" To which it was answered: "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to another; he is the one who did this." And the Philistines went up and burned both the woman and her father. Samson, being angry at them, said: "Since you have done this, I will surely take my revenge on you, and then I will rest." And he struck them with a great slaughter, so that in their amazement he laid them hip and thigh. <note>original: "femorí imponeret"; a literal translation of the idiom for a total and violent defeat.</note> And going down, he lived in a cave in the rock of Etam. Then the Philistines went up into the land of Judah and camped in a place which was later called Lehi, that is, "The Jawbone," where their army was spread out. And the men of the tribe of Judah said to them: "Why have you come up against us?" They replied: "We have come to bind Samson and to pay him back for what he did to us." Therefore, three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave of the rock of Etam and said to Samson: "Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why did you want to do this?" To them he said: "As they did to me, so I have done to them." They said: "We have come to bind you and deliver you into the hands of the Philistines." Samson replied to them: "Swear and promise me that you will not kill me yourselves." They said: "We will not kill you, but we will deliver you bound." They bound him with two new ropes and took him from the rock of Etam. When he had come to the place of the jawbone, and the Philistines came shouting to meet him, the spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson. And just as ropes are accustomed to melt at the heat of fire, so the bonds with which he was tied were broken and loosened. And finding a jawbone—that is, the mandible of a donkey—which was lying there, he snatched it up and killed a thousand men with it and said: "With the jawbone of a donkey, with the mandible of a young ass, I have destroyed them and struck down a thousand men." And when he had finished singing these words, he threw the mandible from his hand and called the name of that place Ramath-lehi, which is interpreted as "The Lifting of the Jawbone." And being very thirsty, he cried out to the Lord and said: "You have given into the hand of your servant this greatest salvation and victory, and behold, I die of thirst and shall fall into the hands of the uncircumcised." And the Lord opened a molar tooth in the jawbone of the donkey and water came out of it; having drunk this, his spirit was refreshed and he recovered his strength. Therefore the name of that place was called "The Spring of Him Who Calls Upon the Jawbone" <note>original: "fons inuocantif de maxilla"; referring to the spring En Hakkore.</note> even to the present day. And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines for twenty years. And he went to Gaza and saw a harlot there and went in to her. When the Philistines had heard and the news had spread among them that Samson had come to the city, they surrounded him, placing guards at the city gate; and they waited all night in silence so that they might kill him as he went out in the morning. But Samson slept until midnight, and rising from there he took hold of both the city gates with their posts and bars, and afterward carried them on his shoulders to the top of the mountain that looks toward Hebron.

**A**fter this he loved a woman who lived in the valley of Sorek, and her name was Delilah. And the leaders of the Philistines came to her and said: "Deceive him and show us in what he has such great strength, and how we might be able to overcome him and afflict him while bound. If you do this, we will each give you eleven hundred pieces of silver." Then Delilah said to Samson: "Show me, I beseech you, in what your greatest strength lies, and what it is that you might be bound with so that you could not break free." Samson replied to her: "If I am bound with seven green bowstrings <note>original: "neruicif funib;"; fresh cords made of animal gut.</note> that are not yet dried but still moist, I shall be weak like other men." The leaders of the Philistines brought to her seven ropes as he had said. With these she bound him while some were hiding in wait with her in the chamber, expecting the matter; they cried out to him: "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" He broke the bonds as if one were to break a thread of flax <note>original: "filu' stuppe"; a coarse fiber from stalks.</note> when it smells fire, and it was not known wherein his strength lay. And Delilah said to him: "Behold, you have mocked me and spoken falsely; at least now tell me what you should be bound with." He replied to her: "If I am bound with new ropes that have never been used for work, I shall be weak like other men." With these Delilah bound him again and the Philistines cried out: "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!"—with an ambush prepared in the chamber. He broke the bonds as if they were thin threads. Delilah said again to him: "How long will you deceive me and speak falsely? Show me how you ought to be bound." And he said: "If you weave the seven locks of my head with a loom and fasten a nail to them, I shall certainly be weak." When Delilah had done this, she said to him: "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" Rising from sleep, he pulled out the nail with the hair and the loom. Delilah said to him: "How can you say you love me, when your soul is not with mine? Three times you have lied to me and would not tell me in what your greatest strength lies." And since she was troublesome to him and stayed with him for many days, she gave him no space to rest, but his soul was weary even unto death.

**T**hen, coming to the truth of the matter, he said to her: "A razor has never come upon my head, because I am a Nazirite—that is, consecrated to the Lord—from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, my strength will depart from me and I shall fail, and be like other men." Seeing that he had confessed all his heart to her, she sent to the leaders of the Philistines and commanded: "Come up once more, for now he has opened to me

<column-break/>

his heart." They came down and brought her the money. She made him sleep upon her knees and recline his head in her lap. She called a barber and shaved the seven locks of his head. And she began to cast him off and repel him from her. Immediately his strength departed; and she said: "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" Rising from sleep, he said in his mind: "I will go out as I did before and shake myself free," not knowing that the Lord had departed from him. When the Philistines had apprehended him, they immediately gouged out his eyes and led him to Gaza bound in chains, and having shut him in prison, they made him grind grain. 

Now his hair was beginning to grow back. And the leaders of the Philistines gathered together to offer magnificent sacrifices to Dagon their god, and the whole city feasted. They ordered that Samson be brought out so that he might be mocked by them. And Samson was brought from prison, and they mocked him. He said to the young man who led him by the hand: "Let me touch the pillars on which the whole house stands, so that I may recline upon them and rest a little." The house was full of men and women; and all the leaders of the Philistines were there. From the roof about three thousand men were watching Samson being mocked. But he, having called upon the Lord, said: "Lord God, remember me, and now restore to me my former strength, my God, that I may avenge myself on my enemies, and receive one vengeance for the loss of my two eyes." And taking hold of both pillars on which the house rested, holding one with his right hand and the other with his left, he said: "Let me die with the Philistines." And when he had done this, the house fell upon all the leaders and all the multitude that was there; and he killed more in his death than he had killed before while living. And his brothers and all his father's household came down and took his body and buried it between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. And he judged Israel for twenty years.

In that time there lived a man from Mount Ephraim named Micah. He said to his mother: "Behold, the eleven hundred pieces of silver which were taken from you, and about which I heard you swear—I have them, they are with me." She replied: "Blessed be my son by the Lord." He returned them to his mother, who said to him: "I have consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord from my hand, that a carved and cast image might be made for my son, and now I give it back to you." He returned them to his father. They took some of the silver and made idols for the *teraphim* <term>household gods or religious ornaments</term>—that is, a priestly garment and the aforementioned images. He had a son whom he made a priest. In those days there was no king in Israel, but everyone did whatever they wanted. There was also another young man from Bethlehem in Judah of that same lineage; he was a Levite and lived there. He set out from the city of Bethlehem to travel wherever he might find a convenient place for himself. When he came to Mount Ephraim and arrived at the house of Micah, he was asked by him: "Where do you come from?" He replied: "I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to live where I can." Micah said: "Stay with me and be to me a father and a priest. I will give you ten pieces of silver annually, a double set of clothing, and those things necessary for me." He agreed and stayed with the man, and was to him like one of his sons. Micah filled his hand and had the young man as a priest. "Now I know that the Lord will do good to me, having a Levite as a priest."

In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of Dan sought a possession for themselves to dwell in. For up to that day they had not received an inheritance among the other tribes. Therefore the children of Dan sent five very strong men from their family, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to explore the land and diligently inspect it; and they said to them: "Go and consider the way." When they had traveled and come to Mount Ephraim and to the house of Micah, they rested there. They recognized the voice of the young Levite and turned aside to him. "Who brought you here? What are you doing here? For what reason did you want to come here?" He replied to them: "Micah provided this and that for me, and hired me for a wage to be his priest." They asked him to consult the Lord, so that they might know if they were proceeding on a prosperous journey. He replied to them: "Go in peace. The Lord looks upon the way you are going." Therefore the five men went and came to Laish; they saw the people living in it without any fear, according to the custom of the Sidonians, secure and quiet, with no one resisting them, possessing great wealth, far from the Sidonians and separated from all men. Returning to their brothers in Zorah and Eshtaol, when they were asked what they had done, they replied: "Arise and let us go up to them. For we have seen a land that is very opulent and fertile. Do not be negligent, do not cease; let us go and possess it. There will be no labor. We will enter a very wide region of secure people, and the Lord will show us a place in which there is no poverty of anything that grows on the earth."

**A**fter six hundred men of the lineage of Dan—that is, from Zorah and Eshtaol—were girded with weapons of war, they went up and stayed in Kiriath-jearim in Judah. From that time the place took the name "The Camp of Dan," and it is behind Kiriath-jearim; from there they crossed into Mount Ephraim. When they came to the house of Micah, the five men who had been sent before to explore the land said to their other brothers: "Do you not know that in these houses there are an ephod, and household idols, and a carved image? See if this pleases you." And when they had turned aside a little, they entered the house of the young Levite who was in the house of Micah and greeted him peacefully. The six hundred armed men stood before the door. But those who had entered the house of the young man took the image, the ephod, the household idols, and the carved image. The priest stood before the door while the six hundred brave men were waiting. The five men said to the youth: "Take the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast image." To them the priest said: "What are you doing?" They responded: "Be silent, put your finger over your mouth and come with us, so that we may have you as a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be a priest in the house of one man, or in a tribe and family in Israel?"

When he heard this, he agreed to their words and took the ephod, the idols, and the carved image and went with them. When they had gone and placed the children, the cattle, and all their precious things before them, and were already a little way from the house of Micah, the men who lived in the houses near Micah cried out and followed behind Dan...

When the children of Israel saw this while in the heat of battle—for the children of Benjamin thought they were fleeing and had already killed thirty of their men—they saw as it were a column of smoke rising from the city. The Benjaminites, looking back, saw the city captured and the flames carried into the heights. Those who had previously feigned flight now turned their faces and resisted strongly. When the children of Benjamin saw this, they turned to flight and took the way of the desert. Their adversaries pursued them there also. But those who had burned the city also met them, and so it happened that they were slaughtered by the enemy from both sides, and there was no rest for those about to die. The next day, rising at dawn, they built an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and they said: "Who did not come up in the army of the Lord from all the tribes of Israel?" For they had made a great oath against those who had not gone up to the Lord at Mizpah, that they should die. For we have all sworn in the name of the Lord that we will not give them our daughters." Therefore they said: "Who is there from all the tribes of Israel who did not go up to the Lord at Mizpah?" And behold, it was found that the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead had not been in that army. When the census was taken in Shiloh, none of them were found.

# OF RUTH
## IN THE DAYS OF ONE <note>Refers to the era "in the days when the judges ruled."</note>

In the days when the judges ruled, a famine occurred in the land. A man from Bethlehem in Judah went to travel in the region of Moab with his wife and two children. He was named Elimelech, and his wife Naomi; his two sons were named Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. Entering the region of Moab, they stayed there. And Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died; and she remained with her sons. They took wives from Moab, one of whom was called Orpah, the other Ruth. They stayed there ten years. And both Mahlon and Chilion died; and the woman remained, bereaved of her two children and her husband. 

She arose to return to her homeland from the region of Moab with both her daughters-in-law. For she had heard that the Lord had looked upon his people and given them food. So she went out from the place of her pilgrimage with both daughters-in-law. And while on the way to return to the land of Judah, she said to them: "Go to the house of your mothers. May the Lord deal mercifully with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me. May He grant you to find rest in the houses of the husbands you shall marry." And she kissed them. They lifted up their voices and began to weep and say: "We will go with you to your people." 

To whom she replied: "Return, my daughters. Why do you come with me? Do I have sons in my womb that you might hope for husbands from them? Return, my daughters, and go; for I am now consumed by old age and not fit for the bond of marriage. Even if I could conceive and bear sons this night, would you want to wait until they grow up and fulfill the years of puberty? You would be old before you could marry. Do not, I pray you, my daughters; for your distress weighs more heavily on me, as the hand of the Lord has gone out against me." 

Lifting up their voices, they began to weep again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and returned; but Ruth clung to her mother-in-law. Naomi said to her: "Behold, your kinswoman has returned to her people and to her gods; go with her." She replied: "Do not press me to leave and go away. Wherever you stay, I will stay. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. The land that receives you in death, in that land I shall die, and there I shall take my place of burial." Naomi, seeing that Ruth had determined with an obstinate mind to go with her, did not wish to oppose her further or persuade her to return to her own. 

They set out together and came to Bethlehem. When they entered the city, a swift report sounded among everyone. The women said: "Is this that Naomi?" To whom she said: "Do not call me Naomi, which means **Beautiful**; but call me Mara, which means **Bitter**, for the Almighty has filled me with great bitterness. I went out full, and the Lord has brought me back empty. Why then do you call me Naomi, whom the Lord has humbled and the Almighty has afflicted?"

So Naomi came with Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, from the land of her pilgrimage. They returned to Bethlehem when the barley was first being harvested. Now Elimelech had a kinsman, a powerful man of great wealth named Boaz. Ruth the Moabite said to her mother-in-law: "If you permit, I will go into the field and gather the ears of grain that escape the hands of the reapers <note>The practice of "gleaning," where the poor were legally allowed to pick up leftovers in the field.</note> if I find favor in the eyes of a merciful leader." She replied: "Go, my daughter." 

So she went and gathered ears of grain behind the backs of the reapers. It happened that the owner of that field was Boaz, who was of the lineage of Elimelech. And behold, he came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers: "The Lord be with you." They answered: "May the Lord bless you." Boaz said to the young man in charge of the reapers: "Whose girl is this?" He replied: "This is the Moabite who came with Naomi from the region of Moab. She asked to gather the remaining ears following the footsteps of the reapers, and from morning until now she has stood in the field, and she has not returned home even for a moment." 

And Boaz said to Ruth: "Listen, daughter. Do not go to gather in another field, nor leave this place, but join my girls and follow where they reap. For I have commanded my servants that no one should be troublesome to you. If you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink the water from which the servants drink." Falling on her face, she bowed to the ground and said to him: "How is it that I have found such favor in your eyes, that you should deign to know me, a foreign woman?" 

He replied: "Everything you have done for your mother-in-law after the death of your husband has been reported to me: how you left your parents and the land in which you were born, and came to a people whom before 

<meta>catchword: whom before</meta>

<column-break/>

you did not know. May the Lord repay you for your work, and may you receive a full reward from the Lord God of Israel, to whom you have come and under whose wings you have taken refuge." She said: "I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have consoled me and spoken to the heart of your servant, though I am not like one of your maidservants."

Boaz said to her: "When it is time to eat, come here and eat bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar." So she sat at the side of the reapers, and he heaped up <term>polenta</term> <note>Roasted grain, a common food for laborers.</note> for her. She ate and was satisfied, and took the leftovers. Then she rose to gather grain according to custom. Boaz commanded his servants, saying: "Even if she wishes to reap with you, do not forbid her. And purposely throw down handfuls from your bundles and let them remain so she may gather them without shame, and let no one rebuke her while she gathers." 

So she gathered in the field until evening. Beating and threshing what she had gathered with a rod, she found about an <term>ephah</term> <note>A dry measure roughly equal to 22 liters or 3/5 of a bushel.</note> of barley, which is three <term>modii</term>. Carrying this, she returned to the city and showed it to her mother-in-law. Moreover, she brought out and gave her the leftovers of the food with which she had been satisfied.

Her mother-in-law said to her: "Where did you gather today, and where did you work? Blessed be he who had pity on you!" She indicated where she had worked and said the man's name was Boaz. Naomi replied: "May he be blessed by the Lord, because he has kept the same kindness toward the living that he showed to the dead." And the mother-in-law said again: "The man is our relative and <term>redeemer</term> <note>original: "eruch," referring to the 'Goel' or kinsman-redeemer who had the right to buy back family land.</note>." Ruth said: "He also told me this: 'Stay with my reapers until all the harvests are gathered.'" Her mother-in-law said: "It is better, my daughter, that you go out with his girls to the harvest, lest someone resist you in another field." 

So she stayed with Boaz's girls and reaped with them until the barley and wheat were stored in the barns. After she returned to her mother-in-law, she heard from her: "My daughter, I shall seek a place where you may rest. Behold, Boaz is by right our kinsman; his reapers are our relatives. Tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor. Wash yourself, therefore, and anoint yourself, and put on your better clothes, and go down to the threshing floor. Let no man see you until he has finished eating and drinking. But when he goes to sleep, note the place where he sleeps, and uncover the cloak covering his feet and lie down. He himself will tell you what you ought to do." She answered: "Whatever you command, I will do."

She went down to the floor and did everything her mother-in-law had commanded. When Boaz had eaten and drunk and become more cheerful, and had gone to sleep next to the heap of grain bundles, she came secretly and, uncovering the cloak from his feet, she lay down. And behold, in the middle of the night, the man was startled and troubled. Seeing a woman lying at his feet, he said to her: "Who are you?" She replied: "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your cloak over your maidservant, for you are a kinsman." 

And he said: "Blessed be you by the Lord, daughter; you have surpassed your earlier kindness with this later one, for you have not followed young men, whether poor or rich. Do not fear; whatever you say, I will do for you. For all the people who live within the gates of my city know you are a virtuous woman. Nor do I deny I am a kinsman, but there is another closer than I. Stay this night, and in the morning, if he wishes to retain you by the right of kinship, the matter is settled well. But if he is unwilling, I will take you without any doubt, as the Lord lives. Sleep until morning."

So she slept at his feet until near dawn. She rose before people could recognize one another, and Boaz said: "Take care that no one knows you came here." And again he said: "Spread out the cloak you are wearing and hold it with both hands." When she extended and held it, he measured out six <term>modii</term> of barley and placed it upon her. Carrying it, she entered the city and came to her mother-in-law, who said to her: "How did you fare, daughter?" She told her everything the man had done for her and said: "Behold, he gave me six measures of barley, saying: 'I do not want you to return empty to your mother-in-law.'" Naomi said: "Wait, daughter, until we see what end the matter has. For the man will not rest until he has fulfilled what he spoke." 

So Boaz went up to the gate and sat there. When he saw the kinsman passing by of whom he had previously spoken, he said to him: "Turn aside for a moment and sit here," calling him by his name. He turned and sat. Then Boaz took ten men from the elders of the city and said to them: "Sit here." When they were seated, he spoke to the kinsman: "Naomi, who has returned from the region of Moab, is selling a portion of the field of our brother Elimelech. I want you to hear this and I tell you before all the witnesses and the elders of my people. If you wish to possess it by right of kinship, buy it and possess it. But if it displeases you, judge this for me so I may know what I ought to do. For there is no kinsman except you who is first, and I who am second." 

He replied: "I will buy the field." Boaz said to him: "When you buy the field from the hand of the woman Ruth the Moabite, who was the wife of the deceased, you must also take her as a wife, to raise up the name of his kinsman in his inheritance." He replied: "I cede the right of kinship, for I must not lose the posterity of my own family. You use my right and privilege, which I profess to freely forfeit."

Now this was an ancient custom in Israel among kinsmen: that if one ceded a right to another, to make the cession firm, the man would take off his shoe and give it to his neighbor. This was the testimony of a cession in Israel. The kinsman said to Boaz: "Take off the shoe." He immediately loosened it from his foot. And Boaz said to the elders and all the people: "You are witnesses this day that I have acquired today all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon from the hand of Naomi; and I have taken Ruth the Moabite, the wife of Mahlon, in marriage, to raise up the name of the deceased in his inheritance, so his name may not be deleted from his family and his brothers. You, I say, are witnesses of this thing." 

All the people at the gate and the elders replied: "We are witnesses. May the Lord make this woman who enters your house like Rachel and Leah, who built the house of Israel, so she may be an example of virtue in Ephrata and have a famous name in Bethlehem. And may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, from the seed the Lord shall give you from this young girl."

So Boaz took Ruth and made her his wife. He went in to her, and the Lord granted her conception, and she bore a son. The women said to Naomi: "Blessed be the Lord, who has not allowed a successor to your family to fail, and may his name be called in Israel. May you have one who consoles your soul and nourishes your old age. For he is born of your daughter-in-law who loves you, and who is much better to you than if you had seven sons." Naomi took the child and placed him in her bosom, and performed the office of nurse and carrier. The neighboring women, congratulating her...

<image-desc>A large ornamental initial 'N' decorated with intertwined vine patterns and animal/mythological figures in blue, red, and green.</image-desc>

**N**o one should think, when they see the prophets written in verses, that they are bound by meter among the Hebrews, or that they have anything similar to the Psalms or the works of Solomon. Rather, as usually happens with the works of Demosthenes <note>A famous Greek orator.</note> and Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note>, they are written in <term>cola and commata</term> <note>original: "cola & commata"; these are rhythmic divisions of prose used to aid breathing and clarity when reading aloud.</note>, who certainly wrote in prose and not in verse. We also, providing for the benefit of readers, have distinguished our new translation by a new style of writing. And first, it must be known concerning Isaiah that he is eloquent in his speech, for he was a man of noble birth and urban elegance, having nothing of rustic speech mixed in. From this, it happens that the translation has not been able to preserve the "flower" of his language as well as others. Next, this must also be added: that he should be called an Evangelist rather than just a prophet. For he has so clearly followed all the mysteries of Christ and the Church that you would think he was not prophesying about the future, but weaving a history of the past. From this, I gather that the authors of that time <note>Jerome is likely referring to the Jewish scholars who translated the Septuagint.</note> did not wish to publish the sacred mysteries of their faith clearly in this volume, lest they "give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine." <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6.</note> You should not ignore how great a labor it is to understand the prophets; no one can easily judge a translation unless they have first understood the ancient readings. We are exposed to the bites of many who, stimulated by envy, despise what they cannot achieve. Therefore, knowing and prudent, I put my hand into the flame. Nevertheless, I pray to these fastidious laborers: just as the Greeks, after the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX) translators.</note>, now read Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion <note>Alternative Greek translations of the Old Testament used in the early Church.</note> either for the study of their doctrine or to better understand the Seventy, so let these people at least deign to have a single translator after their predecessors. Let them read first and despise afterward, lest they seem to condemn things unknown, not out of judgment, but out of a presumption of hatred. The prophet Isaiah, moreover, preached in Jerusalem and Judea, before the ten tribes were led into captivity. <note>The OCR text here contains some garbled phrases regarding his death and burial.</note> Isaiah was of noble birth in Jerusalem; there he prophesied until he suffered a shared death under King Manasseh, being sawn apart. He was buried under the oak of Rogel <note>likely En-rogel</note> near the passage of waters which King Hezekiah had once blocked by building over them.

Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken. "I have nourished and brought up children, but they have despised and rejected me. The ox knows his owner,

<column-break/>

and the donkey his master’s crib; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood." Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity, a wicked seed, ungodly children! They have forsaken the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, they have turned away backward. Why should you be struck anymore, you who increase transgression? The whole head is faint, and the whole heart is grieving. From the sole of the foot even to the top of the head, there is no soundness in it. Wounds and bruises and swelling sores are not bound up, nor cured with medicine, nor soothed with oil. Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire. Strangers devour your region before your face, and it shall be desolate as in a hostile invasion. And the daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field—like a city that is wasted. Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom, and we would have been similar to Gomorrah. Hear the word of the Lord, you princes of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah. "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?" says the Lord. "I am full. I did not want burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fatlings, and the blood of calves, and of lambs, and of goats. When you come before my sight, who has required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Offer sacrifice in vain no longer. Incense is an abomination to me. The new moon and the Sabbath and other festivals I will not bear. Your assemblies are wicked. My soul hates your new moons and your solemnities. They have become a burden to me; I am weary of bearing them. And when you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear you. Your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, be clean. Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes. Cease to do perversely. Learn to do well. Seek judgment, help the oppressed, judge for the fatherless, defend the widow. And come and accuse me," says the Lord. "If your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they be red like crimson, they shall be like white wool. If you are willing and will listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling, and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you, because the mouth of the Lord has spoken." How has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a harlot? Justice once lived in it, but now murderers. Your silver has turned to dross; your wine is mixed with water. Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves. They all love bribes and follow after rewards. They do not judge for the fatherless, and the cause of the widow does not reach them. Therefore the Lord of Hosts, the Strong One of Israel, says: "Alas! I will be comforted over my enemies, and I will be avenged of my foes. And I will turn my hand to you, and I will boil away your dross until it is pure, and I will take away all your tin. And I will restore your judges as they were before, and your counselors as in ancient times. After these things, you shall be called the City of the Just, the Faithful City." Zion shall be redeemed in judgment, and they shall bring her back in justice. And He shall crush the wicked and the sinners together, and those who have forsaken the Lord shall be consumed. For they shall be confounded by the idols to which you sacrificed, and you shall be ashamed of the gardens you had chosen, when you shall be like an oak with falling leaves, and like a garden without water. And your strength shall be like a spark of tow <note>The coarse part of flax or hemp.</note>, and your work like a spark; and both shall burn together, and there shall be no one to extinguish it.

The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. And many people shall go and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths." For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they exercise anymore for war. O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord. For you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob, because they are filled as in former times, and have had soothsayers like the Philistines, and have clung to foreign children. The land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to its treasures. And its land is filled with horses, and its chariots are innumerable. And the land is filled with idols. They have adored the work of their own hands, which their fingers have made. And man is bowed down, and the man is humbled. Do not forgive them! Enter into the rock, hide in a pit in the ground from the face of the fear of the Lord, and from the glory of his majesty. The lofty eyes of man are humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down. But the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. Because the day of the Lord of Hosts shall be upon everyone who is proud and high, and upon everyone who is arrogant, and he shall be humbled. And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, high and erect, and upon all the oaks of Bashan, and upon all the high and elevated mountains, and upon all the high hills, and upon every fortified wall, and upon every ship of Tarshish, and upon everything that is beautiful to the sight. And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the height of men shall be humbled. And the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. And idols shall be utterly crushed. And they shall enter into the caves of the rocks and into the pits of the earth, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to judge the earth.
In that day, a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his images of gold, which he had made for himself to adore, to the moles and the bats. And he shall enter into the clefts of the rocks and into the caverns of the stones from the face of the fear of our Lord, and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth. Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he himself is reputed to be high.

<margin>III</margin>
For behold, the Sovereign Lord of Hosts shall take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the valiant and the strong: all the strength of bread and all the strength of water; the strong man and the man of war, the judge and the prophet, and the soothsayer and the elder; the captain over fifty, and the honorable of face, and the wise counselor among architects, and the prudent in mystical speech. And I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them. And the people shall rush man against man, each one against his neighbor. The child shall riot against the elder, and the base against the noble. For a man shall take hold of his brother, a member of his father’s house, saying: "You have clothing; be our prince, and let this ruin be under your hand." And he shall answer in that day, saying: "I am no healer; and in my house is neither bread nor clothing; do not appoint me prince of the people." For Jerusalem is ruined, and Judah has fallen, because their tongue and their inventions are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty. The look of their face testifies against them; and they have proclaimed their sin like Sodom, nor have they hidden it. Woe to their soul, for evils have been repaid to them! Say to the just man that it is well, for he shall eat the fruit of his inventions. Woe to the wicked man in his evil; for the reward of his hands shall be done to him. As for my people, their oppressors have spoiled them, and women have ruled over them.
O my people, those who call you blessed, they themselves deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps. The Lord stands up to judge, and he stands to be judged...

It shall not be pruned and it shall not be dug; and briars and thorns shall come up; and I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. **I**n the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and elevated; and those things that were under him filled the temple. Seraphim <note>A high order of angels associated with fire and purification.</note> stood upon it: one had six wings, and the other had six wings. Because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of hosts. And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth, and said: Behold, this has touched your lips, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed. Every man shall eat the flesh of his own arm: Manasseh shall eat Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; and together they shall be against Judah. In all these things his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.

**W**oe to those who decree wicked laws, and those who write, have written injustice: to oppress the poor in judgment, and to do violence to the cause of the humble of my people: so that widows might be their prey, and they might rob the orphans. What will you do in the day of visitation, and of the calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee? And where will you leave your glory, so that you do not bow down under the bond, and fall with the slain? In all these things his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger and the staff; in their hands is my indignation. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and I will give him a charge against the people of my wrath: to take the spoils, and to seize the prey, and to tread them down like the mud of the streets. But he will not think so; and his heart will not judge it so. But his heart shall be set to destroy, and to cut off many nations. For he says: Are not my princes all kings? Is not Carchemish like Calno? Is not Arpad like Hamath? Is not Damascus like Samaria? As my hand has found the kingdoms of the idol, so also their graven images of Jerusalem and Samaria. Shall I not, as I have done to Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her statues? And it shall come to pass, when the Lord has performed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem: I will visit <note>In this context, "visit" means to bring judgment or punishment upon.</note> the fruit of the haughty heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of the highness of his eyes. For he has said: By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood; and I have removed the boundaries of the peoples, and I have plundered their princes. And I have pulled down like a mighty man those sitting on high: and my hand has found the wealth of the peoples like a nest. And as eggs are gathered that are left behind, so have I gathered all the earth: and there was none that moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn? As if a rod should lift itself up against him that lifts it, or a staff should exalt itself, which is but wood! Because of this, the Sovereign Lord of hosts shall send leanness among his fat ones: and under his glory there shall burn a burning like the consumption of fire. And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall be kindled, and devour his thorns and briers in one day. The consumption shall be from brevity; it shall consume even to the flesh. And he shall be terrified with terror as if by a scythe(?), because of the smallness of the number; and a child shall write them down.

<margin>30.</margin>
**A**nd it shall come to pass in that day, the remnant of Israel, and those who have escaped from the house of Jacob, shall no more lean upon him who struck them: but they shall lean upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. The remnant shall return; the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them shall return. The consumption decreed shall overflow with justice. For the Lord God of hosts shall make a consumption and a shortening in the midst of all the land. Therefore, thus says the Lord God of hosts: O my people who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of Assyria. He shall strike you with a rod, and lift up his staff over you, in the way of Egypt. For yet a very little while, and my indignation and my wrath shall be accomplished upon their wickedness. And the Lord of hosts shall stir up a scourge against him, according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb: and his rod shall be over the sea, and he shall lift it up in the way of Egypt. And it shall come to pass in that day, that his burden shall be taken away from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck, and the yoke shall rot from the presence of the oil <note>original: "a facie olei"; this is often interpreted as the "anointing" that breaks the yoke of bondage.</note>. He is come to Aiath, he has passed into Migron; at Michmash he has stored his baggage. They have passed over the crossing; Geba is our seat. Ramah was astonished; Gibeah of Saul has fled. Cry out with your voice, O daughter of Gallim; listen, O Laish; poor Anathoth. Madmenah has moved away; the inhabitants of Gebim, strengthen yourselves. There is yet a day that he may stand at Nob. He shall shake his hand against the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. Behold, the Sovereign Lord of hosts shall break the vessel in terror: and those of high stature shall be cut down, and the lofty shall be humbled. And the thickets of the forest shall be cut down with iron, and Lebanon shall fall with its mighty ones.

<margin>33.</margin>
**A**nd there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse: and a flower shall rise up from his root. And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety. And he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord. He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears: but he shall judge the poor with justice, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth. And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked. And justice shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins. The wolf shall dwell with the lamb: and the leopard shall lie down with the kid. The calf and the lion and the sheep shall abide together: and a little child shall lead them. The calf and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall rest together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. And the infant shall play over the hole of the asp: and the weaned child shall put his hand in the den of the basilisk. They shall not hurt, nor shall they kill in all my holy mountain: for the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea. In that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples, him the Gentiles shall beseech; and his sepulcher shall be glorious. And it shall come to pass in that day, the Lord shall set his hand a second time to possess the remnant of his people, which shall be left from the Assyrians, and from Egypt, and from Ethiopia, and from the Elamites, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He shall set up a sign to the nations, and shall gather the outcasts of Israel, and collect the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. And the envy of Ephraim shall be taken away, and the enemies of Judah shall perish. Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not fight against Ephraim.

<column-break/>

And they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines by the sea; together they shall plunder the children of the east. Edom and Moab shall be under the reach of their hand, and the children of Ammon shall be obedient. And the Lord shall desolate the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall lift up his hand over the river in the strength of his spirit. And he shall strike it into seven streams, so that men may pass through it in their shoes. And there shall be a highway for the remnant of my people that shall be left from the Assyrians: as it was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt.

<margin>Heart. 30. <note>likely referring to Chapter 12</note></margin>
**I** will confess to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me; your wrath is turned away, and you have comforted me. Behold, God is my savior: I will act confidently, and I will not fear. Because the Lord is my strength and my praise; and he is become my salvation. You shall draw waters with joy out of the savior's fountains: and you shall say in that day: Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name. Make his inventions known among the people; remember that his name is high. Sing to the Lord because he has done magnificently; announce this in all the earth. Exult and praise, O habitation of Zion, for great in the midst of you is the Holy One of Israel.

<margin>Chap. XIII.</margin>
**T**he burden of Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. Upon the dark mountain lift up a sign; exalt the voice; lift up the hand, and let the leaders enter the gates. I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have called my strong ones in my wrath, those who exult in my glory. The noise of a multitude in the mountains, as of a crowded people. The voice of the sound of kings of nations gathered together. The Lord of hosts has commanded the army of the war coming from a far country, from the foundation of heaven: the Lord and the vessels of his wrath, to destroy the whole land. Howl, for the day of the Lord is near; it shall come as a waste from the Lord. Therefore all hands shall be dissolved: and every heart of man shall melt and be broken. Tortures and pains shall take hold; they shall be in pain as a woman in labor. Each one shall be amazed at his neighbor; their faces shall be as burnt countenances.

**B**ehold, the day of the Lord shall come, cruel and full of indignation, and of wrath and fury: to lay the land desolate, and to crush the sinners thereof out of it. For the stars of heaven and their brightness shall not display their light. The sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not shine in its light. And I will visit the evils upon the world, and against the wicked their iniquity. And I will make the pride of the unfaithful to cease, and I will humble the arrogance of the mighty. A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold. Over this I will trouble the heaven, and the earth shall be moved out of its place, because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts, and because of the day of his fierce wrath. And it shall be as a fleeing doe and as a sheep: and there shall be no one to gather them. Everyone shall turn to his own people, and each shall flee to his own land. Everyone who is found shall be killed: and all who come upon them shall fall by the sword. Their infants shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be plundered, and their wives shall be ravished. Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who do not seek silver, nor desire gold: but with their arrows they shall punish the little ones, and they shall have no pity on the sucklings of the womb: and their eye shall not spare the children. And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, famous in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be even as the Lord subverted Sodom and Gomorrah. It shall not be inhabited forever, and it shall not be founded from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch his tents there, nor shall shepherds rest there. But wild beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with dragons: and ostriches shall dwell there, and the hairy ones <note>original: "pilosi"; likely referring to satyrs or wild goats</note> shall dance there. And owls shall answer one another in her houses, and sirens in the shrines of pleasure. Its time is near to come, and its days shall not be prolonged. For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose out of Israel, and make them rest upon their own ground. The stranger shall be joined to them, and shall adhere to the house of Jacob. And the people shall take them and bring them into their place. And the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the Lord for servants and handmaids: and they shall take those captive who had taken them, and shall subdue their oppressors.

**A**nd it shall come to pass in that day, when the Lord God shall have given you rest from your labor, and from your confusion, and from the hard bondage wherewith you served before, you shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and say: How has the oppressor ceased, how has the tribute rested? The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers that struck the people in indignation with an incurable wound, that subdued the nations in fury, persecuting them cruelly. All the earth is quiet and still; it has rejoiced and exulted. The fir trees also have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying: Since you have slept, no one comes up to cut us down. Hell <note>original: "infernus"; the underworld or Sheol</note> below was troubled at your coming to meet you. It stirred up the giants for you. All the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones, all the princes of the nations. All shall answer and say to you: You also are wounded as we are; you are become like us. Your pride is brought down to hell; your carcass has fallen. The moth shall be spread under you, and worms shall be your covering.

<margin>Chap. XIIII.</margin>
**H**ow have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer <note>original: "lucifer," meaning "light-bringer" or the "morning star"; historically referring to the King of Babylon, later associated with the fall of Satan.</note>, who rose in the morning? You are fallen to the earth, you who did wound the nations: who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God. I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north. I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High. But yet you shall be brought down to hell, into the depth of the pit. Those who see you shall lean toward you and look closely at you: Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms; who made the world a desert, and destroyed its cities, and did not open the prison for his prisoners? All the kings of the nations have slept in glory, every man in his own house. But you are cast out of your grave, like an unprofitable branch, polluted and wrapped among those who were slain by the sword, and have gone down to the foundations of the pit, like a rotting carcass; you shall not have a companion, nor even a burial. For you have destroyed your land, you have killed your people. The seed of the wicked shall not be named forever. Prepare his children for slaughter for the iniquity of their fathers. Let them not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts: and I will perish from Babylon the name, and the remains, and the bud, and the progeny, says the Lord. And I will make it a possession for the hedgehog, and into pools of waters. And I will sweep it with a broom, wearing it away, says the Lord of hosts.

The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: If it be not as I have thought, so it shall be; and as I have reasoned in my mind, so it shall come to pass: that I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and upon my mountains I will tread him under foot. And his yoke shall be taken away from them, and his burden from their shoulder. This is the counsel that I have thought over all the earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who can weaken it? And his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it away?

In the year that King Ahaz died, this burden was made. Rejoice not, all you Philistia, because the rod of him that struck you is broken. For out of the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, and its seed shall be a devouring flying creature. And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the poor shall rest confidently.

...rivers. And I clothe them with my garment: and I have placed sackcloth as their covering. The Lord has given me a learned tongue: so that I might know how to sustain the one who is weary with a word. He awakens me morning by morning, he awakens my ear: that I might listen as a student <note>original: "quasi magistrum", literally "as a master/teacher," but in this context meaning to learn from a master</note>. The Lord God has opened my ear: I do not resist, nor have I turned back. I gave my body to those who strike me, and my cheeks to those who pluck my beard: I have not turned my face away from insults and spitting. The Lord God is my helper: therefore I am not disgraced.
