...had been the priests of the Lord. And the day came, and Elkanah sacrificed; and he gave portions to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave one portion sadly, for he loved Hannah. But the Lord had closed her womb. Her rival <note>Peninnah</note> also afflicted her, and troubled her exceedingly, even so far as to upbraid her for the Lord having closed her womb. And so she did every year, when the time returned for them to go up to the temple of the Lord; and thus she provoked her. But Hannah wept, and did not take food. Then Elkanah her husband said to her: "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart afflicted? Am I not better to you than ten sons?"

So Hannah rose up after she had eaten and drunk in Shiloh. And Eli the priest was sitting upon a seat before the doorposts of the temple of the Lord. And as Hannah was in bitterness of soul, she prayed to the Lord, weeping abundantly; and she made a vow, saying: "O Lord of hosts, if you will indeed look upon the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, and will give to your servant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head." And it happened, as she multiplied her prayers before the Lord, that Eli observed her mouth. For Hannah spoke in her heart, and only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard at all. Eli therefore thought her to be drunk, and said to her: "How long will you be drunk? Digest a little of the wine with which you are soaked." Hannah answering, said: "Not so, my lord; for I am an exceedingly unhappy woman. I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can make one drunk, but I have poured out my soul in the sight of the Lord. Do not count your handmaid as one of the daughters of Belial <note>original: "filia belial," a term meaning a wicked or worthless woman</note>, for out of the abundance of my sorrow and grief have I spoken until now." And Eli said to her: "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant you the petition which you have asked of Him." And she said: "Would that your handmaid may find grace in your eyes." And the woman went on her way, and ate, and her countenance was no longer changed. And they rose early in the morning, and worshipped before the Lord; and they returned, and came into their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and the Lord remembered her.

And it happened after a circle of days that Hannah conceived and bore a son, and called his name Samuel <note>meaning "Asked of God"</note>, because she had asked him of the Lord. And the man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the Lord the solemn sacrifice and his vow. But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband: "I will not go until the infant is weaned, and then I will lead him, and he may appear before the sight of the Lord, and remain there perpetually." And Elkanah her husband said to her: "Do what seems good to you, and stay until you have weaned him; and I pray that the Lord may fulfill His word." So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him. And she took him with her, after she had weaned him, with three calves, and three measures of flour, and a jar of wine, and she brought him to the house of the Lord in Shiloh. But the boy was still a young child. And they sacrificed a calf, and offered the boy to Eli. And Hannah said: "I beseech you, my lord, as your soul lives, I am that woman who stood before you here praying to the Lord. For this child I prayed, and the Lord has granted me my petition which I asked of Him. Therefore I have also lent him to the Lord; all the days he shall be lent to the Lord." And they worshipped the Lord there. And Hannah prayed, and said:

# My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn <note>a symbol of strength and status</note> is exalted in my God.
My mouth is enlarged over my enemies, because I have joyed in your salvation. There is none holy as the Lord is; for there is no other besides you, and there is none strong like our God. Do not multiply speaking high things, boasting. Let old things depart from your mouth, for the Lord is a God of all knowledge, and to Him thoughts are prepared. The bow of the mighty is overcome, and the weak are girt with strength. Those who were full before have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry are filled. Until the barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has become weak. The Lord brings death and gives life; He leads down to hell <note>original: "inferos," the place of the dead</note> and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and He lifts up. He raises up the needy from the dust, and lifts up the poor from the dunghill, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and He has set the world upon them. He will keep the feet of His saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness, because no man shall be strengthened by his own might. The adversaries of the Lord shall fear Him, and upon them shall He thunder in the heavens. The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and He shall give empire to His king, and shall exalt the horn of His Christ <note>original: "christi sui," meaning His anointed one</note>. And Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house; but the boy was a minister in the sight of the Lord before the face of Eli the priest.

# Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial <note>wicked men</note>, not knowing the Lord, nor the office of the priests to the people. But whenever anyone had offered a sacrifice, the servant of the priest would come while the flesh was boiling, and he had a three-pronged flesh-hook in his hand, and he thrust it into the cauldron, or into the kettle, or into the pot, or into the pan; and all that the flesh-hook brought up, the priest took for himself. So they did to all Israel that came to Shiloh. Also before they burnt the fat, the servant of the priest came and said to the one sacrificing: "Give me meat to boil for the priest; for I will not take boiled meat from you, but raw." And the one sacrificing said to him: "Let the fat first be burnt today according to the custom, and then take as much as your soul desires." But he answering would say to him: "Not so; but you shall give it now, or else I will take it by force." Therefore the sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, because they brought men to withdraw from the sacrifice of the Lord. But Samuel ministered before the face of the Lord, being a boy girded with a linen ephod <note>a priestly garment</note>. And his mother made him a little coat, which she brought to him on the appointed days, going up with her husband to offer the solemn sacrifice. And Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, and said: "May the Lord give you seed from this woman for the loan you have made to the Lord." And they went to their own place. And the Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters; and the boy Samuel was magnified before the Lord.

# Now Eli was very old, and he heard all that his sons did to all Israel, and how they slept with the women who waited at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony. And he said: "Why do you do such things, very wicked things, which I hear from all the people? Do not, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear, that you make the Lord's people transgress. If a man sins against a man, the Lord may be appeased for him; but if a man sins against the Lord, who shall pray for him?" And they did not hear the voice of their father, because the Lord would slay them. But the boy Samuel went on and grew, and pleased both God and men. And there came a man of God to Eli, and said to him: "Thus says the Lord: Did I not plainly reveal myself to your father's house, when they were in Egypt in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, and burn incense to me, and to wear 

<column-break/>

the ephod before me; and I gave to your father's house all the sacrifices of the children of Israel. Why have you kicked away my victims and my gifts which I commanded should be offered in the temple? And why have you honored your sons more than me, so that you eat the first-fruits of every sacrifice of Israel my people? Therefore the Lord the God of Israel says: I spoke indeed, that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me; but whoever honors me, I will glorify him, and those who despise me shall be base. Behold, the days come, and I will cut off your arm, and the arm of your father's house, so that there shall not be an old man in your house. And you shall see your rival in the temple, in all the prosperity of Israel; and there shall not be an old man in your house for all days. Nevertheless, I will not altogether take away a man of yours from my altar, but so that your eyes may fail and your soul melt; and a great part of your house shall die when they come to man’s estate. And this shall be a sign to you, that shall come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they shall both die. And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to my heart and my soul; and I will build him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Anointed <note>original: "christo meo"</note> for all days. And it shall come to pass, that whoever remains in your house shall come to be prayed for, and shall offer a piece of silver and a roll of bread, and shall say: Put me, I beseech you, into one part of the priestly office, that I may eat a morsel of bread."

# Now the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious in those days; there was no manifest vision. And it happened one day, Eli lay in his place, and his eyes had grown dim, so that he could not see. And before the lamp of God went out, Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. And the Lord called Samuel. And he answering said: "Here I am." And he ran to Eli and said: "Here I am, for you called me." And he said: "I did not call you; return and sleep." And he went and slept. And the Lord called Samuel again. And Samuel arose and went to Eli, and said: "Here I am, because you called me." And he answered: "I did not call you, my son; return and sleep." Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord been revealed to him. And the Lord called Samuel again the third time. And he arose and went to Eli, and said: "Here I am, because you called me." Then Eli understood that the Lord called the boy, and he said to Samuel: "Go and sleep; and if He calls you hereafter, you shall say: Speak, Lord, for your servant hears." So Samuel went and slept in his place. And the Lord came and stood, and called as He had called before: "Samuel, Samuel." And Samuel said: "Speak, Lord, for your servant hears." And the Lord said to Samuel: "Behold, I do a thing in Israel, which whoever hears, both his ears shall tingle. In that day I will raise up against Eli all the things I have spoken concerning his house; I will begin, and I will make an end. For I have foretold to him that I would judge his house forever because of iniquity, because he knew his sons did wickedly and did not correct them. Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli, that the iniquity of his house shall not be expiated with victims and gifts forever." And Samuel slept until morning, and opened the doors of the house of the Lord. And Samuel feared to tell the vision to Eli. Then Eli called Samuel and said: "Samuel, my son." And he answering said: "I am here." And he asked him: "What is the word that the Lord has spoken to you? I pray you, do not hide it from me. May God do these things to you, and add more, if you hide from me a word of all the words that were spoken to you." So Samuel told him all the words, and did not hide them from him. And he answered: "It is the Lord; let Him do what is good in His eyes." And Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and not one of his words fell to the ground. And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord. And the Lord appeared again in Shiloh, because the Lord had revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh according to the word of the Lord. And the word of Samuel came to all Israel.

# And it came to pass in those days, the Philistines gathered for battle. And Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle, and encamped by the Stone of Help <note>Ebenezer</note>. But the Philistines came to Aphek, and set their army in array against Israel. And when they joined battle, the Philistines turned their backs, and there were slain in that battle, scattered through the fields, about four thousand men. And the people returned to the camp. And the elders of Israel said: "Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord from Shiloh to us, and let it come into the midst of us, that it may save us from the hand of our enemies." So the people sent to Shiloh, and they brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts sitting upon the cherubim; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were with the ark of the covenant of the Lord. And when the ark of the covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel shouted with a great shout, and the earth rang again. And the Philistines heard the sound of the shout, and they said: "What is this sound of a great shout in the camp of the Hebrews?" And they understood that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp. And the Philistines were afraid, saying: "God has come into the camp." And they groaned, saying: "Woe to us! For there was no such great joy yesterday or the day before. Woe to us! Who shall save us from the hand of these high gods? These are the gods that struck Egypt with every plague in the desert. Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you serve the Hebrews as they have served you; take courage and fight." So the Philistines fought, and Israel was struck, and every man fled to his own tent. And there was a very great slaughter, and there fell of Israel thirty thousand footmen. And the ark of God was taken. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died. And a man of Benjamin, running from the army, came to Shiloh that day with his clothes torn and dust sprinkled on his head. And when he had come, Eli sat upon a seat over against the way, watching. For his heart was trembling for the ark of the Lord. And when the man entered the city, he told the news, and all the city wailed. And Eli heard the sound of the outcry, and said: "What is this sound of an uproar?" But he made haste and came, and told Eli. Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes were dim and he could not see. And he said to Eli: "I am he who came from the battle, and I am he who fled from the army today." To whom he said: "What has happened, my son?" And he who brought the news answering, said: "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great ruin among the people; moreover, your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God is taken." And when he had named the ark of the Lord, Eli fell from his seat backward by the door, and his neck being broken, he died. For he was an old man and heavy; and he had judged Israel forty years. And his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near her time. And hearing the news that the ark of the Lord was taken, and her father-in-law was dead, and her husband, she bowed herself and gave birth; for her pains had come upon her.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the early life of Samuel and the Ark of the Covenant, following the transition from Samuel’s birth and his service at Shiloh to the capture of the Ark by the Philistines and its eventual return to Israel, leading into the rise of Saul as the first king.</meta>

The Philistines took the Ark of God and brought it from the Stone of Help <note>Latin: *lapide adiutorii*, also known as Ebenezer</note> into Ashdod. And the Philistines took the Ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon, and they set it next to Dagon <note>The chief deity of the Philistines, often depicted as a fish-god or agricultural deity</note>. When the people of Ashdod rose up the next day at dawn, look—Dagon lay face down on the ground before the Ark of the Lord. They took Dagon and put him back in his place. Again, rising early on the next morning, they found Dagon lying on his face on the ground before the Ark of the Lord. However, the head of Dagon and both palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon remained in its place. For this reason, the priests of Dagon and all who enter his temple do not step upon the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod even to this day. But the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the people of Ashdod, and he destroyed them. Swarms of mice <note>The Latin *ebullierunt* suggests a "boiling over" or swarming of pests</note> broke out in the villages and fields, and there was a great confusion of death in the city and throughout its neighborhoods.

When the men of Ashdod saw this kind of plague, they said: "The Ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, for his hand is harsh upon us and upon our god Dagon." And sending messengers, they gathered all the lords of the Philistines to them and asked: "What shall we do with the Ark of the God of Israel?" The people of Gath responded: "Let the Ark of the God of Israel be carried around." And they carried the Ark of the God of Israel around. But while they were carrying it around, the hand of the Lord brought a very great slaughter upon every city. He struck the men of every city, from the least to the greatest, and tumors <note>Latin: *pudenda*, referring here to painful swellings or hemorrhoids</note> broke out upon them. Therefore, they sent the Ark of God to Ekron. When the Ark of God arrived in Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, saying: "They have brought the Ark of the God of Israel to us, to kill us and our people!" So they sent and gathered all the lords of the Philistines, who said: "Send away the Ark of the God of Israel; let it return to its own place, so that it does not kill us and our people." For there was a fear of death in every city, and the hand of God was very heavy. Even the men who did not die were struck with tumors in their secret parts, and the wailing of every city rose up to heaven.

In the meantime, while the Ark of the Lord was in the land of the Philistines for seven months, the Philistines called for priests and diviners, saying: "What shall we do with the Ark of the Lord? Tell us how we should send it back to its place." They said: "If you send back the Ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but return to him what you owe for your sin. Then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand does not move from you." They asked: "What is it that we must return to him for our offense?" And they answered: "According to the number of the Philistine provinces, you shall make five golden tumors and five golden mice, for the same plague was upon all of you and your lords. You shall make images of your tumors and images of the mice that have devastated the land, and you shall give glory to the God of Israel; perhaps he will lighten his hand from you, and from your gods, and from your land. Why do you harden your hearts, as Egypt and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? Did they not, after he had struck them, let the people go, and they departed? Now therefore, take and make one new cart and two nursing cows upon which no yoke has ever been placed; join them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. You shall take the Ark of the Lord and place it on the cart, and put the golden vessels which you have paid him for your offense into a chest at its side; then send it away to go. And watch: if it goes up by the way of its own borders toward Beth-shemesh, then he has done us this great evil. But if not, we will know that it was not his hand that touched us, but it happened by chance." They did so; and taking two nursing cows, they hitched them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. They placed the Ark of the Lord upon the cart, along with the chest containing the golden mice and the images of the tumors. The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh; they went along one path, lowing as they went, and turned aside neither to the right nor to the left. The lords of the Philistines followed them as far as the borders of Beth-shemesh. Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping wheat in the valley. Raising their eyes, they saw the Ark and were glad to see it. The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stood there. There was a great stone there; they split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the Lord. The Levites took down the Ark of the Lord and the chest that was with it, in which were the golden vessels, and placed them on the large stone. The men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed victims to the Lord that day. The five lords of the Philistines saw this and returned to Ekron that same day. These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the Lord: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron. And the golden mice were according to the number of the Philistine cities in the five provinces, from the fortified city to the unwalled village, as far as the great stone <note>Latin: *Abel magnum*</note> upon which they set the Ark of the Lord, which remained until that day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh. But he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh because they had looked into the Ark of the Lord. He struck seventy men of the people and fifty thousand of the commoners; and the people mourned because the Lord had struck them with a great slaughter. And the men of Beth-shemesh said: "Who is able to stand in the sight of the Lord, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up from us?" They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying: "The Philistines have brought back the Ark of the Lord; come down and bring it up to yourselves."

So the men of Kiriath-jearim came and brought back the Ark of the Lord. They brought it into the house of Abinadab on the hill. They consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the Ark of the Lord. And it happened that from the day the Ark stayed in Kiriath-jearim, many days passed. It was now the twentieth year, and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord. Then Samuel said to the whole house of Israel: "If you are returning to the Lord with all your heart, take away the foreign gods from your midst—the Baals and the Ashtoreths <note>Canaanite deities of storm/fertility and war/love</note>—and prepare your hearts for the Lord. Serve him alone, and he will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines." So the children of Israel took away the Baals and the Ashtoreths and served the Lord alone. Then Samuel said: "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, so that I may pray to the Lord for you." They gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the Lord. They fasted on that day and said there: "We have sinned against the Lord." And Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpah.

<column-break/>

The Philistines heard that the children of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, and the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the children of Israel heard this, they were afraid of the Philistines. They said to Samuel: "Do not cease crying out to the Lord our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines." Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord. Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. As Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines began the battle against Israel; but the Lord thundered with a great crash that day over the Philistines and terrified them, and they were struck down before Israel. The men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down as far as the place below Beth-car. Then Samuel took a stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen; he called the name of that place "The Stone of Help" <note>Ebenezer</note>. He said: "Thus far the Lord has helped us." So the Philistines were humbled, and they did not come into the borders of Israel anymore. The hand of the Lord was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored—from Ekron to Gath—and Israel liberated their borders from the hand of the Philistines. There was also peace between Israel and the Amorites.

Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. Every year he went on a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and he judged Israel in all those places. Then he would return to Ramah, for his house was there, and there he judged Israel. He also built an altar to the Lord there.

But it happened that when Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of the second was Abiah; they were judges in Beersheba. But his sons did not walk in his ways; instead, they turned aside after greed, accepted bribes, and perverted justice. All the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah. They said to him: "Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint for us a king to judge us, just as all the nations have." This word was displeasing in the eyes of Samuel because they said, "Give us a king to judge us." And Samuel prayed to the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel: "Listen to the voice of the people in everything they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them. According to all the works they have done from the day I led them out of Egypt until this day, they have forsaken me and served foreign gods; so they are doing also to you. Now therefore, listen to their voice; however, solemnly warn them and foretell to them the rights of the king who will reign over them."

When Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he spoke them into the ears of the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel: "Listen to their voice and appoint a king for them."

<margin>66.</margin>
There was a man of Benjamin named Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjaminite, a man of great strength. He had a son named Saul, a chosen and goodly man; there was no man among the children of Israel better than he. From his shoulders upward, he stood taller than all the people. Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul’s father, were lost. Kish said to his son Saul: "Take one of the servants with you; rise, go and look for the donkeys." When they had passed through Mount Ephraim and through the land of Shalishah and had not found them, they also passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. They went through the land of Jemini but did not find them. When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to the servant who was with him: "Come, let us return, lest my father stop worrying about the donkeys and become anxious for us." The servant said to him: "Look, there is a man of God in this city, a noble man; everything he says comes true without fail. Let us go there now; perhaps he can tell us about our journey for which we have come." Saul said to his servant: "If we go, what shall we bring to the man? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have no gift to give to the man of God, nor anything else." The servant answered Saul again and said: "Look, I have found in my hand a quarter of a silver shekel; let us give it to the man of God so he may tell us our way." (In the old days in Israel, anyone going to consult God would say: "Come, let us go to the seer." For he who is today called a prophet was in old times called a seer.) Saul said to his servant: "Your word is very good; come, let us go." And they went into the city where the man of God was. As they were climbing the hill to the city, they found girls coming out to draw water and asked them: "Is the seer here?" They answered and said: "He is. Look, he is just ahead of you; hurry now. He came into the city today because there is a sacrifice for the people today on the high place. As you enter the city, you will find him immediately, before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat until he arrives, because he blesses the victim; after that, those who are invited will eat. Now go up, for you will find him today." So they went up into the city. As they were walking in the middle of the city, Samuel appeared, coming out toward them to go up to the high place. Now the Lord had revealed to Samuel’s ear one day before Saul came, saying: "At this very hour tomorrow, I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin; you shall anoint him as leader over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines, for I have looked upon my people; their cry has come to me." When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him: "Look, this is the man I told you about; he shall rule over my people." Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gate and said: "Please tell me, where is the house of the seer?"

Samuel answered him: "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place so that you may eat with me today. I will let you go in the morning, and I will tell you everything that is in your heart. And do not be anxious about the donkeys that were lost three days ago, for they have been found. And for whom is all that is best in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?" Saul answered: "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my family the least among all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken this word to me?" So Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the dining hall...

It also marks the transition to the monarchy as the Israelites demand a king, leading to the introduction of Saul.</summary>

Now, therefore, let us go there, if perhaps he may tell us about our journey for which we have come." Saul said to his servant: "Look, we are going; but what shall we bring to the man of God? The bread is spent in our bags <note>original: *sitarchis*</note>, and there is no gift to give to the man of God, nor do we have anything else." Again the servant answered Saul and said: "Look, I have found in my hand a quarter of a silver shekel <note>original: *stateris argenti*</note>. Let us give it to the man of God so that he may show us our way."

In former times in Israel, everyone going to consult God spoke thus: "Come, let us go to the Seer <note>original: *videntem*</note>." For he who is called a prophet today was called a Seer in former times. Saul said to his servant: "Your word is best. Come, let us go." And they went into the city where the man of God was. As they were climbing the hill to the city, they found girls going out to draw water and said to them: "Is the Seer here?" They answered and said: "He is. Look, he is ahead of you; hurry now. For the people will not eat until he comes, because he blesses the victim, and afterward those who are invited will eat. Therefore, go up now, for today you will find him." 

And they went up into the city. As they were walking in the middle of the city, Samuel appeared to them, coming out toward the high mountain. Now, the Lord had revealed to the ear of Samuel a day before Saul came, saying: "At this very hour tomorrow I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him as leader over my people Israel, and he shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines." When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him: "Look, this is the man of whom I spoke to you; he shall rule over my people." Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gate and said: "Tell me, where is the house of the Seer?" Samuel answered Saul: "I am the Seer. Go up before me to the high place so that you may eat with me today, and I will let you go in the morning, and I will tell you all that is in your heart. And as for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not be anxious, for they have been found. And for whom shall be all the best things of Israel? Shall they not be for you and for all your father’s house?" 

Saul, answering, said: "Am I not a son of Jemini, from the smallest tribe of Israel, and my kin the last among all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why, then, have you spoken this word to me?" So Samuel, taking Saul and his servant, brought them into the dining hall <note>original: *triclinium*</note> and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited. For there were about thirty men. Samuel said to the cook: "Give the portion which I gave to you and told you to set aside with you." The cook took up the shoulder and set it before Saul. Samuel said: "Look, what remained is set before you; eat, for it was intentionally kept for you when I invited the people." And Saul ate with Samuel on that day. They went down from the high place into the town, and he spoke with Saul on the roof. When they rose in the morning and it was already light, Samuel called Saul on the roof, saying: "Rise, that I may send you on your way." Saul rose, and both he and Samuel went out. As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul: "Tell the servant to go on ahead of us and pass by, but you stand still a little while so that I may show you the word of the Lord."

<margin>10.</margin>
**Then** Samuel, taking a vial of oil, poured it over his head and kissed him and said: "Behold, the Lord has anointed you as prince over his inheritance, and you shall deliver his people from the hands of their enemies who are all around them. And this shall be a sign to you that God has anointed you as prince: When you depart from me today, you will find two men near Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin to the south, and they will say to you: 'The donkeys you went to seek have been found; and your father, forgetting the donkeys, is anxious for you and says: What shall I do about my son?' When you depart from there and come further to the oak of Tabor, three men will find you there going up to God at Bethel: one carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another carrying a flask of wine. When they greet you, they will give you two loaves of bread, and you shall receive them from their hand. After these things, you will come to the hill of the Lord where the Philistine outpost is. And when you enter the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, and before them a psaltery, a drum, a flute, and a lyre, and they will be prophesying. And the spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into another man. Therefore, when all these signs happen to you, do whatever your hand finds to do, for the Lord is with you. And you shall go down before me to Gilgal <note>original: *Galgala*</note>, to offer an offering and sacrifice peace victims. You shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you must do." 

When he turned his shoulder to depart from Samuel, God changed his heart, and all these signs came to pass on that day. They came to the aforementioned hill, and look, a troop of prophets met him; and the spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and he prophesied in their midst. All who had known him yesterday and the day before, seeing that he was with the prophets and prophesied, said to one another: "What is this thing that has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" And one said to another: "And who is their father?" Therefore it became a proverb: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" He ceased prophesying and came to the high place. Saul’s uncle said to him and his servant: "Where did you go?" They answered: "To seek the donkeys. When we did not find them, we came to Samuel." Saul’s uncle said to him: "Tell me what Samuel said to you." Saul said to his uncle: "He told us that the donkeys were found." But regarding the matter of the kingdom, he did not tell him what Samuel had spoken to him. 

Samuel called the people together to the Lord at Mizpah <note>original: *Masphat*</note> and said to the children of Israel: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I led Israel out of Egypt and rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kings who afflicted you. But today you have cast away your God, who alone saved you from all your evils and tribulations, and you said: 'No, but set a king over us.' Now therefore, stand before the Lord by your tribes and by your families." Samuel brought forward all the tribes of Israel, and the lot fell to the tribe of Benjamin. He brought forward the tribe of Benjamin and its families, and the lot fell to the family of Matri, and it came down to Saul the son of Kish. They looked for him, and he was not found. After this, they consulted the Lord whether he would come there. The Lord answered: "Look, he is hidden in the house <note>usually translated as "among the baggage"</note>." They ran and brought him from there, and he stood in the midst of the people, and he was taller than all the people from his shoulders upward. Samuel said to all the people: "Surely you see him whom the Lord has chosen, for there is none like him among all the people." And all the people shouted and said: "Long live the king!" <note>original: *vivat rex*</note>. Samuel spoke the law of the kingdom to the people and wrote it in a book and laid it up before the Lord. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home. Saul went to his home in Gibeah <note>original: *Gabaath*</note>, and a part of the army whose hearts God had touched went with him. But the sons of Belial <note>A term meaning "worthless" or "wicked" men</note> said: "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no gifts. But he pretended not to hear.

<margin>11.</margin>
**And** it happened after about a month that Nahash the Ammonite went up and began to fight against Jabesh-Gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash: "Have us as allies and we will serve you." Nahash the Ammonite answered them: "On this condition I will strike a covenant with you: that I may gouge out all your right eyes and make you a disgrace in all Israel." The elders of Jabesh said to him: "Grant us seven days that we may send messengers to all the borders of Israel, and if there is no one to defend us, we will come out to you." The messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and spoke these words in the hearing of the people. All the people lifted up their voices and wept. And look, Saul was coming, following the oxen from the field, and he said: "What is wrong with the people that they are weeping?" And they told him the words of the men of Jabesh. The spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled. Taking both oxen, he cut them into pieces and sent them into all the borders of Israel by the hands of messengers, saying: "Whoever does not come out and follow Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen." Therefore, the fear of the Lord fell upon the people, and they went out as one man. He numbered them in Bezek. There were three hundred thousand of the children of Israel, and thirty thousand men of Judah. They said to the messengers who had come: "Thus you shall say to the men in Jabesh-Gilead: 'Tomorrow there shall be salvation for you when the sun grows hot.'" The messengers went and announced it to the men of Jabesh, who were glad and said: "In the morning we will come out to you, and you shall do to us whatever pleases you." 

On the next day, Saul divided the people into three parts and entered the middle of the camp during the morning watch and struck the Ammonites until the day grew hot. Those who remained were scattered so that not two of them were left together. The people said to Samuel: "Who is it that said, 'Saul shall not reign over us?' Give us the men and we will kill them." Saul said: "No one shall be killed on this day, because today the Lord has worked salvation in Israel." Samuel said to the people: "Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there." All the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord in Gilgal, and they sacrificed peace victims there before the Lord. And Saul 

<column-break/>

and all the men of Israel rejoiced there greatly.
<margin>12.</margin>
**Samuel** said to all Israel: "Look, I have heard your voice according to everything you spoke to me, and I have set a king over you. And now the king walks before you. I have grown old and gray, and my sons are with you. I have lived before you from my youth until this day; here I am. Speak about me before the Lord and before his anointed <note>original: *christo eius*, referring here to the king</note>: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey, if I have slandered anyone, if I have oppressed anyone, if I have accepted a bribe from anyone's hand and despised it today, and I will restore it to you." They said: "You have not slandered us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand." He said to them: "The Lord is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand." And they said: "He is witness." Samuel said to the people: "The Lord, who made Moses and Aaron and led our fathers out of the land of Egypt, is present. Now therefore, stand, that I may contend in judgment against you before the Lord concerning all the mercies of the Lord which he did for you and for your fathers: how Jacob entered Egypt, and your fathers cried to the Lord, and the Lord sent Moses and Aaron and led your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place. 

They forgot the Lord their God, and he delivered them into the hand of Sisera, the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab, and they fought against them. But afterward they cried to the Lord and said: 'We have sinned because we abandoned the Lord and served the Baals and Ashtoreths. Now therefore, deliver us from the hand of our enemies and we will serve you.' And the Lord sent Jerubbaal and Bedan and Jephthah and Samuel and delivered you from the hand of your enemies all around, and you lived confidently. But seeing that Nahash, the king of the children of Ammon, had come against you, you said to me: 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' even though the Lord your God was reigning over you. Now therefore, here is your king whom you have chosen and requested; look, the Lord has given you a king. If you fear the Lord and serve him and hear his voice and do not provoke the mouth of the Lord, both you and the king who reigns over you will be followers of the Lord your God. But if you do not hear the voice of the Lord, but provoke his words, the hand of the Lord will be upon you and upon your fathers. 

And now stand and see this great thing which the Lord is about to do in your sight. Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and he will give thunder <note>original: *voces*, literally "voices"</note> and rain, and you shall know and see that you have done a great evil for yourselves in the sight of the Lord by asking for a king over you." Samuel cried to the Lord, and the Lord gave thunder and rain on that day. All the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel. All the people said to Samuel: "Pray for your servants to the Lord your God that we may not die, for we have added this evil to all our sins, to ask for a king for ourselves." Samuel said to the people: "Do not fear. You have done all this evil; nevertheless, do not turn away from the back of the Lord, but serve the Lord with all your heart. And do not turn aside after vain things which will not profit you or deliver you, because they are vain. For the Lord will not abandon his people for his great name's sake, because the Lord has sworn to make you a people for himself. Far be it from me this sin against the Lord, that I should cease praying for you; I will teach you the good and right way. Only fear the Lord and serve him in truth and with all your heart, for you have seen the magnificent things he has done among you. But if you persevere in malice, both you and your king shall perish together." Saul was thirty years old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years over Israel.

<margin>13.</margin>
**Saul** chose for himself three thousand from Israel: two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and on the mountain of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent back, each to his own tent. Jonathan struck the Philistine outpost which was in Gibeah. When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet throughout all the land, saying: "Let the Hebrews hear." All Israel heard this report: "Saul has struck the Philistine outpost, and Israel has raised itself against the Philistines." The people were called out after Saul to Gilgal. The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen, and the rest of the multitude like the sand which is on the seashore for abundance. They went up and camped in Michmash, to the east of Beth-aven. When the men of Israel saw that they were in a tight spot—for the people were distressed—they hid themselves in caves, in thickets, in rocks, and in holes and pits. 

The Hebrews crossed the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. While Saul was still in Gilgal, all the people who followed him were terrified. He waited seven days according to the appointment of Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people began to slip away from Saul. Saul said: "Bring the burnt offering and the peace offerings to me." And he offered the burnt offering. Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, look—Samuel was coming. Saul went out to meet him to greet him. Samuel said to him: "What have you done?" Saul answered: "Because I saw that the people were slipping away from me, and you had not come by the appointed days, and the Philistines were gathered at Michmash, I said: 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not appeased the face of the Lord.' Compelled by necessity, I offered the burnt offering." 

Samuel said to Saul: "You have acted foolishly; you have not kept the commandments of the Lord your God which he commanded you. If you had not done this, the Lord would have now prepared your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall not stand. The Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart. And the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded." Samuel rose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul numbered the people who were found with him: about six hundred men. Saul and Jonathan his son and the people who were found with them were in Gibeah of Benjamin, while the Philistines were camped in Michmash. Three raiding parties went out from the camp of the Philistines. One party went toward the way of Ophrah <note>original: *Ephra*</note> to the land of Shual; another went by the way of Beth-horon; and the third turned toward the way of the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim toward the desert. 

Now, no blacksmith was to be found in all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken care lest the Hebrews make sword or spear. Therefore all Israel went down to the Philistines so that each one might sharpen his plowshare, his hoe, his axe, and his mattock. The edges of the plowshares, hoes, forks, and axes were blunt, even to the correcting of the goad. When the day of battle came, no sword or spear was found in the hand of all the people who were with Saul and Jonathan, except for Saul and Jonathan his son. The Philistine outpost went out to advance to the pass of Michmash.

<margin>1 Samuel 18</margin>
**I**t came to pass, when David returned after killing the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing to meet King Saul, with timbrels of joy and cornets. And the women sang as they played, saying: "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands." And Saul was exceeding angry, and this saying was displeasing in his eyes. And he said: "They have given David ten thousands, and to me they have given but a thousand. What remains for him but the kingdom itself?" Therefore, Saul did not look upon David with right eyes <note>original: *non rectis oculis* — meaning with jealousy or suspicion</note> from that day forward.

And after some days, the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house. But David played with his hand as he did every day. And Saul held a spear and cast it, thinking that he could pin David to the wall. And David turned away from his face a second time. And Saul feared David because the Lord was with him, and had departed from himself. Therefore, Saul removed him from him and made him a captain over a thousand men; and he went out and came in before the people. In all his ways David acted prudently, and the Lord was with him. And Saul, seeing that he was exceeding prudent, began to beware of him. But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he came in and went out before them.

And Saul said to David: "Behold my elder daughter Merab; her will I give you to wife; only be a valiant man and fight the battles of the Lord." Now Saul thought within himself, saying: "Let not my hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him." But David said to Saul: "Who am I, or what is my life, or my father’s family in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?"

**H**owever, Michal, Saul's daughter, was given to David; and David had Michal as his wife. Michal, the daughter of Saul, loved David; and it was told to Saul, and it pleased him. And Saul said: "I will give her to him, that she may be a stumbling block to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be upon him." And Saul said to David: "In two things you shall be my son-in-law this day." And Saul commanded his servants: "Speak to David secretly, saying: 'Behold, you please the king, and all his servants love you; now therefore be the king’s son-in-law.'" And the servants of Saul spoke all these words in the ears of David. And David said: "Does it seem a small thing to you to be the king’s son-in-law? But I am a poor man and of small ability."

And the king’s messengers reported, saying: "David has spoken such words as these." And Saul said: "Speak thus to David: 'The king requires no dowry, but only a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, that revenge may be taken of the king’s enemies.'" Now Saul thought to deliver David into the hands of the Philistines. And when his servants had told David the words that Saul had said, the saying pleased David, that he should be the king’s son-in-law. And after a few days, David rose up and went with the men that were with him, and he killed two hundred men of the Philistines, and brought their foreskins and numbered them out to the king, that he might be his son-in-law. And Saul gave him Michal his daughter to wife. And Saul saw and understood that the Lord was with David. And Michal, Saul's daughter, loved him. And Saul began to fear David more; and Saul became David’s enemy all his days. And the princes of the Philistines went forth; and from the beginning of their going forth, David behaved himself more prudently than all the servants of Saul, and his name became very famous.

**A**nd Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, the son of Saul, loved David exceedingly. And Jonathan told David, saying: "Saul my father seeks to kill you; therefore, look to yourself, and remain in secret and hide. But I will go out and stand beside my father in the field wherever you are; and I will speak of you to my father."

It culminates in the famous battle where David slays the giant Goliath, sparking Saul's intense jealousy and leading to a complex relationship involving Jonathan's loyalty and Saul's repeated attempts to kill David.</summary>

...and in the same manner he was introduced to him again. After this, war broke out again, and David went out and fought against the Philistines; he struck them with a great slaughter, and they fled from his face. And an evil spirit from the Lord came upon Saul as he sat in his house holding a spear; meanwhile, David was playing the harp with his hand. Saul then sent his guards to David’s house to watch him so that he might be killed in the morning. When Michal, David’s wife, told him this, saying, "Unless you save yourself tonight, tomorrow you shall die," she let him down through a window. So he went, and fled, and escaped. Michal then took an image <note>original: *statuam* — likely a household idol or teraphim</note> and laid it in the bed, and put a goat’s skin with the hair on at its head, and covered it with clothes. When Saul sent messengers to seize David, the answer was given that he was sick. Saul sent the messengers again to see David, saying: "Bring him to me in the bed, so that he may be killed." And when the messengers had come, they found an idol upon the bed, and goat skins at its head. Saul said to Michal: "Why have you mocked me so, and let my enemy go, so that he might flee?" Michal answered Saul: "Because he said to me: 'Let me go, or else I will kill you.'" David, having fled and escaped, came to Samuel in Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. When they saw the company of prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing over them, the spirit of God came upon them, and they also began to prophesy.

<margin>1 Samuel 20</margin>
Then David fled from Naioth, which is in Ramah, and came and spoke before Jonathan: "What have I done? What is my iniquity, and what is my sin against your father, that he seeks my life?" And he said to him: "Far be it; you shall not die. For my father will do nothing, great or small, without first revealing it to me. Why then would my father hide only this thing from me? It shall not be so." David swore again, saying: "Your father certainly knows that I have found grace in your eyes, and he will say: 'Let not Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is only—as I might say—a step between me and death." Jonathan said to David: "Whatever your soul shall say to me, I will do for you." David said to Jonathan: "Behold, tomorrow is the New Moon <note>original: *kalendae* — the first day of the lunar month, observed as a festival with a royal banquet</note>, and I am accustomed to sit by the king to eat. Let me go, therefore, that I may hide myself in the field until the evening of the third day. If your father asks for me, you shall answer him: 'David earnestly asked me that he might run to Bethlehem, his own city, because there are solemn sacrifices there for all his kinsmen.' If he says, 'Very well,' it shall be peace for your servant. But if he is angry, know that his malice is complete. Therefore, show mercy to your servant, because you have brought me, your servant, into a covenant of the Lord with you. But if there is any iniquity in me, kill me yourself, and do not bring me to your father." Jonathan said: "Far be it from you! For it cannot be that if I certainly know my father’s malice is determined against you, I would not tell you." David answered Jonathan: "Who shall tell me if your father answers you harshly about me?" Jonathan said to David: "Come, let us go out into the field." And when they had both gone out into the field, Jonathan said to David: "O Lord God of Israel, if I investigate my father’s mind tomorrow or the day after, and if there is anything good for David and I do not immediately send to you and make it known to you, may the Lord do these things to Jonathan and add more. But if my father’s malice persists against you, I will show it to you <note>original: *revelabo aurem tuam* — literally 'reveal to your ear'</note> and let you go in peace; and may the Lord be with you, as he was with my father. And if I live, you shall show me the mercy of the Lord. But if I die, you shall not take away your mercy from my house forever. When the Lord has rooted out the enemies of David, every one from the earth, let him not take Jonathan from his house, and let the Lord require it from the hand of David’s enemies." So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, and Jonathan took an oath from David because he loved him; for he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan said to him: "Tomorrow is the New Moon, and you will be missed. For your seat will be empty until the evening. You shall go down quickly and come to the place where you must be hidden on the day when it is lawful to work, and you shall sit beside the stone named Ezel. I will shoot three arrows beside it, as if I were practicing at a mark. I will also send a boy, saying to him: 'Go, and bring me the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Behold, the arrows are on this side of you, take them,' then come to me, because there is peace for you and no evil, as the Lord lives. But if I speak thus to the boy, 'Behold, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the Lord has sent you away. And concerning the word which you and I have spoken, let the Lord be between me and you forever." So David went into the field, and the New Moon came, and the king sat down to eat bread. And when the king had sat upon his chair according to the custom, which was by the wall, Jonathan arose, and Abner sat by Saul’s side. And David’s place appeared empty. Saul said nothing that day, for he thought that perhaps something had happened to him so that he was not clean or purified. But when the second day after the New Moon dawned, David’s place appeared empty again. Saul said to Jonathan his son: "Why has the son of Jesse not come to eat, neither yesterday nor today?"

<column-break/>

Jonathan answered Saul: "He begged me earnestly that he might go to Bethlehem, and said: 'Let me go, for there is a solemn sacrifice in the city; one of my brothers has summoned me. Now, if I have found grace in your eyes, I will go and see my brothers.' For this reason, he has not come to the king’s table." Then Saul, being angry with Jonathan, said to him: "You son of a woman who willfully seizes a man <note>original: *fili mulieris ultro virum rapientis* — a harsh idiom implying Jonathan is the rebellious son of a perverse woman</note>, do I not know that you love the son of Jesse to your own confusion, and to the confusion of your mother’s shame? For as long as the son of Jesse lives upon the earth, you shall not be established, nor your kingdom. Therefore, send now and bring him to me, for he is a son of death <note>original: *filius mortis est* — an idiom meaning he is doomed or deserves to die</note>." Jonathan, answering Saul his father, said: "Why shall he die? What has he done?" And Saul caught up a spear to strike him. Then Jonathan understood that it was determined by his father that David should be killed. So Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger, and ate no bread on the second day of the New Moon. For he was grieved for David because his father had put him to shame. And when morning dawned, Jonathan went into the field at the time appointed with David, and a little boy was with him. And he said to his boy: "Go and bring me the arrows which I shoot." And as the boy ran, he shot another arrow beyond the boy. So the boy came to the place of the arrow which Jonathan had shot, and Jonathan cried out behind the boy’s back, saying: "Behold, the arrow is further beyond you." And Jonathan cried out again behind the boy’s back, saying: "Hurry quickly, do not stand still." Jonathan’s boy gathered up the arrows and brought them to his master, and he knew nothing of what was being done; only Jonathan and David knew the matter. Jonathan then gave his weapons to the boy and said to him: "Go, carry them into the city." When the boy was gone, David rose from a place that turned toward the south, and falling prostrate on the ground, he worshipped three times. And kissing each other, they wept together, but David wept more. Jonathan said to David: "Go in peace. What we have both sworn in the name of the Lord, saying 'The Lord be between me and you, and between my seed and your seed forever,' let it stand." And David rose and departed, and Jonathan entered the city.

For I have also appointed my servants to such and such a place. Now, therefore, if you have anything at hand, give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you find." The priest answered David, saying: "I have no common bread at hand, but only holy bread; if the young men are clean, especially from women." David answered and said to him: "Truly, if it concerns women, we have been kept from them since yesterday and the day before, when I came out, and the vessels of the young men were holy. For there was no bread there except the <term>showbread: twelve loaves of bread placed weekly on a golden table in the Sanctuary as an offering to God</term> which had been taken away from before the Lord, so that hot bread might be put there. Saul said to him: "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, giving him bread and a sword, and consulting the Lord for him, so that he should rise up against me and lie in wait, as he does this day?"

Ahimelech, answering the king, said: "And who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king's son-in-law, who goes forth at your command and is glorious in your house? But the king said: "You shall die the death, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house." And the king said to the guards <note>original: *emissariis* — literally 'those sent out' or messengers acting as executioners</note> standing around him: "Turn and kill the priests of the Lord. David said to Abiathar: "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I am guilty of the lives of all your father’s house. Stay with me; do not fear. Whoever seeks my life seeks yours also; with me, you shall be preserved."

<margin>1 Samuel 23</margin>
And they told David, saying: "Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah, and are plundering the threshing floors." Therefore David consulted the Lord, saying: "Shall I go and strike these Philistines?" And the Lord said to David: "Go and strike the Philistines, and you shall save Keilah." But the men who were with David said to him: "Behold, we are afraid even here in Judea; how much more if we go to Keilah against the ranks of the Philistines?"

David consulted the Lord again. And He answered him: "Arise, and go to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand." So David and his men went to Keilah and fought against the Philistines; he drove away their cattle and struck them with a great slaughter, and David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.

Now it happened that when Abiathar the son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he had come down with the ephod in his hand. It was told to Saul that David had come to Keilah. Saul said: "The Lord has delivered him into my hands; for he is shut in, having entered a city that has gates and bars." And Saul commanded all the people to go down to Keilah for war, to besiege David and his men.

When David realized that Saul was openly preparing mischief against him, he said to Abiathar the priest: "Bring the ephod." And David said: "O Lord God of Israel, your servant has heard a rumor that Saul intends to come to Keilah to destroy the city because of me. Will the men of Keilah deliver me into his hands? And will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? O Lord God of Israel, tell your servant." And the Lord said: "He will come down." David said: "Will the men of Keilah deliver me and the men who are with me into Saul's hands?" And the Lord said: "They will deliver you."

Then David and his men, about six hundred, arose and departed from Keilah; they wandered here and there, unsettled. It was told to Saul that David had escaped from Keilah, so he ceased his pursuit. David stayed in the wilderness in very strong places; he remained in a mountain of the desert of Ziph, in a woody mountain. Saul sought him every day, but the Lord did not deliver him into his hand.

David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. And David was in the desert of Ziph, in a forest. And Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose and went to David in the forest, and strengthened his hand in God. He said to him: "Fear not, for the hand of my father Saul shall not find you; you shall reign over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Even my father Saul knows this." And the two of them made a covenant before the Lord. David stayed in the forest, but Jonathan returned to his house.

Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying: "Is not David hiding with us in the safest places of the forest, on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the right side of the desert? Now therefore, as your soul has desired to come down, come down; and it shall be our part to deliver him into the king's hands."

Saul said: "Blessed are you of the Lord, for you have pitied my case. Go therefore and prepare more diligently; act with more curiosity and consider where his foot may be, and who has seen him there; for he thinks of me that I lie in wait for him craftily. Consider and see all the hiding places in which he hides, and return to me with a certain report, so that I may go with you. Even if he hides himself in the earth, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah."

So they arose and went to Ziph before Saul. But David and his men were in the desert of Maon, in the plains, to the right of Jeshimon. When Saul and his companions went to seek him, it was told to David. Immediately he went down to a rock and stayed in the desert of Maon. When Saul heard this, he pursued David into the desert of Maon. Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men were on the other side of the mountain. David despaired of being able to escape from the face of Saul. Thus Saul and his men were encircling David and his men like a crown to capture them.

But a messenger came to Saul, saying: "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have invaded the land." Therefore Saul returned, ceasing to pursue David, and went to meet the Philistines. For this reason, they called that place the Rock of Division <note>original: *petram dividentem* — meaning the rock that separates</note>.

<margin>1 Samuel 24</margin>
David then went up from there and lived in the safest places of En Gedi. And when Saul had returned from pursuing the Philistines, they told him: "Behold, David is in the desert of En Gedi." Saul, taking three thousand chosen men from all Israel, went to seek David and his men, even upon the steepest rocks, which are accessible only to wild goats.

He came to the sheepfolds that were along the way. There was a cave there, which Saul entered to relieve himself <note>original: *purgaret ventrem* — literally 'to purge the belly', a polite idiom for using the latrine</note>. Now David and his men were hiding in the inner part of the cave. And the servants of David said to him: "Behold the day of which the Lord spoke to you: 'I will deliver your enemy to you, that you may do to him as it shall seem good in your eyes.'"

Then David arose and secretly cut off the edge of Saul's cloak. Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul's cloak. He said to his men: "The Lord be merciful to me, that I may not do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed <note>original: *christo domini* — literally 'the Christ/Anointed of the Lord'</note>, to stretch out my hand against him, for he is the Lord’s anointed." And David restrained his men with these words, and did not allow them to rise up against Saul.

Then Saul, rising out of the cave, went on his way. David also arose after him, and going out of the cave, cried out after Saul, saying: "My lord the king!" Saul looked behind him. And David, bowing himself with his face to the ground, worshipped. He said to Saul: "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'David seeks evil against you'? Behold, this day your eyes have seen that the Lord delivered you into my hand in the cave; and I thought to kill you, but my eye spared you. For I said: 'I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, for he is the Lord’s anointed.' Rather, my father, see and recognize the edge of your cloak in my hand. Since I cut off the edge of your cloak and would not stretch out my hand against you, take notice and see that there is no evil in my hand, nor iniquity, nor have I sinned against you. But you lie in wait for my soul to take it away. Let the Lord judge between me and you, and let the Lord avenge me on you. But my hand shall not be upon you. As it is said in the ancient proverb: 'Out of the wicked comes forth wickedness.'"

<column-break/>

"But my hand shall not be upon you. Whom do you pursue, O King of Israel? Whom do you pursue? You pursue a dead dog and a single flea. Let the Lord be judge, and judge between me and you; let Him see and judge my cause, and deliver me out of your hand."

When David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said: "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul lifted up his voice and wept. He said to David: "You are more righteous than I. For you have repaid me with good, while I have repaid you with evil. And you have shown me today the good things you have done for me: how the Lord delivered me into your hand, and you did not kill me. For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go on his way in peace? May the Lord repay you with this reward for what you have done for me this day. And now, because I know that you shall surely reign, and shall hold the kingdom of Israel in your hand, swear to me by the Lord that you will not destroy my seed after me, nor take away my name from my father's house."

And David swore to Saul. Saul then went to his house, while David and his men went up to safer places.

<margin>1 Samuel 25</margin>
Now Samuel died, and all Israel gathered together and mourned him; they buried him in his house in Ramah. And David arose and went down to the desert of Paran.

There was a certain man in the wilderness of Maon, whose possessions were in Carmel; the man was very great, and he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. It happened that his flock was being shorn in Carmel. The name of the man was Nabal, and the name of his wife was Abigail. The woman was very prudent and beautiful, but the man was hard, very wicked, and malicious. He was of the family of Caleb.

When David heard in the desert that Nabal was shearing his flock, he sent ten young men and said to them: "Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal; greet him in my name peacefully, and say: 'Peace be to my brothers, and peace to you, and to your house, and to all that you have. I have heard that your shepherds are shearing. They were with us in the desert, and we never bothered them; nothing of theirs was ever missing all the time they were with us in Carmel. Ask your servants, and they will tell you. Therefore, let these young men find grace in your eyes, for we have come on a good day. Whatever your hand finds, give it to your servants and to your son David.'"

When David's young men came, they spoke all these words to Nabal in David's name, and then they were silent. But Nabal, answering David's servants, said: "Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse? Today, servants who flee from their masters have increased. Shall I then take my bread and my water, and the meat of my cattle that I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men I know not whence they come?"

So David's young men returned by their way, and when they came back, they told him all the words he had said. Then David said to his men: "Let every man gird on his sword." And they each girded on their swords. David also girded on his sword, and about four hundred men followed David, while two hundred stayed with the baggage.

But one of the servants told Abigail, Nabal's wife, saying: "Behold, David sent messengers from the desert to bless our master, but he turned them away. Those men were good enough to us; they did not bother us, nor did anything ever perish all the time we were with them in the desert. They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the days we were with them feeding the flocks. Therefore, know and consider what you should do, for mischief is determined against our master and against his house; and he is such a son of Belial <note>A term for a worthless or wicked person</note> that no one can speak to him."

Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five cooked rams, five measures of parched grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of dried figs, and laid them on donkeys. She said to her servants: "Go before me; behold, I follow after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.

As she rode on her donkey and was descending to the foot of the mountain, David and his men were coming down toward her, and she met them. David had been saying: "Truly in vain have I kept all that this man had in the desert, so that nothing was lost of all that belonged to him; and he has repaid me evil for good. May God do these things to the enemies of David, and add more besides, if I leave of all that belongs to him until the morning so much as one who pisses against the wall <note>original: *mingentem ad parietem* — a Hebrew idiom for a male child or man</note>."

When Abigail saw David, she hurried and dismounted from her donkey, fell before David on her face, and bowed to the ground. She fell at his feet and said: "Upon me, my lord, let this iniquity be. I pray you, let your handmaid speak in your ears, and hear the words of your servant. But I, your handmaid, did not see the young men my lord sent. Now therefore, my lord, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, it is the Lord who has kept you from coming to shed blood and has saved your own hand for you. And now let your enemies, and those who seek evil against my lord, be like Nabal. Therefore, accept this blessing which your handmaid has brought to my lord, and give it to the young men who follow you, my lord. Forgive the iniquity of your handmaid. For the Lord will certainly make a faithful house for my lord, because you, my lord, fight the battles of the Lord. Let no malice be found in you all the days of your life. For if a man ever rises up to pursue you and seek your soul, the soul of my lord shall be kept as if in the bundle of the living with the Lord your God. But the souls of your enemies He shall hurl away as from the middle of a sling. Therefore, when the Lord has done for my lord all the good He has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you leader over Israel, this shall not be a cause of grief or a scruple of heart to my lord, that you have shed innocent blood, or have avenged yourself. And when the Lord has dealt well with my lord, remember your handmaid."

David said to Abigail: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me; and blessed be your speech; and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from coming to shed blood and from avenging myself with my own hand. For truly, as the Lord God of Israel lives, who has kept me back from doing you any evil, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, there would not have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who pisses against the wall."

So David received from her hand all that she had brought him, and said to her: "Go in peace to your house. Behold, I have heard your voice and have honored your face."

And his heart died within him, and he became like a stone. About ten days later, the Lord struck Nabal, and he died. When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said: "Blessed be the Lord, who has judged the cause..."
