<meta>This page continues the narrative of the First Book of Samuel. Following the death of the prophet Samuel, the text follows David’s movements as a fugitive, his conflict with the wealthy Nabal, his second opportunity to kill King Saul, and his eventual tactical decision to live among the Philistines. The page concludes with Saul’s desperate visit to a medium at Endor on the eve of his final battle.</meta>

After the death of Samuel, Nabal is shown to have acted wickedly toward his servant <note>Original: "seruū suū," referring to David as a servant of the kingdom</note>. Nabal returned evil for good, but Abigail intercedes and pacifies David. When Nabal's death was announced to David, Abigail became his wife. David also took Abigail and Ahinoam of Jezreel as his wives.

Now when Samuel died, all Israel gathered and mourned for him, burying him in his house at Ramah. And David, rising up, went down into the desert of Paran. There was a certain man in the wilderness of Maon, and his property was in Carmel; this man was very great, possessing three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. It happened that his flock was being shorn in Carmel. The man's name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. She was a most prudent and beautiful woman, but her husband was harsh, ill-natured, and malicious; he was of the lineage of Caleb.

When David heard in the desert that Nabal was shearing his flock, he sent ten young men, to whom he said: "Go up to Carmel and visit Nabal. Greet him in my name peacefully, saying: 'Peace be to you, to your house, and to all that you have. I have heard that your shepherds were shearing. We never bothered them, nor was anything ever missing from them during all the time they were with us in Carmel. Ask your boys and they will tell you. Therefore, let your young men find grace in your eyes, for we have come on a good day. Whatever your hand finds, give it to your servants and to your son David.'"

When David’s young men arrived, they spoke all these words to Nabal in David’s name, and then waited in silence. But Nabal, answering David's messengers, said: "Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse? Today, servants who flee from their masters have increased. Shall I then take my bread, my water, and the meat of the cattle I have killed for my shearers, and give them to men I do not know?" David said to his men: "Let everyone gird on his sword." And they each girded on their swords; David also girded on his sword. About four hundred men followed David, while two hundred stayed with the baggage.

However, one of the servants told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying: "Behold, David sent messengers from the desert to bless our master, but he turned them away. These men were very good to us, and nothing was ever lost while we were with them in the desert. They were like a wall to us both by night and by day while we were pasturing the flocks. Therefore, consider what you should do, for malice is determined against our master and his house, and he is a son of Belial <note>A Hebrew term meaning "worthless" or "wicked"</note>, so that no one can speak to him."

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five cooked rams, five measures of parched grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of dried figs, and loaded them onto donkeys. She said to her boys: "Go before me; behold, I follow after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal. As she rode on her donkey and descended to the foot of the mountain, David and his men were descending toward her, and she met them. David had been saying: "Truly, I have guarded all that belonged to this man in the desert in vain, so that nothing was lost of all that pertained to him; he has returned me evil for good. May God do these things to the enemies of David, and more besides, if I leave by morning so much as one male <note>Original: "mictētē ad parietē," a literal Hebrew idiom for a male, "one who urinates against a wall"</note> among all who belong to him."

When Abigail saw David, she hurried and dismounted from her donkey, falling prostrate before David and bowing to the earth. Falling at his feet, she said: "Upon me, my lord, let this iniquity be. Let your handmaid speak in your ears, I beseech you, and hear the words of your servant. Let not my lord set his heart against this wicked man Nabal, for according to his name he is a fool <note>The name Nabal literally means "Fool" in Hebrew</note>, and folly is with him. But I, your handmaid, did not see your boys whom you sent. Now therefore, my lord, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, it is the Lord who has kept you from coming to shed blood and has saved your hand for yourself. Now let your enemies, and those who seek evil against my lord, become like Nabal. Therefore, accept this blessing which your handmaid has brought to my lord, and give it to the boys who follow my lord. Forgive the trespass of your servant. For the Lord will certainly make a faithful house for my lord, because my lord fights the battles of the Lord. Let no malice be found in you all the days of your life. If a man ever rises to pursue you and seek your life, the soul of my lord shall be kept in the bundle of the living with the Lord your God. But the souls of your enemies shall be whirled away as if in the force and circle of a sling. When the Lord has done for my lord all the good things he has spoken of you, and has appointed you leader over Israel, let this not be a source of grief or a qualm of heart to my lord—that you shed innocent blood or avenged yourself. And when the Lord has dealt well with my lord, you shall remember your handmaid."

David said to Abigail: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me, and blessed be your speech, and blessed be you, who have kept me today from going to shed blood and from avenging myself with my own hand. Otherwise, as the Lord God of Israel lives, who kept me from doing you harm, if you had not come quickly to meet me, there would not have remained to Nabal by the morning light so much as one male." David then accepted from her hand all she had brought him, and said: "Go in peace to your house; behold, I have heard your voice and honored your presence."

Abigail returned to Nabal, and behold, he was having a feast in his house like the feast of a king. Nabal’s heart was merry, for he was very drunk. She told him nothing, small or great, until morning. At daybreak, when Nabal had slept off the wine, his wife told him these words. His heart died within him, and he became like a stone. When ten days had passed, the Lord struck Nabal and he died. When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said: "Blessed be the Lord, who has judged the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal and has kept his servant from evil; the Lord has returned the malice of Nabal upon his own head." David then sent word to Abigail to take her as his wife. David’s servants came to Abigail at Carmel and spoke to her, saying: "David has sent us to you to take you to himself as a wife." Rising, she bowed facedown to the ground and said: "Behold, let your servant be a handmaid to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." Abigail hurried and rose and mounted a donkey, and five of her young women followed her; she followed David’s messengers and became his wife. David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both were his wives. But Saul had given Michal, his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, who was from Gallim.

David spares Saul and takes his spear and cup, and David says: "Saul, I am more righteous than you." David’s servant returns to the desert of Ziph. David asks the Lord regarding Abigail, and that he might have Michal his wife given back to him, though she had been given to another master.

Saul rose and went down to the desert of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David. Saul camped on the hill of Hachilah, which faces the wilderness by the road. David was staying in the desert, and seeing that Saul had come after him, he sent spies and learned that he had indeed arrived.

<margin>69.</margin>
David rose secretly and came to the place where Saul was. When he saw the spot where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the commander of his army, were sleeping—for Saul slept in the tent with the rest of the people around him—David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother: "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" Abishai said: "I will go down with you." So David and Abishai came to the people by night, and found Saul lying asleep in the tent with his spear fixed in the ground at his head, while Abner and the people slept around him. Abishai said to David: "God has shut your enemy into your hands today. Now therefore, let me pierce him with the spear into the earth just once, and there will be no need for a second stroke." But David said to Abishai: "Do not kill him. For who can stretch out his hand against the Lord's Anointed <term>Christum Domini: This term refers to the ritual of anointing a king with oil, marking him as divinely chosen</term> and be innocent?" David added: "As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strikes him, or his day comes to die, or he goes down into battle and perishes, the Lord forbid that I should stretch out my hand against the Lord's Anointed. Now, take the spear that is at his head and the cup of water, and let us go." So David took the spear and the water cup from Saul’s head and they left. No one saw or knew or woke up, for they were all sleeping because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.

When David had crossed over to the other side and stood on the top of the mountain far off, with a great distance between them, he called out to the people and to Abner son of Ner, saying: "Will you not answer, Abner?" Abner replied: "Who are you who cries out and disturbs the king?" David said to Abner: "Are you not a man? And who else is like you in Israel? Why then have you not guarded your lord the king? For one of the crowd entered to kill the king, your lord. This thing you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you are sons of death because you did not guard your lord, the Lord’s Anointed. Now see where the king’s spear is, and the cup of water that was at his head." Saul recognized David’s voice and said: "Is this your voice, my son David?" David said: "It is my voice, my lord king." And he said: "For what reason does my lord pursue his servant? What have I done? Or what evil is in my hand? Now therefore, my lord king, hear the words of your servant. If the Lord stirs you up against me, let an offering be smelled. But if it be the children of men, they are cursed in the sight of the Lord, for they have cast me out today from living in the inheritance of the Lord, saying: 'Go, serve foreign gods.' Now, let not my blood be shed on the ground before the Lord, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains." Saul said: "I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will never do you harm again, because my life was precious in your eyes today. It appears that I have acted foolishly and have been very ignorant." David answered: "Behold the king’s spear. Let one of the boys come over and take it. The Lord will reward each according to his justice and faith. For the Lord delivered you today into my hand, but I would not lift my hand against the Lord's Anointed. As your life was magnified today in my eyes, so let my life be magnified in the eyes of the Lord, and let Him deliver me from all tribulation." Saul said to David: "Blessed are you, my son David. You shall surely do great things and shall prevail." So David went on his way, and Saul returned to his place.

David flees to Achish, king of Gath; and how David acted so as not to have his wife; and Saul pursues him where it happened. David flees to Achish, king of Gath, and David takes Abigail and Ahinoam of Jezreel as wives.

David said in his heart: "One day I shall fall into the hand of Saul. Is it not better that I flee and find safety in the land of the Philistines, so that Saul may despair and cease to seek me in all the borders of Israel? Thus I shall escape his hands." So David rose and went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath. David lived with Achish in Gath, he and his men and his household—David and his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel. When it was told to Saul that David had fled to Gath, he sought him no more. David said to Achish: "If I have found grace in your eyes, let a place be given to me in one of the cities of this region that I may live there. For why should your servant stay in the royal city with you?" So Achish gave him Ziklag that day. For this reason, Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day. The number of days David lived in the region of the Philistines was four months. David and his men went up and made raids upon the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. For these villages were inhabited in the land of old as one goes toward Shur and the land of Egypt. David struck the whole land and left neither man nor woman alive. Taking the sheep, oxen, donkeys, camels, and clothing, he returned and came to Achish. Achish would say: "Against whom have you raided today?" David would reply: "Against the south of Judah," or "Against the south of Jerahmeel," or "Against the south of the Kenites." David did not leave a man or woman alive to be brought to Gath, saying: "Lest they should speak against us." This David did, and this was his policy all the days he lived in the region of the Philistines. Achish believed David, saying: "He has worked much evil against his people Israel; therefore he shall be my servant forever."

It happened in those days that the Philistines gathered their troops for battle to fight against Israel. Achish said to David: "Know for certain that you and your men shall go out with me in the camp." David said to Achish: "Now you shall know what your servant will do." Achish said to David: "I will make you the guard of my head <note>Meaning a personal bodyguard</note> for all days."

Samuel having died... Saul consults a medium...

Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel had mourned him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. Saul had removed the magicians and fortune-tellers from the land. The Philistines gathered and came and camped in Shunem. Saul gathered all Israel and came to Gilboa. When Saul saw the camp of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly. He consulted the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by priests, nor by prophets. Saul said to his servants: "Seek for me a woman who has a divining spirit <term>Pythonem: Referring to the "Spirit of Python," a classical term used in the Latin Vulgate to describe a medium or necromancer</term>, that I may go to her and inquire through her." His servants said to him: "There is a woman who has a divining spirit in Endor." So Saul disguised himself, putting on other clothes, and went with two men. They came to the woman at night, and he said: "Divine for me by the spirit, and bring up for me whomsoever I shall name to you." The woman said to him: "Behold, you know what Saul has done, and how he has erased the magicians and fortune-tellers from the land. Why do you lay a snare for my life, that I should be killed?" Saul swore to her by the Lord, saying: "As the Lord lives, no evil shall happen to you for this thing." The woman asked: "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said: "Bring up Samuel for me." When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice and said to Saul: "Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul!" The king said to her: "Do not be afraid. What did you see?" The woman said to Saul: "I saw gods ascending from the earth." He asked: "What is his form?" She said: "An old man is coming up, and he is clothed in a cloak." Saul understood it was Samuel, and he bowed his face to the ground and worshipped. Samuel said to Saul: "Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up?" Saul said: "I am in great distress. For the Philistines fight against me, and God has departed from me; He will not hear me, neither by the hand of prophets nor by dreams. Therefore I have called you to show me what I should do." Samuel said: "Why do you ask me, since the Lord has departed from you and gone over to your rival? For the Lord will do to you as He spoke through my hand; He will tear the kingdom out of your hand and give it to your neighbor David. Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord, nor carry out His fierce wrath against Amalek, the Lord has done this thing to you today. Moreover, the Lord will deliver Israel with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow, you and your sons shall be with me; the Lord will also deliver the camp of Israel into the hand of the Philistines." Immediately Saul fell prostrate on the ground, for he was terrified by Samuel’s words, and there was no strength in him because he had not eaten bread all that day. The woman came to Saul and saw that he was greatly troubled, and said to him: "Behold, your handmaid has obeyed your voice; I have put my life in my hand and heard your words which you spoke to me. Now therefore, hear the voice of your handmaid; let me set a morsel of bread before you, so that you may eat and recover strength to go on your journey." He refused, saying: "I will not eat." But his servants and the woman compelled him, and finally, listening to them, he rose from the ground and sat on the bed. The woman had a fatted calf in the house; she hurried and killed it, took flour, mixed it, and baked unleavened bread. She set it before Saul and his servants. When they had eaten, they rose and walked through all that night.

The Philistines were gathered...

The Philistines gathered all their troops at Aphek, while Israel camped by the fountain in Jezreel. The lords of the Philistines marched in hundreds and thousands, but David and his men were in the rear with Achish. The princes of the Philistines said to Achish: "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish said: "Is this not David, who was the servant of Saul, king of Israel? He has been with me for many days or years, and I have found nothing in him from the day he fled to me until this day." But the leaders of the Philistines were angry with him and said: "Let the man return and stay in his place where you appointed him. Let him not go down with us to battle, lest he become our adversary in the fight. For how else could he reconcile himself to his master except with the heads of these men? Is this not the David of whom they sang in dances, saying: 'Saul struck a thousand, and David ten thousand'?" So Achish called David and said: "As the Lord lives, you are upright, and your coming and going in the camp is good in my sight; I have found no evil in you. but you do not please the lords. Therefore return and go in peace, lest you offend the eyes of the princes of the Philistines." David said: "What have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I was in your presence until this day, that I should not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?" Achish answered: "I know you are good in my eyes as an angel of God; but the princes of the Philistines have said: 'He shall not go up with us to battle.' Therefore rise early in the morning, you and your lord’s servants who came with you, and when it is light, depart." So David and his men rose by night to depart in the morning and return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

David came to Ziklag...

When David and his men arrived at Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid from the south into Ziklag; they struck Ziklag and burned it with fire. They took the women captive, from the least to the greatest; they killed no one but led them away and went on their journey. When David and his men came to the city and found it burned with fire, and their wives, sons, and daughters taken captive, David and the people with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no more tears. David's two wives had been taken captive: Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel. David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man was bitter for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the Lord his God. He said to Abiathar the priest, son of Ahimelech: "Bring me the Ephod <term>Ephod: A sacred vestment used by the high priest to discern the will of God</term>." Abiathar brought the ephod to David. David consulted the Lord, saying: "Shall I pursue these raiders, and shall I overtake them?" The Lord said: "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake them and recover the spoil." So David went, he and the six hundred men with him, and came to the brook Besor, where some who were weary stayed behind. David and four hundred men pursued, but two hundred stayed because they were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor. They found an Egyptian man in the field and brought him to David; they gave him bread to eat and water to drink, along with a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. When he had eaten, his spirit returned and he was refreshed, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights. David said to him: "To whom do you belong? Where are you from? And where are you going?" He said: "I am an Egyptian youth, the servant of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me because I began to be sick three days ago. For we raided the south of the Cherethites and the borders of Judah and the south of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire..."

...they had burned Ziklag with fire. And they spoke to David: "Can they be overtaken?" And the Lord said to him: "Pursue them, for you will undoubtedly overtake them and rescue everyone." So David went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook of Besor. Some, being weary, stayed behind, while others continued the pursuit. When David had led the way, behold, they found the Amalekites spread out over the face of the whole land, eating and drinking and celebrating as if it were a festival day, because of all the prey and spoils they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah. And David struck them from evening until the evening of the next day; not one of them escaped except for four hundred young men who mounted camels and fled.

David rescued everything the Amalekites had taken and saved his two wives. Nothing was missing, from the smallest to the greatest, neither sons nor daughters nor any of the spoils they had seized; David brought everything back. He took all the flocks and herds and drove them before him, and the people said: "This is David’s spoil." Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and whom he had ordered to stay at the brook of Besor. They went out to meet David and the people who were with him. As David approached the people, he greeted them peacefully. But every wicked and unjust man among those who had gone with David responded, saying: "Because they did not come with us, we will not give them any of the spoil we recovered; let it be enough for each of them to take his wife and children and depart." But David said: "You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the Lord has given us; He has protected us and delivered the raiders who broke in against us into our hands. No one shall listen to you in this matter. For the share of him who goes down to battle shall be the same as the share of him who stays with the baggage; they shall share alike." This was made a law and a precedent in Israel from that day forward, even to this day. When David came to Ziklag, he sent gifts from the spoil to the elders of Judah, his neighbors, saying: "Receive a blessing from the spoil of the Lord’s enemies." These were for those in Bethel, Ramoth of the South, Jattir, Aroer, Siphmoth, Eshtemoa, Rachal, the cities of the Jerahmeelites, the cities of the Kenites, Hormah, Bor-ashan, Athach, Hebron, and all the other places where David and his men had stayed.

Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines pressed hard upon Saul and his sons, and they killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. The whole weight of the battle turned against Saul; the archers overtook him, and he was severely wounded by them. Saul said to his armor-bearer: "Draw your sword and kill me, lest these uncircumcised <note>A biblical term used by the Israelites to refer to the Philistines, often as a pejorative.</note> come and mock me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he was terrified. Therefore, Saul took his sword and fell upon it. When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him. So Saul died, along with his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men on that same day. When the Israelites who were across the valley and across the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled; and the Philistines came and lived in them.

The next day, the Philistines came to strip the dead, and they found Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa. They cut off his head and stripped him of his armor, sending messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to announce the news in the temples of their idols and to the people. They placed his armor in the temple of Astaroth <note>A Canaanite goddess of war and fertility.</note> and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan. When the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all the most valiant men rose up and traveled all night; they took the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there. They took their bones and buried them in the woods of Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days.

of Saul, that David returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag for two days. On the third day, a man appeared coming from Saul’s camp with his clothes torn and dust on his head. When he came to David, he fell on his face and did obeisance. David said to him: "Where do you come from?" He said: "I have escaped from the camp of Israel." David said to him: "What has happened? Tell me." He said: "The people have fled from the battle, and many have fallen and died; even Saul and his son Jonathan are dead." David asked the young man who told him: "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?" The young man replied: "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and Saul was leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen were closing in on him. Looking behind him, he saw me and called to me. When I answered, 'I am here,' he said to me: 'Who are you?' I said: 'I am an Amalekite.' He said to me: 'Stand over me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, yet my whole life is still in me.' So I stood over him and killed him, for I knew he could not live after his fall. I took the crown that was on his head and the golden band from his arm, and I have brought them here to you, my lord." Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, as did all the men who were with him. They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul,

<column-break/>

for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the Lord and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. David said to the young man who had told him: "Where are you from?" He answered: "I am the son of a resident alien, an Amalekite." David said to him: "Why were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to kill the Lord’s anointed?" <note>David refers to Saul as the "Christ of the Lord" (christum domini) in the Latin text, meaning one who has been ritually anointed with holy oil.</note> David called one of his young men and said: "Go, fall upon him." Then David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and his son Jonathan. He ordered that the people of Judah be taught the Lamentation of the Bow; as it is written in the Book of the Just: <note>Likely the lost Book of Jashar.</note> "Consider, O Israel, those who were killed on your high places. The illustrious of Israel are slain upon your mountains. How have the mighty fallen? Tell it not in Gath, nor announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of first-fruits, for there the shield of the mighty was cast away—the shield of Saul, as if he had not been anointed with oil. From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the arrow of Jonathan never turned back, and the sword of Saul never returned empty. Saul and Jonathan, lovely and beautiful in their life, were not divided even in death. They were swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and delights, who provided golden ornaments for your apparel. How have the mighty fallen in battle? Jonathan was slain in your high places. I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan; you were very dear to me, beyond the love of women. As a mother loves her only son, so did I love you. How have the robust fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"

After this, it came to pass that David consulted the Lord, saying: "Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?" And the Lord said to him: "Go up." David said: "Where shall I go?" He answered: "To Hebron." So David went up, along with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel. David also brought the men who were with him, each with his household, and they dwelt in the towns of Hebron. The men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When it was told to David that the men of Jabesh-Gilead had buried Saul, David sent messengers to them and said: "Blessed are you by the Lord, because you have shown this mercy to your lord Saul and buried him. Now may the Lord show you mercy and truth; I also will reward you for this good deed. Let your hands be strengthened and be men of valor; for though your lord Saul is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."

But Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and led him through the camps, making him king over Gilead, Gessuri, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel. Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. Only the house of Judah followed David. The total time that David remained in Hebron reigning over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. Then Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from the camp of Mahanaim. Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s servants also went out and met them by the pool of Gibeon. When they met, they sat down, one group on one side of the pool and the other group on the other side. Abner said to Joab: "Let the young men rise and play <note>A euphemism for a ritualized or representative combat.</note> before us." Joab replied: "Let them rise." So twelve from Benjamin on the side of Ish-bosheth and twelve of David’s servants rose and went over. Each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his side, and they all fell together. That place was called the Field of the Strong in Gibeon. A very fierce battle broke out that day; Abner and the men of Israel were put to flight by David’s servants.

The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was a very swift runner, like a wild gazelle of the forest. Asahel pursued Abner, turning neither to the right nor to the left. Abner looked back and said: "Is that you, Asahel?" He answered: "It is I." Abner said to him: "Turn to the right or the left; catch one of the young men and take his spoils for yourself." But Asahel would not stop pressing him. Abner spoke to Asahel again: "Stay away from me; do not pursue me, lest I be forced to strike you to the ground, and I will not be able to look your brother Joab in the face." But he refused to listen or turn aside. So Abner struck him in the groin with the butt of his spear, and it went through him, and he died there. Everyone who passed by the place where Asahel fell and died stopped there. But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner as he fled; the sun went down when they reached the hill of the aqueduct, which faces the valley on the road to the desert of Gibeon. The men of Benjamin gathered around Abner in a single troop and stood on the top of a hill. Abner called out to Joab: "Will your sword rage until everyone is destroyed? Do you not know that despair is dangerous? How long will it be before you tell the people to stop pursuing their brothers?" Joab said: "As the Lord lives, if you had not spoken, the people would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning." Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the whole army stopped; they pursued Israel no further, nor did they fight any more. Abner and his men traveled through the plains all that night; they crossed the Jordan, passed through all of Beth-horon, and came to the camp. When Joab returned from pursuing Abner, he gathered all the people; nineteen of David’s servants were missing besides Asahel. But David’s servants had killed three hundred and sixty men of Benjamin and those who were with Abner. They took up Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.

There was a long struggle between the house of Saul and the house of David. David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker every day. Sons were born to David in Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel; the second was Chileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; the third was Absalom, son of Maacah, the daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; the fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital; and the sixth was Ithream, by David's wife Eglah. These were born to David in Hebron.

Now Saul had had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner: "Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?" <note>In the ancient Near East, taking the concubine of a deceased king was seen as a claim to the throne.</note> Abner was very angry at Ish-bosheth’s words and said: "Am I a dog’s head against Judah today?..."

<margin>2 Samuel 4</margin>
**T**he sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, arrived at the house of Ish-bosheth <note>Saul's son and David's rival for the throne</note> in the heat of the day. But David, answering Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, said to them: "As the Lord lives, who has rescued my soul out of all distress, when one told me and said, 'Saul is dead,' thinking that he brought good news, I seized him and slew him in Ziklag, who thought I should have given him a reward for his news. <margin>Concerning Abner</margin>
**I**t was also told to Joab <note>David's general</note> by those reporting: "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has sent him away in peace." And Joab went in to the king and said: "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you; why did you send him away, so that he is gone and departed? Do you not know Abner the son of Ner, that he came for this purpose, to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you do?" Joab then went out from David and sent messengers after Abner, and brought him back from the Well of Sirah, David being unaware. And when Abner had returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside to the middle of the gate to speak to him treacherously. When David heard of the deed, he said: "I and my kingdom are innocent before the Lord forever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner. Let it come upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house. May there never fail to be in the house of Joab one who has a discharge, or who is a leper, or who leans on a staff, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks bread." So Joab and Abishai his brother slew Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel in Gibeon in battle.

<margin>David</margin>
**D**avid said to Abishai and to Joab: "I and my kingdom are innocent before the Lord forever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner. Let it come upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house. Know this day that a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel. But I am yet weak, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. May the Lord reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness." The sons of Saul were also brought to David in Hebron, and their names were clearly distinguished: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; the second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal of Carmel; the third, Absalom the son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.

<margin>Jonathan</margin>
**T**here was also a son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, who was lame in his feet. For when the news concerning Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, his nurse took him up and fled. And as she made haste to flee, he fell and became lame. <note>This refers to Mephibosheth</note> Ish-bosheth also had those who came to him; the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, entered the house in the heat of the day. He was sleeping upon his bed at noon, and the portress of the house, while cleaning wheat, had fallen asleep. Rechab and Baanah his brother entered secretly and struck him in the groin and killed him. Taking his head, they went by way of the desert all night and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David in Hebron, saying to the king: "Behold the head of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul your enemy, who sought your life. And the Lord has avenged my lord the king this day of Saul and of his seed."

<column-break/>

David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months. In Jerusalem he reigned thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah. And the king and all the men who were with him went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land. It was said to David by them: "You shall not come in here unless you take away the blind and the lame," saying, "David shall not come in here." But David took the stronghold of Zion; this is the City of David. For David had proposed on that day a reward for whoever should strike the Jebusites and reach the water-pipes <note>original: "fistulas," often translated as "gutters" or "water shafts"</note> and take away the blind and the lame who hated David’s soul. Therefore it is said in the proverb: "The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple." And David dwelt in the stronghold and called it the City of David. And he built around it from the Millo <note>a rampart or fortification</note> and inwards. And David went on and grew great, and the Lord God of hosts was with him. Hiram king of Tyre also sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, and carpenters, and stonemasons for the walls; and they built David a house. And David perceived that the Lord had confirmed him king over Israel and that he had exalted his kingdom for his people Israel’s sake. David took more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem after he had come from Hebron. And other sons and daughters were born to David. These are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.

<margin>David in Hebron</margin>
**S**o all the elders of Israel came to the king in Hebron, and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the Lord. And they anointed David king over Israel. Ish-bosheth the son of Saul was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah alone followed David.

<margin>The Philistines</margin>
**T**he Philistines came up into the valley of Rephaim. And David consulted the Lord, saying: "Shall I go up to the Philistines? And will you deliver them into my hand?" And the Lord said to David: "Go up, for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand." David therefore came to Baal-perazim, and he struck them there and said: "The Lord has divided my enemies before me as waters are divided." Therefore the name of that place was called Baal-perazim <note>meaning "Lord of Breakthroughs"</note>. And they left their idols there, which David and his men took away. And the Philistines came up yet again and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim. David again consulted the Lord, saying: "Shall I go up against the Philistines? And will you deliver them into my hand?" He answered: "You shall not go up against them, but go around behind them and come upon them from opposite the pear trees <note>original: "pirorum," likely referring to balsam or mulberry trees</note>. And when you hear the sound of a step going in the tops of the pear trees, then you shall join battle; for then the Lord shall go out before your face to strike the army of the Philistines." And David did as the Lord had commanded him, and he struck the Philistines from Geba until one comes to Gezer. David again gathered together the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. And all the people who were with him arose and went from the men of Judah to bring up the Ark of God, upon which is called the name of the Lord of hosts who sits upon the Cherubim over it. And they set the Ark of God upon a new cart and took it from the house of Abinadab, which was in Gibeah. Uzzah <note>original: "Oza"</note> and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drove the new cart. And when they had taken it from the house of Abinadab, they guarded the Ark of God; Ahio went before the Ark. But David and all Israel played before the Lord on all manner of instruments made of wood, and on harps, and lyres, and timbrels, and sistrums, and cymbals.

<margin>The Ark of the Lord</margin>
**D**avid and all the people who were with him also proceeded from Baale-judah <note>original: "Baalim Iuda"</note> to bring up the Ark of God, upon which is called the name of the Lord of hosts who sits upon the Cherubim over it. They set the Ark of God upon a new cart and took it from the house of Abinadab in Gibeah. Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, drove the new cart. When they had taken it from the house of Abinadab, they guarded the Ark of God, and Ahio walked before it. David and all Israel played before the Lord on all manner of crafted wood, harps, lyres, timbrels, sistrums, and cymbals. And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out his hand to the Ark of the Lord and took hold of it, because the oxen were kicking. And the Lord was angry with indignation against Uzzah, and he struck him for his rashness <note>original: "temeritate"</note>; and he died there by the Ark of the Lord. David was grieved because the Lord had struck Uzzah, and the name of that place has been called "The Striking of Uzzah" <note>Perez-uzzah</note> even to this day. And David feared the Lord that day, saying: "How shall the Ark of God come to me?" And he would not bring the Ark of the Lord to himself into the City of David, but he turned it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the Ark of the Lord stayed in the house of Obed-edom for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household. It was told to King David that the Lord had blessed Obed-edom and all that was his because of the Ark of God. So David went and brought up the Ark of God from the house of Obed-edom into the City of David with joy. And there were with David seven choirs and a sacrifice of a calf. When those who bore the Ark of the Lord had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a ram. And David sang <note>original: "psallebat," to sing or play the harp</note> with all his might before the Lord; David was girded with a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel brought up the Ark of the covenant of the Lord with shouting and the sound of the trumpet. And as the Ark of the Lord entered the City of David, Michal the daughter of Saul, looking through a window, saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord; and she despised him in her heart. And they brought in the Ark of God and set it in its place in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it; and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord. When he had finished offering, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts. And he distributed to the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, to everyone a loaf of bread, a piece of roasted beef, and fine flour fried in oil. And all the people departed, everyone to his own house.

<margin>David and the Ark</margin>
**T**he chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, were gathered together again. And David arose and went to Baale-judah to bring up the Ark of God. They set the Ark of God upon a new cart and took it from the house of Abinadab. David returned to bless his own house. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said: "How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the handmaids of his servants, being naked as if one of the lewd fellows <note>original: "scurris"</note> were naked." David said to Michal: "It was before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father and all your house, and commanded me to be king over the people of the Lord, over Israel. I will play and make myself even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes; and with the handmaids of whom you have spoken, I shall appear more glorious." Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child until the day of her death. Nathan said to the king: "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you." But it came to pass that night, behold, the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: "Go and speak to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: Shall you build me a house to dwell in? For I have not dwelt in a house since the day I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt even to this day, but I walked in a tabernacle and in a tent in all the places I traveled with all the children of Israel. Have I ever spoken a word to any of the tribes of Israel whom I commanded to feed my people Israel, saying: Why have you not built me a house of cedar? Now therefore thus shall you say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts..."

“I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. If he commits iniquity, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men. <margin>2 Kings 7</margin>
“Is this the law of man <note>original: "lex adam"; this phrase is famously difficult to translate, suggesting either a decree for humanity or a revelation of a human messiah</note>, O Lord God? For what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord God. For the sake of your word and according to your own heart, you have done all these great things, so that you might make them known to your servant. Therefore you are magnified, O Lord God, because there is none like you, nor is there any God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And what other nation is there on earth like your people Israel, for whom God went to redeem them for himself as a people, to make a name for himself, and to do great and terrible things for them upon the earth, before the face of your people whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, from the nations and their gods? For you have established your people Israel for yourself as an eternal people, and you, Lord God, have become their God. Now therefore, Lord God, the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and his house, uphold it forever, and do as you have spoken, so that your name may be magnified forever, and it may be said: ‘The Lord of hosts is the God over Israel.’ And may the house of your servant David be established before the Lord. Because you, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have revealed this to the ear of your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found the courage in his heart to pray this prayer to you. And now, Lord God, you are God, and your words shall be true. For you have promised these good things to your servant. Begin, therefore, and bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you; for you, Lord God, have spoken, and by your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever.”

<margin>2 Kings 8</margin>
It happened after this that David struck the Philistines and humbled them. And David took the "bit of tribute" <note>original: "frenum tributi"; a metaphorical term for taking control or sovereignty</note> from the hand of the Philistines. And he struck Moab, and measured them with a cord, leveling them to the ground. He measured two cords, one to be put to death and one to be kept alive. And Moab became David's servants under tribute. David also struck Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to extend his dominion over the river Euphrates. And David captured from him one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers; David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for one hundred chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to bring help to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of the Syrians. And David placed a garrison in Syria of Damascus; and Syria became David's servant under tribute. And the Lord preserved David in all things wherever he went. David took the golden shields which the servants of Hadadezer had and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took a very great amount of bronze.

<margin>2 Kings 8</margin>
When Tou, king of Hamath, heard that David had struck down all the strength of Hadadezer, he sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and congratulate him, and to give thanks because he had fought against Hadadezer and struck him down. For Tou was an enemy of Hadadezer. And in his hand were vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and vessels of bronze. These also King David sanctified to the Lord, along with the silver and gold that he had sanctified from all the nations he had subdued: from Syria, and Moab, and the children of Ammon, and the Philistines, and Amalek, and from the spoils of Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah.

<margin>2 Kings 8</margin>
David also made a name for himself when he returned after striking down eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt. He placed guards in Edom and established a garrison, and all of Edom became David's servants; and the Lord preserved David in all things wherever he went. And David reigned over all Israel; and David administered judgment and justice to all his people. Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder. Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were the priests; and Seraiah was the scribe. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites <note>The king's elite personal bodyguards</note>.

Then David said, “Do you think there is anyone left of the house of Saul, so that I may show him mercy for Jonathan’s sake?” Now there was a servant of the house of Saul named Ziba. When the king had called him, he said to him, “Are you Ziba?” and he replied, “I am your servant.” And the king said, “Is there anyone else left of the house of Saul, so that I may show the mercy of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “The son of Jonathan remains, who is crippled in his feet.” He said, “Where is he?” and Ziba told the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel in Lo-debar.” Then King David sent and took him from the house of Machir. When Mephibosheth <note>original: "Misiboseth"</note>, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, he fell on his face and did obeisance. David said, “Mephibosheth,” and he answered, “Behold your servant.” David said to him, “Do not fear, for I will surely show you mercy for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the lands of your father Saul, and you shall eat bread at my table always.” Doing obeisance, he said, “Who am I, your servant, that you should look upon a dead dog such as I?” So the king called Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “Everything that belonged to Saul and to all his house, I have given to your master’s son. You, therefore, and your sons and your servants, shall work the land for him, and you shall bring in the produce so that your master’s son may have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s son, shall always eat at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. Ziba said to the king, “As my lord the king has commanded his servant, so shall your servant do; and Mephibosheth shall eat at your table as one of the king’s sons.” Mephibosheth also had a young son named Mica. And all the household of

<margin>2 Kings 10</margin>
It happened after this that the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place. David said, “I will show mercy to Hanun the son of Nahash, just as his father showed mercy to me.” David therefore sent his servants to comfort him over the death of his father. But when David’s servants came into the land of the children of Ammon, the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun their lord, “Do you think that out of honor for your father David has sent comforters to you? When this was reported to David, he sent to meet them, for the men were very greatly shamed. David commanded them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards grow, and then return.” When the children of Ammon saw that they had insulted David, they sent and hired the Syrians of Rehob and the Syrians of Zobah, twenty thousand footmen, and a thousand men from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand men from Ishtob. When David heard this, he sent Joab and the entire army of warriors. The children of Ammon came out and drew up their battle line at the very entrance of the gate; but the Syrians of Rehob, Zobah, Ishtob, and Maacah were by themselves in the field. Joab, seeing that the battle was prepared against him both in front and behind, chose from all the elite of Israel and drew up his line against the Syrians. The rest of the people he handed over to his brother Abishai, who drew up the line against the children of Ammon. And he said, “If the Syrians are too strong for me, you shall help me. But if the children of Ammon are too strong for you, I will help you. Be a man of courage, and let us fight for our people and for the city of our God; and the Lord will do what is good in his sight.” Then Joab and the people with him entered into battle against the Syrians, who immediately fled from before him. When the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians had fled, they also fled from Abishai and entered the city. Joab returned from the children of Ammon and came to Jerusalem. When the Syrians saw they had fallen before Israel, they gathered together. Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were across the river and led their army; Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, was their leader. When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. The Syrians drew up their line against David and fought him. The Syrians fled from before Israel, and David killed seven hundred chariot teams and forty thousand horsemen of the Syrians; he also struck Shobach the commander, who died there. When all the kings who were under Hadadezer saw they were defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and served them. And the Syrians were afraid to provide help to the children of Ammon any longer.

Why did you approach the wall?’ then you shall say: ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.’” So the messenger went and came to David, and told him all that Joab had commanded. Then the archers shot arrows at your servants from the wall, and some of the king’s servants are dead; and your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.” David said to the messenger: “Thus shall you say to Joab: ‘Do not let this matter break you. For the outcome of war is varied; the sword consumes now this one, now that one. Strengthen your warriors against the city to destroy it, and encourage them.’” When the wife of Uriah heard that her husband Uriah was dead, she mourned for him. When the mourning was over, David sent and brought her into his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. And this thing that David had done was displeasing in the eyes of the Lord.

Thus he did to all the cities of the children of Ammon. Then David and all the army returned to Jerusalem.

**A**fter this, it happened that Absalom, the son of David, had a very beautiful sister named Tamar; and Amnon, the son of David, loved her. He was so tormented because of his sister Tamar that he became ill; for she was a virgin, and it seemed difficult to Amnon to do anything to her. But Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother; and Jonadab was a very clever man. He said to him, "Why are you becoming so thin day by day, O son of the king? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom." And Jonadab said to him:

> Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, "I pray you, let my sister Tamar come and give me food, and prepare some nourishment in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."

So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king:

> I pray you, let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of little cakes <note>original: "sorbitiunculas"</note> in my sight, that I may eat from her hand.

Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him." So Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, and he was lying down. She took flour and kneaded it, and made cakes in his sight and baked them. Then she took what she had baked and poured it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send everyone out from me." When everyone had gone out, Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to her brother Amnon. But when she offered them to him to eat, he took hold of her and said, "Come, lie with me, my sister." She answered him:

> No, my brother, do not force me; for such a thing ought not to be done in Israel. Do not do this wicked thing. As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be like one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.

But he would not listen to her plea; but being stronger than she, he forced her and lay with her. Then Amnon hated her with an exceedingly great hatred; so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Arise, be gone!" But she said to him, "This evil in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her. Instead, he called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out from me and bolt the door after her." She was wearing a robe with long sleeves, for this was how the virgin daughters of the king were dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her. And Tamar put ashes on her head, and tore the long-sleeved robe she was wearing; and she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying out as she went. Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you?

But Absalom urged him, and he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him. Now Absalom had prepared a feast, like the feast of a king. And Absalom commanded his servants, saying:

> Mark well when Amnon's heart is merry with wine; and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; for have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant men.

So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and every man mounted his mule and fled. While they were still on the way, news came to David, saying, "Absalom has killed all the king's sons, and not one of them is left." Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth; and all his servants stood by with their garments torn. But Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother, answered and said, "Let not my lord the king suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons; Amnon alone is dead. For by the mouth of Absalom this has been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar. Now therefore, let not my lord the king take this thing to heart, thinking that all the king's sons are dead; for Amnon alone is dead." But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming by the way of the hillside behind him. And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has happened." As soon as he had finished speaking, the king's sons appeared, and they lifted up their voices and wept; and the king also and all his servants wept with a very great weeping. But Absalom fled and went to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur <note>original: "iessur"</note>. And David mourned for his son every day. So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years. And King David longed to go out to Absalom; for he was comforted concerning Amnon, since he was dead. Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king's heart was toward Absalom. And he sent to Tekoa <note>original: "thecuā"</note> and brought from there a wise woman, and said to her:

And Joab put the words in her mouth. When the woman of Tekoa spoke to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and did obeisance, and said, "Save me, O king!" The king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered:

Then the king answered and said to the woman, "Do not hide from me the thing that I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak." The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As your soul lives, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has spoken. So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. And the king said, "Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face." So Absalom returned to his own house and did not see the king's face.

**Joab** then entered the house to the king and said, "Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants, who have saved your life, and the lives of your sons and daughters, and the lives of your wives and concubines. I realize now that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, you would be pleased. Now, therefore, arise and go out, and speak kindly to your servants. For I swear to you by the Lord, if you do not go out, not one man will stay with you this night. And this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now." So the king arose and sat in the gate. It was announced to all the people that the king was sitting in the gate, and the entire multitude came before the king. Meanwhile, Israel had fled to their own tents.

For I, your servant, said, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself that I may ride on it and go with the king,' for I, your servant, am lame. Moreover, he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city and be buried near the grave of my father and my mother. The king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever you wish; whatever you ask of me, I will do for you." So all the people and the king crossed the Jordan. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place.

The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went with him. All the people of Judah escorted the king, and also half the people of Israel. And behold, all the men of Israel came to the king.

**And they said** to the king, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?" All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our near relative. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten at the king's expense, or has any gift been given to us?" The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and we have more right to David than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than the words of the men of Israel.

**And** there happened to be a wicked man <note>original: "uir belial," a man of Belial/worthless man</note> there named Sheba <note>original: "seba"</note> son of Bichri, a Benjamite. He blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse! Every man to his tents, O Israel!" So all the men of Israel deserted David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed close to their king, from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

And there was a fourth war in Gath, in which there was a very tall man who had six fingers on his hands and six toes on his feet, that is twenty-four in all, and he was of the origin of the giants; and he blasphemed Israel. But Jonathan son of Shimeah, David's brother, struck him. These four were born of the giant in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.

And David spoke to the Lord the words of this song in the day that the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. And he said: "The Lord is my rock and my strength and my savior. My God is my strong one, in him will I hope. And he heard my voice from his temple, and my cry shall come to his ears. The earth was moved and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were moved and shaken, because he was angry. Smoke ascended from his nostrils, and fire from his mouth shall devour; coals were kindled by him. He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet. Because of the brightness in his presence, coals of fire were kindled. The Lord shall thunder from heaven, and the Most High shall give his voice. He sent his arrows and scattered them, lightning and consumed them. They prevented me in the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my firmament. And he led me out into a wide place; he delivered me because I pleased him. The Lord will reward me according to my justice, and according to the cleanness of my hands he will repay me. For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not acted impiously against my God. For all his judgments are in my sight, and his precepts I have not removed from me. And I shall be perfect with him, and I will keep myself from my iniquity. And the Lord will restore me according to my justice, and according to the cleanness of my hands in the sight of his eyes. With the holy you shall be holy; with the robust man you shall be perfect. And the Lord became merciful to the land, and the plague was restrained from Israel.

Their blood shall return upon the head of Joab and upon the head of his descendants forever. But for David and his descendants, and his house, and his throne, let there be peace forever from the Lord." So Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up, attacked him, and killed him; and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness. And the king appointed Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the army in his place, and he appointed Zadok the priest in place of Abiathar. The king also sent and called for Shimei, and said to him: "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there, and do not go out from there to any other place. For on whatever day you go out and cross the Brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall be put to death; your blood shall be upon your own head." And Shimei said to the king: "The word is good; as my lord the king has spoken, so will your servant do." And Shimei lived in Jerusalem for many days.

### Now it happened
Now it happened after three years that Shimei's servants fled to Achish, son of Maacah, the king of Gath. And it was told to Shimei: "Behold, your servants are in Gath." Shimei arose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to Achish to find his servants; and he brought them back from Gath. But it was reported to Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned. The king sent and called him, and said to him: "Did I not make you swear by the Lord, and warn you, saying: 'On whatever day you go out to any other place, know for certain you shall die'? and you answered me: 'The word I have heard is good.' Why then have you not kept the oath of the Lord and the command that I gave you?" And the king said to Shimei: "You know all the evil of which your heart is conscious, which you did to my father David. The Lord has returned your malice upon your own head. But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the Lord forever." So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck him, and he died.

<margin>1 Kings 3</margin>
# The kingdom was established
The kingdom was therefore established in the hand of Solomon, and he was joined by marriage to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. For he took his daughter and brought her into the City of David until he finished building his own house, and the House of the Lord, and the wall around Jerusalem. Nevertheless, the people sacrificed on the high places <note>original: "excelsis" — outdoor altars or shrines that were later forbidden once the Temple was completed</note>, for a temple had not yet been built to the name of the Lord until that day. Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the statutes of his father David, except that he sacrificed and burned incense in the high places. So he went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the greatest high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar in Gibeon. The Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, saying: "Ask what you wish that I may give to you." And Solomon said: "You have shown great mercy to your servant David my father, just as he walked before you in truth, justice, and an upright heart with you. You have kept this great mercy for him, and you have given him a son sitting on his throne, as it is today. And now, O Lord my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father. But I am a little child, and do not know my going out or my coming in. And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a vast people that cannot be numbered or counted for multitude. Give therefore to your servant an understanding heart <note>original: "cor docile" — literally a teachable or docile heart</note> so that he may be able to judge your people, and discern between evil and good. For who is able to judge this people, this great people of yours?" It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked for such a thing. And the Lord said to Solomon: "Because you have asked this word, and have not asked for many days for yourself, nor riches, nor the lives of your enemies, but have asked for wisdom to discern judgment: behold, I have done according to your words. I have given you a wise and understanding heart, such that there has been none like you before you, nor shall any like you arise after you. But I have also given you those things which you did not ask for: namely, riches and glory, so that no one among the kings has been like you in all the days past. And if you walk in my ways, and keep my statutes and my commands as your father walked, I will lengthen your days." And when Solomon awoke, he understood that it was a dream. When he had come to Jerusalem, he stood before the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord and offered burnt offerings, and made peace offerings, and a great feast for all his servants. Then two women who were harlots came to the king and stood before him. One of them said: "I beg you, my lord, I and this woman lived in one house, and I gave birth in a room with her. On the third day after I gave birth, she also gave birth; and we were together, and no one else was in the house with us, except for the two of us. But this woman's son died in the night, for sleeping

<column-break/>

upon him, she smothered him. And rising in the dead of night in silence, she took my son from my side while your handmaid was sleeping, and laid him in her bosom; and her dead son she laid in my bosom. And when I had risen in the morning to give milk to my son, he appeared dead. But when I looked at him more closely in the light of day, I discovered that he was not mine, whom I had borne." The other woman answered: "It is not so; rather, your son is dead, and mine is alive." On the contrary, the first woman said: "You lie! For my son lives, and your son is dead." And in this manner they argued before the king. Then the king said: "This one says: 'My son is alive, and your son is dead,' and that one responds: 'No, but your son is dead, and mine is alive.'" The king therefore said: "Bring me a sword." And when they had brought a sword before the king, he said: "Divide the living child into two parts, and give half to one, and half to the other." Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king—for her heart was moved with compassion for her son: "I beg you, lord, give her the living child, and do not kill him." But the other said: "Let it be neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided." The king answered and said: "Give the living child to the first woman, and let him not be killed. For she is his mother." So all Israel heard the judgment that the king had rendered, and they feared the king, seeing that the wisdom of God was in him to perform judgment.

<margin>1 Kings 4</margin>
## Now King Solomon was
Now King Solomon was reigning over all Israel, and these were the princes whom he had: Azariah the son of Zadok the priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha, the scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the army; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Azariah the son of Nathan was over those who stood before the king; Zabud the son of Nathan, a priest, was the king's friend; Ahishar was governor of the house; and Adoniram the son of Abda was over the tributes.

<margin>2 Chronicles 1</margin>
Now Solomon had twelve governors over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. For each month in a year, each one provided the necessary things. And these are their names: Ben-Hur in Mount Ephraim; Ben-Deker in Makaz, and in Shaalbim, and in Beth-shemesh, and in Elon, and in Beth-hanan; Ben-Hesed in Arubboth—Socoh and all the land of Hepher were his; Ben-Abinadab, who had all the region of Dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as a wife); Baana the son of Ahilud governed Taanach and Megiddo, and all Beth-shean which is beside Zarethan, below Jezreel from Beth-shean as far as Abel-meholah across from Jokmeam; Ben-Geber in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh in Gilead; he was also over all the region of Argob which is in Bashan, sixty great and walled cities which had bronze bars); Ahinadab the son of Iddo was over Mahanaim; Ahimaaz in Naphtali (he also had Basemath the daughter of Solomon in marriage); Baana the son of Hushai in Asher and in Aloth; Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah in Issachar; Shimei the son of Ela in Benjamin; Geber the son of Uri in the land of Gilead, in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, over all things that were in that land. Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand of the sea in multitude, eating and drinking and making merry.
