<margin>2 Chronicles 9</margin>
## But Solomon was
But Solomon was in his dominion and held all the kingdoms from the river of the land of the Philistines to the border of Egypt; they brought him gifts and served him all the days of his life. And Solomon's food for each day was thirty cors <note>A 'cor' (chorus) was a large dry measure, roughly 220–360 liters.</note> of fine flour and sixty cors of meal; ten fat oxen, twenty oxen from the pastures, and a hundred rams, besides the hunting of stags, roebucks, buffalos, and fatted birds. For he held all the region that was across the River, from Tiphsah even to Gaza, and all the kings of those nations; and he had peace on every side round about. And Judah and Israel lived without any fear, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon. And Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen; and the aforementioned governors of the king nourished them. They also provided the necessities for King Solomon’s table with great care in their season. They also brought barley and straw for the horses and beasts of burden to the place where the king was, according to the appointment set for them. God also gave Solomon wisdom and very much prudence, and a breadth of heart like the sand that is on the seashore. And the wisdom of Solomon preceded the wisdom of all the Easterners and the Egyptians, and he was wiser than all men: wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Calcol, and Darda the sons of Mahol; and he was most famous among all the nations round about. Solomon also spoke three thousand parables, and his songs were five thousand. And he disputed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop <note>Hyssop is a small plant used in purification rites, often contrasted with the mighty cedar to show the range of Solomon's knowledge.</note> that grows out of the wall; and he discoursed on beasts, and birds, and reptiles, and fish. And they came from all peoples to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth who heard of his wisdom. Hiram king of Tyre also sent his servants to Solomon, for he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, because Hiram had always been a friend of David. And Solomon sent to Hiram, saying: "You know the will of David my father, and that he could not build a house to the name of the Lord his God because of the wars pressing in on every side, until the Lord put them under the soles of his feet. But now the Lord my God has given me peace round about, and there is no adversary <note>original: "satan" — here used in the general sense of an adversary or accuser.</note> nor evil occurrence. For which reason I intend to build a temple to the name of the Lord my God, as the Lord spoke to David my father, saying: 'Your son, whom I will give in your place upon your throne, he shall build a house to my name.' Command therefore that they cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants; and I will give you whatever wages for your servants you command. For you know that there is no man among my people who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians." And when Hiram had heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said: "Blessed be the Lord God today, who has given David a most wise son over this very great people." And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying: "I have heard whatever you commanded me; I will do all your will regarding the cedar and fir logs. My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will arrange them in rafts on the sea as far as the place you indicate to me; and I will land them there, and you shall take them. And you shall provide the necessities for me, that food may be given to my household." So Hiram gave Solomon cedar and fir timber according to all his desire. And Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat for food for his household, and twenty cors of the purest oil. These things Solomon gave to Hiram every year. The Lord also gave wisdom to Solomon as he had promised him, and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and they both struck a covenant. And King Solomon chose workmen from all Israel, and the levy was thirty thousand men. He sent them to Lebanon...

And for those who prepared the cooked food for the people and for those who did the work. <margin>The command of the king or</margin> The king’s command was to quarry great stones, precious stones for the foundation of the temple, and to square them; these were shaped by Solomon’s masons and the masons of Hiram. **It happened** then in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv (which is the second month), that he began to build the house of the Lord.

<margin>1 Kings 6:b</margin>
**The house** which Solomon built for the Lord had a length of sixty cubits <term>cubit: a unit of measure based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</term>, a width of twenty cubits, and a height of thirty cubits. And the portico in front of the temple was twenty cubits in width, according to the measure of the width of the temple; and it had ten cubits of length in front of the face of the temple. And he made slanted windows in the temple. And he built floors against the wall of the temple all around the walls of the house, encircling the temple and the inner sanctuary; and he made side chambers all around. The first floor was five cubits in width, the middle floor was six cubits in width, and the third floor was seven cubits in width. Moreover, he placed beams in the house around the outside, so that they would not be fastened into the walls of the temple. **The house**, when it was being built, was built with finished stones prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built. The door for the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house; and they went up by winding stairs into the middle chamber, and from the middle into the third. So he built the house and finished it. **And** he covered the house with cedar panels. And he built the structure over the whole house, five cubits high, and covered the house with cedar wood. And the word of the Lord came to Solomon, saying: <margin>1 Kings 6:c</margin> "**This house** which you are building: if you walk in my precepts, and execute my judgments, and keep all my commandments, walking in them, I will fulfill my word to you, which I spoke to your father David. And I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel, and I will not forsake my people Israel."

**And** Solomon built the house and finished it. **And** he built the walls of the house on the inside with cedar boards. From the floor of the house to the top of the wall and up to the ceiling, he covered it with wood of fir <note>original: "maratref," likely a corruption of "meritissimum" or referring to juniper/fir</note>, and he covered the floor of the house with planks of cypress. **And** he built a space of twenty cubits at the rear part of the temple with cedar boards, from the floor to the upper parts; and he made the inner house of the sanctuary into the Holy of Holies. Furthermore, the temple itself before the doors of the sanctuary was forty cubits long. And all the house on the inside was varied with cedar, having its own carvings and subtle, protruding joints; everything was clothed in cedar boards, so that no stone at all could be seen in the wall. Moreover, he had made the inner sanctuary in the middle of the house, in the inner part, so that he might place the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord there. Now the sanctuary was twenty cubits in length, twenty cubits in width, and twenty cubits in height; and he covered it with the purest gold, and he also clothed the altar with cedar. And he closed off the front of the sanctuary with chains of gold. There was nothing in the temple that was not covered in gold. He even covered the entire altar of the sanctuary with gold. **And** he made two cherubim <note>Winged celestial beings representing the presence of God</note> in the sanctuary out of olive wood, ten cubits high. One wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits; that is, they had ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other wing. The second cherub was also ten cubits, of the same measure; and the workmanship was the same in the two cherubim. That is, one cherub had a height of ten cubits, and the second cherub was likewise. And he placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner temple. And the cherubim extended their wings, so that one wing touched one wall, and the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall; and their other wings in the middle of the temple touched each other wing to wing. And he covered the cherubim with gold. And all the walls of the temple around he carved with various engravings and turned work; and he made in them cherubim and palm trees and various pictures as if protruding from the wall and coming forth. **Indeed**, he even covered the floor of the house with gold, inside and out. And at the entrance of the sanctuary, he made doors of olive wood, and doorposts with five angles. And the two doors were of olive wood, and he carved on them pictures of cherubim and the likeness of palm trees and carvings that were very prominent, and he covered them with gold; he covered both the cherubim and the palms and the rest with gold. And at the entrance of the temple, he made four-sided posts of olive wood, and two doors of cypress wood, one following the other; and he carved on them cherubim and palms and very prominent engravings, and he covered everything with gold leaf according to the correct rule. **And** he built the inner court with three rows of polished stones and one row of cedar beams. <margin>1 Kings 6:e</margin> In the fourth year, the house of the Lord was founded in the month of Ziv. And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul (which is the eighth month), the house was perfected in all its design and in all its various parts; and he built it in seven years. Solomon built **his own house** over thirteen years, and brought it to completion. <margin>1 Kings 7:a</margin> **He built** the House of the Forest of Lebanon, one hundred cubits in length, fifty cubits in width, and thirty cubits in height, with four walkways between cedar columns. And he had cut cedar wood for the columns, and he clothed the whole chamber with cedar panels, which was supported by forty-five columns. One row had fifteen columns placed opposite one another, looking toward each other at equal spaces between the columns. And above the columns were square beams, equal in all respects. And the doors were situated alongside the columns. He made it thirty cubits in length and fifty in width. And he placed another portico before the larger portico, and columns and capitals upon its columns. He also made the **Portico of the Throne**, in which the judgment seat is; and he finished it from the floor to the top of the wall. **And** the house in which he sat for judging was in the middle portico of similar workmanship. He also made a **house** for the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Solomon had taken as a wife, of such workmanship as this portico. All these things were made of precious stones, which were cut according to the standard of squareness, both inside—where they were cut with a saw—and from the foundation to the top of the walls, and on the outside even to the great court. And the foundations were of precious stones, large stones of ten or eight cubits. And above these were precious stones cut to a similar measure, and likewise of cedar. And the great court was round, with three rows of cut stones and one row of cut cedars; and also in the inner court of the house of the Lord and in the portico of the house.

On the top of the base was a roundness of one and a half cubits, so manufactured that the basin could be placed upon it, having its own engravings and carvings of various kinds from itself. **He also carved** on those plates which were of bronze: on the corners were cherubim, lions, and palm trees, in the likeness of a standing statue; so that they did not appear engraved but as if they were struck out. In this manner, he made ten bases with similar carving and measurement. **He also made** ten bronze basins. One basin held forty baths and was four cubits; and he placed each basin upon each of the ten bases. And he set five bases on the right side of the temple and five on the left. And Solomon made all the vessels in the house of the Lord: the golden altar, and the golden table upon which the Bread of Presence was placed. And the hinges of the doors of the inner house—the Holy of Holies—and of the doors of the temple were of gold. **And** all the work that Solomon did in the house of the Lord was finished. And he brought in the things that his father David had sanctified: the silver, the gold, and the vessels; and he stored them in the treasures of the house of the Lord.

And though the poles protruded and their ends were visible from the sanctuary in front of the inner sanctuary, they were not visible further outside; and they have been there until this present day. **Then Solomon stood** before the altar of the Lord in the sight of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven and said: "Lord God of Israel, there is no God like you in heaven above or on the earth below, you who keep the covenant and mercy for your servants who walk before you with all their heart. You who have kept for your servant David my father what you spoke to him; you spoke with your mouth and with your hands you have fulfilled it, as this day proves. Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you spoke to him, saying: 'There shall not be taken away from you a man before me to sit on the throne of Israel, provided that your children guard their way so that they walk before me just as you walked in my sight.' And now, Lord God of Israel, let your words be confirmed which you spoke to your servant David my father. But is it truly to be thought that God dwells on earth? If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built! But look toward the prayer of your servant and toward his petitions, Lord my God. Hear the hymn and the prayer which your servant prays before you today, so that your eyes may be open over this house night and day—over the house of which you said: 'My name shall be there'—so that you may hear the prayer by which your servant prays to you in this place. That you may hear the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, whatever they shall pray in this place; and you shall hear in the place of your dwelling in heaven, and when you have heard, you shall be merciful. If a man sins against his neighbor and is held bound by an oath, and comes because of the oath before your altar in your house, you shall hear in heaven and judge your servants: condemning the wicked and bringing his way upon his own head, and justifying the righteous and rewarding him according to his justice. If your people Israel flee from their enemies because they have sinned against you, and they do penance and confess to your name and come and pray and make supplication in this house: hear in heaven, and forgive the sin of your people Israel, and lead them back into the land which you gave to their fathers. If heaven is shut and there is no rain because of their sins, and praying in this place they do penance to your name and are converted from their sins because of their affliction: hear them in heaven, and forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel, and show them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain upon your land which you gave to your people as a possession. If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, or blight, or locusts, or mildew, and if their enemy afflicts them by besieging the gates: every plague, every infirmity, every prayer and supplication that shall happen to any man of your people Israel—if anyone recognizes the plague of his own heart and spreads his hands in this house: you shall hear in heaven, in the place of your dwelling, and you shall be merciful again and act so that you give to each one according to all his ways, just as you see his heart—for you alone know the heart of all the children of men—so that they may fear you all the days they live upon the face of the earth which you gave to our fathers. Furthermore, even the foreigner who is not of your people Israel, when he comes from a far-off land because of your name—for your great name and your strong hand and your outstretched arm will be heard of everywhere—when he comes, therefore, and prays in this place: you shall hear in heaven, in the firmament of your dwelling, and you shall do all those things for which the foreigner calls upon you, so that all the peoples of the earth may learn to fear your name just as your people Israel do, and may prove that your name is invoked over this house which I have built. If your people go out to war against their enemies wherever you send them, they shall pray to you toward the way of the city which you have chosen and toward the house I have built for your name, and you shall hear their prayers and their petitions in heaven and perform their judgment. But if they sin against you—for there is no man who does not sin—and in your anger you deliver them to their enemies and they are led away captive into the land of their enemies, whether far or near, and they do penance in their heart in the place of their captivity and are converted and pray to you in their captivity, saying: 'We have sinned, we have acted unjustly, we have behaved impiously,' and they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies to which they were led captive: and they pray to you toward the way of their land which you gave to their fathers, and the city which you chose, and the temple which I have built for your name: you shall hear their prayer and their petitions in heaven, in the firmament of your throne, and perform their judgment. And you shall be merciful to your people who have sinned against you, and to all their iniquities by which they have transgressed against you, and you shall grant them mercy in the sight of those who hold them captive, so that they may have pity on them. For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you led out of the land of Egypt from the midst of the iron furnace <note>A metaphor for intense suffering or slavery</note>, so that your eyes may be open to the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, and you shall hear them in everything for which they call upon you. For you separated them as an inheritance for yourself from all the peoples of the earth, just as you spoke through Moses your servant when you led our fathers out of Egypt, Lord God."

<margin>9</margin>
**It happened** then, when Solomon had finished praying all this prayer and supplication to the Lord, he rose from before the altar of the Lord, where he had been with both hands stretched out toward heaven. And he stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying: "Blessed be the Lord who has given rest to his people Israel according to all that he spoke; not even one word has failed of all the good things that he spoke through Moses his servant. May the Lord our God be with us just as he was with our fathers; let him not leave us nor cast us away, but let him incline our hearts to him so that we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments and ceremonies and judgments, whatever he commanded our fathers. And let these words, with which I have prayed before the Lord our God

<column-break/>

be near our Lord, day and night, so that he may do justice for his servant and for his people Israel day by day, so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord himself is God and there is no other besides him. Let your heart also be perfect with the Lord our God, that we may walk in his decrees and keep his commandments as it is today." Therefore the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices before the Lord. And Solomon slaughtered peace offerings which he sacrificed to the Lord: twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep. And the king and the children of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord. On that day the king sanctified the middle of the courtyard that was before the house of the Lord. For there he offered burnt offerings and sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the Lord was too small and could not contain the burnt offerings and the sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings. So Solomon held a celebrated festival at that time, and all Israel with him—a great multitude from the entrance of Hamath to the river of Egypt—before the Lord our God for seven days and seven days, that is, fourteen days. And on the eighth day he sent the people away, who, blessing the king, departed to their tents rejoicing and with a cheerful heart because of all the good things the Lord had done for David his servant and for his people Israel.

**It happened** then, when Solomon had finished the building of the house of the Lord and the royal palace and everything he had planned and wanted to do, the Lord appeared to him a second time, just as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. And the Lord said to him: "I have heard your prayer and your supplication which you prayed before me. I have sanctified this house which you have built to put my name there forever, and my eyes and my heart shall be there all days. You also, if you walk before me as your father walked in simplicity of heart and in equity, and do all that I have commanded you, and keep my statutes and my judgments, I will place the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, just as I spoke to David your father, saying: 'There shall not be taken away from you a man of your lineage from the throne of Israel.' But if you and your children turn away from following me and do not keep my commandments and ceremonies which I have set before you, but go and worship foreign gods and adore them, I will take Israel away from the surface of the land I gave them. And the temple which I have sanctified for my name I will cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a story to all peoples. And this house shall be an example. Everyone passing by it will be stunned and will hiss and say: 'Why has the Lord done this to this land and to this house?' And they will answer: 'Because they abandoned the Lord their God who led their fathers out of the land of Egypt and followed foreign gods and adored them and worshipped them. Therefore the Lord has brought all this evil upon them.'" After twenty years had passed since Solomon had built the two houses—that is, the house of the Lord and the royal palace—with Hiram king of Tyre providing Solomon with cedar and fir wood and gold according to everything he needed, then Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee. And Hiram went out from Tyre to see the towns Solomon had given him, and they did not please him. And he said: "Are these the cities you have given me, my brother?" And he called them the Land of Cabul <note>original: "chabul"; traditionally interpreted as "dirty" or "worthless"</note> to this day. Hiram also sent the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold. This is the sum of the expenses which King Solomon offered for building the house of the Lord, and his own house, and the Millo <note>A fortification or terrace in Jerusalem</note>, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer. Pharaoh king of Egypt went up and took Gezer and burned it with fire. And he killed the Canaanite who lived in the city and gave it as a dowry for his daughter, Solomon’s wife. So Solomon built Gezer and lower Beth-horon and Baalath and Palmyra in the land of the wilderness. And he fortified all the villages that belonged to him and were without walls, and the chariot cities and the cities for the horsemen, and whatever he pleased to build in Jerusalem and in Lebanon and in all the land of his power. All the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not of the children of Israel—their children who remained in the land, whom the children of Israel had not been able to exterminate—Solomon made into forced laborers <term>tributarios: people forced to pay tribute, often through labor</term> to this day. But Solomon did not make any of the children of Israel slaves; instead, they were warriors and his ministers and princes and captains and commanders of the chariots and horsemen. There were five hundred and fifty chief officers over all the works of Solomon who had the people under them and commanded the established works. Pharaoh’s daughter went up from the City of David to her own house which Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo. Also three times every year, Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace sacrifices on the altar he had built for the Lord, and he burned incense before the Lord. And the temple was finished. King Solomon also built a fleet in Ezion-geber, which is near Elath on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent his servants in that fleet, sailors and those knowledgeable of the sea, along with Solomon’s servants. And when they came to Ophir, they took gold from there—four hundred and twenty talents—and brought it to King Solomon.

<margin>10</margin>
**But the Queen of Sheba**, having heard of Solomon’s fame in the name of the Lord, came to test him with riddles. And having entered Jerusalem with a great company and riches, with camels carrying spices and infinitely much gold and precious gems, she came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything she had in her heart. And Solomon taught her all the words she proposed; there was no matter that could be hidden from the king which he did not answer for her. When the Queen of Sheba saw all the wisdom of Solomon, and the house he had built, and the food of his table, and the dwellings of his servants, and the orders of those ministering, and their garments, and the cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he offered in the house of the Lord, she no longer had any spirit left in her. And she said to the king: "The report I heard in my own land about your words and your wisdom is true. And I did not believe those telling me until I came myself and my eyes saw it. And I have proved that not even half was told to me. Your wisdom and your works are greater than the rumor I heard. Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants who stand before you always and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God who was pleased with you and placed you on the throne of Israel, because the Lord has loved Israel forever and appointed you king to do judgment and justice." Then she gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold and very many spices and precious gems. Never again were so many spices brought as those which the Queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Also, the fleet of Hiram which carried gold from Ophir brought from Ophir very many almug trees <note>original: "ligna thyina"; a precious, fragrant wood used for fine instruments and architecture</note> and precious gems. And the king made supports for the house of the Lord and the royal palace from the almug trees, and harps and lyres for the singers. No such almug trees have been brought or seen until the present day. King Solomon gave the Queen of Sheba everything she wanted and asked of him, besides those things which he had offered her of his own accord by royal gift. And she returned and went into her own land with her servants.

**Now the weight of gold** offered to Solomon every year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, besides what was brought by the men over the taxes and the merchants and all the kings of the Arabs and the governors of the land.

...and the house for Pharaoh’s daughter. King Solomon had also constructed a throne of ivory, which he overlaid with the finest gold. It was built with six steps, and the top of the throne was rounded at the back. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with two lions standing beside the armrests. Twelve lions stood upon the six steps, six on one side and six on the other. Nothing like it had ever been made for any other kingdom. All the vessels from which King Solomon drank were made of gold, and all the furniture of the House of the Forest of Lebanon was of the purest gold. Silver was not considered of any value in his days, because the King’s fleet sailed the ocean alongside the ships of Hiram <note>original: "regi tharsis" — likely referring to ships of Tarshish, a distant port known for metal trade</note>, and every three years the fleet would return, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Thus, King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom. The whole world desired to see Solomon’s face and to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart. Everyone brought him gifts: vessels of silver and gold, garments, armor, spices, horses, and mules, year after year. Solomon gathered chariots and horses; he had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem. The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees that grow in the lowlands. Horses were brought for Solomon from Egypt and from Kue <note>original: "chua" — a region in Cilicia, modern-day Turkey, famous for horse breeding</note>. The king’s agents purchased them from Kue at a fixed price. A chariot imported from Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse one hundred and fifty. These were also exported through the king's agents to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.

However, King Solomon loved many foreign women: the daughter of Pharaoh, and women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites. These were from the nations about which the Lord had said to the children of Israel: "You shall not intermarry with them, nor shall they marry with you, for they will surely turn your hearts away to follow their gods." Yet Solomon clung to these in most ardent love. He had seven hundred wives of royal rank and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned his heart away. When he was old, his wives led his heart astray to follow foreign gods, and his heart was not entirely devoted to the Lord his God, as the heart of his father David had been. Solomon worshipped Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Chemosh, the god of Moab, and Milcom <note>original: "maloch"</note>, the idol of the Ammonites. Solomon did what was displeasing in the sight of the Lord and did not follow the Lord completely as his father David had done. Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the hill east of Jerusalem, and for Moloch, the idol of the Ammonites. He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and offered sacrifices to their gods. Therefore, the Lord became angry with Solomon because his mind had turned away from the Lord God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him specifically not to follow foreign gods. But Solomon did not keep what the Lord commanded. The Lord said to Solomon: "Because you have done this and have not kept my covenant and my statutes which I commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant. Nevertheless, for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime; I will tear it out of the hand of your son. Yet I will not take away the entire kingdom; I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen." The Lord then raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, of the royal line of Edom. Formerly, when David was in Edom and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, having killed every male in Edom, Hadad—who was then only a young boy—fled to Egypt with some Edomite servants of his father. They set out from Midian and went to Paran, taking men from Paran with them, and came to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, assigned him food, and gave him land. Hadad found great favor in Pharaoh's eyes, so much so that Pharaoh gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, Queen Tahpenes. The sister of Tahpenes bore Hadad a son named Genubath, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s palace, and Genubath lived there among Pharaoh’s own children. When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had slept with his ancestors and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, he said to Pharaoh: "Let me depart, so that I may go to my own country." Pharaoh asked him: "What do you lack here with me that you want to go to your own land?" He replied: "Nothing, but please, let me go." God also raised up another adversary against Solomon: Rezon son of Eliada, who had fled from his master, King Hadadezer of Zobah. He gathered men around him and became a leader of a rebel band after David’s slaughter. They went to Damascus and settled there, making him king in Damascus. He was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon, adding to the trouble caused by Hadad; he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria. Also, Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah and a servant of Solomon whose mother was a widow named Zeruah, raised his hand against the king. This is the reason he rebelled: Solomon was building the Millo <note>a defensive terrace or fortification</note> and closing the breach in the city of his father David. Jeroboam was a capable and powerful man; when Solomon saw how industrious the young man was, he put him in charge of the entire labor force of the house of Joseph.

At that time, when Jeroboam was leaving Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh met him on the road, wearing a new cloak. The two of them were alone in the field. Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces. He said to Jeroboam: "Take ten pieces for yourself, for this is what the Lord God of Israel says: 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and give you ten tribes. But one tribe shall remain his for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel. I will do this because they have forsaken me and worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites. They have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my eyes and keeping my statutes and ordinances as David his father did. However, I will not take the whole kingdom from his hand; I will keep him as ruler all the days of his life for the sake of my servant David, whom I chose and who kept my commandments. But I will take the kingdom from his son’s hand and give it to you—that is, the ten tribes. To his son I will give one tribe, so that my servant David may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I chose to put my Name. I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires; you shall be king over Israel. If you listen to all that I command you and walk in my ways, doing what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and commandments as my servant David did, I will be with you. I will build you a lasting dynasty, just as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you. I will humble David's descendants

<column-break/>

because of this, but not forever.'" Jeroboam lived and troubled Israel all the days of Solomon; this was the mischief of Hadad and the hatred against Israel, and he reigned in Syria as an adversary to Israel, continually threatening until the death of Solomon. After King Solomon had lived ninety-four years and reigned for eighty <note>The Latin text specifies 80/94 years, though standard biblical tradition cites a 40-year reign</note>, he died and was buried in the city of David. The time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam reigned in his place. Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered there to make him king.

When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of this—he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon—he returned from Egypt. They sent for him and called him. Jeroboam and the whole assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam: "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now, therefore, lighten the harsh labor and the heavy yoke your father put on us, and we will serve you." He replied: "Go away for three days, then come back to me." After the people left, King Rehoboam consulted with the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. He asked: "What is your advice? How should I answer these people?" They told him: "If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them, and give them a favorable answer and speak kind words to them, they will be your servants forever." But he rejected the advice the elders gave him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and were serving him. He asked them: "What is your advice? How should we answer these people who said to me, 'Lighten the yoke your father put on us'?" The young men who had grown up with him replied: "Tell these people who said your father's yoke was heavy: 'My little finger is thicker than my father's loins! My father laid on you a heavy yoke; I will make it even heavier. My father scourged you with whips; I will scourge you with scorpions <note>whips fitted with jagged pieces of metal or bone</note>!'" On the third day, Jeroboam and all the people returned to Rehoboam, as the king had instructed. The king answered the people harshly. Rejecting the advice given him by the elders, he followed the advice of the young men and said: "My father made your yoke heavy; I will make it even heavier. My father scourged you with whips; I will scourge you with scorpions." The king did not listen to the people, for this turn of events was from the Lord, to fulfill the word the Lord had spoken through Ahijah to Jeroboam son of Nebat. When all Israel saw that the king refused to listen to them, they answered: "What portion do we have in David? What inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel! Look after your own house, David!" So the Israelites went home. But as for the Israelites who were living in the towns of Judah, Rehoboam still reigned over them. King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was in charge of forced labor, but all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam, however, managed to get into his chariot and flee to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day. When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. Only the tribe of Judah remained loyal to the house of David. When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he mustered the whole house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—one hundred and eighty thousand able-bodied fighting men—to go to war against Israel and to regain the kingdom for Rehoboam son of Solomon.

But this word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: "Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon king of Judah, to the whole house of Benjamin, and to the rest of the people: 'This is what the Lord says: Do not go up to fight against your brothers, the Israelites. Every one of you, go home, for this thing is my doing.'" So they obeyed the word of the Lord and went home again, as the Lord had ordered.

Then Jeroboam fortified Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. From there he went out and built up Penuel. Jeroboam thought to himself: "The kingdom will now likely revert to the house of David if these people go up to offer sacrifices at the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem. Their hearts will return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah; they will kill me and return to him." After seeking advice, the king made two golden calves. He said to the people: "It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt." One he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan. And this thing became a sin; the people came to worship the calf even as far as Dan. Jeroboam built shrines on high places and appointed priests from all sorts of people, even though they were not Levites. He instituted a festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the festival held in Judah, and offered sacrifices on the altar. He did this in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves he had made. At Bethel he also installed priests at the high places he had made. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a month of his own choosing, he offered sacrifices on the altar he had built at Bethel. So he instituted the festival for the Israelites and went up to the altar to burn incense.

By the word of the Lord a man of God came from Judah to Bethel, as Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make an offering. By the word of the Lord he cried out against the altar: "Altar, altar! This is what the Lord says: 'A son named Josiah <note>original: "ioseph" — likely a scribal error for Josiah (Iosias), the king who later destroyed this altar</note> will be born to the house of David. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who now burn incense here, and human bones will be burned on you.'" That same day the man of God gave a sign: "This is the sign the Lord has declared: The altar will be split apart and the ashes on it will be poured out." When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said: "Seize him!" But the hand he stretched out toward the man withered, so that he could not pull it back. Also, the altar was split apart and its ashes poured out according to the sign given by the man of God by the word of the Lord. Then the king said to the man of God: "Intercede with the Lord your God and pray for me that my hand may be restored." So the man of God interceded with the Lord, and the king’s hand was restored and became as it was before. The king said to the man of God: "Come home with me for a meal, and I will give you a gift." But the man of God answered the king: "Even if you were to give me half your possessions, I would not go with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water in this place. For I was commanded by the word of the Lord: 'You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.'" So he took another road and did not return by the way he had come to Bethel.

Now there was a certain old prophet living in Bethel, whose sons came and told him all that the man of God had done there that day. They also told their father what he had said to the king. Their father asked them: "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him which road the man of God from Judah had taken. So he said to his sons: "Saddle..."

**A**fter these words, Jeroboam did not return from his evil way, but on the contrary, he made priests for the high places from among the lowest of the people. Whoever wished to, filled his hand <note>The Hebrew idiom "to fill the hand" means to be ordained or consecrated as a priest</note> and became a priest of the high places. And because of this cause, the house of Jeroboam sinned, and it was overthrown and blotted out from the face of the earth.

<margin>14</margin>
**A**t that time, Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick. Jeroboam said to his wife: "Arise and change your clothing so that you will not be recognized as the wife of Jeroboam, and go to Shiloh, where the prophet Ahijah is, who told me that I would reign over this people. Take in your hand ten loaves of bread, and some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him; he will tell you what shall happen to the boy." Jeroboam's wife did as she was told: and arising, she went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. But he could not see, for his eyes had grown dim with old age. Now the Lord said to Ahijah: "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to consult you about her son who is sick; you shall say this and that to her." When she entered, pretending to be someone else, Ahijah heard the sound of her feet coming through the door and said: "Enter, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? I have been sent to you with a harsh message. Go and tell Jeroboam: 'Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because I exalted you from among the people and made you a leader over my people Israel, and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you—yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing what was pleasing in my sight—but you have done evil above all who were before you, and have made for yourself foreign gods and cast images to provoke me to anger, and have cast me behind your back. Therefore, behold, I will bring evil upon the house of Jeroboam, and I will strike down from Jeroboam every male <note>original: "mingentem ad parietem" — literally "one who urinates against a wall," a common biblical idiom for males</note>, both bond and free in Israel. I will sweep away the remnants of the house of Jeroboam as dung is swept away until it is all gone. Those of Jeroboam's house who die in the city, the dogs shall eat; and those who die in the field, the birds of the air shall devour; for the Lord has spoken it.' You, therefore, arise and go to your house; as your feet enter the city, the boy shall die. All Israel shall mourn him and bury him, for he alone of Jeroboam's family shall come to the grave, because in him there was found some good thing toward the Lord God of Israel in the house of Jeroboam. Moreover, the Lord will raise up for himself a king who shall strike down the house of Jeroboam in this day and in this time. And the Lord God of Israel will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and he will uproot Israel from this good land which he gave to their fathers, and will scatter them beyond the River <note>referring to the Euphrates</note>, because they made for themselves sacred groves <note>original: "lucos" — referring to Asherah poles used in pagan worship</note> to provoke the Lord. And the Lord will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, who sinned and made Israel to sin." So Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. As she crossed the threshold of the house, the boy died. They buried him, and all Israel mourned him, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke by the hand of his servant Ahijah the prophet. As for the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he fought and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Jeroboam reigned for twenty-two years; then he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.

<margin>14</margin>
**M**oreover, Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which the Lord chose out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonitess. Judah did evil in the sight of the Lord, and they provoked him more than all their fathers had done with the sins they committed. For they also built for themselves altars, and statues, and groves on every high hill and under every leafy tree. There were also male cult prostitutes in the land, and they committed all the abominations of the nations which the Lord had driven out before the children of Israel. In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak <note>original: "sesac"</note> king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, and he took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures; he plundered everything. He also took the gold shields which Solomon had made, in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields and committed them to the hands of the captains of the shield-bearers and those who kept watch at the door of the king’s house. Whenever the king went into the house of the Lord, those who held the office would carry them and then bring them back to the

<column-break/>

armory of the shield-bearers. As for the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days. So Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonitess. And Abijah <note>original: "abia"</note> his son reigned in his place.

<margin>15</margin>
**I**n the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijah reigned over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom. He walked in all the sins of his father which he had done before him, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God as was the heart of his father <note>referring to his ancestor David</note>. But for David's sake, the Lord his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, to raise up his son after him and to establish Jerusalem, because David had done what was right in the eyes of the Lord and had not turned aside from anything he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Nevertheless, there was war between Jeroboam and Abijah all the days of his life. As for the rest of the acts of Abijah and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? And there was battle between Abijah and Jeroboam. Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David, and Asa his son reigned in his place.

<margin>15</margin>
**I**n the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa reigned as king of Judah, and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom. Asa did what was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father; he removed the cult prostitutes from the land and purged all the filth of the idols which his fathers had made. Moreover, he even removed his mother Maacah from being a princess because she had made an idol in a grove dedicated to Priapus <note>original: "sacris priapi" — the Latin identifies the pagan idol with the Roman god of fertility, likely referring to an Asherah pole</note>. He destroyed her cave and broke that most shameful idol into pieces and burned it at the brook Kidron; however, the high places were not removed. Nevertheless, Asa’s heart was perfect with the Lord all his days, and he brought into the house of the Lord the things which his father had dedicated and what he himself had vowed: silver, gold, and vessels. There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah, so that no one could go out or come in on the side of Asa king of Judah. Therefore, Asa took all the silver and gold that remained in the treasures of the house of the Lord and in the treasures of the king’s house and gave it into the hands of his servants. He sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who dwelt in Damascus, saying: "There is a treaty between me and you, and between my father and your father. Therefore, I have sent you gifts of silver and gold; I ask that you come and break the treaty you have with Baasha king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me." Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel; he struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, along with the whole land of Naphtali. When Baasha heard this, he stopped building Ramah and returned to Tirzah. Then King Asa made a proclamation throughout all Judah, saying: "Let no one be excused." And they carried away the stones and timber of Ramah with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. As for all the rest of the acts of Asa, all his power, all that he did, and the cities he built, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? However, in his old age, his feet were diseased. He slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.

<margin>15</margin>
**N**adab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah. He reigned over Israel for two years and did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, walking in the ways of his father and in the sins by which he made Israel to sin. Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him and struck him down at Gibbethon, which is a city of the Philistines. For Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon. Thus Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place. As soon as he was king, he struck down the whole house of Jeroboam. He did not leave even one soul of his seed until he had destroyed him, according to the word of the Lord which he had spoken by the hand of his servant Ahijah the Shilonite, because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and by which he made Israel to sin, and because of the offense by which he provoked the Lord God of Israel. As for the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.

<margin>15</margin>
**I**n the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah reigned over all Israel in Tirzah for twenty-four years, and he did evil before the Lord, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sins by which he made Israel to sin. Then the word of the Lord came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying: "Because I exalted you from the dust and made you a leader over my people Israel, yet you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, to provoke me with their sins; behold, I will sweep away the posterity of Baasha and the posterity of his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Those of Baasha's house who die in the city, the dogs shall eat, and those who die in the field, the birds of the air shall devour." As for the rest of the acts of Baasha, whatever he did and his battles, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried in Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place. Now, the word of the Lord had come through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil he did before the Lord, provoking him by the works of his hands so as to be like the house of Jeroboam, and because he had killed him—that is, the prophet son of Hanani <note>This likely refers to Baasha destroying the house of Jeroboam, though the Latin syntax here is complex.</note>. In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha reigned over Israel in Tirzah for two years. His servant Zimri, commander of half the chariotry, rebelled against him. While Elah was in Tirzah drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was in charge of the palace at Tirzah, Zimri rushed in and struck him and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place. As soon as he was reigning and sat on the throne, he struck down the whole house of Baasha; he did not leave a single male, nor any of his kinsmen or friends. Thus Zimri destroyed the whole house of Baasha, according to the word of the Lord which he had spoken against Baasha by the prophet Jehu, because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, who sinned and made Israel to sin, provoking the Lord God of Israel with their vanities. As for the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

<margin>16</margin>
**I**n the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the army was besieging Gibbethon, a city of the Philistines. When the people in the camp heard it said, "Zimri has rebelled and has killed the king," all Israel made Omri <note>original: "amri"</note>, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp. Omri and all Israel with him went up from Gibbethon and besieged Tirzah. When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the palace and burned the royal house over himself, and he died in his sins which he had committed.

<summary>This page chronicles the rapid succession of kings in the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah, focusing on the divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam and the house of Baasha, and the religious reforms of King Asa of Judah.</summary>

Now the rest of the acts of Omri <note>original: "amri"</note> and the battles he fought, and his glory, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab <note>original: "achab"</note> his son reigned in his place.

<margin>Ahab</margin>
Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah. Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years. And Ahab son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord above all who were before him. It was not enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat; moreover, he took as a wife Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and he went and served Baal and worshipped him. And he set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal which he had built in Samaria, and he planted a sacred grove. And Ahab added to his deeds, provoking the Lord God of Israel more than all the kings of Israel who were before him. In his days, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho; he laid its foundations at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of Segub his youngest, according to the word of the Lord which He spoke through Joshua son of Nun.

<margin>Elijah</margin>
And Elijah <note>original: "helýas"</note> the Tishbite, of the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: "As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose sight I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by the words of my mouth."

The word of the Lord came to him, saying: "Depart from here and go toward the east, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith <note>original: "carith"</note>, which is across from the Jordan. And there you shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you."

So he did according to the word of the Lord. When he had gone, he stayed by the brook Cherith, which is across from the Jordan. The ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook.

But after some days, it happened that the brook dried up, for it had not rained upon the earth.

Then the word of the Lord came to him, saying: "Arise and go to Zarephath <note>original: "sareptha"</note> of the Sidonians and stay there; for I have commanded a widow woman there to feed you."

<margin>The widow woman</margin>
He arose and went to Zarephath. And when he had come to the gate of the city, a widow woman appeared gathering wood. He called to her and said: "Give me a little water in a vessel that I may drink." And as she was going to fetch it, he called after her, saying: "Bring me, I pray you, a morsel of bread in your hand." She answered: "As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread, but only as much flour as a fist can hold in a jar <note>original: "hydria"</note>, and a little oil in a flask <note>original: "lecytho"</note>. See, I am gathering two sticks that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and die."

Elijah said to her: "Do not fear; but go and do as you have said. Nevertheless, make me first a little hearth-baked cake <note>original: "subcinericium panem," literally bread baked under the ashes</note> from that flour and bring it to me; afterward you shall make some for yourself and your son. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: 'The jar of flour shall not fail, nor shall the flask of oil be diminished, until the day when the Lord shall give rain upon the face of the earth.'" She went and did according to the word of Elijah; and he ate, and she and her household. And from that day the jar of flour did not fail and the flask of oil was not diminished, according to the word of the Lord which He spoke through Elijah.

<margin>the widow's son died</margin>
After these things, it happened that the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell ill; and the sickness was very severe, so that no breath was left in him. She said therefore to Elijah: "What is there between me and you, O man of God? Have you come to me to bring my iniquities to remembrance and to kill my son?" And Elijah said to her: "Give me your son." And he took him from her bosom and carried him into the upper chamber where he himself stayed, and laid him upon his own bed. And he cried out to the Lord and said: "O Lord my God, have You even brought affliction upon the widow with whom I am staying by killing her son?" And he stretched himself out and measured himself over the boy three times; he cried to the Lord and said: "O Lord my God, I pray You, let this child's soul return into his inward parts." And the Lord heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child returned within him, and he revived. Elijah took the boy and brought him down from the upper chamber into the lower house, and delivered him to his mother, and said to her: "See, your son lives." And the woman said to Elijah: "Now by this I know that you are a man of God, and the word of the Lord in your mouth is true."

After many days, the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying: "Go and show yourself to Ahab, that I may give rain upon the face of the earth." Elijah went therefore to show himself to Ahab. Now there was a grievous famine in Samaria. And Ahab called Obadiah <note>original: "abdiam"</note>, the steward of his house. Now Obadiah feared the Lord greatly. For when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, he took a hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in caves, and fed them with bread and water. Ahab said to Obadiah: "Go throughout the land to all the springs of water and into all the valleys, to see if perhaps we might find grass and save the horses and mules, so that the beasts do not perish entirely." They divided the regions between them to go through them: Ahab went by one way, and Obadiah by another way by himself. While Obadiah was on the way, Elijah met him. When he recognized him, he fell on his face and said: "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" He answered: "It is I. Go and tell your lord: Elijah is here." And he said: "In what have I sinned, that you would deliver me your servant into the hand of Ahab to kill me? As the Lord your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. And when they all answered, 'He is not here,' he took an oath from every kingdom and nation because you were not found. And now you say to me: 'Go and tell your lord: Elijah is here.' When I have departed from you, the Spirit of the Lord will carry you to a place I know not; and I shall go and tell Ahab, and not finding you, he will kill me. But your servant has feared the Lord from his youth. Has it not been told to you, my lord, what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the Lord? How I hid a hundred men of the prophets of the Lord, by fifties and fifties in caves, and fed them with bread and water? And now you say: 'Go and tell your lord: Elijah is here,' so that he may kill me?" Elijah said: "As the Lord of hosts lives, before whose face I stand, I will surely show myself to him today." Obadiah went therefore to meet Ahab and told him; and Ahab came to meet Elijah. And when he saw him, he said: "Is it you, the one who 

<column-break/>

has troubled Israel?" And he said: "I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house, who have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and followed the Baals <note>original: "baalim"</note>. Nevertheless, send now and gather to me all Israel on Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and the four hundred prophets of the groves <note>term: "prophets of the groves" - these are the prophets of Asherah, a Canaanite goddess</note> who eat at Jezebel's table." Ahab sent to all the children of Israel and gathered the prophets on Mount Carmel.

Elijah came near to all the people and said: "How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow Him; but if Baal, follow him." And the people did not answer him a word.

Then Elijah said again to the people: "I alone remain as a prophet of the Lord; but the prophets of Baal are four hundred and fifty men. Let two oxen be given to us; let them choose one ox for themselves, and cutting it into pieces, let them lay it on the wood, but put no fire under it. And I will prepare the other ox and lay it on the wood, and I will put no fire under it. Call upon the names of your gods, and I will call upon the name of my Lord. And the God who answers by fire, let Him be God." All the people answering said: "The proposition Elijah has spoken is very good."

Elijah said to the prophets of Baal: "Choose one ox for yourselves and prepare it first, for you are many; and call upon the names of your gods, but put no fire under it." When they had taken the ox which he gave them, they prepared it; and they called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying: "O Baal, hear us!" But there was no voice, nor anyone who answered. And they leaped over the altar which they had made.

When it was already noon, Elijah mocked them, saying: "Cry with a louder voice! For he is a god, and perhaps he is talking, or in an inn, or on a journey, or surely he is asleep and must be awakened." They cried therefore with a great voice, and cut themselves according to their custom with knives and lancets until they were covered in blood. After noon had passed and while they were prophesying, the time had come when the sacrifice is usually offered; but no voice was heard, nor did anyone answer, nor did anyone pay attention to those praying. Elijah said to the people: "Come near to me." And as the people came near to him, he repaired the altar of the Lord which had been destroyed. He took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the Lord came, saying: "Israel shall be your name." And he built an altar of the stones in the name of the Lord. He made a trench around the altar, about the size of two measures <note>original: "duas amurcas," a measurement of volume, likely two seahs</note>, and he arranged the wood, and divided the ox into members and laid it on the wood and said: "Fill four jars with water and pour it upon the burnt offering and upon the wood." And again he said: "Do this a second time." When they had done it a second time, he said: "Do it even a third time." And they did so; and the water ran around the altar, and the trench of the aqueduct was filled.

When it was now the time for the burnt offering to be offered, Elijah the prophet came near and said: "O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel: show today that You are the God of Israel, and I am Your servant, and that I have done all these things according to Your command. Hear me, O Lord, hear me, that this people may learn that You are the Lord God, and that You have turned their hearts back again." Then the fire of the Lord fell and devoured the burnt offering, and the wood, and the stones; and it licked up the dust and the water that was in the trench. When all the people saw this, they fell on their faces and said: "The Lord Himself is God! The Lord Himself is God!"

Elijah said to them: "Seize the prophets of Baal, and let not even one of them escape." When they had seized them, Elijah led them to the brook Kishon <note>original: "cýson"</note> and killed them there. And Elijah said to Ahab: "Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of much rain." Ahab went up to eat and drink; but Elijah went up to the top of Carmel, and bowing down to the earth, he put his face between his knees. And he said to his servant: "Go up and look toward the sea." When he had gone up and looked, he said: "There is nothing." And again he said to him: "Return seven times."

At the seventh time, behold, a little cloud, like a man's footprint, was rising from the sea. And he said: "Go up and say to Ahab: 'Yoke your chariot and go down, lest the rain overtake you.'" And as they turned this way and that, behold, the heavens grew dark with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. Ahab, mounting his chariot, went to Jezreel. And the hand of the Lord was upon Elijah; and girding up his loins, he ran before Ahab until he came to Jezreel.

Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying: "May the gods do such things to me and add more, if by this hour tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them."

Elijah was afraid, and arising, he went wherever his will carried him. He came to Beersheba of Judah and left his servant there, and he went a day's journey into the wilderness. When he had come and sat under a juniper tree, he requested for his soul that he might die, and said: "It is enough for me, Lord; take my life. For I am no better than my fathers." And he cast himself down and fell asleep in the shadow of the juniper.

And behold, an angel of the Lord touched him and said to him: "Arise and eat." He looked, and behold, at his head was a hearth-baked bread and a vessel of water. He ate therefore and drank, and fell asleep again.

The angel of the Lord returned a second time and touched him, and said to him: "Arise and eat; for a great journey lies before you." When he had arisen, he ate and drank, and walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, even to Horeb, the mountain of God. When he had come there, he stayed in a cave.

And behold, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" And he answered: "I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant. They have destroyed Your altars and killed Your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left, and they seek my life to take it away."

And He said to him: "Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord." And behold, the Lord passed by; and a great and strong wind overturning mountains and crushing rocks before the Lord—but the Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake—but the Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, a fire—but the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, a whistling of a thin breeze <note>term: "whistling of a thin breeze" - often famously translated as the "still small voice"</note>. When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his mantle, and going out, he stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, a voice came to him, saying: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" And he answered: "I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant. They have destroyed Your altars and killed Your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left, and they seek my life to take it away."

And the Lord said to him: "Go and return on your way through the desert to Damascus. When you arrive there, you shall anoint Hazael <note>original: "azahel"</note> as king over Syria, and you shall anoint Jehu <note>original: "iehu"</note> son of Nimshi <note>original: "namsi"</note> as king over Israel; and Elisha <note>original: "helýseum"</note> son of Shaphat <note>original: "saphat"</note>, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place. And it shall be that whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill. And I will leave for Myself in Israel seven thousand men whose knees have not bowed before Baal, and every mouth that has not worshipped him by kissing the hand."
