to cheer himself: for in his labor which he does under the sun, there is no other reward in the days of his life which the Lord has given him: and it is equally good that he should eat and drink and enjoy his portion from the fruit of his labor. This is the gift of the Lord. For he shall not much remember the days of his vanity, because God occupies his heart with delights. Behold another evil that I have seen under the sun, and indeed it is frequent among men: A man to whom God has given riches and substance and honor, and nothing is lacking to his soul of all that he desires; yet God does not give him the power to eat of it, but a stranger shall devour it. This is vanity and a great misery. If a man begets a hundred children, and lives many years, and has many days of age, and his soul makes no use of the goods of his substance, and he lacks a burial: of this man I announce that an untimely birth <note>original: "abortiuus" — referring to a miscarriage or a stillborn child</note> is better than he. For he came in vain, and goes into darkness, and his name shall be blotted out by oblivion. He has not seen the sun nor known the distance between good and evil. Even if he lived two thousand years and did not enjoy good things, do not all things hasten to one place?

<margin>O</margin>**A**ll the labor of man is for his mouth, but his soul is not filled. What more has the wise man than the fool? And what has the poor man, but to go thither where there is life? It is better to see what you may desire than to long for what you know not. But this also is vanity and a presumption of spirit. He who is to be has already been called by name; and it is known that he is a man, and that he cannot contend in judgment against one stronger than himself. Words are many, and they have much vanity in disputing.

<margin>N</margin>**I**s it not better for a man to seek himself in his life, since all the days of his wandering pass like a shadow, the days of his vanity? And in the time that is to come, surely no one can show him what shall be after him under the sun.

<margin>Q</margin>**F**or who knows what is useful for a man in his life, during the number of the days of his vanity? Better is the day of death than the day of birth. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for in the former the end of all men is brought to mind, and the living man considers what is to come. Anger is better than laughter, because through the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected. The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow, and the heart of fools is where there is mirth. It is better to be rebuked by a wise man than to be deceived by the flattery of fools, for like the sound of thorns burning under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool. But this too is vanity. Oppression troubles the wise man and destroys the strength of his heart. Better is the end of a prayer <note>original: "orationis" — can also mean a speech or plea</note> than the beginning; better is the patient man than the arrogant.

<margin>S</margin>**I** knew that there was nothing better than for each one to live in joy and do good in his life; and that their own bodies should be better than they are now? For they even ask the Lord about such things. The wise man is seen with riches, and it is more profitable to those who see the sun. For as wisdom protects, so money protects. But learning and science have this more: that life shall be given to their possessor. Consider the works of God: that no one can correct him whom He has despised. In the good day enjoy good things, and beware of the evil day. For God made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find just complaints against Him. This also I saw in the days of my birth: The just man perishes in his justice, and the wicked man lives a long time in his malice.

<margin>E</margin>**T**here is another evil: do not be more wise than is necessary, lest you become stupid. Do not act too wickedly, and do not be a fool, lest you die before your time. It is good that you support the just man, but also do not withdraw your hand from the other; for he who fears the Lord neglects nothing. Wisdom has strengthened the wise man more than ten princes of the city. For there is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin. But do not apply your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you. For your conscience knows that you also have frequently cursed others. I have tried all things in wisdom; I said, "I will become wise," and wisdom itself receded far from me, much more than it was before. And it is a deep profundity; who shall find it? I have circled all things in my mind, that I might know and consider wisdom and reason, and that I might know the impiety of the fool and the error of the imprudent. And I found a woman more bitter than death, who is a snare for hunters, and her heart is a net; her hands are chains. He who pleases God shall escape her; but he who is a sinner shall be caught by her. Behold, this I have found, said the Preacher <note>original: "ecclesiastes"</note>, one thing and another, that I might find the reason which my soul still seeks and I have not found. One man among a thousand I have found; a woman among all these I have not found. Only this I have found: that God made man upright, and he has entangled himself in infinite questions. Who is such as the wise man? And who has known the resolution of a word?

<margin>S</margin>**T**he wisdom of a man shines in his countenance, and the most powerful one shall change his face. I observe the mouth of the king and the commands of the oath of God. Do not hasten to withdraw from his face, nor remain in an evil work. Because he will do all that he wills, and his word is full of power. Nor can anyone say to him: "Why do you do so?" He who keeps the commandment shall experience no evil. The heart of the wise understands the time and the response. To every business there is a time and opportunity, and much affliction for man; because he is ignorant of things past and things to come, and can know them by no messenger. It is not in the power of man to withhold the spirit <note>original: "spm" / "spiritum" — meaning the breath of life</note>, nor has he power in the day of death, nor is he permitted to rest when war is looming, nor shall impiety save the impious. All these things I have considered, and I gave my heart to all the works that are done under the sun. Sometimes one man rules over another to his own hurt in high places. I saw the wicked buried, who also while they were yet living were in the holy place, and were praised in the city as if for just works. But this also is vanity. Because sentence is not quickly pronounced against the evil, the sons of men perpetrate evils without any fear. Nevertheless, though a sinner does evil a hundred times and is endured through patience, I have known that it shall be well with those who fear the Lord, who revere His face. Let it not be well with the wicked, nor let his days be prolonged, but like a shadow let those pass away who do not fear the face of the Lord. There is also another vanity which is done upon the earth: there are just men to whom evils happen as if they had done the works of the wicked. And there are wicked men who are so secure as if they had the deeds of the just. But this also I judge most vain. Therefore I praised joy, because there was no good for a man under the sun except that he should eat and drink and be glad; and this alone he shall carry with him from his labor in the days of his life which God has given him under the sun. And I applied my heart that I might know wisdom and understand the distraction. And I know the man who day and night takes no sleep with his eyes. And I understood that of all the works of the Lord, man can find no reason for those things that are done under the sun. And the more he labors to seek, the less he finds. Even if the wise man should say he knows it, he will not be able to find it. All these things I have turned over in my heart, that I might curiously understand.

<margin>S</margin>**T**here are just and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God; and yet man knows not whether he be worthy of love or hatred. But all things are kept uncertain for the future, because all things happen alike to the just and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who offers victims and him who despises sacrifices. As the good man is, so also is the sinner; as the perjurer, so is he who swears to the truth. This is the worst among all things that are done under the sun: that the same things happen to all. Whence also the hearts of the sons of men are filled with malice and contempt in their life, and after these things they shall be led down to the underworld. There is no one who lives forever...

<column-break/>

lives, and who has confidence in this matter.

<margin>M</margin>**A** living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they shall die; but the dead know nothing more, nor have they any further reward, for the memory of them is given over to oblivion.

<margin>A</margin>**T**heir love also, and their hatred, and their envy have perished together; nor have they a part in this world, in the work that is carried out under the sun. Go therefore, and eat your bread in joy, and drink your wine with gladness, because your works please the Lord. At all times let your garments be white, and let not oil be lacking from your head. Enjoy life with the wife whom you love all the days of your unstable life, which are given to you under the sun all the time of your vanity; for this is your portion in life, and in the labor with which you labor under the sun. Whatever your hand is able to do, do it instantly; for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom shall be in the underworld <note>original: "inferos"</note> whither you hasten. I turned myself to another thing, and I saw under the sun: that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor grace to the craftsmen; but time and chance happen in all things. Man knows not his end; but as fish are caught with a hook, and as birds with a snare, so are men caught in the evil time, when it shall suddenly come upon them. This wisdom also I have seen under the sun, and have proved it to be very great: A small city, and few men in it; there came against it a great king, and invested it, and built bulwarks around it, and the siege was perfected. And there was found in it a man poor and wise, and he delivered the city by his wisdom, and no one thereafter remembered that poor man. And I said that wisdom is better than strength. Since the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heard. The words of the wise are heard in silence, more than the cry of a prince among fools.

<margin>M</margin>**W**isdom is better than weapons of war; and he who shall offend in one thing shall lose many good things. Dying flies <note>original: "musce morientes" — often translated as 'dead flies'</note> destroy the sweetness of ointment. Wisdom and glory are more precious than a small and temporary folly. The heart of the wise is in his right hand, and the heart of fools is in his left hand. But even a fool walking in the way, since he himself is senseless, esteems all men as fools. If the spirit of power rises up against you, do not leave your place; because healing will make the greatest sins cease. There is also an evil that I saw under the sun, as if an error proceeding from the face of a prince: A fool set in high dignity, and the rich sitting below. I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants upon the earth.

<margin>H</margin>**H**e who digs a pit shall fall into it; and he who breaks down a hedge, a serpent shall bite him. He who moves stones shall be hurt by them; and he who cuts wood shall be wounded by them. If the iron be blunt, and it be not as before, but be blunt, it shall be sharpened with much labor; and wisdom follows industry. If a serpent bites in silence, he who slanders secretly has nothing less. The words of the mouth of a wise man are grace, but the lips of the senseless shall throw him down headlong. The beginning of his words is folly, and the end of his mouth is the worst error.

<margin>S</margin>**T**he fool multiplies words: Man is ignorant of what has been before him; and what shall be after him, who can tell him? The labor of fools shall afflict them, who know not how to go into the city. Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning.

<margin>B</margin>**B**lessed is the land whose king is noble, and whose princes eat in their own time for refreshment and not for luxury. Through slothfulness the rafters shall be brought low, and through the weakness of hands the house shall leak. In laughter they make bread and wine, that the living may feast; and all things obey money. In your thought do not detract from the king, and in the secret of your bedchamber do not curse the rich man; because the birds of the air shall carry your voice, and he who has wings shall announce the sentence.

<margin>M</margin>**C**ast your bread upon the passing waters; for after a long time you shall find it. Give a portion to seven and also to eight, because you know not what evil shall be upon the earth. If the clouds be full, they shall pour out rain upon the earth. If the tree falls to the south or to the north, in whatever place it shall fall, there it shall be. He who observes the wind does not sow; and he who considers the clouds shall never reap. As you know not what is the way of the spirit, and by what reason the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman; so you know not the works of God, who is the maker of all things. In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease; for you know not which shall rather spring up, this or that: And if both together, it shall be better. The light is sweet, and it is delightful for the eyes to see the sun. If a man lives many years, and has rejoiced in all these, he ought to remember the dark time, and the many days; which when they shall come, the vanity of the past shall be rebuked. Rejoice therefore, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart be in good during the days of your youth; and walk in the ways of your heart, and in the sight of your eyes. And know that for all these things the Lord will bring you into judgment. Remove anger from your heart, and put away malice from your flesh. For youth and pleasure are vain.

<margin>M</margin>**R**emember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes, and the years approach of which you shall say: "They do not please me." Before the sun grows dark, and the light, and the moon, and the stars, and the clouds return after the rain. When the keepers of the house <note>the hands</note> shall tremble, and the strongest men <note>the legs</note> shall stagger, and the grinders <note>the teeth</note> shall be idle in small number, and those looking through the holes <note>the eyes</note> shall grow dark. And they shall shut the doors in the street, in the humility of the voice of the grinder, and they shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of song <note>the ears</note> shall grow deaf. Also they shall fear high things, and they shall be afraid in the way; the almond tree shall flourish <note>white hair</note>, the locust shall be made fat, and the caper-berry shall be scattered. Because man shall go into the house of his eternity, and the mourners shall go about in the street. Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden fillet <note>or headband</note> shrinks back, and the pitcher is crushed at the fountain, and the wheel is broken upon the cistern. And the dust returns into its earth whence it was, and the spirit returns to the Lord who gave it. Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher; and all is vanity. And since the Preacher was most wise, he taught the people, and declared what he had done; and searching out, he composed many parables. He sought useful words, and wrote most upright discourses, and full of truth. The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails deeply fastened, which by the counsel of masters are given by one shepherd. More than these, my son, do not require. Of making many books there is no end; and frequent meditation is an affliction of the flesh. Let us all hear together the end of speaking: Fear God and observe His commandments. For this is the whole man. And all things that are done, God will bring into judgment, for every error, whether it be good or evil.

Your name is as oil poured out; therefore the young maidens have loved you. **The Voice of the Church.** Draw me after you; let us run together to the scent of your ointments. **The Voice of the Young Maidens.** The king has brought me into his storerooms. We will exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine. The upright love you. **The Voice of the Synagogue.** I am black but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon. <note>The "Voice of the Synagogue" is often used in medieval commentary to represent the Old Testament people or the soul before grace.</note> **The Voice of the Bride.** Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me. The sons of my mother have fought against me; they made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I have not kept. **The Voice of the Church to Christ.** Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions. **The Voice of Christ to the Church.** If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth and follow after the tracks of the flocks, and feed your young goats beside the tents of the shepherds. I have compared you, my love, to my cavalry in Pharaoh's chariots. Your cheeks are beautiful as a turtledove’s, your neck like necklaces. **The Voice of the Synagogue.** We will make you golden chains, inlaid with silver. **The Voice of the Church.** While the king was at his repose, my spikenard <note>original: "nardus" — a costly aromatic essential oil</note> gave forth its scent. A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall dwell between my breasts. A cluster of henna <note>original: "botrus cypri" — referring to the blossoms of the cypress or henna plant</note> is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of En-Gedi. **The Voice of Christ.** Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold you are beautiful; your eyes are like doves. **The Voice of the Church.** Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and handsome. Our bed is flowery, the beams of our houses are cedar, our rafters are of cypress. **The Voice of Christ.** I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters. **The Voice of the Church.** As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat under the shadow of him whom I had desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat. The king brought me into the wine cellar; he set charity in order within me. Stay me up with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. **The Voice of Christ.** I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you do not stir up nor awaken the beloved until she pleases. **The Voice of the Church.** The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills. My beloved is like a roe or a young hart. Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, peering through the lattices. Behold, my beloved speaks to me: "Rise up, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For now the winter has passed, the rain is over and gone. Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree has brought forth its green figs; the flowering vines have given their scent." **The Voice of Christ.** Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come; my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. Show me your face, let your voice sound in my ears; for your voice is sweet, and your face is comely. **The Voice of the Church to the Brothers.** Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has flourished. **The Voice of the Church.** My beloved is mine and I am his, who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline. Return; be like a roe, my beloved, or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel. **The Voice of the Church regarding negligence.** In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and found him not.

<margin>VI.</margin> I will rise and go about the city; through the streets and the squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. The watchmen who guard the city found me. **The Voice of the Church to the watchmen.** Have you seen him whom my soul loves? When I had passed them a little way, I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who bore me. **The Voice of Christ to the Jews.** I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you do not stir up nor awaken the beloved until she pleases. **The Synagogue.** Who is she that comes up through the desert like a pillar of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, and all the powders of the perfumer? **The Voice of the Church.** Behold the bed of Solomon; sixty valiant men surround it, of the most valiant of Israel, all holding swords and most expert in war. Every man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the fears of the night. King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver, the back of gold, the seat of purple; the middle he covered with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem. **The Voice of the Church regarding the spectacle.** Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal, and on the day of the joy of his heart. **The Voice of Christ to the Church.** How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like doves, besides that which is hidden within. Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, all with twin offspring, and there is none barren among them. Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet. Your cheeks are like a piece of pomegranate, besides that which is hidden within. Your neck is like the tower of David, which is built with bulwarks; a thousand

<column-break/>

shields hang from it, all the armor of the valiant. Your two breasts are like two young twin roes that feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline. I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. **The Voice of Christ to the Bride.** You are all fair, my love, and there is no spot in you. Come from Lebanon, my bride, come from Lebanon, come! You shall be crowned from the top of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one hair of your neck. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the scent of your ointments is above all spices. Your lips, my bride, are a dropping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the scent of your garments is like the scent of frankincense. An enclosed garden is my sister, my bride, an enclosed garden, a fountain sealed. Your plants are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of the orchard. Henna with spikenard, spikenard and saffron, sweet cane <note>original: "fistula" — likely calamus</note> and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes with all the chief ointments. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon. **The Voice of the Bride to the winds.** Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and let its aromatics flow. **The Voice of the Church to Christ.** Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his apple trees. **The Voice of Christ to the Church.** I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved. **The Voice of the Church.** I sleep, and my heart watches. **The Voice of the Bride.** The voice of my beloved knocking: "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled, for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights." **The Bride to the Groom.** I have put off my robe; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? **The Voice of the Church to Christ.** My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch. **The Bride in response to Christ.** I rose up to open to my beloved; my hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the choicest myrrh. I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed by. My soul melted when he spoke. I sought him and found him not; I called and he did not answer me. The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love. **The Voice of the Synagogue.** What manner of one is your beloved of the beloved, O most beautiful of women? What manner of one is your beloved of the beloved, that you have so adjured us? **The Voice of the Church regarding Christ.** My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands. His head is as the finest gold; his locks like the branches of palm trees, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside the rivulets of water, which are washed with milk and sit beside the full streams. His cheeks are as beds of aromatics, planted by the perfumers. His lips are lilies dripping with choice myrrh. His hands are turned gold, full of hyacinths; his belly is ivory, set with sapphires. His legs are columns of marble, which are founded upon bases of gold. His appearance is as Lebanon, chosen as the cedars. His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. **The Voice of the Synagogue to the Bride.** Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful of women? Where has your beloved turned aside, and we will seek him with you? **The Voice of the Church.** My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of aromatics, to feed in the gardens and to gather lilies. I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, who feeds among the lilies. **The Voice of Christ to the Church.** You are beautiful, my love, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army set in array. Turn away your eyes from me, for they have made me flee away. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing, all with twin offspring, and there is none barren among them. As the bark of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, besides your hidden parts. There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and of young maidens there is no number. **The Voice of Christ to the Church.** My dove is one, my perfect one is one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen of her that bore her. The daughters saw her and declared her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her. Who is she that comes forth like the rising morning, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in array? **The Voice of the Church to the Bride.** I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valleys, and to look if the vineyards had flourished and the pomegranates had budded. I knew not; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab. **The Synagogue.** Return, return, O Shulammite; <note>original: "sunamitis" — traditionally identifying the woman as being from Shunem</note> return, return, that we may behold you. **The Voice of the Synagogue.** What will you see in the Shulammite, but the companies of camps? **The Voice of Christ to the Church.** How beautiful are your steps in shoes, O prince's daughter! The joints of your thighs are like necklaces, which are made by the hand of a master. Your navel is like a turned bowl, never wanting liquor. Your belly is like a heap of wheat, set about with lilies. Your two breasts are like two twin roes. Your neck is like a tower of ivory. Your eyes are like the fishponds in Heshbon, which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like the purple of a king joined to the canals. How beautiful you are, and how comely, my dearest, in delights! Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters of grapes. I said: I will go up into the palm tree and will take hold of its fruits; and your breasts shall be as the clusters of the vineyard, and the scent of your mouth like apples. Your throat is like the best wine. **The Voice of the Church regarding Christ.** Worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to ruminate. I am my beloved's, and his turning is toward me. Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field, let us abide in the villages. Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vineyard flourishes, if the flowers bring forth fruit, if the pomegranates have flowered; there I will give you my breasts. The mandrakes <note>original: "mandragore" — plants historically associated with fertility and love</note> have given their scent in our gates. All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you. Who would give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, that I might find you without and kiss you, and now no one would despise me? I will take hold of you and bring you into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who bore me; there you shall teach me, and I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the new wine of my pomegranates. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. **The Voice of Christ to the Jews.** I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not stir up nor awaken the beloved until she pleases. **The Synagogue, responding to the Bride.** Who is she that comes up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? **The Voice of Christ to the Synagogue.** Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated. **The Voice of the Church to Christ.** Put me as a seal upon your heart, and as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as hell. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames. Many waters cannot quench charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it. If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he shall despise it as nothing. Our sister is little and has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister in the day when she is to be spoken to? If she is a wall, let us build upon it bulwarks of silver. If she is a door, let us join it together with boards of cedar. **The Church responds.** I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower, since I am become in his presence as one finding peace. **The Synagogue regarding Christ.** The peaceful one had a vineyard, in that which has people; he let it out to keepers. A man brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver. **The Voice of Christ.** My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who keep its fruits. You who dwell in the gardens, the friends hearken; make me hear your voice. **The Voice of the Church to Christ.** Flee away, my beloved, and be like a roe and a young hart upon the mountains of aromatics.

Here ends THE SONG OF SONGS. <note>original: "SYRASIRIS" — a Latinization of the Hebrew "Shir HaShirim", meaning Song of Songs.</note>

<summary>This page contains the complete text of the Song of Songs, presented as an allegorical dialogue between Christ, the Church, the Synagogue, and the Bride. It uses rich, sensory imagery of gardens, spices, and physical beauty to describe the relationship between God and the soul or the Church.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Book of Wisdom (also known as the Wisdom of Solomon). In the medieval manuscript tradition, this book follows the Song of Songs, transitioning from the allegorical poetry of love to a philosophical and moral treatise on righteousness and the divine nature of Wisdom. While attributed to Solomon, this text was likely composed in Greek in Alexandria during the 1st century BCE, blending Jewish theology with Hellenistic philosophy.</meta>

goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart. For he is found by those who do not tempt him, and he reveals himself to those who have faith in him.

For perverse thoughts separate one from God, and his power, when tested, rebukes the foolish. For wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sin.

For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and will withdraw itself from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be rebuked when iniquity rushes in.

For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and will not acquit a blasphemer <note>original: maledictum, literally "one who speaks evil"</note> of his words. For God is the witness of his heart, and the true searcher of his soul, and the hearer of his tongue.

For the spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.

Therefore, he who speaks unjust things cannot be hidden, nor shall the chastising judgment pass him by.

For there shall be an inquiry into the thoughts of the ungodly, and the report of his words shall come before God, for the punishment of his iniquities.

For the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the noise of murmuring shall not be hidden. Keep yourselves, therefore, from murmuring, which profits nothing, and refrain your tongue from detraction, for a secret word shall not go for naught, and the mouth that lies kills the soul.

Do not seek death in the error of your life, nor bring destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands. For God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living.

For he created all things that they might exist, and he made the nations of the earth healthy; there is no poison of destruction in them, nor is the kingdom of the underworld <note>original: inferorum regnum</note> upon the earth.

<margin>II</margin>
For justice is perpetual and immortal. But injustice is the acquisition of death.

But the ungodly have summoned death with their hands and words; and thinking it a friend, they have fallen away and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy to belong to its side.

<margin>III</margin>
<margin>In Wisdom 2 <note>original: In Sap ii p t</note></margin>
For they said among themselves, thinking not rightly:
> The time of our life is short and tedious, and there is no relief at a person's end, nor is anyone known to have returned from the underworld. For we were born of nothing, and after this we shall be as if we had never been; for the breath in our nostrils is smoke, and our speech a spark to move our heart, which being extinguished, our body shall be ashes, and our spirit shall be poured out like soft air. Our life shall pass away like the trace of a cloud, and shall be dissolved like a mist that is driven away by the rays of the sun and weighed down by its heat. And our name in time shall be forgotten, and no one shall have a memory of our works. For our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no returning from our end; for it is sealed, and no one returns. Come therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use the creatures quickly as in our youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments, and let no flower of the spring pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through. Let none of us be without a share in our decadence; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion and this is our lot. Let us oppress the poor just man, and not spare the widow, nor show reverence to the gray hairs of the aged. But let our strength be the law of justice, for that which is weak is found to be useless. Let us lie in wait for the just man, for he is useless to us and contrary to our works; he reproaches us for sins against the law, and spreads abroad the sins of our way of life. He professes to have the knowledge of God, and calls himself the son of God. He has become a rebuke to our thoughts. He is grievous for us even to behold, for his life is unlike others, and his ways are changed. We are esteemed by him as triflers, and he abstains from our ways as from filthiness; he prefers the latter end of the just, and boasts that he has God for his father. Let us see if his words be true, and let us test what shall happen to him, and we shall know what his end shall be. For if the just man be the true son of God, he will defend him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies. Let us examine him with insults and torture, that we may know his meekness and prove his patience.

<column-break/>

Let us condemn him to a most shameful death; for according to his own words, God shall have care for him.

These things they thought, and they erred, for their own malice blinded them. And they knew not the secrets of God, nor hoped for the reward of justice, nor esteemed the honor of holy souls. For God created man immortal, and made him in the image of his own likeness.

But by the envy of the devil, death entered into the world; and they who are on his side follow him.

But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to die, and their departure was taken for misery, and their going away from us as utter destruction; but they are in peace. And though in the sight of men they suffered torments, their hope is full of immortality. Afflicted in few things, they shall be well rewarded in many; for God proved them and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, and as a whole burnt offering <term>holocaust</term> he accepted them, and in time there shall be respect shown to them.

The just shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among the reeds. They shall judge nations and have dominion over people, and their Lord shall reign forever. They who trust in him shall understand the truth, and the faithful in love shall rest in him; for grace and peace are to his elect.

But the ungodly shall be punished according to their own thoughts, who have neglected the just man and have revolted from the Lord. For he who rejects wisdom and discipline is unhappy; and their hope is vain, and their labors without fruit, and their works useless. Their wives are foolish and their children most wicked. Their offspring is cursed, because happy is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not known the bed of sin; she shall have fruit in the visitation of holy souls.

And the eunuch who has not worked iniquity with his hands, nor thought wicked things against God; for a chosen gift of faith shall be given to him, and a most acceptable lot in the temple of God.

For the fruit of good labors is glorious, and the root of wisdom never fades.

But the children of adulterers shall not come to perfection, and the seed of an unlawful bed shall be rooted out. And if they live long, they shall be counted as nothing, and their last old age shall be without honor. And if they die quickly, they shall have no hope, nor speech in the day of recognition. For the end of a wicked generation is dreadful.

<margin>IV</margin>
O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory! For the memory thereof is immortal, because it is known both with God and with men. When it is present, they imitate it, and they desire it when it has withdrawn itself; and it triumphs crowned forever, winning the reward of undefiled conflicts.

But the multiplied brood of the ungodly shall not thrive, and bastard slips shall not take deep root nor establish a stable foundation. And though they flourish in branches for a time, being weakly set, they shall be shaken by the wind, and through the force of winds they shall be rooted out. For the branches that are not come to perfection shall be broken, and their fruits shall be useless and sour to eat, and fit for nothing. For children that are born of unlawful sleep are witnesses of wickedness against their parents when they are questioned.

<margin>V</margin>
But the just man, if he be overtaken by death, shall be at rest. For venerable old age is not that of long time, nor measured by the number of years; but a man's understanding is gray hair, and a spotless life is old age.

He pleased God and was beloved, and living among sinners, he was translated <note>original: translatus est, meaning "carried away" or "taken up," often referring to Enoch</note>. He was taken away lest malice should change his understanding, or lest deceit should beguile his soul. For the fascination of vanity obscures good things, and the wandering of concupiscence undermines the innocent mind.

Being made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled a long time. For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities.

But the people saw and understood not, nor laid up such things in their hearts: that the grace of God and mercy is with his saints, and that he has respect to his elect. But the just man that is dead condemns the ungodly who are living, and youth soon ended condemns the long life of the unjust.

For they shall see the end of the wise man, and shall not understand what God has designed for him, and why the Lord has secured him. They shall see and shall despise him, but the Lord shall laugh them to scorn. And they shall fall after this without honor, and be a reproach among the dead forever; for he shall burst them when they are puffed up and speechless, and shall shake them from the foundations, and they shall be utterly laid waste. And they shall be in sorrow, and their memory shall perish. They shall come with fear to the thought of their sins, and their iniquities shall stand against them to convict them.

<margin>VI</margin>
Then shall the just stand with great constancy against those who have afflicted them and taken away their labors. Those seeing this shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall be amazed at the suddenness of his unexpected salvation, saying within themselves, repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit:
> These are they whom we had sometime in derision, and for a parable of reproach. We fools esteemed their life madness, and their end without honor. Behold how they are numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding has not risen upon us. We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways, but the way of the Lord we have not known. What has pride profited us? Or what advantage has the boasting of riches brought us? All those things have passed away like a shadow, and like a messenger that runs by; and like a ship that passes through the waves, of which, when it is gone by, the trace cannot be found, nor the path of its keel in the waters. Or as when a bird flies through the air, no proof can be found of its passage, but only the sound of its wings beating the light wind, and parting the air by the force of its flight; she moved her wings and passed through, and after that no sign can be found of her way. Or like an arrow shot at a mark, the divided air presently closed again, so that its passage is not known. So we also being born, immediately ceased to be; and we were able to show no sign of virtue, but were consumed in our own wickedness.

Such things as these the sinners said in hell; for the hope of the ungodly is like dust <note>original: lanugo, literally "down" or "fuzz"</note> which is carried away by the wind, and like a thin froth which is dispersed by the storm, and like smoke which is scattered abroad by the wind, and like the remembrance of a guest of one day that passes by.

But the just shall live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the care of them with the most High. Therefore shall they receive a kingdom of glory and a crown of beauty at the hand of the Lord; for with his right hand he shall cover them, and with his holy arm he shall defend them.

His zeal shall take armor, and he shall arm the creature for the revenge of his enemies. He shall put on justice as a breastplate, and shall take true judgment instead of a helmet. He shall take equity for an invincible shield; and he shall whet his severe wrath as a spear, and the whole world shall fight with him against the unwise.

The shafts of lightning shall go directly from the clouds, as from a well-drawn bow, and shall fly to the mark. And thick hailstones shall be cast as from a stone-bow of wrath. The water of the sea shall rage against them, and the rivers shall run together roughly.

A mighty wind shall stand up against them, and as a whirlwind shall divide them; and their iniquity shall bring all the earth to a desert, and wickedness shall overthrow the thrones of the mighty.

<margin>VII</margin>
<image-desc>Smaller illuminated initial 'A' with foliate scrollwork in red and gold.</image-desc>
Hear therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, you who are judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who rule the multitudes, and please yourselves in the throngs of nations. For power is given you by the Lord, and strength by the most High, who shall examine your works and search out your thoughts. Because being ministers of his kingdom, you have not judged rightly, nor kept the law of justice, nor walked according to the will of God.

### Vain
however, are all men: even those who do not have knowledge. And from those good things which are seen, they could not understand Him who is: nor attending to the works did they acknowledge the craftsman: but either fire, or spirit <note>term: "spiritu" here referring to wind or air</note>: or the swift air, or the circle of the stars: or excessive water: or the sun and the moon, the rulers of the world, they thought to be the gods of gods. If, delighted by the appearance of these, they suspected they were gods, let them know how much more beautiful the Ruler of them is. For the Generator of beauty established all these things. Or if they admire their virtue and power, let them understand from these that He who established these is stronger than they. For from the greatness of the beauty and the creature, the Creator can be seen recognizably. But yet in these there is less complaint. For perhaps they err while they seek and wish to find. For while they are conversant in those works, they inquire: and they are persuaded that the things are good which they see. Again, however, not even these ought to be forgiven. For if they were able to know so much that they could estimate the world: how did they not more easily find the Lord of it?

### Wretched
however, and in the hope of dead things are they, and those who have called gods the works of men's hands: gold and silver, the invention of art: and the likenesses of animals: or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. Or if any craftsman, a smith, has cut a straight tree from the forest: and from this he has scraped off all the bark evenly: and by his art's skill even to the structure: for use in ships: for the use of life and the remnants of their work: he consumes for the preparation of food. And the rest of this which he makes for no use; a crooked and knotty piece of wood: he carves it diligently with his skill. And he figures it according to a shape: and makes it like the image of a man: or compares it to some of the common things, smearing it with red chalk and making its color ruddy. And every spot that is in it: smearing it with red chalk and making a worthy habitation for it: and he places it in a wall and confirms it with iron lest perhaps it fall: looking out for it: knowing that it cannot help itself. For it is an image: and it has need of help. And concerning his substance and his children: and concerning marriages, he makes a vow to inquire: nor is he ashamed to speak with that which is without a soul. And for health indeed he prays to the weak, and for life he asks the dead: and for help: he invokes the useless: and concerning a journey, him who cannot go: and he cannot walk: and concerning following and operation: and concerning the outcome of all things, he asks from it: which is useless to all. Again, he makes it free: he equals it with grief. And for those raging against the floods to make a journey: he is called upon by the wood that carries him: he invokes the wood. For the desire of acquiring thought it out. And the craftsman fabricated it by his wisdom. But you, Father, govern by providence. For you have given a way even in the sea: and a most firm path among the waves: showing that you can save from all things: even if one should approach the sea without a raft. But so that his wisdom might not be empty of works, because of this men trust their souls even to a small piece of wood. And having crossed the sea through the waves, they were delivered. For also when the proud giants were perishing: the seed of hope remained to the world: which was governed by your hand. Blessed however is the wood through which justice comes: but that through which it comes is cursed, both the thing and he who made it. Because indeed the one worked: but the other, since it was fragile, was called a god. Likewise the impious man and his impiety are both hateful to God.

### For indeed
that which is made shall suffer torment with him who made it, or is called so. This also in the idols of the nations there shall be no respect: because the creatures of God were made in a [false] manner; and into a temptation for the souls of men; and into a snare for the feet of the foolish. For the beginning of fornication is the seeking out of idols: and the invention of them is the corruption of life. For they were not from the beginning: nor shall they be forever. For the vanity of these men came into the world. And therefore a brief end of them is found. For a father, grieving with bitter mourning, quickly made an image of his snatched-away son: and him who then had been as a dead man, he now began to worship as a god: and he ordained among his servants sacred rites and mysteries. Then in the process of time, the wicked custom having become hardened: this error was kept as a law. And by the command of the impious, figures were worshipped. Those whom men could not honor in person because they were far off: they brought a figure from afar; making an image of the king whom they wished to honor: so that they might worship him who was absent as if present by their diligence. Moreover, the excellence of the craftsman moved those who were ignorant to the worship of them.

<column-break/>

For he, wishing to please the one who employed him, elaborated the craftsmanship so that he might shape the likeness into something better. But the multitude of men, led away by the beauty of the work, now thought him to be a god who a little before had been honored as a man. And this was the deception of human life: those serving either affection or kings: imposed the incommunicable name <note>The "incommunicable name" refers to the unique name of God (Yahweh), which was wrongly applied to stones and wood.</note> upon stones and wood. And it had not sufficed to have erred concerning the knowledge of God: but living in a great war of ignorance: they called so many and such great evils peace. For either they sacrifice their own children: or they made obscure sacrifices: or they kept vigils full of madness. Neither life nor marriages do they keep pure: but one kills another through envy: or saddens him by adultery. And all things commonly are blood, homicide, theft, and deception, corruption, unfaithfulness, tumult and perjury, the annihilation of good things, the changing of homes, the changing of souls, incest, lust and unchastity, the inconstancy of impurity, and the changing of morals and for eternity. For the worship of unspeakable idols is the cause of every evil: both the beginning and the end. For either they are mad while they rejoice: or they prophesy lies: or they live unjustly: or they quickly forswear themselves. For while they trust in idols which are without life, living evilly they do not hope to be harmed. Therefore, worthily shall things come to them for both: because they thought evilly of God, attending to idols: and lived unjustly in a vow, despising justice. For it is not the power of virtues: but the punishment of sins that always follows the transgression of the wicked.

### Gentle
Lord our God, you are sweet and true: patient and in mercy disposing all things. For even if we sin, we are yours: knowing your greatness. And if we have not sinned: we know that we are counted with you. For to know you is perfect justice; and to know your power and your strength is the root of immortality.

### For not
did the device of man's evil art lead us into error: nor the labor of a shadow of a picture without fruit: an effigy carved through various colors, the sight of which gives concupiscence to the senseless. And he loves the effigy of a dead image without a soul. Evil lovers: worthy are they who have hope in such things: and those who make them: and those who love them: and those who worship them. Just as the potter, pressing the soft earth, laboriously shapes each vessel for our uses. And from the same clay he shapes the vessels that are clean for use, and likewise those which are contrary to this. But what the use of these vessels is, the potter is the judge. Or when with vain labor he shapes a god from the same clay, he who a little before had been made from the earth: and after a little while is called back to the same place where he was. Let him return the debt of the soul which he had. But he has a care: not because he is about to labor: nor because he has a short life: but he contends with goldsmiths and silversmiths: but also he imitates the makers of clay: and he puts forth glory because he shapes vain things. For his heart is ashes, and his hope is empty earth, and his life is viler than clay: he who was ignorant of Him who shaped him: and who inspired into him a soul which works and who inspired a vital spirit. But they estimated our life to be a game, and the conversation of life to be composed for gain, and that it is necessary to acquire from everywhere, even from evil. For this man knows that he offends above all others: he who from earthy matter shapes vessels and carvings. For all the foolish and the wretched are proud of mind beyond measure: enemies of your people: and they commanded it because they thought all the idols of the nations to be gods. Which have neither the use of eyes for seeing: nor nostrils for taking breath: nor ears for hearing: nor fingers of the hands for touching. But also their feet are slow for walking. For a man made them, and he who borrowed his spirit shaped them. For no man can make a god like to God, being mortal: he shapes a dead thing with wicked hands. For he himself is better than these which he worships: because he indeed lived, although he was mortal, but they never. But they also worship the lowest animals: for being compared to the senseless, they are more foolish than these. But neither by sight can any of these animals behold good things: they have escaped the praise of God and His blessing.

### Therefore
by similar things they worthily suffered torments: and by the multitude of beasts they were exterminated. For which torments you well disposed your people, to whom you gave the desire of their own delight, preparing a new taste of food; to those who indeed wanted the desire: even by the signs shown and sent, they might even turn away from this necessary desire: these however, having become of a short time, tasted new food. For it was necessary indeed that they, exercising tyranny, should come to destruction without excuse. But to these only to show how the enemies of them were exterminated. For indeed when the fierce wrath of the beasts came upon them: they were being exterminated by the bites of perverse serpents. But your wrath did not remain forever. But for correction they were troubled for a short time, having a sign of salvation: for a remembrance of the commandment of your law. For he who was turned: was not healed through this which he saw: but through you, the Savior of all. In this, however, you showed to our enemies that you are He who delivers from every evil. For the bites of locusts and flies killed them: and no healing of their soul was found: because they were worthy to be exterminated by such things. But the teeth of venomous dragons did not conquer your sons. For your mercy arriving healed them. For they were examined in memory of your words and were saved: lest they should fall into deep oblivion and not be able to use the help of assistance. For indeed neither herb nor poultice healed them, but your word, O Lord, which heals all things. For you, Lord, have power over life and death, and you lead down to the gates of death and bring back. A man indeed kills through his own malice: and when the spirit has gone out, it does not return: nor will he call back the soul which has been received. For it is impossible to escape your hand.

### Denying
to know you, they were scourged through the strength of your arm: suffering persecution by strange waters and hails and rains: and consumed by fire. For what was wonderful was in the water which extinguishes all things: justice has more power. For the world is the avenger of the just. For at one time the fire was gentle, lest the animals sent to the men should be burned. But so that the impious seeing might know that by divine judgment they suffer persecution. And at another time in the water, it burned everywhere above the power of fire, so that it might exterminate the growth of the wicked land. In place of which, for the holy ones <note>original: "angelo" likely referring to "angelorum esca" (the food of angels) which begins the next section.</note>

### The food of angels
you fed your people. And you provided for them prepared bread from heaven without labor, having every delight and every taste of sweetness. For your substance showed the sweetness of your living things which you have toward your sons. And serving the will of each one, it was converted to what each one wished. But snow and ice sustained the force of fire and did not melt: so that they might know that the burning fire in the hail and the flashing in the rains destroyed the fruits of the enemies. But this again so that the just might be nourished: even they were of their own power: for the nature of your creation, O Lord, serves you the Creator: it burns hot into torment against the unjust and becomes milder for doing good for those who trust in you.

### Therefore
and then transformed into all things, it served the grace of the nurturer of all toward the will of those who were desired by you. So that your children whom you loved, O Lord, might know that it is not the fruits of births that feed men: but your word preserves those who have believed in you. For that which could not be destroyed by fire, being warmed by a small ray of the sun, immediately melted: so that it might be known to all that it is necessary to precede the sun to bless...

-> # PROLOGUE TO THE <-
-> # BOOK OF JESUS <-
-> # SON OF SIRACH <-

---

**M**ANY AND GREAT THINGS HAVE BEEN shown to us through the law and the prophets and the others who followed them in wisdom: in which it is right to praise Israel for the sake of doctrine and wisdom. Since it is necessary that not only those speaking should be prudent, but even strangers should be able both to teach and to write to become most learned. My grandfather Jesus, after he had given himself more to the diligence of reading the law and the prophets and the other books which have been handed down to us from our parents: he himself also wished to write something of these things which pertain to doctrine and wisdom. So that those desiring to learn and becoming more wise in their skill: might desire even more to live a lawful life and be confirmed. I exhort you, therefore, to come with benevolence and to do the reading with more attentive care: and to have pardon in those things in which we may seem, while following the image of wisdom, to fail in the composition of words. For Hebrew words fail in power when they have been translated into another language. And not only these: but even the law itself and the prophets and the rest of the books have no small difference when they are spoken among themselves. For in the thirty-eighth year in the times of King Ptolemy Euergetes <note>original: "eu(er)getis regis"</note>, after I arrived in Egypt and when I had been there for a long time, I found books left there of no small nor contemptible doctrine. Therefore I thought it good and necessary: to add some diligence and labor of interpreting myself. And with much wakefulness and doctrine in a space of time, I brought this book to those things which lead to the end, to give the book also to those who wish to intend their mind and to learn how it is right to instruct their character: who have hastened to lead their life according to the law of the Lord.

<meta>This page transitions from the final commentary on the Book of Wisdom into the beginning of the Book of Sirach (also known as Ecclesiasticus). The text reflects on the nature of wisdom as a gift from God and the practical virtues required to live a righteous life, such as humility, patience, and honoring parents.</meta>

He created wisdom and poured out her prudence. The fountain of wisdom is the word of God on high, and her ways are the eternal commandments.

To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed? And who has known her clever ways? To whom has the instruction of wisdom been revealed? And who has understood her multifaceted entrance?

There is one who is the Most High, the almighty creator, and a King greatly to be feared, sitting upon His throne; he is the ruling God. He himself created her through the Holy Spirit; He saw her, numbered her, and measured her. He poured her out over all His works, and upon all flesh according to His gift, and He has provided her to those who love Him.

The fear of the Lord <note>In this context, "fear" refers to a profound sense of awe, reverence, and holy respect rather than terror.</note> is glory and boasting, gladness and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart, and will give gladness and joy for length of days. It shall be well in the end for the one who fears God, and on the day of his death, he shall be blessed.

The love of God is honorable wisdom; to those to whom she appears in a vision, they love her by the acknowledgment and the sight of her great wonders.

The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; she was created together with the faithful in the womb; she walks with chosen women, and is recognized among the just and the faithful. The fear of the Lord is the religious practice of knowledge. This religious practice will guard and justify the heart, and will give delight and joy.

The fear of the Lord is the crown of wisdom, filling us with peace and the fruit of salvation; He saw her and numbered her, and both are gifts of God. Wisdom will provide knowledge and the understanding of prudence, and she exalts the glory of those who hold onto her.

The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord; her branches are long-lived. In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and the religious practice of knowledge, but wisdom is an abomination to sinners. The fear of the Lord drives away sin, for he who is without fear cannot be justified; for the anger of his pride is his downfall. The patient man will endure until the right time, and afterward, joy shall be restored. Good sense hides his words until the proper time, and the lips of many shall tell of his understanding.

In the treasures of wisdom is the meaning of instruction, but the worship of God is an abomination to a sinner.

My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. Humble your heart and endure; incline your ear and receive the words of understanding, and do not be hasty in the time of darkness. Wait for God's endurance; join yourself to God and endure, so that your life may increase in your final days. Accept everything that is applied to you; endure in sorrow, and have patience in your humility. For gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable men are tested in the furnace of humiliation.

Believe in God and He will recover you; direct your way and hope in Him. Keep His fear, and grow old in it.

You who fear the Lord, wait for His mercy; and do not turn away from Him, lest you fall.

You who fear the Lord, believe in Him, and your reward shall not be void.

You who fear the Lord, hope in Him, and mercy shall come to you for your delight.

You who fear the Lord, love Him, and your hearts shall be illuminated.

Look, my children, at the nations of men, and know that no one has hoped in the Lord and been confounded. Or who has remained in His commandments and been forsaken? Or who has called upon Him and been despised? For God is pious and merciful; He will forgive sins in the day of tribulation, and He is the protector of all who seek Him in truth.

Woe to the double heart and to wicked lips, and to hands that do evil, and to the sinner who enters the earth by two ways.

Woe to those of a dissolved heart who do not believe in God, and therefore they shall not be protected by Him.

Woe to those who have lost endurance, and who have forsaken the right ways and turned aside into crooked ways. What will they do when the Lord begins to look upon them?

Those who fear the Lord will not be incredulous of His word, and those who love Him will keep His way.

Those who fear the Lord will seek what is well-pleasing to Him, and those who love Him shall be filled with His law.

Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts, and in His sight they will sanctify their souls.

Those who fear the Lord keep His commandments, and they will have patience until His inspection, saying: "If we do not perform penance, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, and not into the hands of men." For according to His greatness, so also is His mercy with Him.

The children of wisdom are the church of the righteous, and their nation is obedience and love.

Children, hear the judgment of your father, and act in such a way that you may be saved. For God has honored the father in the children, and seeking the judgment of the mother, He has confirmed it upon the children.

He who loves God will pray for his sins and will restrain himself from them; he will be heard in his daily prayer. And he who honors his mother is like one who stores up a treasure.

He who honors his father shall have joy in his own children, and on the day of his prayer, he shall be heard.

He who honors his father shall live a longer life, and he who obeys his father shall bring refreshment to his mother.

He who fears the Lord honors his parents, and will serve those who begot him as if they were his masters, in work and word, and in all patience.

Honor your father so that a blessing from God may come upon you, and that his blessing may remain until the end. The blessing of a father strengthens the houses of children, but the curse of a mother roots out the foundations. Do not glory in the shame of your father, for his shame is no glory to you, but confusion. For the glory of a man comes from the honor of his father, and a father without honor is the disgrace of a son.

Son, support your father in his old age, and do not grieve him during his life. Even if his mind fails, give him pardon, and do not despise him in your own strength. For the alms given to a father shall not be forgotten; for in place of the sin of your mother, good shall be repaid to you. It shall be built up for you in justice, and in the day of tribulation you shall be remembered; and your sins shall melt away like ice in fair weather.

How bad is the reputation of one who forsakes his father, and he who exasperates his mother is cursed by God.

Son, perform your works in meekness, and you shall be loved above the glory of men. The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find grace before God. For great is the power of God alone, and He is honored by the humble.

Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search into things stronger than you; but always think upon those things which God has commanded you. Do not be curious about His many works, for it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden. Do not search in many ways into superfluous matters, and do not be curious about his many works. For many things have been shown to you that are beyond the understanding of men. Their own suspicion has supplanted many, and held their senses in vanity. Without eyes, you will not see; and without knowledge, you will not have it in the end. And why do you say, "I know much," in place of "I do not wish to"?

A heart entering two ways shall not have rest, and the perverse of heart shall be scandalized in them. A wicked heart shall be burdened with sorrows, and the sinner adds sin upon sin.

There shall be no health for the congregation of the proud, for the shrub of sin shall be rooted in them, and it shall not be understood.

<column-break/>

<margin>Chapter 1 <note>The marginal numbering follows the structure of this specific manuscript's commentary or lesson divisions rather than modern biblical chapters.</note></margin>
The heart of the wise will understand a parable, and a good ear will hear wisdom with all desire. A wise and understanding heart will abstain from sins and will have success in works of justice.

<margin>Chapter 2</margin>
Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving resists sins. God is the provider for him who returns a favor; He remembers it in the time to come, and in the time of his infirmity, he shall find a firm support.

<margin>Chapter 3</margin>
Son, do not defraud the poor of alms, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor. Do not despise a hungry soul, and do not exasperate the poor man in his poverty. Do not afflict the heart of the needy, and do not delay a gift to one in distress. Do not reject a petitioner in his affliction, and do not turn your face away from the needy. Do not turn your eyes away from the poor out of anger, and do not leave an opening for those who seek to curse you behind your back. For the curse of one who curses you in the bitterness of his soul is heard; He who made him will hear him.

<margin>Chapter 4</margin>
Make yourself affable to the congregation of the poor, and humble your soul to the elder, and humble your head to the great man.

<margin>Chapter 5</margin>
Incline your ear to the poor without sadness; pay your debt and answer him peacefully in meekness. Deliver him who suffers injury from the hand of the proud, and do not be faint-hearted in your soul. Be like a father to orphans, and as a husband to their mother. Then you shall be like an obedient son of the Most High, and He will have mercy on you more than a mother.

<margin>Chapter 6</margin>
Wisdom inspires life in her children; she takes up those who seek her and will go before them in the way of justice. He who loves her loves life, and those who watch for her shall embrace her delight. He who holds her shall inherit life, and wherever she enters, God will bless. Those who serve her shall be obedient to the Holy One, and God loves those who love her. He who hears her shall judge the nations, and he who gazes upon her shall remain confident. If he believes in her, he shall inherit her, and his descendants shall be in confirmation. For she walks with him in temptation, and at first she chooses him. She will bring fear, dread, and trial upon him, and she will torment him with the tribulation of her doctrine until she tries him in his thoughts and can trust his soul. Then she will strengthen him, lead him on a straight path, gladden him, and reveal her secrets to him. She will heap upon him the knowledge and understanding of justice. But if he goes astray, she will forsake him and deliver him into the hands of his enemy.

<margin>Chapter 7</margin>
Son, observe the time and avoid evil. For the sake of your soul, do not be ashamed to speak the truth. For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace. Do not accept a person against your own face, <note>Original: "faciem adversus faciem tuam"—likely meaning "do not show favoritism that compromises your integrity."</note> nor let a lie be against your soul. Do not stand in awe of your neighbor in your downfall, nor withhold a word in the time of salvation. Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty, for wisdom is recognized by the tongue; sense, knowledge, and doctrine are known in the word of the wise, and firmness in works of justice. In no way speak against the word of truth, and be ashamed of the lie of your lack of instruction. Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not subject yourself to every man for the sake of sin. Do not resist against the face of the powerful, nor strive against the current of the river. Struggle for justice for the sake of your soul, and even unto death, fight for justice; and God will fight against your enemies for you. Do not be hasty with your tongue, nor useless and remiss in your works. Do not be like a lion in your house, overturning those of your household and oppressing those subject to you. Let not your hand be stretched out to receive, and closed when it comes to giving.

<margin>Chapter 8</margin>
Do not pay attention to dishonest possessions, and do not say, "I have enough for my life," for it will profit nothing in the time of vengeance and darkness. Do not follow your own strength in your desires, and do not say, "I was able," or "Who shall subject me because of my works?" For God will surely take vengeance. Do not say, "I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?" For the Most High is a patient payer of debts. Do not be without fear concerning the forgiveness of sins, nor add sin upon sin. And do not say, "The mercy of the Lord is great; He will have mercy on the multitude of my sins." For mercy and wrath quickly approach from Him, and His wrath looks upon sinners. Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For His wrath shall come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance He will destroy you. Do not be anxious for unjust riches, for they shall not profit you in the day of darkness and vengeance.

<margin>Chapter 9</margin>
Do not winnow in every wind, and do not go into every path; for so the sinner is proved by a double tongue. Be steadfast in the way of the Lord, and in the truth of your understanding and knowledge; and let the word of peace and justice follow you. Be meek to hear the word so that you may understand, and with wisdom bring forth a true answer. If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be over your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word and be confounded. Honor and glory are in the speech of the wise, but the tongue of the imprudent is his own undoing. Do not be called a whisperer, and do not be caught and confounded by your own tongue. For shame and condemnation are upon the thief, and the worst condemnation is upon the double-tongued. But to the whisperer there is hatred, enmity, and reproach. Justify the small and the great alike, and do not become an enemy to your neighbor in place of a friend. For the wicked shall inherit reproach and shame, and so shall every envious and double-tongued sinner.

<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
Do not extol yourself in the thoughts of your soul like a bull, lest perhaps your strength be shattered by your folly, and it eat your leaves and destroy your fruits, and you be left like a dry tree in the desert. For a wicked soul will destroy the one who possesses it, and will give him over to the joy of his enemy, and lead him into the lot of the impious.

<margin>Chapter 11</margin>
A sweet word multiplies friends and mitigates enemies, and a gracious tongue will abound in a good man. Let many be at peace with you, but let your counselor be one among a thousand. If you possess a friend, prove him in temptation, and do not easily trust him. For there is a friend according to his own time, who will not remain in the day of tribulation. And there is a friend who turns to enmity, and there is a friend who will reveal hatred, strife, and reproaches.

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
Moreover, a friend is a companion at the table, but he will not remain in the day of necessity. If a friend remains steadfast, he shall be to you as an equal, and will act confidently with those of your household. If he humbles himself against you and hides himself from your face, you shall have a good and unanimous friendship. Separate yourself from your enemies, and be careful with your friends. A faithful friend is a strong protection; he who finds him finds a treasure. There is no comparison to a faithful friend, and no weight of gold or silver is worthy against the goodness of his faith. A faithful friend is the medicine of life and immortality, and those who fear the Lord shall find him. He who fears the Lord shall have an equally good friendship, for his friend shall be like him.

<margin>Chapter 13</margin>
Son, receive instruction from your youth, and even unto your gray hairs, you shall find wisdom. Come to her like one who plows and sows, and wait for her good fruits. For in her work you shall labor a little while, and you shall soon eat of her produce. How very harsh wisdom is to unlearned men, and the heartless man will not remain in her. She will be like a heavy stone of trial upon them, and they will not delay to cast her away. For the wisdom of doctrine is according to her name, and she is not manifest to many.

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>
But to those by whom she is recognized, she remains until the sight of God. Hear, my son, and receive the counsel of understanding, and do not reject my advice. Put your feet into her fetters, and your neck into her collar.

It emphasizes themes of humility, honoring parents, charity toward the poor, and the value of faithful friendship.</summary>
