<column-break/>

They indicated to me that in the whole world there is a dispersed people who used new laws, and contrary to the custom of all nations they contemn the commands of kings, and violate the concord of all regions by their own dissension. When this was demonstrated, we see that one nation is rebellious against every race of men... they use laws... and they disturb the peace and concord of the subjects... we have ordered that whosoever Haman... who is placed over the matters and is second after the king, and whom we worship in the place of a father, they should be destroyed with their wives and children as enemies, and no one should pity them... in the twelfth month of Adar in the present year, so that these wicked men on one day descending [to death] might restore the peace which they have disturbed.

<margin>Remember, O Lord</margin>
Remember: the exemplar of the letter. Because you should know that this place does not... Mordecai... his prayer... Lord, remembering all the works of the Lord.

<margin>Of all things...</margin>
> Lord, Lord, Almighty King: all things are in your power, and there is no one who can resist your will. If you have decreed to save us, we shall be delivered immediately. You made heaven and earth and whatever is contained in the circuit of the sky. You are the Lord of all, and there is no one who resists your majesty. You know all things: and you know that it was not through pride or contempt or any desire that I did this—that I did not adore the proud Haman. For I was ready to kiss even the traces of his feet for the salvation of Israel. But I feared lest I should transfer the honor of my Lord to a man, and lest I should adore anyone except my God. And now, O Lord King, God of Abraham, have mercy on your people, because they wish to destroy us and blot out your inheritance. Do not despise your portion which you redeemed from Egypt. Hear my prayer, and be merciful to your lot and your cord, and turn our mourning into joy, so that we living may praise your name, O Lord, and do not close the mouths of those who sing to you.

<margin>Which when she heard...</margin>
And all Israel cried out to the Lord with like mind and supplication, because certain death hung over them. Queen Esther also fled to the Lord, fearing the danger that was imminent. And when she had laid aside her royal garments, she took up robes suitable for mourning and weeping, and instead of various ointments, she filled her head with ashes... and she humbled her body with fasts; and all the places in which she was previously accustomed to rejoice, she filled with signs of her grief. And she prayed to the Lord God of Israel, saying: My Lord, you who are our King alone, help me, a solitary woman, who has no other helper but you. My danger is in my hands. I heard from my father, Lord, that you took Israel from all nations and our fathers... that they might possess an eternal inheritance; and you have done as you spoke. We have sinned in your sight, and therefore you have delivered us into the hands of our enemies, for we worshipped their gods. You are just, O Lord. And now it does not suffice them that they oppress us with the hardest servitude, but attributing the strength of their hands to the power of idols, they wish to change your promise and blot out your inheritance, and close the mouths of those praising you and extinguish the glory of your temple and your altar, so that they may open the mouths of the nations and praise the strength of idols, and proclaim a carnal king forever. Do not deliver, O Lord, your scepter to those who are nothing... but turn their counsel upon them, and show forth him who began to act against us. Remember, O Lord, and show yourself to us in the time of our tribulation, and give me confidence... King of gods and of all power. Give a well-ordered speech in my mouth in the presence of the lion <note>The "lion" here is a metaphor for the King (Artaxerxes/Ahasuerus).</note>, and turn his heart into a hatred of our enemy, so that he and the others who consent to him may perish. But deliver us by your hand, and come to my help, I who have no other but you, Lord, who have knowledge of all things. And you know that I hate the glory of the wicked, and detest the bed of the uncircumcised and of every stranger. You know my necessity, that I loathe the sign of my pride and glory which is upon my head in the days of my ostentation... and that I do not wear it in the days of my silence, and that I have not eaten at the table of Haman, nor has the king’s banquet pleased me, and I have not drunk the wine of libations... nor has your handmaid rejoiced from the time I was translated hither until the present day, except in you, Lord God of Abraham. O God, powerful above all, hear the voice of those who have no other hope, and deliver us from the hand of the wicked, and rescue me from my fear.

<margin>King Artaxerxes...</margin>
Which things... he found added in the common edition. He commanded: and Mordecai sent this word to Esther that she should go in to the king and petition for her people and for her country. "Remember," he said, "the days of your humility... how you were brought up by my hand; because Haman, the second after the king, has spoken against us unto death. And you, call upon the Lord, and speak to the king for us, and deliver us from death." <note>The following section of the transcription is highly repetitive and contains many OCR errors; it describes the scene where Esther, after three days of fasting, arrays herself in splendor and approaches the king's throne.</note> And when the queen arrived... she had with her two handmaids, and upon one she leaned as if for support... her body was delicate... and the other handmaid followed. Her face was like a rose, and her eyes were gracious and shining, but her soul was hidden in sorrow and excessive fear. Having entered through the order of the doors, she stood before the king where he sat upon the throne of his kingdom, clothed in royal robes and shining with gold and precious stones; he was terrible in aspect. And when he had lifted his face, showing the fury of his heart with burning eyes, the queen collapsed, her color turning pale, and she leaned her weary head upon her handmaid. And God turned the spirit of the king into mildness, and in haste and fear he leaped from his throne and sustained her in his arms... until she recovered. "What is it, Esther? I am your brother. Do not fear; you shall not die. For our law is not for you, but for all others. Approach and touch the scepter." And as she remained silent, he lifted the golden scepter and laid it upon her neck, and he kissed her. "Why do you not speak to me?" she asked. She responded, "I saw you, my lord, like an angel of God, and my heart was troubled by the fear of your glory. For you are wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of graces." And while she was speaking, she again fainted...

<meta>This page concludes the "Additions to Esther" (Vulgate Esther 16), which contains the decree of King Artaxerxes rehabilitating the Jews and condemning Haman. It then transitions directly into the Book of 1 Maccabees, beginning with a traditional prologue followed by the history of Alexander the Great and the subsequent persecution of the Jews under Antiochus Epiphanes.</meta>

Which matter is proved both from ancient histories and from those things which are currently being done: for it was seen that some were attempting to corrupt the highest power of kings. Wherefore, provision must be made for the peace and quiet of all. Nor should one think that if we command all these things <note>Referring to the king's previous decrees influenced by Haman</note> it is because of a fickle mind, but rather that we judge according to the quality and necessity of the times for the public good. For Haman, the son of Hammedatha <note>original: "aman-tiorē amachā"</note>, a man utterly alien to our blood, was received by us as a guest; and we extended to him such humanity that he was called our father. But he, overcome by the arrogance of his mind, endeavored to deprive us of our kingdom and our life. By various and deceitful craftiness, he sought the destruction of Mordecai <note>original: "adamū"</note>, by whose loyalty we live, and also the daughter of the Most High, the partner of our kingdom. He thought that by their death he might find an opportunity to betray our empire to the Macedonians. But we find no fault in the Jews, whom this most wicked of mortals had marked for death; on the contrary, we find that they live by just laws and are children of the Most High. Therefore, know that the letters he sent in our name are void. For this reason, he who plotted this has been hanged before the gates of this city, Shushan, with all his kindred; God has rendered to him the reward he deserved. Therefore, let this decree be published in all cities, that the Jews may safely follow their own laws. And you shall assist them, so that on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar, they may defend themselves against those who would attack them. For the Almighty God has turned this day of mourning into joy for them. Therefore, you shall also celebrate this day with all gladness among your other festival days, so that it may be known in the future that all who faithfully obey receive a worthy reward for their loyalty. But any city or province that does not observe this shall be destroyed by sword and fire, proving itself faithless not only to men but also to the gods.

# THE PROLOGUE
# TO THE BOOK OF MAC-
# CABEES BEGINS

The BOOKS of the Maccabees record the battles of Mattathias the Hebrew. They set forth the story and the noble Maccabees with their two triumphs; the books are named from these leaders. This history was unknown to the Romans. The history of the Maccabees describes what was done under King Antiochus, how they suffered many things, yet remained standing; they did not only suffer in the flames but also rejoice in the honors to which they pass.

# DER, SON OF PHILIP,
# THE MACEDONIAN,

who was the first to reign in Greece, coming out of the land of Kittim <note>original: "cethim," referring to Greece or the Mediterranean islands</note>, had defeated Darius, king of the Persians and Medes: he established many battles, and took the strongholds of all, and slew the kings of the earth. And he passed even to the ends of the earth, and took the spoils of many nations; and the earth was silent before him. And he gathered power and a very strong army, and his heart was exalted and lifted up. And he obtained the regions of the nations and their rulers, and they became tributary to him. And after these things, he fell upon his bed and knew that he should die.

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin>
And he called his noble servants, who had been brought up with him from his youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was yet alive. And his servants reigned for twelve years, and Alexander died. And his servants obtained the kingdom, each one in his own place; and they all put crowns upon themselves after his death, and their sons after them for many years, and evils were multiplied on the earth. And there went out from them a wicked root, Antiochus the Illustrious <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note>, son of king Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome; and he reigned in the hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks. In those days, there went out of Israel wicked sons, and they persuaded many, saying:
<margin>b</margin>
"Let us go and make a covenant <term>testamentum</term> <note>meaning a formal alliance or treaty</note> with the nations that are round about us; for since we departed from them, many evils have befallen us." And the word seemed good in their eyes. And some of the people determined to do this, and went to the king; and he gave them power to follow the justice of the nations. And they built a gymnasium <term>gymnasium</term> <note>a Greek athletic school, which was controversial because athletes exercised naked, contrary to Jewish modesty</note> in Jerusalem according to the laws of the nations. And they made themselves uncircumcised, and departed from the holy covenant, and were joined to the nations, and were sold to do evil. And when the kingdom was prepared in the sight of Antiochus, he began to reign over the land of Egypt, that he might reign over two kingdoms.
<margin>c</margin>
And he entered into Egypt with a heavy multitude, with chariots, and elephants, and horsemen, and a great number of ships. And he moved war against Ptolemy, the king of Egypt; and Ptolemy was afraid of his presence and fled, and many fell wounded. And he took the strong cities in the land of Egypt, and he took the spoils of the land of Egypt. And Antiochus turned back, after he had smitten Egypt, in the hundred and forty-third year, and went up to Jerusalem with a heavy multitude. And he entered into the sanctuary with pride, and took the golden altar, and the candlestick of light, and all its vessels, and the table of proposition <term>mensam ppositionis</term> <note>the Table of Shewbread</note>, and the pouring vessels, and the vials, and the little mortars of gold, and the veil, and the crowns, and the golden ornament that was before the temple; and he broke all in pieces. And he took the silver, and the gold, and the precious vessels; and he took the hidden treasures which he found. And when he had taken all away, he departed into his own land. And he made a great slaughter of men, and spoke with great pride. And there was great mourning in Israel and in every place where they were. And the princes and the ancients mourned; the young men and the virgins were made feeble, and the beauty of the women was changed. Every bridegroom took up lamentation, and they that sat in the marriage bed mourned. And the earth was moved for the inhabitants thereof, and all the house of Jacob was covered with confusion. And after two full years, the king sent the chief collector of tributes into the cities of Judah, and he came to Jerusalem with a great multitude. And he spoke to them peaceable words in deceit, and they believed him. And he fell upon the city suddenly and struck it with a great slaughter, and destroyed much people in Israel. And he took the spoils of the city and burnt it with fire, and threw down the houses thereof and the walls thereof round about. And they took the women and the children captive and possessed the cattle. And they built the City of David with a great and strong wall, and with strong towers, and it was made a fortress for them. And they placed there a sinful nation, wicked men, and they grew strong in it. And they stored up armor and food, and gathered together the spoils of Jerusalem, and laid them up there; and they became a great snare. And this was a place to lie in wait against the sanctuary, and an evil devil in Israel. And they shed innocent blood round about the sanctuary and defiled the holy place. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them, and it became a habitation of strangers, and she became a stranger to her own seed, and her children left her. Her sanctuary was desolate like a wilderness; her festival days were turned into mourning, her sabbaths into reproach, her honors into nothing. According to her glory, so was her ignominy multiplied, and her high station was turned into mourning.
<margin>e</margin>
And king Antiochus wrote to all his kingdom, that all the people should be one. And every one should leave his own law. And all nations agreed according to the word of king Antiochus. And many of Israel consented to him, and they sacrificed to idols and defiled the sabbath. And king Antiochus sent books by the hands of messengers to Jerusalem and to all the cities of Judah: that they should follow the law of the nations of the earth, and should forbid burnt offerings and sacrifices and atonements to be made in the temple of God, and should forbid the sabbaths and the solemn days to be celebrated. And he commanded the holy places to be defiled, and the holy temple. And they commanded altars to be built in the temple, and idols, and swine's flesh to be immolated, and common beasts; and to leave their sons uncircumcised, and to defile their souls with all uncleanness and abominations, so that they might forget the law and change all the justifications of God. And whosoever would not do according to the word of king Antiochus should die. According to all these words he wrote to his whole kingdom; and he appointed rulers over the people to compel these things to be done. And they commanded the cities of Judah to sacrifice. And many of the people were gathered to them that had forsaken the law of the Lord; and they committed evils upon the land. And they drove the people of Israel into hiding places and into the secret places of fugitives. On the fifteenth day of the month of Chislev <note>original: "casleu"</note>, <insert>second book of maccabees</insert>
<margin>f</margin>
in the hundred and forty-fifth year, they built the abomination of desolation upon the altar of God; and they built altars throughout all the cities of Judah round about. And they burnt incense and sacrificed before the doors of the houses and in the streets. And they burnt the books of the law of God with fire, tearing them to pieces. And with whomsoever the books of the covenant of the Lord were found, and whosoever observed the law of the Lord, they were put to death according to the edict of the king. <margin>311</margin> By their power they did these things to the people of Israel who were found in the cities month by month. And on the twenty-fifth day of the month, they sacrificed upon the altar which was over against the [holy] altar. And the women who circumcised their children were put to death according to the command of king Antiochus. And they hanged the children by their necks throughout all their houses, and those who had circumcised them they put to death. And many of the people of Israel determined with themselves that they would not eat unclean things; and they chose rather to die than to be defiled with unclean foods. And they would not break the holy law of the Lord, and they were tortured and died. And there was very great wrath upon the people.

In those days arose Mattathias, the son of John, the son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib, from Jerusalem, and he dwelt on the mountain of Modin. And he had five sons: John, who was surnamed Gaddi; and Simeon, who was surnamed Thassi; and Judas, who was surnamed Maccabeus; and Eleazar, who was surnamed Avaran; and Jonathan, who was surnamed Apphus. These saw the evils that were done among the people of Judah and in Jerusalem.

And they immediately went out to them and set the battle against them on the Sabbath day. And they said to them: "Resist no further! And they stirred up the battle against them. But they did not answer them, nor did they cast a stone at them, nor did they block up the hidden places, saying: "Let us all die in our innocence <note>original: "simplicitate"</note>, and heaven and earth shall be witnesses over us that you destroy us unjustly." And they brought war upon them on the Sabbaths, and they died—they and their wives, and their children, and their cattle—up to a thousand souls of men. And Mattathias and his friends learned of it, and they mourned for them greatly.

**T**hen there were gathered to them the mighty in strength from Israel, every volunteer for the Law; and all those who fled from the evils were added to them, and they became a source of strength to them. And they gathered an army and struck the sinners in their wrath and the wicked men in their indignation, and the rest fled to the nations to escape. And Mattathias and his friends went around and destroyed the altars, and they circumcised the uncircumcised boys—as many as they found within the borders of Israel—by force. And they pursued the children of pride, and the work prospered in their hands; and they rescued the Law from the hands of the Gentiles and from the hands of the kings, and they did not allow the sinner to triumph <note>original: "non dederunt cornu peccatori," literally "did not give the horn to the sinner." The horn is a biblical symbol for power and pride.</note>.

<margin>1 Maccabees</margin>
**E**nd the days of Mattathias’s life drew near, and he said to his sons: "Now pride and punishment are strengthened, and the time of destruction, and the wrath of indignation. Now, O sons, be emulators of the Law and give your lives for the covenant of your fathers. Remember the works of the fathers which they did in their generations, and you shall receive great glory and an eternal name. Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was credited to him as righteousness? Joseph, in the time of his distress, kept the commandment and became lord of Egypt. Phinehas our father, by being zealous with the zeal of God, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Joshua, while he fulfilled the word, became a leader in Israel. Caleb, while he bore witness in the assembly, received an inheritance. David, in his mercy, obtained the seat of the kingdom forever. Elijah, while he was zealous with the zeal of the Law, was taken up into heaven. Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>The Hebrew names for Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego</note>, by believing, were delivered from the flame of fire. Daniel, in his innocence, was delivered from the mouth of the lions. And so, consider throughout generation after generation that all who hope in Him are not weakened. And do not fear the words of a sinful man, for his glory is but dung and worms. Today he is lifted up, and tomorrow he shall not be found, because he is returned to his earth and his thought has perished. You, therefore, my sons, take courage and act manfully in the Law, for in it you shall be glorious. And behold, Simon your brother; I know that he is a man of counsel—listen to him always, and he shall be a father to you. And Judas Maccabeus, mighty in strength from his youth, let him be the leader of your army, and he shall lead the people's war. And you shall bring to yourselves all those who observe the Law, and you shall avenge the wrongs of your people. Render retribution to the nations, and attend to the precept of the Law."

**A**nd when he had blessed them, he was joined to his fathers. And he died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year <note>Approximately 166 BC in the Seleucid calendar</note>, and he was buried by his sons in the tombs of his fathers in Modin, and all Israel mourned him with great mourning.

**A**nd Judas, who was called Maccabeus, rose up in his place. And all his brothers helped him, as did all who had joined themselves to his father, and they fought the battle of Israel with joy. And he extended the glory of his people, and put on a breastplate like a giant, and girded himself with his weapons of war in battles, and protected the camp with his sword. He became like a lion in his works, and like a lion's whelp roaring in the hunt. And he pursued the wicked, searching them out, and those who troubled his people he burned with flames. And the enemies were repulsed for fear of him, and all the workers of iniquity were troubled. And salvation was directed by his hand, and he grieved many kings and gladdened Jacob <note>meaning the nation of Israel</note> by his works, and his memory is blessed forever. And he traveled through the cities of Judah and destroyed the impious from them, and turned away wrath from Israel. And his name was renowned even to the ends of the earth, and he gathered those who were perishing.

**A**nd Apollonius gathered the nations, and a great and mighty force from Samaria to fight against Israel. And Judas knew of it and went out to meet him, and he struck him and killed him. And many fell wounded, and the rest fled, and he took their spoils. And Judas took the sword of Apollonius and was fighting with it all his days. And Seron, the prince of the army of Syria, heard that Judas had gathered a congregation and an assembly of the faithful with him, and he said: "I will make a name for myself, and I will be glorified in the kingdom, and I will defeat Judas and those who are with him, who have despised the king's word." And he prepared himself, and the camp of the impious went up with him—mighty helpers to take vengeance on the children of Israel. And they approached as far as Beth-horon, and Judas went out to meet him with a few men. But when they saw the army coming to meet them, they said to Judas: "How shall we, being few, be able to fight against so great and so strong a multitude? For we are exhausted from fasting today." And Judas said: "It is an easy thing for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; and there is no difference in the sight of the God of heaven to deliver by many or by few. For the victory of battle is not in the multitude of the army, but strength is from heaven. They come to us in a multitude of insolence and pride, to destroy us and our wives

<column-break/>

and our children, and to despoil us. But we will fight for our lives and our laws, and the Lord Himself will crush them before our face. You, however, do not fear them." And when he ceased speaking, he leaped upon them suddenly, and Seron and his army were crushed in his sight. And he pursued him down the descent of Beth-horon as far as the plain. And eight hundred men of them fell, and the rest fled into the land of the Philistines. And the fear of Judas fell upon his brothers, and dread upon all the nations round about them. And his name reached the king, and all the nations spoke of the battles of Judas.

**B**ut a messenger came and told Seron <note>Though the Latin says Seron, context suggests it refers to the king's officers</note>, the leader of King Antiochus's army, that Judas had gathered a very strong military camp from his whole kingdom. And the king opened his treasury and gave pay to the army for a year, and commanded them to be ready for everything. And he saw that the money had failed from the treasuries, and the tributes of the region were small because of the dissension and the plague he had brought upon the land—to take away the laws which had been from the earliest days. And he feared that he would not have enough, as he had once and twice before, for the expenses and gifts which he had given with a liberal hand—for he had abounded more than the kings who had been before him. And he was greatly dismayed in his mind, and he thought to go into Persia to receive the tributes of the regions and to gather much silver. And he left Lysias, a noble man of the royal lineage, over the king’s business from the river Euphrates to the borders of Egypt, and to raise Antiochus his son until he should return. And he delivered to him half of the army and the elephants, and commanded him concerning all that he wished, and concerning the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem: that he should send an army against them to crush and uproot the strength of Israel and the remnants of Jerusalem, and to take away the memory of their place, and to settle the children of strangers in all their borders and distribute their land by lot. And the king took the remaining part of the army and departed from Antioch, the city of his kingdom, in the one hundred and forty-seventh year; and he crossed the river Euphrates and traveled through the upper regions. And Lysias chose Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes, and Nicanor, and Gorgias—powerful men from among the king’s friends—and sent with them forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen to come into the land of Judah and destroy it according to the king’s word. And they set out with all their power and came and camped near Emmaus in the plain country. And the merchants of the regions heard their name and took very much silver and gold, and servants, and came into the camp to buy the children of Israel as slaves. And the armies of Syria and the land of the foreigners were added to them. And Judas and his brothers saw that evils were multiplied and the armies were approaching their borders; and they knew the words of the king, which he had commanded the people to do for their destruction and consumption. And each man said to his neighbor: "Let us raise up the ruin of our people, and let us fight for our people and our holy things." And a gathering was assembled to be ready for battle, and to pray, and to ask for mercy and compassions. And Jerusalem was not inhabited, but was like a desert; there was no one of her holy ones who entered or went out, and the sanctuary was trodden down, and the children of foreigners were in the citadel—there was the dwelling of the Gentiles. And joy was taken away from Jacob, and the pipe and the lute failed there. And they gathered together and came to Mizpah <note>original: "masphat"</note> over against Jerusalem, because the place of prayer in Israel had formerly been in Mizpah. And they fasted that day, and put on sackcloth and put ashes on their heads, and tore their garments. And they laid open the book of the Law, in which the Gentiles sought the likeness of their idols. And they brought the priestly ornaments and the firstfruits and the tithes, and they brought forward the Nazirites who had completed their days. And they cried with a loud voice toward heaven, saying: "What shall we do with these, and where shall we lead them? For Your holy things are trodden down and contaminated, and Your priests are in mourning and humiliation. And behold, the nations have gathered against us to destroy us. You know what they plot against us. How shall we be able to stand before their face unless You help us?" And they sounded the trumpets with a loud voice. And after this, Judas appointed leaders of the people: tribunes, and centurions, and commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten. And he said to those who were building houses, and betrothing wives, and planting vineyards, and to the fearful, that each man should return to his own house according to the Law. And they moved the camp and placed it to the south of Emmaus. And Judas said: "Gird yourselves and be powerful sons, and be ready in the morning to fight against these nations that have gathered against us to destroy us and our holy things. For it is better for us to die in war than to see the evils of our nation and the holy things. But as the will shall be in heaven, so let it be done."

**A**nd Gorgias took five thousand men and a thousand chosen horsemen, and they moved the camp by night to approach the camp of the Jews and strike them suddenly; and the men who were from the citadel were their guides. And they saw the camp of the Gentiles, strong and armored, and the cavalry around them, and these men were trained for battle. Remember how our fathers were saved in the Red Sea when Pharaoh followed them with a great army. And now let us cry to heaven, and the Lord will have mercy on us and will be mindful of the covenant of our fathers, and He will crush this army before our face today; and all the nations shall know that there is one who redeems and delivers Israel." And the foreigners raised their eyes and saw them coming against them, and they went out of the camp to battle. And those who were with Judas sounded the trumpets, and they joined battle, and the nations were broken and fled into the plain. But the hindmost fell by the sword. But stand now against our enemies and fight them, and afterward you shall take the spoils confidently." And while Judas was still speaking these words, behold, a certain part appeared looking out from the mountain, and it saw that they were turned to flight and the camp was set on fire; for the smoke that was seen declared what had happened. When they saw this, they were greatly afraid, seeing at the same time both Judas and his army in the plain ready for battle. And they all fled into the land of the foreigners. And Judas returned to the spoils of the camp, and they took much gold and silver, and hyacinth-blue and sea-purple, and great riches. And returning, they sang a hymn and blessed God in heaven, because He is good, because His mercy endures forever. And there was a great salvation in Israel on that day. But whoever of the foreigners escaped came and told Lysias all that had happened. When he heard these things, he was dismayed and his spirit failed...

**A**nd when Lysias saw the flight of his men and the boldness of the Jews—and that they were ready either to live or to die bravely—he went away to Antioch and chose soldiers so that he might return to Judea with many more.

And they saw the sanctuary deserted, the altar profaned, the gates burned, and plants growing in the courtyards as if in a forest or on the mountains, and the <term>pastoforia</term> <note>These were side-chambers or store-rooms used by priests in the Temple.</note> pulled down. And he considered what to do with the altar of burnt offerings, which had been profaned. A good plan occurred to them: to pull it down, lest it should be a reproach to them because the Gentiles had contaminated it. So they pulled it down and stored the stones in a fitting place on the mountain of the House <note>The Temple Mount.</note> until a prophet should come and give an answer concerning them. And they took whole stones according to the law and built a new altar according to the one that was there before. They built up the holy places and the parts within the house; they sanctified the interior and the courtyards. They made new holy vessels and brought the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table into the temple. They put incense upon the altar and lit the lamps that were upon the lampstand, and they shone in the temple. They placed loaves of bread upon the table, hung the veils, and finished all the works they had undertaken. They rose early before morning on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month—this is the month of <term>Casleu</term> <note>The Jewish month of Kislev, roughly December.</note>—in the one hundred and forty-eighth year. And they offered sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings which they had made. According to the time and according to the day on which the Gentiles had contaminated it, on that very day it was renewed with songs, and lutes, and harps, and cymbals. And all the people fell upon their faces, and they adored and blessed him in heaven who had prospered them. They celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days, and they offered burnt offerings with joy, and sacrifices of salvation and praise. They adorned the front of the temple with golden crowns and small shields, and they dedicated the gates and the chambers and put doors on them. And there was very great joy among the people, and the reproach of the Gentiles was turned away. And Judas and his brothers and the whole assembly of Israel decreed that the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept in their season from year to year for eight days, from the twenty-fifth day of the month of Casleu, with joy and gladness. At that time they also built up Mount Zion and high walls and strong towers all around it, lest the Gentiles should ever come and trample it as they had done before. And he placed an army there to guard it, and he fortified it to guard Bethsuram, so that the people might have a stronghold against the face of Idumea.

**A**nd it happened that when the nations round about heard that the altar and the sanctuary were built as before, they were very angry. When Judas and the people heard these words, a great assembly met to consider what they should do for their brothers who were in tribulation and were being attacked by them. And Judas said to Simon his brother: "Choose men for yourself and go and deliver your brothers in Galilee; I and my brother Jonathan will go into the land of Gilead." And three thousand men were assigned to Simon to go into Galilee, and eight thousand men to Judas for Gilead. Simon went into Galilee and joined many battles with the nations, and the nations were crushed before him, and he pursued them to the gate of Ptolemais. And about three thousand men of the nations fell, and he took their spoils. He took those who were in Galilee and in Arbatta, with their wives and children and all that they had, and brought them into Judea with great joy. Judas Maccabeus and Jonathan his brother crossed the Jordan and traveled a three-days' journey through the desert. And the Nabateans met them and received them peaceably, and told them all the things that had happened to their brothers in Gilead, and how many of them were trapped in Bozrah, and Bosor, and in Alema, and in Casphor, and Maked, and Carnaim—all these were strong and large cities. They were also held shut up in the other cities of Gilead, and they had planned to move their army against the cities the next day, to seize and destroy them all in one day. Then Judas and his army suddenly turned their way into the desert of Bozrah and occupied the city; he killed every male at the edge of the sword, took all their spoils, and burned the city with fire. They rose from there at night and went as far as the stronghold. And it happened at daybreak, when they lifted their eyes, behold, there was a people without number, carrying ladders and engines to take the stronghold and attack them. And Judas saw that the battle had begun, and the cry of the battle went up to heaven like a trumpet, and a great cry from the city. And he said to his army: "Fight today for our brothers!"

And he came in three ranks behind them, and they sounded the trumpets and cried out in prayer. And the camp of Timotheus knew that it was Maccabeus, and they fled from his face. They crossed the Jordan into the great plain over against Beth-shan. And Judas was gathering those who lagged behind and exhorting the people all along the way until they came into the land of Judah. And they went up to Mount Zion with joy and gladness and offered burnt offerings because not one of them had fallen until they returned in peace.

**A**nd in the days when Judas and Jonathan were in the land of Gilead, and Simon his brother was in Galilee over against Ptolemais, Joseph the son of Zechariah and Azarias, the leaders of the forces, heard of the good deeds and the battles that had been done, and they said: "Let us also make a name for ourselves, and let us go fight against the nations that are around us." **A**nd King Antiochus was traveling through the upper regions, and he heard that there was a city, Elymais in Persia, most noble and rich in silver and gold. <meta>This page continues the narrative of the First Book of Maccabees, following the death of King Antiochus IV Epiphanes. It details the reign of his young son, Antiochus V Eupator, the ongoing wars led by Judas Maccabeus, the rise of the usurper Demetrius, and the first formal diplomatic contact between the Jews and the Roman Republic.</meta>

The king arrived before daybreak and spurred his army into an assault against Beth-zechariah <note>original: "beth-zacara"</note>. Those who were on horses and others followed. They appeared and marked their positions. The mercenary armies arrived, numbering one hundred thousand footmen, twenty thousand horsemen, and thirty-two elephants trained for war. They came through Idumea and approached Beth-zur, where they fought for many days. They built siege engines, but the defenders came out and burned them with fire, fighting manfully. 

Then Judas withdrew from the citadel and moved his camp to Beth-zechariah, opposite the king's camp. The king rose early and spurred his army's charge toward Beth-zechariah; the armies prepared themselves for battle and sounded the trumpets. To provoke the elephants to battle, they showed them the blood of grapes and mulberries <note>original: "sanguinem uue & mori"; a historical tactic used to incite war elephants by showing them red liquid.</note>. They divided the beasts among the legions, and for every elephant, there were a thousand men in coats of mail with brass helmets on their heads, and five hundred chosen horsemen assigned to each beast. These horsemen stayed wherever the beast was, following it wherever it went and never departing from it. Firm wooden towers were fastened upon each beast to protect them, containing siege engines and thirty-two <note>The number 32 likely refers to the total soldiers associated with the unit, as ancient sources vary on how many men a single elephant tower could actually hold.</note> strong men who fought from above, along with the beast's driver. The rest of the cavalry was stationed on either side to harass the enemy and to charge forward while packed in their legions.

When the sun shone upon the shields of gold and brass, the mountains sparkled with them like flaming torches. Part of the king’s army was deployed across the high mountains and others through the low valleys; they marched cautiously and in order. Everyone who heard the noise of their multitude, the marching of the crowd, and the clashing of their armor was moved, for the army was vast and strong. Judas and his army approached for battle, and six hundred men of the king’s army fell. 

Eleazar, son of Saura <note>Also known as Eleazar Avaran, the brother of Judas.</note>, saw one of the beasts armored with royal mail, standing taller than all the other beasts. It seemed to him that the king was upon it. He gave himself up to deliver his people and to acquire an eternal name. He ran boldly toward it into the midst of the legion, slaying to the right and left so that they fell away from him on both sides. He went under the feet of the elephant, placed himself beneath it, and killed it. It fell to the earth upon him, and he died there. The Jews, seeing the strength of the king and the violence of his army, turned away from them. 

The king’s camp then went up against Jerusalem. The king's camp approached Judah at Mount Zion. They made peace with those in Beth-zur, who left the city because they had no food to endure a siege, as it was a Sabbatical year <note>original: "annus erat septimus"; every seventh year, the land was left fallow and no crops were harvested.</note> for the land. The king took Beth-zur and stationed a garrison there to guard it. He turned his camp toward the sanctuary for many days and set up catapults, engines, fire-throwers, stone-throwing machines, darts, and "scorpions" <note>A "scorpion" was a type of heavy bolt-throwing engine.</note> to shoot arrows and slings. The Jews also built engines against the enemy's engines and fought for many days. However, there were no provisions found because it was the seventh year, and those who had remained in Judea from among the Gentiles had consumed the last of the stores kept for emergencies. Only a few men remained in the sanctuary, as hunger had overwhelmed them, and they were scattered, each to his own place. 

Then Lysias heard that Philip—whom King Antiochus had appointed while he was still alive to raise his son Antiochus to reign—had returned from Persia and Media with the army that went with him, and was seeking to take over the affairs of the kingdom. Lysias hurried to say to the king and the leaders of the army: "We are failing daily, our food is scarce, the place we are besieging is well-fortified, and the business of the kingdom rests upon us. Now, therefore, let us give our right hands to these men and make peace with them and their whole nation. Let us decree that they may live by their own laws as they did before. For it is because of their laws, which we tried to destroy, that they are angry and have done all these things." This speech pleased the king and the princes. He sent word to the Jews to make peace, and they accepted it. The king and the princes swore an oath to them, and they came out of the fortification. But when the king entered Mount Zion and saw the strength of the place, he quickly broke the oath he had sworn and commanded the wall to be destroyed all around. Then he departed in haste and returned to Antioch, where he found Philip ruling the city. He fought against him and took the city by force.

In the one hundred and fifty-first year <note>Approximately 161 BCE.</note>, Demetrius, son of Seleucus, escaped from the city of Rome and went up with a few men to a city by the sea and reigned there. As he was entering the palace of his ancestors, his army seized Antiochus and Lysias to bring them to him. When this was made known to him, he said, "Do not let me see their faces." So the army killed them, and Demetrius sat upon the throne of his kingdom. Then all the wicked and godless men of Israel came to him, led by Alchimus, who wished to be made High Priest. They accused the people to the king, saying: "Judas and his brothers have destroyed all your friends and driven us out of our land. Now, therefore, send a man whom you trust to see all the destruction he has caused us and the king’s lands, and let him punish all his friends." 

The king chose Bacchides, one of his friends, who ruled beyond the River <note>The Euphrates.</note>, a great man in the kingdom and faithful to the king. He sent him and the wicked Alchimus, whom he confirmed in the priesthood, and commanded him to take vengeance on the children of Israel. They arose and came with a large army into the land of Judah. They sent messengers to Judas and his brothers with deceitful words of peace, but Judas did not heed their words, for he saw they had come with a great army. 

A group of scribes gathered before Alchimus and Bacchides, seeking a just settlement. The Hasideans <note>original: "assidei"; a sect of pious Jews particularly devoted to the Law.</note> were the first among the children of Israel to seek peace from them. For they said, "A man who is a priest of the seed of Aaron has come; he will not deceive us." He spoke peaceful words to them and swore an oath, saying: "We will bring no harm to you or your friends." They believed him. But he seized sixty of them and killed them in a single day, according to the word that is written: "The flesh of your saints and their blood they have shed around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them." <note>A quotation of Psalm 79.</note> Fear and trembling fell upon all the people, for they said: "There is no truth or justice in them, for they have broken the covenant and the oath they swore." 

Bacchides moved his camp from Jerusalem and settled in Beth-zetha. He sent and seized many of those who had deserted him, and some of the people he slaughtered and threw into a great pit. He committed the region to Alchimus and left him an army to help him. Bacchides returned to the king, and Alchimus struggled for the high priesthood. All who troubled their own people gathered to him; they gained control of the land of Judah and caused great harm in Israel. 

Judas saw all the evil Alchimus and his followers were doing to the children of Israel—far more than the Gentiles had done. He went out into all the borders of Judea and took vengeance on the men who had deserted, so they ceased to go out into the countryside. But Alchimus saw that Judas and those with him were prevailing and realized he could not withstand them. He returned to the king and accused them of many crimes. Then the king sent Nicanor, one of his most noble princes, who bore a grudge against Israel, and commanded him to exterminate the people. Nicanor came to Jerusalem with a great army and sent to

<column-break/>

Judas and his brothers with deceitful words of peace, saying: "Let there be no fight between me and you; I will come with a few men to see your faces in peace." He came to Judas, and they greeted each other peaceably, though the enemies were prepared to kidnap Judas. When Judas realized Nicanor had come to him with deceit, he was afraid and refused to see his face again. Nicanor realized his plan had been discovered and went out to fight Judas near Caphar-salama. About five thousand of Nicanor’s men fell, and the rest fled into the City of David. 

After this, Nicanor went up to Mount Zion. Some of the priests and the elders of the people went out to greet him in peace and to show him the burnt offerings being offered for the king. But he mocked them, despised them, defiled them, and spoke arrogantly. He swore in anger, saying: "Unless Judas and his army are delivered into my hands, as soon as I return in safety, I will burn down this house!" And he went out in great rage. The priests entered and stood before the altar and the temple, and weeping, they said: "You chose this house to have your name called upon in it, to be a house of prayer and petition for your people. Take vengeance on this man and his army; let them fall by the sword. Remember their blasphemies and do not allow them to continue."

Nicanor departed from Jerusalem and camped at Beth-horon, where the Syrian army met him. Judas camped in Adasa with three thousand men, and Judas prayed, saying: "Lord, when the messengers of King Sennacherib blasphemed, your angel went out and struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them. So crush this army before us today, so that others may know he has spoken wickedly against your sanctuary; judge him according to his malice." The armies joined battle on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar <note>Adar is roughly February/March.</note>, and Nicanor’s camp was crushed; he was the first to fall in the battle. When his army saw that Nicanor had fallen, they threw down their arms and fled. The Jews pursued them a day's journey from Adasa until they reached Gazara, sounding the signal trumpets after them. People came out from all the surrounding villages of Judea and hemmed them in, turning them back toward their pursuers. All fell by the sword; not a single one was left. The Jews took the spoils and the prey. They cut off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had stretched out so arrogantly, and they hung them up near Jerusalem. The people rejoiced greatly and kept that day with great gladness. They ordained that this day should be kept every year on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. And the land of Judah was quiet for a few days.

Now Judas heard of the name of the Romans: that they are mighty in power and agree to everything requested of them, establishing friendships with all who approach them. He heard of their battles and the brave deeds they did in Galatia, how they conquered them and made them pay tribute; and what they did in the land of Spain to gain control of the silver and gold mines there. By their counsel and patience, they possessed the whole place, even though it was very far from them. They crushed kings who came against them from the ends of the earth and struck them with a great blow; the rest pay them tribute every year. They also defeated Philip and Perseus, king of the Macedonians <note>original: "citheorum"; likely a scribal error for Kittim or Macedonians.</note>, and others who took up arms against them. They crushed them in war and made them subjects. Even Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, who went to fight them with one hundred and twenty elephants, cavalry, chariots, and a massive army, was defeated by them. They took him alive and decreed that he and those who reigned after him should pay a great tribute, give hostages, and cede territory—including the regions of India, Media, and Lydia, some of their best provinces. They took these from him and gave them to King Eumenes. 

Judas also heard how the Greeks had planned to come and destroy them, but the Romans learned of it and sent a single general against them. They fought, and many of the Greeks fell; the Romans led away their wives and children as captives, plundered them, took possession of their land, destroyed their walls, and reduced them to slavery to this day. They destroyed and brought under their power all other kingdoms and islands that had ever resisted them. But with their friends and those who relied on them, they maintained friendship. They conquered kingdoms both near and far, and whoever heard their name was afraid of them. Those whom they wish to help to reign, do reign; and those they wish to depose, they depose; they have been greatly exalted. 

Yet in all this, none of them wears a crown or is clothed in purple for self-glorification. They have established a senate for themselves, where three hundred and fifty <note>original: ".cccl."; usually historical sources say 320.</note> senators consult daily, constantly deliberating for the multitude so that they may act properly. They commit their government to one man each year to rule over all their land, and all obey that one person, and there is no envy or jealousy among them. 

So Judas chose Eupolemus son of John, son of Accos, and Jason son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to establish a treaty of friendship and alliance, to lift the yoke of the Greeks from them, for they saw that the kingdom of the Greeks was reducing Israel to slavery. They went to Rome—a very long journey—entered the Senate, and said: "Judas Maccabeus and his brothers and the people of the Jews have sent us to you to establish an alliance and peace with you, and to enroll us as your allies and friends." The proposal pleased them. This is the copy of the letter they wrote back on tablets of brass and sent to Jerusalem to remain there as a memorial of peace and alliance:

They built fortified cities in Judea: the fortification in Jericho, and in Amman, and in Beth-horon, and Bethel, and Thamnata, and Pharathon, and Tephon, with high walls and gates and bars. All the lawless men plotted, saying: "Behold, Jonathan and those with him live in silence and confidence. Now therefore, let us bring Bacchides, and he will capture them all in one night." They went and gave him this advice. He rose to come with a great army and sent letters secretly to his allies in Judea to seize Jonathan and those with him, but they could not because their counsel became known to them.

And all the armies of his fathers were friendly to him.

And Demetrius sent to Jonathan, saying: "I will not only do these things for you and your nation, but I will illustrate you and your nation with glory when it shall be opportune."

"Now therefore, you will do well if you send me help, because all my army has deserted me." And Jonathan sent him three thousand chosen men, and they came to Antioch; and the king was delighted by their arrival. And those who were of the city, a hundred and twenty thousand men, gathered together, and they wished to kill the king. And the king fled into the palace, and those who were of the city occupied the streets of the city and began to fight. And the king called the Jews for help, and they all gathered together to him. And they were scattered through the city, and they killed in that day a hundred thousand men, and they set the city on fire, and they took many spoils on that day, and they delivered the king. And those who were of the city saw that the Jews had obtained the city as they wished, and they were weakened in their minds, and they cried out to the king with prayers, saying: "Give us your right hand, and let the Jews cease attacking us and the city." And they threw down their arms and made peace. And the Jews were glorified in the sight of the king and in the sight of all who were in his kingdom, and they were renowned in the kingdom and returned to Jerusalem having many spoils. And King Demetrius sat on the seat of his kingdom, and the land was silent in his sight. And he lied about whatever he had said, and he alienated himself from Jonathan, and he did not repay him according to the benefits he had given him, and he vexed him greatly.

After these things, however, came Antiochus <note>Antiochus VI Dionysus, the young son of Alexander Balas</note>, quite a boy, and he reigned and placed the crown upon himself. And the whole army gathered to him, whom Demetrius had scattered, and they fought against him, and they fled and turned their backs. And Tryphon took the beasts <note>War elephants</note> and obtained Antioch. And the young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying: "I confirm you in the priesthood, and I appoint you over the four districts, that you may be among the king's friends." And he sent him golden vessels and service, and gave him the power of drinking from gold, and to be in purple, and to have a golden buckle. And they appointed Simon his brother as governor from the borders of Tyre to the borders of Egypt. And Jonathan went out and traveled across the river through the cities, and the whole army of Syria gathered to him for help. And he came to Ascalon, and they of the city met him honorably; and they went from there to Gaza, and those who were in Gaza shut themselves in, and he besieged it. And he burned the things that were in the circuit of the city and spoiled them. And the Gazans requested Jonathan, and he gave them his right hand <note>A gesture of peace or a pact</note>, and he took their sons as hostages and sent them into Jerusalem, and he traveled through the region as far as Damascus.

And Jonathan heard that the chief commanders of Demetrius had come into Galilee with a great army, wishing to remove him from the business of the kingdom, and he went to meet them. His brother Simon, however, he left in the province. And Simon approached Beth-zur and fought against it for many days and shut them in. And they requested from him to receive his right hand, and he gave it to them. And he cast them out from there and took the city and placed a garrison there. And Jonathan and his camp moved to the waters of Gennesaret <note>The Sea of Galilee</note>, and before light they watched in the plain of Hazor. And behold, the camp of the foreigners met them in the plain, and they were stretching an ambush for him in the mountains. He himself, however, met them. But the ambush rose up from their places and attacked, and all those who were on Jonathan's side fled, and no one was left of them except Mattathias the son of Absalom and Judas the son of Chalphi, the leaders of the military of the army. And Jonathan rent his clothes and put earth upon his head and prayed. And he returned to them in battle and turned them into flight, and they fought. And those who were fleeing from his side saw it, and they returned to him and pursued with him as far as Hazor to their camp, and they were there. And there fell of the foreigners on that day three thousand men, and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.

And Jonathan saw that the time favored him, and he chose men and sent them to Rome to renew friendship. And to the Spartans and to other places he sent letters according to the same form. And they went to Rome and entered the senate-house and said: "Jonathan the high priest and the nation of the Jews have sent us that we might renew the friendship and alliance according to the former way." And they gave them letters for them through the places, that they might lead them into the land of Judah with peace. And this is the copy of the letters which Jonathan wrote to the Spartans: "Jonathan the high priest, and the elders of the nation, and the priests, and the rest of the people of the Jews, to the Spartans their brothers, greeting. Already long ago letters were sent to Onias the high priest from Arius, who was reigning among you, that you are our brothers, as the writing below contains. And Onias received the man who was sent with honor, and received the letters in which it was signified concerning alliance and friendship. And we, though we were in need of none of these things, having for comfort the holy books that are in our hands, preferred to send to you to renew the brotherhood and friendship, lest perhaps we should become strangers to you. For much time has passed since you sent to us. We therefore at all times without intermission, on the feast days and the other days when it is fitting, are mindful of you in the sacrifices which we offer and in our observances. As it is right and becoming to remember brothers. We rejoice therefore concerning your glory. But many tribulations and many battles have surrounded us, and the kings who are in the circuit have fought against us. We were unwilling therefore to be troublesome to you or to the rest of our allies and friends in any of these things. For we have had help from heaven, and we have been delivered, and our enemies have been humbled. We have chosen therefore Numenius the son of Antiochus and Antipater the son of Jason, and we have sent them to the Romans to renew with them the friendship and the former alliance. We have commanded them therefore that they come also to you and salute you, and deliver to you our letters concerning the renewal of our brotherhood. And now you will do well responding to us regarding these things."

And when Jonathan had heard that the commanders of Demetrius had returned with a much greater army than before, to fight against him, he went out from Jerusalem and met them in the region of Amathis; for he had not given them space to enter into his own region. And he sent scouts into their camp. And they returned and told him that they were preparing to come upon him by night. When the sun had set, however, Jonathan commanded his men to watch and to be in arms ready for battle the whole night, and he placed guards around the circuit of the camp. And the adversaries heard that Jonathan was ready with his men for war, and they feared and were terrified in their heart, and they lit fires in their camp <note>To hide their retreat</note>. Jonathan, however, and those who were with him did not know it until morning, for they saw the lights burning. And Jonathan pursued them and did not overtake them, for they had crossed the river Eleutherus. And Jonathan turned aside to the Arabs who are called Zabadeans, and he struck them and took their spoils. And he joined up and came to Damascus and traveled through all that region. Simon, however, went out and came as far as Ascalon and to the nearest garrisons, and he turned aside into Joppa and occupied it. For he had heard that they wished to hand over the garrison to the parties of Demetrius, and he placed guards there to keep it. And Jonathan returned and called together the elders of the people, and he thought with them to build fortifications in Judea, and to build walls in Jerusalem, and to raise a great mound in the middle of the citadel, and the city, so that he might separate it from the city, that it might be unique, and that they might neither sell nor buy. And the Jews gathered together.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Maccabean Revolt, specifically focusing on the transition of leadership from the captured Jonathan Apphus to his brother Simon Thassi. It details the treachery of the Seleucid general Tryphon, the diplomatic efforts with Rome and King Antiochus VII, and the construction of the famous family monument at Modein.</meta>

And he went to Joppa and cast out those who were in it. And he remained there to stay. And he went out from Gaza to King Antiochus: and he came to see if he might be seen. And when he lay down to fight under his own right. And seeing the matter... And they went out from each other: having an army. And when he was to meet him with forty thousand chosen men for battle. And he came to Beth-zur. And Tryphon <note>A Seleucid general and usurper</note> came because he came with the whole army in one appearance to extend his hand. And he saw him. And he received him with honor, and commended him to his friends: and gave him gifts. And he commanded his armies to obey him, just as himself. And he said to Jonathan:

"Why have you troubled all the people when there is no war for us? And now send them back to their homes. Choose for yourself a few men who may be with you: and come with me to Ptolemais <note>Ancient Acre</note>: and I will deliver it to you, and the rest of the strongholds and the army with all those who were in charge of affairs: and I will turn back and depart."

And he believed him: and did as he said: and dismissed the army. And they departed into the land of Judah. But he kept with him three thousand men, of whom he sent back two thousand into Galilee; but a thousand came with him. But as he entered Ptolemais, the people of Ptolemais shut the gates and seized him; and all who had come with him they killed with the sword. And Tryphon sent an army and horsemen into Galilee and into the great plain, to destroy all the associates of Jonathan. But they, when they knew that he was captured and that Jonathan and all who were with him had perished, encouraged each other: and went out prepared for war. And those who came to pursue them, seeing that it was a matter of life for them, turned back. But they came with peace into the land of Judah and they mourned Jonathan and those who had been with him greatly; and Israel mourned with great mourning. And all the nations that were in their circle sought to destroy them. For they said: "They have no prince or helper. Now therefore let us fight them and take away the memory of them from men."

**S**imon went out and gathered an army: and met Tryphon in the great plain. And those who came to pursue them, seeing that it was a matter of life for them, returned to Judea to Jerusalem. And he gathered the people and exhorted them, saying: "You know how much I and my brothers and the house of my father have done for the laws and for the holy things, and the distresses we have seen. Because of these things all my brothers have perished for the sake of Israel, and I alone am left. And now, may it not happen to me to spare my life in any time of tribulation. For I am not better than my brothers. I will see to the vengeance of my nation and the sanctuary, and of our wives: because all the nations are gathered together to crush us for the sake of enmity."

And the spirit of the people was kindled as soon as they heard these words: and they answered with a loud voice, saying: "You are our leader in the place of Judas and Jonathan your brother. Fight our battle, and whatever you say to us, we will do." And he gathered all the fighting men: and hastened to finish all the walls of Jerusalem: and fortified it all around. And he sent Jonathan the son of Absalom and with him a new army into Joppa. And having cast out those who were in it, he himself remained there. And Tryphon moved from Ptolemais with a great army to come into the land of Judah: and Jonathan was with him in custody. Simon, however, encamped in Adida against the face of the plain. And Tryphon knew that Simon had risen in the place of Jonathan his brother; and because he was about to join battle with him, he sent legates to him, saying: "For the silver which Jonathan your brother owed to the king's account for his affairs, we have detained him. And now send a hundred talents of silver, and his two sons as hostages, so that being dismissed he may not flee from us: and we will release him."

And Simon knew that he spoke with deceit to him; nevertheless, he ordered the silver and the boys to be given, lest he should take great enmity toward the people of Israel, who might say: "Because he did not send the silver and the boys, therefore Jonathan perished." And he sent the talents and the boys; and [Tryphon] lied, and did not release Jonathan. And after this Tryphon came to enter the region to crush it, and they circled by the way that leads to Adora. And Simon and his camp marched in every place wherever they went. But those who were in the fortress sent legates to Tryphon, that he should hasten to come through the desert and send them food. And Tryphon prepared all his cavalry to come that night. But there was very much snow, and he did not come into Gilead. And when he approached Bascama, he killed Jonathan and his sons there. And Tryphon turned back and went into his own land.

And Simon sent and took the bones of Jonathan his brother: and buried him in Modein, in the city of his fathers. And all Israel mourned him with great mourning, and lamented him for many days. And Simon built over the tomb of his father and his brothers a building high to the sight, with polished stone behind and before. And he set up seven pyramids, one against another, for his father and mother and four brothers. And he placed large columns around them, and upon the columns armor for an eternal memory, and next to the armor carved ships, which might be seen by all who sail the sea. This is the tomb which he made in Modein, even to this day.

But Tryphon, while he was making a journey with the young King Antiochus, killed him by deceit and reigned in his place, and placed upon himself the crown of Asia, and caused a great plague in the land. And Simon built the fortresses of Judea, fortifying them with high towers and great walls, and gates and bars, and placed food in the strongholds. And Simon chose men and sent to King Antiochus, that he should grant a remission to the region, because all the acts of Tryphon had been done for destruction. And King Antiochus wrote back to him thus, and wrote such a letter:

<margin>IIS</margin>
**K**ing Antiochus to Simon the high priest and to the friends of the king and to the nation of the Jews, greetings. Since certain pestilent men have obtained the kingdom of my fathers, I wish to reclaim the kingdom and restore it as it was before. And I have made a selection of a great army, and made ships of war. I wish to pass through the regions to take vengeance on those who have corrupted our region and who have desolated many cities in my kingdom. Now therefore I confirm to you all the offerings which the kings before me released to you, and whatever other gifts they released to you. And I have permitted you to make a minting of your own coinage in your region. Jerusalem and the holy things shall be free; and all the weapons you have made, and the fortresses you have built and which you hold, let them remain to you. And every debt of the king, and the things that shall be the king's from this time and for all time, are remitted to you. When we have obtained our kingdom, we will glorify you and your nation and the temple with great glory, so that your glory may be manifested in all the earth.

In the one hundred and seventy-fourth year <note>Approximately 138 BCE</note>, Antiochus went out into the land of his fathers, and all the armies gathered to him, so that few were left with Tryphon. And King Antiochus pursued him, and he came to Dora fleeing, which is by the sea. For he knew that evils were gathered against him, and the army had left him. And Antiochus encamped at Dora with a hundred and twenty thousand men of war and eight thousand horsemen. And he surrounded the city, and the ships approached from the sea; and he harassed the city from land and sea, and allowed no one to enter or go out.

In these days Numenius and those who were with him came from the city of Rome, having letters written to kings and regions, in which these things were contained: "Lucius, consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy, greetings. The legates of the Jews have come to us, our friends, renewing the ancient friendship and society, sent by Simon the prince of the priests and the people of the Jews. They also brought a golden shield of a thousand pounds. It pleased us therefore to write to kings and regions, that they should not bring evils upon them, nor fight them and their cities and their region, nor bring help to those fighting them. It seemed good to us to receive the shield from them. If any pestilent men have fled from their region to you, deliver them to Simon the prince of the priests, that he may take vengeance on them according to his law." These same things he wrote to King Demetrius and to Attalus, and to Ariarathes and Arsaces, and to all regions: and to Lampsacus, and to the Spartans, and to Delos, and to Myndus, and to Sicyon, and to Caria, and to Samos, and Pamphylia, and Lycia, and Halicarnassus, and to Rhodes, and Phaselis, and to Cos, and to Side, and to Aradus, and Gortyna, and in Cyprus, and Cyrene. A copy of these they wrote to Simon the prince of the priests.

But King Antiochus encamped at Dora for the second time, always moving his hands against it and making machines. And he shut in Tryphon, lest he should go out. And Simon sent him two thousand chosen men for help, and silver and gold, and many vessels. And he would not receive them, but broke all things which he had agreed with him before, and alienated himself from him. And he sent Athenobius, one of his friends, to him, to meet him, saying: "You hold Joppa and Gazara, and the fortress which is in Jerusalem, which are cities of my kingdom. You have desolated their borders and made a great plague in the land, and have ruled through many places in my kingdom. Now therefore deliver the cities which you have occupied, and the tributes of the places in which you have ruled outside the borders of Judea. Otherwise, give for them five hundred talents of silver; and for the extermination you have made, and for the tributes of the cities, another five hundred talents. Otherwise, we will come and fight you."

And Athenobius, the friend of the king, came to Jerusalem and saw the glory of Simon and his splendor in gold and silver, and much apparatus, and he was amazed; and he reported the words of the king. And Simon answered him and said to him: "We have neither taken foreign land, nor do we hold the property of others, but the inheritance of our fathers <note>original: "hereditatem patrum nostrorum"</note>, which was possessed by our enemies for a time without justice. We, having the opportunity, claim the inheritance of our fathers. For concerning Joppa and Gazara which you demand, they themselves caused a great plague among the people and in our region. For these we give a hundred talents." And Athenobius did not answer him a word. Returning with anger to the king, he reported these words to him, and the glory of Simon, and all that he saw. And the king was angry with great wrath. Cendebeus, the commander of the maritime coast, moved the army to Dora and proceeded to Judea, and built up Kedron and fortified it with gates and walls: and began to irritate the people, and to trample Judea, and to capture the people and kill them. And he built Kedron and placed horsemen and an army there, so that going out they might patrol the way of Judea, as the king appointed him.

**A**nd King Antiochus, son of Demetrius, sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon the priest and prince of the Jewish nation, and to the whole nation; and they were contained in this manner: "King Antiochus to Simon the great priest and to the nation of the Jews, greetings. I have made a choice of a multitude of an army, and made ships of war. I wish to proceed through the regions, to take vengeance on those who have corrupted our region and who have desolated many cities in the king..."
