<margin>Athenobius</margin> But against them, he had hardly applied the camp in Dora, but they moved out always with hands and machines being made. And he shut in Tryphon lest he should escape: and Simon sent him two thousand chosen men as an aid: and silver and gold: and many vessels. And he refused to receive them, but broke all that he had covenanted with him before, and alienated himself from him. And he sent to him Athenobius, one of his friends, to treat with him, saying: "You hold Joppa and Gazara, and the fortress that is in Jerusalem—cities of my kingdom. You have desolated their borders and made a great plague upon the land, and you have dominated many places in my kingdom. Now therefore, hand over the cities which you have occupied, and the tributes of the places in which you have dominated outside the borders of Judea. Otherwise, give for them five hundred talents of silver: and for the extermination of the dominions and the tribute of the cities, another five hundred talents: it should be held likely that you be sent." And Athenobius, the friend of the king, came into Jerusalem, and he saw the glory of Simon and the display of gold and silver, and the abundant equipment: and he was astonished. And he reported the words of the king. And Simon answered and said to him: "We have neither taken foreign land, nor do we hold the property of others: but the inheritance of our fathers, which was unjustly possessed for some time by our enemies. We, however, having the opportunity, are reclaiming the inheritance of our fathers. For concerning Joppa and Gazara, which you demand, they themselves caused much plague among the people and in our region: for these we give a hundred talents." And he did not answer him a word. But returning with wrath to the king, he reported these words to him, and the glory of Simon, and all that he saw. And the king was exceedingly angry. But Tryphon fled in a ship to Orthosia. And the king appointed Cendebeus as commander of the maritime coast, and gave him an army of horsemen and footmen: and he commanded him to move the camp against the face of Judea. And he commanded him to rebuild Kedron, and to block the gates of the city, and to war against the people. But the king pursued Tryphon. And Cendebeus reached Jamnia, and began to provoke the common people, and to trample Judea, and to take the people captive, and to rebuild Kedron. And he stationed horsemen and an army there, so that going out, they might patrol the roads of Judea just as the king had appointed for him.

<margin>John</margin> Then John <note>John Hyrcanus, Simon's son</note> went up from Gazara and reported to Simon his father what Cendebeus had done among their people. And Simon called his two elder sons, Judas and John, and said to them: "I and my brothers and the house of my father have fought the enemies of Israel from our youth until this day, and it has prospered in our hands to deliver Israel several times. But now I am old; you be in my place and the place of my brother, and go out and fight for our nation. And may the help from heaven be with you." And he chose from the region twenty thousand warlike men and horsemen, and they set out toward Cendebeus, and slept in Modein. And they rose in the morning and went into the plain. And behold, a copious army met them, of footmen and horsemen, and there was a rushing stream between them.

<margin>Kedron</margin> <margin>Azotus</margin> And he moved the camp against their face, he and his people. And he saw the people trembling to cross the stream, and he crossed first: and the men saw him and crossed after him. And he divided the people in the midst of the horsemen. But the cavalry of the adversaries was exceedingly numerous. And they shouted with the sacred trumpets, and Cendebeus and his army were turned to flight, and many of them fell wounded; but the rest entered into flight. Then Judas and John were wounded; but John pursued them until he came to Kedron, which he had built. And they fled as far as the towers that were in the field of Azotus, and he burned them with fire. And two thousand of their men fell, and he returned into Judea in peace.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin> And Ptolemy the son of Abubus was appointed commander in the plain of Jericho, and he had much silver and gold. For he was the son-in-law of the high priest. And his heart was exalted, and he wished to obtain the region, and he plotted deceit against Simon and his sons to remove them. Now Simon, traveling through the cities that were in the region of Judea and taking care of them, went down into Jericho, he and Mattathias his son, and Judas. In the year one hundred and seventy-seven, in the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat. And the son of Abubus received them into a little fortress called Dok <note>original: "doch"</note> with deceit, which he had built. And he made a great feast for them, and hid men there. And when Simon and his sons were drunk, Ptolemy rose with his men, and they took their weapons and entered the great feast, and they killed him and his two sons, and certain of his servants. And he committed a great betrayal in Israel, and returned evil for good. And Ptolemy wrote these things and sent to the king, that he might send him an army for help and hand over the region and their cities to him. And he sent others to Gazara to kill John: and to the tribunes he sent letters to come to him so that he might give them silver and gold and many gifts. And others he sent to occupy Jerusalem and the mountain of the temple. And a certain man running, reported to John in Gazara that his father and his brothers had perished, and that he has sent people to kill you also. But when he heard it, he was vehemently terrified, and he seized the men who had come to destroy him, and killed them. For he knew that they were seeking to destroy him. The rest of the words of John and of his wars and the virtues by which he acted bravely, and the building of the walls which he constructed, and his deeds—these are written in the book of the days of his priesthood, from the time he was made high priest after his father.

<margin>The Letter.</margin> To the brethren who are Jews everywhere, greetings namely, and good peace. May God do good to you, and remember his covenant, which he spoke to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, his faithful servants. And may he give to all of you a heart so that you may worship him and do his will with a great heart and a willing mind. May he open your heart in his law and in his precepts, and make peace. May the Lord hear your prayers and be reconciled to you, and not desert you in the evil time. And now we are here praying for you. While Demetrius was reigning, in the year one hundred and sixty-nine. We Jews wrote to you in the tribulation and the attack which came upon us in those years since Jason withdrew from the holy land and the kingdom. They burned the gate and shed innocent blood. And we prayed to the Lord and were heard, and we offered sacrifice and fine flour, and we lit the lamps and set out the loaves. And now celebrate the days of the Feast of Booths <note>This refers to Hanukkah, often called the "Sukkot of the month of Kislev" in early traditions.</note> in the month of Kislev.

<margin>Another Letter.</margin> In the year one hundred and eighty-eight. The people who are in Jerusalem and in Judea, and the senate, and Judas, to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the race of the anointed priests, and to those Jews who are in Egypt, greeting and health. Delivered from great perils by God, we give him magnificent thanks, as those who have fought against such a king. For he himself made those who fought against us and the holy city to boil out from Persia. For when the leader himself was in Persia, and with him an immeasurable army, he fell in the temple of Nanea <note>A Persian/Mesopotamian goddess often identified with Artemis or Aphrodite</note>: deceived by the counsel of the priests of Nanea. For Antiochus and his friends had come to dwell with her, as if to receive much money by way of a dowry. And when the priests of Nanea had set it out, and he with a few had entered within the enclosure of the temple, they closed the temple when Antiochus had entered; and opening a hidden entrance of the temple, throwing stones, they struck the leaders and divided their limbs, and decapitating them, they threw their severed heads outside. Blessed be God through all things, who handed over the impious.

<margin>Nehemiah</margin> Therefore, as we are about to celebrate the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Kislev, we thought it necessary to signify to you: that you also may keep the day of the Feast of Booths, and the day of the fire which was given when Nehemiah, having built the temple and the altar, offered sacrifices. For also when our fathers were being led into Persia, the priests who were then worshippers of God, having taken the fire from the altar, secretly hid it in a valley where there was a deep and dry pit: and in it they preserved it, so that the place was unknown to everyone. But when many years had passed, and it pleased God that Nehemiah should be sent from the king of the Persians: those priests, whose [descendants] he made descend to seek the fire—and as they told us, they did not find fire but thick water. And he ordered them to draw it and bring it to him. And the priest Nehemiah ordered the sacrifices which had been placed [on the altar] to be sprinkled with that water, and the wood which had been placed over them. And this was done. And the time came when the sun shone forth, which before was in a cloud. A great fire was kindled, so that all wondered. Moreover, all the priests made a prayer while the sacrifice was being consumed: Jonathan leading the beginning, with the rest responding; and the others had their prayer in this manner:

<margin>Prayer</margin> > O Lord, Lord God, creator of all, terrible and strong, just and merciful, who alone are good and king, and alone excellent; alone just and almighty and eternal, who deliver Israel from every evil, who made the fathers chosen and sanctified them. Receive the sacrifice for your whole people Israel, and guard your portion and sanctify it. Gather our dispersion, and deliver those who serve the nations, and look upon the despised and the abominable: so that the nations may know that you are our God. Afflict those who oppress us and act with insult in pride. Establish your people in your holy place, just as Moses said.

And the priests sang hymns until the sacrifice was consumed. With the remaining water, Nehemiah ordered the larger stones to be drenched. When that was done, a flame was kindled from them: but it was consumed by the light that shone from the altar. But when the matter was made manifest, and it was reported to the king of the Persians that in the place where the priests who had been deported had hidden the fire, water appeared, from which Nehemiah and those who were with him purified the sacrifices. Moreover, the king considered, and examining the matter diligently, he made a temple [at the site]. And if any were given [the water], they received many good things; he took from it and distributed it. Moreover, Nehemiah called this place "Nephthar," which is interpreted as "purification." But it is called "Nephi" by many.

If those things which were gathered by the priests for the congregation of the people were true. And from now on he showed much—that is, it appeared—concerning the evil-doing of the Lord, and it had been shown to many, he made a show of this as when Solomon prayed that the place might be made holy for the Great God; he manifested this, which is wisdom, and he led out the passing of the holy ones and fulfilled the completion. <note>This section refers to the legendary accounts of the Temple fire and Nehemiah's library mentioned in the introductory letters of 2 Maccabees.</note> As the masters of the laws were saying—that is, to defend the rights of the needy—and the ancient offering of the holy. For what Moses commanded was reported: that it was for sin, and it was consumed in like manner; and Solomon celebrated the dedication for eight days. They also included these same things in the descriptions and memoirs of Nehemiah. And how he established a library and gathered books from the regions, and those of the prophets, and of David, and the letters of the kings, and concerning votive offerings. Similarly, Judas <note>Judas Maccabeus</note> also gathered all those things which had been lost through the war that happened to us, and they are with us. If, therefore, you have need of these, send those who will bring them to you. And so, we are about to perform the purification; you will do well if you keep these days. But God, who delivered his people and restored the inheritance to all, and the kingdom, and the priesthood, and the sanctuary—as he promised in the law—we hope that he will soon have mercy on us and gather us from under the whole heaven into the holy place. For he has rescued us from great perils and has cleansed the place. Now, concerning Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, and the purification of the great temple, and the dedication of the altar, and also the wars which were fought against Antiochus the Illustrious and his son Eupator, and the visions that came from heaven to those who acted bravely for the Jews, so that they vindicated the whole region, though they were few, and put to flight the barbarian multitude, and recovered the temple famous throughout the whole world, and liberated the city, and restored the laws that were to be abolished, the Lord being gracious to them with all tranquility. These things, which were comprised in five books by Jason of Cyrene, we have attempted to summarize in one volume. For considering the multitude of books and the difficulty for those wishing to enter into historical narratives because of the mass of matters, we have provided help for those who wish to read for the sake of mental delight, and for the studious so that they might more easily commit things to memory, and that utility might be conferred upon all readers. And indeed, for ourselves who have taken up this work for the sake of abbreviating it, we have assumed no easy labor, but rather a business full of late nights and sweat. Just as those who prepare a banquet and seek to please the will of others, we willingly undergo the labor for the sake of the many. Entrusting the truth of details to the original author, we ourselves study to follow the given form of abbreviating. For just as the architect of a new house must care for the entire structure, but he who paints and adorns the upper parts must seek out what is necessary, so it must be judged for us. To collect the contents and order the discourse and carefully prepare each point is the duty of the author of a history. But to follow brevity of speech and to pursue the execution of the matters is to be granted to the abridger. Here, therefore, let us begin the narrative; let it suffice to have said this much of the preface. For it is foolish to overflow with words before the history begins, but then be brief in the history itself.

When, therefore, the holy city was inhabited in all peace, and the laws were still very well kept because of the piety of Onias the high priest and his mind hating evil, it happened that even the kings and princes held the place worthy of the highest honor and illustrated the temple with the greatest gifts, so that Seleucus, king of Asia, provided from his own revenues all the expenses pertaining to the service of the sacrifices. But Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, having been appointed overseer of the temple, contended against the high priest to bring about something unjust in the city. And when he could not overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius, the son of Tharseas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, and told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of innumerable sums of money, and that the common riches were immense, which did not belong to the account of the sacrifices, and that it was possible for all these things to fall under the power of the king. And when Apollonius had come to the king, he told him of the reported money. The king, having called Heliodorus, who was over his affairs, sent him with commands to transport the aforesaid money. And immediately Heliodorus set out on the journey, in appearance as if he were to pass through the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but in truth to fulfill the king's purpose. But when he had come to Jerusalem and had been kindly received in the city by the high priest, he told of the information given about the money and revealed the cause for which he was present, and he asked if these things were truly so. Then the high priest showed that these were deposits for the livelihood of widows and orphans, and that some belonged to Hyrcanus, son of Tobias, a very noble man, unlike what the impious Simon had reported; and that in all there were four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. He said it was utterly impossible to deceive those who had trusted in the place and the temple, which is honored throughout the whole world for its veneration and holiness. But Heliodorus, because of the commands he had from the king, said that in any case the money must be brought to the king's treasury. A day being appointed, Heliodorus entered to arrange the matter, and there was no small trepidation throughout the whole city. The priests cast themselves before the altar in their priestly vestments, and with tears they called upon him from heaven who had made the law concerning deposits, that he might keep them safe for those who had deposited them. Now, whoever saw the face of the high priest was wounded in mind; for his countenance and changed color declared the inner grief of his mind. For a certain sadness was poured over him, and a horror of the body, through which the grief of his heart was manifest to those who saw him. Others also rushed out of their houses in crowds, joining in public supplication because the place was about to come into contempt. Women, girded with sackcloth under their breasts, flocked through the streets; and the virgins who were shut up ran out to Onias, others to the walls, and some looked out of the windows. All of them, stretching out their hands to heaven, made supplication. And indeed, the combined sorrow of the whole multitude and the expectation of the great high priest in his great agony was piteous.

But they called upon the Almighty Lord that the things committed to them might be preserved with all integrity for those who had committed them. Heliodorus, however, executed what was decreed, and he was present with his guards at that place near the treasury. But the spirit of the Almighty God made a great evidence of his manifestation, so that all who had dared to obey him, falling down by the power of God, were dissolved in reason and turned to fear. For there appeared to them a certain horseman having a terrible rider, adorned with the best ornaments; and with an onset he struck Heliodorus with his forefeet, and he who sat upon the horse seemed to have golden armor. And two other young men also appeared, great in strength, beautiful in glory, and beautiful in dress, who stood by him on either side and scourged him without ceasing, inflicting many wounds. Suddenly Heliodorus fell to the ground, and they snatched him up, consumed by much darkness, and having put him in a litter, they cast him out. And he, who with many followers and guards had entered the aforesaid treasury, was carried out, with no one able to bring him help, the power of God being clearly recognized. And he indeed lay speechless by divine power, and deprived of all hope and safety. But they blessed the Lord because he had magnified his place; and the temple, which a little before was full of fear and tumult, was filled with joy and gladness when the Almighty Lord appeared. Then indeed some of the friends of Heliodorus immediately begged Onias to call upon the Most High to grant life to him who was at his last gasp. The high priest, considering lest the king might suspect some malice had been done by the Jews against Heliodorus, offered a saving sacrifice for the man's health. And when the high priest was praying, the same young men, clothed in the same vestments, stood by Heliodorus and said: "Give thanks to Onias the priest, for for his sake the Lord has granted you life. And you, having been scourged by God, announce to all the great works of God and his power." And having said these things, they disappeared. Heliodorus, however, having offered a sacrifice to God and promised great vows to him who had granted him life, and having given thanks to Onias, took his army and returned to the king. And he testified to all the works of the Great God which he had seen with his own eyes. When the king asked Heliodorus who might be a fit man to be sent once more to Jerusalem, he said: "If you have any enemy or a traitor to your kingdom, send him there, and you shall receive him back scourged, if indeed he escapes; because in that place there is truly a certain power of God. For he who has his dwelling in heaven is the visitor and protector of that place, and those who come to do evil he strikes and destroys." Therefore, the matter of Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury stands thus.

<column-break/>

But Simon, the aforementioned informer concerning the money and his country, spoke ill of Onias, as if Onias himself had instigated Heliodorus and had been the inciter of evils; and he dared to call the provider for the city and the defender of his nation and the emulator of the law of God a traitor to the kingdom. But when the enmities proceeded so far that through some of Simon's associates murders were committed, Onias, considering the danger of the contention and that Apollonius, the son of Menestheus, the governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was raging to increase Simon's malice, went to the king. Not as an accuser of the citizens, but considering the common utility of the whole multitude within himself. For he saw that without royal providence it was impossible for peace to be given to affairs, and that Simon could not cease from his folly.

But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, who was called the Illustrious <note>Original: "Epiphanes"</note>, took the kingdom, Jason, the brother of Onias, ambitiously sought the high priesthood, promising the king three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from other revenues. Besides this, he promised another hundred and fifty if it were granted to his power to establish a gymnasium and a place for youth <note>Original: "ephebiam"</note>, and to enroll those who were in Jerusalem as "Antiochians." When the king had granted this and he had obtained the principality, he immediately began to transfer his countrymen to the Greek custom. And having set aside those things which had been granted to the Jews by the kings out of humanity, through John the father of that Eupolemus who had gone on an embassy to the Romans for friendship and alliance, he destroyed the lawful rights of the citizens and established perverse institutions. For he dared to establish a gymnasium under the very citadel and to place the best of the youths in brothels. This was not the beginning, but a certain increase and progress of Greek and foreign conversation, because of the nefarious and unheard-of wickedness of the impious Jason, no priest. So much so that the priests were no longer intent on the service of the altar, but despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened to participate in the spectacle of the wrestling ground and its unjust distributions, and in the exercise of the discus. And holding the honors of their fathers as nothing, they thought the Greek glories to be the best. For the sake of these things, a dangerous contention came upon them, and they followed the customs of those whose enemies they had been, and they desired to be like them in all things. For to act impiously against the divine laws does not pass without punishment, as the following time will declare.

When the quinquennial games were being celebrated at Tyre, and the king was present, the wicked Jason sent from Jerusalem men to carry three hundred drachmas of silver for the sacrifice of Hercules. But those who carried them asked that they should not be spent on a sacrifice, as was not fitting, but should be devoted to other expenses. These things were indeed offered by him who sent them for the sacrifice of Hercules, but on account of those present, they were given for the building of triremes <note>warships with three banks of oars</note>. Now Apollonius, the son of Menestheus, was sent into Egypt on account of the enthronement of King Ptolemy Philometor. When Antiochus knew that he was made a stranger to the affairs of the kingdom, he provided for his own utility, and setting out from there, he came to Joppa and then to Jerusalem. And being magnificently received by Jason and the city, he entered with torchlights and praises; and from there he turned his army into Phoenicia.

And after a period of three years, Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the aforementioned Simon, to carry money to the king and to bring back answers concerning necessary business. But he, having been commended to the king, when he had magnified the appearance of his power, took the priesthood for himself by outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver. Having received the king's mandates, he came, having nothing indeed worthy of the priesthood, but having the mind of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a wild beast. And Jason indeed, who had supplanted his own brother, was himself deceived and fled into the country of the Ammonites. Menelaus, however, obtained the principality, but concerning the money promised to the king, he did nothing, though Sostratus, who was over the city, made a demand for it; for to him belonged the collection of the revenues. For which cause both were called to the king. Menelaus was removed from the priesthood, and his brother Lysimachus was substituted; and Sostratus was made governor of Cyprus.

But while these things were being done, it happened that the people of Tarsus and Mallus moved a sedition because they had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king's concubine. Therefore the king went in haste to appease them, leaving Andronicus, a man of high rank, as his deputy. Then Menelaus, thinking he had found an opportune time, having stolen some golden vessels of the temple, gave them to Andronicus, and others he sold at Tyre and in the neighboring cities. When Onias knew this for certain, he rebuked him, keeping himself in a safe place at Antioch near Daphne. Whereupon Menelaus, coming to Andronicus, begged him to kill Onias. And when he had come to Onias and had given him his right hand with an oath—though he was suspected—he persuaded him to come out of the sanctuary, and immediately he slew him, not fearing justice. For which cause not only the Jews, but also other nations, were indignant and took it heavily for the unjust death of so great a man. But when the king returned from the places of Cilicia, the Jews of the city, and the Greeks likewise, went to him, complaining of the unjust death of Onias. Antiochus, therefore, was struck with grief in his mind, and being moved to mercy, he shed tears, remembering the sobriety and modesty of the deceased. And being kindled in mind, he commanded that Andronicus be stripped of his purple and led through all the city, and in the same place where he had committed the impiety against Onias, the sacrilegious man was killed, the Lord rendering to him a worthy punishment.

But when the rumor was multiplied throughout the city of the sacrileges committed by Lysimachus by the counsel of Menelaus, and the multitude was gathered against Lysimachus—for much gold had already been carried away—the crowds rising up and filled with anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began to use unjust violence, under a certain leader, a tyrant equal in age and madness. But when they perceived the attempt of Lysimachus, some snatched up stones, others strong clubs, and some began to throw ashes at Lysimachus. And many indeed were wounded, and some were struck down; but all of them they drove to flight, and the sacrilegious man himself they killed near the treasury. Concerning these things, a judgment began to be agitated against Menelaus. When the king came to Tyre, three men sent from the elders pleaded the cause before him. **T**herefore, Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy Macron, a high-ranking official who eventually supported the Jews but here acts as a corrupt intermediary.</note>, for the sake of cooling the king's anger, approached him and drew him away from his intended judgment. He acquitted Menelaus, who was the author of all the wickedness, of the charges against him. However, he condemned to death the wretched men <note>Deputies from the Jewish Council (Gerousia) who had come to accuse Menelaus of stealing Temple vessels.</note> who, even if they had pleaded their case before barbarians, would have been judged innocent. Those who had pleaded for their city, their people, and the sacred vessels quickly suffered this unjust penalty. For this reason, even the citizens of Tyre, being indignant at such cruelty, were most liberal in providing for their burial. But Menelaus, because of the greed of those in power, remained in office, growing in malice and plotting against his own citizens.

**A**t the same time, Antiochus prepared his second expedition into Egypt. It then happened that throughout the entire city of Jerusalem, for forty days, there were seen horsemen galloping through the air, wearing robes of gold and armed with spears like companies of soldiers. One could see the ranks of horses in motion, hand-to-hand combat, the clashing of shields, a multitude of helmets, drawn swords, the casting of missiles, the flash of golden armor, and every kind of breastplate. Because of this, everyone prayed that these omens might turn out for good. But when a false rumor spread that Antiochus had died, Jason <note>The Hellenizing former High Priest who had been ousted by Menelaus.</note> took no fewer than a thousand men and suddenly attacked the city. As the people fled to the walls and the city was finally taken, Menelaus fled to the citadel. Jason, however, did not spare his fellow citizens in the slaughter; he did not realize that success against one's own kinsmen is the greatest of misfortunes, thinking instead that he was taking trophies from enemies rather than from his own people. Yet, he did not obtain the high priesthood; he ended his conspiracy in confusion and fled again into the land of the Ammonites. At the last, he was hemmed in by Aretas, the tyrant of the Arabs, and fled from city to city. Hated by all as a fugitive from the laws and abominable as an enemy of his country and citizens, he was finally cast out into Egypt. He, who had driven many from their own country, perished in exile among the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans; Jason hoped for refuge there because of a legendary (but unlikely) shared ancestry between Spartans and Jews.</note>, thinking he would find refuge there due to their kinship. And he who had left many unburied was himself cast out unlamented and unburied, neither honored with a foreign funeral nor participating in the tomb of his fathers.

**W**hen these events were reported, the king suspected that all Judea was about to desert him. Therefore, departing from Egypt with a mind enraged like a wild beast, he took the city by force of arms. He commanded his soldiers to kill and not spare any they met, and to go up into the houses to slay. There was a slaughter of young and old, the destruction of women and children, and the killing of virgins and infants. In three days, eighty thousand were slain, forty thousand were imprisoned, and no fewer were sold into slavery. But this was not enough for him. He even dared to enter the Temple, the holiest in all the world, with Menelaus as his guide—the man who was the betrayer of the laws and his country. Taking the holy vessels in his wicked hands, which had been placed there by other kings and cities for the decoration and glory of the place, he handled them unworthily and polluted them. Antiochus, alienated in his mind, did not consider that the Lord was angry for a little while because of the sins of the inhabitants of the city, which is why this neglect happened to the Holy Place. Otherwise, had they not been involved in many sins—just as happened to Heliodorus <note>The Syrian official sent to rob the Temple in a previous chapter, who was stopped by a divine apparition.</note>, who was sent by King Seleucus to plunder the treasury—this man too, as soon as he arrived, would have been scourged and repulsed. But God did not choose the people for the sake of the place, but rather the place for the sake of the people. Therefore, the place itself became a partaker in the people's misfortunes, but afterward, it will be a partner in their blessings. That which was abandoned in the wrath of the Almighty shall be exalted again with great glory when the Great Lord is reconciled.

**T**herefore, Antiochus, having carried off one thousand eight hundred talents from the Temple, quickly departed for Antioch. In his pride, he thought he could make the land navigable and the sea passable by foot, such was the elation of his mind and heart. To afflict the people, he left governors: at Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian by birth and more cruel in character than the one who appointed him; at Mount Gerizim <note>The site of the Samaritan temple.</note>, Andronicus and Menelaus, who oppressed the citizens more grievously than the others. And as he was set against the Jews, he sent the hateful prince Apollonius with an army of twenty-two thousand, commanding him to kill all men of full age and to sell the women and younger ones. When he arrived at Jerusalem, pretending peace, he waited until the Sabbath day. Then, while the Jews were keeping the holy day, he commanded his men to take up arms. He massacred all who had come out to the spectacle and, running through the city with armed men, he destroyed a vast multitude.

**B**ut Judas Maccabeus, who was the tenth <note>Meaning he was one of ten leaders or was the tenth man in his initial band.</note>, had retreated into a desert place. There he lived with his followers among the wild beasts in the mountains, and they ate only herbs <note>original: "feni cibi" - literally 'hay-food,' referring to wild vegetation.</note> so that they might not participate in the ritual pollution.

**B**ut not long after, the king sent an elderly man from Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers and of God; and also to contaminate the Temple in Jerusalem and name it after Jupiter Olympus, and likewise the temple in Gerizim after Jupiter the Hospitable, as those who inhabited the place had requested. This incursion of evils was most bitter and grievous for everyone. For the Temple was full of luxury and gluttony, and men dallied with harlots; women entered the sacred buildings and brought in things that were forbidden. The altar was full of illicit things prohibited by the law. Neither were the Sabbaths kept, nor the ancient solemn days observed, nor did anyone simply confess himself to be a Jew. They were led by bitter necessity to the sacrifices on the king’s birthday; and when the festival of Dionysus <note>The Greek god of wine (Bacchus).</note> was celebrated, they were compelled to walk in procession wearing crowns of ivy. A decree went out to the neighboring Greek cities, at the suggestion of the Ptolemies, that they should act in the same way against the Jews, forcing them to sacrifice; and that those who refused to adopt the customs of the Gentiles should be killed. One could see the misery. For two women were accused of having circumcised their children; these were led publicly through the city with their infants hanging at their breasts and then cast down headlong from the walls. Others had gathered in nearby caves to celebrate the Sabbath day in secret; when they were betrayed to Philip, they were burned with fire, because they hesitated to help themselves for the sake of religion and their observance of the day. Now I beseech those who shall read this book not to be discouraged by these adverse events, but to consider that these things happened not for the destruction but for the correction of our race. Indeed, it is a sign of great benefit when sinners are not allowed to go on in their own way for a long time, but are immediately met with retribution. For the Lord does not wait patiently as he does with other nations, to punish them in the fullness of their sins when the day of judgment comes. He has dealt thus with us so that, our sins not having reached their limit, He might not take vengeance on us at the end. For this reason, He never removes His mercy from us; **C**orrecting us with adversity or through tribulation, He does not forsake His people. But let these few words be said for the admonition of the readers; now we must come to the narrative.

he did, and may he establish the same wisdom for them. He replied <note>Eleazar the scribe, who is refusing to eat forbidden pig meat.</note> that he would rather be sent to the grave prematurely and without honor than come to old age through such deceit; for he would not have the youth think that Eleazar, at ninety years old, had crossed over to the customs of the heathens. It would be unworthy of my years, he said, if for the sake of a brief and corruptible span of life I should occupy this body and thus bring a stain and a disgrace upon my old age. For even if I am delivered from the punishments of men in the present time, I shall not escape the hand of the Almighty, whether living or dead. Therefore, by bravely departing this life, I shall show myself worthy of my old age. And I shall leave a noble example to the young if, with a ready and constant mind, I suffer an honorable death for the sake of our venerable and most holy laws. Having said these things, he was immediately dragged to the torture. Those who led him, who shortly before had been mild, were turned into rage because of the words he had spoken, which they considered to be said out of arrogance. But when he was being crushed by the blows, he groaned and said: "Lord, you who have the holy knowledge, you clearly know that although I could be delivered from death, I endure grievous pains of the body; but in my soul, I am glad to suffer these things because of my fear of You." And so this man departed from life, leaving the memory of his death as an example of virtue and fortitude, not only to the young but to the whole nation.

**I**t also happened that seven brothers with their mother were seized and compelled by the king to eat swine's flesh against the law, being tortured with whips and scourges. But one of them, who was the first, said thus: "What do you seek, and what do you wish to learn from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of God and our fathers." The king, being angry, commanded frying pans and brazen pots to be heated. When they were heated, he commanded that the tongue of him who had spoken first be cut out; and having the skin of his head pulled off, they also cut off the extremities of his hands and feet while his other brothers and his mother looked on. And when he was now rendered useless in every part, he commanded him to be brought to the fire and to be fried in the pan while still breathing. While he was being tortured there for a long time, the others, together with their mother, encouraged one another to die bravely, saying: "The Lord God will look upon the truth and will have compassion on us, as Moses declared in his protestation song: 'and He will be comforted in His servants.'" When the first had died in this manner, they brought the next one to be mocked; and having pulled off the skin of his head with the hair, they asked him if he would eat before being punished in every single limb of his body. But he answered in his native language <note>Aramaic or Hebrew.</note>, saying: "I will not do it." Because of this, he also received the same cruel torment. And when he was at his last breath, he spoke thus: "You, most wicked man, destroy us in this present life, but the King of the world will raise us up, who die for His laws, in the resurrection of eternal life." After him, the third was mocked, and when his tongue was demanded, he quickly put it out and courageously stretched forth his hands, saying with confidence: "I received these from heaven, but for the sake of God's laws I despise them, because I hope to receive them back from Him." So much so that the king and those who were with him wondered at the young man's spirit, that he considered the tortures as nothing. When he was dead, they tormented the fourth in the same way; when he was near death, he spoke thus: "It is better, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God, to be raised up again by Him; but for you, there shall be no resurrection to life." When they brought the fifth, they tormented him. But he, looking at the king, said: "Having power among men, although you are corruptible, you do what you will. But do not think that our race is forsaken by God. Endure patiently, and you shall see His great power, how He will torment you and your seed." After him, they brought the sixth, and he, being ready to die, spoke thus: "Do not be deceived in vain. For we suffer these things for our own sakes, because we have sinned against our God; and things worthy of admiration have happened. But do not think that you will go unpunished, since you have begun to fight against God." But the mother was marvelous above measure and worthy of honorable memory; she saw her seven sons perish within the space of one day and bore it with a good courage because of the hope she had in God. She encouraged each of them in her native language, being filled with wisdom; and joining a man's heart to a woman's thought, she said to them: "I do not know how you appeared in my womb; for I did not give you spirit and soul and life, nor did I join together the limbs of each of you. But the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man and found out the beginning of all, will in His mercy give you back spirit and life again, as you now despise yourselves for the sake of His laws." Antiochus, thinking he was being despised and suspecting her voice was one of reproach—while the youngest was still alive—not only encouraged him with words but also affirmed with an oath that he would make him rich and happy and take him for a friend if he would turn from the laws of his fathers. But when the young man would not listen, the king called the mother and persuaded her to advise the youth for his own sake—poor woman. But after he had argued with her with many words, she promised she would persuade her son. So, leaning toward him and mocking the cruel tyrant, she said in her native language: "My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, and gave you milk and nursed you for three years, and brought you up to this age. I beseech you, look upon heaven and earth and all that is in them, and understand that God made them out of nothing, and the race of man likewise. So let it be that you do not fear this executioner, but being made worthy of your brothers, accept death, so that in that mercy I may receive you again with your brothers." While she was yet speaking, the young man said: "What are you waiting for? I do not obey the command of the king, but the command of the law which was given to us by Moses. But you, who have been the author of all the evils against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God. For we suffer these things for our sins. And though the Lord our God is angry with us for a little while for our rebuke and correction, He will be reconciled again to His servants. But you, O wicked and most flagitious of all men, do not be puffed up in vain with empty hopes, while you rage against His servants; for you have not yet escaped the judgment of God. For our brothers, having now sustained a brief pain, are under the covenant of eternal life. But you, by the judgment of God, shall pay the just penalty for your pride. I, like my brothers, give up my soul and body for the laws of my fathers, calling upon God to be quickly merciful to our nation, and that you, by torments and stripes, may confess that He alone is God. And may the wrath of the Almighty, which has been justly brought upon all our race, cease in me and my brothers." Then the king, being bitter with rage, raged against him more cruelly than against all the others, taking it ill that he was mocked. And so this one died holy, trusting in the Lord in all things. Last of all, after the sons, the mother also was consumed. Therefore, concerning the sacrifices of the Jews and the excessive cruelty, let this much be said.

Now when Maccabeus had gathered a multitude, he became invincible to the Gentiles; for the wrath of the Lord was turned into mercy. Coming upon castles and cities unawares, he burned them; and occupying strategic places, he inflicted no small slaughter on the enemies. He carried out these excursions mostly by night, and the fame of his valor was spread abroad everywhere. When Philip saw that the man gained ground by degrees and frequently...

<meta>This page marks a major transition in the manuscript. It concludes the prefatory material and shifts into a Latin translation of Flavius Josephus’s "Antiquities of the Jews," Book 1. Josephus was a first-century Romano-Jewish historian, and this text serves as his retelling of the Biblical Book of Genesis for a Greco-Roman audience. The text moves from a philosophical defense of Moses as a lawgiver directly into the Seven Days of Creation.</meta>

...to those returning: so that they may have a most happy life. And so that they do not deviate from virtue <note>The text is mid-sentence, discussing the benefits of following divine law.</note> or fall into the greatest calamities. Desiring these things, with God as his teacher, Moses provided for his people through a constitution of laws, starting not from himself or other men, nor from their own customs, but by raising their minds to God and the craftsmanship of the world. He persuaded them that we humans are the most precious of God’s works among all creatures; thus, having found them obedient to his teachings, he might more easily persuade them of the rest.

While other lawgivers follow human fables or present their gods as sacrilegious beings through their constitutions, often providing an excuse for sins through the malice of their stories, our lawgiver, declaring God to be the highest virtue, opened and prepared these things for men. He showed that those who would not understand or believe such things should be corrected with just lashes. Therefore, I beg the readers to examine this writing with an attentive mind. For if one considers the logic of this design, nothing seen here is inconsistent with the majesty or mercy of God. We recognize that all things regarding the nature of the world are in harmony: some things the Lawgiver expressed with great dignity as befitting the Beginning; others he described allegorically with proper decency; and those things that could be said clearly, he declared honorably. For those wishing to consider the individual causes of things, this contemplation provides much and is deeply philosophical. I will refrain from speaking more on this now, but if God grants us time, I will attempt to write about it through this work. I shall now turn to the narration of events, beginning with what Moses said regarding the craftsmanship of the world. These things were found recorded in the sacred books.

# IN THE BEGINNING

God created heaven and earth. But while the earth did not yet come into view and was hidden by the depth of darkness, and the Spirit of God moved over it, God commanded light to be made. This being done, He considered the whole space, separating the light from the darkness. To the light, God gave the name Day; the other He called Night. The morning He called "morning," and the evening "evening." And this was the first day. Moses, however, says "one day." <note>A reference to the Hebrew phrasing "Day One" rather than "First Day."</note> I ought to explain the reason for this now, as I promised to explain the causes of each thing briefly, but that discussion is better suited for a more necessary time. After this, on the second day, He placed the sky above all things; distinguishing it from the others, He established it by divine precept. It appeared like crystal, yet it held the moisture and rain to sustain the life of those below; thus God fashioned the air. On the third day, the earth stood firm, as God poured out all the seas. On that day, the strength of herbs and seeds suddenly rose up. On the fourth day, God adorned the heavens with the sun, the moon, and the other stars, which clearly designate the distinctions of the seasons for us. Then He created all the animals: those that swim and those that fly, some in the deep and others in the air. He joined them in pairs so that the cause of their reproduction might be established and their kind could be multiplied and grow. On the sixth day, He created the quadruped sex <note>land animals</note> and finally Man was formed. God said all that He had made was good. These were made in six days. On the seventh day, He is said to have rested from the works of His hands. Whence we also ought to be vacant from our own labors on that day; we call it the Sabbath, which in the Hebrew language signifies "rest." After the seventh day, Moses begins to give an account of Adam. He says that Man was formed from the clay of the earth and given a soul by the inspiration of the Spirit. This man was called Adam, which in the Hebrew language signifies "red," because he was born from red earth. God presented the animals to Adam, according to their masculine and feminine kinds, and Adam imposed names upon them according to their natures. But seeing that Adam did not have a companion for procreation and found no delight in being alone while seeing the other animals coupled, God, while Adam was sleeping, took a rib from his side and fashioned a living creature. When she was brought to him, he knew she had been formed from himself. In the Hebrew language, she is called "Woman" <note>original: "mulier"</note>, but he also gave her the name "Eve," which signifies "Mother of All." On that day, God planted a paradise toward the East <margin><unclear>itay d d' d d’ s r' m' i' u' i' t i l' i' d' p' i' d' r i' d' e' r</unclear></margin> filled with germinating flowers and other things pleasing to the mind of the Creator, including the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. He commanded the man and his wife to have care for this garden. This place is watered by one river which flows around the whole earth and is divided into four parts. One is named Pishon <note>original: "Phison"</note>, which means "fullness"; it flows into India and is called the Ganges by the Greeks. The Euphrates and Tigris flow into the Red Sea; the name Euphrates signifies "flower," and the Tigris is named for its narrow and rapid flow. The Gihon <note>original: "Gyon"</note> flows through Egypt, signifying that which comes from the East; the Greeks call it the Nile.

<image-desc>A circular globe or cosmological map in green and blue tones, divided into sections and featuring detailed interior markings, possibly representing the earth or a planisphere.</image-desc>

God therefore permitted them to taste of the other plants but commanded them to abstain from the forbidden one, foretelling that if they touched it, they would perish in their bodies. But the Devil, being envious, placed in their minds the desire to disobey God’s precept. He persuaded them that by eating of the plant, they would gain the knowledge of good and evil, and thus lead a more happy life. By these words, the woman was seduced to taste of the fruit, and she gave it to her husband. Having done this, they became aware of their own nature and were ashamed, covering themselves with leaves. When God came to the garden, Adam and his wife hid themselves. But God called them, and they, being unable to hide their sin, confessed. Adam asked for mercy, saying he had been seduced by the woman, who in turn blamed the serpent. God then imposed punishment upon them: the woman would suffer pain in childbirth, and Adam would have to labor upon the earth, which was previously abundant for his pleasure. He foretold that they would live in misery and toil until they returned to the earth from which they were made. He also cursed the serpent, taking away its voice and making it crawl upon its belly, placing enmity between it and mankind.

<meta>This page continues the genealogy of the descendants of Noah, specifically focusing on the sons of Ham and Shem, and the life of the patriarch Abraham. It follows the narrative of Flavius Josephus's "Antiquities of the Jews," Book 1, detailing the origins of various nations and Abraham's journey to Egypt.</meta>

How they arrived in this world was established by these four men, who gathered together as unrefined people in the neighboring lands. Meroe <note>original: "Meneuothaut," a likely corruption of the name associated with the Ethiopian capital Meroe</note>, the son of Cush, did not lose the name derived from his own person when he established his name. Through Meroe, the inhabitants are now called Ethiopians, while his son Sabas <note>original: "sabatheum"</note> is named by his neighbors. The Sabines were formerly named after the son of Cush, but are now called Sabatenians by the Greeks, with the region itself named Justina. Through the region of Meroe and Sabatano, the name was established. Yet even the name of Sabinus as a specific person was not lost, but the region of Ramis <note>referring to Raamah</note> was named by the man Medre. And Thiraus <note>Tiras</note> with the region of Justina Meroeth. 

To the Ethiopians who possess the land, the Nile is called the "Fini." Among the eight sons of Cush, the Caruaians were a people of the same stock, and the youngest son did not lose his own name in his calling. Sidon <note>original: "Sydoni"</note> is called "A" <note>likely a scribal error or abbreviation</note> among the Egyptians. Phut, when he founded Libya, called the people Phutites after his own name. And a river in Meroe is named for the Arabs. It will happen that the land of the Greeks, which is in the record of the law, will be seen by the eyes of the region; having a certain boundary, it lost the Gergesites <note>original: "geresos"</note> when I see the borders of the Samaritans; thus, at first, we did not have the book of the law. The Hebrews call their deserter one who dwells near the mountain called Aphroditus.

Noah lived for three hundred and fifty years after the flood, and up to twenty-five years <note>The chronology here is confused in the transcription, likely referring to the total of 950 years</note> according to my words. Because they were seen to know things on the earth, admiration gave them their own time. The Hebrews, however, settled in Sopare; many times they came into the land of the Greeks through this river. These people, when the world was made: it was the choice of certain sons of the sons of Ham <note>original: "cham"</note> in their congregation, some of whom were cursed. But another, fleeing the curse, were the sons of Canaan. Regarding these, all names were given. For Shem <note>original: "Sem"</note>, five sons were joined in the region called Assyria, in that same habitation from the river Euphrates to the sea. Elam, the son of Shem, is the prince from whom the Elamites arose in Assyria. Asshur founded Nineveh <note>original: "niniui(m)"</note>. Arphaxad <note>original: "Arphaxat"</note> named those who are called Chaldeans the Arphaxadites, being the ruler over them. Aram founded the Aramaeans, whom the Greeks call Syrians. Lud established the Ludites, now called Lydians. These are the five sons. From Aram, four nations arose: the Aramaeans, and those in Meroe who are called by their own region. 

Armenia was generated from these, as were the Bactrians; but the Mesa were called Mesanaeans by everyone. From Arphaxad were sons from whom two Hebrews were found. Eber begat Joktan <note>original: "iatam"</note> and Peleg <note>original: "falech"</note>. Peleg was so named because of the division of habitations; for "Peleg" in Hebrew signifies "division." Joktan, the son of Shem, had sons: Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab <note>These names are transcribed with Latin variants: "helmothat saleph, asar mothae irac, adoram usal diclel. abimahel. saba. saphat et euila(m) ybel"</note>. These are the sons of Arphaxad. Eber begat Reu <note>original: "ragau"</note>; he begat Serug <note>original: "seruc"</note>. To him was born Nahor. These are from Peleg and his son Eber: his son Serug, who in memory begat the son Nahor, who begat Terah <note>original: "thare"</note>. To him was born Abram, who became Abraham. This is the twelfth generation from Noah; it was the two hundred and ninetieth year after the flood that Abraham was born. Terah begat Abraham in his seventieth year. 

Nahor was born in the 70th year. And Haran was begat by Terah. From Terah came Nahor. <note>The text here lists several names including Sarah and Lot</note> Haran had a son named Lot. Sarah and Milcah were daughters. Haran died in the land of the Chaldeans, but he had not lost his generation. But Nahor begat Lot according to the name of his brother's son. Milcah was joined to her brother Abraham. Furthermore, Terah, when they hated the Chaldeans, died in the place of Aram <note>Haran</note> in Mesopotamia, where the burial of the dying Terah was. He lived 205 years. Life in the land of men was becoming rare: it was gradually shortened until the years were 255, then 150. Nachor, Sela, Serug, Abraham, and Sarah. Lot was the son of Bethuel. These were from Nahor. Bethuel begat Rebekah. Abraham took Lot, the son of his brother Haran, and his wife Sarah. They left the Chaldeans; they wished to migrate by the Lord's will into the land of the Canaanites to inhabit it. Abraham came to Canaan after seventy-five years. He began to announce many things from God. First, he proclaimed the Lord as the creator of the world and of charity to those who attended to things happily. As the first prophet, he wished each thing to be given and to consist in wisdom. He came from the sea, and taught how the sun and moon follow their courses, and how the heavens are tempered. For a power lives and made the order through its own beauty. He came before them because they were so at first: though he came by many ways, it is not necessary to enjoy power by one's own will, but to possess it. Thus the justice of the Lord is manifest to man, to whom alone honor and thanksgiving should be given. 

Because of this wisdom, he chose with greater reason to dwell with the Chaldeans and others of Mesopotamia. Thus it is proclaimed of him that in the place of the Canaanites he constituted a place for the prophet where he established an altar for the praise of the Lord. Where Abraham is named, Berosus <note>A Babylonian historian often quoted by Josephus</note> mentions him: for he says there was a generation among the Chaldeans as is seen above, to be better understood. Nicolaus of Damascus <note>A historian and friend of Herod the Great</note> says in his fourth book that Abraham was king of Damascus. Abraham reigned in Damascus, coming with an army from the land above Babylon called the Chaldeans. After much time, he arose from this region to the land now called Canaan, where he dwelt and was multiplied. Even to this day, a village is named after Abraham among the Damascenes.

<column-break/>

He was establishing many things as from the Lord, even in the land of Damascus. The Egyptians differ in various customs and keep their own laws, but they came to a discussion of the truth. Abraham demonstrated to each one the words he held. He showed that from their inventions, the truth was small. He convinced the Assyrians of Arithmetic and the Egyptians of the inventions of Astronomy <note>original: "astrologia," used here in the classical sense of astronomy</note>. For the Lord's son came into Egypt through the land of Damascus. When he returned to the part of Canaan, he and Lot separated because of the pasture of the land. They divided the land through justice: Abraham took the place in the city of Hebron, which is seven years older than the Egyptian Tanis <note>original: "panidus"</note>. Lot inhabited the land near the river, not far from the city of the Sodomites, which was once good but now destroyed by sins in the judgment of God. At that time, the Assyrians held sway; many kings came to the Assyrian king, including Bera, Birsha, Shinab, Shemeber <note>original transcription: "ballas-balas-smibar-us-synobore-us"</note>. Each had their own prince. These served the King of Assyria for twelve years, but in the thirteenth year, the sons of the Sodomites attempted to break the yoke. The Assyrians led an army against them under Chedorlaomer <note>original: "chodorlaomor"</note>. They attacked Sodom and Gomorrah. In a great fight in the valley, which was previously called the wooded vale but was shortened. 

The Sodomites were obsessed by the Assyrians for five years. The Assyrians were victorious. They seized Lot and the goods of Sodom. Abraham, when he heard this, did not hesitate. He prepared to conquer the Egyptians <note>likely meaning the Eastern kings</note> and rescue his kinsman. Abraham, with the servants he had, pursued them. They achieved a victory by God. In the battle against the Assyrians, they conquered four kings. When he returned from the Assyrians, it was most beautiful and glorious. Abraham saw that the victory over the Assyrians was the truth of the Lord. The King of Sodom met him, but Melchizedek also received him. His name signifies "Just King" <note>original: "significauert iustur"</note>. He was the king of Salem, which is now Jerusalem. Melchizedek was a priest of the Most High God, providing abundance to the victors. Abraham continued his years. The King of Sodom offered him the goods, but Abraham favored nothing for himself, returning the property to the king. 

Later, through a prophecy of the Lord, it was said that his descendants would be in servitude for four hundred years in a foreign land. This signified the many years his children would be afflicted, until they reached the number of the victors. Abraham was dwelling in Hebron in the land of Canaan. When he was 100 years old, the Lord promised a son. Sarah, however, was barren and gave her Egyptian handmaid <note>Hagar</note> to Abraham so she might bear a child. When she conceived, she was afflicted by Sarah and fled, but an angel commanded her to return. The child was named Ishmael <note>original: "mahel"</note>, which signifies "God obeys" or "God hears." Seven years later, when Abraham was 100 years old, the promise of a son by Sarah was renewed. They were at Damascus, and it appeared beautifully. 

They were named. And there were servants and children in the time of the Sodomites. The Lord's truth and justice was with him. The time of the Assyrians was such that they received many parts. The pride of the princes was great. Abraham returned the tithes.

Behold, even those who see these things find that there is danger in acting for the good. It is evident that the fathers <note>The "fathers" here likely refers to the older brothers as tribal patriarchs.</note> were exasperated because they were embittered by what had been prepared for him; again, pride brings forth not humility but a solitary state. Even the son of the master <note>original: "arbis filium"; likely a corruption of "heris filium" (the master's son) or "arboris" (of the tree/lineage).</note> is made exasperated by pride. In the name of Joseph, he sought to empty the body and soul through this scourge. Although pride is dangerous to others, he did not hate the other sons more. Hence, because Joseph was beloved by his father, the sons began to hate their brother. For this reason, he narrated the dreams which he saw to his father and brothers; they served to accumulate the hatred that existed before. On account of these things, men began to envy and exasperate him. And what he said appeared to the humble and the just. Many, indeed, out of pride, feared this gathering of things; for the brothers saw that they did not fear justice; they saw that they presumed something from anyone. So that the saying of the brothers might be despised, he found and reported a dream for his own cause. Nevertheless, it was truly done that in time his sheaf <note>original: "munuipulum"; a corruption of "manipulum," the bundle of grain from Joseph's first dream.</note> stood up from the earth—the earth, as if from prophecy. And they ran to him to worship him as if he were a lord. These things were truly sent in justice and brought to pass in the magnitude of the vision. And then, just as he prophesied, it was made known to him. Those who see the father in justice dreaming, from there they shone back. By a plan in iron <note>Possibly a reference to the harshness of their intent or the "iron" of their will.</note> they did not reach the father, because then they also received the power of the judge, and they saw even more grave figures of justice. And so everyone turned again toward the justice or the vision inclined over Joseph. Truly, in a much greater way, because they were not the first. But he says then that they saw the sun, the moon, and the stars alone in Joseph; truly, because of their sheaf, they provided a bad fortune for the justice prepared for the father. Again, it was not according to standing custom: for the fathers were also able to see what this signified for the sons. He, however, rejoiced in the dream; by looking back, not then at his brothers and in pride, but he delighted to recall the history. He magnifies the father according to the dream; nevertheless, he announced Joseph as a happy son to him. Again, it was done by God's gift <note>original: "lariante do"; likely "largiente Deo".</note> that he should be honored by the father, which is worthy to be adored. The moon and the sun represent the father and the mother. By the author of the stars, the mother is included in all things, as it is a prophecy of the future king. Namely, the father Jacob and the mother Rachel: because Joseph’s twelve <insert>brethren</insert> are the stars, and the moon is the father <note>In the biblical text, the sun usually represents the father and the moon the mother.</note>. Because then for Joseph, that son of pride: they did not look upon him in pride to the danger of the just, but in envy, for they despaired that he excelled them. And all things they wished to turn upon Joseph, yet the good things which were signified made everyone possess the dream. So that they might rejoice as if concerning themselves, all were able to do so; this was certainly to be shared with the prophets. What they did was set free: not following unjust paths, they directed themselves. And so when the sons of these had become fierce, they saw according to the saying of the prophets toward the land; but they said if the sons of Israel are seen, the spirit of prophecy are the leaders. For they saw that justice was the precursor. The gods among whom they had their life visited what was done by their fathers against Joseph, etc.

Likewise, it also happened then that he appeared to the father as a precursor; for he came to the father and it was bitter, because while Reuben was the eldest, he came to worship in Shechem unexpectedly. # The Deeds of Moses

He had been a leader: whoever followed him from that place, he would lead them along the way. And when they had set out to prepare the paths, they did not think to resist the present circumstances. He asserted that he wished to reach **Memphis** and the sea; no city was able to resist them. When these people were beset by such evils, it seemed right to trust in the response of God and the gods, so that they might surrender themselves to the present circumstances. **Moses** and the leaders took charge, just like the army of the Hebrews. With him as the leader, the sea was to be crossed by his guidance and consent. Amid the hidden dangers and the number of those in peril—where he affirmed that everything was in abundance—Moses said: "Have confidence." For he would obtain their prayers, benefits, and victory. Upon his arrival, the priests who wished to do so would proclaim the divine will. Moses, however, was sent in turn to those he had once wished to attend him. Finally, the king, having become suspicious and diligent, looked upon him with disfavor because of what he had seen the army accomplish; he despised him as if he were one of the prophets of the Jews who had come promising the help of the God of the Hebrews. And now he had come with craftiness to take the Hebrews away; he even rejoiced to work against him, since he was entirely determined that Moses should depart from his presence.

Moses, however, considered the enemies among them; using his ingenuity, he took charge of the army as a fitting leader, and for that reason, many departed together. Furthermore, after three weeks, they made their presence visible. In the **City of the Ethiopians**, it became known that he had arrived there; it was said that all things had been done by the skill of Moses from his birth. And as they were perishing in that city, many things soon showed themselves again—namely, how much the water was delayed. Moses, however, not being overcome by Pharaoh, remained in suspense. # HERE BEGINS BOOK III.
## CONCERNING THE SUPPOSED SITUATION.

**H**aving set out, therefore, by the salvation of the Lord, they gave thanks for their return <note>The text likely refers to their "return" to freedom or to the land of their ancestors</note>, carrying provisions in the manner Moses had commanded them to bring. Already, as necessity and the lack of water pressed upon them, the soil proved difficult, and they found themselves in need of help. From this point, no animals could thrive, and <unclear>until</unclear> <unclear>clear</unclear> their land was sterile; no new fruits were seen to grow from it. It was necessary for the Hebrews to hasten through the region, for they had once lived there <note>A reference to the patriarchs' time in Canaan and the surrounding deserts</note>, from which they could divine their absence. They carried with them from Egypt foods <unclear>already</unclear> by Moses' command. And they drank of the water which they had then drawn. But when they found that the water was failing after a journey of twelve days, they encountered water in this soil, but it was at once bitter and scarce. This occurred to them at a place they reached at midday. They called the place "the bitter waters of the sea," as Moses himself named it. It was called *Amara* in the Hebrew language <note>original: "Amara"; This refers to Marah (Exodus 15:23), which means "bitter" in Hebrew</note>. Just as <unclear>Lucy</unclear> <note>Likely a corruption of a name or the word "lux," light</note>, they were exhausted by the violence of the journey and the lack of food, which had completely failed them. They were utterly worn out. Furthermore, there was a stench there, and they could not endure the sin of such an outcry; yet some consolation was proved to them, which had been found for thousands of people. They had heard of this place from those who had seen it while walking through lonely places: that it was bitter, and a harsh omen for those who took food; the ground was possessed by neither men nor animals. It seemed, therefore, that Moses was placed in a narrow strait by the people, and similarly dear ones, so that they might return in vain. For they had not found an entrance into the land where they might have been satisfied, and they feared dying like wild beasts. While their spirit failed, they turned to madness and murmuring out of hatred. Moses taught them in words: they confessed all their sustenance was in Moses' own hands. Some others, however, prayed to Moses that the aforementioned bitterness might be turned to sweetness, as they found it neither in the aforementioned <unclear>place</unclear> nor in others; they asked how it might be done for their health. Moses, however, <unclear>turned</unclear> toward benefits and toward the prayer of those who had been held in the malice of the present situation. He granted them a great grace. Taking the tip of the rod which he carried, Moses divided the aforementioned bitter water, and along its length, he performed a miracle. He cast a small piece of wood into it, so that he might satisfy the people just as God had prepared the water for them. Through the power and glory of prophecy, just as it had been bitter, it was made ready. There, what was granted by the divine will came to pass. Thus, he ordered that if they found they were able to draw the poured water, they should do so. **H**e also made the altar of incense of acacia wood, being a square of one cubit on each side, and two cubits in height. From its corners proceeded horns. He overlaid it with the purest gold, with its grate, walls, and horns. He made a golden crown around it, and two golden rings under the crown on each side, so that bars might be put into them and the altar could be carried. The bars themselves he made of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold plates. He also composed the oil for the ointment of sanctification and the incense of the purest spices, by the work of a perfumer.

**H**e also made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood, being a square of five cubits, and three cubits in height. Its horns proceeded from the corners; he overlaid it with bronze plates. For its use, he prepared various bronze vessels: pots, tongs, flesh-hooks, hooks, and fire-pans. He made its grate in the manner of a net of bronze, and under it in the middle of the altar was a hearth. He cast four rings for the four ends of the grate to receive the bars for carrying. These bars he also made of acacia wood and overlaid them with bronze plates. He inserted them into the rings which projected from the sides of the altar. That altar was not solid, but hollow, made of boards and empty inside. **H**e also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle. **H**e made the court, on the southern side of which were hangings of fine twisted linen, a hundred cubits long. There were twenty bronze columns with their bases; the capitals of the columns and all the carvings were of silver. Likewise on the northern side, the hangings, columns, bases, and capitals were of the same measures and metals. On that part which looks toward the sea, there were hangings of fifty cubits, ten columns, and as many bases. The capitals of the columns and all the carvings were silver. Moreover, toward the east he prepared fifty cubits, in which the hangings of one side had fifteen cubits, three columns, and as many bases. And on the other side, fifteen cubits, with three columns and as many bases. In the entrance of the court, he made a hanging variegated with blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen, having twenty cubits in length; the height was five cubits, according to the measure which all the hangings of the court had. The columns at the entrance were four with bronze bases; their capitals and carvings were silver. They made the pegs of the court all around of bronze.

Through these things, no interruption occurred if they remained strong in their fear and were obedient to the ritual of the sacrifices. They were soon urged to protect these laws, even when prohibited by the stirrings of the faithless among them. Their conscience alone was their guide, lest they stray from the laws of Moses <note>The text here emphasizes the internal moral compass of the Hebrews in following the Mosaic code despite external pressures</note>. Through the deeds of the Lord, their broken spirits in the camps were mended, even when they seemed to be on the verge of ruin. Yet, when the time for healing arrived, the murmurings of the people often sought to replace the established order. Despite the rigors they faced, the divine laws remained a source of wonder, having been given by God to be observed with prayers to the Lord. Now, let us record the history as the truth dictates.
