# THE BEGINNING OF BOOK 4
## THUS THE HEBREWS

**H**arsh difficulties in the desolate region and a lack of necessities began to drive the Hebrews toward adversity and to spark discord. They were unable to move forward or to remain obedient. Even if they realized they could not overcome their enemies without divine help, many nonetheless murmured and blamed Moses, seeing themselves as victims of poverty rather than recipients of the solace they had been promised. They claimed that the Lord had ceased to speak through Moses. Moses, seeing this uprising of the murmuring crowd, sought to console them, even as they could no longer endure what they called his tyranny <note>This "tyranny" refers to the perceived heavy-handed leadership of Moses during the long desert migration</note>. Believing their journey was leading to nothing, the Hebrews considered returning to Egypt or launching a war against the Canaanites. Moses warned them that victory was impossible without the will and aid of the Lord. He urged the people not to let their anger lead them to a premature end. Gradually, the Hebrews moved toward the desert borders of Canaan. Though many were obedient, a faction arose that did not fear the warnings of the prophet Moses, and their murmurs flew through the camp. They rushed toward the Canaanites, but were driven back into the wilderness. Disregarding Moses's advice, they suffered a great defeat, realizing too late that divine protection had been withdrawn due to their rebellion.

**K**orah <note>original: "Chore," a prominent Levite who led a famous rebellion against Moses's authority as recorded in the Book of Numbers</note>, a nobleman of the Hebrew race and a man of great wealth, possessed a great talent for speaking and influencing the people. Driven by a massive envy, he began to challenge the leadership of Moses. He saw that Moses held much power and suspected that the honors being distributed were part of a secret design for his own family's gain. He began to cry out to the people, calling Moses cruel and accusing him of usurping the honor of the priesthood under the guise of prophecy. He specifically targeted the appointment of Aaron, Moses's brother, to the high priesthood, claiming it was done through trickery rather than divine command. Korah argued that if such honors were to be granted, they should be given based on the will of the people and the merit of wealth and nobility, rather than through Moses's private selection. This message found a receptive audience among the common people, who began to stir against the republic <note>The term "republic" here refers to the organized communal government of the tribes</note>. They accused Moses of granting the most dignified priesthood to his own kin and suggested that he had treated the rest of the people with contempt. Moses, facing these slanders and the irritation of the people, remained devoted to his duty. He spoke to Korah and the two hundred and fifty leaders who followed him, telling them that while they were all worthy of honor, the decision regarding the priesthood belonged to the Lord alone. He proposed a trial: let each man bring his censer and incense, and let God show whom He has chosen for this holy office.

<column-break/>

They were prostrated by a passion for power that no other could have held. Moses declared that if he had sinned in this, let the Lord judge. He noted that they were all of the same faith and the same community, yet they sought to pour out discord. He accused the rebels of seeking to accumulate power for themselves under the pretext of seeking the common good. Korah, however, did not cease his efforts; he continued to urge the people to choose their own priests, claiming that Moses's true goal was to make himself a judge over all. Moses stood firm, asserting that the priesthood was not a prize to be seized by violence or trickery, but a sacred trust. He noted that he had not sought these honors for himself or his sons, but had followed the immutable will of God. He challenged Korah to a trial of the censers <note>term: "censer," a vessel for burning incense used in religious ceremonies; in this context, it serves as the instrument of a divine "trial by fire"</note>, where the Lord would manifest His choice through the rising smoke. He warned that they should not persist in their pride, for the Lord recognizes those who are truly His. 

The leaders of the community, including Dathan and Abiram <note>original: "Dattan & Abiron," leaders from the tribe of Reuben who joined Korah's rebellion</note>, refused to even meet with Moses, accusing him of leading them out of a land of plenty only to kill them in the desert and rule over them. They treated his summons with mockery and remained in their tents, further inciting the crowd. Moses, moved by their stubbornness, called upon the Lord to vindicate his leadership. He asked that if these men died a natural death, then the people might believe he was a fraud; but if the earth itself were to open and swallow them, then they would know that he acted by divine authority. As he spoke, the very ground beneath the tents of the rebels began to tremble. The people watched in terror as a great chasm opened, consuming the rebels, their families, and all their possessions. At the same moment, a divine fire broke out among the two hundred and fifty men offering incense, consuming them as well. Thus, the rebellion was ended not by the hand of man, but by a terrifying display of divine judgment that reaffirmed the chosen status of Aaron and the leadership of Moses.

<summary>This page concludes the third book of Josephus's history and begins the fourth, focusing on the hardships of the desert and the dramatic rebellion led by Korah against the authority of Moses and Aaron.</summary>
<keywords>Josephus, Moses, Aaron, Korah, Dathan, Abiram, rebellion, priesthood, censers, divine judgment, desert wanderings, Antiquities of the Jews</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Book 4 of Josephus’s *Antiquities of the Jews*, transitioning from the aftermath of Korah's rebellion to the military conquests of the Transjordan. The previous page detailed the complaints of the Hebrews against Moses's leadership; here, divine signs and military victories re-establish his authority.</meta>

From the smoke and the burning ritual, Eleazar, son of Aaron, took the censers <note>These were the bronze pans used for incense by the rebels; they were hammered into plates to cover the altar as a warning</note>, so that the altar of the Lord or their descendants would clearly illustrate this power of the Lord. Aaron, however, was believed to possess a much greater divine faculty. While many continued to grow in their greatness and friendship, others grew in malice. Therefore, lest the people judge Moses for the fate of the ark, and so that the whole nation would not be found culpable before the Lord, Moses sought to demonstrate his favor. They had studied the will of the Lord regarding the Ark, and Moses had long labored for it.

Though many were seeking to turn back, they soon humbly changed their minds when Moses beckoned them. Moses, seeing the virtue which they could in no way ignore, warned that a new order of things was emerging. He instructed that the rods of the tribes be brought, each marked with a name, and placed within the Tabernacle. On the following day, when he brought them forth, it was known that each would receive his own. While the others remained unchanged, the rod of Aaron had germinated a branch and had brought forth almonds <note>original: "mala," here referring to the fruit of the almond tree, a traditional sign of Aaron's chosen status</note>, flourishing with vigor. Then, those who saw this vision were struck with awe and yielded to the will of the Lord, for the grace of the Lord through Aaron was certain. This way having been found, the sedition of the Hebrews, which had been so great, finally grew quiet.

After these things, the Lord ordained the service of the Levites. Moses’s authority was confirmed as he went about the mountain for the sake of the service. The multitude, though poor, was distributed according to the divine judgment. The life of the people was suspended upon the Lord’s will, and the service of the principals was accepted by the people.

<margin>After these things, concerning the victory and wars of the Hebrews</margin>
**Post** After this, Moses wished to mobilize the army. Sihon, the king who defended the region against the Arabs and the desert river <note>The Arnon River, a significant boundary in the Transjordan</note>, divided the Moabites and the Amorites. This king sought to defend his goods and the land against the multitude of men. Sihon, the king of that region, received the messengers sent by Moses who prayed for passage, but Sihon did not believe in a peaceful victory. He prohibited the Hebrews from crossing the Arnon river. When Moses saw the hostile mystery of the Amorites, he did not allow his people to fall into fear. He approached them, and the Lord preceded him. Even though Sihon sought to resist, the Hebrews processed with arms and prepared for battle. Through the Lord of hosts, the victory of the Hebrews was swift, and the multitude was overcome as they moved rapidly.

<column-break/>

As the Hebrews pressed upon them, the Amorites reached a point of despair concerning their empire and victory. They did not dare to hasten to the main conflict. For because the Hebrews had progressed into the mountains, the justice of the Lord was seen. They did not flee the fight but stood with confidence. Thus the Hebrews, facing the multitude on the mountain, broke the resistance. The Hebrews, having labored for victory, used their slings <note>original: "fundibula"</note> and weapons. The Amorites were unable to withstand the strength of the slingers from a distance. Because the Lord granted a huge victory to the Hebrews, they pressed the battle further. At that time, it was willed that the Lord of hosts would grant the primary military success. Aaron and the Hebrews achieved a famous victory, and those who had been flatterers now fell. Under Moses’s will, the army entered into the service of taking spoils. With their slings and great desire, they realized they could conquer more. And so the Hebrews, seeing the Lord was with them, grew bolder. They possessed the land that the Lord had opened to them. The victory flowed like a wave across the Arnon river into the land of the Amorites, all the way to the river Jordan. To the western part of these regions, the water of the Jordan provided a boundary. While they held this path, Og, the king of Gilead and Bashan, also came against them. But the Hebrews, through their will and strength, defeated him as well, and his army was overcome. Moses then moved the army toward the mountain by the river Jordan.

<margin>Concerning Og, king of Bashan, and the victory of the Hebrews</margin>
Og was a king of great magnitude and strength. It was said that he was of a marvelous stature, and the clarity of his body was seen by all. In his ferocity and magnitude, he was not easily overcome. He reigned at Rabbath, and his fame was great. He possessed an iron bed <note>The OCR "baluami fēre corio" likely refers to the "lectum ferreum" or iron bed of Og, which Josephus describes as being four cubits wide and nine cubits long</note>, which served as a testament to his massive size. He was a great victor in strength, yet he fell before the Hebrews. The Hebrews, confident in their victory, possessed the way forward.

<meta>This page continues the narrative transition from the period of the Judges—specifically following the death of Eli’s sons and the return of the Ark—to the establishment of the Israelite monarchy under Saul.</meta>

It was determined that the people should not return to their previous state of governance. At that time, the Divine Spirit willed that they be ruled by a king called by God. Whatever nobility was inherent in your ancestors' countenances was found in him. This occurred when the form was revealed to Samuel: a man of great beauty and physical stature, who surpassed others in his appearance. 

This was Saul. His father’s young donkeys had wandered from the field, in which they had previously been a source of much joy. The father sent his son to find them, accompanied by a single servant. When they had searched through the countryside and the donkeys were still missing, they arrived at a place where they began to lose their way. Saul suggested they turn back, lest his father begin to worry more about them than about the lost animals. <note>Saul’s concern for his father’s mental state shows an early glimpse of his character before he assumed the throne.</note>

When their provisions were exhausted, the servant who was with him said that they should perhaps visit a man of God nearby. Saul worried that they had no gifts to offer the man who might use his foresight to help them. The servant replied that he had a small portion of silver to give. As they approached the city, they met young women going out to draw water and asked where the prophet lived. They were told he was attending a sacrificial feast, as Samuel had arrived to lead the people in a sacred meal. 

Samuel, sitting in his house, had been prepared by a divine word regarding who was coming. When they arrived, Samuel saw Saul and knew he was the one destined to rule the Hebrews. Saul approached Samuel, not knowing who he was, and asked him to point out the house of the seer. Samuel revealed that he himself was the prophet. He invited Saul to the feast, informed him that the donkeys had already been found, and declared that all the good things of the kingdom were destined for him. 

Saul replied humbly, stating he was not worthy, as he came from the smallest branch of the tribes. <note>Saul refers here to the Tribe of Benjamin, which was significantly reduced in power during the period of the Judges.</note> Samuel led him to the feast, placing him in the seat of honor above the other guests.

Samuel then instructed the cook to set aside a choice portion of meat for Saul. After they had spent the day and night together, Samuel called Saul at dawn to set him on his way. Samuel ordered the servant to go on ahead so that he might speak a private word of divine significance to Saul. When they were alone, Samuel took a vessel of oil and poured it over the young man’s head, kissing him. "The Lord has anointed you to be prince over his inheritance," he said. 

As a sign that this was truly from God, Samuel predicted three things: first, that Saul would meet two men near Rachel’s tomb who would tell him the donkeys were found; second, that he would meet three men carrying gifts; and third, that he would encounter a company of prophets and be filled with the Divine Spirit himself. 

When these signs were fulfilled, Saul’s heart was changed. Later, he met his kinsman, who asked where he had been. Saul mentioned the found donkeys but, out of modesty or perhaps fear of disbelief, remained silent regarding the matter of the kingdom. 

Samuel then called all the people to Gilgal <note>original: "Isgalatha"</note> to formally choose a king by lot. When the lot fell to Saul, he could not be found, for he had hidden himself among the baggage. This was seen as a sign of his great temperance and lack of worldly ambition. When they finally brought him out, he stood head and shoulders above all the people. Samuel cried out, "See the man the Lord has chosen!" and the people shouted, "Long live the King!" Samuel wrote the laws of the kingdom in a book and placed it before the Lord. While most honored him, some troublemakers despised him and brought him no gifts, but Saul held his peace.

### After some time, King Nahash of the Ammonites increased his honor through war
Nahash had inflicted many evils upon the Jews living across the Jordan. He besieged their cities and sought to crush their strength. 

<column-break/>

He imposed a cruel condition on those he conquered: he would only grant them peace if he could gouge out their right eyes. <note>This was a calculated military tactic. In ancient warfare, a soldier’s shield covered his left eye, meaning the loss of the right eye rendered a man entirely useless in battle.</note> The inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead, facing this terror, sent messengers to Saul. When the news arrived, the people wept. Saul, moved by the Spirit, took a yoke of oxen, hewed them in pieces, and sent them throughout Israel, declaring that the same would happen to the livestock of anyone who did not follow him into battle. 

A massive army was gathered—three hundred thousand from Israel and thirty thousand from the tribe of Judah. They crossed the Jordan and launched a surprise attack on the Ammonites during the morning watch. The victory was total; Nahash was defeated, and the region was liberated. This triumph silenced Saul's critics. The people were so delighted with Saul's leadership that they suggested those who had previously mocked him should be put to death, but Saul refused, saying that no man should be killed on a day when the Lord had wrought such salvation.

<unclear>The following section of the manuscript is heavily corrupted with repetitive characters and fragmented syntax, appearing to describe the re-confirmation of the kingship at Gilgal and Samuel's concluding exhortations to the people regarding their transition from a government of judges to a monarchy.</unclear> 

Samuel reminded them of their history from the time of Moses and Aaron, arguing that God had always been their true protector. He challenged them to testify if he had ever taken anything from them or treated them unjustly. The people confirmed his integrity. Samuel then warned that both they and their king must remain faithful to God’s commands, or the hand of the Lord would be against them as it was against their fathers. To prove his words were backed by divine power, he called for a sign—thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, a rare occurrence—which terrified the people into repentance.

It marks the formal transition of Israel from a collection of tribes led by Judges to a unified monarchy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the early Israelite monarchy. Having previously described Saul's selection as king, the text now moves to the first major crisis of his reign: the confrontation with the Philistines and Saul's failure to obey the prophetic instructions of Samuel.</meta>

Much misfortune followed. This became even more prominent regarding the tribes, who again came to Samuel to be called together so they might discuss the war with him. This plan pleased everyone. However, Samuel insisted that they must wait for the commands of God. He instructed that victims should be prepared for sacrifice, and that he would come to Saul when the seventh day was completed so they might offer sacrifices and entrust their affairs to God. 

But when the seventh day arrived and Samuel had not yet come, and Saul saw that the hope he had offered was failing, he grew anxious because Samuel delayed so long. Indeed, there was a great tumult among the Hebrews. When they saw the army of their enemies looming against them, they began to slip away and scatter in haste. Saul, being in great distress and fearing that he might lose the opportunity to perform what was required by God's will, took it upon himself to offer the sacrifice because the people were trembling with fear. 

As Saul was finishing the sacrifice, it was announced that Samuel had arrived. Saul went out to meet him. Samuel asked why he had acted contrary to his arrival, especially since it had been promised that he would come to perform the rite. Saul responded to Samuel, saying that he had been overcome by the circumstances and the pressure of time, rather than a lack of obedience; he claimed that because the enemy was threatening them, he could no longer wait and risk being caught in the enemies' trap. 

But Samuel then declared that the kingdom would not remain with Saul's son. He showed that because Saul had not followed the righteous will of God, the kingship would be given to another. 

At that time, the Philistines held such power over the land, as has been declared before, that they did not allow any blacksmith to work in the entire region. This was done so that the Hebrews would not be able to manufacture weapons for themselves. Because of this, when the Philistines approached, the Hebrews found themselves without the means to defend their people or restore their popular standing. 

The enemy had gathered a massive force, and the situation seemed desperate. The Hebrews prepared to face the enemy camps, even though they lacked proper armor. Fear returned to the enemy as well, yet they held their camp upon a high cliff, a place of great length and height, which was very difficult to approach.

...that his son would not be the one to conquer. As he changed his path so that they might not recognize you, he wished to kill you openly there. And he taught him the outcome of the event immediately, as if it were a holy message. Therefore, he did not delay but came, and when he arrived, everyone came out to meet him. But he ordered a sacrifice to be celebrated, and it happened that the sons of Jesse were to be purified at the altar first. 

When the elder sons of Jesse had come, the prophet believed by his countenance and his goodness that **this man would be the king**; but divine providence rejected him. To Samuel, who was seeking one he judged worthy but did not know, the Spirit announced inwardly: this man must be joined in mind and spirit, for the mind is to be judged anew from that which pleases men. 

To this, the response was given that he should not look upon the beauty of youth or his stature, for God does not look upon physical beauty, but looks upon the heart for what is kingly <note>original: "facie cor regalem aspicere" - a reference to the famous biblical principle that "man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."</note>, which undoubtedly includes virtue. For he is prophetically beautiful who shines with piety, justice, and strength; he is splendid in obedience, and from these acts the beauty of the soul is established. 

When everyone had been led through, Samuel asked Jesse to bring his other sons. He made five others come. Samuel called those who were present, but he was uncertain why the king of Israel was not among these five. Samuel then consulted Jesse regarding the beauty of the sons' forms, asking if he chose any of these to be king. When he responded "none," he asked again: did he have others? He had one more. He said there was another named **David**, a shepherd, who was tending the sheep. Samuel ordered him to be brought quickly, saying it was impossible for everyone to sit down until he arrived. 

When David arrived, looking most beautiful and kingly, Samuel looked upon the boy and the Spirit of God indicated that this was the one who pleased Him. When David had sat down, it was whispered to him by God's providence that he was the one; he was the son whom He himself had chosen. This clearly honored Samuel, and he silently spoke and signified to him that he was chosen by God to reign, warning him that he must be just and obey the commandments; for thus the kingdom would remain for a long time, and he would have a famous and illustrious lordship, and would conquer the Philistines and whatever nations or rebels he might face. Samuel, having finished these matters, departed to his own place.

But after this, the Spirit departed from Saul, and he began to be vexed by an evil spirit <note>The "evil spirit" (demonia) was historically interpreted as a divine withdrawal of favor resulting in melancholy or madness.</note>. Saul fell into a certain passion and found himself seized by demons; they brought on suffocations and anguishes. Therefore, since the physicians could find no remedy for his health, those who were wise taught that a just man should be brought to him. They ordered this man to come, so that when he went to him, he might soothe the warlike disturbance of his mind through song and make him clean. 

Saul did not ignore this and sought a man of such song. When one of his servants told him that he had seen a certain son of Jesse in Bethlehem, a youth beautiful and decorous in age, and very worthy in other studies, and also learned in playing the lyre <term>cithara</term> <note>The cithara was a stringed instrument similar to a lyre or harp, used in antiquity for both secular and sacred music.</note> and singing hymns, and moreover an exceptional warrior; Saul sent a messenger to Jesse [asking] that he should send his son David to the king. Jesse gave David gifts to be carried to Saul. When David arrived, Saul rejoiced. He made him his armor-bearer and honored him in all things. He was delighted by him when the intrusion of demons occurred; for when he came to him, by playing hymns and singing to the lyre, he called Saul back from the oppression of madness.

<column-break/>

After these things, the **Amalekites** again prepared for war. A great time had passed, and since they were neighbors, they were tempting fate. They came to the city of the Idumeans. Saul led his army out against them, placing his camp on a mountain, while the Philistines left their camp to go toward the mountain where Saul was. 

The army was divided between the mountains, and there came forth a certain Philistine named **Goliath** from the city of Gath, a very powerful man whose height was six cubits and a span. <note>A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm (18 inches); this would make Goliath nearly 10 feet tall.</note> Because of the greatness of his body, he wore a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels; he carried a spear so large that only a man of his size could wield it, and his spear-head was not light. 

Goliath stood in the midst of the lines and sent out a great voice, saying: "Why should Saul and the Hebrews come out to fight? I will release you from danger. What necessity is there for both armies to perish? Let a man be given from those among you who will fight in a contest, and let him end the war for everyone. Let it be that the side of the one who is conquered shall serve the one who conquers. Is it not just that the danger of all be decided by one?" Having said these things, he returned to his own. On the next day he came again, and for forty days he challenged them under the same conditions. Saul and his army were terrified; they stood in battle array but none dared to go out. 

Saul had sent David back to his father to tend the sheep. Not long after, David was sent by his father to his brothers to bring them food and see how they fared. When Goliath again came out and provocatively asked if there was no man here who wished to fight him, David was speaking to his brothers as his father had commanded. Hearing the giant's boast, he told his brothers he was ready to fight the enemy alone. His eldest brother, Eliab, was indignant and rebuked him, telling him to return to his father and his sheep. 

But David did not depart; he spoke to the soldiers, saying he wished to fight the Philistine. They judged his will to be from God. Word reached Saul, who called the youth to him. Saul marveled at his confidence but said, "You are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth." David responded that he had killed both a lion and a bear that had taken a lamb from his flock <note>David uses his experience as a shepherd to prove his qualifications as a warrior.</note>. He said the Philistine who reproached the army of the living God would be like one of those beasts. 

Saul, seeing the youth's spirit, armed him with his own armor—a bronze helmet and a coat of mail. But David, having not tested them, found he could not walk.

David took a stone, put it in his sling, and struck Goliath in the forehead. The giant fell to the earth. David ran and, standing over him, cut off his head. 

When the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled. The Hebrew army raised a shout and pursued them to the gates of Gath and Ascalon. Saul and the people celebrated David's victory. The women came out with cymbals and tambourines, singing, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands." This began the jealousy of Saul toward David...

David then took Abigail to be his wife, along with Ahinoam of Jezreel. Michal, Saul’s daughter, had been given to another.

Abishai wanted to strike Saul with a spear, but David forbade him, saying, "Do not destroy him, for who can stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be guiltless?" David took the spear and the water jug from near Saul's head and went to the other side of the hill. He called out to Abner, Saul’s general, rebuking him for not guarding the king. Saul recognized David’s voice and again repented of his pursuit, calling David his son.

<meta>This page transitions from the final days of King Saul's reign to the beginning of David's rule. It covers the tragic end of Saul at the Battle of Mount Gilboa and the subsequent report brought to David by an Amalekite messenger, following the historical account of Flavius Josephus.</meta>

...when they had announced the matter to their leaders. But a greater destiny called Saul: that this should be his fortune. They placed it in Hercules’ hands <note>original: "herculēte" — likely a scribal or OCR corruption referring to a divine or heroic fate</note> and fortified themselves with the help of his strength; they were devoted to taking the field on horseback. While the king remained there, he came to the battle with such material as the camp had brought. Four individuals provoked him: and the victory in Judea was reported. With the death of Saul, a certain Amalekite arrived with a gift of great value. He sought David where he was born; David asked who he was. He responded that he was of the Hebrew descent, but diminished, and had escaped after the few things he had lost. He said the Philistines had not caught him, but that the soldiers of the Hebrews had fallen.

King Saul was wounded, and his son bore the brunt of the battle. Seeing his confidence in the war was lost and the enemy’s assault was pressing, he feared the coming cohort. Therefore, he turned to his own. The Philistines sent archers; they fought with fierce spirits. At the approach of the enemy, many fell. When the host fell there, the Hebrew line was turned to flight. A great slaughter was made as the enemy pursued them. When Saul arrived at his own kings, the Philistines rushed upon them with chariots and all the terror of the battle.

A few did not flee, seeing the death of the king's sons before their eyes. Saul, seeing his hope of victory extinguished and his body wounded, spoke to his armor-bearer. He asked him to draw his sword and kill him before the uncircumcised enemies could reach him. The armor-bearer, however, did not dare to kill the king. Therefore, Saul took his own sword, and placing it against his breast, he fell upon it. <note>Josephus follows the biblical account of Saul’s suicide but adds details regarding the armor-bearer's refusal and subsequent suicide.</note> A certain Amalekite then approached David. He claimed that he had stood over Saul and, at the king’s request, finished him off because he was already dying. He brought the crown from Saul’s head and the armlet from his arm as proof, hoping for a reward.

When the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead <note>original: "iabef galaad"</note> heard what had happened to Saul and his sons—that the Philistines had stripped their bodies and hung them on the walls of the city of Beth-shan (which is now called Scythopolis)—they were moved by the memory of Saul's past kindnesses. All their most valiant men rose and traveled through the night to Beth-shan. They took down the bodies of Saul and his sons from the walls and brought them to Jabesh, where they burned the remains and buried the bones under a great tree in a place called the Field. They fasted for seven days and mourned the king and his sons. <note>The men of Jabesh-Gilead were historically loyal to Saul because he had rescued their city from the Ammonites at the start of his reign.</note> Saul died after reigning twenty years, or as some say, twenty-two years, ending the line of the house of Kish.

# THE SEVENTH BOOK BEGINS
## THE LIFE OF DAVID

**A**fter these things were done, David had been pursuing the Amalekites for two days. He had achieved a victory in the fight against those who had raided his camp. Then a messenger came from the camp of Saul, with his clothes torn and dust upon his head. He fell before David to deliver the news. He reported that the people of Israel had fled and that many had fallen, including Saul and his son Jonathan. David was struck with great grief. He and the men with him wept and fasted until evening for the king and for the fallen of Israel. 

<column-break/>

When David heard of the victory of the Philistines and the deaths of Saul and his sons, he did not rejoice in his enemy's fall but lamented the loss of his leaders. He composed a song of mourning for them, praising their bravery and the gentleness they had shown in life. David then inquired of God and was told to go to Hebron in the land of Judah.

**A**bner, however, the son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army—a man of great influence and power—took Ishbosheth, the remaining son of Saul, and led him across the Jordan to Mahanaim. There, he proclaimed him king over all Israel, except for the tribe of Judah. Judah, meanwhile, had gathered at Hebron and anointed David as their king. Thus began a long conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David. Abner was determined to maintain the power of Saul’s lineage, while David’s strength grew daily. <note>This marks the beginning of the civil war between the northern tribes (Israel) and the southern tribe (Judah).</note> Eventually, the people began to see that the favor of God had moved to David. Even Abner began to realize that the kingdom was destined for David, as Samuel had prophesied years before. The text details the skirmishes between the two factions, specifically the battle at the Pool of Gibeon where the young men of both sides fought. David remained patient, waiting for the tribes to unite under his leadership.

<summary>This page concludes Book VI of Josephus' Antiquities with the death of Saul at Mount Gilboa and the rescue of his remains by the men of Jabesh-Gilead. It begins Book VII, detailing David's mourning and the division of the kingdom between David in Judah and Ishbosheth in the north.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the history of David’s reign. The previous page concluded with the death of Abner and David’s consolidation of power. This section transitions into David’s foreign wars and his personal moral failure regarding Uriah the Hittite.</meta>

Therefore, no one should wonder at what happened unexpectedly; for friendship and victory had already preceded it. David, taking this opportunity, sent messengers to Hanun, the king of the Ammonites, because his father had died; David wished to show that the friendship he had held with Hanun's father would continue with the son. However, the nobles of the Ammonites did not receive this embassy well. They incited their king against David with insulting words, saying that David had sent spies, not to renew friendship, but to scout their fortified camp so that he might return to conquer it. Hanun, following this shallow advice, treated David's messengers with injury. He shaved off half of their beards and cut their garments off as far as the middle of their hips, and then sent them back to David.

David, considering such a great insult to be completely intolerable, sent an army against the Ammonites and placed Joab in command. The Ammonites, prepared for this, gathered to their aid the kings of Syria, Galadia, and Maacah <note>original: "macephanū" – likely referring to the King of Maacah</note>, along with a hundred thousand infantry and chariots. David, seeing how they appeared to excel in strength, called upon the Lord all the more, placing all hope of victory in God. He sent Joab with a brave army against them. When Joab arrived at Rabbah, the city of the Ammonites, he saw the enemy army arranged in two places outside the walls. For the Syrians and the auxiliary infantry were in the field, while the Ammonites were at the gates. 

Joab, having divided his army, chose the best men for himself and directed them against the Syrians; the remaining part of the army he sent against the Ammonites. Over that side, he appointed his brother Abishai <note>original: "Abēſa"</note> to command. When the lines were drawn, Joab said to his brother: "If the Syrians overcome me, you come to my aid; but if the Ammonites overcome you, I will help you." Therefore, Joab began to fight against the Syrians; and as they were unable to withstand their first attack, the enemy were turned to flight. Seeing this, the Ammonites also turned to flight and retreated into the city. Joab returned to Jerusalem as a victor. 

The Syrian king, however, did not remain quiet after having wronged David; he requested aid from the king of the Syrians who ruled across the Euphrates River. When his army arrived, David met them with his own army and, making an attack, killed twenty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry. When the Syrian king saw he could not defeat David, he sent legates to him and sought peace. Thus, with the Ammonites left alone, David again sent Joab with the army to besiege their city, Rabbah. He himself remained in Jerusalem.

Meanwhile, while David was living in Jerusalem, one day when he was walking upon the roof of the palace, he saw a woman washing herself in a bath, who was of very beautiful appearance. When it was reported to David that she was the wife of Uriah, he ordered her to be brought to him, and he lay with her. When the woman found herself pregnant, she reported it to David. David, fearing that she might be exposed to public infamy, sent word to Joab to send Uriah back to him. When Uriah arrived, David asked him how the army was doing. After this, he ordered him to go to his house and wash his feet <note>A common ancient euphemism for resting at home with one's wife</note>. Uriah, however, remained in the royal house. David asked him why he had not gone to his house. Uriah replied that it was not fitting for him to rest in his house while the army of the Lord remained in the field. David detained him for three days and then sent him back to the army, giving a letter to Joab in which he commanded that Uriah be placed in the front line where the fighting was most fierce, so that he might be killed. Joab fulfilled David’s command and placed Uriah in the front line. While they were fighting at the city walls, Uriah was killed, and many others with him.

# THE BEGINNING OF BOOK VIII

## CONCERNING SOLOMON'S YOUTH

In the preceding book, we declared how many years of David’s youth remained, the great evils he fought in war, and how he deserved to live to a great age. Now, we see that Solomon his son, while still a young man, took up the government of the kingdom. We also consider the sedition of Adonijah, although he had been solemnly invited; joined with Joab and Abiathar, who were then in high standing. Adonijah sought the height of power, while Solomon was still young. Adonijah acted without the king's knowledge, but Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, provided for the situation, ensuring that David made Solomon king and that he should rule from the palace. Adonijah, though not a wise man, had expected the kingdom to be his by right of birth, yet by the will of God, it was granted to Solomon.

Adonijah later requested, through the king’s mother, that he be allowed to marry Abishag <note>The young woman who had cared for David in his final days</note>. Although Adonijah claimed he wanted her for his own comfort, Solomon suspected a play for the throne, as marrying a former king's concubine was often a political claim to the crown. Therefore, Solomon, sitting upon the throne of the kingdom, saw this as a threat to the oath of peace. He ordered Adonijah to be put to death. After this, Solomon called Abiathar the priest. He spared him from death because he had served David and carried the Ark of the Lord, but he removed him from the priestly honor. Thus was fulfilled what the prophet Samuel had predicted regarding the house of Eli <note>Abiathar was the last of the line of Eli, whose downfall was prophesied in 1 Samuel</note>.

In place of Abiathar, Zadok was made the high priest. As for Joab, when he heard what had happened to Adonijah, he fled to the sanctuary and took hold of the horns of the altar. Solomon ordered Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, to remove him. Joab refused to leave, saying he would rather die in that holy place. When Benaiah reported this to the king, Solomon commanded him to strike him down even there, to avenge the blood Joab had shed in the past. Thus Joab was buried, and Benaiah was placed over the military in his stead.

Solomon then consolidated his kingdom. He made an alliance with Pharaoh, the king of the Egyptians, and took his daughter as his wife. He began building the walls of Jerusalem, making them much stronger and higher than they were before. He governed with great justice and followed the mandates of his fathers. He went to Gibeon to celebrate a great sacrifice on the altar that Moses had made. There, the Lord appeared to him in a dream and told him to ask for whatever he desired.

<column-break/>

Solomon, however, asked for wisdom and an understanding heart, so that he might be worthy to govern the people; he did not ask for riches or long life, but for the ability to judge the many people under his care. This request pleased the Lord, who granted him not only wisdom such as no man had ever possessed, but also riches and glory beyond all other kings. Solomon, awakening from his sleep, returned to Jerusalem and offered spiritual sacrifices before the Tabernacle.

Shortly thereafter, a difficult case was brought before the king for judgment. Two women who lived in the same house came before him. They had both given birth at the same time, but during the night, one of the infants died. The mother of the dead child took the living child from the other woman’s side while she slept and replaced it with the dead one. When the second woman woke and saw the dead child, she recognized it was not hers. They argued before the king, both claiming the living child.

Solomon, seeing that there was no witness to the deed, ordered a sword to be brought. He commanded that the living child be cut in half, so that each woman might have one part. At this, the real mother, filled with love and misery for her son, cried out to the king to give the child to the other woman rather than kill it. But the false mother agreed to the division, saying, "Let it be neither mine nor hers." By this, the king knew the true mother and ordered the child to be returned to the woman who had shown mercy. All the people marvelled at this divine wisdom in their king.

<margin>C</margin>
The king also established governors over the provinces to manage the kingdom’s affairs. One was in the land of Galilee, and another was the son-in-law of Solomon, having married his daughter Basemath. Others were placed over the regions of Bashan and Gilead, overseeing the great cities there.

<margin>D</margin>
The daily provisions for Solomon’s court were immense: many measures of fine flour and meal, and a great number of oxen and fatted sheep, besides deer and birds. His fame grew because of his peace and the abundance of his reign.

<margin>O</margin>
God gave Solomon such vast wisdom that he surpassed the wisdom of the ancients, including the famous wise men of Egypt and the Hebrews like Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda. He composed three thousand parables and a thousand songs. He spoke with knowledge about all plants, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows on the wall, and about all animals, birds, and fish. There was no part of nature he did not understand. Furthermore, he possessed the power to cast out demons, leaving behind incantations by which people are cured. This method of healing remains among us to this day. I myself have seen a man named Eleazar, in the presence of the Emperor Vespasian and his sons, cure those possessed by demons using a ring and the incantations of Solomon.

### Dius Mentions This:

Dius <note>original: "dios" — referring to Dius the Phoenician, an ancient historian</note>, the writer of ancient things, who translated histories from the Phoenician language for the Greeks, mentions this. He records that Hiram, the son of Abibalus, succeeded to the kingdom. He lived fifty-three years and reigned thirty-four. This Hiram enlarged the spaces of the land and dedicated a golden column in the temple of Jupiter. Furthermore, he cut timber from Mount Lebanon for the roofs of temples and destroyed ancient shrines to build new ones, specifically the temple of Hercules and Astarte <term>Astarte: a major Phoenician goddess of fertility and war</term>. 

It is also recorded that Hiram once increased the labor of the workers and that Solomon sent to him certain riddles to be solved. He requested that if he could not solve them, he should pay a fine of many drachmae <note>original: "darchma" — a Greek silver coin</note>. When Hiram could not solve them, a man named Abdemon <note>original: "abdamo"</note>, a Tyrian by birth, was sent to solve the riddles that Solomon had proposed. He solved them and proposed others in return, which Solomon could not solve, and thus he had to pay back a sum of drachmae. This is what Dius narrates about Solomon and Hiram.

When King Solomon saw the walls of the Tyrians, he desired to build other cities with great firmness. In the desert of lower Syria, he built a very large city, a journey of two days from Upper Syria and one day from the Euphrates. He chose this place because it had an abundance of water and very cold springs. In the desert, Solomon began to build this city, which is near the river. This city, because of its location and its eminent walls, the Syrians called Tadmor <note>original: "tadamir"</note>, which the Greeks call Palmyra. 

King Solomon was supreme in all these things. Nor did he cease to rule with justice and the fear of the Lord. The wisdom of God was in Solomon, and it was constant. The years from the time of Abraham until Solomon are calculated as one thousand and fifty years. 

<margin>The origin of the title Pharaoh</margin> 

The kings of Egypt were called Pharaohs. Before the time of Solomon, the title Pharaoh was used by those who commanded. For Pharaoh, according to the Egyptians, signifies "king." I have found in other books that after Solomon, no other king of Egypt was called by the name Pharaoh. Later, the queens were called by their own names, such as the queen who came to Solomon, of whom no further mention is made here. Thus, the books of the kings agree on many things.

**The King** also commanded that from the mountains of Lebanon, machines should be used for labor, and he placed a multitude of servants there to exercise vigilance. Every year, a selection of men was made for this service.

<column-break/>

Therefore, no heroes of ferocity were in the city. Solomon had servants who were from the remnants of the subject nations, whom he used as laborers for the ironwork and the chariots. There were five hundred commanders who oversaw these works. 

Solomon also prepared many ships on the Red Sea, in a place called Ezion-Geber <note>original: "fclonauher" — an ancient port city</note>, in the city of Berenice. This region belongs to the Hebrews. Through the benefit of King Hiram, who sent skilled sailors and pilots experienced in maritime matters, Solomon's ships sailed to a place that was once called Ophir <note>original: "opỹhira"</note>, but is now called the Land of Gold, in India. From there, they collected four hundred talents of gold for King Solomon.

**The Queen of Sheba** <note>original: "fỹba" — likely Sheba or Saba</note>, who is called the Queen of the Ethiopians, was a woman of most excellent wisdom. Hearing of the fame and virtue of Solomon, she desired to experience his wisdom for herself. She came with many gifts to test him with hard questions. When she arrived, Solomon showed her great hospitality and solved every question she proposed. She was overwhelmed with amazement at his wisdom and the magnificence of his palace, the order of his servants, and the discipline of his house. She observed the sacrifices of the priests at the altar, which were performed with great devotion. She said that although she had heard much of his wisdom and his kingdom, the reality far exceeded the reports. She blessed the servants and friends of Solomon who were privileged to hear his wisdom every day. She gave him many gifts: gold, and an abundance of spices, and precious stones. It is said that the balsam <term>Balsam: a highly prized aromatic resin used in medicine and perfume</term> which we now have in our land was first brought by her as a gift to the king. Solomon, in turn, gave her many good things and allowed her to choose whatever she desired from his own treasures. 

At that same time, much gold, precious stones, and "almug" <note>original: "puchlt/pumicite" — referring to almug or algum wood</note> wood were brought to the king. From this wood, he made musical instruments—harps and psalteries—with which they sang divine hymns. Of all the wood brought to King Solomon, this was the most excellent in beauty and magnitude. No one should think this wood is like that which we see today, for it has a natural sweetness and was used for the most precious works. 

Solomon also had many chariots and horses. The number of his horses grew to twenty thousand. King Solomon took great care to have the most beautiful horses, and they were adorned so that they appeared with great speed and beauty. He also appointed horsemen for them.

For a long time they sang of these things. After Solomon lived, he was stirred up by an invincible adversary named Hadad, whose old hatred had this cause: Hadad was a boy of the royal family of Edom. When Joab, the commander of the Hebrew army, was wasting the land, the boy fled to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, who received him with great affection. He gave him a house and a province to inhabit. When he reached a certain age, Pharaoh loved him so much that he gave him his wife’s sister, named Tahpenes, as a wife, by whom he had a son. When he heard in Egypt of the deaths of David and Joab, he went to Pharaoh and asked to be permitted to return to his own country. When Pharaoh asked what he lacked or what evil he had suffered that he hurried to leave, he could not be stayed. He was dismissed. At that time, Solomon was being invaded because of his transgressions; through sins, the land was divided. Hadad came from Pharaoh into Edom. Since he could not gather a nation because Solomon held the garrisons, he rose up and went to Syria. There he found a man who had fled from his master, and they formed a friendship. He had a great multitude of bandits with him; they went up and took Syria and Rezon became king. Then he was said to be an adversary who afflicted the province of Solomon.

At this time, Jeroboam the son of Nebat raged against Solomon. He was a boy left by his father, and Solomon, seeing him to be a robust and strenuous young man, appointed him over the guard of the walls when he was working on the fortifications in Jerusalem. He praised his nature and put him in charge of the tribe of Joseph. Not long after, when Jeroboam was coming to Jerusalem, a prophet of God named Ahijah met him. He took Jeroboam aside to a quiet place and tore his own new cloak into twelve pieces; he told Jeroboam to take ten pieces. He predicted that God willed to take the kingdom from Solomon and his son, leaving them two tribes, and giving ten to Jeroboam, because Solomon had been drawn away by women and had subjected himself to the filth of their worship. "This is the reason God has loosened his bond with Solomon. Be virtuous, that you may possess this palm of honor, just as David wished to be." Jeroboam, clarified by the prophet's words, did not remain quiet; he saw an open path and, having come to the assembly, he used the words of the prophet to persuade the people to withdraw from Solomon. When Solomon learned of his will and deceit, he sought to apprehend and kill him. Jeroboam fled to Shishak, the king of Egypt.

<column-break/>

He stayed there until the death of Solomon. Solomon died after forty years <note>The Hebrew Bible says 40; Josephus often says 80</note> of reigning and lived ninety-four years. He was buried in Jerusalem. His felicity and wisdom excelled all kings; but he was perverted by the love of women. Because of the evils that came upon the Hebrews, this must be explained.

After the death of Solomon, his son Rehoboam succeeded to the kingdom, born of an Ammonite woman named Naamah. The leaders of the people sent for Jeroboam. When he came, they went to Rehoboam. It was decided they would meet at Shechem, where he was to be ordained king. The leaders and Jeroboam asked Rehoboam to lighten their burden and be better than his father, who had placed a heavy yoke and command upon them. They said if he ruled with gentleness rather than fear, they would love him. He told them to return in three days. This kept them in suspense. He sought advice on how to answer. The elders, who knew the nature of the people, advised him to speak mildly to the people and the king’s followers, and thus bind the people to him as subjects. But he left this excellent counsel and went to the young men with whom he had been educated. They, not thinking of what was better, told him to speak harshly to the people. 

When the third day came and the people were in suspense to hear the king’s words, hoping for clemency, he followed the advice of the youths and responded harshly. He told them that his father had been a burden, but he would be a greater one. The people, grieving at such words, cried out with a great voice that they had no share in David or the house of his father. They abandoned the Temple his father had built and were inflamed with bitterness. Rehoboam sent Adoram to persuade them to return, but the people stoned him to death. Rehoboam, burning with fear and fearing he might suffer evil, mounted his chariot and fled to Jerusalem. The ten tribes together chose Jeroboam as their king. Thus the house of David lost the kingdom. Rehoboam gathered one hundred and eighty thousand chosen warriors to fight the people and bring them back to servitude. But he was prohibited by the prophet Shemaiah <note>original: "addo p pham" — likely referring to Shemaiah or Iddo</note> from making war. He said it was God's will that the kingdom be divided. Rehoboam stayed in his garrison. Now the reign of Jeroboam over the ten tribes and Rehoboam over the two tribes will be explained.

The kingdom that Jeroboam established was not stable, for he feared that if the people went to Jerusalem to worship at the festivals, they might repent and return to Rehoboam. He thought of an evil plan. He made two golden calves and placed one in Bethel and the other in Dan. He built shrines for them. He addressed the people, saying they should not weary themselves by going to Jerusalem, for God is in every place. "These are your gods," he said, "who led you out of Egypt." He dedicated one in Bethel and the other in Dan. This was the beginning of evils for the Hebrews, as they withdrew from the author of their life. Jeroboam also made priests, not from the tribe of Levi, but from whoever wished to be a priest. This was a violation of the law. While Jeroboam was celebrating a festival he had invented and stood by the altar, a prophet from Jerusalem named Jadon <note>original: "iadas" — Josephus calls him Jadon; the Bible leaves him unnamed as the "Man of God"</note> came, sent by God. He cried out against the altar, prophesying that a descendant of David named Josiah would one day destroy the false priests upon it. As a sign that this was from God, the altar suddenly split and the ashes were poured upon the ground. Jeroboam stretched out his hand to seize the prophet, but his hand withered and he could not pull it back. He begged the prophet to supplicate God that his hand might be restored.

### The Prophet and the King

<column-break/>

Although his hand appeared to be restored to its natural state <note>This refers to a miracle where King Jeroboam’s hand withered when he tried to seize a prophet, then was healed by the prophet's prayer</note>, his impiety did not rest then. Instead, the prophet warned him again upon his arrival that it was not the Lord’s will for him to enter, nor to taste any bread or water there. He stated that this was a command from God: that he should return by a different road than the one he had used to travel there. 

While the prophet was following this path of abstinence, a certain old man—referred to here as a **false prophet**—approached him. This man sought to bring the prophet back to eat with him, eventually overcoming his resolve by falsely claiming that he had been sent by the Lord with a message to bring him home.

# The Deeds of the Kings of Judah and Israel

### The Victory of Abijah over Jeroboam

He might possess and contemplate better things; it would be a small thing for the divine power. He rules and will be conquered; it is that which yields to the greatness of virtue. This entire matter regarding Abijah <note>original: "abrae," likely a transcription error for "Abiae"</note> is philosophical. To this end, during the confrontation, Jeroboam was told he should by no means do this. Abijah lived, and because he had at one time repented of his sins, he expiated them. Abijah, however, in his victory, again trusted in this: that although he seemed to have smaller numbers, he believed he could prevail against the untamed enemy. That confidence came from the priests, the altar, the trumpets, and the shouting as they attacked the enemy. Jeroboam trusted in his army. He was defeated, and the confidence in victory faded, so that peace proceeded from Abijah. For such was the invincible nature of the war, and the confidence with which he won, that neither the ages nor the barbarians could weaken the army of Jeroboam as much as God did in granting this most famous victory. Because of this, the strength of the enemy was broken in war, and their most fortified cities fell, including Bethel <note>original: "babilum," likely a transcription error for "Bethel"</note> and its regions; Jeroboam had held all under his dominion, but after this defeat he was shattered and had no further strength to resist. However much time Abijah lived after this victory, he survived only a short time before he died, having reigned for three years. He was buried in Jerusalem, in the tombs of his ancestors.

<margin>King Asa</margin>
### The Reign of Asa

It is said his son reigned 20 years <note>Biblical sources state 41 years; the "XX" may be a transcription error or refer to a specific period</note>, by the name of Asa. For ten of those years, he lived in peace. His son Asa succeeded him. His mother was called Maachah. During his reign, his early years were peaceful for ten years.

<margin>Jeroboam</margin>
### The End of the House of Jeroboam

Jeroboam reigned for twenty-two years and then died. He was succeeded by his son Nadab in the year of Asa’s reign. Because he had been evil and followed the path of his father’s crimes for two years, he was slain by Baasha, the son of Ahijah, who had stood against him in the army. While he was besieged and taken by treachery, he died at the hands of Baasha, son of Ahijah. After his death, Baasha took power and, as the prophet had foretold, he wiped out the entire house of Jeroboam, so that they were torn by dogs and birds. This was the abominable end of Jeroboam, a divine victory over the merits of kings who had turned to evil. The King of Jerusalem, meanwhile, always seemed to progress toward perfection; nothing was lacking in his piety or his guarding of the laws. He composed his affairs well, removing all wickedness and the abominations of idols.

### The War Against the Ethiopians

He had in his army chosen men, armed with shields and spears from the tribe of Judah and Benjamin. In the tenth year of his reign, while he was at rest, a victory came to Asa against a very great army. Zerah <note>original: "Hara"</note>, the King of the Ethiopians, came with 800,000 infantry, 10,000 cavalry, and 700 chariots. When he reached the territory of Judah with his army, Asa met him. They set their camps against each other in the valley called Zephathah <note>original: "ronaullo"</note>, near Mareshah. When he saw the multitude of Ethiopians, Asa prayed to God to make him victorious. He confessed to the Lord that He is the one who can help the few against the many and make the weak prevail over the strong. A sign of victory was shown to Asa, and with divine help, he prevailed in the war. He struck down many Ethiopians and pursued the rest as far as the region of Gerar. After the defeat of the enemy, he turned to the plundering of the city of Gerar. As he returned from the victory, the prophet Azariah met him.

<margin>Azara</margin>
### The Prophecy of Azariah

The prophet Azariah, a wise man, met him and told them that the victory had been granted by God because they proved themselves just. He warned that they must continue to call upon the name of the Lord. If they remained in His commands, they would always prevail over enemies and have a happy life. But if they abandoned religion, they would fall into a state where there is no true king, no teaching priest, and no law. Hearing this, the king and the people exhibited great zeal for justice. King Asa was not merely a king in name; he observed the laws diligently and kept the peace for many years.

<margin>Jeroboam</margin>
<unclear>

Asa, however, seeing the wickedness of the successors of Jeroboam, continued to rely on God as his helper. When Baasha began to build Ramah to prevent anyone from going to King Asa in Judah, Asa took the silver and gold from the temple and sent it to Ben-Hadad <note>original: "ficadr"</note>, the King of the Damascenes, to break his treaty with Baasha. The King of Damascus accepted the money and sent his commanders to attack the cities of Israel, such as Ijon and Abel-maim.

<column-break/>

When Baasha heard this, he abandoned his work on Ramah and returned. He had intended to use the fortified city as a base against Asa.

<margin>King Asa</margin>
Afterwards, Asa’s reign continued, and Baasha was succeeded by his son Elah <note>original: "belen/helen"</note>. He reigned for two years before he was struck down by the word of the Lord. While he was feasting, his servant Zimri <note>original: "Zaree/Zambri"</note> killed him and took the throne, wiping out the entire house of Baasha.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Kingdom of Israel during the reign of King Ahab, specifically focusing on his conflict with the prophet Elijah and the transition into the narrative of Naboth’s vineyard and the wars with Syria.</meta>

# The Deeds of the Kings of Israel

### The Prophet Elijah and the Contest on Mount Carmel

**Column 1**

King Ahab had sent out men to seek water and grass for the animals. At that time, Obadiah <note>The steward of Ahab’s palace who remained a faithful worshiper of God.</note>, who was in charge of the king’s house, met the prophet Elijah. During the time when Jezebel <note>Ahab's queen, notorious for her promotion of the god Baal.</note> was killing the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah had taken a hundred prophets and hid them in caves by fifties, feeding them with bread and water. When Obadiah went on the king’s orders, Elijah met him. Obadiah asked him who he was, and Elijah told him to go to Ahab and say, "I am here." Obadiah responded in fear, asking what wrong he had done that he should be sent to his death. He explained that Ahab had searched every kingdom and nation for Elijah, and if the Spirit of the Lord should carry Elijah away to an unknown place after Obadiah announced his presence, the king would surely kill him.

Elijah, however, remained firm and told him that he would certainly show himself to Ahab that day. When Obadiah told the king that he had seen Elijah, Ahab soon went to meet him. When they met, Ahab accused him of being the one who disturbed the Hebrew people. Elijah, with no fear, replied to the king that he was not the one who disturbed Israel, but rather the king himself and his father’s house, because they had forsaken the true God to follow the idols of Baal <note>A Canaanite weather and fertility god.</note> and the foreign gods of the provinces. Elijah then commanded the king to gather all the people at Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves <note>Original: "luco," referring to the prophets of Asherah, often associated with sacred groves.</note>.

When they had all come to the mountain by the king’s command, Elijah stood in their midst and said: "How long will you waver between two minds? <note>Original: "qu’ ad usqz dū sū mentes haberz," a paraphrase of "How long will you limp between two opinions?"</note> If the Lord is the true God, then follow Him. If Baal is god, go to him." When the people did not respond, Elijah proposed a test to prove the truth. He suggested they take two bulls; the prophets of Baal would choose one and place it on an altar without putting fire under it, and he would do the same with the other. They would then call upon their gods, and the God who answered with fire to consume the sacrifice would be recognized as the true God. The people agreed to this.

The prophets of Baal went first. From morning until noon, they called out to their gods. Elijah mocked them, saying they should cry with a louder voice, for perhaps their god was talking, or away on a journey, or perhaps he was sleeping and needed to be awakened. They continued until the afternoon, cutting themselves with swords until they were covered in blood, but there was no voice and no response.

Elijah then called the people to him. He took twelve stones, representing the twelve tribes of the Hebrew people, and rebuilt the altar of the Lord. He prepared the sacrifice and ordered that water from a spring be poured over the altar and the wood three times, until the water filled a trench around it. Standing there, he prayed to the Lord. Immediately, fire fell from heaven and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and even licked up the water in the trench. When the people saw this, they fell on their faces and shouted that the Lord is the true God. 

Shortly after, a great rain began to fall. Ahab went in his chariot to Jezreel, and Elijah, girded with strength, ran before the chariot. When Jezebel heard of what had been done and how the prophets had been killed, she threatened Elijah. Fearing for his life, Elijah fled into the wilderness. He sat down under a tree and asked to die, but an angel touched him and provided bread and water. Strengthened by this food, he walked for forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, just as Moses had once received the Law there.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

The narrative then turns to the matter of the possession of land and a certain vineyard. Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, which was near the palace of King Ahab. Ahab spoke to Naboth, asking to buy the vineyard or exchange it for a better one so he could use it as a vegetable garden. However, Naboth refused, saying it was the inheritance of his fathers and he could not give it up. 

Ahab returned to his house heavy and displeased. When Jezebel saw him, she asked why he was so troubled. After he explained Naboth’s refusal, Jezebel told him to be of good cheer, for she would give him the vineyard. She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his ring, ordering the elders of the city to falsely accuse Naboth of blasphemy. Consequently, Naboth was taken out and stoned to death. 

When Elijah heard of this, he was sent to Ahab to pronounce judgment, telling the king that in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, they would also lick the king's own blood. 

The text also records the conflicts with Ben-Hadad, the king of Syria. Ben-Hadad gathered his entire army and thirty-two kings with him to besiege Samaria. He sent messengers to Ahab with arrogant demands, claiming Ahab’s silver, gold, wives, and children as his own. Ahab initially submitted, but when the demands became even more intrusive, he consulted the elders of the land and refused. This led to a series of battles where, despite the great numbers of the Syrian army, the forces of Israel were granted victory by divine intervention to show that the Lord is God not only of the hills but also of the valleys.

# JEHOSHAPHAT THEREFORE
<margin>Chapter One</margin>
**J**EHOSHAPHAT therefore, having returned to **Jerusalem** after the war which he had waged with **Ahab** against the King of **Syria**, was met by the prophet **Jehu**. And he [the prophet] blamed him for why he permitted himself to be allied with **Ahab**, an impious and wicked man. If he had commanded you to be killed, if it had been his intention to destroy them, just as he had done to those he led into captivity in war; but to slaughter him would not have been a punishment, but a wicked loss of divine power. Upon hearing this, the king sent someone to the house of **Elisha** <note>original: "Helisei"</note> to lead him to punishment, fearing that some ruinous event might occur if he continued to live. The cause for such a harsh command was the siege by the king of Syria, who had come against the king of Israel with opposing force. He had come believing he could resist, but he felt the skill of the siege-works closing in, and had besieged the city with a tumultuous fortification. Against those whom the Lord sent against them—the Syrians—they were binding them by machines for capturing the city and by a lack of food. 

This condition was brought upon the besieged city. When the siege had proceeded so long that the lack of food prevailed over everything, and out of the horror of hunger they sold the **head of a donkey** for eighty silver pieces, and they purchased a small measure of **pigeon dung** <note>original: "fimi columbarii"; this refers to extreme famine where even waste products or low-grade pulse were sold at high prices</note> for five silver pieces. Horror gripped the entire city, lest the cares of their strength wither through the disaster of hunger; and sorrow grew in the citadels among the guards, lest they be stained by the enemy or the enemy be informed of their actions. 

While this was happening, a certain woman cried out to another woman—one truly skilled in divine matters—concerning a thing they could not foresee. She said, "Do not look at what is hidden or whether you can snatch something away." When the other said it was better to ask, the king deigned to listen. He ordered her to state her grievance or say whatever she wished. She confessed that she had made a pact with another woman, her neighbor and friend: because of their extreme want, they would take turns slaughtering their sons so that they might both eat them. She said that on the first day she had killed her son and shared the portion; but now the other woman, breaking the pact, had hidden her own son so as not to eat him. 

When the king heard this, he was moved by vehement affliction and tore his clothes at this cruel turn of events. For a long time, he wished to make Elisha’s presence ineffective because he would not supplicate God, who prevails for those who pray to Him to take away all violence. Suddenly he sent a man to take off Elisha's head. The messenger therefore hurried, shouting against the prophet, but the servants were in hiding...

Elisha’s words were these: "I know that you will be a great and powerful king." But he also foresaw that Hazael would dash children against stones and rip open the bellies of pregnant women.

Hazael then went to the king and announced only good news: that he would gain his life and recover. However, he was acting against the prophet’s warning. <margin>The death of Uzziah</margin>
He had entered the city. Once roused, he built many towers and gathered a multitude of citizens, providing them with great fortifications and instructing many. At that time, they also possessed an innumerable multitude of animals; for the land was rich and fertile, serving as pasture for the cultivators. He held a great interest in planting and sowing, and these crops yielded much fruit. He also raised altars everywhere in his fields, and he fortified an army of many thousands of the strongest men, who by their own strength could govern many riches. He constructed an army for their cohorts and armed them with weapons. He provided them with everything: the bow, the shield, the breastplate, and many machines for hurling projectiles. Everywhere, engines were prepared for the purpose of conquering, including javelins and grappling hooks. For a long time, he persisted in these things, and there was nothing that could be done that he did not prepare. But a mortal, drawn against the immortal substance, wished to act against it at all times. Yet the immortal substance is piety toward the Lord and the keeping of His commandments. The heart of King Uzziah <note>original: "ozias"</note> was lifted up because of his prosperity, and descending into his father's ways, he thought he could declare himself master, and his eyes apprehended the magnitude of his possessions. During a general festival, he entered the temple of the Lord to occupy the priestly role and to offer a gift upon the golden altar. And the priest Azariah, of the priestly line, along with other priests, forbade him and commanded him to exit the temple. He attempted to do what was spoken of as forbidden, for the priesthood must be retained by the priests, lest one incur death. He shouted at them in the sight of the people, and a splendor <note>The text here refers to the biblical account of leprosy appearing on his forehead like a sudden light or stroke.</note> broke out upon him. At the hour he ascended the temple, in the place called Eroge <note>original: "erogo", referring to En-Rogel</note>, a part of the mountain to the west split in half. It rolled forward for four furlongs <note>original: "vii. stadia", though Josephus says four</note> toward the east, such that it closed the road and overwhelmed the king's gardens. Thus, while the priests were standing in the temple, his sin was made manifest. A mark appeared upon his person so that he could not escape. Fourfold confusion fell upon him, and he was afflicted. He who thought he had sufficient power now saw his judgment fulfilled. <margin>The judgment of the Lord</margin> This act was beyond human nature, and as the hand of the Lord pressed upon him, he suffered this passion. He was removed from the city and lived apart, while his son Jotham <note>original: "ioathan"</note> governed the kingdom. All the army of the Lord was deserted by him. He lived seventy-six years, of which he reigned fifty-two. He was buried alone in his own gardens.

<margin>148</margin> In the fourth year of the reign of the king of Israel, the son of Ahaz, Hezekiah, began to reign in Jerusalem. He was a religious victor. Then Hezekiah called for a great festival of Unleavened Bread <note>term: "azymis", the Passover festival</note> in Jerusalem. He sent messengers throughout Israel and Judah, warning them not to remain in their evil ways but to return to the ancient worship of God. He promised that if they came to Jerusalem, they would find grace and feast together. When they arrived, King Hezekiah and the leaders offered sacrifices: seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven he-goats. The priests laid their hands upon them as a sin offering for the king and the people. They offered burnt offerings with songs and the sounding of cymbals and harps, just as in the days of David. The rest of the sacrifices were so numerous that they could hardly be counted. Indeed, they sacrificed seventy bulls and one hundred rams.
