<meta>This page continues the history of the late Kingdom of Judah, picking up from the reign of Jehoiakim and transitioning into the final days of Jerusalem under King Zedekiah, the Babylonian siege, and the ministry of the prophet Jeremiah.</meta>

Baruch had hidden the net <note>original: "rete," likely referring to the scroll or the snare of the king's anger</note>, and when he had brought the book to King Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedecye"</note>, the King, in the depths of his soul, had cast aside his sadness; but when he heard what was written in the books, he did not merely tear the book but committed it to the fire, and ordered Jeremiah and Baruch to be brought to him by messengers. They, however, were hiding. Not much time later, a great force reached Babylon. Zedekiah acted with you <note>the people</note> as you yourselves walked, such was his condition; he was to suffer many things, even as he suspected. The common faith of the army everywhere ought to be known: if then the strongest and most beautiful man falls, then his lord and those who rebuilt the walls were commanded to be buried; his son was taken by death. The religious name of his family was known everywhere. He was led to Babylon, in which also the prophet Ezekiel was led out, while the king was still a boy in this state, in the year 96. Of the kings, he was the 13th. His successor had a mother named Honor <note>likely Nehushta</note>. He was called Jehoiachin <note>original: "ioiachim"</note> by Zedekiah. And so King Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchad"</note> showed him favor, for he hastened to come to him when he invaded. Fearing lest the common people would remember the former peace and help the invader, he invested the army at Jerusalem in the royal seat.

Jehoiachin, when he had arrived, was kind as is right, and not wishing to see the city perish on his account or to be deceived, took his mother with his kinsmen to meet the king, going out to him. And above all this, for the sake of their lives, they used pure things because he did not know he was a parent. Nor did they kill him: he opened the city to him. He himself had wanted to keep faith, and all the gifts which he guarded were then changed. He took whatever remained of the wealth. Ten thousand eight hundred and thirty-two were led away; he took Jehoiachin and his mother and aunt and led them to Babylon, where he shut up the multitude. The fathers of Jehoiachin were to live in prison. Then the king promoted Jehoiachin, son of Jehoiachin, through his brother’s mother, through Zedekiah. Our Zedekiah was twenty-one years old, twelve years before his father: for neither he nor his brother was clothed with much when he was a private citizen in the greatest place. 

Wherefore Jeremiah the prophet—that is, he who had come frequently—represented all justice and deserted impurity, urging them to cultivate justice and not to approach wicked leaders or false prophets who he said would seduce them; for they sang prophecies before the fall and the Assyrians, and therefore they did not wish to fight and win. There was nothing in the grass, nor were we found in these things. Zedekiah, however, while he heard Jeremiah saying these things, felt from the first as though they were speaking even then. And when he was superseded by the tribunals, again fearing for himself, he was of an averse mind toward the prophet: but he went where he wished. The prophet spoke to Zedekiah, trembling for the future of his own will, when he was in charge of Jerusalem. But Zedekiah was against Nebuchadnezzar, and in agreement with Zedekiah, the prophet Jeremiah said again that the city would be fortified and then plundered by Babylon: Jeremiah said, "He has come to lead you into Babylon." Although all things were spoken harshly, they came to pass just as these prophets interpreted and explained.

**Meanwhile**, when Nebuchadnezzar realized that Zedekiah, whom he had established as king, intended to come only into friendship with himself, he began to look upon him with an army, and when he came against Zedekiah at Babylon, this was a just war of siege. Then they came to Jerusalem. The King, hearing of the Egyptians <note>the Pharaoh's army</note>, because Zedekiah had come to them at the time of the siege, took up the oath of war by fleeing: for he had broken the siege. Nebuchadnezzar, when he had resumed the siege, ran to meet the Egyptians who had come out, and they were surely overcome and turned to flight from all of Syria. Meanwhile, the false prophets seduced Zedekiah, saying that Nebuchadnezzar would not come to Jerusalem and conquer or return. And they said all those who were captives in Babylon would be led back through the gates of the temple. Jeremiah, in a false manner <note>according to his critics</note>, tried to prove the opposite, saying those who persuaded the king were doing evil: when nothing of their own was in the prophecy, that the kings would come and Jerusalem would return to ruin. It would be besieged by force. And the people would be corrupted by hunger. The captives would be led away, and the divine temple and church would be led into the fire, the city overturned. And the Babylonian king alone would perpetrate this upon them. And so the city did not believe the prophet, and the wicked of the time deserted to impious Babylon. They thought, "We shall rebuild the house of Jerusalem." 

Many believed Jeremiah, but the princes and the impious of that time spoke against him according to their own minds, and they added to his troubles. Jeremiah, however, when he had wished to go into his own country, which is Anathoth, thirty stadia from Jerusalem, was seized at the watch-tower when it was time to go out, because they thought he was deserting to the Babylonians. He said their words were false, but they wished to prepare for their own impiety. The prince turned him back: they did not listen to the truth. To the judges and magistrates, he suffered words and torture; he was kept as a survivor, for he endured much. At this very time, neither for King Zedekiah was there peace, nor did King Nebuchadnezzar return over Egypt, but they came to wound the city and besieged Jerusalem with great zeal on the tenth day of the month.

**To** the people of Jerusalem, indeed, while poor in goods, other great evils entered: hunger, the languor of disease pressed upon them. Jeremiah, while he was in custody, warned the people to receive the king of Babylon, opening the gates: for he said that by doing this they could be saved, otherwise they would be destroyed at the root; but they would not be sent out, nor would they die of hunger but at the hands of the enemies. He declared they should go out to the fortified Chaldeans to avoid death. The princes heard these things, and amidst the evils they suffered, they attacked him with words. They said the king should kill this man who was near him because he broke their spirits; they judged his promises as evil and softening the people, while the king fought for the safety of the country, but he moved or induced them to flee. The king sent words in prayer: he said he did not see himself praying unless at a later time, so that they might not happen; he prohibited those wishing to send him into prison. Jeremiah was bound with hunger in a pit <note>cistern</note> full of dregs and water, so that he might die by being submerged. Jeremiah was submerged up to his throat and lips; he was in the pit to die. One of the king's servants, decorated with honor, an Ethiopian by race <note>Ebed-Melech</note>, reported the prophet's plight to the king, saying they had done evil to his friend, for he was submerged in fear and dying. And by the king's command, they came to find him; when he heard the prophet, he sent eighty men so that...

<column-break/>

...with ropes and rags <note>original: "fenuque & fumu[m]," likely mis-transcribed for "pannos," old rags</note> and some joined to him, they clothed the king's word: they extracted Jeremiah with haste. Because he was smoking <note>perhaps meaning dirty or faint</note> with clean things, when they wanted to pull him out, he then committed himself to the guard. He who had shut the prophet in prison came before the king: if he were declared immune. He said if he had anything to say, it must be believed by the victor, who was almost dead from human suffering. He joined himself then to the king of Babylon, and he did not false those words: "If it happens then, do not speak. Our death is condemned." 

The king promised he would not kill him nor hand him over to the princes. He said if the Chaldeans were allowed to come, nothing would be punished, nor the city destroyed by fire, nor would Zedekiah, his mother, and himself be dressed as authors of this evil. Thus Jerusalem was besieged as they attacked. Making carts with machines for the siege, King Nebuchadnezzar returned, and he was able to use machines from the walls in the traditional manner. Our city was perishing. Because hunger bloodied the city, they resisted most pressingly, but they languished from labor. They opened the way to our king, but the Babylonian enemy dissolved them. The Babylonians arrived in the city again; Jerusalem, for its own safety, was consumed in Judea. They labored in the night and in despair ran to destroy the enemy's machines. Under King Zedekiah, in his 11th year, the city was wasted by hunger. By stones thrown from the towers, the enemy was opposed. The city was captured in the 11th year of Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the 11th month. But the prince of Babylon, who was at the siege for King Nebuchadnezzar, came into Jerusalem, and he was the first of all who came: Nebuzaradan <note>original: "nabu sardon"</note>, the judge who cared for the cities of Media, came at midnight and entered the temple. Zedekiah, recognizing this, took his own sons and friends and fled from the city toward the king's gardens. The kings ordered the way into Judea. Those who encountered them seized them. He was seen in the way; those who helped were few, as the enemies were close in the province. They fled from place to place. Nothing was taken to the king himself, but his sons were led to King Nebuchadnezzar to die. 

When the king received them, he asked about the commands and where they wished to go. The impious king was pressed and led away. He was to be held by those who were wicked. To King Zedekiah, he then struck his sons before his very eyes, and the princes; he saw all the wickedness. He escaped death but was saved for Babylon. Zedekiah the emperor, when the king finished with Babylon, was led into Babylon. In the time of his father the king, he served in Babylon, according to the word of Jeremiah. Thus he who came to Babylon was also the subject of Ezekiel the prophet. The princes came and spoke of the infidelity of men, because they were not conquered by this which was prepared. 

In the 11th year and 10th month, on the 6th day, Nebuchadnezzar ordered his prince Nebuzaradan <note>original: "nabuzardam"</note> into Jerusalem to overturn the temple, the city, and the regalia. He was prepared to save them on the way for service in Babylon. Arriving in Jerusalem in the 11th year of Zedekiah, he subverted the temple. He took the golden and silver vessels and much wealth which had belonged to Solomon: the columns, the golden table, and the candelabrum. He came when the temple had served for many years. In the 18th year of King Nebuchadnezzar, he subverted the temple and the city. It had stood since Solomon for many years. From the beginning of the world <note>the year of Adam</note> to the devastation of the temple, there were 4514 years, 10 months, and 10 days. The number is manifested by the deeds. Nebuzaradan, after he destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, was favorable and desiring to fortify them; he made a registry of the authors of the temple and the friends who had been armed. When they came, Nebuzaradan opened it to the king in the city of Riblah <note>original: "reblas"</note>. The king ordered the high priest's head to be cut off, and the heads of all the princes. King Zedekiah was led as a victor into Babylon by the command of the kings.

Jotham, and after him Uriah, had died. Following him were Hoshea and then Shallum, these being from the tribe of Issachar. Asfarax <note>This likely refers to Ashpenaz, the chief of the court officials mentioned in the Book of Daniel.</note> said that at this time no son would be born there, though it is said he was the son of the deceased. Afterwards, they appointed a leader over the poor who remained in the land of the Jews: his name was Gedaliah <note>original: "godolia"</note>, the son of Ahikam, a man of most noble birth. Through the presence of Ahikam, they found the prophet Jeremiah. For the king had commanded that Jeremiah could either go to Babylon, remain in the land, or go wherever he wished. Gedaliah, acting as the primary leader, received him in the village of Mizpah <note>original: "masphat"</note>. There he instructed the people to be moved as the royal decree had stated, and told them they ought not to fear the king of the Babylonians. He demonstrated how the aforementioned king had permitted the conquered to remain in the land, and that they should also revere the prophet, as he had not prophesied anything but the truth. They found that the holy man had indeed been a true prophet for many years. If they had stayed for a long time, they would have remained as they wished.

<margin>Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon</margin>
Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon—who was the first to bring the kingdoms of the conquered lands under his yoke by the Lord's will—had allowed Gedaliah to remain in Mizpah. There, among the remnants of the conquered land of Jerusalem, those who had survived gathered and came to Gedaliah in Mizpah. Their leaders were Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jozas, and Ishmael, who was of the royal family. When these leaders saw that Gedaliah treated them kindly with his own resources, it was warned at that time that Ishmael, the king of Jerusalem <note>original: "hirmosolima"; likely a corruption referring to Baalis, King of the Ammonites, who instigated Ishmael.</note>, intended to seize Gedaliah. However, Gedaliah did not keep a Babylonian guard; he sought to comfort the land, as many were weary from those days. He believed Ishmael would remain faithful. Asfarax, however, wished to stay according to his words, just as had been prophesied through Jeremiah. When Gedaliah found himself in despair, Ishmael desired to remain in that land so that people would come to him; in this, he deceived Gedaliah, even as Asfarax wished to move forward. Ishmael, having been invited to a meal by Gedaliah, murdered him and all the Jews who were in the land. They were supposed to remain under the king, but Johanan the son of Amari, fearing the Chaldeans, went toward the king of Egypt. Gedaliah's official Asfarax wished to return but was unwilling. Asfarax wanted them to remain in that land; not only should they not delay, but they should call the prophet Jeremiah back into Egypt.

At this end, it is said the king of Assyria sent word to Zedekiah, the conquered king, that the king of Babylon was coming into Egypt, at which time he would see the subjects provided for him. But there was little time left to rule, and the men remained in Assyria. Later, those returning from Egypt and Assyria came back to Jerusalem, for they observed the words of the Lord spoken through the king and Jeremiah.

And from being a conqueror, he had moved against all the neighboring nations, including the Moabites. When he had them under his power, he then settled his own people there. He led the king and the people of the Hebrews who were there into the Babylonian captivity. The leader said: "Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, himself took captives away from Samaria." Not long after this, the king of Babylon came again and took the more noble men, even those from the royal line of Zedekiah. Those who were found to be beautiful in body and face were ordered to be castrated <note>term: castrari (eunuchs) — a common practice for court officials in ancient Near Eastern empires to ensure total loyalty to the monarch.</note> so that, under the diligent prohibition of their tutors, they might be kept chaste. He took care that they should possess wisdom and learning, being chosen as the best among such a group. Afterwards, they so prevailed in knowledge that they were honored by the king.

However, Daniel thought with his companions that he should not defile himself with the royal food, because he had received a holy covenant. Daniel, however, said that they should be given their own food for ten days, and he would see if they lost anything in the eyes of the king; for by abstaining for a long time, they appeared in a spiritual royal countenance. When they had prayed together and returned and were seen, those who had been received were persuaded by Daniel concerning the royal food.

A short time later, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed a dream, which Daniel interpreted at that time. For he had seen a very large and wonderful statue. Its head was of gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, and its feet were partly of iron and partly of clay. Then he saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands, which struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay and crushed them. Daniel then explained the dream: "You are the head of gold. After you shall rise another kingdom less than yours, and a third kingdom of bronze. The fourth kingdom shall be like iron. But because you saw the feet divided, the kingdom shall be divided." Concerning the magicians of God <note>original: "de magis dei"</note> who are dedicated in fullness: whether there is any faith to be had in them, and in their judging of things to come. If anyone should seek to inquire of them, let them know beforehand: they know of the state of our affairs and what ought to be done quickly toward God, according to what the divine sentence judges. Our kingdom shall also be established forever, and he shall be established as the most just of all kings. Upon hearing this, the king ordered the holy magician <note>This refers to Daniel, who was often categorized among the "magi" or wise men of the Babylonian court.</note> to be brought in the aforementioned months. And since he knew how the outcomes of things are made and the reason of all matters, the king raised him up above all others with honors, rewards, and gifts; and they sustained the prophecy. Among kings, such a cause was a matter of great wonder.

**N**ebuchadnezzar the second, therefore, who is also called the younger, was joined to the prophet in the Latin tongue <note>original: "latiali lingua"</note> and was king of the kings of Babylon. Concerning those subjugated in the land. And there are hay and woods in Babylon: he shall suffer the paths of the wild beast, the king to rule the land. And after much time, when these things were discussed, the estates of the sacred bread remained. Yet what they have brought in the king's part in war, these things also those who do not serve as soldiers—but who labor by plowing the land—desire. When they have harvested and are at the height of their labor, the king commands it all to be gathered. And if they owe it to the king, they offer it. Whether they are soldiers or judges, or if they fulfill a false accusation. And when they have slept with every luxury or reading, others keep watch; for out of love for him, no one dares to leave him while he sleeps, or to go down and see to their own affairs. Instead, they consider this one work necessary: that they keep watch over the prudent king. Why then is the king not seen as the most powerful of all? Since he has such obedient service.

Then Zorobabel <note>Zerubbabel, the leader of the Jewish exiles</note> began to dispute about women and truth, saying: Indeed, you have ordered thus. Wine is strong. Perhaps the king also moves those who obey. But the beauty of women is more powerful than all these. For a woman conceived the king; and women gave birth to and nourished those who plant the vines from which wine flows. There is nothing that we do not have from women. Even clothing and ornament and cultivation are changed and preserved primarily by women: and thus we cannot be separated from women. Even if we possess much gold and silver, and whatever else is precious, as soon as we see a beautiful woman, we deliver all good things to oblivion. We gape at her, astonished: and it is clear we would leave all we possess, provided that we might enjoy the beauty desired by lovers. Often even fathers and mothers are forgotten for a mistress, and they are willing to die together with them for their country. So especially trusting in the beauty of women, we ourselves labor and tolerate every turn of fortune. When we have undergone and done much, we offer it to our wives as if to a master. I once saw the most powerful king with his concubine named Apama <note>original: "apamā alapi filiā" - Apame, daughter of Bartacus</note>, sitting at his right hand. She took the crown from his head and placed it on her own, and he tolerated every force from her. When she laughed, he laughed. And when she was angry, he was confused and sad: he would soothe the woman with flatteries, begging her. It is a pleasure for him to be humbled, if in some way she is held back or conquered. 

After these things, the nobles and satraps looking at one another, the same man, Zerubbabel, began to dispute concerning the truth. While all see that a woman is stronger than wine, or a king is more powerful, it is certain that Truth conquers all things and will conquer again. For if the earth is vast, and the heights are nourished by what is swift, these all are governed by the will of God, who is truth. For God is true and just, and from that same truth all things proceed: it is the strongest judgment. They shall not act against the truth, for no unjust victory prevails. Nor do mortal things which seem strong prevail against the truth. For Truth is immortal and eternal: it is not perceived by beauty alone, nor captured by price, nor by the magnitude of riches. It takes away everything else: discerning just and royal things from those which are shown to be unjust or wicked. When Zerubbabel had finished his discourse on the truth, the multitude praised him, saying he had spoken best, for he alone possessed truth, the invincible strength. Then King Darius commanded him to ask for whatever he wished, and he said he would grant him everything because he had appeared wiser and more prudent. He bid him sit with him and be called his kinsman. Then Zerubbabel reminded the king of the vows he had made to God when taking the kingdom. The vow he had promised was: to rebuild Jerusalem and the Temple, and to return the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried to Babylon. This request he made because he sought wisdom and prudence. King Darius, rejoicing in this, rose and kissed him: and he ordered the satraps that Zerubbabel and those with him should go to the building of the temple. And he commanded the magistrates of Syria and Phoenicia to bring cedar wood from Lebanon to build Jerusalem and the city of God. He ordered all the Jews to be free who wished to return to Judea. He prohibited any official from taking their crops, and ordered that the Jews should possess their land without tribute. He also commanded the Samaritans and those who lived in humble Syria to return what they held of the Jews, and moreover to give gold for the building of the temple. And he permitted their sacrifices and the long-prepared offerings. All the expense, and the sacred vestments in which they would serve in the temple, he ordered to be given, as well as for the rest of the priests and the Levites' musical instruments. He commanded that these be paid from his own treasury. And he ordered a certain amount of money to be provided for the guards of the city and the temple each year for their necessities. It was decreed that what Cyrus had begun before him should be fulfilled and restored, and all things Darius defined should be sent. But above all, Zerubbabel was granted gifts from the royal house. Looking up to heaven, he gave thanks to God with his head bowed for the wisdom by which he was granted victory, saying:

<column-break/>

in no way was I worthy of this loss... he commanded that thanks be given. The king then allowed him to depart. They came to all the Jews... and he opened it to the Jews. They heard what the king had done. For the Jews, days were enjoyed in joy, and they celebrated the reconstruction of their homeland with festive rejoicing. They were provided with food and drink. With joy and pleasantness they sang with pipes and cymbals. And the rest of the multitude of Jews went up with games to Jerusalem. There were 85 others... four hundred and... servants bought. And when the first month had come since they arrived from Babylon, Jeshua the high priest and Zerubbabel gathered them in Jerusalem. They celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles at that time, and the offerings that belonged to the days: and they returned the sacrifices of the Sabbaths and all the festive victims. And on the first day of the seventh month, they began to distribute the money they had given to the stone-cutters and builders, and to those providing food. They brought cedar wood from Mount Lebanon to the port of Joppa, but they encountered resistance from those across the river. They had Jeshua and his brothers and sons, who gave themselves to the work of examining the Jews and the building of the temple. They finished the temple, the priests with their solemn garments and ornaments, and the Levites and sons of Asaph made praise to God. But many of the elders and priests remembered the beauty of the former temple, and seeing the current smallness, they wept. But others were moved to joy. The people rejoiced in the recent completion of the temple; nor was the memory of the former beauty mentioned. The sound of joy exceeded the sound of the weeping of the priests and Levites. 

When the Samaritans heard the sound, they came to the temple. They saw the work being completed. Zerubbabel and Jeshua and the heads of the tribes said it was impossible for them to be joined in the work. For Cyrus first, and now Darius, had committed the building of the temple to them alone. You may worship God in this temple, but the building is for us. After the Samaritans heard this, they persuaded the kings of Syria to prohibit the innovation of the temple. They came to Jerusalem, Sisinnies the governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and Sathrabuzanes with many others, and interrogated the Jews on whose authority they built the temple. Zerubbabel and Jeshua responded: This temple was built long ago by a great king of ours and lasted for many times. But because our fathers sinned against God, it was given into the hands of the Chaldeans, and they were taken captive to Babylon. Afterward, King Cyrus in the first year of his reign ordered that the temple be rebuilt. He ordered that all the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken be returned to Zerubbabel to be brought back to the temple. And by the command of King Cyrus we have come to rebuild. Under King Darius the work was continued. And they made a report of these names. Zerubbabel and Jeshua made this clear. And those who were with him did not cease from the building. 

Darius, when he had read the letter of the Samaritans, ordered the archives to be searched. They found in the records of Cyrus what he had ordered the Jews concerning the temple. Darius the king, reading this, found all the things that Cyrus had ordered. He commanded them to assist the Jews by offering animals for sacrifice: gold, rams, lambs, and kids. Likewise oil and wine, as the priests required. And that they should pray for the health of the king. And those who would go against these mandates would be punished. The king asserted this. They also found the decree of Cyrus as it had been recorded, and the building of the temple continued.

From where, with God's help, he received permission from the king to excellently rebuild the walls and complete the temple. When he found favor among those people <note>The neighbors of Jerusalem, such as the Samaritans and Ammonites</note>, they were greatly troubled and brought many grievances against us when they realized we wished to repair our structures. Let us trust in the Lord, for He who invaded them can dissolve their plans; and day and night we shall not abandon our spirit. When the time for working arrived, and when resources were lacking, he sent machines to the walls so that the work would not be divided. Through the city and the neighboring settlement, he willed it to be done with his own people. Thus, the state was restored beyond what it had been for years. However, he accelerated the construction and finished the walls, even though those who were plotting snares wanted to hinder his will and incited many against the Jews. Nehemiah himself sought to ensure that they would not be separated. When they were pressed, he often sent to you in love; and because of the many armed groups against us, a rumor spread through the land that they might almost abandon the work. 

On the contrary, he was disturbed by nothing and did not abandon the works of his people; instead, the guards with arms took the greatest care. He remained so that he would not fail the desire of the city. He recognized that after the wall was fortified, it was truly a wall of buildings. He commanded that all should work armed by day, and the builders and carriers should be girded with swords and place shields near them. So that if any force should attack, they would be ready for war, and he signaled by a trumpet blast that they should resist, lest they be attacked while naked and unarmed. He himself at night, with the guards, took very little sleep before the work was finished. This labor was sustained for two years and four months, and so at that time the wall of Jerusalem was perfected in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of **Xerxes**, in the ninth month. And because the wall was completed, Nehemiah with all the people sacrificed to God for the building of the wall; and for many days they feasted, while the surrounding nations were greatly indignant. Nehemiah, seeing that there were few people living in the city, asked the priests and Levites to come from the villages to remain in the city. And he built for them at his own expense. He also commanded that the settlers should bring the fruits of their crops to Jerusalem so that the priests and Levites would have food and remain in the land. By this occasion, the great city was filled with a multitude of men. And he wrote all these other good works worthy of praise. Having come to old age, he died, a man benign by nature and just; and having perfected Jerusalem, he left the walls of the Jerusalemites. These things were perfected in the twenty-eighth year of the reign, in the ninth month.

After the death of Xerxes, his kingdom fell to his son **Ahasuerus**, whom they called **Artaxerxes**. During his reign, the care for the Jews was perfected, and peace was established with their wives and children. For when Artaxerxes accepted the kingdom, he ordained one hundred twenty-seven satrapies from India to Ethiopia. In the third year of his reign, he made a banquet for all his subjects and the leaders of the nations, prepared for one hundred and eighty days. Afterward, he fed the people for seven days in a celebration held in Susa. For a pavilion had been erected with silver columns and purple veils extended over them, so that it might hold many thousands of guests. With golden vessels and precious stones, he prepared both a banquet and a spectacle for them. He had commanded the stewards that they should not force anyone to drink, but offer drink to each according to their wish, so they might drink as much as they desired rather than being told what to do; he conceded that each should feast as they wanted. He had also commanded that a separate drink be prepared for the women and the queen, and a banquet was made by her within the palace where the king's royal women were. On the third day, however, wishing to show the excellence of his wife's beauty, who surpassed all women in loveliness, the king sent for her. But she ignored the law, for she knew it was forbidden for the wives of the king to be seen by strangers. And she would not come. Messengers were sent to her repeatedly, telling her the truth, yet she still would not come.

Whereupon the king was moved to anger, and he called to him seven of the wise men who interpreted the laws for him, to know what should be done because his wife, though called, did not come. One of them, named **Muchaeus** <note>original: "eir lery uffintiano" / "Muchaeus" in Josephus</note>, said: "The injury is not done to you alone, but to all the leaders; for if this is allowed, wives will despise their husbands." He argued that her conduct was a shame to the king's banquet. Therefore, he urged that she should be punished and that a decree should go out that every man should be master in his own house. This decree was sent out. When the king's anger cooled, his friends persuaded him to cast out the memory of his former wife and seek throughout the kingdom for beautiful virgins, from whom he might choose a new wife. The king was moved by this; he ordered that throughout the kingdom young virgins be chosen and brought to the palace. Among the many who were brought, there was a certain girl found in Babylon, deprived of both parents, who was raised by her uncle named **Mordecai** <note>original: "mardocheu"</note>. She was of exceeding grace. She was called **Esther**, and she surpassed all in beauty, and the grace of her sight delighted the king. All the virgins were kept under the care of a eunuch, and they were prepared with sweet odors and abundance of ointments to irrigate their bodies for six months. Out of the number of forty thousand <note>A traditional high estimate found in some medieval commentaries</note>, when they were brought to the king's chamber, the king was delighted by Esther. He was led by love and chose her as his wife, celebrating the nuptials in the seventh year of his reign. He commanded a great feast to be celebrated.

<column-break/>

Throughout the whole empire, there was joy. After this, he placed the crown upon the head of Esther. It was not known then from what nation she came. But her messenger, Mordecai, sat at the gate of the palace to know what would happen to the girl. At that time, the king had made a law that no one should approach him unless called; if anyone approached uninvited, they would be put to death unless the king extended his golden scepter to save them. Those who were allowed to approach would kiss it. 

During that time, two eunuchs, **Bagathan** and **Thares**, sought to kill the king. Mordecai heard of this and reported the plot to the king. The king, having found the truth, ordered them to be crucified. He ordered that Mordecai be recorded among the benefactors of the king and commanded that he should stay within the palace. At that time, there was a man with the king named **Haman** <note>original: "aman"</note>, son of Hammedatha, of the race of the Amalekites. By the king's command, he was to be honored and adored by all. But Mordecai would not adore him, for it was against his laws. Haman was moved to great anger when he saw this and inquired who he was. When he found he was a Jew, he thought it a small thing to punish Mordecai alone; he decided to destroy the whole race. For he hated the Jews because they had formerly destroyed the Amalekites, from whom he was descended. He went to the king and said that there was a certain people scattered through the kingdom that was useless, not following the king's laws nor practicing his religion, but being strange and hostile. He suggested they should be rooted out. "Lest there be any loss to your treasury," Haman said, "I promise to give ten thousand talents of my own substance to the king if you allow me to destroy them." The king, however, granted him the money and told him to do with the people as he wished. The king then issued a decree to this effect: 

"The Great King Artaxerxes, from India even to Ethiopia, to the one hundred twenty-seven provinces subject to him. Having rule over many nations and having subjected the whole world, I wish not to abuse the magnitude of my power but to govern my subjects with clemency and leniency. I desire that they may lead their lives without fear and in peace. However, my counselors have informed me that there is a certain people who do not mix with others and who resist our orders, following their own laws and bringing dissension to the nations. Therefore, we have ordained that they, with their wives and children, shall be destroyed by the sword on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, and no one should pity them. Thus, those who are our enemies may be destroyed in one day, and peace may be restored to our empire."

This decree was sent through all the provinces and cities. The Jews were in great mourning. Mordecai, when he learned this, tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went through the city crying out against the slaughter of an innocent people. When the queen saw Mordecai in such a miserable state at the gate, she wanted to call him in, but he refused. The queen then sent her eunuch, **Hatach**, to Mordecai to ask why he was in such a state and would not put off his sackcloth. Mordecai told him everything, including the decree and the promise of money Haman had made to the king for the destruction of the Jews. He sent word to the queen that she must go to the king and supplicate for her people, and not to think that being in the palace would save her. 

When the queen heard this, she sent word back to Mordecai saying that if she entered to the king without being called, she would face death. But Mordecai sent back a message saying that if she remained silent, help would come to the Jews from another place because of their sins, but she and her father's house would perish. Esther then commanded Mordecai to gather all the people to fast and pray for three days, as she and her maidens would also do; then she would go to the king, and if she must die, she would die. Mordecai did as Esther commanded and prayed to the king of heaven to preserve his people. He prayed that God would forgive their sins and liberate them from the threat. He explained that he had not refused to bow to Haman out of pride, but because he would not give the honor due to God to any man. Esther also prayed to the God of her fathers, with tears, that her speech might be persuasive and that she might find favor in the king's eyes, so that the king's heart might be changed and she might save her people. 

After three days of fasting, Esther took off her mourning garments and dressed in royal robes. She went with two maidens, one of whom she leaned upon, while the other followed carrying her train. Her face was flushed with beauty, yet her heart was full of fear. She approached the king. When she saw the king sitting on his throne, clothed in gold and precious stones, his appearance was terrifying.

...perfect and immutable, though he afflicted the Jews. After the death of Joiada <note>original: "iudo," a variant of Joiada</note>, his son **Jaddua** succeeded to the high priesthood. His brother was **Manasseh**, as Josephus records. After the death of Joseph the governor, who had done many evils to the Jews, his successor sent by Darius was **Sanballat** <note>original: "sanaballach," the governor of Samaria</note>; both were temporary rulers. <margin>Sanballat</margin>
After Darius was defeated by the flower of the Macedonians while fighting at the river Issus, and escaped into exile from **Alexander**, he prepared again for a later war. Darius, the leader of the Medes, standing above the river, said after he had camped at the field of Cilicia and taken booty, he came to the places of Pamphylia. The elders and leaders in Jerusalem were indignant that Manasseh, the brother of the high priest, had taken as a wife the daughter of the foreigner Sanballat. They daily ordered him to either separate from his wife or be barred from the altar. Manasseh, however, came to his father-in-law Sanballat and said that while he loved the honor of the priesthood, he did not wish to be separated from his daughter, whom he loved greatly. Sanballat, hearing this, promised to give him not only a priesthood but a governorship and the honor of all places, provided he did not dismiss his daughter. He told him that with the help of Darius, he would build a temple like the one in Jerusalem on Mount Gerizim. Hearing this promise, Manasseh remained with his father-in-law Sanballat. Meanwhile, Jaddua, the high priest in Jerusalem, heard that Alexander was coming to Judea to conquer it, and he sought the mind of God in prayer.

The Jewish priest was then given a vision, and the Lord appeared and told him to be of good courage: they should decorate the city and open the gates, and the people should dress in white, while he and the priests should meet the King in their sacred robes. When he heard the King was not far from the city, he went out with the multitude of priests to a certain place called **Sapha** <note>original: "saph̄m," meaning "the watchtower," also known as Mount Scopus</note>, from which place Jerusalem and the Temple can be seen. When Alexander arrived and saw the high priest in his sacred garments, with the golden miter on his head and the golden plate upon which the Name of God was written, Alexander approached alone, adored the Name, and first saluted the high priest. All the priests greeted him with one voice. The kings of Syria who were with Alexander were stupefied and thought the King's mind was corrupted.

<margin>Parmenio</margin>
**Parmenio**, the general of the army, asked Alexander: "Why, after you have adored the Name, do you grant such grace to the Jews?" Alexander replied: "I did not adore him, but the God whose high priest he is. For while I was in Macedonia, a figure in this very habit appeared to me in a dream. When I asked if I could conquer Asia, he exhorted me not to delay, but to cross over confidently, for he would be my guide and deliver the Persian power into my hands. Therefore, seeing this man now, I remember the vision and trust that by his help I shall achieve all that I have in my heart." After Alexander spoke this, he honored the high priest and went up into the Temple to offer sacrifice to God according to the priest's direction. Alexander himself offered magnificent gifts to the priesthood.

<margin>Daniel</margin>
After this, the priests showed him the **Book of Daniel**, in which it was written that a Greek would destroy the Persian empire <note>Referring to Daniel 8:21</note>. Believing himself to be that person, he was filled with joy. The next day, he called the people and asked what they desired. The high priest asked that they might live by their ancestral laws and that every seventh year <note>The Sabbatical Year</note> they be free from tribute. He granted all these things freely. Alexander then departed Jerusalem for the neighboring cities, where he was received honorably. The Samaritans then came to him, and seeing the honor given to Jerusalem, they began to claim they were Jews.

For these Samaritans, as we said before, have this custom: when they see the Jews in calamity, they deny they are Jews; but when they see the Jews prospering, they claim to be Jews, tracing their descent from Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh. At that time, King Darius, hearing that Alexander had crossed the Hellespont and defeated his satraps, gathered a great army of horse and foot to meet him. Sanballat, after the departure of Alexander, went to Darius to accuse the Jews. But Darius was defeated by Alexander, and Alexander took the mother, wife, and children of King Darius. Alexander then came to Syria, took Damascus, and besieged Tyre. From there, Alexander sent letters to Jaddua the high priest, asking for aid and provisions for his army and seeking friendship. The high priest responded that he had sworn an oath to Darius and would not change it while Darius lived.

<column-break/>

When Darius was defeated, Alexander was indignant and threatened to march against Jerusalem. Sanballat, hearing of Alexander's victory, changed his loyalty from Darius to Alexander. He took seven thousand of his own men and came to Alexander during the siege of Tyre, saying he preferred him as lord over Darius. He petitioned Alexander to build the temple on Mount Gerizim for his son-in-law Manasseh. Alexander granted this. Sanballat then built the temple with great haste and installed Manasseh as high priest. Shortly after beginning this work, Sanballat died. Alexander, having captured Syria, marched toward Jerusalem with his army, intending to be harsh toward the Jews because of their previous refusal of aid. But as recorded, the meeting at Sapha changed his heart.

After Alexander had subdued the world, he died <note>in 323 BCE</note>, and he left his empire to be divided among his successors. Among the priests, Onias succeeded his father. Jerusalem then fell under the power of **Ptolemy son of Lagus** <note>Ptolemy I Soter</note>, who seized Egypt. 

->Here ends the eleventh book of Josephus' Jewish Antiquities.<-

## HERE BEGINS BOOK XII

After Alexander, the king of the Macedonians, had died, his empire and Judea were divided. Many brothers and successors were left. Antigonus seized Asia; Seleucus took Babylon and Antioch in Syria; and Cassander obtained Macedonia. **Ptolemy son of Lagus** took possession of Egypt. They entered into wars with one another over the division of the empire. All these things happened under Ptolemy son of Lagus, who was called "Soter" <note>meaning "Savior"</note>. This King Ptolemy entered the city of Jerusalem by deceit on the Sabbath day. While the Jews suspected nothing and were at rest, he suddenly seized the city and treated them with cruelty. A witness to this is Agatharchides <note>original: "tabat̄eredeſ," a corruption of Agatharchides</note>, who wrote: "There is a nation that inhabits a great and strong city called Jerusalem, which they allowed to fall into Ptolemy's hands because of their superfluous superstition [regarding the Sabbath]." Ptolemy took many captives from the mountains of Judea and Samaria to Egypt, where he made them serve in his army and fortresses. After forty years, his son **Ptolemy Philadelphus** succeeded him.

This Ptolemy Philadelphus was a lover of learning. It is said he built a great library. While he was studying to collect all the world's volumes, **Demetrius of Phalerum**, who was in charge of the library, told the king that he had collected thousands of books, but that the laws of the Jews were missing. He said they were written in the Hebrew tongue and would require much labor to translate into Greek, as the Hebrew language is similar to the Syrian but has its own unique pronunciation. He suggested the King should not spare money to have these laws translated for the royal library. Ptolemy, wanting to show his devotion to learning, agreed. Then **Aristeas**, a friend of the king, who was held in high regard, suggested that if the king wanted to obtain these laws from the Jews, he should first release the Jewish captives taken by his father. He argued that it was inconsistent to ask for their sacred laws while keeping their people in servitude.

### The Royal Banquet and the Wisdom of the Elders

# The Arrival of the Translators

The king invited them to recline for the feast, each according to where they had sat before. After they were all seated, he said: "As you have come from that life," <note>Referring to their journey from Jerusalem to Egypt</note> for he spoke from his great heart. He himself wrote the order of their seating in turn. The King, however, marveled at the slenderness of their limbs <note>original: "tenuitate membrorum"</note> because they encompassed so much wisdom. When they were all assembled together, they stood before the Lord. "I was with you as you advised!" he said. For the nature of men follows this: it is delighted even unto tears when a person has truly grieved; they heard him happily, that is, as one truly rejoicing in God. 

The king ordered that everything should be provided to each person just as it was to be kept for their service. He omitted nothing to show the kindness he had toward those who had come to him; it was clear that his friends and followers celebrated this. He ordered that the guest quarters be prepared quickly, so they would have a place to sleep. 

And so, he called his steward <note>original: "darchonem," a scribal variant for 'archon' or 'architriclinum,' the master of the feast</note> and ordered him to provide for the security of each individual so they might live safely. For when the banquet was arranged, the king sat in order so that they might be brought forward as we see fit; everyone was served alike. He took care that no food should be corrupted <note>original: "carrupta vitarit"; likely referring to the provision of Kosher food for the Jewish elders</note>. Instead, while others enjoyed different things, the steward was entrusted to ensure the masters were served correctly. I have learned that during the time of peace, they were allowed to eat according to their customs.

As he joined them, he ordered that they should be treated with the honor due to elders. When they had come and he saw them coming—for he was concerned with mercy—he prepared to honor the Lord. After they had reclined, he again ordered the steward to minister as usual; to those who came to God, he spoke words. Both the King and the priests <note>original: "sacerdof"</note> offered sacrifices; the King, who provided them life and food, commanded one of the elders named **Eleazar** <note>The High Priest of Jerusalem who sent the translators</note> to offer a prayer. He stood in the midst of them and asked for good things, praying that he might be filled with glory. When he had spoken according to his words, he was received with favor and council. 

The King treated the philosophers with those favors, and he sat with them to begin the discourse, approaching the contemplation of what stood before them. As he had answered cautiously to God and those things which were being planted, the King said: "This day shall be for your preservation." But let the word be sent that he might have the power to do your will. He said that this was how the matter should be ruled.

### The Translation Begins

After twelve days, the king called **Demetrius**, who was over the library <note>Demetrius of Phalerum, the librarian of Alexandria</note>. He committed the elders to him and led them to the prepared place. To each of the elders, he gave three silver bowls of great value. For the older among the elders, he provided a guard. They reached a certain small island <note>The island of Pharos, where the famous lighthouse stood</note> joined to the land by a bridge. There they were to give themselves to the task, and he made arrangements for prayer and business; they were to stand where the King would lead them individually. He had the interpretation brought to them, and in the presence of God, the work was to be fulfilled. And so, they sat individually. They were served and worked laboriously, making the interpretation with caution until the ninth hour. And as Demetrius helped them together, they compared their work with one another; from these things, they prepared the final wording. 

After some time had passed and they came before the King, they were greeted and returned to the same place. They washed their hands in the sea and, having been purified, returned to their life of living and reading. Thus, they interpreted the entire Law and the spiritual meaning over seventy-two days. Demetrius asked them to read the work aloud; it was read and found to be concordant. They prayed that he who lives might know.

All who were present came to the King, and he read the Law itself and all that had been interpreted. He was joyful and asked that this interpretation be preserved for **Ptolemy** <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note>. They requested that those who saw it should make the elements manifest. It was judged that what they knew should remain unchangeable in its purity. The King, rejoicing in his will, called together those who were present—the neighbors and the wise—and praised their labors. 

He asked Demetrius why no one from the poets, or the historians, or the writers of prose had ever discussed this Law. Demetrius replied: "No one dared to touch these laws previously because they are venerable and divine." He noted that when **Theopompus** <note>A Greek historian</note> wanted to write something of this history, his mind was disturbed for eighty days because he saw a voice and a sound like a thunderclap. Because he wanted to bring divine things out to impure men, he ceased writing until he was restored by God with clarity. Likewise, a certain writer of tragedies named **Theodectes** <note>A Greek tragic poet</note> wanted to write about certain things in the divine volume, but he suffered from cataracts in his eyes. He ceased his work and was shown divine indulgence.

The King, having heard this, said he wished to dismiss the interpreters to their own homes. He told them they should come to visit him frequently. He gave to each of them two talents of wrought gold and two silver bowls, and a golden cup, and one couch with golden feet. To the High Priest Eleazar, he sent ten couches with silver feet and all the necessary furniture, along with thirty golden cups, ten robes, and purple cloth, and a beautiful crown, and fine linen, and vessels for libation, and golden bowls to be vowed to God. He sent a letter to Eleazar with prayers: that if any of the elders wished to come back to him, they should be returned with favor, because he delighted greatly in having conversation with learned men and wished to bestow his wealth upon them. This honor and glory is seen under **Ptolemy Philadelphus**, King of Egypt.

# Historical Context of the Jews in Egypt

Now, the story is told of how the Jews were brought into Egypt by other kings and their successors, and how **Alexander the Great** <note>The conqueror of the Persian Empire</note> also gave them great honors when they came to the city. And in his own metropolis, the city of **Antioch**, he judged the Jews to be worthy of the republic and its elements.

But

<column-break/>

They intended royal honor along with their dwellings thereafter, and he showed the Jews that they should come into his region. The King read the interpreted Law as promised. So that they and the foreigners would not be harmed, he himself provided money for their needs. As the people of Antioch were established, they were given money so that they would not be less than the others. For in the time of **Vespasian**, both the King and the Jews endured many evils; they were conquered by force, yet it seemed they were restored to their own God.

Know that under the empire of the great monarch <note>likely referring to the Seleucid rulers or the later Roman era mentioned above</note> many evils were suffered, beyond what they had committed. For as they sailed into Egypt in the time of Ptolemy, they came to that city and saw it. But with the life of this city and its calamities... suddenly... by the order of Ptolemy... his kingdom was dissipated. 

King Ptolemy was the greatest of them. With great force, he went against the Jews and against **Antiochus**. They saw that Antiochus was troubled and that no one could stand against the fate of the covenant. Ptolemy then took all things with a quiet equality for the Jews who lived in his kingdom. <meta>This page continues the history of the Tobiad family during the Hellenistic period. ### The Rise of Joseph and the Cleverness of Hyrcanus

# Joseph the Tax Collector

Having fulfilled his embassy and reported on the status and funds, Joseph was praised by the mouth of King Ptolemy and Queen Cleopatra. Because he had come to the kings and barons <note>The text uses "baronibus," likely a medieval Latin substitution for "magnates" or "courtiers"</note> with a spirit of friendship, he received mutual rewards from them. He prepared to meet the expectations of those arriving with vessels and furniture which were valued at six thousand drachmas <term>drachma: a silver coin representing a day's wage for a laborer</term>. It happened at that time that the elites and magnates from various cities came to Alexandria to bid on the tax-farming rights which Ptolemy held over the nations. Seeing Joseph on the road, they mocked his poverty, as he seemed a person of modest means to the Alexandrians. 

When Joseph arrived for the assembly before the king, they hastened to meet him. Joseph was seen then as a man of great character. Ptolemy, who was residing in Jerusalem <note>The Latin here is confused; historically, Joseph met the king in Egypt</note>, received him with hospitality. Seeing Joseph, the king soon recognized him as a young and liberal-minded man. King Ptolemy therefore commanded him to sit with him after the first greeting. Joseph gave thanks and sought to win his friendship further. 

Then Joseph said: "That the king's father and my father <note>Referring to the High Priest Onias, Joseph's uncle</note> should have a sincere mind toward one another is well known." He explained why his uncle had been slow in paying the tribute, finding favor through his goodwill, and the king began to love him even more. He was permitted to stay and feast with the king. When the time came for the tax auctions in Alexandria, Joseph was present to represent the Jews before the king. 

On the day the king opened the bids for the taxes and fiscal duties which the noble procurators <term>procurator: a financial agent or tax administrator</term> collected across Syria and Samaria, the bids reached eight thousand talents <term>talent: an immense unit of currency, roughly 6,000 drachmas</term>. Joseph then spoke to the king, saying this was a small amount of money. He promised he would double the bid if the tax rights for those provinces were granted to him. The king, hearing this, realized he could increase his revenue. However, he asked Joseph if he had any guarantors <note>original: "ydonous testey," likely 'idoneos testes' or sureties</note> who could verify his ability to pay. Joseph wittily replied to the king and his friends: "I have the most honorable and reliable sureties: you, O King, and the Queen." The king, pleased by his wit and boldness, entrusted the taxes to him. He announced to those who previously held the taxes that Joseph was now the tax-farmer. 

Joseph, having obtained the authority, requested an escort of two thousand soldiers from the king to help him collect the funds. He departed Alexandria for Syria and arrived at Ascalon <note>A major coastal city</note> to demand the taxes. The people of Ascalon mocked him and refused to pay. Joseph seized twenty of their leading men, executed them, and sent their confiscated property—totaling a thousand talents—to the king. He sent word to the king of what he had done. Ptolemy, praising his prudence and firmness, allowed him to continue. The inhabitants of Syria and Scythopolis <note>Modern-day Beth Shean</note>, hearing of the fate of Ascalon, paid their taxes without delay. Joseph thus collected great sums and made a vast profit from the taxes, which he paid every year, sending gifts also to the King and Queen Cleopatra and their friends to maintain his power. 

Joseph ruled in this manner for twenty-two years. He had seven sons by one wife and one son named Hyrcanus by the daughter of his brother. <margin>The birth of Hyrcanus</margin> It is told that once, while Joseph was in Alexandria with his brother, he desired a certain dancer. His brother, wishing to prevent Joseph from disgracing himself with a commoner, placed his own daughter in Joseph's bed while Joseph was drunk. Joseph, believing her to be the dancer, slept with his niece. When he learned the truth the next morning, he praised his brother for saving his reputation and took the girl as his wife, from whom Hyrcanus was born. 

By the age of thirteen, Hyrcanus showed great spirit and prudence. Joseph wanted to see which of his sons was most fit to succeed him, so he sent them to various teachers and finally tested them. He loved Hyrcanus above his other sons because of his natural goodness. Once, Joseph sent him on a journey into the wilderness with oxen to sow the land. When they arrived, Hyrcanus found he lacked the straps <note>original: "lora"</note> to hitch the oxen. The other servants thought he would have to return home, but Hyrcanus killed ten of the oxen, used their meat to feed the workers, and fashioned the hides into straps to continue the work. When Joseph heard of this, he marveled at the boy's resourcefulness. However, his older brothers grew jealous of him. 

Later, a son was born to King Ptolemy in Egypt. All the leaders of Syria and the subject provinces prepared to celebrate the child’s birth.

<column-break/>

Joseph, hearing of the journey to Egypt, called his sons and asked who would go to the king in his place, for he was too old to travel. The older brothers refused, saying they were not suited for such a courtly gathering. Hyrcanus, however, affirmed he could go. He asked his father for ten thousand drachmas for the journey. Joseph, pleased by his son's sobriety and readiness, prepared him for the journey to Alexandria. He gave Hyrcanus a letter to Arion, his financial agent in Alexandria, who held his collected tax money, instructing Arion to provide Hyrcanus with whatever funds he needed. Joseph expected he would need perhaps ten talents to provide gifts for the king. 

When Hyrcanus arrived in Alexandria, he delivered the letter. Arion, however, was hesitant. He asked Hyrcanus why he required so much money, noting that Joseph usually only requested small amounts. Hyrcanus replied firmly that he was there on his father's business and demanded the funds. When Arion continued to resist, Hyrcanus had him imprisoned. Arion eventually relented and provided the money. 

King Ptolemy, hearing that Joseph had sent his son, sent a messenger to Hyrcanus, asking why he had not yet come to the court. Hyrcanus replied that he was waiting to acquire gifts worthy of the king’s majesty. He explained that he would not appear before the king without offerings, as he wished to honor the king just as his father did. Arion, meanwhile, had reported to the king that the youth was acting with a boldness that bordered on arrogance. 

When Hyrcanus finally came before the king, he was received as Joseph's son and treated with friendship. During a royal banquet, the other courtiers, wishing to mock the boy, conspired against him. They instructed the servants to place all the bones from their meat onto Hyrcanus’s plate. When the king saw the pile of bones before Hyrcanus, he asked: "Hyrcanus, have you eaten all this meat yourself?"

Hyrcanus wittily replied: "My lord, it is only natural. For dogs eat both the meat and the bones, as you see the other guests have done, leaving their plates empty. But men eat only the meat and leave the bones behind, as I have done." 

The king was delighted by this clever response and ordered the court to applaud him. Hyrcanus then spent his money to buy one hundred young boys and one hundred young girls as gifts for the King and Queen, paying a talent for each. This magnificent generosity surpassed all the other guests. 

When it came time to depart, the king honored Hyrcanus with many gifts and sent letters to his father and brothers. However, when his brothers heard of his success and the favor he found with the king, they went out to meet him on the road, intending to kill him. Hyrcanus, defended by his followers, fought them and killed two of his brothers. 

Hyrcanus eventually returned to Jerusalem, but his father Joseph was dead <note>Historical accounts suggest Joseph was still alive, but their relationship was severed</note>, and the city was divided between those who supported the older brothers and those who supported Hyrcanus. Fearing for his life, Hyrcanus retreated beyond the Jordan River. There he built a great fortress of white stone, which he named Tyros <note>modern-day Iraq al-Amir in Jordan</note>. He lived there for many years, collecting taxes from the local tribes and ruling as a lord in the wilderness until the time of the king's death.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Jewish people during the Hellenistic period, shifting focus from the exploits of Hyrcanus the Tobiad to the rise of King Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the subsequent persecution of the Jewish faith, and the beginning of the Maccabean revolt.</meta>

<margin>The face of the Jews.</margin>
The face of the Jews. For some, after the manner of wild beasts, claimed the same lineage as the Lacedaemonians <note>original: "lacedemonies"; referring to the Spartans</note>, asserting they had a kinship with Abraham. It happened that from these persons, he [the king] thought it necessary to insinuate further. This same "face" or appearance is also seen in matters concerning the common interest. Furthermore, a certain one of our people has written in a quadrangular script regarding this notable matter: a seal of joining, an eagle carrying a dragon in its claws. In the letters destined for the king by the Spartans, this word was held:
<margin>Hyrcanus, who after the death of his father</margin>
Hyrcanus, who after the death of his father Joseph, while his brothers did not wish to vex him, sat in counsel regarding the war... and he retreated, and conducted a very strong occupation beyond the Jordan. For up to eight years, he took up the raising of animals; he built a great and high tower, and structures of diverse masonry. On the external parts, he spent much on construction, and leveled many spacious areas in length where he had built, making houses for use, for sleep, and for dining, until he had made a great multitude of caves capable of holding chariots, which would enjoy diversity. And if these were called by the name of caves, so that the common slander might visit them, he would have known the words of the guardian... he had cut off many wonders with words. And perhaps again in these many things, a great omen would strike, and he destroyed the paradise with arms; and having completed such a place, he named it Tyre <note>original: "tyrum"; this refers to the fortress Birtha or Iraq al-Amir in modern Jordan</note>. This is located between Arabia and Judea, at the Jordan, far from the region of Heshbon. Hyrcanus lived there during the time that Seleucus reigned in Syria. But when Seleucus died, his brother Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, obtained the kingdom. Also, when Ptolemy the king of Egypt died, he left his kingdom to his young sons. It was then that Hyrcanus, after he saw the sons of Seleucus and Antiochus... But Hyrcanus, seeing Antiochus become king and possessing great power, and fearing that he might suffer dangers from him because of the attacks he had made against the Arabs, took his own life by his own hand. King Antiochus then applied all his substance and habitation to himself. At the same time, after the death of Onias the high priest, Antiochus again... after Ptolemy Epiphanes died. While Onias was still an infant, we shall narrate those details in their proper place.
<margin>Antiochus who again</margin>
Antiochus then again took away the priesthood and gave it to his younger brother named Onias. This man was threefold <note>likely referring to his divided loyalties</note>, who was so prompt in acting thus. He, being expelled from his life of action, named himself Jason. But the other Onias... from his uncle, and thus from Antiochus, he named himself Menelaus. A sedition then occurred between the brothers. The greater part of the people aided Jason because they favored him. They went in fervor to King Antiochus, praying that they might be allowed to abandon their ancestral laws and observe the city according to the custom and rite of the Greeks. They asked the king for permission to build a gymnasium <term>gymnasium: a Greek school for athletics and culture, which traditional Jews saw as a symbol of pagan Hellenization</term> in Jerusalem. And when the king had granted it, they skillfully concealed their circumcision <note>original: "fua uelarent"; a practice called epispasm to look like Greeks</note>, so that they certainly differed in nothing from the Greeks. Leaving the ancestral law, they brought themselves to that kind of life. Antiochus, seeing his kingdom proceeding well, wished also to reign over Egypt. He looked down upon the sons of Ptolemy as youths who were not strong enough to rule such great affairs. The king thought to approach the city of Pelusium with great power; and by deceit, he occupied it. He took the city of Memphis, and took all the riches, and departing, he took all from the Jews. Ptolemy therefore, having been king, made him king...
<margin>Returned through it</margin>
Antiochus, however, wanting to do as he had intended, was expelled not only from Alexandria but from all Egypt. Returning from Egypt at that time, he turned his love toward the city of Jerusalem. Fearing the power of that son... in the 143rd year after the time of the first Seleucus, in the 145th Olympiad, on the 25th day of the month of Chislev <note>original: "nisf castri"; likely a corruption of the Hebrew month Chislev</note>, which the Greeks call Apelleios. He took the city... to those who favored his will. Entering the city of Jerusalem, he held many in order by his wisdom... he stripped the temple of its ornaments. He took the vessels, the golden lamps, the golden altar, the table, and the sacred veils made of fine linen and scarlet. Leaving nothing of the treasures of the place, he arrived at a maximum of profit. For he also prohibited the sacrifice and offering which they used to offer to God. He led away some into captivity... up to ten thousand... and he destroyed the walls. He built a citadel <term>citadel: the Akra, a fortress used to control the Jewish population</term> in the lower part of the city, which was high and more eminent than the temple, and fortified it with high walls and towers, placing a Macedonian guard within. These were impious men. From them, the people suffered many evils. He also built an altar in the sanctuary, and upon it he sacrificed pigs, an offering which is seen as not sacred by the laws.
<margin>He compelled them</margin>
He therefore compelled the people to relinquish their fatherland's ways and to worship idols, and to build shrines in every city and even temples for gods; to set up altars and sacrifice pigs upon them every day by decree. If anyone refused to eat the meat of these, they were totally destroyed. But many were constant and did not submit to those who compelled them to be deprived of justice and the mandate. Again, others acted toward the Jewish servants out of love for the king. Some of the multitude, however, acted execrably against the law. Because of this, every day they were afflicted and suffered bitter torments. For they suffered lashes and crucifixions; while they were yet alive, they were even slightly pierced. Those who were found to have circumcised were hung from crosses with their parents. And if any book of the Holy Law was found, or anyone learned in the Law, they were put to death. Thus the Jews were afflicted with these vile things, and they did not deserve to be called Jews, and they called themselves Medes, and prayed in the language of their fathers. A certain man, Apollonius, held the king's authority in Jerusalem. He reported to Antiochus Epiphanes... For the greater provinces claimed a certain ancient superstition among the Jews regarding the Sabbath day... they offered sacrifices to these gods. But some men and judges came to us, thinking we were Jews. And why did they nourish us... then again from the race of their fathers and the Medes... Apollonius from Micanor...

<column-break/>

<margin>from these let no one henceforth</margin>
From these let no one henceforth molest them... and he gave thanks. The temple which had been built on Mount Gerizim, which was said to have belonged to no god as of yet, they first called by the name of the Greek gods <note>historically, Zeus Hellenios</note>. This writing, however, protects the truth everywhere among those who narrate diligently. We shall resolve this regarding the younger Hebrews. Here, the former Samaritans... Simon and Nicanor and the Samaritans set forth in a public report... it was prepared for the younger Jews... We resolve therefore the open dispute of the Jews and Samaritans, and how they came to be called by that name.
<margin>And indeed this</margin>
And indeed at this time there was a man living in the village of Modein <note>original: "modoicū"</note>, a Jew by name Mattathias, the son of John, the son of Simon, the son of Asamoneus, from a venerable family of Jerusalem. He had five sons: John, who was called Gaddi; Simon, who was called Thassi; Judas, who was called Maccabeus; Eleazar, who was called Auran; and Jonathan, who was called Apphus.
<margin>This Mattathias</margin>
This Mattathias and his sons lamented the state of affairs, the city captured, the temple stripped, and the common people slandered. He said it would be better for them to be deprived of life by death than to live such a life under these laws.
<margin>They came however</margin>
The king's officers came to the village of Modein, to the village of the Jews where things were seen to be prepared as ordered; there they established that they ought to sacrifice according to the king's command. First they called upon Mattathias; and they made him... others obeyed the orders of the powerful authority. But he and his sons followed the path of justification.
<margin>Neither however</margin>
Neither did they... and they sacrificed in the middle thus with their own weapons. But Mattathias... when he saw the blood poured out upon the altar, he commanded the altar to be destroyed.
<margin>To those who are zealous</margin>
To those who are zealous for the ancestral laws and religion... they followed him into true service, leaving behind their possessions; and many with their wives and children went with him. The king's judges heard these things... they were in Jerusalem... and by their words they tried to bend them so they would choose one thing as good rather than evil. When they did not listen to their words, the friends [of the king] flowed together to the caves... they attacked them on the Sabbath day; nor did they see any honor in going out to save themselves. For it is the part of talkative men to be silent. They died with their wives and children... from the victory of Hyrcanus... Mattathias discovered that they wished to perish... for if they did this, they would not be saved... he said they must fight; even if they were conquered. This Mattathias said... we must fight, and this shall be our precedent. Our custom of fighting and our hope in God... Mattathias gathered an armed hand and went out: he wished to destroy the altars, and he wished for the divine excellence of the Jews. For his life... and he commanded the boys to be circumcised, expelling those who prohibited this. He extended his mind... calling together his own. And standing at the altar, he said: "I, for the sons of God... I commend to you to observe the ancestral laws... but rather guard and defend them." The king had wished... he wished for divine excellence... to follow justice in all things... you ought to favor the people more than the love of ancestors... this life... but through your virtue... into a life of service... and one day by your holiness... to love the Lord... and even if they have minor victories. And if they constrain you, help one another with substance and virtue. Simon is not lacking in the wisdom of the brothers; he shall be a father to you. Judas, however, the military leader, has hope in truth and fortitude, to defend his people and fight the enemies. Take up your arms and religion, and cherish their truth." Mattathias, having spoken these things and prayed to the Lord while he had life, that his laws might be served, died... and he was buried in Modein with great mourning from the sons of the Jews.
<margin>Succession occurred</margin>
The governance of affairs succeeded to his son, Judas Maccabeus, with his brothers helping him with a primary spirit. He approached with religion; and they wished to offer the action of the laws, purifying the temple from all evils. They made Judas the leader of the armed Jews. He went out against the enemies. Apollonius encountered him. And in the battle, he slew many of them; Apollonius was killed and his army destroyed, and taking much spoil from the army of the enemies, he departed. The leader of lower Syria, Seron, heard that Judas had brought many to Judea, and he wondered at his virtue... he came to the village... Judas, seeing those who were with him preparing to fight, when he saw the fewness of the people, exhorted them saying: "Victories are not won through a multitude, but through that which you believe. If you have piety and holiness, you have the most daring example, for justice and God have fought for us; he has often conquered many." And saying that justice... through the multitude... he turned them to flight. And he pursued them into the plain. Eight hundred of them fell... When King Antiochus saw the virtue of Judas and the congregation of his forces... he prepared his forces... our wisdom then distributed... he returned everything through the sedition of the nations. For when he had a great matter... he deliberated first to go to Persia, to gather tribute. He left the governance of the nation to Lysias, while he himself set out...

# Lysias

And Judas and his brothers saw that evils were multiplied and the army was approaching their borders. And they knew the words of the king, which he commanded the people to do for their destruction and consumption. And each said to his neighbor: "Let us raise up the ruin of our people, and let us fight for our people and our sanctuary." And the assembly was gathered so that they might be ready for war, and that they might pray and ask for mercy and compassion.

And when it was day, Judas appeared in the field with only three thousand men, who did not have armor or swords as they wished. And those who were with Judas sounded the trumpets. And they joined battle, and the nations were crushed and fled into the plain. And Judas returned, and his army following him. For he said to the people: "Do not covet the spoils, for battle is near us; Gorgias and his army are in the mountain near us.
