While Judas was still speaking these words, behold, a certain part appeared looking out from the mountain. And he saw that they were turned to flight and had set the camp on fire. For the smoke that was seen declared what had been done. When they saw these things, they feared greatly, looking at the same time at Judas in the field ready for battle. And they all fled into the land of the foreigners. And Judas returned to the spoils of the camp, and they took much gold and silver, and blue and sea-purple fabric, and great riches. And returning, they sang a hymn and blessed the Lord in heaven, because he is good, because his mercy endures forever. And there was a great salvation in Israel on that day. But whoever of the foreigners escaped came and told Lysias all that had happened. When he heard these things, he was dismayed and fainted in his mind, because things had not happened in Israel as he wished, or as the king had commanded.

And Judas fought against the children of Esau in Idumaea, and those who were in Akrabattene, because they surrounded the Israelites, and he struck them with a great blow.

<meta>This page follows the previous account of the Jewish uprising under Judas Maccabeus. The preceding text focused on the purification of the Temple (Hanukkah) and early regional skirmishes. This section transitions to the death of the Seleucid King Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the subsequent military campaign of his young successor, Antiochus V Eupator, against the Judean forces.</meta>

...the king's testament <note>original: "mographum," likely a corruption of "chirographum" or "testamentum"</note> or his final will. At that time, Antiochus was in the upper provinces, having learned that the temple of the new dominion was unfaithful to the established order. For there were those who appeared to have sinned; and the cause of all these things in that region was the news that Antiochus had been repelled by the Lord. He had been sent with a great force, but many were slain in the field of the Jerusalemites where a great devastation was made. The king was crushed and resisted by God, just as the general opinion believed. Antiochus, foreseeing his end, called Philip, one of his friends, and appointed him ruler over all his kingdom. He gave him the diadem, his robe, and his ring, and commanded him to bring them to his son Antiochus, and to raise him so that he might rule the empire.

<margin>The death of Antiochus</margin>
And so Antiochus died in the year 149 <note>of the Seleucid era, approximately 164 BCE</note>. When Lysias learned of the king's death, he announced it; he appointed the king's son Antiochus, whom he had raised, to reign in his place, and he called him Eupator <note>meaning "of a good father"</note>.

<margin>Judas besieges the citadel</margin>
At that time, those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem <note>the Akra, a Seleucid fortress overlooking the Temple</note> were causing great harm to the Israelites and those adjacent to the Lord's house. They were constantly seeking to do evil in the Temple, and as these things occurred, Judas deliberated on how to destroy the citadel. Gathering all the people, he besieged the citadel and constructed siege machines and built up mounds of earth, laboring with great effort. Some of those who were besieged escaped and, gathering other ungodly men, they went to Antioch to the King, praying that he would not desert them. They claimed they had been loyal but were now suffering because they obeyed the king's commands and had forsaken their ancestral religion. When Judas saw that the king had heard this, he prepared himself. Indeed, the messengers told the king that unless he sent help immediately, the citadel would be lost. Hearing this, the young Antiochus was very angry and called his generals and friends, commanding them to gather the army and foreign mercenaries. He gathered 100,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, and 32 elephants trained for war. They marched through Idumea with Lysias, and the Maccabees came to Beth-zacharia <note>a strategic location south of Jerusalem</note>. They reached Bethsura and besieged it, but the Jews fought back and burned their siege engines.

When Judas heard of the king's arrival, he left the siege of the citadel and moved to where the camp was stationed, at a place called Beth-zacharia, which was ten miles from the enemy. The King, moving before dawn, directed his army toward the Maccabees. He prepared the ranks and had the elephants follow. Because of the narrowness of the pass, he positioned the infantry and cavalry in defensive lines, with a thousand footmen and five hundred horsemen protecting each elephant. The elephants carried high wooden towers and archers. The rest of the army was spread across the mountains on both sides to harass the enemy with noise and terror. The sun shone on their gold and bronze shields, making the mountains glisten and tremble. Judas and his men approached, and six hundred of the king's men were slain. <margin>Eleazar</margin> Eleazar, the brother of Judas, who was called Avaran, saw one of the elephants adorned with royal harnesses and taller than the others. Thinking the king was upon it, he rushed through the ranks, killing men on the right and left. He went under the elephant and stabbed it from beneath; the elephant fell dying upon him, crushing Eleazar to death. The Jews, seeing the king's strength and the onset of his army, retreated to Jerusalem. The king's forces then went up to Jerusalem, and he sent a division to Bethsura. Antiochus's army besieged the city for a long time. They were in need of food because it was a Sabbatical year <note>a year of rest for the land, occurring every seventh year, when no crops were sown or harvested</note>.

During this time, Jerusalem was also besieged. The defenders fought back bravely, constructing their own machines against those of the king. However, they ran out of food because of the Sabbatical year, and many fled the Temple due to hunger, leaving only a few to defend the holy place. At this time, Lysias heard that Philip, whom King Antiochus had appointed to raise his son, had returned from Persia and Media with the king's army and was seeking to take control of the government. Therefore, Lysias urged the King to make peace with the Jews, saying that the siege was taking too long, food was scarce, and the affairs of the kingdom required their attention elsewhere. He suggested they allow the Jews to live according to their own laws as they did before. The King and the leaders agreed and sent a promise of peace to the Jews, which they accepted. The King and the princes swore an oath to them. But when the King entered Mount Zion and saw the strength of the fortifications, he broke the oath he had sworn and commanded that the wall surrounding the site be torn down. Then he departed in haste and returned to Antioch. Lysias found Philip in control of the city, but he fought against him and took the city by force. Meanwhile, the Jews were relieved of the immediate threat but mourned the loss of their defenses and the treachery of the king.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'E' at the start of the second column, intricately designed with floral or scroll-like patterns within the letter's body.</image-desc>
Even with the announcement of the king's death, his friends remained venerable. He had sent his son to be raised so that he might take up the principality. In those days, there was no peace. Those who fled to Asia were many. The news of King Antiochus's death reached everyone, leaving behind a great mourning. The case of Jerusalem was similar to that of the people. They had to organize their own affairs. Confiding in the King's justice, they sought help. Judas and the Jews were determined to maintain their laws. Many great battles were fought in the region of Judea. With God's help, they stood against the signs of the enemy. In Heliopolis and elsewhere, the people sought to restore the Temple. Many were gathered, and the remnant of the people sought refuge in Egypt <note>this refers to the high priest Onias fleeing to Egypt to build a temple at Leontopolis</note> where they lived among the animals and the fields. The place was given to them by the king of Egypt. They built a temple there similar to the one in Jerusalem, though smaller. This caused much dispute among the priests and the people. Some said the service should only be in Jerusalem, while others defended the new temple in Egypt. This became a matter of great debate in Alexandria before King Ptolemy. The king eventually ruled in favor of the Jerusalem temple's tradition, though the temple in Egypt remained for many years.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Maccabean Revolt from Josephus’s *Antiquities of the Jews*, specifically the transition from the end of Book 12 to the beginning of Book 13. It chronicles the final victories and death of Judas Maccabeus and the rise of his brother Jonathan.</meta>

...they are without. Others, however, fearing for themselves, thought the matter harmful; and seeing the deeds done, they rightly expected divine vengeance for the crime. An army was sent from Rome, from which he had fled <note>This refers to Demetrius I Soter, who escaped Rome to seize the Seleucid throne</note>; they determined to show no mercy to the Jewish nation. Nicanor, arriving in Jerusalem, wished to fight against Judas. He attempted to capture him by deceit, sending a message of peace, claiming he came with no desire for war but only to swear an oath that they would suffer no ill from him. Nicanor, speaking thus, met with Judas, who had no suspicion. However, once the pledge was given, Judas's suspicion grew. When they greeted each other, Nicanor gave a signal, and his men attempted to seize Judas. Having sensed the ambush, the matter became known to Judas, and he retreated to his own men. Nicanor then moved against Jerusalem, coming down from the citadel <note>The Akra</note>; some of the priests met him, showing him the sacrifices they offered for the king. But he swore he would destroy the temple unless they surrendered Judas. 

Nicanor and Judas then met in battle; Judas prayed to God to liberate them, for they had done no evil in Jerusalem. The Jews fought bravely. Amidst these and other defenses against the Syrians, Judas defeated Nicanor. Nicanor was killed in the battle, and his army, seeing their leader fallen, turned to flight. The Jews pursued them, sounding the trumpets to signal their victory. When the people in the villages heard the signal, they came out and cut off the fugitives. Not one of the enemies escaped; five thousand fell <note>Josephus and the Book of Maccabees usually cite larger numbers, but the manuscript here suggests five or nine thousand</note>. This victory for Judas occurred on the thirteenth day of the month which the Jews call Adar, and the Macedonians call Dystros. For a short time after this war, the land of the Jews had peace and rest from calamities, though soon they returned to conflict.

At that time, Alcimus <note>original: "iethim... & wacham," referring to Jakim/Alcimus</note>, whom they wished to depose from the high priesthood, was struck by a plague from God while he was attempting to tear down the wall of the inner court of the temple. He fell to the ground, lost his speech, and died in great agony after having held the priesthood for three years. 

After his death, Judas decided to seek an alliance with Rome, having heard of their fame and how they had conquered the Gauls, the Spaniards, and the Carthaginians of Libya, as well as Greece and many kings. He sent Eupolemus, son of John, and Jason, son of Eleazar, to Rome <margin>150.</margin> to ask the Romans to be their allies and friends, and to write to King Demetrius to stop his oppression. When the ambassadors arrived in Rome, the Senate received them kindly and entered into a treaty, which they inscribed on bronze tablets and placed in the Capitol. The decree was as follows: "No one under Roman jurisdiction shall make war against the Jewish nation, nor provide aid to those who fight them; nor shall the Jews aid the enemies of Rome. If any change is to be made to this treaty, it shall be done by common consent." This was the first friendship and alliance between the Romans and the Jews. 

When King Demetrius heard of Nicanor’s death and the destruction of his army, he sent Bacchides again into Judea with a new force. They marched from Antioch and encamped at Arbela. Judas, with only three thousand men <note>OCR suggests "eight hundred" remained after others fled</note>, went out to meet them at Berzetho. Many of Judas’s men were terrified by the size of the enemy army and fled, leaving only eight hundred men. Judas, though distressed, exhorted those remaining to fight bravely for their glory and their nation. The battle was fierce; Judas and his men attacked the right wing where Bacchides was and broke their line, pursuing them as far as Mount Azotus. But the left wing of the enemy encircled Judas from behind. Surrounded and fighting with great courage, Judas was struck by a sword and fell. Jonathan and Simon recovered his body and buried him in the tomb of his fathers at Modin, mourning him for many days. All Israel wept for him.

<column-break/>

...to do; he was a great and warlike man, always ready to do and to suffer all things for his people. Through his leadership, great glory and protection came to his people; he liberated them from the bitterness of oppression, especially the priesthood and the servants of the Lord. — Here ends the twelfth book of Josephus's Jewish Antiquities.

From now on, I release you from the poll tax, the salt tax, and the crown gold which you used to offer us. I also give up the third part of the grain and the half of the fruit from the trees. I also decree that any Jews who were taken captive from the land of Judah into any part of my kingdom shall be set free without ransom. No one shall impose burdens on them, for Jonathan has shown himself a friend of our mind. And even if 30,000 Jews wish to serve in my army, they shall receive pay just as the royal troops do. I also grant 15,000 drachmas of silver annually from the king's accounts for the restoration of the Temple. Despite these promises and flatteries of Demetrius, the Jews did not believe him, for they remembered the great evils he had done to them. They preferred Alexander, who had first offered them peace. Alexander then gathered a great force and marched against Demetrius. In the battle, the left wing of Demetrius’s army fled, but Demetrius himself stood bravely and fought among a few of his enemies. He was pursued, and though he fell into a muddy pit, he continued to fight until he was overcome by many wounds and died. Thus was the end of Demetrius, who reigned for twelve years. Alexander, having taken the kingdom of Syria, wrote to Ptolemy, the king of Egypt, asking for his daughter’s hand in marriage. Ptolemy, the king of Egypt, freely accepted the proposal, having seen that Demetrius was dead. He commanded Alexander to meet him at Ptolemais for the wedding.

Jonathan came to the king and offered him many gifts. He was treated with great honor by both kings. Then King Alexander commanded that Jonathan be clothed in purple and sit upon a throne with him. Those who had come to speak against Jonathan, seeing him so honored and clothed in purple, fled away so that they would not suffer harm. King Alexander loved Jonathan and inscribed him as his first friend and made him a governor.

The Jews pursued them, and the king was saved along with his wife and children.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Maccabean period, specifically the transition of leadership from Jonathan Apphus to his brother Simon Thassi. It details the philosophical divisions among the Jews, the military campaigns against the Seleucid forces of Demetrius II, and the treacherous rise of Tryphon, who captures Jonathan by deceit.</meta>

Farewell. The ambassadors returned to the Laodiceans and the free people, and we will offer him this message concerning friendship toward you all.

At the same time, there were three sects <note>The Latin 'hereses' here refers to schools of thought or sects, not 'heresy' in the modern sense.</note> of the Jews, which held differing views on human affairs. The group called the **Pharisees** claimed that all things were governed by providence <note>Latin: 'providentia'; the text discusses the complex balance between fate and free will.</note>; the Pharisees said that fate ruled some things, but in others, human choice could prevail. The **Essenes**, however, confirmed that all things are under fate, and that nothing happens to men except by its decree. The **Sadducees** take away fate entirely, concluding it is not a factor in human affairs; instead, they place all things under human power, such that we ourselves are the authors of our good or ill fortune according to our own wisdom. But we shall clarify more of these matters elsewhere.

As for the rest, after the civil war of the Jews, an army wanting to dominate Judea gathered a larger force against **Jonathan**. But when Jonathan learned of this, he went to meet them and did not wish to delay until they entered Judea. He pitched his camp not far from the enemies in Judea and sent scouts to examine the enemy camp. When they returned to report everything, they noted that the enemy guards had planned an attack by night. Jonathan kept his army in arms and warned them to be of brave heart, and if necessary, to fight by night. He then placed guards at all the enemy's points of approach. But when the enemies learned that Jonathan had discovered their plan, they were disturbed that they could not carry out their ambush against the Jews. Lighting many fires in their camp so that the Jews would think they were staying there, they all fled. 

When Jonathan came to the camp in the morning, he found it deserted. Seeing they had fled, he pursued them but was unable to catch them, for they had crossed the **Eleutherus River**. Returning to Arabia, Jonathan turned his forces there, took much plunder and captives, and arrived in Damascus, where he stationed his men. **Simon**, meanwhile, traveled through Judea and Palestine as far as Ascalon, fortifying the strongholds. When he heard that the garrison had made a pact, he came to **Joppa** and occupied it, placing a guard there; for he had heard the Jews intended to surrender the city to Demetrius. 

When Jonathan and Simon, the leaders of the Jews, returned to Jerusalem, they gathered all the people in a council. They persuaded them to reconstruct the destroyed walls of Jerusalem and the part of the Temple, to fortify it with towers, and to build another wall in the middle of the city so that the enemy camp would be cut off from the flow of supplies and the strongholds of the province would be made safer. When they consented to this, Jonathan took care of building the walls, while Simon fortified the province. 

**Demetrius**, meanwhile, having crossed into Parthia and wishing to defeat **Arsaces**, the king of the Parthians, came to the enemy to obtain the upper provinces, so that he might later recover the kingdom from the defeated and scattered forces. He sent an embassy to Arsaces to ask for help, promising to help him in the war he had begun. Arsaces sent a force against him to see if he could defeat the Parthians and recover his strength, and then later defeat **Tryphon** and drive him far from Syria. They captured King Demetrius, defeated him, and led him away conquered to Arsaces. Demetrius was kept alive in the war and treated with honor.

<margin>T</margin>
**Tryphon**, however, when he learned that Demetrius had been captured, persisted in his current efforts; for he hoped that while Demetrius was alive, he could seize the kingdom if he could gain the goodwill and friendship of the Jews which they had with Arsaces. For if he could see Jonathan removed and gain access to the leadership, he thought he could destroy Jonathan through deceit and guile. He came toward Antioch and then to **Scythopolis** <note>Also known as Beth Shean.</note>, where Jonathan met him with forty thousand chosen warriors, prepared for battle. **Tryphon**, seeing Jonathan ready for battle, feared him and commanded his own men to obey Jonathan, wishing to confirm his faith to the Jews and dispel suspicion, so that they might fear nothing from the invitation. He then urged Jonathan to dismiss his army so they would not be weary for no reason, as there was no war present, and requested him to come with a few men to **Ptolemais**, so he could hand over the city and the government to him. Jonathan, suspecting nothing and believing Tryphon spoke in good faith, dismissed his army. He kept only three thousand with him, of whom he left two thousand in Galilee; with only a thousand, he came to Ptolemais with Tryphon. 

When he entered Ptolemais, they closed the gates on the Jews who had entered with him; they captured Jonathan alive and killed everyone who had entered with him. **Tryphon** then sent forces to Galilee to kill the remaining two thousand. But when the news reached them that Jonathan was captured, they prepared their arms and went out. And when those sent by Tryphon saw that they were ready to fight, they returned to Tryphon without causing trouble. Those in Jerusalem, hearing that Jonathan was captured and his fellow soldiers killed, mourned his destruction and were in great distress, fearing that after Jonathan's death, their neighbors would invade them—which is exactly what happened. For when the neighbors heard of Jonathan's death, they all wanted to go to war, lacking only a leader. 

**Tryphon**, gathering a large army, decided to come to Judea to destroy everyone. **Simon**, seeing the danger to Jerusalem, began to encourage them with his speech, which gave them courage so they would not fear Tryphon but look forward. Gathering the people in the Temple, he spoke thus: "You know, men of Judea, that I am ready to die like my father and brothers for our laws..."

<column-break/>

"...and preserve them with help. For I see that you have lost a leader and the wars have increased against you." When Simon had said this to the people, they took courage from his boldness and cried out with one voice, saying: "You are our leader in place of your brothers, and we will obey you in all things." **Simon**, coming forward, gathered all the warriors and hastened to reconstruct the city wall, fortifying it with high and strong towers. He also sent his friend Jonathan, son of Absalom, with soldiers to Joppa, commanding the inhabitants to face the enemy, for he feared they would surrender the city to Tryphon. He himself remained in Jerusalem. 

**Tryphon** moved from Ptolemais with a large army and came toward Judea, leading Jonathan as a prisoner. **Simon** met him with his forces at the city of Adida, which is on a hill, from where the whole plain can be seen. When Tryphon heard that the Jews had appointed Simon as their leader, he turned to deceit and guile. He sent ambassadors to Simon saying that he held Jonathan for no other reason than because of the money he owed the royal treasury. He promised that if Simon sent a hundred talents of silver and Jonathan’s two sons as hostages, he would release him. Simon, though he realized this was a trick of Tryphon's, sent the silver and the boys anyway, so that the people would not say he let his brother perish for the sake of money. He gathered the people and explained that Tryphon's words were full of deceit and traps, but it was better for the Jews to send the money and the sons so that they would not be blamed for Jonathan’s death. 

Tryphon, having received the silver and the sons of Jonathan, did not release Jonathan. Instead, he attempted to go by way of Idumea to ascend to Jerusalem. Simon, however, moved his camp to every place Tryphon went. While those in the citadel of Jerusalem sent messengers to Tryphon asking him to come to them quickly and bring supplies, Tryphon prepared his cavalry to reach Jerusalem that night, but a great snowstorm fell and hindered his march. Failing in this, he went to Syria. Coming to the land of Gilead, he ordered Jonathan to be killed and buried there, and then he reached Antioch. 

**Simon** came to the city of Basca and recovered the bones of Jonathan, burying him in his own city of **Modin** next to his father. Simon built a magnificent monument for his father and brothers of high, polished stone. He erected seven pyramids, one for each of his parents and brothers, and around them he set up great pillars and carved suits of armor and ships, which can still be seen today. This tomb of Jonathan has been preserved in honor by the Jews. 

Simon, now the leader of the Jews, restored the walls and towers. He also took the city of Gazara and cleansed it of idols. After this, the garrison in the citadel of Jerusalem, having no supplies, surrendered to Simon. He did not destroy them but allowed them to depart. He entered the citadel with palm branches and music, and it was decreed that this day should be celebrated annually. Simon then ordered the hill on which the citadel stood to be leveled so that the Temple would be higher than it, and the work continued for three years until the hill was made level with the plain.

After the captivity of Demetrius, who was held by Arsaces of Parthia, Simon's rule was prosperous. But Tryphon, after he had killed the young King **Antiochus** (whom he called 'Theos'), seized the kingdom for himself. He had been the guardian of the boy, but through treachery, he claimed the crown and reigned for three years. However, he was not favored by the soldiers, who preferred **Antiochus Sidetes**, the brother of Demetrius. Antiochus had sent letters to Simon and the Jews from the islands of the sea, seeking their friendship and promising to confirm their liberties. Antiochus eventually invaded the kingdom to drive out Tryphon. Tryphon fled to **Dora**, a fortress where he was besieged. Antiochus accepted the help of Simon, who sent two thousand chosen soldiers and money to assist in the war against Tryphon.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Hasmonean dynasty, moving from the death of Simon Thassi to the reign of his son, John Hyrcanus I. It details the internal treachery of Ptolemy, the invasion by the Seleucid king Antiochus VII Sidetes, and Hyrcanus’s eventual stabilization of the kingdom through an alliance with Rome and the expansion into Samaria.</meta>

In the same year, Ptolemy—the son-in-law of Simon—who acted with treachery, sent armed men to seize Simon's son John, who was also called **Hyrcanus**. But John, having sensed the danger, fled to the city [Jerusalem], trusting in the people's goodwill toward his father's memory. Ptolemy attempted to enter, but he was excluded from the gates. 

Hyrcanus then besieged Ptolemy at a fortress named **Dagon**, located above Jericho. There, Ptolemy held Hyrcanus’s mother and brothers captive. Whenever Hyrcanus attacked the walls, Ptolemy would bring the mother and brothers out and scourge them, threatening to throw them headlong if Hyrcanus did not lift the siege. Although Hyrcanus was moved by his mother's suffering, she cried out from the walls, urging him not to stop on her account, but to take vengeance for the sake of his family. She considered a death by torture to be a small thing if the enemy were punished for his crimes. However, seeing his mother beaten, Hyrcanus's resolve would falter, and he would draw back the siege. Because of this, the siege was prolonged until the arrival of the "seventh year," in which the Jews are commanded to rest <note>original: "anno... septimo"; this refers to the Sabbatical Year or Shmita, which required a cessation of military activity.</note>. Ptolemy then killed the mother and brothers and fled to Zeno, the tyrant of Philadelphia <note>Modern-day Amman, Jordan.</note>.

**Antiochus** [VII Sidetes], seeking to avenge the defeats of his predecessors, invaded Judea in the first year of Hyrcanus's reign, which was the 162nd Olympiad. He devastated the countryside and hemmed Hyrcanus into the city [Jerusalem]. Antiochus set up a massive siege with a hundred towers, each seven stories high, and stationed divisions of soldiers to encircle the walls. He dug a great and deep trench to prevent escape. Hyrcanus, facing a shortage of food, expelled those who were not fit for battle from the city to conserve supplies. These poor people wandered between the walls and the enemy lines in a miserable state. However, when the **Feast of Tabernacles** <note>A major Jewish pilgrimage festival.</note> arrived, Hyrcanus took pity and readmitted them. 

Hyrcanus sent ambassadors to Antiochus asking for a seven-day truce for the festival. Antiochus, being a man of great piety, not only granted the truce but sent a magnificent sacrifice: bulls with gilded horns and cups filled with all manner of spices. For this reason, the people called him "Antiochus the Pious." 

<note>original: "Antiochus ypsimaco"; Likely a reference to Antiochus Epiphanes, the "madman" who preceded him and desecrated the Temple.</note> Unlike the earlier Antiochus, who had sacrificed swine on the altar and sought to abolish Jewish law, this Antiochus was praised for his respect for religion. Hyrcanus, impressed by this kindness, sent an embassy of the most powerful citizens to negotiate for the restoration of their native laws. Antiochus rejected the advice of those who urged him to destroy the Jews entirely and instead agreed to peace, provided that the Jews laid down their arms, paid tribute for Joppa and other cities outside Judea, and gave hostages. Hyrcanus agreed to all terms except the placement of a permanent garrison in the city. He paid three hundred talents of silver and gave his own brother as a hostage. When Antiochus received these, he lifted the siege and departed as a friend.

Hyrcanus then opened the tomb of David—the first of the Jewish kings to do so—and took out three thousand talents of gold. With this wealth, he was the first of the Jews to maintain a force of foreign mercenaries. He also accompanied Antiochus on an expedition against the **Parthians**. 

**Nicolaus of Damascus** <note>A famous historian and advisor to Herod the Great.</note> mentions this in his history, noting that Antiochus set up a trophy by the Lycus River and waited two days for the Jews to celebrate a festival on which it was not lawful for them to travel. 

After the death of Antiochus in battle against the Parthians, Hyrcanus immediately launched an expedition into **Syria**, finding the cities deserted of defenders. He took Medaba, Samega, and the surrounding regions. He also captured **Mount Gerizim** and destroyed the temple that the Samaritans had built there—which had stood for two hundred years. Afterward, he took the cities of Adora and Marissa, and having subdued all the Idumeans, he permitted them to remain in the land only if they were circumcised and followed the laws of Moses. Out of a desire to keep their ancestral home, they submitted to circumcision and became, from that time on, reckoned as Jews. 

Seeking to renew his friendship with the **Romans**, Hyrcanus sent an embassy to them. The Senate received them warmly. The consul Fannius <note>Gaius Fannius, consul in 122 BCE.</note> introduced the ambassadors—Simon son of Dositheus, Apollonius son of Alexander, and Diodorus son of Jason—who were men of the highest character. 

<column-break/>

The Senate decreed that the friendship be renewed and that the cities taken by Antiochus be restored to the Jews. They also prohibited the king from marching through Jewish territory and mandated that the Romans defend the Jews as their allies. 

Meanwhile, after the death of Antiochus Sidetes, Demetrius II (Nicator) returned to the throne, but he was soon unpopular. The people turned to **Ptolemy Physcon**, who sent an army under **Alexander Zabinas**. In the ensuing battle, Demetrius was defeated and fled to his wife Cleopatra at Ptolemais, but she refused to receive him. He was eventually captured and killed. 

Hyrcanus, seeing the Seleucid Empire crumbling into civil war between various claimants, ceased to be a subject of the Macedonians and lived in peace. At this time, he turned his attention toward the city of **Samaria**, which was very well fortified. He sent his two sons, **Aristobulus** and **Antigonus**, to conduct the siege. They dug a double trench around the city. The Samaritans called upon **Antiochus Cyzicenus** for help. He came with a large force but was defeated by the brothers and fled toward Scythopolis. 

A miraculous event is recorded regarding the high priest Hyrcanus during this time. While he was alone in the Temple offering incense in the Holy of Holies, he heard a voice saying that his sons had just conquered Antiochus. When he came out of the sanctuary, he shared this news with the people, and it was soon confirmed that the victory had happened at that exact moment.

Those who were malicious and desired to break their concord went to Aristobulus and told him of Antigonus's victory and his pomp, claiming he intended to overthrow the king during the Feast of Tabernacles. They told Aristobulus that he had not come as a subject but as a king. Aristobulus, influenced by these reports, decided to test him so as not to appear to be acting on mere suspicion. He stationed his guards in a dark, underground passage <note>Known as Strato's Tower.</note>. He gave orders that no one should be armed, but he sent word to Antigonus to come to him. He instructed the guards that if Antigonus came unarmed, they should let him pass, but if he came in arms, they should kill him. 

The Queen, however, and the conspirators persuaded the messenger to tell Antigonus exactly the opposite: that the King had heard he had a beautiful new suit of armor and wished to see him in it. Therefore, Antigonus, suspecting no guile and trusting in his brother's affection, put on his arms and proceeded to his brother. When he reached the dark passage, he was immediately struck down and died. When his death was revealed, it showed the power of envy and slander. Aristobulus, realizing the truth, was moved by deep repentance, but he could not turn his mind and soul from the tragedy. This distress corrupted his internal organs; he began to vomit blood. As a servant was carrying away the blood, he accidentally slipped and spilled it on the very spot where the stains of Antigonus's blood still remained. Those who saw it cried out that it was divine judgment. Aristobulus, hearing the outcry and learning the cause, groaned and said: "Can I hide my impious and cruel deeds from the eye of God? Why does my impious body still hold my soul? How long must I pay for my mother and brothers whom I killed?" Then, having lost much blood, he expired. He reigned for one year and was called a "Philhellene," that is, a lover of the Greeks. He was a man of modest character and innate shame, as testified by the historian Strabo.

And when many frequent reports were given of Aristobulus’s actions, she died ten days after he had occupied two locations, and much of the military from the people of Lebanon and <unclear>Sicoar</unclear> <note>likely referring to the region of Iturea</note> were deprived. When the leaders saw this, they came to Hyrcanus concerning the kingdom, so that they might take counsel regarding the standing affairs. For this matter was as she had previously declared; then they held the son of the queen. They were those who, if they were judged to be useful, possessed a strong people and most skilled money, and an abundance of resources; but she herself was failing in body, just as her mind labored with heavy burdens.

When Queen Alexandra had said these things, she died not long after: she was in her ninth year of honor, and her age was seventy-three. She had been much weakened and never succumbed to her duties. She laid down the clever care of the kingdom; and whatever she wished, she brought to pass as she had ordered. And while victory kindled the realm, she led the kingdom to our greatest calamity through many dangers and labors. Which, while they possessed it, in a short time they would lose through the desire for power. And she left this persistent habit of her race to her heirs: and she proved by a wicked reason that she deprived her friends; and she filled the kingdom with much inferiority after her death by a perverse disposition; but because she had done this thing, which then while they lived, in the whole land: since.

# THE BEGINNING OF BOOK XIV
## [THE DESCENDANTS] OF ALEXANDER

And in the manner demonstrated in the previous volume, speaking of our times, we hasten to provide another account in the record of deeds performed. For since our history and ancient matters indicate, it behooves those through the antiquity of the narration to apply devotion and to study the explanation of things properly, so that with some delight they may know the experience of things. Above all, indeed, the honesty of truth and to speak the truth, so that readers may be able to believe in the assistance of things. 

The most certain deeds truly began in the **one hundred and seventy-seventh Olympiad** <note>roughly 72–68 BCE, though the Roman consuls mentioned below suggest 60 BCE</note>, when Quintus Metellus and Lucius Afranius were consuls: Aristobulus prepared for war against Hyrcanus; and after a battle was fought, the soldiers of Hyrcanus, terrified by the men, fled to Aristobulus. After this was done, Hyrcanus fled in his flight to the citadel where the wife of Aristobulus and his sons were held. And when Aristobulus came for reconciliation, where he might know the surrender, he received that he who was there should enjoy his own possession as a private citizen. And when they had disposed of these things, and in the temple had exchanged oaths and right hands in turn, Aristobulus took the royal power, and Hyrcanus lived as a private citizen in the house of Aristobulus.

In that place there was a certain man of a divided race: **Antipater** <note>The father of Herod the Great and an Idumaean nobleman</note>, a friend of Hyrcanus, who was then shut in flight. Aristobulus accepted him through Hyrcanus. This <note>Nicholas of Damascus</note> seems to have been of the most noble race of those who returned from Babylon to Judea. He truly is the one regarding whom Herod his son, because he ruled the Jews, was later to become a contact, of whom we shall speak in his own time. This Antipater was a leader of the whole coast of **Idumaea** <note>the region south of Judea</note> under King Alexander and Queen Alexandra; he was a friend of our people and prepared his military for this matter with the counsel of the greatest lords. And when he perceived that Aristobulus would be an invader of Hyrcanus’s affairs, he saw it through a vision: he warned many to neglect him while they saw Aristobulus as impetuous. He did this for the sake of peace. 

He frequently urged Hyrcanus to flee, and not to change the friendship of his brother at any time, nor to be persuaded by those who spoke of justice. He offered prayers in Damascus. At first, Hyrcanus did not believe these words, as he was good by nature and easily agreed to visitation. Indeed, his innocence and his mind made it seem that he was on a serious path. But Aristobulus was of a different nature, being harsh and arrogant. When Antipater saw that Hyrcanus did not admit his words, he in no way ceased in those days to bring accusations about his brother Aristobulus; and when he wished to entice him, he urged him to flee to **Aretas** <note>Aretas III, King of the Nabataeans</note>, the king of the Arabs, who would be a provider of aid. He who was of this party urged Hyrcanus to depart. And when he saw the matter departing to the borders, Antipater went privately to the king of the Arabs, seeking trust from Aretas: that he would not betray him when he fled to him. And when he had accepted the pledge of Aretas, he returned to Hyrcanus in Jerusalem. After this, he led Hyrcanus and Antipater out of the city by night; after much travel, they arrived at the royal city where the palace of King Aretas was. Antipater then asked Aretas, the king of the Arabs, to lead Hyrcanus back to Judea, and he did this every day without any release. Along with gifts he pressed him. Hyrcanus truly promised Aretas that if he restored his father’s kingdom, he would return all the land and the twelve cities which his father **Alexander** <note>Alexander Jannaeus</note> had taken from the Arabs. These were: Nabata, Alabata, Talathone, and others.

<column-break/>

He led him out for a long time. Aristobulus, indeed, received his friends; when he had heard of the submission, he prepared for the battle against Aristobulus. And when Aristobulus came into the valley of his strength, they replied to his son Aristobulus that the republic was dissolved. The King of the Arabs was now disturbed, as many more gathered to besiege Aristobulus. Indeed, the sun was passing when Aristobulus presented himself. And these arts were of our people's race when the siege was imminent. At this time, during our celebrated days, a precious victim was seen through the darkness when the master returned. 

There was a certain man, righteous and beloved by God, named **Onias** <note>referring to Honi Ha-Ma'agel, "the Circle-Maker," a Jewish miracle-worker</note>, who, when he gave prayers in turn, was now released. And just as he had spent his prayer so that this sedition might be given up, his prayers were heard. But they did not stop, even as it was being undone: and when they forced Onias to curse Aristobulus, he spoke out. Since he was a man of great grace, the people gave him change through prayer. And they established all things everywhere. And then those who, out of faith in him so that he might persuade them of the destruction of the temple, heard him and then he perished <note>Honi was stoned to death for refusing to curse either side of the civil war</note>; and so they announced these things against Hyrcanus and those who were with Aristobulus. And then, being led away from the altar, they struck our man. 

At the festival, Aristobulus prepared a price for the celebrated things; in which solemnity, many were offered. But they were harsh to him, and Aristobulus was pressed: he announced that no man should come; he told Aristobulus and the priests that they should give a thousand drachmas for each head, which they did. But when they had taken the money, they did not return the animals; and it was true malevolence. While these things were being done above regarding the plundering of the victims, the priests came to the Lord, and a message was sent to Aristobulus and Aretas regarding this mind. A famine fell upon all the power, and at that time a measure of grain cost eleven drachmas.

In other matters, while they were warring, **Scaurus** <note>Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, a Roman general and diplomat</note> was sent to Syria. When he arrived there, he prepared the city of Damascus, which had been occupied shortly before. At that time, envoys from Hyrcanus and Aristobulus came to him. Aristobulus promised him four hundred talents; so much was offered to satisfy the mind. Scaurus favored Aristobulus because he was generous and high-minded, whereas he saw Hyrcanus as poor and stingy. Scaurus, because he preferred the faith of Aristobulus, lifted the siege, ordering Aretas the King of the Arabs to withdraw, lest he appear as an enemy to the Romans. Scaurus then returned to Damascus. Aristobulus, however, with a large army, prepared an army against Hyrcanus. When they fought, many thousands were captured: including <unclear>Celafoni</unclear>, the brother of Aristobulus. 

Not long after, when **Pompey** <note>Pompey the Great</note> had come to Damascus and had traveled through lower Syria, envoys came to him from Egypt, Syria, and Judea. They brought him gifts of victory. Aristobulus came and hurried through the pass; and thus a gift was offered, which he had named during the war. I saw this gift in the temple of the Capitol in Rome: it had the inscription "Aristobulus, son of Alexander," for Aristobulus was of the race of the Jews. In that time, they came to Pompey, and the same appeared for Hyrcanus. He accused Aristobulus, and Scaurus, Gabinius, and others, whom he claimed had been bribed by Hyrcanus in turn; he accused them of things worthy of death. Pompey accepted him also, and he came to Damascus at the present time. Pompey then followed the lineage from the places of Jerusalem: those who, while they differed in life, excelled in art. 

After this, they appointed men over the city. And while it was in his hand, Hyrcanus did not prevail. After this he came toward Jerusalem and Judea. Where the sons of the tyrant were, and when he had taken Heliopolis and Chalcis, he ascended into the middle and made the matter come to pass. When the two brothers, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, had now come with their wealth, Hyrcanus and Antipater accused Aristobulus that he, being younger in birth, had seized power by force and had stolen the ships, and they nurtured accusations against him. They said his victory was gained by slaughter. To this, testimony was given by many of the best men of Judea who were persuaded. 

Aristobulus, however, proved his brother's weakness through a natural and inherent nature: he lived with a hasty mind, and he had taken the kingdom through wicked ambition. He feared that he would be deprived by another, and he prepared to be called king. And he had those neighbors who had helped him, whom he surpassed in purple and robes and other ornaments, so that the neighbors wondered; but he came to offer himself to Pompey. Pompey, however, when he had heard this, blamed Aristobulus for the violence. For when they came to Pompey, and he saw the neighbors and peace were needed, he came to decide. Aristobulus, because Pompey had overseen the matter, did not want to remain. He surrendered and hurried away. He gave an exposition of his position in Damascus, reading the Roman laws against Aristobulus. When he had crossed Pella and Scythopolis, he delayed; when the messengers from Judea came to him, they reported that he was over the mountain in the place named **Alexandrium** <note>a Hasmonean fortress</note>, where Aristobulus was superior. Pompey sent a destination to him, and they came. When Aristobulus had come, he prepared for the invasion. But here the matter was deprived. He simulated submission to Pompey through his works.

<margin>Herod, by the command of Hyrcanus and because of his many virtues, comes to Jerusalem; soon Malichus plots against Herod.</margin>
**After Antipater was killed**, Herod, lest he should dwell upon the howling of this current storm, determined to march with an army against Malichus. Cassius <note>Gaius Cassius Longinus, the Roman proconsul and assassin of Caesar</note>, however, who after many gifts had been given to him by Malichus, ordered him to confess his desire for power, lest he become the cause of a war. Thus, Cassius and Malichus were suspicious of one another; for Malichus pretended to be a friend. When Herod approached the city for a feast day, Malichus prepared an ambush, but he was cautious, as the time for open war was being reserved for later.
<margin>Herod kills Malichus.</margin>
**After this** more famous celebration, Herod, being somewhat emboldened, gathered his forces to enter Jerusalem. When Malichus learned of this, he turned his heart toward Hyrcanus <note>Hyrcanus II, the High Priest and nominal ruler of Judea</note>, trying to prevent Herod’s arrival by a deceptive decree. Hyrcanus, at Malichus's urging, sent word to Herod that he ought not to bring such a multitude into the city, as it was already crowded. Herod, however, disregarded the command and entered the city by night. Then Malichus, fearing for his safety, did not abandon his pretense of friendship; and as the king’s <term>apparatus</term> <note>the royal attendants and officials</note> gathered, he acted as if he loved the ancient kingdom and Herod's lineage, though they were secretly at odds. It pleased Herod to note this deception while he waited for his revenge, responding with both gifts and flatteries. Cassius, however, sent word to Herod that he should put Malichus to death for his cruelty. There were a thousand commands given regarding the trap; Herod was warned, but he did not hesitate. When Malichus came forward, crowned and offering gifts, Herod's servants, acting as if they were preparing lodgings for their guests, instead fell upon him. As Malichus was surrounded by soldiers with drawn swords, he was struck down. The man breathed his last, and the city streets were filled with the blood of his wounds before he could even cry out.
<margin>A certain Felix prepares a tumult against Herod but is soon killed by Herod.</margin>
**Thus Malichus** paid the penalty for his iniquity. Hyrcanus, when he saw the fate of Malichus, was stunned, until Herod told him that the deed was done for his own safety. Hyrcanus then remained silent, for Herod’s power was now great and he was feared by many. After Cassius departed from Syria, a great disturbance arose in Jerusalem. A certain Felix <note>a supporter of the late Malichus</note> armed a multitude to attack Herod's brother, Phasael. Herod, however, hastened to his aid and defeated the attackers. Though he desired to bring peace, foreign elements and those loyal to the old factions continued to invade. In the city, Hyrcanus was accused of showing favor to the enemies of Herod; but Felix was eventually suppressed and his rebellion broken.
<margin>Antigonus strives to return but is defeated.</margin>
**Antigonus** <note>Antigonus II Mattathias, the last Hasmonean king, son of Aristobulus II</note> seized the heavily fortified place of Masada. But Herod soon liberated the way and drove him back. This was a time of great shifting loyalties and betrayals. It was also during this time that Herod sought an alliance through marriage with the house of Hyrcanus <note>the marriage to Mariamne I</note>, defending the family of the High Priest against the sons of Aristobulus. He sought to demonstrate that he was not a mere plunderer, but a protector. Meanwhile, Mark Antony, who had been a general under Caesar, was now rising to power in the East.

**After this** more famous celebration, Herod, being somewhat emboldened, gathered his forces to enter Jerusalem. When Malichus learned of this, he turned his heart toward Hyrcanus, trying to prevent Herod's arrival. Hyrcanus, by the command given to Herod, said that he ought not to bring a multitude into the city. Herod, however, entered the city by night against the command. Then Malichus, fearing for his safety, did not abandon his pretense, and the king prepared to meet Herod. They were deeply at odds with one another. It pleased Herod to note this and to remain observant toward him, even with gifts and flatteries. Cassius, however, ordered Herod to kill Malichus for his cruelty. There were a thousand commands given, but Herod did not want this. When Malichus arrived, crowned and offering gifts, Herod's servants, as if preparing lodgings, killed Malichus with swords. He breathed his last and died in the streets of the city.

<meta>This page follows the account of the political instability in Judea during the Roman civil wars. Following the assassination of Antipater, his son Herod has been forced to navigate the treacherous rivalry between Roman factions and the local Hasmonean claimants, specifically Antigonus, who has allied with the Parthian Empire to seize the throne.</meta>

...the destruction of such great things. They brought Hyrcanus and Phasael <note>Phasael was Herod's elder brother and governor of Jerusalem</note>, the brother of Herod, in chains. Herod, however, being most powerful in his resolve, chose to resist where he could not win by voice; he prepared to depart. Taking his sister, and the daughter of Alexander <note>Mariamne I, the Hasmonean princess whom Herod married to bolster his legitimacy</note> whom he held in marriage despite her youth, along with his two brothers Joseph and Pheroras, and all his necessary servants, he hurried to depart from Judea, fleeing with a retreating column. Yet no one was more distressed than Herod himself; as he pursued the journey, he pitied them all. He saw the women wailing because they were leaving their fatherland and expected no good for themselves.

**H**erod, however, maintained his spirit with the authority of the matter and a greatness of soul against all such piety <note>original: *pietatem*, here meaning familial duty or emotional distress</note>. He encouraged each one to trust him and not to give themselves over to fear, for their only hope of safety lay in their flight. Those who were with Herod tried to sustain their spirits with these persuasions. Herod himself was nearly driven to despair when his mother’s carriage overturned, placing her in great danger; he could hardly endure it. Out of his passion and love, and fearing the enemies would capture them while they were delayed, he drew his sword to kill himself. He preferred to deprive himself of life rather than see his family fall into the hands of the enemy. However, his companions prevented him, saying it was better to persevere for the sake of his people. Overcome by their words, he repented of the act he had contemplated, and they continued with speed to the fortress called Masada <note>A rugged natural fortress overlooking the Dead Sea</note>. There, while he assessed his power, he realized that many from the province were joining him. When he reached Idumaea, where he met his kin, he deposited his mother, his sister Mariamne, and the other women at the town of Masada, providing them with enough water and other supplies to withstand a siege. He then set out with his two brothers, Joseph and Pheroras, toward Petra, a city of Arabia. Meanwhile, the Parthians <note>An empire from the East, ancient rivals of Rome</note> took Jerusalem by force and plundered the palace. Hyrcanus and Phasael remained there in distress, held until the heat of the conflict subsided. Antigonus, who had promised the Parthians money and women, had Herod's kin as his primary target, but Herod had already led them away. Since the Parthians did not find the promised money, they laid waste to the provinces and the most powerful city of Marissa. Antigonus, having earned the trust of the Parthians, held Hyrcanus and Phasael as a small triumph over the Jews. He feared that the multitude might later restore Hyrcanus to the high priesthood <term>High Priesthood</term> <note>Jewish law required the High Priest to be physically "unblemished"</note>, so he cut off Hyrcanus's ears. He did this so that even if the people wanted to, the old man could never again hold that sacred office, as his body was no longer whole. The Parthians wanted to keep Phasael alive, but since he could not endure the shame and had no sword to end his life, he struck his head against a stone and finished his life. It is said that Antigonus sent a physician to him under the pretense of healing the wound, but ordered him to apply poisonous medicines to the gashes. Yet, before he breathed his last, Phasael learned from a woman that his brother Herod had escaped the Parthians; he died bravely, knowing that one remained who would avenge his death. Herod, not deterred by the magnitude of these surrounding evils, was made more resolute by them. Unaware that Phasael was already dead, he intended to ransom his brother from the King of Arabia, offering Phasael's son as a hostage. But hearing that his brother had perished, he decided to flee to Egypt to see Cleopatra, and from there to proceed to Antony <note>Mark Antony, the Roman Triumvir</note>. Arriving in Alexandria, he was received by Cleopatra, who wished to use him for her own purposes, but he hurried toward Rome to see Antony. Despite sailing in the winter, he reached Pamphylia and eventually arrived in Italy. He hurried to Antony and recounted the tragedies that had befallen Judea: how his brother Phasael had been killed by the Parthians, how Hyrcanus was held captive with his ears cut off, and how Antigonus had promised the Parthians a thousand talents and five hundred women of Herod's own kin. He described how he had escaped with the women by night and the many calamities he had suffered.

**A**t this hearing, Antony cried out with a most miserable voice for Herod, both because of the dignity of the man and the memory of the friendship with Herod’s father, Antipater, who had faithfully served the Romans in their wars. He took him to Caesar <note>Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus</note>. Caesar, when he was asked by Antony on behalf of Herod, was even more ready to help. Messala and Atratinus then introduced Herod to the Senate, recounting his father's benefits to the Romans and accusing Antigonus of being a manifest enemy, not only for his previous actions but because he had accepted the kingship from the Parthians in neglect of the Romans. When the Senate was moved by this, Antony said it would be advantageous for the war against the Parthians if Herod were appointed King of the Jews. When the whole Senate agreed, they decreed it so. This was the highest honor Antony could give Herod, to have him restored to power so unexpectedly. They never expected the Romans would give a kingdom to one who was not of the priestly lineage <note>The Hasmoneans were both kings and priests; Herod was an Idumaean, making his appointment a radical break from tradition</note>.

<column-break/>

When these matters were concluded, he was ordered to descend from Italy to Judea. When he arrived in Ptolemais, it was announced that Herod and Antony were allied. Herod gathered a small army of foreigners and Jews and marched through Galilee against Antigonus. He was compelled to act with speed to liberate those besieged at Masada. Many in Judea, out of hatred for the adversary, joined him. As he fought, many who had rebelled were reduced to flight. He hurried to Masada to rescue his kinsmen. When he arrived, his countrymen helped him. Herod rewarded those who were faithful. For while Antigonus tried to occupy the land with frauds and plundering, Herod, knowing the land well, took back the fortresses and proceeded toward Jerusalem. There was great enthusiasm for Herod on the western side of the city. He pitched his camp near Jerusalem, while his brother's killers and the supporters of Antigonus frequently harassed his troops. Herod proclaimed near the walls that he came for the good of the people and not for their destruction, even toward those who had been his enemies. Antigonus, however, shouted from the walls, calling Herod a "half-Jew" and unworthy of the throne, saying that the honor of the kingship should only be given to the priestly line. As these blasphemies were voiced by both sides, Antigonus’s men began to throw missiles from the towers. Herod then ordered his troops to retire to winter quarters in the areas around Jerusalem, as Antigonus’s soldiers had laid waste to the immediate vicinity. When the Roman troops <note>Under the commander Silo</note> threatened to depart because of a lack of supplies, Herod ensured they were provided with everything they needed—corn, oil, and cattle—so that no necessity would be lacking. He sent his brother Joseph to Idumaea to prevent any uprisings there, while he himself remained to guard the grain stores. In this, Herod did not rest. He took several cities, including Joppa, and eventually moved toward the caves of Galilee where many of the rebels were hiding. He used great ingenuity to reach these caves, lowering soldiers in chests by ropes from the cliffs to smoke out and destroy the brigands who were harassing the countryside. This victory in Galilee further solidified his control. He then returned to Samaria and prepared for the final march against Jerusalem, having proven his valor and his ability to provide for both his soldiers and the people.

<summary>Herod flees a Parthian-backed coup in Jerusalem, secures his family at Masada, and travels to Rome where the Senate officially declares him King of Judea. Returning with Roman support, he begins a military campaign to reclaim his kingdom from his rival, Antigonus.</summary>

### These things having been finished, he soon acquired the power. In the consulship of Marcus Agrippa and Caninius Gallus, in the 185th Olympiad.
In the certain month of the celebration, on the 27th day. Sosius, when he had offered a golden crown to the Lord God, returned from Jerusalem and led the bound Antigonus to Antony. Herod, however, did not want Antigonus to live at Rome and declare to the Senate that he was of royal lineage. Herod, being an outsider <note>term: *alienigena* - Herod was an Idumaean, not a Hasmonean Jew, which challenged his legitimacy</note>, feared that the kingdom might not remain his. He compelled Antony with much money to have Antigonus executed.

with the soldiers. He also omits granting the crown <note>original: "conū," likely "coronam"</note> to Jaffa <note>Jaffa was a strategic port city; the text likely refers to the ongoing territorial disputes involving Cleopatra VII</note>. If he had detained him on his journey home through a petition, he would have dishonored this man with a harsh reputation. And as they had previously suppressed him, he said this: "The King will not despise those who had not made preparations for every eventuality." He proclaims this man as the heir who should restore the foundations, and he recovers the honors of others which had been cast down by Antigonus <note>Antigonus was the last Hasmonean king, whom Herod defeated with Roman help</note>. Each person is praised by the light of Herod. He acted with a slow but steady goodwill toward all, and with great desire, he anticipated him in every way. When all things were fulfilled according to his petition, he changed his position from a lower sphere; and because of this, he was truly honored, and he made it known that he should be called by the name of Cleopatra, who had been heard before. Here, by these means, they turned back toward the same things.

They ceased to be ungenerous toward Herod, as they had previously held him to be as good as dead; they now chose to see him as a living man. For they feasted sumptuously with Herod. Indeed, he was protected by divine providence <note>original: "divina providentia"</note> which brought Herod back at that time; it had made him safe and secure, even while the will of the people remained in flux.

And with his will helping his speech, they were in effect: it is brought before Herod.

...directs toward Herod. Praying to avert the first dissension of the war. For just as it is argued, the past excesses of the deeds done [were such] that he could not draw strength for himself.

**Herod**, however, so as not to give the impression that he had fled, nor to remain quietly silent, wished to handle matters with a determined and forceful spirit. The Arabs, however, had secured the way; but he himself was seen to go, lest anything among the captives in the clouds <note>original: "nūba," likely a corruption of "nubibus" or referring to a specific foggy region</note> should be lost, and lest if they should leave the camp for the rest of the day, he should be seen as leading a decisive battle. He examined all small things, lest by degrees those who are caught should perish. These things he deliberated upon during the journey, and he cleverly managed the other failings of his health; and mostly at sea, he thought that in an uncertain outcome he should extend certain things. Here, in his own battle, there is a reward. When he had demanded the return of the captives with a prior request, your own [position] also did not fall through your own [fault], but through a faithless occupation, since his own people were announced as perishing. Thus it seems through the duration of the pledges, you also diminish the highest part of your dignity. But he himself was able to use such force when he had so perversely and valiantly guarded his own interests; he indeed confessed to many the end of his fates in envy. The same thing, however, remained unmoved among the gifts, and then it seems he was present. And even then he greatly disturbed the highest parts, and now [he approached] the prior fortresses; he was scarcely able to be at peace. He wore down the years on the road, where many stood together in his presence. When he departed from the ship in secret, passing through the play, they then came into the statue in the forum.

But if Hyrcanus should arrive, who alone among the Parthians <note>Hyrcanus II had been mutilated and taken as a prisoner to Babylon by the Parthians to prevent him from serving as High Priest again</note> was accustomed to the proper customs and affairs of the kings: it could be established, though faith would hardly remain for what was promised. He would mock the occasion, as he alone was not allowed to be [king]. Since the Jews [saw] the occasion of such an evil for Hyrcanus, they judged Hyrcanus. He looked back at the small model and the governance of affairs as if toward a king: he believed he should preserve everything. But in Judea, the multitude, together with their spirits, [went] to Hyrcanus so that he should not be sufficiently overwhelmed. They saw him in the monument... lest he should know Herod had killed many in his own family. Because he specifically is seen to be used for evil, I judge that he should be preserved, and so he made a confession... and so Herod is announced as the judge of those condemned. By which pledges, and having brought the presents of the king, he seeks Hyrcanus [and] Alexander <note>Likely referring to the Hasmonean family members Herod was monitoring</note> but his own... Hyrcanus... but they saw your own skill. Many on the road were then overwhelmed... many failed in spirit. Hyrcanus... others... looked out from there. When the wealthy were seen to be carried away in spirit... into which... Hyrcanus... to the thing itself... he should prepare for the journey. Because so much from the deeds of the Hyrcanians was not... in the new way they trust and fail... to Herod then... whatever is to his own... in the new... Judea from the Parthians. Hyrcanus the king of his own... then Hyrcanus [trusted] in the conspiracy.

<meta>This page continues from the account of Herod’s diplomatic efforts with Rome. It transitions from his external political security to the internal collapse of his household, specifically the intrigues leading to the execution of his wife, the Hasmonean princess Mariamne I, and the subsequent psychological decline of the king.</meta>

And with a feigned voice he spoke: "Let it not be a precedent for me that I have associated myself [with such things]; let it be done to me thus." So it was said in spirit: but he was sent among the others where he had loosened his habit. King Herod also had raised an outcry once more; and the circle of the Herodian court <note>original: "herodiam," here likely referring to the family faction or a corruption of the name</note> was gasping in a more bitter hatred, then and there being substituted, through which the breeze and the nourishment of help might hold them. In a bloody discourse, the cleansing of all was sought. When so many conditions were holding you here, the sentence was changed into a greater danger. Then, some of those who were faithful to the royal decree subsided out of sorrow; they were added to the utility of the kingdom in Herod's eyes. But Salome, the sister of Herod—a cunning and singular woman—since she was then present, all things were again held through her, who, being the lover of her own interests, brought [Mariamne's] youth into judgment.

Alexandra <note>Mariamne's mother</note> then seeing that she was to be destroyed unless she should petition Herod, and being violently disgusted by the situation, sought to be made a spectator through the streets; she advised the example: she blamed all the misfortunes and deeds of her daughter, and in the sight of all the judges, she declared that Mariamne had conquered through evil and unjust vices. Which behavior, proceeding from her, was detestable; for it was a blow against a most just woman who had done her favors. Nor did she stop there where she fell: she was making her face sorrowful with her eyes and changing her color, and even tearing her hair in a pompous display. Alexandra, however, was mixing irony with the children; but with loud words to the honest, she then appeared to loosen herself. This grief was a pretender to life, but with the pain of Herod being slaughtered <note>original: "mactantne," referring to the metaphorical or physical "killing" of the spirit or the upcoming execution</note>, she was again in fear: so that she might sufficiently indicate to Herod her noble birth; again they tell of the ritual of Herod's slaughter.

Mariamne, they say, the wife of Herod, thus looked upon the gestures of her servants with piety: and she polluted <note>or "surpassed"</note> the greatness of many years. Modest in her soul, nor did her beauty of body fail, which lived in her affability; she said she would rather be a victor than be made so here. She spoke to the victor and yet not in fear, as she was led for the second time. For at that time he ran to her; he was following the mouth of others in his immoderate companionship toward her. Secondly, he said: Herod turned from this and slaughtered Mariamne: this deed of the impious favored the Herodians; he established the madness in the marriage and handed over the state: so that faith then might be led here, a small feast of trouble having arisen. After these internal things, he showed himself an equal to Herod; then he exercised himself in that time, inviting the voices of all, for he was softening toward everything.

The latter half contains repetitive legalistic summaries concerning Herod's judgments and the "truth" of his reign in relation to Roman law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the history of Herod the Great’s reign, moving from his architectural achievements—specifically the expansion of the Temple Mount—into the political maneuvers described at the opening of Book 16 of the Antiquities, involving his sons and his relationship with the Roman statesman Marcus Agrippa.</meta>

A great wall surrounded the side, which was a thousand stadia <note>original: "mille stadiorum"; a stadium was about 600 feet, making this a massive enclosure</note> in circumference. Herod, however, enclosed it from the inner parts with a sixth wall <note>interpreted as a reference to the various boundary layers of the Temple</note>, binding it with lead so that the space within the circuit might be filled. Again, he enclosed a sixth area within that, made of many squares, having measurements at the front; on both sides the flanks were fitted together so firmly that they were essentially immovable. Beside this sacred work, which was a defiant undertaking, he built down to the foundations in a short time. 

There was a ditch made at that time, but later a larger level surface was completed. On every side, porticoes <note>term: portico — a porch or walkway with a roof supported by columns</note> could be seen from afar, a magnificent connection of the whole. From that time, this portico wall was strongly fortified by masonry, and other walls made the sacred precinct an extraordinary enclosure. On the eastern side, the length of the portico was doubled, built with extremely high walls. The sheer nature of the work made it seem as though it could withstand any siege or attempt to tear down the fortifications. Through the side of the mountain, he had a cavernous passage constructed, as Herod had ordered this to be done during a time of great concern. This fortification of Herod's was kept ready, as he presented it to his friends for their own safety and followed the instructions and warnings of the Romans.

On the western side, there were gates standing; one looked toward the palace <note>original: "rutia," likely a corruption of "regia" or the royal palace</note>, protected by a wall; two led to the suburbs; and the fourth descended by many steps to the lower valley. The western side looked toward the east, and again to the eastern valley. The southern tract also had gates. In the middle of this southern side, the portico was built double in length, stretching from the east all the way to the western valley. 

It is worthy of the highest justice to narrate these things, which were done by Herod alone. This was a spectacle more illustrious than any other that can be seen; if any other part had been attended to, it would be the gates upon which it stood. It truly seemed at that time that these were not works of the earth; they were so immense that the mind struggles to measure their force. Rows of columns stood there, bound to the length of the wall. The thickness of the columns was such that three men could barely clasp their hands around one; their length was fifteen feet, and they were made of the finest wood <note>original: "fustibus," though Josephus describes stone columns, the manuscript here suggests wood or decorated shafts</note>. 

The number of columns was one hundred and sixty-two. Their capitals were sculpted in the Corinthian style <note>term: Corinthian style — an ornate Greek architectural style characterized by carved acanthus leaves on the tops of columns</note>, a work of marvelous skill. There were four rows of columns, dividing the space. Two of these rows were made in the same way, with a width of thirty feet and a height of fifty feet. The middle row had a width of forty-five feet and a height of one hundred feet. Around this, the upper apparatus was built of wood, joined together in various polished figures, so that the beauty of the joints was visible. Because they were formerly walls, nothing stood in the way of the sacred beauty.

Inside the wall, on the southern and northern parts, there were inscriptions on the walls; on the eastern path, there were notices in various languages <note>original: "uice mēta," referring to the Soreg or warning signs</note> that no foreigner or woman should enter the inner sanctuary. Within the sanctuary, burnt offerings were placed for God. Herod did not prohibit anyone from bringing gifts, but he took care of the inner and outer walls and their preparation. Herod chose a number of priests, five hundred in one group and five thousand in another, to be instructed in the building arts. These were trained for the service and honor of the holy place. Since the time was uncertain, the temple was dedicated again through the immediate assumption of duties by the priests as established by law. The construction and completion by Herod was an abundant and lasting work.

<column-break/>

# BOOK XVI BEGINS

**After the construction** of the temple, Herod administered all affairs with great care, so that the city and provinces might have a more refined culture than before. He sent messengers to many places. Herod sought to resolve any confusion and to see his sons, who had been sent to Rome for their education. 

At that time, Herod sailed to Italy, desiring to greet Caesar <note>Augustus</note> and to see his sons who were living there. Herod wished to see them provoked to excellence in their conduct. When Herod arrived in Rome, he was received most clearly and honorably by his own people. He took his sons from the care of their tutors and brought them before Caesar. The priesthood was under his power until he died, and he also met with Agrippa <note>Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Augustus's right-hand man</note>. Herod then arranged for the priestly robes to be kept under Roman custody. 

The king appointed that this power should be seen as coming from the Romans, and even from the time of Claudius, this power remained. Herod then established a residence for the festive celebrations of the people. Caesar advised Herod that he should bring his sons, Alexander and Aristobulus, back to their own home. They were of a magnificent stature and had a very beautiful form. It seemed a great salvation for Herod to have them back, as it was an unexpected hope. 

Herod was seen as a man of great favor, and the people accepted the youths. However, some brothers and others began to spread rumors and vanity against Herod, seeking to turn his favor away from his sons. They sowed fear and deception, trying to tear the sons away from him. It was whispered that Herod should be wary. 

To secure his lineage, Herod married Aristobulus to the daughter of Salome <note>Berenice</note>, and Alexander to the daughter of Archelaus, the king of Cappadocia <note>Glaphyra</note>. He hoped this would bring peace. Meanwhile, Agrippa hurried from Italy to Asia, and Herod went to meet him. Herod hosted Agrippa with great display and showed him the perpetual path and the vestibule of the temple. Agrippa stayed with Herod and was impressed by the people. Herod thanked him for the voyage. When Herod and Agrippa were together, Herod sought justice for his province and for the Jews. 

<note>The following section in the OCR contains significant repetition and fragmented Latin phrases regarding Herod's interactions with Agrippa and his provincial administration.</note>

Herod traveled with Agrippa through the provinces, showing him the royal houses and the justice he had established. They visited various places together, and Herod petitioned Agrippa on behalf of the inhabitants, seeking to have their burdens reduced. Agrippa, seeing Herod's labor and the greatness of the works he had performed, granted many favors to the province. Through Herod's intervention, Agrippa showed great justice and fidelity to the people. Herod was seen as a protector of the laws and a friend of Rome. Agrippa then returned to Rome, having seen the nobility of Herod’s kingdom and the justice he had enacted for his people.
