Suspicion and hatred began to press upon him; regarding the Jewish affairs, they wished them to be handled without the annoyance of Peter <note>original: "petri"; likely a scribal error for "patris," referring to Herod as a father</note>. For these men had spoken to Agrippa concerning Herod's divine council, and he himself was gratified by this affection, and again he had summoned Herod for both purposes.

Indeed, having returned to Syria, where he heard from others what had been done regarding the affairs of the Jews, Herod’s pleasure turned to horror, and the days became more bitter and evil. For upon coming to Jerusalem, where he had gathered the whole people, he announced everything from the embassy, holding an assembly. He reported to them his presence before the king <note>Caesar Augustus</note> from the delegation, which the Jews in Egypt had sought, so that he might live in Syria without violence. And it came to pass that Herod was accustomed to being a prince over his own, and that he had been in a fourth part <term>Tetrarch: a ruler of one-fourth of a kingdom</term> among his brothers, bringing him to the judgment seat. Among his own Jews, with the highest presentation, the king was blinded by these things, not without the Lord in Judea. He proceeded toward those detested seditions and received them more bitterly. At that time, Herod’s hatred and suspicion regarding the sons of Mariamne grew, and the people were always born in them by vow: you bold men, in the name of Syllaeus <note>original: "silay"; an official from Nabataea who frequently plotted against Herod</note>, who wish to claim authority. And when Herod commanded those young men, he prayed: the memory of their mother <note>Mariamne I</note>, which had been untimely, was used to direct them against Herod. The young men were so eager for Herod that their own evil seemed like a prayer. Herod’s heirs and his sister Salome exercised hatred against one another. The mode of this hatred was most similar to that of the daughter of Mariamne; Alexander and Aristobulus had come to their husbands in honest standing, but Salome, with a malicious mind, wished to slander them with false accusations. They could have told the truth to the young men, which was altogether most deserved. As one grievance was brought in for the death of their mother, they were confounded, nor could they be justly excluded from the threat. They were stirring up sedition to avenge the one who had been honored. Finally, those young men were the authors of greatness among the Jews. But most of all, the malice of Salome and the neighborhood of others, while looking toward them, distracted their minds; she harassed them as if she were raving with some evil. And since Alexander was an heir of Mariamne, he was known to be in conflict with Herod. When he had been with Agrippa, and the people were better disposed, Alexander’s voice broke out in hatred against Herod. He brought news to Judea of an accuser <note>original: "mxtore/mxtadore"; corrupted form of 'accusatore' or 'Antipatrem'</note> for himself, which they could least endure, calling them to vengeance. Caesar [Augustus] also brought in Aristobulus from Cappadocia in the hope that he might live, so that through him, Herod might receive Alexander. But Herod, slandering him in Judea, approached Caesar with Alexander to be judged by the Lord <note>Caesar</note>. Caesar truly judged Herod and Herod’s sons as just; and so that even today no son could be overlooked, he assigned Aristobulus his place. 

The domestic household of Salome lived in this way. At that time, Herod took Alexander's affection as an occasion for the young men’s wives to be incited, which happened unjustly because he preferred his own wives over the Jewish ones, who would inherit the kingdom. They stood against the sons of Mariamne. Herod saw all of this in Judea: let Herod know his other son from Judea <note>referring to Antipater, his first-born son by Doris</note>, so that with the seal placed upon him, Herod moved against Alexander. If Alexander and Aristobulus appeared defeated, they were nevertheless heirs. Herod was moved by the brothers' affliction, though he had accused them. The accuser <note>Antipater</note> was brought from elsewhere. Alexander and the others were born into suspicion. These were miserable years. Herod followed the will of the accuser, wishing it to be done according to the truth, and he wanted Aristobulus to be with him. Because of the insult to Salome, they were raging with fear; it became manifest through her love for the accuser. The accusations came to Herod, and he humbled the sons of Mariamne, wanting to grant greater honor to the accuser. Herod and Alexander then went before Caesar; Herod said the forum was being exasperated. Every day, the corruption of Mariamne’s sons was seen. Malice grew daily between the brothers. Herod, using this wickedness, was in a fury, as if the sons of Mariamne had been noted as just. He called the sons back to the truth. 

He took the sons of Mariamne and brought them to Rome; he came to Caesar’s charity. Herod accused the sons of Mariamne regarding Judea. He called them to the accuser's piety. The father thought his sons were seeking his death. Caesar saw himself as the judge of the whole matter. He saw the boys were in danger. Having read the complaints, he did not wish to leave the sons to be destroyed. Now Caesar was forced to witness Herod being polluted by these slanders. Why do you labor in these reports? He provided assistance to the son and thought the accuser was proven. Those who wished Herod justice wanted to give Alexander back to the will of the accuser. Such hatred existed that they stood worthy of judgment. I wish to report the true horror and hatred the accuser demonstrated. Indeed, Alexander and Aristobulus, while Salome honored them, saw the evil. They wished to return evil for honor. I did not want to share this audacity, but Caesar, with a more just heart, brought Herod’s peace to the situation. By his speech, he checked the hatred and the accusations. This was not a fable or a source of shame among men.

When Herod was defeated in his open accusation, and saw the flow of tears, he was relieved of the heavy charge. He was brought to the accusation of the sons, which was more just; though they were difficult in their defense, they could provide the confidence of an honest mind to their father. Caesar detested the accusation and wanted the family to be reconciled through justice. Caesar saw to the reconciliation.

<column-break/>

Herod, though not appearing shameless in his sorrow, gradually purged himself. When it was done, Caesar stood as the authority over the lands. He told Herod that it was foolish to play with the fate of his son Alexander. Alexander appeared in hatred toward the accuser, but through Caesar’s justice, the son appeared restored to the father. We must not change our minds toward Herod through this faction; he must abhor what he did. For Caesar returned him to his former life, though he had thought to destroy his own sons. If indeed it was done in this manner, the son would be absolved. If truly he had a perverted nature, he would be handed over to the Jews as a Jewish son. 

And so, to Herod, the son appeared as a victim of calumny. It was confessed that all things were done by the accuser. Herod saw his sons again. They came to justice. Let no one think this was done by perversion. It appeared they had been in danger. Herod was called "Father" by the Jews. They came to the truth. Justice was given to Herod. The wife's faction had perished. Caesar spoke to Herod about the sons.

Herod’s labor bore fruit; the violated life was restored. Caesar said he had acted as a father. Herod returned to Judea with his sons. He gave them honors. Caesar had shown the way. Herod returned to his kingdom, having been restored to his sons by the Romans. Caesar had returned the son to Herod in honor. This was the truth of Herod's house. Alexander and Aristobulus were restored to their place. Herod's first-born son <note>Antipater</note> was also given his station, but the shadow of the accuser remained. Herod returned to his children. He came to the truth. Caesar, acting as the father of the world, had brought peace.

# The Benefits 
Furthermore, it is almost impossible to fully explain the **benefits** which Herod bestowed upon the foreign nations: both in the construction of these works and the useful buildings provided to various republics and cities. Most noble and memorable is the temple built from its foundations in **Rhodes**; he himself constructed the port for the Phoenicians at great expense. He also provided many talents for the construction of ships. He rebuilt the metropolis <note>Likely referring to Nicopolis, the "City of Victory" built to honor Augustus</note> from its ruins and established many conditions for public places near the lands of the **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans</note>. And in the city of Antioch <note>The OCR reads "gip patria," but historical context confirms the great street of Antioch</note>, he paved a vast, long civic street with stone, decorating it with a portico <term>portico|a covered walkway supported by columns</term> on both sides to provide both ornament and pleasure for the inhabitants. Furthermore, he bestowed an honor worthy of the name upon the **Olympic games** in terms of their decoration. Having observed that the games were declining due to a lack of funds, he dedicated a source of revenue to ensure the celebration and its festive decoration would continue. Because of this, he was named a perpetual **agonotheta** <term>agonotheta|a supervisor or judge of the sacred games</term> for all time.

Many have observed a contradiction in Herod’s will. For if one looks at the generous gifts of his spirit, which he gave to all men, who could deny that he possessed an **overflowing soul**? If, however, one looks at the **torments and injuries** he inflicted upon his subjects and those of his own household, he appears harsh, fierce, and utterly alienated from all piety. Thus we find that people believe his will was composed of contrary elements. Indeed, he focused on one single cause: the preservation of his **dominion**. For while he maintained a massive outward show of largess and munificence, he did so for his own current hopes, even if time compelled him to lay waste to his subjects through great expense, especially when he turned to injustice to cover his costs. When he began to be overwhelmed by the hatred of his subjects because of his violence toward others, he sought to be corrected—or so it appeared—through his usual habit of spending money. As for his family, if any words were cast against him, he would treat them as slaves, stripping them of their status...

# The Accession of Archelaus and the Passover Riots

...they approached Caesar on your behalf. May all the gods above see to it that among those who draw near, the uprooted are at least fragile. On the contrary, **Archelaus**, because he had stood before all the soldiers to be greeted, appeared equal to their expectations; yet the Jews were entirely excluded. First, indeed, he spoke openly and clearly in a salutary manner, having been led by hand after those who arrived by ship, so that they might follow him as if they had prepared everything in my manner by mutual agreement. Then, by a leap of fate, he prepared himself in the order of his rank. After this, they read through the records to see whether anything had yet been written to him or to **Herod’s fortress** <note>original: "iherodem castellum"; likely referring to the Antonia Fortress or Herodium</note>. Let it be sent in his writing. For he held power in this way, by the force of the command, and so forth.

***

**Archelaus**, even if he then seemed to hold the upper hand, nevertheless most abundantly and for six days straight obeyed the king's edict concerning praises, celebrating many favors; while with great applause he spoke of these honors. While the whole city was led toward greater and nearly headlong emotions, Archelaus sat upon the tribunal and promised them that he would appear as a kind friend. By speaking and by his instructions, he prepared them so that by the union of all their favor, his speech might be dearer than mere benevolence. He began to give them many thanks, because the suspicion of evil thoughts regarding his father’s actions toward him was replaced by an affection for the king's magnificent honor. He asked and prayed that they would not honor him with the title of King out of fear. For although he had been invested with the dignity of power by **Herod**, who wished him to succeed, he sought to confirm his justice outside of the royal realm <note>original: "extra regium"; implying he sought Roman confirmation before officially taking the title</note>. For this reason, he did not hasten to have the diadem placed upon him in Jerusalem; he did not wish to receive an ambiguous honor, fearing that it might generate much trouble for his safety until those in order of merit and will should judge his rule to be firm. If indeed his kindness seemed good to **Caesar**, he would prepare with the necessity of a benevolent spirit. He urged himself to hasten, so that he might show himself to be better than his father. The confused multitude of the common people sought his favor, and they did not widely challenge his will with their praises. And indeed, as Archelaus spoke with such gentleness, the more they increased their promises to him. Already he had made concessions to those bringing petitions; some demanded the lightening of public duties <note>original: "publicae functionis"; referring to taxes or civic labor</note> with a great shout; others expected the release of those imprisoned by Herod. Others made great vows for things he did not at all approve, and they strove to abolish the public union. Archelaus, being in no way contrary or harsh, gave a kind judgment to those who had suffered, hoping the justice of the kingdom would surpass the past. For this reason, he hastened to offer sacrifices to God, celebrating the completed rites.

***

**S**edition, however, began again after it seemed that the whole journey was being attempted. They waited for an outside movement; with tumultuous voices, they demanded the causes of Herod’s majesty be investigated, and many poor and outspoken men, having lost their fear of Herod, sought honor. Moreover, men of high standing did this by striking before the waters—that is, during the days in which that warning stands through the friendship and the losses Herod had caused. Having completed the gifts which they gave according to their will, a great number of merchants demanded that Archelaus remove those who had held office under Herod. Many Jews also demanded that the **High Priest** <note>original: "pontifice"</note> whom Herod had appointed be removed, and that a man who was pure and according to the laws be promoted to the high priesthood. **Archelaus**, although he bore this with difficulty, nonetheless hastened to prevent a forceful outbreak until the journey he was preparing for was ready; for he could not easily prevail unless by force of will and justice. He sought to avoid everything that was being done and to meet their prayers with mercy. He spoke against the dispersion, saying that he did not want a conflict of dissension or a massive struggle. He urged concord until he could return from Caesar with a firm kingdom. He advised them to avoid ruining their own safety by chance while they struggled. Archelaus seemed to be speaking to two groups: then they called the younger men and exhorted them with words. But they cried out that Archelaus spoke perversely; they were determined to fulfill their own lust for rebellion more than the rule of justice.

***

And then those friends of Herod came to the youths, and the same things were done; with no judgment changed, they grew more fervent. They said these things were just: unless Caesar himself came on the journey, nothing could be taken away. A great multitude of people was brought in, and the seditions became more entwined. Many were seen to be skilled in temptation; the time was full of soldiers as if a sacrifice were to be made. That festival is called **Passover** <note>original: "Paschalium illa festiuitas"</note>; it is for the veneration and memory of the departure from Egypt. A great and innumerable multitude of people gathered during that solemn time. A great abundance of people from the whole region converged, many being vexed by the religious fasts of Herod. Although the multitude was in the middle, they avoided words that friends provided. Archelaus, fearing he would lose his authority, ordered a cohort of armed men to restrain their onset; if the multitude of others should impose themselves, they were to repel them. Many came to the divine will with a great shout, and the soldiers committed injuries and horrors in their onset. Very many were scattered, and many failed with great loss. Archelaus, however, thought to persuade them of everything unless he broke the onset of the multitude. The city's justice perished so that they might repel others from their counsel. The leaders of the seditious ones left the honor of the soldiers, and through this invention, they rested. But the Passover was celebrated as if from a cult of things; it seemed to the Jews that on that day the duties of the festival were abandoned. They pressed against the wall and made a spectacle of their burden. Very many then commended themselves to **Philip**, his brother, who was in the royal court and household. **Salome**, the sister of Herod, also ordered all her family to act. She said in words that she would collaborate with Archelaus so that Caesar might firm up the kingdom; in truth, however, she prepared to accuse him before Caesar with those who had been at the temple.

<column-break/>

They prepared for his death so that he would not be dear to Archelaus or Caesar's children; the Jews possessed a portion of Caesar's treasure, yet it failed Archelaus. Then, through a scheme in the court, he saw that Herod's confirmation had been made by the judgment of Archelaus's division <note>original: "herodis confirmatio[n]e et fuisse arbitrio archelas diuitioneris"</note>. However, Archelaus again withdrew and waited for Caesar's command. Many preferred to approach Caesar, for they did not wish to fulfill the judgment as if it were finished. Many spent days sailing to Rome; among them was **Antipas** <note>original: "antipater"; historically Antipas, Herod's other son and rival for the throne</note>, the heir of Herod, who prepared to take the whole kingdom for himself. **Salome** and the heralds of Herod permitted this, so that Antipas might be made the heir instead of Archelaus. They arrived with a show of benign friendship, but it was for this purpose. Archelaus arrived in the region of **Idumea**. The leaders of the promise came, and a multitude was proclaimed as one honorable thing: they prepared for his presence. Especially when he had come to the King, he deserved to have an heir in all clear matters. It was seen that Archelaus, being the elder, should receive the kingdom from Caesar. Yet all friends cried out against Archelaus for the sedition. Even if there was some benevolence from the land, Archelaus said he would be the victor against the royal confirmation. He hastened into Idumea, as if he could prepare himself by the king's merits. He labored so that the authority of Archelaus might be deposed before Caesar. He accepted the inheritance and whatever had been prepared from the land's affairs. Caesar then looked upon their various claims of justice. Caesar himself, by his presence, judged the Jews and the divine justice of the promise. For Herod had not wished for the son to act as heir in that way previously. When Caesar saw the promise Archelaus held, he prepared to take what was true. Archelaus had commanded that the effect be carried out. Many had come to see the truth of the invention, and a unique heir was seen among the Jews. Many of Herod's party were scattered, yet many wondered about the succession of the kingdom. All the military multitude and the coronation came to the blessed royal court. Many causes were seen as if the king had already been given by Caesar. It was prepared so that Herod's promise of an heir would be made one with Caesar. He went out from the fortress of Idumea; many believed it had proceeded from a divine matter. But many Jews in their truth preferred the light and helped many of Herod's party. They prepared to stand by the Herodian house. The multitude prepared to stand by the king of the nation. It was prepared so that he might show himself in various turns. It was seen that he should receive it firmly by the will of Caesar. Especially concerning the empire, he was opposed in turns. Many had died in the struggle; the multitude had been defeated in the succession, so that the kingdom of the Jews was found in the promise. Caesar did not want the Jews to be defeated. He then granted the honor of Herod to the defeated ones of the land. Archelaus then held the testimony and firmness of the victor. He prepared against those who were against the Jews. Archelaus then appeared to obey, yet he was made master over the multitude of the Jews.

***

**I**t began to be brought before Caesar concerning the multitude of the land. When Antipas saw that he was the heir to the true inheritance, and Archelaus saw the victory over the Jews, Archelaus sought to provide. Archelaus saw that his victory was in the inheritance. He prepared to be the victor in humility. The victory over the hostile works was judged by the gods for Archelaus. He saw the necessity of the king. The multitude came, and that which Archelaus did concerning the victory of the Jews was seen as his. For he had performed the merits of the victory over Antipas. Archelaus acted as victor. When Archelaus saw them equally, the succession of arms was corrupted. To Caesar and the Jews, Archelaus was the heir of merit. Then in the management of Idumea, the multitude of Herod's house had prepared everything for the victor because of Caesar. The preparation of the land was established. The funeral and the burial were performed by divine law. It is established that he was Herod's and had suffered. Archelaus mediated this to Caesar. Those who acted for Herod among the Jews were mediated by him. He, the victor by the merits of his honors, held power. Caesar mediated the will of the multitude so that all might act as Herod had deserved. Then the Jews and all things came into that power. Therefore, he deserved to come into the royal court.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Judean province under Roman rule, transitioning from the regional projects of Herod Antipas to the governorship of Pontius Pilate. It contains the famous (and historically debated) passage regarding Jesus of Nazareth and begins a scandalous narrative involving the Temple of Isis in Rome.</meta>

<initial>H</initial>erod Antipas went into his own country and, having arranged his affairs with the <term>procurator</term> <note>A Roman financial agent or provincial governor.</note> of Syria, Valerius Gratus, who had been appointed by Rome, he earned the favor of his friends and leveled the ground for a new city. This is how he went about his business while he was overseeing the territory. 

Herod then turned toward the city of Tiberias, named after the Emperor Tiberius, arming himself with the support of those who had followed him. He desired to name the city after him. Daily, he surveyed the region near the Lake of Gennesaret <note>Also known as the Sea of Galilee.</note> where there are hot springs not far from the site of Emmaus. He joined his city to this site. Many people flowed into this city, both voluntarily and by force, so that the region of Galilee would be well-populated. <margin>Chapter 11</margin> A hundred and ten regions were under his embrace; from these, he took citizens to be cared for, even those who were considered unfit for war. Many of the noble class came there to dwell, as well as the wealthy and the poor from all over, for whom moving there was not difficult. Herod himself gave them favor and ruled the city; he exulted with many of those who were young and did not wish to leave that city. He built private houses from the finest materials and also provided a place for judgment. He broke the old rules of settlement; he placed the law above the previous inhabitants, even if the location was considered an ancient burial ground.

<initial>P</initial>ilate, however, the governor, led his army from Caesarea to be stationed in Jerusalem. He did this to maintain order among the Jews. He brought with him the <term>effigies</term> <note>Images of the Emperor on military standards, which Jews considered idols.</note> of Caesar, which are on the military standards. These images were brought in by night, which was a departure from previous practice. The images of Caesar were brought into the city by his command, whereas previous <term>rectors</term> <note>Governors or leaders.</note> of Judea had entered without such divisions. This signaled a change that the citizens soon noticed. 

When the Jews discovered this invasion of their customs, they came in a great multitude to the city. The standards that had been placed there were a violation of their law. Pilate, having learned of the protest, remained in his palace. The Jews pleaded with him for five days and nights, prostrating themselves. On the next day, Pilate sat upon his judgment seat in the stadium and summoned the people as if to give them an answer, but he had secretly placed armed soldiers around them. When the Jews persisted in their petition, he gave a signal to the soldiers to surround them and threatened them with death unless they accepted the images of Caesar. But they, as if by one signal, threw themselves upon the ground and bared their necks, saying they would rather die than see their laws transgressed. Pilate, marveling at their religious conviction, ordered the standards to be carried back from Jerusalem to Caesarea.

<initial>F</initial>uit autem hiisdem temporibus <note>original: "At this same time lived Jesus..."</note> At this same time lived Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works, and a teacher of all those who receive the truth with pleasure. He drew to himself many of the Jews and many also from the Gentiles. <gloss>He was the Christ.</gloss> When Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men among us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him; for he appeared to them alive again the third day, as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him. And the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day.

<column-break/>

<initial>I</initial>nterim at this same time, another misfortune <note>The OCR for this column is heavily corrupted with repetitive "invīade" strings, but the context clearly follows Josephus's account of the scandal of Paulina in the Temple of Isis.</note> fell upon the Jews. There appeared among them a great trouble. It happened in Rome that a certain woman named Paulina, of great nobility and chastity, was deceived by a man named Decius Mundus. This man was deeply in love with her, but she rejected his advances. 

<initial>B</initial>ecause of his obsession, he devised a plan with the priests of the Temple of Isis. At this time, the cult of Isis was popular in Rome. The priests were bribed to tell Paulina that the god Anubis desired her presence in the temple. Being a devout woman, she received this news with joy and obtained permission from her husband to go to the temple for a night of sacred communion with the god. 

However, it was Decius Mundus who lay in wait for her. In the darkness of the temple, she believed she was with the god Anubis, when in fact it was Mundus. After the deed was done, Mundus later mocked her in public, revealing that he had enjoyed her favors under the guise of the god. 

<initial>C</initial>irca this time, when Paulina realized the deception, she informed her husband, and the matter reached the Emperor Tiberius. The Emperor ordered the priests of Isis to be crucified and the temple to be destroyed. Mundus, however, was only exiled, as it was felt his crime was one of passion. 

<initial>S</initial>ed but these things were not the only troubles of the time...

...it was: and in those conversations, it had broken out to such an extent that some wished to be free; they sought to restore the Republic <note>original: "rēp." for "rem publicam"</note> and at the same time prayed to the river and its greatness, which might make them one. <meta>This page transitions from the immediate aftermath of Caligula’s assassination to the reign of King Herod Agrippa I and the subsequent governance of Judea. # X.

With honor and under his leadership: Because he wished for the forces to have rescued Simon <note>This likely refers to Simon Kantheras, whom Agrippa appointed as High Priest</note>; he had a daughter who was a great heir. King Agrippa, having made a compact with the Jews and those in Jerusalem, had sent everyone in compensation. Finally, he had relaxed many claims. Regarding their former woman, the skilled Syla, he often reflected upon her. Furthermore, Agrippa—beyond everything he had sent from the Octavian gate—announced that the previous proclamations were void and he would lead a peaceful life. Having gathered his resources, he established statues as a sign of joy; this greatly disturbed Agrippa, for he judged the destruction of the ancestral laws to be a destruction of all Judea. For this cause, Agrippa hurried himself to the mission, and with all his cavalry. Since he himself judged this excessively, a new discipline was joined: he introduced an army to the Jews. Publicly, he had sent a four-day closure of the treasury, raging against the law. But indeed, those of Judea who stand against dark superstition say that Caesar must be observed in these things; he favored the paths of the law, and all knew his attention had been fixed upon the sources of Caesar’s inspiration. He recognized that the proclamation would be dissolved not long after by Caesar himself, to whom he sent a simulation of the way, having introduced a plan so that he might recently give to Caesar and inquire what the hour of light would provide. Justly, he stands for the Jewish rites of their fathers, which not only provided for the gods, but also for those by whose rites they persisted.

<margin>Bernice, the daughter of Agrippa, flourished with the exceptional honor of chastity.</margin>
**B**ernice, however, his sister, was of exceptional honor and chastity; for when they were in need due to their circumstances, she did not waver from her devotion. But afterward, she rendered a full account to the Jewish judges while the world was astonished: so that the Jews here might seek a carefully celebrated likeness, showing the presence of the centurions; she was greatly blessed, or she established herself here as justice. Standing before the Jewish judges, she was convicted by the evidence.

<margin>The killing of James and John by Agrippa.</margin>

<margin>Josephus tells of himself and his lineage</margin>
It is not right for us to be silent about our lineage, and about those who have followed this honor. We speak of Josephus, the son of Matthias, from the lineage of priests from Jerusalem <note>original: "hyerusalē"</note>. He was first from the twenty-four courses <note>The OCR says "twenty"; the Jewish priesthood was divided into 24 "courses" or families that took turns serving in the Temple</note> which is our lineage, and taken from the highest rank, from which our Jewish nation took its origin, and from which our people began to have rulers who came here from other kings. Our record speaks of this matter: those who were kings through succession by a son. For they were named from other kings, but from our own nation through many peoples in Jerusalem they took their origin, just as is now proposed from the sacred books concerning these histories of our affairs.

For the **First** book commemorates the creation of the world and the formation of man, and afterward the flood and those things which happened to the Jews in Egypt.
The **Second** concerns those things which happened to them afterward in the wilderness and the laws which were given by Moses.
The **Third** tells what was done in the wilderness, and the judges from many nations who took up the Judean cause, as is said in the sacred books.
The **Fourth** tells those things which were done concerning Saul and David, the kings of the Jews.
The **Fifth** tells of Solomon’s construction of the temple and of his many virtues.
The **Sixth** tells of Amaziah, king of the Jews, and of other kings who came after him.
The **Seventh** tells of the Babylonian captivity of the kings.
The **Eighth** tells of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and of many things which were done under him.
The **Ninth** tells those things concerning King Antiochus and many things which were done under him.
The **Tenth** tells those things which were done concerning John the High Priest <note>term: "pontifice"; refers to John Hyrcanus I</note>.
The **Eleventh** tells of Cassius and Herod, kings of the Jews.
The **Twelfth** tells of Herod and many things which were done under him.
The **Thirteenth** tells those things which it says concerning Archelaus and Herod.
The **Fourteenth** tells of Syria and many things which were done under it.
The **Fifteenth** tells of Claudius and many things which were done under him.
The **Sixteenth** tells of Spain <note>original: "hyppānia"; this is a likely scribal error or OCR corruption, as Book 16 usually focuses on Herod’s sons and Agrippa</note> and many things which were done under it.
The **Seventeenth** tells those things which were done afterward and of the calamities of the Jews.
The **Eighteenth** tells of the Jewish war and of their calamities.
The **Nineteenth** tells of the victory of Vespasian and of many things which were done under him.
The **Twentieth** tells of the calamities of the Jews and of many things which were done afterward.

**And concerning this Jewish war and their calamities, above in seven books.**

<column-break/>

Since the war which the Jews waged with the Romans was almost the greatest of all that have happened in our times—either of those we have heard of or those which neighboring nations have experienced by their own valor or fortune—and since certain people, who were not present themselves but composed this history from hearsay, have written various and empty accounts, and seem to have invented things out of their own zeal, and others out of hatred for the Jews have confirmed a perversion of the matter, while others, seeking to flatter the Romans, have confirmed their own version of Roman affairs, and have nowhere established a true history. 

Since I, Flavius, who previously wrote for the barbarians <note>referring to non-Greek speakers, such as those in Mesopotamia</note> in my native language <note>Aramaic</note> concerning the divine things that took place in Jerusalem, have now also established it in the Greek voice <note>The Latin text here is a translation of Josephus’s later Greek version</note> for those who are governed under the Roman Empire, so that it may speak a true history. 

However, it does not seem so to many, since some things happened through their own valor or fortune as if it were the greatest. And since certain people, who were not present themselves but composed this history from hearsay, have been part of various and empty matters, and seem to have invented things out of their own zeal, and others out of hatred for the Jews have confirmed a perversion of the matter, while others, seeking to flatter the Romans, have confirmed their own version of Roman affairs, and have nowhere established a true history.

...moving against Alexander <note>Likely referring to Alexander Jannaeus or his son Alexander, heirs to the Hasmonean dynasty</note>. Fearing from here that, having been warned, they might teach him to strive to endure. Thus, having collected his forces, he departed from there to his own lands. Fearing the sudden attacks of Hyrcanus, and not being ignorant that the danger of sedition in the city was suspected by him, he withdrew to Scythopolis <note>A major city of the Decapolis, now Beth Shean</note>, where Hyrcanus was coming toward him in ambush. But fearing from here that, having been warned, they might teach that they would approach Scythopolis by their own will, and then move against him, he sends to them; when they had spoken for some time, he worthily received their opinion. For up to that point, Hyrcanus had feigned a false friendship with them, so that he might hold them as suspected beneficiaries. Coming then to Scythopolis, he was eager to know his will concerning himself. Since he gave him no suspicion and promised friendship, and honored him with many gifts as a wealthier man: though either his own mildness made him suspect, or a portion of the men around him had been the judge of his will, whom he knew would soon be a mortal end. Since it was certain that chains would be made for him even before he had been there, he rested from arms. Although Hyrcanus, wishing this man to be a neighbor and friend to him, was not ignorant of what he knew he could do to harm him, yet he held him not only as his friend and domestic, but they had a most recent treaty and friendship between them, so that they both might mutually endure the coming wars together. Indeed, Hyrcanus wished that Hyrcania and Samaria <note>Regions of the Levant</note> should perish for this friend of his, along with all the other regions of the Jews which the Jews had previously destroyed and demolished; and again he builds cities for them. Or perhaps at that time he even wished to help the Jews. To those for whom it is suspected that it was for the safety of Aristobulus, he wished, after divine veneration, to favor Hyrcanus with the favor of the Jews from the city of Jerusalem. For he had come to him with many thousands of armed men; of the games <note>The Latin 'ioci' may be a corruption of a name or technical term</note>, however, it is said from here that Hyrcanus was then a friend to the Jews, if the games again gave him the favor of the Jews. But Hyrcanus, who then presided over the regions of the Jews, thought by a certain proximity and for the sake of friendship that the Jews were not behaving worthily. Since he then ruled the affairs of the Jews, they knew that they could then overcome the Jews again with Hyrcanus as the heir of his power, who would soon again be made of the power of the Jews; then Hyrcanus began to be ruled by the Jews again. And war began between him and Aristobulus. And when they were shaken by civil sedition, the Jews again drove themselves to be ruled for Hyrcanus. Hyrcanus indeed was ruled again. If indeed then they were not able to endure one, fearing from here lest again the power should go to Hyrcanus instead of surrender: and he flees to Alexandria <note>The fortress of Alexandreion</note>; he began to fortify the defenses of the city greatly with valleys and again with fortified walls and towers. For in this way he hoped he could defend himself from those who would again pursue or besiege him. But Herod, wanting to conquer the mind of the younger Aristobulus through Marion <note>the tyrant of Chalcis who had invaded Galilee</note>, knew that he could more easily win the aid of the Jews through Hyrcanus and Herod’s father-in-law. When Herod came to Judea and victory was obtained in the battle, he restored Hyrcanus in such a way that Hyrcanus regarded Herod as a king <unclear>exēltas</unclear>; indeed, it seemed he was held in such familiarity that he was no longer a despised subject. Herod affirmed Hyrcanus with the greatest respect. Herod took a wife from the lineage of Hyrcanus, the woman named Mariamne, daughter of Alexander, the son of Aristobulus <note>Mariamne was the granddaughter of both Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, intended to unite the rival Hasmonean factions</note>. While the brother of Alexander sought discord, the girl Mariamne joined the peacemaker Aristobulus, the brother of Hyrcanus whom Pompey had killed. After Hyrcanus was received, it happened by chance that Caesar came in victory toward the Philippians, and they brought news of the meeting with Antiochus in Syria. Then the Jewish elites sent an embassy to Antony, and again the Jewish nobles congratulated the victor, but their situation was then repossessed. For at that time, more honor was given to Hyrcanus. Herod, however, soothed Antony with great gifts <note>Herod was famous for using bribes to secure Roman favor</note> so that he would not even hear a single word of the accusations against him. And so they departed. Then again, the Jewish leaders came to Antony when he had arrived in Daphne <note>near Antioch</note>, laying out their complaints. They were led by those who excelled in eloquence and logic, accusing Herod. Hyrcanus was also cautious, for Antony favored him. Antony declared Herod and his brother <note>Phasael</note> as tetrarchs, entrusting the government of Hyrcanus's realm to them. The Jewish envoys took this poorly; the victor <note>Antony</note> threw fifteen of them into prison. They then ran to Jerusalem in a tumult; eighty of the envoys were sent to the legate of Syria, meeting at Tyre, where they sought to complain about Herod. But the Jews were struck down by the soldiers. Lest he should draw back, Antony sent soldiers to kill the defeated and those whom Hyrcanus ordered to be handed over for burial. Yet they did not escape the unrest that was seen, and for a long time they irritated Antony, so that he became unfriendly toward the Jews.

<margin>Antony</margin>
With the arrival of the King of the Parthians <note>Pacorus I</note> to the Jews, many talents and five hundred women were promised to drive out Herod and Hyrcanus. While Pacorus prepared the soldiers, Herod had already surrendered some of his forces. The Parthian king sought the kingdom; the Jewish scouts heard of the adversity of the soldiers. The army was in the garrison for Antigone <note>Antigonus Mattathias, the Hasmonean rival to Herod</note>, and the multitude of Jews ran to Antigonus of their own accord to find a way to live. The guards who came were given warnings. Antigonus and the Jews who were traitors then took the temple itself. After this, part of the multitude took refuge, and Herod, vexed by the King of the Parthians, sought to kill Pacorus and remain in the place he held. When the Jewish leaders came to the village and Hyrcanus offered gifts to Herod, Barzapharnes was furious; he wanted to take the king and the soldiers. He took Phasael and Hyrcanus as prisoners for the Parthians. Not long after, the Parthians moved toward Herod, wanting to shut him in the city. But Herod, being very prudent, provided for his soldiers against the greedy enemies. Knowing this, the Parthians moved quickly. He believed his brother and the girl <note>Mariamne</note> were being held on the road. He prepared himself secretly against the Parthians, moving toward the fortress of Masada <note>Marda/Masada</note>. Along the way, he met Jews who attacked him. Herod, though fleeing, received them with a victor's spirit. His brother <unclear>safarip</unclear> <note>Phasael</note> helped him. They reached the defenses of Masada. Afterward, when the soldiers prevailed, the war was unappeasable. They then appointed Antigonus as king, and they mutilated Phasael, Herod’s brother, and Hyrcanus.

### The War Against the Arabs and the Speech of Herod

...neighbors, and it seemed that no part of the lordship existed apart. Through this, he did not speak again; nor was there a ready combativeness of words, but rather the steady power of your voice alone. 

When it seemed his strength was called forth by these predictions, no faith in an invincible fate could be sustained unless it was harmed by the assembly. With these words, Herod miserably exhorted them: where he saw them eagerly celebrating the sacred rites. And then, with his army, he crossed the Jordan. <margin>Crossing the Jordan.</margin> Having set up camp in the district of Philadelphia <note>The OCR "abbethis" likely refers to the region around Philadelphia/Amman</note>, he moved for battle, desiring a swift engagement. Herod, however, ordered that none of your people be brought to him, and because he was organizing his confused ranks for battle, he commanded the infantry to join the ascent. If he seemed to rage with a multitude, his eagerness was unmatched; when he saw his neighbors making a move in desperation, he did not persuade them to see what was done. There, in that month, the multitude of adversaries perished, with no interval between the deeds. Truly, none yielded in flight, even those who were entangled; it helped to compel them. He even blocked those fleeing into the precipices, and the water proved an impediment. 

### Herod's Great Victory

Great things were revealed by Herod: this was his victory. He stripped the neighboring areas and believed so much in his success that within days, when thousands joined him, the multitude came to the lush lands. After these were settled, Herod again moved his army through the neighboring villas, and he overcame the Arabs with a great blow. <margin>Victory over Arabs.</margin> The concern of the defendants surpassed that bitter anxiety: for it did not seem that they met Herod as a victor, but rather as one who came to betray the commands. For his victory did not seem merely human; some divine quality in Herod was proclaimed here as he came against the enemy. He was seen on the plains, warned by the divine. He approached without a crown <note>original: "sine diademate"</note>, in a private garment and habit, but it was stated that the victory was won through the leap of his spirit and not by difficulty. He said, "I, the king, have made this fate my own before Caesar." Even if one doubted, it was said in every way that he did not rest until he had seen the neighboring lands. Truly, the ancestral aids were his toward victory, and he was impressed by many fates. With the death of Herod’s rivals, he might be well-deserving of grace.

### Herod Before Caesar Augustus

Caesar <note>Referencing Octavian, later Augustus</note>, also commending those who helped, gave the best counsel for life. His words were truthful toward peace, even in the most anxious times. He promised the victory of the provinces and even the focus of war itself. But he had previously chosen a more elegant love: so that he might see friendship in the victor, a victor over fate. For even if I am a neighbor to the defeated, and they sought their fortune, Herod's victory would not be defiled. These are the kinds of friends who are loved. But for Caesar, he was not false in his invincibility. Nor was the kingdom truly given for wealth. For as he ruled with force, when friends were needed, he acted severely. If he was able to derive hope into the greatness of the fatherland, he did so because Mark Antony had perished. Herod hurried to become a friend to this new fate. 

The victor Herod joined in friendship. He acted well, as it is read. And after this, Herod did not doubt his own friendship; he placed such honor upon him and signed it with Caesar’s indulgence. He asked that a certain suppliant who had met Antony be absolved and recalled to the banquet. Caesar permitted him to come through victory to his fatherland. Herod led Caesar through and preceded him with a present countenance. He exhibited unique hospitality to all the men and even distributed the ancestral army. Because they traveled through arid places to their fatherland, he ensured there was water, as if coming from the West; thus, the defeated were suddenly given what they hoped for. Beyond these benefits, Caesar extended Herod's kingdom with victory, including the lands Cleopatra had joined with Antony. He reached all of Syria. 

### The Building of Cities and Temples

From here, carried by a flow of happiness, he lifted his spirit. He indulged his fatherland with the greatest predicted obedience. He restored the Temple <note>The Second Temple in Jerusalem, Herod's most famous project</note>, which he himself frequented, embracing the ancient elements with walls, and his singular munificence was made equal to it. He also desired forts and towers to be given in honor of his friends. When he built this royal house in the upper part of the city, which surpassed even the Temple in splendor, he named one the Caesareum and the other the Agrippium after his friends. 

In Samaria, he surrounded a town with beautiful walls and called the city Sebaste <note>Sebaste is the Greek equivalent of the Latin "Augusta"</note>. He dedicated it to thousands of inhabitants and held it as a most fertile land. There he placed a great and high temple, and the area was three furlongs; he dedicated it to Caesar. He placed another temple of white marble at the source of the Jordan. That place is called the Panium <note>Paneas, modern Banias, associated with the god Pan</note>, where a precipice drops down into a deep abyss containing a vast amount of standing water. From there, a spring arises. Some think the Jordan begins here. 

Herod did not leave any place without honor for Caesar. He loved the Roman connection so boldly that he preferred victory in the neighborhood. The most famous palace of all was inspected, made of white stone, showing the greatness of the neighboring power. For in that maritime region, they had navigated to the ports. But the difficulty of the harbor was great, with few places for ships to seek refuge. But Herod, by his liberality, overcame the nature of the place; he constructed a port larger than the Piraeus <note>The famous port of Athens</note>, and it remains for other ships. Despite the difficulty of the sea, its beauty conquered, so that nothing arduous appeared to stand in his way.

Archelaus took charge of the arrangements for the person <note>original: "ministratione personae"</note>. All this royal finery was fitting for the funeral procession. The body was laid out as if it were still breathing, though it was empty of life. The body was covered in purple, with a golden crown placed upon his head, and a diadem and gold were set upon him. A scepter was placed in his right hand. Around the bier, his sons and a multitude of his relatives formed the ranks. The guards, the Thracians, the Germans, and the Gauls <note>Herod’s elite foreign bodyguards</note> marched in battle order, preceding the body. The rest of the army followed, armed and under their commanders, moving in their proper ranks. Five hundred servants followed, carrying sweet-smelling spices. The body was carried to Herodium <note>Herod’s palace-fortress and tomb south of Jerusalem</note>, for there the king had commanded he be buried. Such was the end of Herod.

# BOOK II BEGINS.

## BUT CONCERNING THE DISTURBANCES
The beginning of the disturbances <note>original: "turbarum"</note> arose from the hope Archelaus had for the entire kingdom. He observed the traditional mourning for his father. According to the Jewish custom, this lasted seven days, after which he provided a funeral feast for the multitude. This custom is so strictly observed among the Jews <margin>Herod’s death</margin> that anyone who neglects it is considered impious. Afterward, dressed in white robes, he proceeded to the Temple. There, he was received with various shouts of favor by the people. He sat upon a high throne, also made of gold, and received the common people most humanely. He responded to their acclamations by promising to be better than his father. He told them that although he had the power of the kingdom, he would refuse the title of "King" until **Caesar** <note>Augustus Caesar, the Roman Emperor</note> confirmed the will of his father and appointed him as successor. For this reason, even at **Jericho**, he had refused the diadem when the soldiers wanted to place it on his head. He promised that if he were confirmed, their alacrity and goodwill would be rewarded, and he would appear better to them than his father had been. At this, the multitude, moved by his words, began to test him with petitions. Some shouted for a reduction in taxes, others for the abolition of duties, and some demanded that prisoners be released. To all of these, he nodded in agreement to persuade them and win their favor. Then he turned to the sacrifices and made supplications. But behold, after midday, a sudden distress was called forth by new agitators <note>original: "fladoribus"</note>. While the public mourning for the king was ending, they began to wail for those whom Herod had executed for tearing down the golden eagle <note>The "sophists" Matthias and Judas, who led a religious protest against a Roman eagle Herod placed over the Temple gate</note>. Their grief was not silent, but very loud, with many weeping and persistently shouting that those who had been killed for the laws of their fathers should be avenged. They demanded that the king punish the friends of Herod. Although Archelaus <margin>Archelaus</margin> was in a hurry to depart for Rome and wished to avoid health-shaking conflict, he tried to restrain them with warnings, but they turned to sedition. They would not listen to reason, for the festival day was near <note>Passover</note>, and a vast multitude from the countryside had flowed into the city for the sacrifice. These people began to lament the teachers of the law <note>referred to here as "sophists"</note>. Archelaus, though he was a harsh man, feared a total uprising. He sent a commander with a troop of soldiers to stop the ringleaders of the sedition, but the crowd drove them off with stones.

### The Rise of Agrippa and the Conflict with Rome

He ordered these matters to be alleged so as to deceive. For he hoped that the fame of his name would be venerable everywhere if he established it. I observe, however, that after he received the kingdom, he <note>Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great</note> came to him. For a long time, he went before Agrippa: Caesar <note>the Emperor Caligula, also known as Gaius</note> greeted him and honored him so much that he called him King of Judea, following the reign of Philip in the neighboring region. And setting aside delays, he who would be called Herod <note>Agrippa I often used the name Herod in official contexts</note> arrived; Herod's trusts were founded in his piety and thanksgiving. For it is incredible to see how he came to the royalty of Judea and what his journey was. Since at that time his beginnings were being established. For even if Herod <note>Agrippa</note> had come into Judea, he held the kingdom of Judea in that place. For Agrippa again withdrew himself from the whole, as they wished to doubt whether they should worship him with the same honor.

When Herod <note>Agrippa</note> came to him: in turn, for such great clemency toward him, he returned honor according to his strength. Immediately, Agrippa had been an accuser. From the inheritance which Caesar decided to choose, he thus released Herod <note>Antipas</note> to Spain <note>This refers to the exile of Herod Antipas to Lugdunum, often associated with Spain/Gaul in these texts</note>. To whom Caesar had used insults as an abuse of neighborhood. For he did not think then that he should be called by that choice. Caesar, invincible in his own piety, spoke of a denarius of money to the army in Jerusalem; and he, being pious, would have been consecrated in the temple, were he not to have taken it up. He nevertheless conquered in Judea, while the arrival of the religious soldiers was expected. Through the world, he [Petronius] heard many things while he labored there; he was a leader to the Jews and was touched by them. The Jews, however, rejoiced then that the pious fame had come. Quickly, all things changed in turn.

#### The Miraculous Sands of the Belus River

From there he came to the city of Ptolemais <note>Modern-day Acre</note>. Near there flows a small river called the Belus <note>A river famous in antiquity as the source of sand for glassmaking</note>, which is very small; next to it is the tomb of Memnon. Here, next to the source, a most wonderful sight is seen at the base of the fig tree. There is a round valley, within a hundred cubits, and at the base lies what they call the "sand" <note>term: Vitreous sand, used to make glass</note>. ### The Standoff at Jerusalem and the Succession of Claudius

**N**ero, as we have said above, was struck by a great terror when he heard of these deeds. In his heart there was distress; upon his face, a stupor mixed with fear. **I**t occurred to him that Vespasian was the man for these two necessary requirements. <meta>This page continues the narrative of the Roman campaign in Galilee. Having previously described Vespasian’s preparations and the movement of the legions, the text now focuses on the siege of a highly fortified Jewish city (likely Jotapata) and the psychological and tactical duel between the Roman commander Vespasian and the Jewish leader Josephus.</meta>

Therefore, the laboring [of the men] and the lack of water <note>original: "humore." In the context of the siege of Jotapata, this likely refers to the famous water shortage Josephus managed through trickery.</note> had made them grow faint; this situation had much helped the work of the enemy. To the Romans, this seemed a clear sign of their coming rule, which would be seen as a command from above.

How did the Roman cause stand? Vespasian believed he had already begun to take the city. He had hoped for a great outcome when he saw the maneuvers of Josephus and his obstinacy. Vespasian was encouraged, trusting in his own cunning and hoping for a swifter victory. <margin>Josephus</margin> Josephus, meanwhile, prepared as if for a total siege. At that time, the Romans invaded a most fortified place, one of the four principal cities. Some Romans invaded not only by command and for the sake of victory, but also out of hope. They hoped for victory not through justice, but through strength, which is a rarer hope. ...of the nations. For clearly where the boundaries of the land turn back, those of the Galileans also end them: all their rural lands are fully restored by cultivation and are rich in abundance; there is no field that is not worked by tillers. Indeed, the entire region is full of cities, and everywhere it is populous due to the frequency of villages, so much so that even the smallest village has over fifteen thousand inhabitants. <note>This high population figure is famously cited by the historian Josephus, though modern scholars often debate its literal accuracy.</note> Finally, if the standard of living is lower in the whole region, it is nevertheless superior in courage. Since the Galileans are born among foreigners and are surrounded on all sides by neighboring nations, they are perpetually practiced in wars. Nor are their rural lands ever empty of men, or the small region empty of people. For those who inhabit it are ready for the sake of defense, and those who are less warlike are overcome by the multitude; and the men sustain a bellicose populace. And these are again neighbors to the people living through Iturea and through Syria. Furthermore, although their region is vast, it is not fruitful in every part, nor does it have the wealth of safety in the whole region. However, as much as there is, it is so fertile and productive that it abounds in every kind of fruit that is born from the earth. They are productive for cultivation in every single detail, and it is such that the fruits of the Gospel <note>The translator here uses "evangelei," likely interpreting the fertility of the land as a metaphor for the spread of the Christian message or simply noting the region's biblical significance.</note> in a certain part of it bring about a rich and ready cultivation; so that although there lie some things which seem to be less fertile of noble sowers, yet the very least of their vines are scarcely without fruit because of the proximity of the Marian mountains. And this manner of life under Caesar, the Jews preserve to this very day. Also in the <unclear>sagitibus</unclear> of grain, just as was done by those Jews at that time. # IN THE NAME OF CHRIST BEGINS THE LETTER OF ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, TO BRAULIO OF ZARAGOZA

<note>original: "IN XPI NOIE" (In Christi Nomine). Scribes often used "XPI," a Greek abbreviation (Chi-Rho), to represent the name of Christ.</note>

A greeting to my lord and servant of the faith. To Bishop Braulio, [from] Bishop Isidore. With all my heart I have longed to see your face, and <unclear>uoxatā</unclear> to fulfill that longing: concerning my prayers: <unclear>ang' moniar</unclear>. May the grace of God the Father be present, granted through your prayers: so that in this life your presence may be fulfilled and in the future life you may be led into the company of the blessed in the joys of God. And I shall use my strength or virtue, but it is truly our most excellent [grace] and I see your virtue filled with humility. <note>Braulio frequently praises Isidore's humility despite his immense learning.</note> May your dignity remain forever... in this life and the next, most blessed one. # HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ETYMOLOGIES, ON DISCIPLINE AND ART

<image-desc>A large ornamental initial 'D' marks the beginning of the text. The transcription identifies it as "ISCIPLINADISCENDO" but the initial letter is a D, forming the word "DISCIPLINA." The initial is blue with detailed red and gold scrollwork and floral motifs contained within its vertical bar.</image-desc>

## DISCIPLINE FROM LEARNING
<note>The heading puns on the Latin words "Disciplina" and "Discere" (to learn).</note>

<margin>In the 14th Book, seek paradise</margin>

Discipline takes its name from learning <note>original: "a discendo"</note>. Whence it is also called science <note>original: "scientia," meaning knowledge</note>. Because no one knows unless they learn. Otherwise, discipline is so named because it is "full of learning" <note>original: "discit plena"</note>. For to learn is to hold onto proper rules. Others say the name is derived from a Greek origin <unclear>archef... accūte</unclear>... But regarding these arts, if one wishes to speak carefully, the Hebrew origins <unclear>hebrayca omniū</unclear> of grammar should be held... He is therefore said to tell a history...

**O**n the seven <term>liberal disciplines</term> <note>The "Liberal Arts" were the core curriculum of medieval education, thought to be the knowledge necessary for a free person.</note>
The first is grammar, which is the knowledge of speaking. The second is rhetoric, which is considered necessary especially in civil questions because of its use and beauty of eloquence. The third is dialectic, also named logic, which separates truth from falsehoods by very subtle disputations. The fourth is arithmetic, which contains the causes and divisions of numbers. The fifth is music, which consists of songs and chants. The sixth is geometry, which deals with the measures and dimensions of the earth. The seventh is astronomy, which accounts for the law of the stars.

<margin>the hand of the sender <note>original: "missis manus"</note></margin>

**O**n common letters
The beginnings of the art of grammar are common letters, which scribes and accountants know. <unclear>Gr̄ dīsciplinū... un̄ & littera</unclear>. Letters are the signs of things and the memories of time. Lest they flee into oblivion, the letter is held. For a thing which is seen or heard, lest it vanish from memory, is fixed by the shine of letters. In the reasoning of "letter" <note>original: "l̄rī"</note>, they are said to be so named as if they were "paths for those reading" <note>original: "legētris"</note>, because they offer a path to reading. Latin and Greek letters seem to have arisen from the Hebrew. Among those, the first is called <note>original: "Aleph"</note>. <unclear>Deū x̄i emitu... nū ap latinos a.</unclear> <note>The text here discusses the phonetic and spiritual significance of the letter 'A' as the first sound.</note> ...Seventeen elements of letters. The Hebrew letters... <unclear>chaldeoy p̄abrā</unclear>... <note>Isidore provides a legendary history of the alphabet's development.</note> ...The use of Greek letters was discovered by <unclear>r̄d rēie arc</unclear>... <note>Isidore typically credits Cadmus with bringing letters to Greece.</note> Cadmus, the son of Agenor, first brought seventeen letters to the Greeks: A, B, G, D, E, I, K, L, M, N, O, P, R, S, T. To these, Palamedes during the Trojan War added three: H, X, Ω. After him, Simonides added another three letters: Ψ, Ξ, Φ. Pythagoras of Samos first formed the letter Y as an example of human life. Its lower stem represents the early path of life <unclear>figur̄. iūetā q̄p̄o</unclear>... while the fork above represents the two paths: if a person chooses the right-hand path, they lead a life of ease and virtue; if the left, they meet labor and ruin <unclear>si adle be & labore mātū</unclear>... <note>The "Pythagorean Y" was a common medieval metaphor for the moral choice between virtue and vice.</note> ...The letter <note>original: "theca"</note> <note>representing the Greek Theta</note> was used as a sign for a judge to signify death <note>original: "theta ap̄ut mortem"</note>, for the letter 'T' signifies death <note>original: "t a morte"</note>. <unclear>V u & r̄ hep mēia elūm</unclear>... <note>The remainder of this column becomes heavily corrupted in the OCR transcription, appearing as strings of disjointed letters.</note> <unclear>l̄ra chau. e figurā dmonstrar... h q l̄ r d in dū inat h m h l i t h d s t s r s d t s t l u u u t s r d</unclear>...

<column-break/>

<note>The second column begins with further corrupted OCR, likely representing technical linguistic descriptions of vowels and consonants that the transcription was unable to process clearly.</note>

...vowels and consonants. Vowels are those that can be uttered by themselves... Consonants, because they are perceived through themselves, do not make a full sound unless they adhere to vowels. <unclear>In num̄ie ſī uibic lastine effiūuer</unclear>... Of the consonants, some are semivowels, which begin with a vowel sound like 'f, l, r, s, m, n.' Others are called mutes, because they do not have a sound unless a vowel is added. <unclear>o munoale dmr ūsq; q r̄lla ſonut d d d d d</unclear>... <note>Isidore is explaining the phonetic differences between sounds that can be sustained (vowels/semivowels) and those that are "muted" or stopped.</note> ...<unclear>sonates uocalef au & sein uocalef & mure; aurik sūt... m d̄ p̄ u d u d i q ſonanti h̄rt; ne uat</unclear>... <note>Extensive OCR corruption follows, consisting of repetitive character strings.</note> <unclear>t d r h; ī deā ſuu l̄ r d u m f d d p r i t d d i s d s... fragor; reliq d m̄ d n . m̄ p q s r r h s d t d r r d u l s d l r l s d s.</unclear>

**O**n grammar.
Grammar is the science of speaking correctly and is the origin and foundation of liberal letters. This discipline is suited for the use of the word in the life of the present. <note>original: "uitae p̄sentis"</note>. The parts of the art of speaking truly are... <unclear>rono fūame sūt artia f q n̄ uec; nam amp̄ . d̄ m q̄. u. lra i m l d i m i s u q r d u r n l u n s. u. u m. u d u n s. d r d s i d ū d.</unclear> <note>The text continues with technical definitions of the components of grammar, though the OCR is largely illegible.</note>

<summary>This page provides a comprehensive table of contents for the twenty books of Isidore's encyclopedia and begins Book I, defining the liberal arts and exploring the origins and phonetics of the alphabet.</summary>
