...enigma. But others think, as seen in the view of certain people like Peter, that it is not what children know, but because it appears differently to them. Peter says that everyone who does this is seen as "outward," that is, one who simulates doing one thing while actually doing another. The name, moreover, is derived from *iron* <note>original: "yro"</note>, that is, from "simulation." Donatus, however, says irony is where one thing is understood by another. He says there are many types of this: namely, irony and enigma. And thus a distinction is made between irony and enigma. In irony, only the pronunciation alone is to be interpreted. In an enigma, however, one thing is understood for another through the similarity of things. Just as through the 318 servants of Abraham, the name of Jesus <note>original: "yhu"</note> and the sign of his cross are honored through figurative representation <note>In Greek numerals, 318 is represented by TIH; T resembles a cross, and IH are the first two letters of Jesus' name in Greek.</note>. Having said these things, let us return the focus of our pen to the orders and names of the books, so that we may pursue what remains.

## Letters, moreover, are the indices of things and the signs of words. There is such power in them that the words of those who are absent speak to us without a voice. For they introduce things through the eyes, not through the ears.

## Asinius Pollio was the first to make a library public in Rome; for previously they were held by kings. But then Ptolemy held this role. This was first Ptolemy Philadelphus, the son of Ptolemy Lathyrus <note>Usually identified as the son of Ptolemy I Soter, the founder of the library of Alexandria.</note>. He added this to the name and fame of his kingdom, so that he might make it more illustrious in all books. He furnished a library of 70,000 books.
<margin>But the Greeks established the "Lathyric" letters for the Athenians.</margin>

## Among the Greeks, however, Pisistratus is said to have been the first to establish a library. This was later increased by Xerxes, the king of the Persians, and was afterwards brought to Rome.

## A certain king of Egypt named Ptolemy sought out a great multitude of books. Among these, he also requested the books of the Divine Law from the Jews, translated into the Greek language. This task was assigned to seventy interpreters in Alexandria. Being placed in individual cells, they wrote everything so harmoniously through the Holy Spirit that nothing discrepant was found in their manuscripts, either in words or in order.

## Orations, epistles, and sermons are contained not in large books, but in "quaternions" <note>Small booklets made of four folded sheets.</note>. "Oration" <note>original: "Oratio"</note> is so named, as if it were "the reason of the mouth" <note>original: "oris ratio"</note>; for an oration is a vocal discourse poured out through the mouth. They are called "epistles" in Greek, but in Latin "missive" <note>letters that are sent</note>. For in Greek, *apostole* means "a sending." An "epistle" in Greek is called "that which is sent." "Sermons" <note>original: "Sermones"</note> are so named because they occur between two or more people where speech happens, as if they were "intertwinings" <note>original: "seryones"</note>; that is, those things which are born from conversation.

## A "corpus" <note>body</note> of books is that which consists of many books.
<margin>He published this work concerning illustrious men.</margin>
For we also call "canons" the "rules" by which the bodies of books are contained. Or they are called *kanones* in Greek and *regulae* in Latin, because they show the system for living rightly. Others say a "canon" is a rule that is never drawn away from rectitude. Others say a "canon" is a "carpenter's square" <note>original: "amussim"</note>, since it does not judge unfairly or unjustly.

## We call it a "page" <note>original: "Pagina"</note> because the sheets are seen to be "fastened together" <note>original: "conpaginata"</note> to one another, so that one is made from two or more sheets. Or it comes from "fixing" <note>original: "pangendo"</note>, because the poems by which the verses of the pages are gathered are made by "fixing," that is, by writing; hence it is called a page.
<margin>Others say it is called "page" from "fixing," that is, from "fastening."</margin>

## A "quaternion" is so called from the number of four sheets, or from a "quaternity" of books, because four volumes make up one "body."

## "Wax" <note>original: "Cera"</note> is so called in Greek because it is written with four letter-elements. Or "wax" is named from "chalk" <note>original: "creta"</note>, because one writes upon it.
<margin>Wax is used in painted or written tablets and other necessary things.</margin>

<margin>Concerning the Trinity</margin>
**There are three persons in the Godhead**: Father and Son and Holy Spirit. One God: one principle. Not three gods. Nor three principles. The Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another <note>original: "non aliud pater: aliud filius: aliud spiritus sanctus"</note>, but all are one and the same. One nature: one end: and just as all things are one, so also all things are of one nature. Unity remains in the persons: and all things universal and the Son: and the Holy Spirit: one in three: one from the whole Trinity in person. One, that is, unity: but by communion: in three persons through themselves so the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another. But through themselves one God. But in the assumed persons. They are one, however, in the persons: where one wills, so also every [will] of God. These are the three persons where they remember one God: in three persons. Whence also the Holy Spirit [has] the property; the Son, the Holy Spirit are said to proceed from the Father and the Son: so that...

Both are held by their own thirst, the faithless Jews and the Saracens, in the times of the harvest. For through the harvest, the sons of this world—who are judged by the merits of the righteous and assigned to perpetual burning—are represented by the chaff. Those, however, who arrive at the true measure of the wheat and are judged as righteous, are preserved in the granary of the Lord, which is to say, the heavenly kingdoms. As it is said through Solomon in Proverbs 7, whatever things are said in righteousness concern this world, while the unfaithful Jews and heretics, who are cast into eternal fire, shall be burned like chaff. Truly, the Lord returns the reward of righteousness to the just on the Day of Judgment, and they shall live forever. This is also shown in many ways through the prophets, as in the fourth Psalm. One of these is described in Isaiah, who preaches that the Jews who were subservient in mind will be judged, but true rewards will be given to the righteous through the judgment of the Lord’s justice. As it is written: "It shall not be a time of harvest for the faithless Jews," but on the Day of Judgment they shall depart from God and receive their reward in torments. And the Lord shall be over those who worshipped a false lord. As Isaiah says, they shall receive burning in the fire. As it is written: "It shall be in that day there will be no light, but cold and frost. That day shall not be known to the Lord, but in the evening there shall be light." By this he demonstrates that in the final time of the world, the Gentiles shall come to Christ; they who wandered in darkness throughout the whole time of the world shall know the truth. Truly the faithless Jews, who thought themselves to have light, shall be blinded by the coming darkness on the Day of Judgment. The Jews were in darkness, but light came to the Gentiles, as the prophet testifies: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." Isaiah says: "Truth shall dwell in the righteous, and righteousness shall fill the earth." By this word he teaches that Christ has come upon the earth, who justifies all who believe in him, and through Christ all truth has shone in the world. Whence the Lord says: "I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."

A **Monastery** <note>original: "Monasterium"</note> is one, although there may be many scattered throughout the world, which are joined by the single charity of one's neighbor and governed by one Spirit who dwells over all these. "Monastery" is a Greek word <note>original: "monasterium graecum est"</note> which in Latin is called "solitude" <note>original: "solitudo"</note>. For *monas* in Greek is called "one" in Latin <note>Greek *monos*: single/alone</note>. From this, the "monk" <note>original: "monachus"</note> is also named, because he is alone, either in a community <note>original: "coenobio"</note> or in the desert. Yet it is one monastery though many dwell there, through one charity and through one Spirit, of which the Lord says: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Isaiah demonstrated this through Christ, who is the head of the monastery, as it is written: "In that day Christ shall have one monastery, and it shall be filled with the glory of the Lord." Whence Christ says in the Gospel: "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up." For Christ is the root of justice, and all who grow from him produce the fruit of righteousness.

**Christianity** <note>original: "Xpianismus"</note> took its name from Christ. For example, Christ is named from *chrisma*, that is, "anointing" <note>original: "unctione"</note>. For the Jews used to anoint their kings and priests with chrism, whence they were also called "christs" <note>meaning "anointed ones"</note>. In the time of Tiberius Caesar, Christ the Son of God, sent by the Father, came into the world as was predicted before by the prophets; he was anointed with the chrism of the Holy Spirit, whence he is called Christ. Of whom the prophet says: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." Christ is also called "Savior" <note>original: "salvator"</note>, because he saved all who believe in him. For "Christ" is Greek; in Latin he is called "the Anointed" <note>original: "unctus"</note>. In Hebrew he is "Messiah" <note>original: "messias"</note>; in Latin he is called "Christ," and also in Latin he is called "Savior." All the nations who believe in Christ are called "Christians" from Christ. Whence it is said through the prophet: "And a new name shall be called upon you, which the mouth of the Lord shall name." A Christian in Latin is called "anointed," one who is touched with the chrism of the Holy Spirit.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK VIII: ON THE CHURCH AND THE SYNAGOGUE

## THE CHURCH IN GREEK

<image-desc>A large, ornate illuminated initial 'E' in blue and red. The interior of the letter is filled with complex interlace patterns in blue on a plain background, while the exterior is surrounded by fine red line-work and decorative flourishes that extend into the margin.</image-desc>

**Ecclesia** <note>The Church</note> in Greek is named from a "convocation" or "calling together" <note>original: "convocatione"</note>, for the reason that it calls all people to itself. It is called **Catholic** because it is diffused throughout the entire world, or because it is universal—that is, perfect in the precepts of God and in all doctrines. Whence the Lord says: "Upon this rock I will build my church." **Peter** <note>original: "Petrus"</note> in Greek is called "firmness" <note>original: "firmitas"</note> in Latin, whence comes that saying: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." The Church was gathered by Christ from all nations, whence it is also called Catholic, as Isaiah says: "I will bring them into my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer; my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples." For Christ is the root of justice. Whence the prophet says: "In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, and he who shall rise to rule the nations, in him the nations shall hope." Whence Christ also says in the Gospel: "There shall be one fold and one shepherd."

There are two kinds of citizens who dwell in the world, as the prophet says: one that serves the one true God, the other that worships idols. Whence Christ says in the Gospel: "One is my dove, one is my perfect one, she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." For there is one Church in the world which is joined by the one charity of Christ and ruled by the one Spirit, which is gathered from many nations. As Isaiah says: "It shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it." Whence also the prophet says in the Psalm: "Holiness becomes your house, O Lord, unto length of days." Whence the Lord says in the Gospel: "The gates of hell shall not prevail against it"—that is, vices, crimes, and various heresies which lead men to hell. The Church is one because there is one faith, one baptism, and one God who is above all, and through all, and in us all.

**Heresy** <note>original: "Haeresis"</note> in Greek is named from "choice" <note>original: "electione"</note>, because each person chooses for himself that which seems to be better, such as the Jews and Gentiles who did not wish to leave their choices for Christian truth. True Christians are those who remain in the true Catholic faith, of whom the prophet says: "There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism." True Christians, who guard the true faith of Christ, avoid heresies, which deceive through plausible words. Whence it is written: "There are ways which seem right to men, but their ends lead to death." And the Lord says in the Gospel: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves." Whence the prophet says in the Psalm: "Their throat is an open sepulcher; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues," and likewise: "Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." True Christians remain in the charity of Christ and flee heresies, and are called Christians from Christ. As it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, where it says: "We know of this heresy, that everywhere it is spoken against." For "heresy" is named from choice, like the Jews and Gentiles who chose against the truth of Christ. True Christians were named Christians from Christ. Whence it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "The Lord began to teach in Antioch, where they were first called Christians."

<column-break/>

...they ought to have taken up, who were later called heretics because they did not wish to freely preach the truth. God situated all things in the world like a tree which has a root and fruit, of which tree Christ speaks: "Make the tree good and its fruit good," which signifies the Church filled with the faith of Christ and with Christians, gathered from all nations. As the prophet says: "The whole earth is filled with his glory." Truly, heretics are those who deserted the truth of God and worshipped their own error. Whence he says through Isaiah: "Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, putting darkness for light and light for darkness." For heretics do this, who would not preach the truth of God and Christ. And the prophet Isaiah predicted: "Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight." For this is said to the heretics who trust in their own wisdom and refuse the truth of God. But in the time of judgment, they shall receive the reward of their works, as the prophet says: "As the tongue of fire devours the stubble and the heat of the flame consumes it, so their root shall be as dross and their bud shall go up as dust." For they cast away the law of the Lord and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. Christian heretics are those who reject Christ and adhere to the doctrines of men; on the Day of Judgment, they shall be condemned to eternal fire. But the time of the harvest of the righteous shall come, in which the righteous shall be refreshed, and the faithless Jews, Saracens, and heretics shall be plunged into eternal fire.

Because we have begun to speak of the heresy and schism of Christians, and have set forth all prior things, here a just reason seems to be that we should insert all things regarding heresies and schisms below. Concerning the heresy of both Testaments, we shall mention all heretics and schismatics: what heresy and schism are, what each heresy is, who were their authors, and why it is said that all nations shall come to the Church, those who persevere in the true faith. Whence it is written: "One is my dove, my perfect one is one, she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." For Christ is the root of justice, whence the prophet says: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it."

Because, however, mention of only a few heresies is made in this part, let us not terrify the reader with a long, prolix discourse. In earlier times, Jews came to Christ, who had perished through many heresies. For the Church is one, which prepares rewards for those believing in Christ; truly heretics, who contradict Christ, shall be plunged into eternal fire. Whence it is written: "Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves." Whence the prophet says: "Their throat is an open sepulcher; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues," and likewise: "Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." These are the Christian heretics who went out from the Church of Christ, and the faithless Jews and Saracens. Whence it is written: "Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, putting darkness for light and light for darkness." These are the heretics who call men away from the truth.

# Philosophy
<margin>A lover of wisdom</margin>
**Philosophy** is a Greek term, which is called in Latin a **Lover of Wisdom**. For a philosopher is a lover of wisdom. Indeed, philosophers are those who possess the knowledge of divine and human things, and who hold the principle of living well. The name "philosopher" was first used among the Greeks. For previously they were called "Sages" <note>original: *sapientes*</note>; but those who did not lose the perfect sense of things by calling themselves "Sages" were humbled; they said they were not sages, but were simply called "philosophers," that is, lovers of wisdom. He who calls himself a lover of wisdom does so because the perfect knowledge of things is not easily attained; he desired it, of course, for the sake of perfect reason.

...I speak of pollution: however, it does not defile by itself unless the will of the person judging it is involved. For example, it might come from an excess of food, or from the blood, or from the will of lust, or it may be recognized as happening because the body was mocked by nocturnal dreams. If it happened because of the past, it recalls the will back to the mind; if for the future, it recalls it for a response. In this matter, that which comes from the movement of the mind is divination.

<margin>Pyromancy</margin>
**Pyromancy** <note>original: *Piromancia*</note> is named from fire <note>original: *ab igne*</note>: because in it they call upon the fate of demons, or they foresee the future from fire, just as it was predicted in it by the reasoning of mixed blood; and so they say they predict the future. But to do this is divination.

<margin>Aeromancy</margin>
**Aeromancy** is named from the air: because in it they call upon the movement of demons, or they foresee the future from the variety of the air; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Hydromancy</margin>
**Hydromancy** is named from water: either from the variety of waters, or from the will of demons by the reasoning of mixed blood, or they foresee the future from water; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Geomancy</margin>
**Geomancy** is named from the earth: either from the variety of the earth, or from the will of demons by the reasoning of mixed blood, or they foresee the future from the earth; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Necromancy</margin>
**Necromancy** is named from the dead <note>original: *a mortuis*</note>: the dead are summoned by the will of demons by the reasoning of mixed blood; or they foresee the future from the dead; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Illusions</margin>
**Illusions** <note>original: *Prestigia*</note> are so called because they blind the eyes, and thus they deceive by the reasoning of mixed blood or by the will of demons; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Mathematicians</margin>
**Mathematicians** <note>In the medieval context, *mathematici* often referred to astrologers or those who predicted the future by the stars.</note> are those who predict the future by the reasoning of the stars, or from the variety of the stars, or by the will of demons by the reasoning of mixed blood. But to do this is divination.

<margin>Lots</margin>
**Lots** <note>original: *Sors*</note> are named from reason: because in them they call upon the reason of demons, or they foresee the future from lots; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Augury</margin>
**Augury** is named from birds <note>original: *ab auibus*</note>: because in their flight they call upon demons, or they foresee the future from birds; just as doing this is divination.

<margin>Auspices</margin>
**Auspices** are named from birds: because in their flight they call upon demons, or they foresee the future from birds; just as doing this is divination.

<margin>Prophecy</margin>
**Prophecy** <note>original: *Vaticinatio*</note> is named from the seer <note>original: *a uate*</note>: because in the mind of the seer they call upon demons, or they foresee the future from the seer; but to do this is divination.

<margin>Diabolic Crime</margin>
A **Diabolic crime** is when they foresee the future by the will of demons, or from the will of demons; but to do this is divination.

What is called **Physics**: the art of the reasoning of things to come, since there are various things happening at various times; the reasoning does not determine to predict the future by various fevers, but by what happens from various things. The reasoning is not varied by the various mind, but what happens is predicted from various times; the reasoning is not varied by various minds. Because of the variety of times, there are the minds of demons, and thus the minds of men; and so by the variety of the mind, the reasoning of future things is predicted. Physics is spoken of from the reasoning of things to come, which is used by those who foresee the future from the course of the stars.

Because in the course of the stars the future is predicted, for this reason they foresee the future from the course of the stars; they are those who foresee the future from the course of the stars, just as the star which they foresee from the mind of the course of the stars. Just as a star from the mind of the stars: because by the variety of the stars there are the minds of demons, and thus the minds of men; and so by the variety of the mind, the reasoning of future things is predicted.

The **tempter** <note>original: *temptator*</note>, because he is present in the things to be tempted, becomes known through established reasons; especially through that which he sees, through that which he hears, or through that which is in the mind. And they call this the "will of demons," because they call upon the minds of demons.

<margin>The Devil</margin>
**The Devil** <note>original: *Diabolus*</note> is interpreted as "falling downward" or "flowing": because in him his mind is the reasoning of one falling, and it is from the reasoning of the fall of demons.

<margin>Satan</margin>
**Satan** <note>original: *Sathanas*</note> is interpreted as "the adversary" or "the prevaricator": because in him his mind is the reasoning of an adversary.

<margin>Demon</margin>
**Demon** is interpreted as "one who knows": because in him his mind is the reasoning of one who knows.

<margin>Antichrist</margin>
**Antichrist** is interpreted as "contrary to Christ": because in him his mind is the reasoning of contrariety.

<margin>Beelzebub</margin>
**Beelzebub** is interpreted as "lord of flies" <note>original: *uir muscarum*</note> or "having flies": because in him his mind is the reasoning of one who flies.

<margin>Belial</margin>
**Belial** is interpreted as "without a yoke" or "without God": because in him his mind is the reasoning of one who wanders.

<margin>Behemoth</margin>
**Behemoth** is interpreted as "animal" or "quadruped": because in him his mind is the reasoning of foolishness.

<margin>Leviathan</margin>
**Leviathan** is interpreted as "their addition" or "the twisted dragon": because in him his mind is the reasoning of perversity.

<margin>The World</margin>
**The World** <note>original: *Mundus*</note> is so called because in it the reasoning of future things is predicted by the variety of the mind. Whence it is called "mundus": because the reasoning of future things is predicted in the mind <note>The scribe is attempting a folk etymology connecting *mundus* (world) with *mens/mente* (mind).</note>. The World is said to be that in which there are the four elements.

<margin>The Four Elements</margin>
**Fire, Air, Water, Earth.**

<margin>Fire</margin>
**Fire** <note>original: *Ignis*</note> is named from fire: because in it his mind is the reasoning of the will.

<margin>Air</margin>
**Air** <note>original: *Aer*</note> is named from air: because in it his mind is the reasoning of the will.

<margin>Water</margin>
**Water** <note>original: *Aqua*</note> is named from water: because in it his mind is the reasoning of the will.

<margin>Earth</margin>
**Earth** <note>original: *Terra*</note> is named from earth: because in it his mind is the reasoning of the will.

<margin>Stars</margin>
**Stars** <note>original: *Stelle*</note> are named from "standing" <note>original: *a stando*</note>: because in them his mind is the reasoning of the will.

<margin>Sun</margin>
The **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*</note> is so called because it alone shines, or because it dissolves the darkness.

<margin>Moon</margin>
The **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*</note> is so called because it shines in the night, or because it receives light from another.

<margin>Mercury</margin>
**Mercury** is named from merchandise <note>original: *a mercibus*</note>: because in it his mind is the reasoning of one who trades.

<margin>Mars</margin>
**Mars** is named from the sea <note>original: *a mare*</note> or from Mars: because in it his mind is the reasoning of one who wars.

<margin>Jupiter</margin>
**Jupiter** is named from "helping" <note>original: *a iuuando*</note> or from "father": because in it his mind is the reasoning of one who helps.

<margin>Saturn</margin>
**Saturn** is named from "to satisfy" <note>original: *a saturo*</note> or from "sowing": because in it his mind is the reasoning of one who satisfies.

<margin>Venus</margin>
**Venus** is named from "venerating" <note>original: *a uenerando*</note> or from Venus: because in it his mind is the reasoning of one who venerates.

<margin>Diana</margin>
**Diana** is named from "day" <note>original: *a die*</note> or from Diana: because in it his mind is the reasoning of one who gives day. Since she shines in the night, she is called Diana because she shines as day in the night. Or because she is seen in the night.

...waters of Galatia. People believe that **Magog** is the origin of the **Goths** <note>original: "Gothos"</note> based on the similarity of the last syllable. The term **wife** <note>original: "uxor"</note> is derived from "unctor" <note>one who anoints</note>; from which the common word for wife is said to be as if it were "unxor." For it was an ancient custom that new brides, upon entering their husband's house, would anoint the doorposts with oil. Others believe the name comes from the "joining" <note>original: "iunxit"</note> of the couple, as if they are bound together. A man stands as a husband, and a woman as a wife; they are joined in a single bond. They are called "under the man" because they are under the power of the husband... <unclear>b b m u l l a r ꝫ</unclear>. This nature is confirmed by the honorable name of "matron," if they have already borne children... <unclear>r u r n u d o r r ꝫ</unclear>. A common wife is sometimes called a "concubine," who is kept alongside the house... <unclear>h u n o m r ꝫ</unclear>. From this, the word for a woman who remains with one man is "wife," while others wander.

**Kingdom** <note>original: "**R**egnum"</note> is named from **Kings** <note>original: "regibus"</note>. For the name of kings comes from "ruling" <note>original: "regendi"</note>; just as a "rector" <note>guide/governor</note> is one who directs the mind. Thus, in Egypt, even if it is only one city that is governed, or elsewhere, it is not properly called a kingdom; rather, it refers to a glorious tradition. Indeed, in the times of the Romans, it was ordered among them... a king will be so if he acts rightly; if he does not, he will not be. <note>original: "rex eris si recte facias; si non facias, non eris." This was a popular Roman school rhyme used by Isidore to define the moral requirements of kingship.</note> For the name of king is not held by one who does not govern. Therefore, kings are named for their ruling. The name is given so that they may correct their people. For the name of king is lost by sinning. <note>Isidore argues that a king's title is dependent on his virtue.</note>

Hence, in olden times, they used to call leaders "vindex" <note>avenger/protector</note>. Kings were seen as those who kept everything in order... A king should be firm in form... according to the law. A ruler is one who directs the work... <unclear>r i q r r ꝫ rꝫ r d ꝫ n ꝫ n v ꝫ</unclear>. The name of **Consuls** <note>original: "Consules"</note> is said to come from "consulting" <note>original: "consulendo"</note>, for they provide counsel to the people. Others say they are named from "tempering" <note>original: "consulendo"</note> the affairs of the state. They were established for one year so that they would not become arrogant through long-standing power. After they leave office, they are called "proconsuls."

...you shall say: because you act... <unclear>rꝫ u r n r m u r r ī r r ī s s</unclear>.
[The text here becomes highly fragmented, repeating various phonetic abbreviations and remnants of the discussion on civic titles.]
...the name... for the soul... the body... for the sake of the republic... help... for the soldiers... to the judge... for the word... they are called... through the years... through the individual... for the memory of the law... for the name... for the truth...

**Leader** <note>original: "**D**ux"</note> is the one who leads the army. Because he truly leads his own, he is named "Emperor" <note>original: "imperatorem"</note> by the consent of others; this is proclaimed according to custom. From where does this come? An Emperor takes a name of the highest sublimity. This title converts those he wishes to conquer, and he also acts as an "organizer" <note>original: "ordinator"</note> because he holds the supreme position. Thus, in the word "Emperor" <note>original: "imperium"</note>, there is the lordship of the world under one head for the human race.

To this, the **family** <note>original: "familia"</note> belongs: those who are under one head and are neighbors, and are measured by two origins. A family is also clearly distinguished by the decorations of its ancestral places. The Greeks call them by "paragonia" <note>a lineage or line of descent</note>. From this, the family and the origin of the ancestors are named in the dowry and the offspring they produce.

<margin>People</margin>
A **People** <note>original: "Populus"</note> is a human multitude associated by a consensus of law and a harmonious community. "People" is named after the "many" <note>original: "pylos" in Greek, meaning crowd/multitude</note>, which refers to a multitude; or from "plebs" <note>original: "plebe"</note>, which refers to the community.

<margin>Affines</margin>
We are said to be held as **Affines** <note>original: "Adfinis"; those related by marriage rather than blood</note> in either public or private matters. Likewise, the partners of a wife and a husband are called affines. Affinity consists of four degrees. In the first degree are those who come from a true blood relationship and through the labors of the female sex. A free woman is grave and fierce. Truly, those who are in a state of infamy are weak. In a public sense, an **affine** <note>In this context, it refers to boundaries or borders</note> is called a royal road, a local road, a public road, a river, or those things which pertain to the state of the republic. Those called **local roads** <note>original: "Viae uicinalis"</note> are the villas, which they call public villages. Local roads are those which lead into villages, or which lead from villages into public ones. Furthermore, **public roads** are called those which lead to the king or to the army. **Overseers** <note>original: "Prouisores"</note> are indeed those who take care of the rivers or roads, and keep watch over the republic, or have care of it. An **Advocate** <note>original: "Aduocatus"</note> is one who calls every friend to his case, or who strives to defend every person in his cause. An **Adversary** <note>original: "Aduersarius"</note> is said to be he who opposes another and attacks his cause. A **Tenant** <note>original: "Inquilinus"</note> is the name for one who lives in another’s villas; from which they are also called **inhabitants** <note>original: "incolae"</note>. Indeed, inhabitants are those who live in foreign places and cities, not born there, but inhabiting them for a time. A **Stranger** <note>original: "Aduena"</note> is said to be one who, coming from another land, <unclear>dwells</unclear> in an unknown fatherland. A **Neighbor** <note>original: "Accola"</note> is the name for he who lives in a foreign land and tills it. An **Exile** <note>original: "Exul"</unclear> is also said to be he who lives in a strange region, or who is sent into banishment. A **Foreigner** <note>original: "Peregrinus"</note> is the name for one who lives in foreign kingdoms, or who migrates from place to place. An **Outsider** <note>original: "Extraneus"</note> is said to be one who was not born of the same land, or not of the same villa. From this they are called "extranei," because they are born "from without" <note>original: "extra nati"</note>. An **Alien** <note>original: "Alienus"</note> is said to be one who is not of the same parentage, or who comes from another region. One to be **admonished** <note>original: "Admonendus"</note> is he who warns others to do well or to cease doing evil. One **arriving** or **coming** is said to be he who comes from afar, or is about to come from afar. Indeed, those who come from afar are called the "arriving." A **footprint** <note>original: "uestigium"</note> is so called because it is trodden by the foot. The **heel** <note>original: "Calcaneus"</note> is so called because it is pressed by the heels, or because one walks upon the heels. **Property** <note>original: "Manicipium"; usually referring to slaves or formal property</note> is whatever can be bought and sold, or whatever men buy or sell. Such as estates, slaves, and money. And they are called "mancipia" because they are "taken by the hand" <note>original: "manu capiantur"</note>, so that when they are bought, they are marked. A **Purchase** <note>original: "Emtio"</note> is so named because it is bought, and it passes from the right of one to another. A purchase is whenever it occurs, whether from a good thing or a bad thing. Such as to buy and to sell, and to give and to receive. A **Buyer** <note>original: "Emtor"</note> is he who buys things. From wherever he may buy, whether from a good thing or a bad thing. From wherever he may buy, whether from a good thing or a bad thing. From wherever he may buy, whether from a good thing or a bad thing. <note>Repetition in original</note> From wherever a thing is bought, he is called a buyer. A **Purchased Thing** is that which has been bought. A **Seller** <note>original: "Venditor"</note> is he who sells his things, or whatever he has for sale. A **Sale** <note>original: "Venditio"</note> is so named because things are sold, or whatever he has for sale. From wherever it is sold, it is called a sale. A **Sold Thing** is that which has been sold. Purchase and sale consist of four modes. The first mode is through writing. The second mode is through money. The third mode is through witnesses. The fourth mode is through delivery <note>original: "traditum"</note>, regarding which modes it is also written in the laws. A **Donation** <note>original: "Donatio"</note> is so named because things are given, whether of valuable things or <unclear>lesser</unclear> things. A **Donor** is he who gives his things. A **Gift** <note>original: "Donum"</note> is the thing which is given. **Gift-places** <note>original: "Donaria"</note> are the places where gifts are placed, such as temples or altars, or in whatever places gifts are placed, they are called *donaria*.

**Agnates** <note>original: "Agnati"; paternal relatives</note> are those joined by legal kinship through persons of the male sex, as if born "to the father" <note>original: "a patre nati"</note>. Such as a brother born of the same father, a brother's son, and a grandson from him. Likewise, a paternal uncle and the son of a paternal uncle, and a grandson from him. However, those joined through persons of the female sex are not agnates, but are otherwise **cognates** by natural law, such as a sister's son and a grandson from her. Likewise, a maternal uncle and the son of a maternal uncle and a grandson from him. Also, a maternal aunt and the son of a maternal aunt and a grandson from her.

<margin>Regarding affinities and degrees</margin>
There are **two** types of agnates. One consists of those whom the law admits to succession. The other consists of those who are under legal power. Furthermore, this is the difference between agnates and cognates: those who descend from males are called agnates, but those from females are called cognates. Likewise, agnates are said to be from one clan and the name of a man. Cognates are said to be "natural," as if "born together" <note>original: "simul nati"</note>. For they are called cognates as if "born in common" <note>original: "communi nati"</note>, that is, descending from one birth and coming through the female, who are not agnates but are otherwise cognates by natural law. Affinity consists of four degrees. The first degree is from a husband and wife. The second degree is from a father and mother. The third degree is from brothers and sisters. The fourth degree is from grandfathers and great-grandfathers, or from grandsons and great-grandsons. From this it is called **affinity** <note>original: "adfinitas"</note>, as if it were the "end" <note>original: "finis"</note> of two lineages.

<margin>Regarding heirs</margin>
They are called **Heirs** <note>original: "Heredes"</note> either because they "cling" <note>original: "haereant"</note> to those whom they succeed, or because they were previously called *heri* instead of masters, for the word itself has the name of mastery. From this also "master" <note>original: "herus"</note> is said. A **legal heir** is he who comes into the inheritance from his own house and family. They are called heirs because they inherit the goods of the deceased. An **Inheritance** is so named because things are left to the heirs, or whatever pertains to the inheritance. It is called **Hereditary** because it comes from the inheritance.

<column-break/>

The **Paternal Aunt** <note>original: "Amita"</note> is the father's sister, as if "another mother" <note>original: "alia mater"</note>. The paternal aunt’s husband is a maternal uncle, because the maternal uncle is the mother’s brother. **Cousins** <note>original: "Amitini"</note> are those born from two sisters, just as from a paternal aunt and a mother, joined as if by the thin kinship of a paternal aunt. Female cousins are also born from the same sisters. She who is born of a paternal aunt is called a female cousin. He who is born of a paternal aunt is called a male cousin. Likewise, those born of a father and mother are called *amitini*. Likewise, those born of brothers and sisters are called *amitini*.

The **Paternal Uncle** <note>original: "Patruus"</note> is the father's brother, as if "another father" <note>original: "alter pater" </note>. The paternal uncle's wife is a paternal aunt, because the paternal aunt is the father's sister. **Paternal Cousins** <note>original: "Patrueles"</note> are those born from two brothers, just as their sisters are called paternal cousins. A **Great-Uncle** <note>paternal</note> is the grandfather's brother. A **Great-Aunt** <note>paternal</note> is the grandfather's sister. A **Great-Great-Uncle** is the great-grandfather's brother. A **Great-Great-Aunt** is the great-grandfather's sister. A **Great-Great-Great-Uncle** is the great-great-grandfather's brother. A **Great-Great-Great-Aunt** is the great-great-grandfather's sister. An **Atpatruus** <note>Great-great-great-great-uncle</note> is the great-great-great-grandfather's brother. An **Atamita** <note>Great-great-great-great-aunt</note> is the great-great-great-grandfather's sister.

The **Maternal Aunt** <note>original: "Matertera"</note> is the mother's sister, as if "another mother" <note>original: "mater altera"</note>. The maternal aunt’s husband is a paternal uncle, just as the paternal aunt’s husband is a maternal uncle. **Maternal Cousins** <note>original: "Materterini"</note> are those born from two sisters, just as their sisters are called maternal cousins. A **Great-Aunt** <note>maternal</note> is the grandmother's sister. A **Great-Great-Aunt** is the great-grandmother's sister. A **Great-Great-Great-Aunt** is the great-great-grandmother's sister. An **Atmatertera** <note>Great-great-great-great-aunt</note> is the great-great-great-grandmother's sister.

A **Maternal Relative** <note>original: "Matruelis"</note> is the mother's brother, as if "another mother" <note>original: "mater alter"</note>. The *matruelis*' wife is a paternal aunt, just as the paternal uncle's wife is a paternal aunt. Those born from a brother and sister are called *matrueles*. The **Maternal Uncle** <note>original: "Auunculus"</note> is the mother's brother. A **Great-Uncle** <note>maternal</note> is the grandmother's brother. A **Great-Great-Uncle** is the great-grandmother's brother. A **Great-Great-Great-Uncle** is the great-great-grandmother's brother. An **Atauunculus** <note>Great-great-great-great-uncle</note> is the great-great-great-grandmother's brother.

**Inheritance** is the succession into the goods of the deceased. It is named "Inheritance" from the word for "Heir." The strengths of inheritance are the right of succeeding and the right of obtaining possession. Inheritance comes from several modes: either from a will, or from the law, or from the wish of the deceased, or from nature.

<meta>This page concludes the definitions of marriage and family from Book IX of Isidore of Seville's *Etymologies* and transitions into an alphabetical glossary of terms. In this place, it signifies the right of marrying, unless an adversary prevents the right of the person they wish to join. In a union, whether it is made for the love of a husband—almost like a masculine force <note>The text here plays on a folk etymology connecting "maritus" (husband) and "mas" (male)</note>—it is the male who enters into the state of marriage. He is called a husband <note>original: "maritus"</note> from his "masculine" strength. A **Betrothed** <note>original: "Sponsus"</note> is named from "promising" <note>original: "spondendo"</note>. For in the use of marriage records, it was the custom to make mutual guarantees, in which they promised <note>original: "spondebant"</note> one another their future roles in marriage and gave defenders. Hence the man is admitted as a **betrothed** <note>original: "sponsus"</note> from the vow of the man and from the act of promising; and the bride <note>original: "sponsa"</note> likewise. Furthermore, where you promise <note>original: "spondes"</note>, he is called the **betrothed** <note>original: "sponsus"</note>, meaning the "one who promised"; and she is called the **bride** <note>original: "sponsa"</note>, meaning the "one promised." They are so called because they give earnest money <note>original: "arrabant"</note> and provide guarantors. **Earnest money** <note>original: "Arrabo"</note>, that is, a good legal victory, which makes the agreement firm and corporate. For the earnest money is given not so that the thing itself is added, but so that the pledge remains with the giver; they call it earnest money from the payment of the promise, given so that the promise is fulfilled. Truly, we properly call it **earnest money** <note>original: "arram"</note> from "pleasing," from which the promise arose. We say **prenuptial** because it stands before those marrying. Whomever the husband takes as a bride, she is the **paranymph** <note>In ancient Greek tradition, the bridesmaid or "best man" equivalent who escorted the bride</note>. For a **nymph** <note>original: "nympha"</note> is what we call a bride who has been promised.

### The Tree of Consanguinity
<note>This diagram maps the legal degrees of kinship, used by the Church to determine who was allowed to marry without committing incest.</note>

| Degree | Relationship (Latin/English) |
| :--- | :--- |
| I | Pater & Mater (Father & Mother) |
| II | Frater & Soror (Brother & Sister) |
| III | Filius & Filia (Son & Daughter) |
| IV | Nepos & Neptis (Grandson & Granddaughter) |
| V | Pronepos & Proneptis (Great-grandson & Great-granddaughter) |
| VI | Abnepos & Abneptis (Great-great-grandson & Great-great-granddaughter) |
| VII | Abpatruus (Great-great-great uncle) |

**Affinity** <note>Relationship by marriage rather than blood</note> is a bond of persons coming through marriage, a name that alludes to the binding office. **Spouses** <note>original: "Coniuges"</note> are named from the "yoke" <note>original: "iugo"</note>, because they are joined in marriage. For a yoke is where a pair lies joined together; the word is also said to mean "joining in turn." Nor is there any removal because of the age of the flesh. Younger people are called **spouses** when the marriage yoke is imposed for the purpose of joining; it was customary for certain preparations for the wedding to be made with rings which joined them for life. Hence **nuptials** <note>original: "nuptiae"</note> are named because at the wedding, the brides veil <note>original: "nubent"</note> their heads. To "veil" <note>original: "obnubere"</note> means to cover. This is seen in the changing of garments; those are "unveiled" who do not yet veil their faces. A **wife** is called *uxor* as if from "anointing" the man’s threshold <note>original: "unxerēt"</note>. For among the ancients, when the marrying girls came to the threshold of the husband, they would smear the doorposts with wool and anoint them with oil; and she is called a wife <note>original: "uxor"</note> because they would "anoint" <note>original: "unxerent"</note>. This was done so that she would not stumble at the threshold when she joined him, and once joined, they should not be separated. She is called a **married woman** <note>original: "marita"</note> because she is called to the wedding. From this also, "matrimony" is named. **Nuptials** are for husbands or for mothers of families. For "matrimony" <note>original: "matrimonium"</note> is named from "mother" <note>original: "matre"</note>. Mothers of families are those who give birth. Truly, she is not called a mother of the family until the solemnities have been performed in the husband's family. A **monogamist** <note>original: "monogam"</note> is one who has only one marriage. **Monofiles** are those of one husband. **Digamy** refers to those with two marriages, whether husbands or wives. **Widowhood** <note>original: "viduitas"</note> is the state when the life of the husband has ended; it is a state of being "void" of a man after his death. A "widow" is one who is desolate, nor should she prefer any other...

**Slippery** <note>original: "Lubricus"</note> means slick. **Lamp** is a vessel of light. **Lucid** means bright. **Lucifer** is the morning star. **Gains** <note>original: "Lucra"</note> means profits. **I wrestle** means I fight. **Grove** <note>original: "Lucus"</note> is a wood. **I play** means I joke. **Loin** <note>original: "Lumbus"</note> is a part of the body. **Light** <note>original: "Lumen"</note> is light. **Moon** is a planet. **Lupercalia** are festivals dedicated to Pan. **Wolf** is a predatory animal. **Lurid** means pale. **Nightingale** <note>original: "Lusciniola"</note> is a bird. **Lustrum** is a space of five years. **Yellow** <note>original: "Luteus"</note> means saffron-colored. **Mud** <note>original: "Lutum"</note> is filth. **Light** <note>original: "Lux"</note> is splendor. **Luxury** is pleasure. **Excess** <note>original: "Luxus"</note> is the same. **Water** <note>original: "Lympha"</note> is water. **Lynceus** was a certain man who could see through walls. **Lynx** is a spotted animal.

**Mass** <note>original: "Massa"</note> is properly said of that in which much honey or water is mixed. It is also used for a "mass," that is, a multitude or a collection of hearts into one. **To sacrifice** <note>original: "Mactare"</note> is properly said to offer a victim with force; hence those who slay the victims are called "mactati." **Stain** <note>original: "Macula"</note> is the dirt on a garment. **More** means plus. **Master** <note>original: "Magister"</note> is a teacher. **Magistrate** is a dignity. **Magnanimous** means brave. **Magnate** means noble. **Magnificent** means honorable. **Magus** is of a wise man. **Majesty** is royal dignity. **May** is a month. **Cheek** <note>original: "Mala"</note> is the jaw. **Slanderous** is one who speaks ill. **Malice** is wickedness. **Bad** is not good. **To command** means to prescribe. **I chew** <note>original: "Mando"</note> means I eat. **Morning** is the dawn. **I remain** means I wait. **Manes** are the souls of the dead. **Sleeve** <note>original: "Manica"</note> is a covering for the hands. **Maniple** is a bundle. **Tame** means mild. **Tablecloth** <note>original: "Mantēle"</note> is a napkin. **Mantile** is a vessel. **Manual** is a small book. **I manumit** means I free from slavery.

...of nature. **Nobility of dress**: Nobility through the splendor of one’s clothing. **Noble people**. **Nobility** is not an inheritance for those whose ancestors were noble. **Nobles** are those who possess no virtue of their own. **Nobility** is innocence. **Nobility** without virtue is like a blighted fig tree. Not everyone born of a royal lineage is royal: rather, it is the one who performs royal deeds. Nor is everyone born of nobles truly noble. For God can raise up children of Abraham from the stones. <note>A reference to Matthew 3:9</note> For just as the flowers of the dead have a scent but do not live, so also nobles born of an illustrious family, unless they brighten their soul with their own virtues, may seem to bloom, but they do not truly live. <meta>This page continues the alphabetical Latin glossary, focusing on the letter 'P'. An **agreement** <note>original: "pactio"</note> is the meeting of two or more into the same pleasure and consensus. An **agreement** is made by treaty. A **pact** <note>original: "pactum"</note> is a law that joins faith and obedience to the gods. A **pact** is that by which we place our lives and our affairs under the care and counsel of God. A **pact** is also called a treaty, friendship, or society, as when one has "pacted" with a king. A **pact** is what is transacted between the contracting parties. A **pedagogue** <note>original: "paedagogus"</note> is a leader of boys. **Almost** <note>original: "paene"</note> means nearly. A **district** <note>original: "pagus"</note> is called a village where people dwell, and those who live in these districts are called **pagans**. A **district** is divided land and villages, and those who come from the districts are called **pagans**. **Pagus** for village. A **page** <note>original: "pagina"</note> is a part of a small book. A **small page** <note>original: "paginula"</note> is a tiny page. **Pago** means a joint or structure. **Paguridis** is a type of sea crab. A **spade** <note>original: "pala"</note> is a rustic iron tool, as are stakes, vulturiis <note>likely a specific type of heavy tool</note>, and hoes. **Pala** can also mean a type of garment. **Openly** <note>original: "palam"</note> means manifest. **Palam** is openly; that is, "see": it is open to everyone. **Palatinal** pertains to the palace. **Palatine** pertains to the palace. A **palace** <note>original: "palatium"</note> is a royal house. A **palace** is the place where kings live. The **Palatine** is a hill in Rome. A **palace** is said to be where a king dwells. **Pale** means chaff. **Chaff** <note>original: "palea"</note> is the skin that hangs from the neck of an ox; **chaff** is also a wicker twig. **Chaff** is what is threshed from wheat. A **dewlap** <note>original: "palear"</note> is the "chaff" of oxen. The **dewlaps** of oxen are what hang from them. **Palearis** pertains to chaff. **Pales** is the goddess of shepherds. A **palaestra** is a place where naked men were exercised. **Palaestra** is the force of exercising. **Palaestra** is a contest or the power of exercising. **Palaestral** pertains to the palaestra. **Palaestric** pertains to the palaestra. A **palaestrita** is one who exercises in the palaestra. The **Palilia** is a festival day of the goddess Pales. **Palinbachia** <note>original: "palimbaccheus"</note> is how we call a thing back to previous states. A **palindrome** is said to be where words are read backward. **Palingenesia** is a renewed generation. A **palinode** <note>original: "palinodia"</note> is a repeated voice; a **palinodium** is a repeated song. **Paliurus** is a type of thorn. The **Palladium** is the image of Pallas that fell from heaven. **Palladius** pertains to the palladium. **Pallas** is the goddess of wisdom. **To be pale** <note>original: "palleo"</note> is to turn pale. **Pallescens** means beginning to grow pale. **Pallid** is one who is overcome by paleness. A **pallium** is the garment of philosophers and a certain Greek robe. A **palliolum** is a small pallium. The **palm** <note>original: "palma"</note> is the inner part of the hand. **Palmarius** is one who deserves the palm. A **palmarium** is a place where palms are, or a place where the palm is given to victors. **Palmatus** is one who has the palm. A **palmes** is a branch of a vine. **Palmipedalis** is five palms long. A **palmo** is the space of one palm. A **palmula** is a small palm. A **palmus** is a measure of four fingers. **To stroke** <note>original: "palpare"</note> is to touch softly. A **palpator** is one who strokes or flatters. **Eyelids** <note>original: "palpebrae"</note> are the coverings of the eyes. **Palpitation** is the movement of the heart. **To palpitate** is to move frequently. **To stroke** <note>original: "palpo"</note> is to touch gently. A **paludamentum** is a military garment. **Marshes** <note>original: "paludes"</note> are watery places. A **stake** <note>original: "palus"</note> is a post fixed in the earth. A **marsh** <note>original: "palus"</note> is a watery place. **Paluster** pertains to a marsh. A **tendril** <note>original: "pampinus"</note> is the leaf of a vine. **Pampineus** pertains to a vine-tendril. **Pan** is the god of shepherds. **Panacea** is a kind of herb, or a medicine for all diseases. **Panaceus** pertains to panacea. A **bread-basket** <note>original: "panarium"</note> is a vessel in which bread is stored. **Panathenaea** is a festival day in Athens in honor of Minerva. A **pancratiastes** is one who exercises in the pancratium. A **pancratium** is a kind of exercise <note>a Greek combat sport combining wrestling and boxing</note>. **Pancratic** pertains to the pancratium. **Pandects** are books in which all laws are contained. **To spread** <note>original: "pandere"</note> is to open. **To stretch** <note>original: "pandiculari"</note> is to extend the limbs. **Pandiculation** is the extension of the limbs. A **pot-bellied man** <note>original: "pandox"</note> is one who has a large belly. A **pandura** is a type of musical instrument; **panduria** is another name for it. A **panegyric** is a speech spoken in praise of someone. A **panegyris** is a gathering of people, a festival, or public praise. **To fix** <note>original: "pangere"</note> is to sing or to fix/fasten. **Pangonia** is a type of gemstone. **Panicium** is a type of grain. A **panicula** is a small panicle. **Paniculum** is a small panic-grain. **Paniculus** is a small cloth or rag <note>The text appears to conflate botanical terms with "panniculus," a rag</note>. **Bread** <note>original: "panis"</note> is food made from flour; bread is the food of humans. A **bread-eater** <note>original: "panivorus"</note> is one who eats bread. A **rag** <note>original: "panniculus"</note> is a small piece of cloth. **Ragged** <note>original: "pannosus"</note> is one who is clothed in rags. A **cloth** <note>original: "pannus"</note> is a woolen garment. **Pannuceus** pertains to cloth. **Panomphaeus** is a surname of Jupiter <note>meaning 'the source of all voices'</note>. **Panoply** is a complete set of armor. **Panoptes** is he who sees all things. **Panos** is a type of gemstone. A **baker** <note>original: "panovius"</note> is one who sells bread. A **splay-footed man** <note>original: "pansa"</note> is one who has broad feet. The **belly** <note>original: "pantex"</note> is the stomach. **Pantheology** is a discourse about the gods. The **Pantheon** is a temple of all the gods. A **panther** <note>original: "panthera"</note> is a kind of animal. A **pantomime** <note>original: "pantomimus"</note> is one who imitates all things. A **pantomime** is an actor.

**O**MNIBUS ANIMANTIBUS <note>To all living things</note> Adam first gave names, calling each one a name from its own state, according to the nature in which or where it might serve. The nations, however, gave names to each animal from their own language. Adam, truly, did not use the Latin language, nor Greek, or any barbarian tongue, but that which was before the flood, which is called **Hebrew**. # Of Beasts
The word <term>bestiae</term> properly belongs to bears, wolves, lions, leopards, tigers, dogs, and others which savage either with mouth or claws, snakes excepted. They are called "beasts" from the force <note>Latin: "vis"</note> with which they savage. Whence they are also called "wild" <note>Latin: "ferae"</note> because they enjoy natural liberty and are moved by the desire of their own ferocity. They are of free will, and wander here and there, and are carried where their spirit leads them. Their name passed from Greek origin into Latin. For the Greeks call them <term>theras</term>, which we call <term>feras</term> by a corrupted name. The **Pard** <note>The leopard or panther</note> is second from the lion; a varied genus, and very swift, and headlong for blood. For it rushes to death with a leap. The **Leopard** is born from the adultery of a lioness and a pard, and makes a third origin, just as Pliny says in his Natural History: the lion mates with a female pard, or the pard with a lioness, and from both degenerate offspring are created, like mules and hinnies. The **Panther** is a friend to all animals except dragons. It is called <term>panthera</term> either because it is the friend of all animals except the dragon, or because it rejoices in the universality of its kind, and whatever it receives, it returns. For <term>pan</term> in Greek means "all." This animal is distinguished by various small circles, as some are distinguished by small and tawny eyes. They say it gives birth only once; whence one alone destroys the womb with its claws. Whence others, like mice, give birth only once, and there is only one male. When it is called Panther, it is called Panther because whatever is said is special, and sometimes one is said to be rarer, whence it is said "beyond, beyond," the final thing is said to be beyond measure.

<meta>This page continues the medieval encyclopedia's bestiary, moving from the lions of the previous page into a detailed catalog of serpents, creeping things, and aquatic life. <margin>concerning serpents</margin>
The **Asp** <note>original: "aspis"</note>, as Isidore says, is a serpent; it is called <term>aspis</term> in Greek from the "application" <note>Latin: "adhibendo"</note> of venom; whence it is also called <term>aspis</term> as if it were "at the sting" <note>Latin: "adpis"</note>. For the asp is said to be found with its venom applied <note>held ready</note>: thus it is named from applying and not letting go of its venom. Alternatively, it is called <term>aspis</term> from "scattering" <note>Latin: "spargendo"</note> venom: because wherever it bites, the venom is scattered in that vicinity and diffused throughout the whole body; hence it is called <term>aspis</term> as if it were "at the scattering" <note>Latin: "adspis"</note>. There are many and diverse kinds of these, just as there are diverse effects and strengths of their venom. The **Dipsas** <note>original: "dipsas"</note> is its Greek name, which in Latin is called the **Thirsty One** <note>original: "sitiens"</note>: because whoever it bites perishes from thirst. The **Hypnalis** is a type of asp that kills whoever it bites through sleep, as Isidore says. And Cleopatra applied this to herself so that she might end her life in a death like a deep slumber. The **Hemorrhous** <note>original: "hemmorhois"</note> is a type of asp that, when it bites someone, causes them to lose so much blood that death follows once the veins are drained. The **Prester** is a serpent that, when it bites, causes the victim to swell up; once distended by this excessive swelling, the victim rots and dies. The **Seps** is a serpent that immediately consumes whoever it bites, so that the person seems to entirely liquefy in the asp's mouth. The **Cerastes** is a serpent that has horns on its head like a ram, from which it takes its name. The **Jaculus** is a flying serpent that throws itself from trees onto passersby, from which it takes its name <note>The name is related to "javelin" or "hurling."</note>. The **Amphisbaena** is so called because it has two heads: one in its proper place and another at the tail; it runs from both directions with glowing eyes. The **Scytale** <note>original: "scytale"</note> is so called because it is of such great variety that it appears to be a painted picture; whence it is called <term>scytale</term> as if it were "a painting" <note>Latin: "pictura"</note>. The **Boa** is so called because it follows cattle <note>Latin: "boves"</note> and sucks their udders, from which it takes its name. These things Isidore says. The **Asp** is said to have such great prudence that it shuts its ears against enchanters so that it might not hear their voices: it presses one ear against the earth and plugs the other with its tail, lest it hear the voice of the one casting spells.

<margin>concerning the dipsas</margin>
The **Dipsas** is said to be a small but virulent serpent, and it has such a strength of venom that whoever it bites is overcome by such a thirst that it can in no way be satisfied, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the hypnalis</margin>
The **Hypnalis** is called a type of asp that immediately sends whoever it bites into a deep sleep; from this it takes its name, being called <term>ypnalis</term> from <term>ypnos</term>, which is "sleep," as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the hemorrhous</margin>
The **Hemorrhous** is called a type of asp that, when it bites someone, causes so much blood to be emitted that death follows, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the prester</margin>
The **Prester** is a serpent that, when it bites, causes the victim to swell; from this excessive swelling, the victim rots and dies, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the seps</margin>
The **Seps** is a serpent that immediately consumes whoever it bites, so that the person seems to entirely liquefy in the asp's mouth, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the cerastes</margin>
The **Cerastes** is a serpent that has horns on its head like a ram, from which it takes its name, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the jaculus</margin>
The **Jaculus** is called a flying serpent that throws itself from trees onto passersby, from which it takes its name, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the amphisbaena</margin>
The **Amphisbaena** is so called because it has two heads: one in its proper place and another at its tail; it runs from both directions with glowing eyes, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the scytale</margin>
The **Scytale** is so called because it is of such great variety that it appears to be a painted picture; whence it is called <term>scytale</term> as if it were "a painting," as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the boa</margin>
The **Boa** is so called because it follows cattle and sucks their udders, from which it takes its name, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the salamander</margin>
The **Salamander** is called an animal that lives in fire and extinguishes fire, from which it takes its name, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the stellio</margin>
The **Stellio** <note>A type of spotted lizard.</note> is an animal named for its variety of "stars" <note>Latin: "stellarum"</note>, from which it takes its name, as Isidore says.

<margin>concerning the scorpion</margin>
The **Scorpion** is a worm that lives in the earth and has a sting in its tail with which it strikes, from which it takes its name, as Isidore says.

<column-break/>

...it has a sting in its tail with which it strikes...

A **Worm** <note>original: "vermis"</note>, as Isidore says, is an animal that is mostly born from flesh, or from wood, or from any other earthly thing, without blood and without bones; from this it takes its name, as Isidore says. <margin>concerning worms</margin> There are, however, many and diverse kinds of worms, just as there are diverse things from which they are born. The **Earthworm** <note>original: "lumbricus"</note> is called a worm of the earth, which comes out of the ground after rain. The **Moth** <note>original: "tinea"</note> is called a worm of garments, which consumes clothing. The **Louse** <note>original: "pediculus"</note> is called a worm of the head, which is born from the body of a human. The **Flea** <note>original: "pullex"</note> is called a worm that is born from dust. The **Bedbug** <note>original: "cimex"</note> is called a worm of beds, which is born from moisture. These things Isidore says.

**Fish** <note>original: "pisces"</note> are so named because <margin>concerning fish</margin> they are "fed" <note>Latin: <term>pasco</term></note>; hence a "pool" <note>Latin: <term>piscina</term></note> is also so named, as Isidore says. Pools and estuaries are so named, they say, because the tide <note>original: "aestu"</note> rushes in and recedes; everything whether far or near: but because the source which is in their vicinity both flows in and, as it were, expels this from itself, so they say. Indeed, an estuary <term>estuarium: a tidal opening where the sea meets a river source</term> pours forth from itself; from here its abundance leaps out through its own veins and draws itself back again: this is what they say concerning the rise and fall of the tides.

### About the tides and the straits of the sea.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK 13: ON THE EARTH AND PARADISE

<image-desc>A large, elaborate red initial T decorated with white scrollwork patterns and circular motifs inside the letter body.</image-desc>

**T**he Earth <term>Terra: the element of soil and the world at large</term> is situated in the middle part of the universe, positioned at an equal interval from all parts of heaven like a center in the middle of a circle, whence it is also called *terra*, because upon it life is "trodden" <note>original: "teritur," a medieval etymological link between terra and treading</note>. For the Earth is said to be "worn" <note>original: "trita"</note>. For life itself is called earth because it brings forth fruit. And it is called "arid," because the water has dried up <note>original: "aruit"</note> upon it. For even arid water is that which flows through a dry place. It is indeed solid, because it is sustained through the whole world. From the lower part indeed, it is excluded from this same heaven by the surrounding neighborhood on all sides.

### ABOUT THE GLOBE.

The globe <note>original: "orbis"</note> is named from the roundness of its form, because it is like a wheel; whence also a small wheel is called an *orbiculus*. For the Ocean, flowing around it on all sides, encompasses its borders and divides it into three parts, of which one is called Asia, the second Europe, and the third Africa. The ancients divided these three parts, but not equally; for Asia reaches from the south through the north to the east, while Europe goes from the north to the west, and Africa also from the south to the west. Whence it is manifest that [Asia] holds two parts of the globe, while Europe and Africa hold the other. Between both of them, however, the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> enters from the Ocean.

### About Asia and its parts.

Asia was named after the name of a certain woman who held the empire of the East among the ancients. This lies in the third part of the globe toward the east, bounded by the rising of the sun in the east, by the ocean in the south, by our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> in the west, and by the Maeotian marsh <note>The Sea of Azov</note> and the Tanais river <note>The Don</note> in the north. It has, moreover, many provinces and regions, whose names and locations I shall briefly set forth, taking the beginning from Paradise.

<margin>Cyrene</margin>
It rises up. Cyrene is situated on the summit of a mountain. From it, the district of its neighbor was named the Aretic region <note>original: "arēticula"; likely referring to the Cyrenaic Pentapolis</note>. It is a region previously rare in rains, but now appearing with an abundance of dew: for those parts of the land itself which are held by those living nearby were not then deserted by the dew. For that which was later the will of the gods in the warming of things which existed before has perished, yet so much dew was not lacking. First, to the right, that city preserves me, and only so much dew is lacking in which a multitude of citizens live in the City of the Sun <note>original: "urbe solis"; likely Heliopolis or a symbolic reference to Cyrene's climate</note>, yet they fulfill political duties.

Next, however, is the region of the sea which seems to have the city of Babylon. And then, then, the land is always silent, not as it is said of many things, but concerning the things in which each person is instructed. The text follows the structure of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, though it contains significant repetitive scribal errors or corruptions in the descriptive passages.</summary>

--- Page 447 ---
<meta>This page continues the encyclopedic survey of human habitation from Book XV of Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies. Having previously discussed cities and roads, the text now moves into the specific architectural components of buildings, the nature of fortifications, types of tombs, rural dwellings, and the legal and physical division of land. It concludes by transitioning into Book XVI, which deals with the materials of the earth.</meta>

standing walls made of cement. **Winding passages** <note>original: "Anfractus"</note> refer to two walls joined together. An **emicilla** is a wall that follows a curved path to enclose a city. **Antae** <note>original: "Antas"; these are pilasters or pier-like structures at the ends of walls</note> are the outermost parts of a wall. An **angle** <note>original: "Angulus"</note> is the point where all visible members of the structure meet. **Vaults** <note>original: "Camarae"</note> are those structures that are curved. **Rafters** <note>original: "Canterii"</note> are the useful channels through which accidental water may flow out. **Outlets** <note>original: "Pronumina"</note> in pools are where the water flow is diverted; however, **pools** <note>original: "lacus"</note> are generally named from the basin where water remains from the downflow. For a pool is where water flows together. **Pits** <note>original: "Lacunae"</note> are cut off from pools; they are named so because they do not have the form of a proper lake, but are places where water shines on the ground if there is an abundance of snow. **Before the doors** <note>original: "Ante ostia"</note>: a door <note>original: "ostium"</note> is named from those who stand before the door at the outer entrance. An **entrance** <note>original: "Aditum"</note> is named as if it were an "approach" <note>original: "obitus"</note> to the entry of a city or a whole house; the **sacred** part <note>original: "sacre hanc"</note> is where sacrifice is made. To **reflect an image** <note>original: "Immaginem reddere"</note> refers to the likeness of another, echoing in a space where voices are returned by resonance. An **area** is either a place for building or a floor on which grain is threshed; **areas** are named from "being dry" <note>original: "areo"</note> because they were worked to be dry first. A **machine**, as Varro says, is a building for climbing or lifting anything high. They are called **machines** <note>original: "machinae"</note> because those who ascend in them fear <note>original: "metuatur"</note> for their safety. Among these, columns stand as part of the walls or substance. **Columns** are called "celestial" because they stand tall. They are called **columns** <note>original: "Columnae"</note> because they support the mass and weight of the entire building. **Statues** are columns that they have made to a specific measure. **Capitals** <note>original: "Capitella"</note> are "little houses" <note>original: "domitella"</note> at the top. The **top** <note>original: "Summum"</note> is the peak <note>original: "fastigium"</note>. Any stones used for fortification are part of this. **Bases** <note>original: "Bases"</note> are the foundations of columns which often support the weight for future structures. An **apse** <note>original: "Bapsis"</note> is formed with gold near the site of the peak. **Columns** are made so they do not mimic each other in length and roundness. **Enclosure** <note>original: "Circunndari"</note> in three or four columns provides the stability of firmness. **Enclosure** in two ranks are worn down for those standing by, resulting in the haste and abundance of the standing building. **Cymatia** <note>original: "Cimas"</note>, which are the capitals of columns, reach to the highest peak. They are called **cymatia** from "summit" <note>original: "summitate"</note>, spoken of as the capitals of columns. Here, by design, capitals are placed above the capitals of the columns, and it is called "super-imposed" <note>original: "super missa"</note>. **Architraves** <note>original: "Epulite"</note> and **cornices** <note>original: "coronæ"</note> are named from the summit and the decoration of the "heads" <note>the capitals</note>. **Gades** <note>perhaps a corruption of "Gadus" or a specific vessel</note> is a basin from which a bronze aqueduct is formed where the root stands. **Cariat** <note>referring to Caryatids</note> is named from the "knee" <note>original: "genum"</note> or the manner of a reed. There are reeds from which a measure is formed, using the masculine for the feminine; it stands upright at the foundation of the columns and is named from its straightness.

### On fortifications.

**City walls** <note>original: "Moenia"</note> are the walls of a city, properly those parts that are fortified. A **wall** <note>original: "Murus"</note> is named from a "sharp stone" <note>original: "murice"</note> because they conclude all things into one within themselves. They are properly called **walls** <note>original: "Muri"</note>, but **moenia** are those which are outside the city. For walls in a city are spoken of as being in houses. A **rampart** <note>original: "Vallum"</note> is that which is provided for those things which are for defense. A **valley** <note>original: "Vallis"</note> is from where it rises up and precedes the guard. Walls, however, are **ramparts** made of stakes <note>original: "fustes"</note>, and "valli" are the stakes which fortify the rampart. A **valley** is named from its "face" and its fortified emptiness; if there is a space, it is called an **interval**. It is named from the rampart or from those things fortified outside the city. A **mound** <note>original: "Agger"</note> is made from those things gathered nearby to fill a space. The **mound** itself is named from "piling up" <note>original: "adgestu"</note>, by which ditches and ramparts are protected from vice and walls, and the way is fortified. They call it a **mound**, which is a heap of far-off and eminent earth. A **stone wall** <note>original: "Maceria"</note> is properly seen as a wall. A **maceria** is either formed in sight, and those first walls made of earth are so named, which are built in the form of buildings, two-in-one, in length and hardness. Note, therefore, all things around the stronger and often fortified standing structures. There is a cause for being fortified, which is the "seventh city," and for those who hold the same. In which a field calls to no receptacles.

It is called fortified, that is, the most protected places of buildings. They are called **pavilions** <note>original: "Papiliones"</note> from the likeness of a peacock <note>original: "pavonis"</note>; they are established if they abound greatly in brilliance of this kind. Like those small huts which are venerated with attentive light and are named by those who are called nearby.

A **tomb** <note>original: "Sepulchrum"</note> is named from the "buried" <note>original: "sepulto"</note>, because of those buried in their own home.
