For they are **monuments** <note>original: "Monumenta"</note> because they move the mind <note>original: "in mente moveant"</note> to the memory of the deceased. When it is a monument, so it is a tomb. When it is called a **monument**, it is for the sake of memory. Why does he call it a monument? For the admonition of where to come. Thus, "monuments" and "memory" are counted as the same name. A **mound** <note>original: "Tumulus"</note> is named as if "fearing the chamber" <note>original: "timens cellam"</note>. A **sarcophagus** <note>original: "Sarcofagus"</note> is that which consumes the body; *sarx* <note>original: "sarcis"</note> means flesh, and *phagein* <note>original: "fagus"</note> means "I eat." **Mausoleums** <note>original: "Mausolea"</note> are from "basolea" or the monuments of a king, named after Mausolus, the Egyptian king <note>Mausolus was actually Carian, but Isidore or the scribe attributes him to Egypt here</note>. <meta>This page transitions from the architectural components discussed on the previous page into Book XVI of the Etymologies, which focuses on the "materials of the earth," specifically stones and gems. The text uses the physical properties of minerals—such as hardness, weight, and color—as allegories for human morality and spiritual states, a common practice in medieval lapidaries.</meta>

In this way, so do all enemies. Limbs move correctly when they provide for what is worldly and laughed at; thus the sinner is called a "stone." <note>The author is drawing a moral parallel between the cold, unfeeling nature of a stone and the heart of a sinner.</note> Truly, sin hardens just like a stone, and it is said to be "right" only in that it is always falling <note>original: "sepere montis," likely a corruption of "semper ruit," referring to the downward gravity of stone and sin</note>. For the property of a stone is to be heavy. Indeed, a stone <note>original: "lapis"</note> is so named because it is "striking the foot" <note>original: "laedens pes"</note>, because it is said to both press down and strike. There is a verse about this:
> The foot is said to be struck; from "striking," the stone takes its name.

So too the sinner provides for what the righteous man laughs at, and he crushes and presses upon the just. The verse says:
> Thus the sinner is a stone, and the world has these stones.

These stones are many and varied in their properties. For some are precious and are useful for temperance, chastity, and other virtues. Others are medicinal and are effective against various portents. For there are words within portents, herbs among serpents, and stones within limbs; there are also stones found in herbs, animals, and serpents, as is said in the book of the "Mind of the Lord." <note>This likely refers to a lost or specific lapidary authority or a misreading of a title like "Liber de naturis rerum."</note> Others are common and numerous: some are white, such as marbles; some are reddish, such as tiles; some are black, such as coals. A reddish color signifies the fire of concupiscence <note>Lust or strong worldly desire.</note> which wishes to weigh down the limbs. Black signifies a sinner who loves earthly things. White, however, signifies a bright and clean mind, as is said everywhere in the text of the Scriptures. For it is said of the Bride in the Song of Songs: "My beloved is white and ruddy" <note>Song of Solomon 5:10. In medieval exegesis, "white" represented purity and "ruddy" represented the blood of Christ's passion.</note>; that is, pure in himself and reddened toward us through charity. Because of this, he is my beloved, and thus he is called ruddy through his passion and white through his purity. 

And stones are considered according to other significations:
I. That it is abundant, just as the sinner abounds in the world.
II. That it is hard in perversity, just as the sinner is in iniquity.
III. That it is heavy in malice, just as the sinner is in sin.
IIII. That it is a source of mockery, just as the sinner is in the world.
V. That it is crushing, just as the sinner is toward the righteous.
VI. They are called "broken wood gathered together" <note>original: "fractur lignis recollicti"</note> because just as they fail in the fire having the property of earth, so do sinners fail in spiritual matters. 

Likewise, it is said that walls fail because of these stones—that is, from the harmony of minds—because if they fail, this verse about the stone is spoken:
> The world did not hold you because it learned you were a stone.
For a stone is a small world in itself: in spirit, in God, in the earth, in the soul, and in other things.

### Regarding stones in general:

**S**tones <note>original: "Lapides"</note> are named from "striking the foot" <note>original: "ledendo pede"</note>. Whence the verse:
> The foot is said to be struck; from "striking," the stone takes its name.
Some stones are precious; others are common. Precious stones are those that serve for the decoration of a king or are effective for medicinal cure, such as gems. Common stones are those prepared for the construction of walls, such as rocks and flints. These represent external things in weak souls or in spiritual matters. For one perceives firmness and holds God in the mind through faith, which is the goal <note>original: "meta"</note>, the stone, the rock. And it is said that a small world exists within it. For the world is spoken of in a precious stone. The world is described as a multitude of harmonies. And hence it is said that there are many evils in the world, because there are many precious things: temperance, human chastity, and other human virtues against serpents and other things. They are hard and smooth. For they seem to be filled to such an extent that their properties differ among themselves, just as human virtues: some of the mind, some of joy, some of purity, some of chastity, some of temperance; they are defined by these other properties. Likewise, a rock profits human virtue only when removed from others, just as in spiritual matters. Likewise, marble filled by God is called a "world," just as a rock is called "the world." Just as a rock is called smooth, so the purity of the mind is called a rock.

<margin>About the properties of the magnet in particular</margin>

**M**agnets <note>original: "Magnetes"; the Lodestone</note> are stones of an iron color, slightly attracting iron. In terms of its power, it is said to be "human" in its temperance; it is called "purity of mind," and so in other things. Someone is called a "small world" in himself, just as he is called such in other things; and here he is called a stone, just as in the world he is called a rock, and so on.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Book XVI of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies—which covers minerals and measurements—into the beginning of Book XVII, dedicated to agriculture. The text maintains continuity by moving from the physical properties of materials (metals and stones) to the methods of weighing them, and finally to the cultivation of the earth that produces them.</meta>

**Measurement** is a certain limit in its time and body. For it consists of either a span of time, or the length, width, or height of bodies, or their weights. <meta>This page continues the transition into Book XVII of Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies, shifting from the general study of the earth and agriculture to the specific classification of trees and fruits. The text relies heavily on classical authorities, particularly Isidore and the poet Virgil, to define the nature of various botanical species.</meta>

<margin>Definition of a tree</margin>
Because there are many types of trees that are admirable for their size, quality, and strength, it is right that this subject be treated thoroughly. We must first deal with those which are fruitful in the field. Regarding this, Isidore, in the seventeenth book <note>Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, Book XVII, Chapter 7</note>, sets down this difference between trees and herbs: A **tree** is that which has a tall body and branches reaching upward, such as the cedar. An **herb** is that which flowers and produces seed as soon as it is born. Furthermore, some trees have branches that never lose their leaves, such as the laurel, the olive, and the palm; others do lose them, such as the fig and the apple tree.

<margin>Kinds of trees</margin>
**A**mong trees, some are fruit-bearing, others non-fruit-bearing; some are wild, others domesticated. Isidore writes in book seventeen: A tree is called "fruit-bearing" where the countryside is cultivated or where fruit is sought; that which grows in the woodland and whose fruit is not sought is "non-fruit-bearing," such as the fir, the pine, and the alder, which lack fruit but not timber.

<margin>The Fir</margin>
The **fir** <note>original: *abies*</note> is a tall tree, full of branches, with a few sharp, hard leaves at the top, similar to the pine. This tree is rough and sparse, with clean, dry foliage; its wood is white, light, and resinous. Once polished, it hardens so that it may be split and used for walls. It is often rough at the top and resinous at the root. It grows on high mountains, as Virgil says in the second book of the *Georgics*: "We see the fir born in the mountains, resinous and hard." Its wood is durable and, as Isidore says in book seventeen, it is not easily split.

<margin>The Strawberry Tree</margin>
The **strawberry tree** <note>original: *arbutus*; likely *Arbutus unedo*</note> is a tree that the Greeks call *comaron*. Some think this tree should be called *arbutum*, or that the place where they grow is an *arbustum*, but this is false. The tree is not called *arbutum*; rather, one is the fruit and the other is the tree. Specifically, the tree is the *arbutus*, and the fruit is the *arbutum*. Regarding the strawberry tree, Virgil says in the second book of the *Georgics*: "The rough strawberry tree is grafted with the nut of the chestnut," and so forth. Isidore speaks the truth and also says that its fruit is called *memaecylon*, which is eaten immediately. To many, the strawberry tree is called *memecylon*. However, Isidore says that *memecylon* is specifically the name for the fruit of the strawberry tree, which is fatty, rare, round, and branched, appearing like a small breast—whence the name *mamilla* <note>Latin for "nipple" or "little breast"</note> seems to be derived. Many use the word *arbutus* for the place where they grow, but the tree itself is called *arbutus*.

<margin>The Alaternus</margin>
The **alaternus** <note>likely the Mediterranean buckthorn, *Rhamnus alaternus*</note> is a resinous tree of the mountains whose leaves are round and serrated, and which stings the touch like a nettle. Virgil mentions this in the second book of the *Georgics*: "Commonly the alaternus is among the branches in the mountains."

<margin>The Alder</margin>
The **alder** <note>original: *alnus*</note> is a tree growing in swamps and on riverbanks, loving the water and growing to a great height. It is quickly used up in consumption, though it is useful for walls and soft for stretching. When it is in the water, it is extremely hard. Its wood is red, and when it is painted, it is clean. Virgil says of it in the second book of the *Georgics*: "The alder in the swamps, and the pine in the woodland." Isidore says in book seventeen that the tree is called *alnus* because it is "nourished by the river" <note>original: *alatur amne*—a typical medieval folk etymology</note>, that is, it is fed by the water near which it grows.

<margin>The Almond</margin>
The **almond** <note>original: *amygdalus*</note> is a tree which is said to bloom first. Virgil says in the first book of the *Georgics* that the almond blooms in the woodland and soon bears fruit in the autumn. Isidore says in book seventeen that it is called *amygdala* in Greek, but in Latin it is the "long nut" <note>original: *nux longa*</note>. Its nut is also called *amygdalum*, just as the fruit of the apple tree is an apple. In Greek, however, the nut is called *amygdala*, and the tree itself is called *amygdalus*.

<margin>Tree Barks</margin>
The **barks** of a tree are sometimes wrinkled, sometimes smooth, sometimes thick, and sometimes thin. Isidore, in book seventeen, defines "bark" <note>original: *cortex*</note> as the outermost part of trees, while the "inner bark" <note>original: *liber*</note> is that which is under the bark and stands before the wood.

<margin>Definition of Fruit</margin>
**F**ruit <note>original: *pomum*, used broadly for any orchard fruit</note> is every kind of produce that a tree brings forth. It is called *pomum* from the fact that it "feeds" <note>original: *pascat*</note> man or animals. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called *pomum*, every kind of fruit that a tree produces; hence it is named from "feeding" <note>original: *pascendo*</note>. What is called *pomum* in Latin is called *opos* in Greek, meaning "juice," because it is eaten immediately or because juice is squeezed from it. This is also why *opion* <note>opium</note> is named, as it comes from the poppy.

<margin>Species of Apples</margin>
There are many species of **apples** <note>The Latin *malum* can mean "apple" specifically or "fruit" generally</note>, and they are called by various names, as Isidore says in book seventeen. It is called *malum* because it is a fruit and is born on the branches of a tree; it is named *malum* because it hangs from the branches and soon falls to the ground. The word *malum* is derived from the Greek *melon*. These are the species of apples: the **Matian apple**, named after its creator Matius, which is a fatty and round fruit. The **orbicular apple**, because it is round. The **Cudian apple**, which is "precocious" <note>early-ripening</note> and matures before others. The **Cestian apple**, which is "of Cestius," having a sweet scent but rotting quickly. The **fragrant apple**, which has a sweet smell and is seen to have a pleasant, spiced flavor. The **sweet apple**, which is sweet, broad, somewhat dark, and smooth. The **mountain apple**, which is called *montanum*, is modest in size and has little juice. Regarding the tree itself, it is said to be branched, some more than others, and some smaller. The leaves of the apple tree tend toward a round shape. There is also a tree whose fruit is thinner and less round. The **bitter apple** is so called because it is bitter. The **citrine apple** is so called because it is the color of a citron <note>yellow</note>.

<column-break/>

nature and it was called a "pill" <note>original: *pilula*</note> if it came from the fruit. He says "blushing" <note>original: *pruitio*, likely a corruption of *punicio* or related to redness</note> is first a sign of beauty; and because the fruit is filled... so it grew stiff. And as the tree fruits and is purged... whence it is called **Cestian**... because for the reds and by a certain King Cestianus: because they are in the earth like a red fruit. And it is said to be well named as a fruit. An apple is also called a **Punic apple** <note>The pomegranate</note> because it abounds in the Punic region <note>Carthage</note>, and because the fruit has much tartness. The **Persian apple** <note>The peach</note> is so called because it was born in the region of Persia. The **precocious apple** <note>The apricot, *malum praecoquum*</note> because it matures before other fruits. The **Matian apple** is named after the author Matius, and it is a fatty and thin apple fruit.

<margin>Tree Bud</margin>
It is called the **bud** <note>original: *gemma*</note> of the tree, which is at the very top where it begins to flower. It is called *gemma* because it is like a precious gem, or because it begins to "gem" <note>to bud or sparkle</note>, that is, to flower. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called a bud where it first begins to flower, either because it is at the summit of the tree, or because, like a gem, once opened, it shows color and brightness.

<margin>Tree Foliage</margin>
It is called the **foliage** <note>original: *frons*</note> where the leaves are born and the branches begin to form. Isidore says in book seventeen: He calls the *frons* that which is at the top of the tree where the leaves are born. It is said "to be leafy" <note>original: *frondere*</note> where it makes foliage.

<margin>Tree Leaves</margin>
They are called **leaves** <note>original: *folia*</note>, which are born on the branches of the tree. It is called a leaf (*folium*) because it "flies" <note>original: *folat*, a folk etymology</note> from the branches and soon falls to the ground. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called *folium* because it flies from the branches and soon falls to the ground.

<margin>Tree Flower</margin>
It is called the **flower** of the tree, which is on the branches before the fruit. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called a flower (*flos*) because it quickly "flows away" <note>original: *defluat*</note> and falls from the branches.

<margin>Tree Seed</margin>
It is called the **seed** of the tree, which is inside the fruit. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called seed (*semen*) because it is in the fruit of the tree so that it may be "sown" <note>original: *seminetur*</note> to make another tree.

<margin>Tree Root</margin>
It is called the **root** of the tree, which is under the earth and sustains the tree. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called a root because it is under the earth and supports the tree.

<margin>Tree Branches</margin>
They are called the **branches** of the tree, which are born from the trunk and produce leaves. Isidore says in book seventeen: They are called branches (*rami*) because they are born from the trunk and produce leaves.

<margin>Tree Twig</margin>
It is called the **twig** <note>original: *vimen*</note> of the tree, which is born on the trunk; it is thin and suitable for binding. It is called *vimen* from *viendo*, that is, "binding." Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called a *vimen* because it is fit for *viciendum*, that is, for binding.

<margin>Tree Stock</margin>
It is called the **stock** <note>original: *stirps*</note> of the tree, which is born from the earth and sustains the tree. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called the stock because it arises from the earth and supports the tree.

<margin>Fungus</margin>
It is called **fungus** because it is like a sponge; hence it is named fungus because it is a lover of water and quickly drinks it up. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called fungus...

<margin>The Plum Tree</margin>
The **plum tree** <note>original: *prunus*</note> is the tree that produces the plum, and it is called a plum because it is a fatty and sweet fruit. Isidore says in book seventeen: The plum tree is so called because it is a tree of sweet and fatty apples.

<margin>The Pear Tree</margin>
The **pear tree** <note>original: *pirus*</note> is the tree that produces the pear, and it is called a pear because it is a thin and long fruit. Isidore says in book seventeen: The pear tree is so called because it is a tree of thin and long apples.

<margin>The Fig Tree</margin>
The **fig tree** <note>original: *ficus*</note> is the tree that produces the fig, and it is called a fig because it is a fatty and sweet fruit. Isidore says in book seventeen: The fig tree is so called because it is a tree of fatty and sweet apples.

<margin>The Punic Tree</margin>
The **Punic tree** <note>The pomegranate</note> is the tree called the Punic apple because it abounds in the Punic region. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called Punic because it is the tree of the Punic apple.

<margin>The Palm Tree</margin>
The **palm tree** is the tree called the palm, and it is called palm because it is a tree of round and fatty fruit. Isidore says in book seventeen: It is called palm because it is a tree of round and fatty apples.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of trees and fruits, providing etymological definitions and physical descriptions based on Isidore of Seville and Virgil. It covers deciduous and evergreen trees, orchard fruits like apples and pears, and the anatomical parts of a tree from root to bud.</summary>

### On Aromatic Trees

There are many aromatic trees in India and Arabia which bear leaves throughout the entire year and are never without fruit. Among these is **Frankincense** <note>original: *Thus*</note>. The frankincense tree grows in the middle of Arabia in a place called Saba; hence it is also called "Sabaean frankincense." The appearance of the frankincense tree is similar to the lentisk <note>the mastic tree</note>. The juice of the tree is white like gum or terebinth; it is cut or split with iron tools in the summer, from which a liquid drips that is called frankincense. It is called *thurid* as if it were *thus*, because it burns <note>original: *pignat*, likely *pinguefecat* or *pyrat*</note> upon the altar. The bark and mastic of the frankincense tree are also utilized. **Myrrh** is a tree of Arabia, eight cubits high, similar to a thorn bush but with twisted and thorny branches. Its "tear" or distillation that flows spontaneously is better; that which is forcefully extracted is of lower quality. It is named by metaphor because it is bitter <note>original: *amara*</note> to the taste. **Stacte** is the name given to the myrrh that flows spontaneously from the tree, dripping before the bark is even cut. The myrrh tree is so named because it is bitter. **Bdellium** is the tear of a tree that grows in Arabia; it is translucent, strong-smelling, and black in color. It has the power of loosening and softening, and it is used to soften hardness in the body. **Costus** is a shrub produced in India; its root is considered the best part, which is commonly called "aromatic." **Balsam** is a small shrub, sticky and fragrant, whose wood is called *xylobalsamum* <note>wood-balsam</note>, its fruit is called *carpobalsamum* <note>fruit-balsam</note>, and its tear is called *opobalsamum* <note>sap-balsam</note>. Regarding this, Pliny says that balsam surpasses all other aromatics, and it grows only in Judea. But now it abounds more in Egypt, where it is also called a "vineyard." The virtue of balsam is twofold: one from the tear, another from the bark, and another expressed from the fruit.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on plants and medicinal herbs into Book XVIII, which covers the vocabulary of war, combat, and military instruments. which is seen. All these are called wars. Battles are specific to individuals, whereas wars belong to parties, such as the Punic War. Battles are parts of these, just as there are many battles in one war. Enmity exists in the mind; war is in the ritual; a fight is in the deed. But these terms are often used interchangeably. War <note>original: *bellum*</note> however, received its name from the fact that it is a harsh thing and "least beautiful" <note>original: *minime bella*</note>, that is, least good—just as a "grove" <note>original: *lucus*</note> is named from "least light" <note>original: *minime lucendo*</note>. In wars, one fights in four ways: either by land or by sea, and either secretly or openly. They are said to be "hand-to-hand" <note>original: *cominus*</note> when they fight with joined hands, and "at a distance" <note>original: *eminus*</note> when a javelin is thrown. A battle <note>original: *proelium*</note> is properly the work of those who fight with the hand, whence "battle" comes from the fact that one fights there with the "thumb" <note>original: *pollice*</note>. In battles, first there is the exercise, then the contest <note>original: *agon*</note>, and thirdly the victory. There are four types of fighting in battles, which were mentioned above. War is like the affair of those fighting, ready for the fight. In battles, an honest defense is called a "propugnation" <unclear>without deceit</unclear>. It is called "proclivous" for a fight or a struggle. Later the words were changed and they were called "wars." Others say they are called "prizes" <note>original: *praemia*</note> from the rewards, or it does this or that, like an enemy for an enemy. Or named from <unclear>applause</unclear> and a long prize. Wars are called similar to a prize, but in turn it is called what seems to the defender to be near. Battles are <unclear>called</unclear> fights. Truly, instead of fights, some are without iron. Four things in war: the fight for waters, flight, victory, and peace. Peace <note>original: *pax*</note> is a name that seems to be superior. Later it was accepted near the waters. For which proper name peace and the end of peace are fought over in the wild. In a festival, it is spoken from "striking" <note>original: *feriendo*</note>, just as the prize is spoken. The battle battles the war. From "doing," "faith" is said; "fear" <note>original: *pauor*</note> from "trembling," but for all the provinces. They help with the fear of ruin, which rises again from fear. Truly the unconquered are conquered by enemies.

### All
civil wars are those where not only an adversary but also a friend strikes. Likewise, they are called an adversary, I say, a judge in battle; they are called enemies or they conquer. One having been conquered, namely enemies, the enemy overcomes or they conquer; they are called the conquered or the victor. Victors are said to conquer by force or to expel. So that victory is also earned. A certain victory, however, is the joy of the enemies at the end of the victories. Then there is the authority of victory which is called a harmonious rumor; and these praises for the salutations. To us, victory at the end is called victory properly. The Pompeian victory, from which the standards and trophies show a harmonious war and battle, just as from victory it is called a "procession" <note>original: *pompa*</note> and a "trophy." This is also the prize of the victory of vows. Trophies are called <term>APO TOU TROPOU</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ τρόπου</note>, that is, from the turning of the enemies and their flight. Give victory to those driven in flight, which is called victory in the hand. It is spoken after so much victory of the victors. Likewise, a triumph is owed to a victory. A triumph is when a leader comes among the people and they display the victory; they celebrate the victor from the army. This victor is superior in his three vows. A triumph, or "to triumph," is called thus in Latin, that is, when an emperor enters the city with victory; the emperor is truly honored by the victory. From the first, the leader is led in triumph; it seems a consolation, as if the three-fold heat were brought. Thirdly, for three. Then, however, the Romans would triumph when they had conquered in battle or led a faction in the habit of a warrior. Whatever, however, in history is in our palm, a golden crown is given, which simulates the palm. Here, because without history he stands to have fled, victory, the laurel and a tree without flowers is the way, because they are the victors or they are carried in the "toga picta" <note>an embroidered robe worn by generals in their triumphs</note> triumphantly, and it is called the crown of the victor. One of the conquered as if to the victory in the cliffs which were called crowns for victory, which is said of the unconquered, victory is called a rumor because they are called "spoils" <note>original: *spolia*</note>. And this I do for the sake of speaking of the village in deeds, just as I am said to walk. Superior, indeed, he was made to sit above where the victory, because the victory is distinct and great, approaching by day and in a red color through lines, as in the arms of the lampreys whose likeness it was, or from the executioner of tragedies. That is, victory through the arrival of health whose immortality is the abundance of human community. Either those conquered who meet at the end, or in the authority and distinction of the victors. From the spoils, they name the enemies afterward. The conquered are the companions of the spoken word properly. Just as in victory it is called "spoil," so "plunder" <note>original: *praeda*</note> is said of the divided field properly. Proper to bodies, the enemy, the war, are called plunder. From which plunder is properly said to belong to the victor. These are called spoils from the taking away from the conquered enemies because they are said to be carried by hand. That is, that besides the appearance and their own division, because the victors and the labor are served in the assembly, they are said to be expelled from the spoils or victories. **On the instruments of war.**

<margin>S</margin>
### Signs
of war are those which give incitement to the fight, or which rule the army by the force of wars. It is said to be a conflict through fights, and the prizes of victory for the unconquered victory. For before a few cities, the victors are conquered between the tokens. Truly the proper signs are the eagle, dragons, and standards. From glory and audacity, or because it was seen equally in arms. They are spoken by the voice of the enemy's javelin; they carry forward the eagles by their step. In appearance they had appeared because those famous in victories, the javelin was seen and carried away. From the legion the sign was named. Standards <note>original: *prela*</note> were called signs in figures; in appearance, words are subject to all men, or in these, figures show the things carried, as the victory of a warlike sign. To tear out in the wars of command, in the diminishing and the scales. A trumpet <note>original: *tubrum*</note> or a bundle of hay, the youths had to announce; here they were also called "manipuli" <note>literally "handfuls," referring to the hay bundles used as early Roman standards</note>. <meta>This page transitions from the vocabulary of war and military conflict on the previous page into the terminology of public spectacles and games. Following the structure of Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*, the text explores how the Latin names for entertainment, racing, and theater are derived from their physical forms or symbolic meanings.</meta>

**Column 1**

Spectacles are among all the pleasures of the human race, not only because they are for delight but also because they are spread throughout the whole world; it is said that anyone may be led to madness by them. 
Circus games: so called because they are celebrated in a circus. Scenic games: so called because they are performed on stages.

<margin>On spectacles</margin>
Spectacles <note>original: *spectacula*</note> are generally named from this: they are so called from "looking" <note>original: *aspectu*</note>, just as "playthings" <note>original: *ludicra*</note> are named from "play" <note>original: *ludo*</note>, and vice versa. For spectacles are named from the games, and games from "spectating." There are four kinds of them. Therefore, they are called spectacles for the sake of spectating, because the eyes are fixed upon them.

<margin>On games</margin>
However, they are called playthings <note>original: *ludicra*</note> because they are practiced in the fields, or in gymnasiums, or in theaters. From this, games <note>original: *ludi*</note> are named either from "play" <note>original: *ludo*</note> or from "luxury" <note>original: *luxu*</note>, and vice versa: for spectacles are named from the games, and games from spectating, because they were invented for the pleasures of the soul alone. Truly, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a bishop whose encyclopedia was the standard reference for word origins in the Middle Ages.</note> says, "pleasure" <note>original: *voluptas*</note> is so called because it belongs to a "turning mind" <note>original: *animi volubilis*</note>, or pleasure is named from "flying" <note>original: *volatu*</note>, because the force of delight is fleeting, flying quickly in its very impulse, and it perishes and passes away forever. Hence, games are named either from play, or from luxury, or from "sport" <note>original: *lusu*</note>, or from play which is in the movement of the mind; the cause of the name is varied, just as "playthings" is the proper name for those things practiced in the fields or in gymnasiums.

<margin>On the number of chariots</margin>
According to how they are practiced, games are called by various names. Some are "gymnic" <note>athletic or gymnastic</note>, others are equestrian, others musical, others scenic; and again they are called "votive" when they are rendered as a vow for some danger, others are public, others are for funerals. Hence a "plaything" is what occurs in gymnasiums, or in theaters, or in the fields; thus games are named either from play or from luxury.

<margin>On the contest</margin>
Contest <note>original: *Agone*</note>: so called because it is performed in gymnasiums, as it is a struggle <note>original: *certamen*</note> where one contends for virtue. It is called "agony" <note>original: *agonia*</note> because it is said to pertain to the contest. Hence they are also called "agonists" <note>original: *agonistae*</note> because they fight in the contest to contend for virtue.

<margin>On circus games</margin>
Charioteers <note>original: *quadrigarii*</note> first established four horses in a chariot so that there would be four, on account of the four elements of the world, or on account of the four seasons of the year, or on account of the four circles of the world, or on account of the four circles of fortune.

<margin>On the circus</margin>
The circus is named from "circuit" <note>original: *circuitu*</note> because it has a circuit, or from "roundabout" <note>original: *circu*</note> because they run there around the turning posts. Hence they also call it a "circum" because it is a surrounding or the path of a circle.

<margin>On the four-horse chariot</margin>
It is called a *quadriga* because it has four horses, just as a *triga* has three and a *biga* has two.

<margin>On the chariot</margin>
The chariot <note>original: *currus*</note> is named from "running" <note>original: *currendo*</note> or from a "course" <note>original: *cursu*</note>, because it is in motion.

<margin>On the ornaments of the circus</margin>
The ornaments of the circus are: the turning posts <note>original: *meta*</note>, the central barrier <note>original: *spina*</note>, the gates <note>original: *ostia*</note>, the water channel <note>original: *euripus*</note>, and the obelisks.

<margin>On the turning post</margin>
The turning post <note>original: *meta*</note> is named from "measuring" <note>original: *metendo*</note>, because the chariots are measured there.

<margin>On the gates</margin>
The gates <note>original: *ostia*</note> are what they call the place from which the horses are released.

<margin>On charioteers</margin>
He is called a charioteer <note>original: *auriga*</note> because he "gilds" <note>original: *aurat*</note> the horses, or because their necks were accustomed to be adorned with "gold" <note>original: *auro*</note>, or because he manages the horses.

<margin>On the colors of the horses</margin>
There are four colors in the four-horse chariots, either because of the four elements of the world, or the four seasons of the year, or the four circles of the world.

<margin>On the procession</margin>
The procession <note>original: *pompa*</note> was first named from Pompey, or from *pompa* because there is a certain display of finery or a certain adornment.

<margin>On the chariot</margin>
They wished to use a chariot of four horses in a *quadriga* because there are four elements of the world, or because there are four seasons of the year.

<margin>On the chariot</margin>
The chariot is named from a course, or from running, or from the chariot because the chariot runs there.

<margin>On the deceased</margin>
Spectacles are also celebrated for the deceased, so that the dead may seem to be seen by the dead.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

Furthermore, there are four kinds of colors, because of the four elements of the world, or the four seasons of the year.

<margin>On the theater</margin>
The theater is a spectacle in which playthings are celebrated; it is named either from "theory" <note>original: *theoria*</note> because there is a vision there, or from theater because a spectacle is held there.

<margin>On the stage</margin>
The stage <note>original: *scena*</note> is the place in the theater where the actors perform, named from *scena* because there is a shadow <note>original: *umbra*</note> there.

<margin>On the orchestra</margin>
The orchestra is the place in the theater where the dancers perform.

<margin>On the proscenium</margin>
The proscenium is the name for the place in front of the stage.

<margin>On the pulpit</margin>
The pulpit <note>original: *pulpitum*</note> is the place in the theater where the tragic and comic actors perform.

<margin>On the seating tiers</margin>
They are called *podia* because there are seats there.

<margin>On the postscenium</margin>
The postscenium is the name for the place behind the stage.

<margin>On tragic actors</margin>
They are called tragic actors because they act in tragic songs.

<margin>On comic actors</margin>
They are called comic actors because they act in comedies.

<margin>On actors</margin>
The term *histriones* is used ambiguously, because they are performers <note>original: *histriones*</note>, or ambiguously because he is an actor.

<margin>On mimes</margin>
Mimes are so called because they perform a mime.

<margin>On dancers</margin>
Dancers <note>original: *saltatores*</note> are so called because they leap <note>original: *saltant*</note>.

<margin>On equestrian games</margin>
The equestrian game is where horsemen contend.

<margin>On net-fighters</margin>
Net-fighters <note>original: *retiarii*</note> are so called because they carry a net <note>original: *rete*</note> to catch their opponent.

<margin>On the pursuers</margin>
The pursuers <note>original: *secutores*</note> are so called because they follow <note>original: *sequuntur*</note> their opponent.

<margin>On lasso-fighters</margin>
Lasso-fighters <note>original: *laquearii*</note> are so called because they carry a lasso <note>original: *laqueum*</note> to catch their opponent.

<margin>On the light-armed skirmishers</margin>
The skirmishers <note>original: *uelites*</note> are so called because they run swiftly <note>original: *uelociter*</note>.

<margin>On wild beasts</margin>
Wild beasts <note>original: *ferae*</note> are so called because they rage fiercely <note>original: *ferociter*</note>.

<margin>On the game board</margin>
It is called a board <note>original: *tabula*</note> on which one plays with dice.

<margin>On the die</margin>
A knucklebone <note>original: *talus*</note> is so called because one plays with a knucklebone.

<margin>On the dice</margin>
Dice <note>original: *tesserae*</note> are so called because they have four corners.

<margin>On the counters</margin>
Counters <note>original: *calculi*</note> are so called because one plays with small stones.

<margin>On the game of hazard</margin>
It is called *alea* because one plays in it.

<margin>On the name of the dice</margin>
Regarding the name of the dice: it is because one plays with *tesserae*.

<margin>On the throws</margin>
The various movements or throws that occur in a game are called "throws" <note>original: *iactus*</note> because they are thrown quickly and as if in points; hence it is called a throw.

It reflects the medieval tradition of associating physical objects and cultural practices with symbolic groups of four, such as the seasons and the elements.</summary>

### ->BOOK XVIII BEGINS: ON SHIPS, BUILDINGS, AND CERTAIN TERMS<-
<note>The manuscript label says Book 18, but the content actually begins Book 19 of Isidore’s encyclopedia.</note>

The ingenuity of the *arefoci* <note>likely a corruption of *Argo*, the first ship</note> stood out as unsurpassed, and by the art of a most fortified vehicle. This they call a ship; thereafter it must be called the truth. **Ship** <note>original: *navis*</note>: from "knowing" <note>original: *nosse*</note> because it is suitable to "busily perform" <note>original: *navet*</note>, that is, they act truly: or as far as they are busy, or from which they "fly" <note>original: *volant*</note>: because their fates are swifter. Just as the *clerus* is said to want to expel you from the ship: whether it be swift, or like those who are called "fated." It is certain, however, that it was first invented by the Cretans, because he who was of the Colchians also rode it, since they first came into this sea. These followed the custom of other seas. But a ship is called *adica* by divine power. If, however, it is called by "busied power," the shipbuilder <note>original: *naufactor*</note> is primary. For a "busy ship" is the same as that which comes by itself, or it carries the oarsman: it would be called a ship-handler. That which is called from the *lamo* <note>unclear technical term, possibly a pool or marsh</note>: because these neighbors do not move. If the ships were truly faster in their custom, they are indeed called "sciffs" <note>original: *scip’tra*</note>. Whence their age, I pray, because they are carried ready: and fortified because that which does not reach them is prey. Whence that is also said where they are in need because they possess with their hands. To this point there was prudence. But truly, the sight of the swifter ships besides the sea was seen to fix this. That is the first strength, which of the ships was the ship when it was also built to be carried swiftly. From the foundation of this fabric, the ship is said to have been invented. Whence also by misuse the ships are called *fete rices*: because it would have a curved wall. A large ship will arise because they call it by its hardness. From which it is ordered, that is, it is written before the prow, or "great." The **Carpasian ship** is named from victory; so the **Rhodian** from Rhodes; so the **Alexandrian** from Alexandria. Everywhere they are called "winged." But ships are called *m'inope* because they are burdened with strength. That is, by weights: another strength of the sailor. **Rustic** strength ships were called from that which had a "beak" <note>original: *rostra*</note> on the front. It was first called a "beak" <note>original: *rostrum*</note> whether it follows on land or in sea. Whence also ships are called "beaked," because they are made from hollowed wood: which is the strength of the ships. The addition of **oars** <note>original: *remoru*</note> was said from these: because they call them "runners" <note>original: *dromu*</note>; or from "dromedaries" just as wood or a sharp empty thing which they carry. They call it "delayed" from the sea. But for the sake of speed they act with **anchors**: which in the front made the vehicle of the ships. Those ships which in their custom they call "loose hulls" <note>original: *carinas*</note> are made. That is, truly the first ones made. A **skiff** <note>original: *capha* or *scapha*</note> because it is a "whale." A lookout point is called a "mirror of life." It is called "wise" <note>original: *sophos*</note>, that is, smooth. A **bark** <note>original: *barca*</note> is that which had gathered the wedges of the ships, carried to that. Whence from here at first it seemed they took up the oar. Whence, as if by the spirit, they call it returning to the port truly, the oars of the ship having been poured out with force. For the ship they are prepared primarily, which indeed they call from these: which was the strength to these: which is called the **beak** <note>original: *rostrum*</note>, which he had prepared elsewhere to be seen at this side. The *miroparon* <note>a pirate vessel</note> is as if it prepares a wall. Whence also the skiff from immense fates, which is called from their strength which provides for ships. By which they are strong; by which they are brief. At first called by readers from the marshes by their weight. From whatever history, which also appear in the prow of the Saxons according to custom. **Swift ships** <note>original: *celoces*</note> because they are called "velocity" they are seen. **Runners** <note>original: *dromis*</note> truly are likely agile and more fit for the service of the fleet. Every hull is seen for those... Brief ships are those which are made with one order of oars. Those of Gades <note>Cádiz</note>: according to custom from a triple order. As if from those who at once and at a single water. Whence they call: that is truly a spread out street. By the oar of the ship the hull is called a "breeze," which is made into a single one, that is truly pacified. Whence he throws strength and those made for the honor of their own. Whence also it is called a "ship-let" <note>original: *nauia*</note> which is called by a long name, as a **cymba** <note>skiff</note> or a **caupula** <note>small boat</note> had been. As this is called "gray": because they use them in the marshes. A **wicker-boat** <note>original: *cratis*</note> is made of skiffs from the edge: which is also a wheel of raw hide which provides for ships. In the prow of the ships according to custom, as when the linens and the hull are named from "carrying." These and the "fore-memory" are seen. The hull is a ship of Ammon which they strike from the heat. Because the ship is of various rafts. That is, it is gray, made from one hollowed piece of wood. And in the deep it is said, that is, as the first.

The **stern** <note>original: *puppis*</note> is the posterior part of the ship; just as the anterior part is the **prow** <note>original: *prora*</note>. The **skiff** <note>original: *cymba*</note> is a place in the ship at the middle. The **cervus** <note>likely "stag," a part of the ship</note> is named from the "hind," which by custom is named either from the side of coming or from the carrying mouth. Or the *calataria* of ships, that is, preserving. The **prow** from that which was first made: so that they might come. That is, the strength of the heights. <margin>mixture</margin> A mixture of color has threads and is made from flax <note>original: *lino*; the fiber used for linen</note> itself. A *linostema* garment is made from a mixture of flax and wool. By the Greeks, it is called *linostema*: woven from flax and a flaxen warp <note>original: *stamine*; the set of stationary threads on a loom</note>. Flax is a green herb, so called because it is soft and supple, and draws [moisture] to itself; and through a process when treated with water, it reaches its intended appearance. And it is the same that weaves. *Cinota* [are so called] because they stand rigid in likeness. That is: eyelashes woven from flax, or those which contract chaff. *Velonici* tunics are those which are woven from boards <note>likely referring to a stiffened or structured fabric</note>. An *exaenia* garment is transparent, and is named so because the body shines through it as if in glass. An *exania* garment is of a Phoenician color <note>original: *punicei*; the deep red or purple associated with ancient Phoenicia</note>, and is named so because dyed clothes are brought from there. A *galna* garment is of a yellow color, named as if it were *galbina* <note>a pale greenish-yellow</note>; hence the resin *galbanum* is also named. *Ralla*, that is, very thin; some call a thin garment what we call *ralla* in common speech. Rags <note>original: *panni*</note> are named either from *panno* [cloth] or from the Greeks because it is *p[h]os* <note>original: likely *phos*, light/shining</note>, or they are named from hanging <note>original: *pendendo*</note>. ...

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*, concluding Book 19 on clothing and materials before transitioning into Book 20, which covers household tools, food, and drink. The author uses his characteristic method of explaining the nature of objects through the perceived origins of their names.</meta>

... or bears hard coverings. Leather <note>original: *corium*</note> is named from "hide" <note>original: *corio*</note> because it is hard. Afterward, however, it is softened in many ways according to the required measure and use. Once it has been prepared, it is then called a skin <note>original: *pellis*</note>.

<margin>On skins.</margin>
The skin is named from "driving away" <note>original: *pellendo*</note> enemies, or from "driving off" the cold. This is also why we call shields *peltae*, as they are made from skins. Leather, however, is named from its thickness <note>original: *corio*</note> because it becomes hard. A fleece <note>original: *vellus*</note> is named from "plucking" <note>original: *vellendo*</note>, because it used to be plucked from the sheep before the practice of shearing was invented. The toga is so named because it is "covering" <note>original: *tegens*</note> the whole body. From this also come "roof-coverers" <note>original: *tectoria*</note> and those who cover a house are called "roofers" <note>original: *tectoria*</note>. Garment <note>original: *vestis*</note> is named from "binding" <note>original: *vinctu*</note>. Hence, an enwrapped person is said to be "dressed" <note>original: *investis*</note>. A traveling cloak <note>original: *penula*</note> is as if it were "almost a small villa" <note>original: *pene uila*</note>, just like a "peninsula" <note>original: *peninsula*</note>; for it covers the body deep within. The *lacerna* cloak is named because it has rough fringes <note>original: *laciniis*</note>, or because it is made of wool shreds <note>original: *laniis*</note>; that is, a shredded wrap on this side and that, and so it is called a garment. The *birrus* cloak is named from its color, because it is red; for in Greek, *birron* means "red" <note>original: *rubeum*</note>. The *sagum* is called a Gallic cloak. The *chlamys* is Greek, but it is interpreted into Latin; it is said that every *chlamys* is Greek in origin.

<margin>On wools.</margin>
Wools <note>original: *lanae*</note> are named from "shredding" <note>original: *laniatione*</note> or from "softness" <note>original: *lenitate*</note>. From this also the term "fleeces" is used. *Canna*—that is, wool—is a Greek term. For when it is shredded, it is so called.

<margin>On outer garments.</margin>
The *amictus* <note>a wrap or mantle</note> is that which we wrap around ourselves. In this usage, the Greeks call it an *amictus*. It is named from "binding" <note>original: *vinciedo*</note>, because it binds the body. Thus we have the *amictus*, or the *aliculum* <note>a short cape</note>. The tunic <note>original: *tunica*</note> is named from "protecting" <note>original: *tuendo*</note> the body, as if it were a *tuonica*. The toga is so named because it "covers" <note>original: *tegat*</note>. The *pallium* <note>a Greek-style cloak</note> is named from "skins" <note>original: *pellibus*</note>, because in ancient times they used skins in place of garments. In the same way, the toga comes from "covering" <note>original: *tegendo*</note>.

<margin>On footwear.</margin>
Footwear <note>original: *calceamenta*</note> is named from the "heel" <note>original: *calce*</note>, with which the feet are protected. Gallic shoes <note>original: *gallicae*</note> are named from the origin of that nation. *Socci* <note>slippers</note> are as if "dried" <note>original: *seccati*</note>, because they are used in dry places. Hence also *crepidae* <note>sandals</note> are named, from the "rattle" <note>original: *crepitu*</note> they make. Leggings <note>original: *ocreae*</note> are so called because they cover the shins <note>original: *crura*</note>. From this also *cothurni* <note>buskins/boots</note> are named.

<margin>On legumes.</margin>
Legumes are those things which grow from themselves into a fruit. Hence they are also called "crops" <note>original: *fruges*</note>, because they come into fruit, things which grow from the earth besides trees or herbs. These are beans, peas, vetch, lentils, and chickpeas. They are called legumes because they are "gathered" <note>original: *leguntur*</note> by hand, not like a "harvest" <note>original: *messis*</note>, which is cut down from the crop.

# BOOK 20 BEGINS. FROM THE TESTIMONY OF THE MANUSCRIPTS, THIS IS BOOK 6.

### FIRST, DAEDALUS

<margin>On the tools of smiths.</margin>
Daedalus is said to be the first inventor of the smith's art. He was the first inventor of saws, the adze, the compass, the drill, glue, and the scraper. He was also the one who described the art of building, and first applied it to structures. An awl <note>original: *subula*</note> is named from "driving under" <note>original: *subigendo*</note>, with which a cobbler prepares stitches. Needles <note>original: *acubus*</note> are named from a "distaff" <note>original: *colu*</note> or from their "tip" <note>original: *cacumine*</note>, because they are sharp. A saw <note>original: *serra*</note> is named from being "serrated," because it is sharp. Whence also a saw is named from "cutting" <note>original: *sertione*</note>, or because it enters into the wood.

<column-break/>

...it is divided without resistance. Where there is no other, another is for the madman. Witnesses <note>original: *adstenti*</note> are claimed, and it is not poured out again in excessive abundance; it is beaten and worked in special ways, which it finds thus stretched out with fear in those ways. In that which is wealth: for it is not foreseen... <note>This section appears to be a fragmented or corrupted insertion of moral or legal text regarding wealth (*opulentia*) and poverty (*inopia*), interrupting the flow of the culinary etymologies.</note> Poverty is the opposite of wealth; for it is not foreseen. A shepherd <note>original: *opilio*</note> is named from "wealth" <note>original: *opulendo*</note>. Whether he might foresee two successors... the goat... which is called the interior... from this, he turns, see then.

<margin>On bread.</margin>
Bread <note>original: *panis*</note> is so named because it is served with every food, or because it feeds <note>original: *pascat*</note> every animal. Bakers <note>original: *pistores*</note> are named from "pounding" <note>original: *pisando*</note>, for they discovered the grain-mills when calling upon Ceres <note>the goddess of agriculture</note>. <note>The corrupted section regarding poverty and wealth is repeated here in the transcription.</note> Poverty is the opposite of wealth; for it is not foreseen. A shepherd is named from wealth... which are four from itself. The goat... which is called the interior... see then. *Subaitericii* bread is as if cooked "among the embers" or in the ashes. *Libanei* bread is that which is cooked in a baking pan.

<margin>On porridge.</margin>
Porridge <note>original: *puls*</note> is so named because our fathers used it for their sustenance before the life of bread was invented. From this also the *pultarii* <note>porridge-pots</note> which make porridge are named. From this also the term *pulticum* is used.

<margin>On wine.</margin>

<margin>On honey.</margin>
Honey <note>original: *mel*</note> is named from "honey" <note>original: *melle*</note> because it is soft <note>original: *molle*</note>.

<margin>On oil.</margin>
Oil <note>original: *oleum*</note> is so named because it is smooth. From this also the olive <note>original: *oliua*</note> is named.

<meta>This page marks a significant transition in the manuscript. While the previous page concluded a section of natural history and etymologies based on Isidore of Seville—discussing the properties of herbs like sage and parsnip—this page begins a new section of biblical scholarship. It introduces the "Monarchian Prologue" to the Gospel of John, a traditional preface found in many early medieval Latin Bibles that provides a theological and biographical introduction to the evangelist.</meta>

### HERE BEGIN THE
### ARGUMENTS OF JOHN
### THE DISCIPLE
### ON PHILOSOPHY <note>original: *DE PHI*. This is an abbreviation likely for *Philosophia* or *Physica*, referring to the spiritual or "physical" nature of John’s theological inquiry.</note>

This is John the Evangelist, one of the disciples of God, who was chosen by God as a virgin. God called him away from his wedding when he intended to marry. A twofold testimony of his virginity is given in the Gospel: first, that he is said to be beloved by God above the others; and second, that God <note>referring to Christ on the cross</note> entrusted his mother to him, so that a virgin might protect a virgin. Finally, making manifest in the Gospel what he himself was, and beginning the work of the incorruptible Word, he alone testifies that the Word was made flesh and that the light was not overcome by the darkness. He records the first sign that God performed at the wedding <note>the wedding at Cana</note>, so that by showing this, he might demonstrate to readers that where the Lord is invited, the wine of the [old] wedding must fail, and as the old things are changed, all the new things instituted by Christ should appear.

Regarding this, each individual thing arranged in order maintains the faith of the writer, so that those wishing to know might be told why, at the beginning of the Gospel, it is not the generation and birth of the flesh <note>referring to the genealogies found in Matthew and Luke</note> that is described, but rather the Spirit and the Word. This was written in the Gospel for a reason: for in one place he says, "In the beginning was the Word" <note>original: *In principio erat verbum*</note>, and in another, "The Word was made flesh" <note>original: *verbum caro factum est*</note>.

For he begins with the generation of the Son of God, by which he was begotten of the Father, and afterwards returns to the Mother, by whom he was begotten of the Virgin. Hence, in the first chapter of the Gospel, we see the person of John whom Christ calls to himself, and in the last chapter, the person of John whom Christ seeks for himself. By the grace of this judgment, Christ made John's state manifest; indeed, Christ most deeply hinted that in seeking this man for himself, he wished him to remain in him. After he [the Word] came forth from the Father's bosom, so that through the eternal and invisible he might become visible through the flesh, he took his own flesh into himself, so that he might first exhibit in himself the grace of a new formation and the justice of the resurrection.

And he desires that this man [John] should come to him, in whose body the soul would be sacrificed, and whose death would not occur except through him. And to John, who sought him, he also bore witness that he would not die <note>a reference to the tradition that John did not suffer a natural death or was "preserved" until Christ's return</note>, showing in the written Gospel that this is exactly what he willed. This is the matter.

For the faith is spoken through each detail of the Gospel, so that in no other way except through these individual parts is Christ to be recognized by us as God, both concerning God and concerning himself.

This is John the Evangelist, one of the Twelve, who, since he was chosen by the Lord and loved more than the others because of his chastity and purity, is said to have written the Gospel in Asia after the Lord’s Passion.

When he had already written the Gospel in Asia, after he had written the Apocalypse on the island of Patmos, he wrote his Gospel at the request of the bishops of Asia, so that in it he might more fully reveal the divinity of Christ.

<summary>This page contains the "Monarchian Prologue" to the Gospel of John, detailing John's virginity, his special relationship with Christ, and the theological purpose behind his Gospel's unique focus on the "Word made flesh." It also notes the tradition that he wrote his Gospel in Asia after the Apocalypse to combat heresies regarding Christ's divinity.</summary>

--- Page 464 ---
<meta>This page marks a sudden and significant shift in the manuscript's subject matter. While the previous page concluded a theological introduction to the Gospel of John, this page begins a completely different text: the *Isagoge* (Introduction) of Johannitius. Johannitius is the Latinized name of Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873 AD), a Nestorian Christian scholar in Baghdad who translated Greek medical works into Arabic and Syriac. This text became the foundational introductory textbook for medical students in medieval Europe, summarizing the complex system of the Greek physician Galen.</meta>

# HERE BEGIN THE INTRODUCTIONS OF JOHANNITIUS, DISCIPLE OF JOHN OF ALEXANDRIA, ON THE ART OF GALEN <note>original: *TEGNI GALIENI*. The "Tegni" or *Ars Medica* was Galen's most famous introductory work.</note> CONCERNING THE REASONING OF MEDICINE <note>original: *DE PHISICA RATIONE*. In this period, "physics" refers to the study of nature and the physical body, essentially medicine.</note>.

->MEDICINE IS DIVIDED<-

into two parts: namely, into theory and practice. Of these, theory is called vision and contemplation—that is, for the purpose of understanding **natural things**, **non-natural things**, and **things against nature** <note>These three categories formed the basis of medieval diagnosis: what the body is (natural), how we live (non-natural), and what goes wrong (against nature)</note>. Practice, however, is the operation; it is called the "sight of science," which is to say how you ought to work within those same three categories. Theory is divided into three parts: the knowledge of natural things, non-natural things, and things against nature. The knowledge of natural things is divided into seven modes: namely, elements, mixtures, humors, members, virtues, spirits, and operations.

**M**Elements are the smallest particles of the body, which cannot be divided into smaller particles. There are four elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth. Fire is hot and dry; air is hot and moist; water is cold and moist; and earth is cold and dry. The diversity of mixtures <note>also called "complexions"</note> is spoken of in eight ways: four simple and four composite. The simple ones are heat, coldness, moisture, and dryness. The composite ones are heat and moisture, heat and dryness, coldness and moisture, and coldness and dryness. A ninth mixture is called "equal," which is found in temperate bodies.

**A**certain heat flows from celestial powers, another from terrestrial elements, and another from the light of fires. Yet all these heats are of one kind. One should think similarly regarding coldness, for coldness flows from celestial influence, from terrestrial quality, and from watery moisture. One should think the same of moisture and dryness. Thus it is clear that just as there are four elements, so there are four qualities, four humors, four principal members, four spirits, four principal virtues, and four principal operations.

**V**ence <note>The scribe uses "Vnde" frequently as a transitional "therefore" or "and so."</note> each one of these four humors consists of two qualities. Blood is hot and moist. Red bile <note>choler</note> is hot and dry. Black bile <note>melancholy</note> is cold and dry. Phlegm is cold and moist. It is called red bile because it is born from the redness of fire; black bile from the blackness of earth; phlegm from the whiteness of water; and blood from the redness of air. Although some say all humors are born from all four elements, each humor participates more in one specific element, from which it takes its name: blood from air, red bile from fire, black bile from earth, and phlegm from water.

**T**emperance <note>health</note> is a certain quality mixed from the four qualities, existing in every body according to its nature. Malice <note>dyscrasia or illness</note> is a certain quality mixed from the four qualities, existing in every body against its nature. Thus, some malice is called simple, and some composite. Simple malice consists of only one quality, such as only heat or only coldness. Composite malice consists of two qualities, such as heat and dryness, or coldness and moisture.

**M**alice of the members <note>organs or limbs</note> occurs when the members cease their natural function. This happens in two ways: either because of a bad complexion <note>imbalance of heat/cold/moist/dry</note> or because of a bad composition <note>structural deformity</note>. A bad complexion is when a member is changed from its natural balance into another. A bad composition is when the members do not function according to their duty, as is the case in those with contractures or paralysis.

**M**embers are parts of the body created from the humors. Some are principal and others are not. There are four principal members: the heart, the brain, the liver, and the testicles. The heart is the beginning of life and the source of heat. The brain is the beginning of sense and motion. The liver is the beginning of nutrition. The testicles are the beginning of generation. Non-principal members are those that serve the principal ones, such as nerves, veins, and arteries. Nerves serve the brain for motion and sense. Veins serve the liver for nutrition. Arteries serve the heart for natural heat.

**S**pirit is a certain subtle and airy substance from which proceeds the animal, vital, and natural power. Thus there are four principal spirits: animal, vital, natural, and generative. The vital spirit is born in the heart; the animal spirit in the brain; the natural spirit in the liver; and the generative spirit in the testicles. It is called the vital "vision" or virtue because life is preserved by it; the animal virtue because the soul <note>Latin: *anima*</note> operates through it; and the natural virtue because nature is ruled by it.

**V**irtue is a certain force acting in the body, from which animal, vital, and natural operations proceed. This is divided into two parts: natural virtue and animal virtue. Natural virtue is divided into two parts: nutritive and generative. Nutritive virtue is divided into four parts: appetitive <note>the urge to take in food</note>, retentive, digestive, and expulsive. The appetitive virtue seeks food; the retentive retains it; the digestive digests it; and the expulsive expels waste.

**S**ense is the power perceiving exterior things and bringing them to the brain. There are five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Sight perceives colors; hearing perceives sounds; smell perceives odors; taste perceives flavors; and touch perceives heat, cold, moisture, dryness, and other tangible qualities.

**C**olor is a certain quality existing in the body, proceeding from the four humors. There are four principal colors: red, white, black, and blue-gray <note>original: *glaucus*</note>. Red is born from red bile; white from phlegm; black from black bile; and blue-gray from blood. From these four colors, many others are born according to the mixing of humors. Thus some color is called fiery, some airy, some watery, and some earthy. These all vary according to the quality of the humors. Red bile is also called yellow or saffron; black bile is livid or black; phlegm is pale or green. <note>The text here provides an exhaustive list of shades and their corresponding humor-mixes, used by medieval doctors to diagnose patients by their skin tone or urine color.</note> Red color is born from blood; pale from red bile; ashen from black bile; green from red bile mixed with phlegm; black from "over-cooked" black bile; and white from phlegm. It is said that color is the "vision" of the humors. And just as there are four humors, so there are four principal colors, four elements, and four qualities. All these are **natural things** and belong to physics. Physics is the science that treats natural things, non-natural things, and things against nature. Natural things are those just discussed. Non-natural things are six: air, food and drink, motion and rest, sleep and waking, emptiness and fullness <note>evacuation and repletion</note>, and the accidents of the mind <note>emotions</note>. Things against nature are three: disease, the cause of disease, and the accident <note>symptom</note>. Disease is a state against nature; the cause is that which induces it; and the accident is that which follows it. All these belong to physics so that through them the human body may be preserved in health and freed from disease. This is done through medicines of four kinds: potion, electuary, ointment, and plaster. A potion is liquid medicine taken by mouth; an electuary is a solid medicine taken by mouth; an ointment is liquid applied externally; and a plaster is solid applied externally. And thus ends the first part of physics. Amen.

<column-break/>

**...us, foam and bubbles.** <note>This column appears to start mid-sentence or mid-list regarding urine or humor appearances.</note> The first humors of spring are clear or egg-white like. There are four red colors: red, clear, ruddy, and blue-gray. In phlegm there are seven: white, pale, ashen, green, livid, black, and bright. In bile there are four: citron, yolk-colored, leek-green, and copper-rust green. In black bile there are two: natural and against nature. Phlegm has three types: sweet, sour, and salty. The color of phlegm varies according to the quality of the humors; for instance, pale humor is phlegm mixed with red bile, while ashen is phlegm mixed with black bile.

**M**otion and rest are spoken of in four ways: local motion <note>moving from place to place</note>, motion of alteration <note>changing quality</note>, motion of increase, and motion of decrease. Rest is the cessation of motion. Similarly, one must consider the motions of the mind, such as anger, joy, fear, sadness, and anxiety. Anger and joy cause heat to diffuse outward. Fear and sadness cause heat to contract inward. Anxiety causes heat and spirit to diffuse both inward and outward.

**A**ges are four: namely adolescence, youth, old age, and senility. Adolescence is hot and moist and lasts until 25 years. Youth is hot and dry and lasts until 40. Old age is cold and dry and lasts until 60. Senility is cold and moist and lasts until the end of life. A person's complexion varies with age: adolescence is in its natural balance, youth has more heat and dryness, old age has more cold and dryness, and senility has more cold and moisture.

**V**irtue is a certain natural, vital, and animal force. Natural virtue resides in the liver, vital in the heart, and animal in the brain. Natural virtue is divided into nutritive and generative; generative is divided into the formative and the seed-producing. It is said that natural virtue nourishes and generates the body, vital virtue preserves life, and animal virtue operates through sense and motion.

**T**he third species of color is that which arises from the "burning" <note>original: *adustione*</note> of the humors. Thus some color is called black, some green, some livid, and some pale. Black comes from the burning of black bile; green from the burning of red bile; livid from the burning of blood; and pale from the burning of phlegm. These vary by the intensity of the "burning": dusky from a little, obscure from medium, and dark from great burning.

**M**alice of the members is twofold: in bad complexion and in bad composition. Natural malice is that which is present from birth, while accidental malice comes after birth. One must think similarly regarding the principal members.

**M**embers that are principal are four: heart, brain, liver, and testicles. The heart is the principle of life; the brain the principle of sense and motion; the liver the principle of nutrition; and the testicles the principle of generation. Just as there are four principal members, there are four principal spirits, virtues, and operations. All these belong to physics.

<margin>240.</margin>
<margin>Among the medicines</margin>
**S**pirit: the vital spirit is born in the heart and diffused through the arteries; the animal in the brain and diffused through the nerves; the natural in the liver and diffused through the veins. It is said that the spirit is the "carrier of virtue" <note>original: *uector uirtutis*</note>. Just as spirit is carried through the members, so virtue is diffused through the spirit itself.

**F**ever is a foreign heat kindled in the heart and diffused through the arteries into the whole body, harming natural actions. It is divided into three parts: ephemeral, putrid, and hectic. Ephemeral is that which resides in the spirit <note>lasting only a day</note>. Putrid is that which resides in the humors. Hectic is that which resides in the solid members. Ephemeral fever is said to be of one day; putrid is long-lasting; hectic is seen to be incurable. These types vary according to causes and times.

**M**edicine is divided into two parts: theory and practice. Theory into three: knowledge of natural, non-natural, and against-nature things. Practice into three: knowledge of diet <note>original: *uictus*</note>, medication, and surgery <note>original: *cyrurgie*</note>. Diet rules the body through food and drink. Medication cures the body through contrary qualities <note>e.g., treating a "cold" disease with "hot" medicine</note>. Surgery heals the body through the operation of the hands. Medicine is the science of the healthy, the sick, and the "neutral" <note>those neither fully sick nor fully well, such as convalescents or the elderly</note>. All these things belong to physics.

For from these things, the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> holds that man and every thing composed of elements is formed. For the active and the passive are always brought back into harmony with one another. And it must be known that health consists in acting and being acted upon <note>original: "agere et pati". Thus, when heat, moisture, cold, and dryness are present in the body in a way that is not according to nature, then suffering <note>original: "passio", the root of our word "patient"</note> occurs. Diseases arise from humor and cold when they are not according to nature in the body—for example, if there is a humor in the body that is unnatural or superfluous. Disease is a passing thing in a man that exists beyond nature. Diseases exist in man and have causes through which they are created.

Disease in man is fourfold: namely, fever, abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note>, disease of the humor, and disease in the limbs and in their composition. Disease of the humor occurs in three parts, as in a hectic fever <note>original: "febre ethica". A persistent, wasting fever often associated with the solid parts of the body.</note>. Disease in the solid limbs is found in hectic fever, and it occurs in those same limbs where the hectic fever resides. Disease in the limbs in their composition is also like that in the limbs where there is hectic fever. It must be known that a bad humor in the body causes many infirmities. Diseases in the limbs where they reside occur in various ways: such as in the internal organs like the stomach, liver, heart, spleen, and others. For they cause and produce many and diverse sufferings. Thus, where there is a bad and cold humor, such as in the stomach and liver, then a daily fever <note>original: "febris cotidiana"</note> is produced, and so on for the others.

Diseases which arise from burnt liquid <note>original: "adusta pituita"</note> and dry phlegm are daily fevers. Diseases which arise from blood are tertian fevers <note>original: "febres tertiane", fevers that occur every other day.</note>. **Diseases** are of such a kind as they may be; just as in a fever, a disease may arise from a humor, yet in their movement there is both heat and cold according to the material from which it is made. Whether he recognizes the signs from the face: if the face and lips are swollen, he might soon be <unclear>healed</unclear>. If the face is whitish, remedies for the head will be difficult. ¶ Here is a sign: if the countenance changes for no apparent cause, and [the patient] is twenty-one years old, and if the face changes its appearance [further], a judgment [on the outcome] will be seen. 

¶ But if anyone is awakened by pain and joined with weakness according to their habit, or if they should sleep <unclear>deeply</unclear>, this is announced as a sign of death besides any other occurrence; it shows a sign of death. 

¶ He who in sickness grows moist with sweat, if the humors soon come to a state of health, let him seek how the humors soon work toward health. If it should be otherwise, I see that it shows a sign not of death but of lingering weakness.
