<meta>This page transitions from the specific liturgical calendar of the previous page to a general treatise on "Computus"—the medieval science of calculating time and the dates of movable feasts like Easter. It provides the mathematical and mnemonic rules used by monks to navigate the Roman calendar system and the lunar cycle.</meta>

Concerning the days of the months which are numbered by Kalends, Nones, and Ides.
It can be known through this verse: <insert>Method for numbering the months</insert>
The beginning of the month holds the front in the first order.
And the Nones [fall on] the seventh or the fifth [day].
Afterward, [the count] gave the Ides through eighteen [days before the next Kalends].
Then follow the Ides. Once that name has been spoken,
On the next day of fate, you shall begin to count the remaining days
From the Kalends of the following month. Moreover, in numbering the months,
we use these verses: <insert>Other very clear proofs and rules</insert>
June, April, September, and November [have thirty days]. <note>This is a Latin version of the "Thirty days hath September" mnemonic.</note>
February has twenty-eight or nine.
To all the rest, thirty-one is the one.
In a leap year <term>bissextile year: a year with an extra day, so called because the "sixth day before the Kalends of March" was counted twice</term>, February has twenty-nine days.
In any given month, however, there are three principal days:
namely, the Kalends, the Nones, and the Ides. "Kalends" are named from *calo*,
that is, "I call," because in ancient times the priest used to call the common people to the Capitol
and there announce to them how many days there were until the Nones.
"Nones" are named as if *nundine* <note>original: nundine; refers to market days held every ninth day</note>, because then the country folk would come to the city
for their trade, and it was then announced to them
when the Ides would be. "Ides" are named from *iduando*, that is, "dividing,"
because they divide the months almost through the middle. <insert>Calculation of the epacts.</insert>
If you wish to know the epacts <term>epacts: the age of the moon in days on January 1st, used to harmonize the solar and lunar calendars</term>, find which year it is in the nineteen-year cycle,
multiply that number by eleven, and whatever results from that,
divide by thirty; what remains are the epacts for that year.
If indeed nothing remains, consider thirty as the epacts.
And this is seen here: <insert>Rule for finding the epacts.</insert>
On the Kalends of January, there are as many epacts
as there were on the Kalends of January in the preceding year,
with eleven added. <insert>Calculation of the epacts.</insert>
And as often as the moon has thirty [days] on the Kalends of April, you shall have those same epacts
for the whole year. <insert>Concerning the cycle.</insert> You will find the nineteen-year cycle if, from the Kalends of January
of the present year, you subtract one, and divide by nineteen;
what remains is the year of the nineteen-year cycle. <insert>Concerning the epacts.</insert>
We call the epacts nothing other than the additions of the moon,
which increase by eleven days each year relative to the solar course.
For the sun completes its course in three hundred sixty-five days
and six hours. The moon, however, completes it in twelve lunations, which are three hundred fifty-four days;
whence eleven days remain, which are called epacts. <insert>Concerning the cycle.</insert>
Why is it called the nineteen-year cycle? Because in nineteen years,
it returns to the same limit. <insert>Concerning the embolism.</insert> Embolism
is interpreted as "super-abundance," because that year better begins from the Kalends of January
which always has three hundred eighty-four days <note>An "embolismic" year in the lunar calendar adds a 13th month to stay in sync with the sun</note>,
and this happens seven times within nineteen years. <insert>Concerning a common year.</insert>
It is called a common year
when the year has only twelve lunations and three hundred fifty-four days.
The first embolism is in the third year, when the epacts are thirty.
The second in the eighth year, when the epacts are twenty-two.
The third in the eleventh year, when the epacts are eleven.
The fourth in the fourteenth year, when the epacts are thirty.
The fifth in the seventeenth year, when the epacts are twenty-two.
The sixth in the nineteenth year, when the epacts are eleven.
The seventh is in the second year, when the epacts are twenty-two,
and then the "leap of the moon" <term>saltus lune: a mathematical adjustment where the moon's age is skipped forward by one day to keep the cycle accurate</term> occurs. <insert>Concerning the leap of the moon.</insert>
It is called the leap of the moon when the moon is seen one day earlier
than it ought to be seen by the art of calculation. <insert>Concerning the limits of the months.</insert>
The month of January has its own limits, that is, for Septuagesima,
Lent, Easter, Rogation days, and Pentecost.
On the Kalends of January, if there were zero epacts,
then the limit of Septuagesima <note>The start of the pre-Lenten season</note> will be on the ninth day before the Kalends of February,
and the limit of Lent on the sixth day before the Ides of February,
and the limit of Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of April,
and the limit of Rogation days on the seventh day before the Kalends of May,
and the limit of Pentecost on the sixth day before the Ides of May.
If, however, there was one epact, then the limit of Septuagesima will be
on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, and so on for the others. <insert>Limits of the moon.</insert>
If you wish to know the limit of Easter, find which year it is in the nineteen-year cycle,
multiply that number by nineteen,
and whatever results from that, divide by thirty;
and what remains is the limit of Easter.
If indeed nothing remains, take thirty as the limit.
And this is seen here: <insert>Rule for finding the limit of Easter.</insert>
On the Kalends of April, the limit of Easter is the same
as it was on the Kalends of April in the preceding year,
with eleven added. <insert>Concerning Septuagesima.</insert>
On the day of the moon which will always be against the Nones of February,
on the next Sunday, we shall have Septuagesima.
